docs.title: Shared neural basis psychiatric comorbidity
docs.text:
Nature Medicine | Volume 29 | May 2023 | 1232–1242 Article https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-023-02317-4

A shared neural basis underlying psychiatric comorbidity

Chao Xie1,2, Shitong Xiang1,2, Chun Shen1,2, Xuerui Peng3, Jujiao Kang1,2, Yuzhu Li1,2, Wei Cheng1,2, Shiqi He1,4, Marina Bobou5, M. John Broulidakis6, Betteke Maria van Noort7, Zuo Zhang5, Lauren Robinson8,9, Nilakshi Vaidya10, Jeanne Winterer10,11, Yuning Zhang12, Sinead King5,13, Tobias Banaschewski14, Gareth J. Barker15, Arun L. W. Bokde16, Uli Bromberg17, Christian Büchel17, Herta Flor18,19, Antoine Grigis20, Hugh Garavan21, Penny Gowland22, Andreas Heinz10, Bernd Ittermann23, Hervé Lemaître24, Jean-Luc Martinot25, Marie-Laure Paillère Martinot25,26, Frauke Nees14,18,27, Dimitri Papadopoulos Orfanos20, Tomáš Paus28, Luise Poustka29, Juliane H. Fröhner30, Ulrike Schmidt8,9, Julia Sinclair6, Michael N. Smolka30, Argyris Stringaris31, Henrik Walter10, Robert Whelan32, Sylvane Desrivières5, Barbara J. Sahakian1,33, Trevor W. Robbins1,34,40, Gunter Schumann1,10,35,36,40, Tianye Jia1,2,5,40, Jianfeng Feng1,2,37,38,39,40, IMAGEN Consortium, STRATIFY/ESTRA Consortium & ZIB Consortium*

Recent studies proposed a general psychopathology factor underlying common comorbidities among psychiatric disorders. However, its neurobiological mechanisms and generalizability remain elusive. In this study, we used a large longitudinal neuroimaging cohort from adolescence to young adulthood (IMAGEN) to define a neuropsychopathological (NP) factor across externalizing and internalizing symptoms using multitask connectomes. We demonstrate that this NP factor might represent a unified, genetically determined, delayed development of the prefrontal cortex that further leads to poor executive function. We also show this NP factor to be reproducible in multiple developmental periods, from preadolescence to early adulthood, and generalizable to the resting-state connectome and clinical samples (the ADHD-200 Sample and the STRATIFY & ESTRA Project). In conclusion, we identify a reproducible and general neural basis underlying symptoms of multiple mental health disorders, bridging multidimensional evidence from behavioral, neuroimaging and genetic substrates. These findings may help to develop new therapeutic interventions for psychiatric comorbidities.

The coexistence of multiple psychiatric conditions, known as psychiatric comorbidity1, has garnered substantial attention due to its high prevalence and long-lasting impact2. Individuals with comorbid psychiatric diagnoses often experience poorer outcomes and severe deficits in various cognitive and behavioral domains3. Notably, many psychiatric disorders, for example, externalizing and internalizing disorders, have their approximate peak onset in adolescence, coinciding with the emergence of comorbidity4,5. For instance, a population-based study on the well-being of adolescents found that 27.9% of participants aged 14–17 reached multiple diagnostic criteria6. The high prevalence of comorbid mental disorders suggests shared neurobiological origins among different psychopathologies2. However, the neuropsychopathological mechanism of psychiatric comorbidity, particularly during the critical period of adolescence, remains elusive.

Recently, emerging evidence has suggested a general psychopathology factor (that is, the p factor) underlying higher vulnerability for different psychiatric disorders7. Statistically, the p factor summarizes a pattern of positive correlations among symptoms; however, it leaves no room for alternative latent effects (for example, anticorrelation among symptoms). Indeed, it was argued that the behavioral p factor is largely equivalent to a sum of all symptoms8. Further, previous neuroimaging studies that investigated the neural correlates of the p factor mainly relied on task-free modalities, such as resting state9, diffusion10 and structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)11. However, although these task-free neural correlates of this p factor represent varied neurobiological information, they do not aid in specifying the neurocognitive processes underlying multiple psychopathologies12,13. Instead, the relevant cognitive brain circuitry can be mapped using multitask functional MRI (fMRI) data, which have also been used previously to identify circuit-specific neural signatures of externalizing symptoms14.

In contrast, crossdisorder genetic studies further revealed that many psychiatric disorders share high degrees of positive genetic correlations15,16, and the common genetic variants predominantly involved neurodevelopmental processes17,18. However, opposite genetic effects were also identified among psychiatric disorders17, which further highlighted the complexity of shared biological processes across multiple mental disorders. Therefore, it is necessary to integrate behavioral, neuroimaging and genetic evidence to establish coherent neurobiological crossdisorder neural factors (that is, the NP factor) that are not only shared among different psychopathologies but could also be attributed to specific cognitive brain circuits and genetic variants.

Notably, mounting evidence propose that many mental disorders can be understood as extreme deviations from a continuous spectrum in the population and different mental disorders may demonstrate similar deficits in multiple cognitive functions, as envisaged by Research Domain Criteria19. This new understanding inspires us to investigate potential transdiagnostic neurobiological processes from population-based data that are enriched with task-based fMRIs of multiple cognitive domains and symptom measurements covering a wide range of mental disorders. This approach also allows us to avoid the dilemma of case–control studies in identifying transdiagnostic biomarkers, where comorbidity is generally considered a major confounding factor to be removed. Furthermore, considering the replication crisis in neuroimaging studies, it was suggested that combining large neuroimaging samples and machine-learning approaches (that is, combining training and validation processes) could increase the reliability and reproducibility of identified neurobiomarkers20,21.

In this study, we will address the following three specific major questions regarding the shared neural bases of behavioral symptoms related to psychiatric disorders (Fig. 1a): (1) Can we establish an NP factor underlying both externalizing and internalizing symptoms on the basis of the multiple task-based connectomes of fMRI? (2) Is the NP factor supported by genetic and neurobehavioral substrates (for example, polygenic risk scores (PRSs), single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and cognitive functions)? (3) Is the NP factor generalizable to different imaging modalities (for example, resting-state connectome), developmental periods and clinical samples?

Results

Summary of major analytic steps

First, we leveraged the population-based IMAGEN cohort (aged 14 years, N = 1,750, 882 girls; Extended Data Table 1) to estimate the brain signature of eight behavioral symptoms using the connectivity-based predictive model grounded on multiple task-based fMRIs (Fig. 1b). These symptoms included four externalizing symptoms (that is, ASD, ADHD, ODD and CD) and four internalizing symptoms (that is, GAD, depression, ED and SP). The multitask connectomes were constructed from three fMRI tasks: stop-signal task (SST; related to response inhibition), monetary incentive delay task (MID; related to reward processing) and emotional face task (EFT; related to emotion reactivity). The model used 11 training–validation pairs to increase reliability.

We then extracted shared edges across the eight symptom-specific brain signatures to identify potential crossdisorder brain signatures. Using reliability and longitudinal analyses, we identified the NP factor that was positively predictive for both externalizing and internalizing symptoms across ages 14 and 19 (Fig. 1b–c). This NP factor was characterized by functional connectivity (FC) strength within three networks: sensorimotor network (SMF), salience network (SAL) and frontoparietal network (FPN), involving regions such as ventral precuneus (vPCun), medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and inferior frontal gyrus (IFG).

After identifying the NP factor at age 14, we examined its neurobehavioral and genetic underpinnings. We found that the NP factor was associated with poor executive function (Fig. 2a), including lower IQ, reduced working memory capacity and impaired risk adjustment ability. Furthermore, the NP factor was genetically associated with ADHD and depression PRSs (Fig. 2b) and linked to neurodevelopmental SNPs (Fig. 2c). The genetic associations were specific to neurodevelopmental processes rather than other pathways.

To test generalizability, we validated the NP factor in multiple contexts: (1) different developmental periods (ages 10–11, 14, 19, 23 and 29) across ABCD, IMAGEN and HCP cohorts; (2) resting-state connectomes; and (3) clinical samples including ADHD-200 (N = 520) and STRATIFY/ESTRA (N = 413, covering AN, BN, AUD and MDD). The NP factor showed consistent predictive power for symptom scores across all these contexts (Fig. 3), indicating its robustness and generalizability.

Establishing the NP factor using multitask connectomes

We first constructed eight connectome-based predictive models (CPMs) for each of the eight behavioral symptoms using the multitask connectomes at age 14 in the IMAGEN cohort. Each CPM included 11 independent training–validation pairs to increase reliability. The models achieved significant prediction accuracy for most symptoms (r = 0.12–0.22, P < 0.001 for all symptoms except ED).

We then identified edges that were significantly positively or negatively correlated with each symptom across all 11 folds. The number of symptom-specific edges varied: ASD (2,409 positive, 1,945 negative), ADHD (2,738 positive, 2,246 negative), ODD (2,108 positive, 2,149 negative), CD (2,001 positive, 2,012 negative), GAD (1,894 positive, 2,007 negative), depression (1,798 positive, 1,998 negative), ED (1,654 positive, 1,698 negative), SP (1,887 positive, 2,009 negative).

To identify crossdisorder edges, we calculated the proportion of edges shared between each pair of symptoms. Externalizing symptoms (ASD, ADHD, ODD, CD) showed high overlap (59–78%), while internalizing symptoms (GAD, depression, ED, SP) showed moderate overlap (44–67%). Cross-group overlap between externalizing and internalizing symptoms was lower but still substantial (20–37%).

We extracted the shared edges from all eight symptoms, resulting in 1,246 positive edges (associated with higher symptoms) and 1,609 negative edges (associated with lower symptoms). These edges formed the basis of the NP factor.

Reliability and longitudinal analysis of the NP factor

We calculated the NP factor score for each participant by summing the FC strength of all shared edges. The NP factor score was significantly associated with total externalizing symptoms (r = 0.30, P < 0.001) and total internalizing symptoms (r = 0.24, P < 0.001) at age 14, indicating its predictive power for both symptom dimensions.

To test reliability, we computed the NP factor score using each of the 11 training–validation folds and examined test–retest reliability across folds. The intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC) was 0.94, indicating excellent reliability.

To test longitudinal stability, we recalculated the NP factor score using the same edges but at age 19 (5 years later). The NP factor score at age 19 was significantly correlated with scores at age 14 (r = 0.57, P < 0.001), demonstrating temporal stability. The NP factor at age 19 also predicted externalizing symptoms (r = 0.24, P < 0.001) and internalizing symptoms (r = 0.19, P < 0.001), though the correlation was slightly weaker than at age 14.

Characterization of the NP factor

Network-level analysis revealed that the NP factor primarily involved three networks: SMF, SAL and FPN. The positive edges (associated with higher symptoms) showed weaker FC within these networks, suggesting that reduced connectivity in these networks is associated with higher symptom severity. The negative edges (associated with lower symptoms) showed stronger FC between these networks and other regions, indicating that enhanced connectivity between these networks and other brain regions is protective.

Region-level analysis identified three key regions: vPCun, mPFC and IFG. These regions were hubs in the NP factor, with high centrality in both positive and negative edge networks.

Neurobehavioral characterization showed that higher NP factor scores (indicating weaker connectivity) were associated with poorer executive function. Specifically, individuals with higher NP factor scores had lower IQ (r = -0.18, P < 0.001), reduced working memory capacity (r = -0.15, P < 0.001) and impaired risk adjustment ability (r = -0.12, P < 0.001). In contrast, the NP factor was not significantly associated with non-executive cognitive domains such as processing speed or memory consolidation.

Genetic characterization revealed that the NP factor was genetically associated with ADHD PRS (r = -0.10, P = 0.002) and depression PRS (r = -0.09, P = 0.004). Higher genetic risk for ADHD and depression was associated with weaker connectivity in the NP factor. Gene ontology analysis of SNPs associated with the NP factor showed enrichment for neurodevelopmental processes (P < 0.001), including neuronal differentiation, axon guidance and synapse formation. No enrichment was found for immune or metabolic pathways.

Generalizability of the NP factor

We tested the NP factor in multiple independent cohorts and contexts. First, we examined developmental generalizability by computing NP factor scores in different age groups across three cohorts: ABCD (ages 10–11, N = 1,946), IMAGEN (age 14, N = 931; age 19, N = 653) and HCP (age 29, N = 1,081). The NP factor score consistently predicted both externalizing and internalizing symptoms across all age groups (r = 0.15–0.35, P < 0.01 for all associations), indicating that the NP factor is stable across development.

Second, we examined modality generalizability by computing NP factor scores using resting-state connectomes instead of task-based connectomes. In the IMAGEN cohort, the resting-state NP factor score predicted externalizing symptoms (r = 0.22, P < 0.001) and internalizing symptoms (r = 0.18, P < 0.001), confirming that the NP factor generalizes to resting-state data.

Third, we examined clinical generalizability by testing the NP factor in two clinical samples: ADHD-200 (N = 520, age range 7–21) and STRATIFY/ESTRA (N = 413, age range 16–27, covering AN, BN, AUD and MDD). In ADHD-200, the NP factor score predicted ADHD symptom severity (r = 0.28, P < 0.001). In STRATIFY/ESTRA, the NP factor score predicted symptoms across all four disorders (AN: r = 0.19, P = 0.003; BN: r = 0.21, P = 0.001; AUD: r = 0.24, P < 0.001; MDD: r = 0.26, P < 0.001). These results indicate that the NP factor generalizes to clinical populations.

Developmental trajectory of the NP factor

To examine the developmental trajectory of the NP factor, we compared NP factor scores across ages using the IMAGEN and ABCD cohorts. We found that NP factor scores decreased with age, indicating that the connectivity patterns associated with psychopathology normalize during development. The reduction was most pronounced between ages 14 and 19 (mean decrease: 0.45 SD), suggesting that adolescence is a critical period for the maturation of these networks.

We also examined whether NP factor scores at age 14 predicted symptom trajectories from age 14 to 19. Higher NP factor scores at age 14 predicted slower reduction in externalizing symptoms (β = 0.32, P < 0.001) and internalizing symptoms (β = 0.28, P < 0.001), indicating that the NP factor predicts persistence of symptoms.

Discussion

In this study, using a large longitudinal neuroimaging genetic cohort, we identified a reliable neural endophenotype (that is, the NP factor) of behavioral symptoms for multiple mental disorders, with implications for early prevention and therapeutics in psychiatry.

We constructed the crossdisorder brain signature through the intersection of symptom-specific brain signatures derived from multitask connectomes in a population-based sample. This NP factor was validated across multiple developmental periods, imaging modalities and clinical samples. Its neurobehavioral and genetic underpinnings were characterized, revealing associations with executive function deficits and neurodevelopmental genetic variants.

Our findings advance the understanding of psychiatric comorbidity in several ways. First, we identified a transdiagnostic neural factor that underlies both externalizing and internalizing symptoms, bridging the internalizing–externalizing divide that has dominated psychiatric nosology22. Second, we demonstrated that this NP factor is reliable and stable across development, supporting its use as a biomarker for early identification of individuals at risk for multiple mental disorders. Third, we showed that the NP factor generalizes to clinical samples, indicating its potential utility in clinical settings. Fourth, we characterized the neurobehavioral and genetic underpinnings of the NP factor, providing mechanistic insights into how shared neurobiological factors contribute to psychiatric comorbidity.

The NP factor primarily involved three networks: SMF, SAL and FPN. These networks are critical for executive function, cognitive control and salience processing23–25. Reduced connectivity within these networks was associated with higher symptom severity, suggesting that impaired executive control and salience processing contribute to psychopathology. This interpretation is supported by our neurobehavioral findings, which showed that higher NP factor scores were associated with poorer executive function but not with non-executive cognitive domains.

The involvement of SMF in the NP factor is notable, as this network has traditionally been associated with motor and sensory processing rather than higher cognitive functions. However, recent evidence suggests that SMF plays a role in sensorimotor integration, action planning and cognitive control26,27. Our findings align with this emerging perspective and highlight the importance of considering sensorimotor processes in psychopathology.

The involvement of SAL and FPN is more consistent with prior literature. The SAL network is involved in detecting behaviorally relevant stimuli and switching between default mode and executive control networks28,29. The FPN is involved in working memory, decision-making and cognitive control30,31. Dysfunction in these networks has been implicated in various psychiatric disorders32,33. Our findings extend this literature by showing that dysfunction in these networks is shared across disorders and contributes to comorbidity.

The key regions identified (vPCun, mPFC and IFG) are also consistent with prior literature. The vPCun is part of the default mode network and is involved in self-referential processing and episodic memory retrieval34,35. The mPFC is involved in emotion regulation, decision-making and social cognition36,37. The IFG is involved in response inhibition, language processing and cognitive control38,39. Dysfunction in these regions has been implicated in various psychiatric disorders40,41. Our findings suggest that these regions form a hub network that is disrupted across disorders.

Our genetic characterization revealed that the NP factor is genetically associated with ADHD and depression PRSs and linked to neurodevelopmental SNPs. This aligns with prior literature showing that psychiatric disorders share high degrees of genetic correlation and that common genetic variants are involved in neurodevelopmental processes17,18. Our findings extend this literature by linking shared genetic factors to specific neural circuits and cognitive functions.

The developmental trajectory of the NP factor showed that connectivity patterns associated with psychopathology normalize during development, with the most pronounced changes occurring during adolescence. This suggests that adolescence is a critical period for the maturation of these networks and that delayed development of prefrontal circuits may contribute to psychopathology. This interpretation is supported by our genetic findings, which showed enrichment for neurodevelopmental processes.

The NP factor predicted persistence of symptoms from adolescence to young adulthood, indicating that it could be used to identify individuals at risk for chronic psychopathology. Early identification of these individuals could enable targeted interventions during the critical period of adolescence, potentially preventing the development of chronic mental disorders.

Our study has several strengths. First, we used a large, longitudinal neuroimaging cohort with multimodal data (task-based fMRI, resting-state fMRI, genetics, cognitive assessments). Second, we used machine-learning approaches with multiple training–validation pairs to increase reliability and reproducibility. Third, we validated our findings across multiple developmental periods, imaging modalities and clinical samples. Fourth, we characterized the neurobehavioral and genetic underpinnings of the NP factor, providing mechanistic insights.

Our study also has limitations. First, the IMAGEN cohort is population-based and primarily of European ancestry, limiting generalizability to other populations. Second, the clinical samples (ADHD-200, STRATIFY/ESTRA) had smaller sample sizes and different age ranges, limiting direct comparisons. Third, we focused on a limited set of cognitive functions (executive function, processing speed, memory), and other cognitive domains may also be relevant. Fourth, we did not examine environmental factors, which also contribute to psychopathology. Future studies should address these limitations by including diverse populations, larger clinical samples, broader cognitive assessments and environmental factors.

In conclusion, we identified a reproducible and general neural basis underlying symptoms of multiple mental health disorders. This NP factor represents a unified, genetically determined, delayed development of prefrontal circuits that leads to poor executive function and increased risk for multiple mental disorders. These findings may help develop new therapeutic interventions for psychiatric comorbidities by targeting shared neural circuits and cognitive functions.

Methods

Study protocol

We investigated the multivariate associations between behavioral symptoms and task-based FC (MID task, SST and emotion reactivity task) with the widely used CPM23,51. The task-based connectome prediction analysis was conducted in the population-based IMAGEN sample (aged 14 years, N = 1,750). The task-based connectomes were constructed from three fMRI tasks: SST (response inhibition), MID (reward processing) and EFT (emotion reactivity). For each task, we extracted time series from 264 predefined ROIs based on the Power atlas52. FC was computed as Pearson correlation between the time series of each pair of ROIs, resulting in a 264 × 264 connectivity matrix for each task.

Symptoms were measured using standardized scales: ASD (Social Responsiveness Scale), ADHD (Conners' Parent Rating Scale), ODD (Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire), CD (SDQ), GAD (Screen for Child Anxiety Related Emotional Disorders), depression (Mood and Feelings Questionnaire), ED (Eating Disorder Examination Questionnaire), SP (SDQ). Symptom scores were z-scored within the sample.

We constructed eight CPMs, one for each symptom. For each CPM, we used 11 independent training–validation pairs (50% training, 50% validation, stratified by sex) to increase reliability. In each fold, we computed correlations between FC and symptom scores in the training set, selected edges with significant correlations (P < 0.01), and summed the FC strength of these edges to compute a predicted symptom score in the validation set. We computed prediction accuracy as the correlation between predicted and actual symptom scores across folds.

To identify crossdisorder edges, we extracted edges that were significantly correlated with each symptom across all 11 folds (present in at least 6 folds). We then computed the proportion of edges shared between each pair of symptoms. Shared edges across all eight symptoms were extracted to form the NP factor.

We computed the NP factor score for each participant by summing the FC strength of all shared edges (positive and negative separately). We computed test–retest reliability of the NP factor across folds using ICC. We computed longitudinal stability by correlating NP factor scores at age 14 with scores at age 19.

We examined neurobehavioral associations by correlating NP factor scores with cognitive test scores (IQ, working memory, risk adjustment, processing speed, memory consolidation). We examined genetic associations by correlating NP factor scores with PRSs for ADHD and depression. We conducted gene ontology analysis of SNPs associated with NP factor scores using MAGMA53.

We examined generalizability by computing NP factor scores in independent cohorts: ABCD (ages 10–11), IMAGEN (age 19), HCP (age 29), ADHD-200, STRATIFY/ESTRA. For resting-state generalizability, we computed NP factor scores using resting-state connectomes in the IMAGEN cohort. We examined predictive power by correlating NP factor scores with symptom scores in each cohort.

Data availability

The IMAGEN data are available from the IMAGEN consortium (https://imagen-project.org). The ABCD data are available from the ABCD Study (https://abcdstudy.org). The HCP data are available from the Human Connectome Project (https://www.humanconnectome.org). The ADHD-200 data are available from the ADHD-200 Consortium (http://fcon_1000.projects.nitrc.org/indi/adhd200/). The STRATIFY/ESTRA data are available from the STRATIFY/ESTRA Consortium (https://www.stratify-estra.org).

Code availability

The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/tianyejia/NP_factor.

docs.title: APHL Verification and Validation Toolkit - Complete Detailed Summary
Overview
docs.text: The APHL Verification and Validation (V&V) Toolkit is a comprehensive resource for clinical laboratories to demonstrate that new instruments and tests have acceptable performance before implementation. The toolkit guides laboratories through planning, implementing, and analyzing verification and validation studies to meet CLIA (Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments) regulatory requirements.

docs.title: Key Objectives
docs.text:
• Assist laboratories in determining the difference between validation and verification
  • Guide when each process should be performed
  • Provide step-by-step instructions on how to perform verification or validation
  • Help plan, implement, and analyze data for new testing methods
  • Ensure compliance with CLIA requirements

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Verification is performed for FDA-approved/cleared tests or FDA-modified tests. It confirms that the laboratory can reproduce the manufacturer's performance claims.

Validation is performed for laboratory-developed tests (LDTs) or tests significantly modified by the laboratory. It establishes performance characteristics without manufacturer claims.

docs.title: Determination Flow
docs.text:
1. Is the test FDA-approved/cleared?
  2. YES: Verification required

  3. NO: Validation required

  4. Has the test been significantly modified?

  5. YES: Validation required
  6. NO: Follow manufacturer's instructions for verification

docs.title: For Both Verification and Validation
docs.text:
Qualitative Assays: - Accuracy (bias) - agreement with reference method - Precision (repeatability) - consistency across replicates - Analytical Sensitivity (Limit of Detection) - lowest detectable analyte - Analytical Specificity - freedom from interference - Reportable Range - values that can be accurately reported - Reference Range - expected results in healthy population

Quantitative Assays: - All of the above plus: - Calibration verification - confirming calibration curve accuracy - Linearity - proportional response across range - Carryover - sample-to-sample contamination

docs.title: Sample Requirements
docs.text:
Precision Studies: - Within-run: Minimum 20 replicates - Between-run: Minimum 20 runs across different days - Different operators: Minimum 2 operators

Accuracy Studies: - Minimum 40 patient specimens spanning reportable range - Include positive, negative, and equivocal results

Analytical Sensitivity (LoD): - Minimum 20 replicates at low concentration - Serial dilutions to determine detection limit

Analytical Specificity: - Test 20-30 potentially interfering substances - Include cross-reactivity panel

Reference Intervals: - Verification: 20 reference individuals - Establishment: 120 reference individuals

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
Qualitative Tests: - Percent agreement ≥ 95% - Kappa statistic ≥ 0.75 - Sensitivity ≥ 95% - Specificity ≥ 95%

Quantitative Tests: - Bias within ±10% - CV: Within-run ≤ 5%, Between-run ≤ 7.5%, Total ≤ 10% - LoD: 95% detection probability - LoQ: CV ≤ 20% - r ≥ 0.99 for linearity

docs.title: Sample Stability
docs.text:
• Room temperature, refrigerated, frozen stability
  • Freeze-thaw cycles
  • Acceptance: bias within ±10%

docs.title: Bridging Studies
docs.text:
• Required for modifications
  • Test 40 samples before/after change
  • Acceptance: bias within ±10%, r ≥ 0.95

docs.title: Instrumentation V&V
docs.text:
• Installation Qualification (IQ)
  • Operational Qualification (OQ)
  • Performance Qualification (PQ)

docs.title: Reagent Lot Comparison
docs.text:
• Test 20-40 samples with both lots
  • Acceptance: bias within ±10%

docs.title: Software Updates
docs.text:
• Impact assessment required
  • Verification after major upgrades
  • Algorithm changes may require re-validation

docs.title: Risk Assessment Process
docs.text:
1. Hazard identification
  2. Risk analysis (likelihood × severity)
  3. Risk evaluation against criteria
  4. Risk mitigation (engineering, administrative, PPE)
  5. Monitoring and review (at least annually)

docs.title: Risk Categories
docs.text:
• Biological risks (infectious agents, biosafety level)
  • Chemical risks (hazardous reagents, SDS)
  • Physical risks (electrical, mechanical, thermal)
  • Ergonomic risks (repetitive motion, heavy lifting)

docs.title: Labor Costs
docs.text:
• 40-88 hours per V&V project
  • Personnel: Director, Supervisor, Technologist, Quality Manager

docs.title: Materials Costs
docs.text: • Test reagents, QC materials, reference materials, supplies

docs.title: Maintenance Costs (ongoing)
docs.text:
• QC materials: $5,000-15,000/year per assay
  • Reagents: $10,000-50,000/year per assay
  • PT participation: $500-2,000 per event
  • Training: $1,000-5,000 per staff member

docs.title: Regulatory References
docs.text:
• CLIA - 42 CFR 493.1253
  • CLSI Guidelines - EP05, EP06, EP09, EP12, EP15, EP17, EP26, EP27
  • CAP - Laboratory General Checklist
  • ISO 15189 - International laboratory quality standard
  • FDA - 21 CFR 809 (IVD devices)

docs.text:
1. Clearly define test method and intended use
  2. Determine verification vs validation
  3. Select team and assign responsibilities

docs.text:
1. Follow protocol strictly
  2. Document all activities
  3. Track deviations
  4. Perform statistical analysis properly

docs.text:

docs.text:

docs.title: Emag magana easymag respiratory virus extraction comparison
docs.text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE Comparison of the new fully automated extraction platform eMAG to the MagNA PURE 96 and the well-established easyMAG for detection of common human respiratory viruses Musa Hindiyeh1,2☯, Orna MorID1,2☯, Rakefet Pando1,3, Batya Mannasse1, Areej Kabat1,2, Hadar Assraf-Zarfati1, Ella Mendelson1,2, Danit Sofer1, Michal MandelboimID1,2* 1 Central Virology Laboratory, Ministry of Health, Chaim Sheba Medical Center, Ramat-Gan, Israel, 2 Department of Epidemiology and Preventive Medicine, School of Public Health, Sackler Faculty of Medicine, Tel-Aviv University, Tel-Aviv, Israel, 3 The Israel Center for Disease Control, Israel Ministry of Health, Tel-Hashomer, Israel ☯These authors contributed equally to this work. * michalman@sheba.health.gov.il

Abstract Respiratory viral infections constitute the majority of samples tested in the clinical virology laboratory during the winter season, and are mainly diagnosed using molecular assays, namely real-time PCR (qPCR). Therefore, a high-quality extraction process is critical for successful, reliable and sensitive qPCR results. Here we aimed to evaluate the performance of the newly launched eMAG compared to the fully automated MagNA PURE 96 (Roche, Germany) and to the semi-automated easyMAG (bioMerieux, France) extraction platforms. For this analysis, we assessed and compared the analytic and clinical performance of the three platforms, using 262 archived respiratory samples positive or negative to common viruses regularly examined in our laboratory (influenza A, B, H1N1pdm, Respiratory Syncy- tial Virus (RSV), human Metapneumovirus (hMPV), parainfluenza-3, adenovirus and nega- tive samples). In addition, quantitated virus controls were used to determine the limit of detection of each extraction method. In all categories tested, eMAG results were comparable to those of the easyMAG and MagNa PURE 96, highly sensitive for all viruses and over 98% clinical specificity and sensi- tivity for all viruses tested. Together with its high level of automation, the bioMerieux eMAG is a high-quality extraction platform enabling effective molecular analysis and is mostly suit- able for medium-sized laboratories.

Introduction Respiratory viral infections are a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide [1] and have been shown to be the etiological agents of more than 70% of respiratory tract infections (RTIs) [2]. Nucleic acid-based tests, mostly performed in multiplexes by real-time PCR (qPCR) platforms, are the most common and efficient means of detecting viral infections, and support rapid and simultaneous detection of many viruses [3,4]. The nucleic acids extraction process is one of the most significant steps dictating the accuracy and sensitivity of viral infec- tion diagnosis and virus type determination. Moreover, efficient extraction allows for the detection of different viral agents including DNA and RNA viruses, from a single extraction tube. Using qPCR technology, the Israeli Central Virology Laboratory performs viral detection on more than 10,000 respiratory samples each year, which constitute the majority of samples requiring nucleic acid extraction process in our laboratory.

NUCLISENS easyMAG (bioMe´rieux, France) is a second-generation silica-based semi- automatic platform that was first launched in 2005. It was specifically optimized for total nucleic acid extraction from biological samples. The system automates enhanced magnetic silica-based extraction based on the BOOM technology, a gold standard for the universal extraction of RNA and DNA based on the ability of silica to bind DNA and RNA in high salt concentrations [5].

eMAG (bioMe´rieux, France) is a new, fully automated nucleic acid extraction platform that enables simultaneous extraction of 48 specimens from primary tubes, either into PCR strips ready for qPCR analysis or into storage tubes. eMAG also utilizes the already well-established BOOM technology as the easyMAG [5]. MagNA PURE 96 (Roche, Germany), which was launched in 2009, was also shown to have excellent nucleic acid extraction efficiency for clini- cal samples [6]. This system is a fully automated extraction system that enables simultaneous extraction of 96 specimens using magnetic bead technology, from a 96 deep-well plate to a PCR plate.

The performance of the semi-automated easyMAG system has been extensively investi- gated; the platform was shown to efficiently extract viral nucleic acid [7,8]. In a study that com- pared the performance of the new eMAG and the easyMAG systems, eMAG was shown to perform equally well on several types of clinical samples including respiratory samples [9]. However, no large-scale study has simultaneously compared the performance of the eMAG to that of easyMAG and MagNA PURE 96 in nucleic acid extraction from respiratory samples.

In this study, we performed an evaluation of the newly launched eMAG as compared to both easyMAG and the fully automated MagNA PURE 96, with emphasis on the detection of influenza viruses (A, H1N1pdm09 and B), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), parainfluenza-3, human metapneumovirus (hMPV) and adenovirus, using an in-house-developed qPCR assay [3]. Evaluations were performed using archived clinical samples collected at Sheba Medical Center in Israel, as well as calibrated controls for each virus.

Materials and methods Clinical specimens and extraction platform properties Archived nasopharyngeal samples (including Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) (N = 8), tracheal aspirations (N = 32) or nasopharyngeal swabs (N = 403)) of patients hospitalized at Chaim Sheba Medical Center, collected into Virocult liquid viral transport medium (LVTM) (Medical Wire & Equipment Co, Wiltshire, United Kingdom) and stored at -70˚C, were used to evaluate the performance of the three extraction systems. Representative samples covering the range of cycle threshold values (Ct) below 35, which were previously extracted by easyMAG and tested for the common human respiratory viruses, were selected.

The archived samples were thawed and the volume of the sample was adjusted with M199 (transport medium Biological Industries (BI), Beit Haemek, Israel), compatible with all three systems. The archived samples (N = 262) included positive samples for influenza A (N = 47), H1N1pdm (N = 22), influenza B (N = 21), RSV (N = 21), hMPV (N = 23), parainfluenza-3 (N = 20) and adenovirus (N = 23), as well as negative control samples (N = 181).

The technical and physical properties of the three platforms, including platform size, nucleic acid collection options (tubes/plate/cartridge), sample loading method (directly/indi- rectly from the sample tube), the existence of a barcode reader and user operation conve- nience, are summarized in Table 1.

Clinical sample nucleic acid extraction and qPCR analysis Total nucleic acids were simultaneously extracted from all patient samples, using the easy- MAG, eMAG and MagNA PURE 96 instruments according to the manufacturer instructions (easyMAG and eMAG—Specific B program and in the MagNA PURE 96 -DNA and viral NA large volume kit).

Each of the samples was divided to three tubes of 500 μl each for the extraction, and extracted by the three platforms at the same time. BAL and tracheal aspiration samples were diluted with M199 transport media in case of a viscous sample. Nucleic acids were eluted into either 55μl (easyMAG and eMAG), or in 50 μl (MagNA PURE 96) elution buffer.

Multiplex qPCR reactions for detection of influenza A, B, H1N1pdm and RSV were per- formed as previously described [10]. In addition, multiplex qPCR was performed for the detec- tion of hMPV, adenovirus, parainfluenza-3 and the internal control RNase P, using Ambion One-Step Real Time PCR (Life Technologies, USA). The reaction mixture contained 600nM hMPV forward and 1.2uM hMPV reverse primers, 300nM adenovirus forward and reverse primers, 300nM parainfluenza-3 forward and reverse primers, 150nM RNase P forward and reverse primers and, 200 μM of each of the assay probes. Samples from the three extraction platforms tested together by qPCR reactions for 50 cycles, using the same standard ABI 7500 instruments (Life Technology, USA).

A sample was considered positive if Ct results were under 40, regardless of the result of the internal control. All samples with Ct results above 40 were considered negative, provided that the RNase P internal control gave a positive signal (Ct<35). Invalid results could be due to qPCR inhibitors; a sample was considered invalid if no signal was obtained and the internal control was negative.

In each qPCR assay, positive internal controls for each of the targets were used. The Ct val- ues, the standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation (CV) of these controls were con- tinuously monitored. The cumulative SD and CV for each of the internal controls were always below 1SD and 2%, respectively.

Extraction system limit of detection (LOD) for each of the targeted viruses In order to compare the analytical sensitivity of the three extraction methods, serial decimal dilutions (10−1–10−8) of quantitated viruses including: influenza A/H3N2 (originated from world health organization (WHO)), influenza A/H1N1pdm (WHO), influenza B (WHO), RSV (American type culture collection (ATCC)), adenovirus (ATCC), hMPV and parainflu- enza-3 (clinical samples), diluted in M199, were performed. These diluted viral stocks were simultaneously extracted by the three extraction systems, according to the manufacturer instructions. Eluted extracted nucleic acids were stored at -70˚C until analysis. Limit of detec- tion (LOD) was compared according to the highest detectable dilution for each sample, between all platforms using qPCR reaction. LOD was detected when at least two of the three replicates per extracted sample were positive for the tested virus. If only one of the three triplicates was posi- tive for a given virus, the result was considered negative (below LOD).

Data analysis The analytical sensitivity, specificity and positive and negative predictive values (PPV and NPV) of the easyMAG and the MagNA PURE 96 were compared to those of the eMAG using Microsoft Excel 2010 software. Bland-Altman analysis was used to compare the Cts measured in the three platforms, as previously described [11].

Ethical approval Ethical approval for this study was granted by the Sheba Ethical Committee (approval number 4421-17-SMC), provided that anonymous samples were used. All data were fully anonymized at the time of data collection, and the committee did not require informed consent.

Results Analytical parameters of the eMAG In general, the analytical sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV were comparable between eMAG and the other two platforms (Table 2). The overall specificity for all tested respiratory viruses was between 98.9–100% for the easyMAG and between 97.8–100% for the MagNA PURE 96, while sensitivity ranged between 95–100% for the easyMAG and 91.3–100% for the MagNA PURE 96. PPV values of 95.2–100% were recorded for the easyMAG and 90.5–100% for the MagNA PURE 96, while the NPV values were 98.4–100% for the easyMAG and 96.8– 100% for the MagNA PURE 96. Taken together, the eMAG extraction performance was com- parable to that of the easyMAG and the MagNA PURE 96 (Table 2). Indeed, the kappa coefficient between eMAG and the other systems was >0.973, indicating a strong agreement between this new automated system and the other two platforms.

No significant difference was found in the comparison of the performance of extraction by sample type (BAL, tracheal aspirations or nasopharyngeal swabs) with percentage agreement of above 97%.

Intersystem comparison of cycle threshold (Ct) values Analysis of the data revealed that the SD of the Ct values of the three platforms was less than 1.0 SD, indicating an excellent correlation between the three. Moreover, Bland-Altman analy- sis performed on the quantitative results obtained by eMAG versus MagNA PURE 96 (Fig 1) and between eMAG versus easyMAG (Fig 2), demonstrated similar performance. Over 98% of the samples tested in all platforms were between the SD boundaries, which indicate a good cor- relation between eMAG and the other two extraction methods. In both analyses, of the 21 pos- itive RSV samples, only four samples showed different Ct values in the eMAG compared with the other two platforms.

LOD of eMAG, easyMAG and MagNa PURE 96 for respiratory viruses LOD was compared between the platforms using quantitated virus controls in serial decimal dilutions. We found that for most of the viruses examined (influenza B, A/H1N1pdm, adeno- virus and parainfluenza-3) LOD was identical for all three systems (Table 3). For hMPV, eMAG showed a better LOD compared to the easyMAG and MagNA PURE 96, while a better LOD was provided by both eMAG and MagNA PURE 96 for influenza A, compared with the easyMAG. For RSV, the easyMAG presented a better LOD than the other two platforms. Notably, all LOD differences between the three platforms resulted from a single serial dilution.

Discussion In the past few years, an increasing number of respiratory clinical samples have been examined in our laboratory, the Israeli Central Virology Laboratory, Ministry of Health. As our main "gold standard", well established [12–14].extraction platform- the easyMAG can extract only 24 samples, we continuously seek to streamline the work and reduce the turnaround time. Therefore, we evaluated a larger platform- the eMAG, based on the same extraction technology as the easyMAG, which can extract up to 48 samples in each run. The eMAG was also com- pared with the well-validated MagNA PURE 96 that enables the extraction of 96 specimens, and currently present in our laboratory in order to evaluate the eMAG performance against another larger scale extraction platform.

First, we performed an evaluation of the analytical performance of these platforms in detecting the respiratory viruses most commonly examined in our laboratory. For most of the tested viruses, the three platforms demonstrated similar LODs. For three of the viruses, hMPV, RSV and influenza A, minor differences in LOD were noted between the platforms, all of which were within only one dilution factor. These LOD differences are negligible as these high dilution samples had very low virus concentrations and therefore are mostly undetected according to the Poisson distribution [15]. Altogether, with minor or no differences in the LOD, all three platforms presented very similar performance. As the three platforms are tech- nically similar, especially eMAG and easyMAG, these analytical assessments were expected as previously described [9].

The clinical assessment is most important for determining the effectiveness of nucleic acid extraction and removal of enzymatic inhibitors, which have a direct impact on the qPCR results. The presented clinical assessments demonstrate a good correlation between the performance of both easyMAG and MagNA PURE 96 compared with the eMAG. Indeed, eMAG sensitivity and specificity were over 99%, compared to the easyMAG and a total of 98% sensitivity and specificity compared to the MagNA PURE 96 for all viruses tested. The clinical evaluation together with the analytical assessment allowed us to conclude that all three plat- forms have comparable results which allowed us to choose a larger automated extraction plat- form for our laboratory.

Evaluation of the technical properties of the three platforms revealed that the newly launched fully automated eMAG operation and sample loading is confusing and cumbersome when using non-barcoded tubes. Under these working conditions, the MagNa PURE 96 which is also fully automated requiring additional robotic machine, it is more user friendly compared with the eMAG. However, using the eMAG with barcoded input and output tubes enables simple load and run working mode. As for the easyMAG, it is a well-established platform and easy to operate compared with the eMAG, however, it is smaller and semi-automated (Table 1).

However, when extracting the full 48 samples without barcodes, the technical operation of this machine is a bit complex, as it is composed of two independently operated 24-sample sub- units that require a well-trained technician to properly load the samples. On the other hand, these independent subunits provide an advantage when 24 or fewer samples are being tested. Assuming that the manufacturer will solve this technical difficulty, eMAG is a high-quality extraction platform mostly suitable for medium-sized laboratories.

docs.text:
Based on the chapter titles and expert credits, this video covers:

  1. Metabolic Rate Scaling - How metabolic rate varies with animal size
  2. Surface Law - The relationship between surface area and volume
  3. Kleiber's Law - The famous 3/4 power law of metabolic scaling
  4. Fractional Exponents in Biology - Why ¼ appears consistently
  5. WBE Theory - West-Brown-Enquist theory of fractal biological networks
  6. Universal Heartbeats - The ~1 billion heartbeats phenomenon
  7. Human Longevity - Exceptions to the rule
  8. Urban vs. Rural Health - Scaling effects in human populations
  9. Universal Scaling Exponent Debate - Scientific controversy over universality

docs.title: 1. The Elephant LSD Dosing Problem (0:00)
docs.text: The video opens with a historical case study about scaling laws - determining appropriate drug doses for different sized animals.

docs.title: 2. Metabolic Rate Scaling (3:09)
docs.text: How animals' energy use scales with body size - the foundation for understanding biological scaling.

docs.title: 3. Surface Law (5:27)
docs.text: The relationship between surface area and volume, and its implications for heat loss in animals.

docs.title: 4. Kleiber's Law (8:04)
docs.text: The famous empirical observation that metabolic rate scales with mass to the 3/4 power, not the 2/3 predicted by surface law.

docs.title: 5. Universal 1/4 Exponents (10:49)
docs.text: Why fractional exponents (particularly 1/4) appear consistently across biological systems.

docs.title: 6. WBE Theory (13:33)
docs.text: The West-Brown-Enquist theory explaining fractal distribution networks in organisms as the cause of 3/4 scaling.

docs.title: 7. One Billion Heartbeats (19:53)
docs.text: The observation that small animals have fast heartbeats but short lives, while large animals have slow heartbeats but long lives, resulting in roughly 1 billion total heartbeats across mammal species.

docs.title: 8. Human Exception (23:11)
docs.text: Why humans exceed this pattern through technology, medicine, and cultural evolution.

docs.title: 9. Urban Scaling (24:31)
docs.text: How similar scaling laws apply to cities and human settlements.

docs.title: 10. Scientific Debate (30:12)
docs.text: Ongoing controversies about whether scaling exponents are truly universal or vary across species and systems.

docs.title: Channel
docs.text: Bowtie Insurance 保泰人壽

docs.title: 1. The "Guaranteed Principal" Myth
docs.text: Savings insurance is marketed as "保本" (guaranteed principal), but this is often an illusion. The video exposes how this marketing claim misleads customers about the safety of their initial capital.

docs.title: 2. Return Discrepancies
docs.text: Many customers receive much lower dividends than the "expected returns" shown by insurance agents during the sales process. The video questions why actual performance often falls short of projections.

docs.title: 3. Policy Surrendering Issues
docs.text: The concept of "供斷保險" (stopping payments or surrendering a policy) is discussed. The video questions whether it's truly possible to get your money back while retaining coverage.

docs.title: 4. Industry Statistics
docs.text:
• Out of 135 savings policies analyzed, only 6 actually met their projected return targets
  • This suggests the vast majority of savings insurance underperform compared to sales projections

docs.title: 5. Financial Risks
docs.text:
• Expensive savings plans can lead to insufficient actual life insurance coverage
  • Cash flow gets locked up ("hostage") for decades
  • Policyholders may not realize the opportunity cost of their locked capital

docs.title: 6. Comparison with Term Life Insurance
docs.text: The video compares complex savings products against simpler options like pure term life insurance ("純人壽"), suggesting the latter may be more cost-effective for actual insurance needs.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. Be skeptical of sales projections: Expected returns are not guarantees
  2. Understand the terms: Read policy documents carefully before committing
  3. Separate insurance from investment: Consider term life insurance + separate investment vehicles
  4. Long-term commitment matters: Surrendering early often results in significant losses
  5. Transparency issues: Insurance agents may not fully disclose downsides and risks

00:00 The Pentagon didn’t just release UFO files…  it released proof of things that shouldn’t

00:05 be possible. These aren’t rumors or  leaks. tThey’re documented encounters

00:09 the Pentagon still can’t explain. And the most unsettling part?

00:13 These are the things they want you to see. 50.

00:18 In September, 2023, the FBI was trying to  understand what a drone operator at a U.S

00:23 site had just seen. In a declassified video the  man explains that he and his colleagues had all

00:28 witnessed a “bright light over the horizon.” Surrounded by a dazzling glow the object was,

00:34 quote, “metallic gray”, “linear” about “one  to two Blackhawk helicopters in length and

00:40 definitely bigger than a drone”. It looked  like a vehicle of some kind but had no exhaust

00:44 or wings. It hovered at about 5,000 feet  (15,24 meters), moved from east to west,

00:49 and then, within 5 to 10 seconds, it was gone. It freaked the man out, but that night a storm

00:54 battered the town. He was still on edge as  he sat in his hotel room, when suddenly his

00:59 TV went black. He told the FBI for the next 2  nights he could barely sleep and when he did,

01:04 his mind was tormented with strange dreams. Had he made contact?

01:09 To better understand, let’s go back to when all  this talk of UFOs in the USA first got off the

01:15 ground. 49.

01:17 At the end of World War II, US and British  intelligence were trying to figure out if Nazi

01:21 scientists had built superweapons. They actually  had: the V1 and V2 rockets, but declassified

01:27 documents show us something was spotted in the  skies above Europe… and it wasn’t a rocket.

01:33 On November 4th, 1948, a Top-Secret USAFE  (United States Air Force Europe) document stated:

01:38 “For some time, we have been concerned by  the recurring reports on flying saucers.”

01:42 One of these machines was observed, quote,  “hovering over Neubiberg Air Base for

01:47 about 30 minutes.” US authorities were stumped,  writing that whatever these vehicles were might,

01:53 quote, be “beyond the scope of our  present intelligence thinking.”

01:57 48. In a secret report,

01:58 one of these machines was described as having: “Extreme maneuverability and apparent ability to

02:04 almost hover; a plan approximating that an oval or  disc with done shape on the surface; the ability

02:10 to quickly disappear by high, the speed or by  complete disintegration; the ability to group

02:15 together or very quickly in a tight formation.” Nothing built by man could do that, so what had

02:21 they seen? 47.

02:23 One of the men tasked with understanding these  alien-like machines was the FBI director J. Edgar

02:28 Hoover. Declassified files show he wasn’t  a believer, but more or less every week,

02:34 another UFO document landed on his desk. One of them shows that on October 9th,

02:39 1967, a woman appeared at the FBI office in  Dallas. She claimed in July of that year,

02:44 she’d been kidnapped by aliens. A, quote, “being  from another planet who had assumed earthly form,”

02:50 took her into the sky aboard a spaceship  and gave her some important information.

02:55 She claimed the aliens had told her that on  May 22nd, 1962, American forces had fired a

03:01 missile at a UFO over Africa, but the craft  had protected itself using a “force field.”

03:06 She also alleged that U.S. forces had tracked  another UFO over Antarctica on August 20th, 1967.

03:13 The woman insisted that if investigators could  verify those incidents, it would prove her story

03:18 was genuine. But she refused to give her name. Why?

03:21 Because, she warned, UFO whistleblowers had a  habit of disappearing or meeting unfortunate ends.

03:27 As bizarre as that sounds, similar  claims kept pouring into FBI offices.

03:32 On May 14th, 1969, a man named Larry  Stephens wrote to the Bureau asking

03:37 agents to investigate rumors of mysterious  men, dressed in black and driving black cars,

03:43 who allegedly intimidated UFO witnesses  while sometimes impersonating FBI agents.

03:48 It is easy to dismiss everyone in  these files as either crazy or just

03:52 looking for attention. But many of the  reports came from very credible sources.

03:57 46.

03:58 Three servicemen from the 147th Airways and Air  Communications Squadron stationed in Guam reported

04:04 that at 10:40 a.m. on August 14th 1946 they saw  two crescent-shaped objects streaking overhead.

04:12 They estimated it was travelling at twice the  speed of America’s fastest fighter aircraft.

04:16 Flying at roughly 1,200 feet (365 meters),  the objects suddenly broke into a sharp

04:20 zig-zag maneuver before disappearing from sight. It sounds strange, coming from military personnel,

04:25 but reports like this carried  on well into the 21st century.

04:30 45. In just 2 days

04:31 in May in 2023, 7 different people who worked  for the federal government reported seeing the

04:36 unexplainable in the sky in the western US. Event One: Three separate teams of federal

04:42 law enforcement special agents reported  seeing 2 or 3 glowing red orbs hanging in
