33:04 Then, on the very same day the major witnessed  the discs, military personnel at Davis-Monthan

33:10 Air Force Base in Arizona reported something  equally weird. 12 unidentified objects flying in

33:16 formation at estimated speeds of between 1,500  and 2,000 miles per hour (2,414 - 3,218 kph).

33:21 It was the kind of performance that was beyond  anything publicly known to exist in the 1950s.

33:27 The legendary Lockheed SR-71  Blackbird wouldn’t emerge from

33:31 the secret world of Area 51 until the mid-1960s. And these super-fast vehicle sightings weren’t

33:37 only confined to the US. 6.

33:39 In September 1953, NATO warships participating  in Operation Mainbrace were crossing the North

33:44 Atlantic. During the mission, a Danish  naval commander and his crew reported

33:49 a glowing triangular object tearing across the  sky at roughly 900 miles per hour (1,448 kph).

33:54 It was also glowing with an eerie blue light. Over the following weeks, more sightings

33:59 emerged from personnel involved in the  exercise. None of them were explained.

34:03 Then right after came an incident in Yorkshire,  northern England. RAF personnel reported that

34:08 an unidentified object appeared to shadow one of  their Meteor jet fighters in flight. One airman

34:14 later described the object as a silver disc. “It stopped its descent and hung in the air,

34:19 rotating as if on its own axis,” he said. “Then it  accelerated at an incredible speed to the West.”

34:25 But what happened when investigators believed  they’d found not just a sighting, but actual

34:30 physical evidence? 5.

34:32 Arthur Stansel, a technician connected to the  Nevada Test Site, would later become part of

34:37 UFO legend. In a sworn statement, he claimed  that on May 21st 1953, he’d helped recover part

34:43 of a crashed UFO near Kingman, Arizona. According to his account, the object was

34:49 “constructed of an unfamiliar metal which  resembled brushed aluminum.” He said he and

34:54 several other men dug it out of the sand where  it had partially embedded itself after impact.

34:58 The craft, he claimed, was oval-shaped, roughly 30  feet (9 meters) in diameter, with two swivel seats

35:04 and a cabin filled with strange instruments. He later described it as something so many

35:08 people had seen all over the world – “a  teardrop-shaped cigar... a streamlined cigar.”

35:14 Then came the detail that would one day  make Americans feel like they weren’t alone.

35:18 “A tent pitched near the object sheltered the  dead remains of the only occupant,” he stated.

35:24 Occupant, as in… alien. So what exactly had Stansel claimed to have seen?

35:29 In his own words, the being was  “about 4 feet (1.21 meters) tall,

35:32 with a dark brown complexion, and had two eyes,  two nostrils, two ears, and a small mouth.” He

35:38 said it wore “a silvery metallic suit” along  with a skullcap made from the same material.

35:43 And according to Stansel, he wasn’t  alone. Other technicians present that

35:47 day supposedly saw the same thing. And now comes the strangest part.

35:51 4. In classified government documents,

35:54 intelligence officials reportedly referred to  Arthur Stansel using the name Fritz Werner.

35:59 Those files describe how Stansel and other  technicians were allegedly transported to the

36:04 crash site aboard a bus with blacked-out windows. Then, in 2024, another document surfaced online

36:10 relating to Werner. It appeared to  contain messages exchanged between a

36:14 U.S. government official and Christopher  Mellon, the former Senate Intelligence

36:19 Committee staffer who later became involved  in the Pentagon’s investigation into UAPs.

36:24 In the exchange, the official suggested that the  truth about the Kingman crash would leave people

36:29 “slack-jawed.” He spoke about the incident  as though it remained an active matter

36:33 even into the 2020s, reportedly saying: “We’re  vacuuming up info”. That’s the kind of language

36:39 that could be interpreted as an admission  that authorities were still suppressing or

36:44 collecting information connected to the case. If genuine, the messages appeared to suggest

36:49 that a supposedly high-ranking official  believed there was at least some truth

36:54 behind Stansel’s extraordinary claims. Unfortunately, the latest tranche of

36:58 released documents doesn’t appear to add  much concrete evidence to the Kingman story.

37:02 But the allegations remind us of  something that went down in the UK.

37:06 3. After years of

37:08 sightings – and growing distrust in CIA-linked  UFO investigations – the Condon Committee was

37:13 formed. It was a project funded by the U.S.  Air Force and the University of Colorado to

37:18 scientifically study unidentified flying objects. One of the cases that got the committee’s

37:23 attention took place in 1956 at  RAF Bentwaters in Suffolk, England.

37:27 Radar operators tracked an object moving  at several thousand miles per hour. Then,

37:32 suddenly, the radar began showing dozens  of them. According to the reports,

37:36 the equipment was checked and found to be  functioning properly. Witnesses said smaller

37:40 objects appeared to dart around a much larger  one, and multiple servicemen observed the event.

37:46 Something very similar happened nearby at  RAF Lakenheath. There, the object wasn’t

37:50 only picked up on radar, it was reportedly  seen visually as well. Witnesses described

37:55 it stopping dead in the sky, accelerating  instantly, and moving at extraordinary speeds.

38:00 Lakenheath personnel contacted RAF Neatishead,  also in Suffolk, which scrambled a de Havilland

38:06 Venom night fighter to intercept the target. The Venom’s two-man crew later reported that they

38:10 had the object both on radar and in direct  visual sight. Then, without warning,

38:14 the target appeared behind them before they could  react. Eventually, the jet ran low on fuel and was

38:20 forced to break off the pursuit and land. The Condon Report would later describe the

38:23 encounter as the “most puzzling and  unusual case” it had ever examined.

38:28 So what exactly were these objects  that seemed capable of outrunning and

38:32 outmaneuvering military aircraft? Were they connected to the same

38:35 phenomena reported by American test pilots  and radar crews across the Cold War world?

38:41 2. X-15 pilot

38:43 Joseph Walker was flying at Mach 4 when he said  into the radio: “Two UFOs just passed overhead.”

38:48 They flew right past him, and were doing 3,400 mph  (5,471 kph), as fast as any plane in existence.

38:54 He said he got within about 200 feet (61 meters)  of them and saw they were disc-shaped. Walker

38:59 never got to speak about UFOs later in his life,  he died in a group formation accident in 1966.

39:06 But his words resonated with Major Robert  White, another X-15 pilot. He was traveling

39:11 at 314,000 feet (95,707 meters) when  he saw several objects flying nearby.

39:16 He told Time magazine, “There are  things out there. There absolutely are!”

39:20 This last one is important. 1.

39:23 In 2014, The Guardian posed a question: “Rather  than covering up the existence of aliens,

39:28 could it be that the real conspiracy has  been persuading us to believe in them?”

39:33 The article referred to what appeared to be  a CIA-linked psychological operation in which

39:37 fake classified UFO documents were deliberately  circulated to the public. The documents became

39:43 known as Majestic 12 papers – secret files  ostensibly proving top U.S. officials had

39:48 concealed evidence of alien contact for decades. Except the documents were exposed as forgeries.

39:54 Disinformation designed to inflame  UFO hysteria rather than calm it down.

39:59 The fallout destroyed UFO researcher, Paul  Bennewitz. After receiving supposedly leaked

40:04 information from Air Force intelligence sources,  he became convinced extraterrestrials were

40:09 operating on Earth. He later suffered  a severe psychological breakdown.

40:13 So for years, the files show us that  intelligence agencies had warned that the

40:17 American public was vulnerable to mass hysteria  surrounding UFOs. Yet there were allegations

40:23 that elements inside the national security  world had actively fueled those same fears.

40:28 Why? No one knows.

40:29 But some researchers point toward  the Psychological Strategy Board,

40:33 a Cold War-era body created to coordinate American  psychological operations and propaganda efforts.

40:39 Few ideas can capture the public imagination  more effectively than UFOs and little green men.

40:45 All the documents you’ve heard about  today are real. But as history shows,

40:49 facts and fiction have a habit of becoming  tangled, especially when governments, fear,

40:54 propaganda, and the unknown collide. The truth is out there, somewhere,

40:59 and it might be very human. Or, maybe, it’s not.

41:02 But if you’re looking for proof, it’s not  just buried in Pentagon files anymore.

41:06 It’s in close encounters, witnessed  up close by trained personnel who knew

41:11 exactly what should and shouldn’t  be in their skies. Find out what

41:14 they saw in “Actual Video Of US Military  Intercepting UFO’s”. Or watch this instead.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Americans Have Turned Against AI
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: Americans Have Turned Against AI
  • Video ID: 14Uc2WCSPiw
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Millions of Americans will open  ChatGPT in the next 10 minutes…

00:03 And most of them believe it's making  the world worse. Half the country uses

00:07 AI now. Yet only 16% of Americans  think it will be good for society.

00:12 It’s the lowest level of optimism any  major technology has launched with.

00:16 The people building AI call it humanity's greatest

00:18 breakthrough. The people using it describe  something closer to a hostage situation.

00:23 So how did the fastest-adopted technology of  our lifetime also become one of the most hated?

00:28 You might expect that it’s the older  generations that are pushing back on

00:31 the AI revolution. After all, every new  technology has faced resistance from

00:36 people who didn't grow up with it. But that's not what's happening.

00:39 The biggest users of AI are Americans  under 30. They use it for schoolwork,

00:44 job applications, coding, brainstorming,  and as a substitute for Google. By every

00:49 indicator, they should be AI's biggest fans. Instead, they're some of its biggest critics.

00:54 A Gallup study found the share of Gen Z who  say AI makes them feel angry climbed from

00:58 22% to 31% by early 2026. And according to Pew  Research, 40% of young Americans said it would

01:05 make the country worse than better. But this isn't just a Gen Z story.

01:09 Trust in AI is collapsing all  across the U.S. Two thirds of

01:13 people think it's being developed too  quickly. 59% don't trust the companies

01:17 building it. And most don't believe the  government can keep it under control.

01:20 Yet people keep using it. ChatGPT alone is  used by 44% of American adults, more than

01:27 double its share in 2023. That's the AI paradox.

01:31 So why does adoption keep accelerating  if confidence keeps falling?

01:34 For most people, it wasn’t really adopted.  Workplaces began implementing it in their

01:39 workflow. Schools added it to assignments. Apps  and search engines displayed it as a main feature.

01:44 People had no other choice. It was forced  upon them. AI didn’t earn their trust.

01:49 They have no other option.

01:51 The shift happened so gradually  that most people barely noticed it.

01:54 Until suddenly, it was everywhere.

01:56 The moment you open Google and search  for something, you’re hit with a block

02:00 of AI-written text answering the question  before you even reach the search results.

02:04 The company that’s supposed to help you find  information is now deciding what you see first.

02:09 And it works.

02:10 60% of Americans say they read the summaries  regularly, because there’s no way to avoid

02:15 them. The moment Google started answering  the question itself, the experience changed.

02:20 And the more the internet degraded, the less  people trusted it. In 2021, 37% of Americans said

02:26 the spread of AI worried them more than it excited  them. By 2025, that number had climbed to 50%,

02:32 even though most people hadn't been personally  affected by AI in a professional capacity.

02:37 That would soon change.

02:39 In April 2025, Tobi Lütke,  Shopify’s chief executive,

02:43 posted a memo to his staff. Before any team could  ask him for a bigger budget or another employee,

02:47 they had to prove that a machine  couldn’t do the work first. Lütke

02:51 insisted that “reflexive AI use  was the new baseline expectation”.

02:55 Shopify wasn’t the only  company going all in on AI.

02:59 Language learning platform Duolingo was next. CEO,  Luis von Ahn, told his staff the company was going

03:04 “AI-first.” It would rely on AI before hiring,  reduce the number of contractors, and weigh AI

03:10 use in performance reviews. Within a week, 148 new  courses were shipped, it was work that would take

03:17 staff years to develop. The same AI implementation  turned up at Box, at Fiverr, and other firms.

03:23 The wording barely changed. Run the software  before you ask for new hires or extra money.

03:28 Then the pushback happened.

03:29 Longtime Duolingo users filmed themselves deleting  the app in protest. Staff started asking if they

03:34 had to use AI well or just use it. Almost a year  later Luis von Ahn walked his decision back.

03:40 He acknowledged that the AI-written code was  hard to debug and the lessons weren’t reliable.

03:45 But the damage had been done.

03:47 And it was just the beginning.

03:48 The fear of AI taking jobs is real, so in the  summer of 2025, a Stanford economist named Erik

03:54 Brynjolfsson decided to look into it. His team at  the Digital Economy Lab pulled the records from

03:59 ADP, the firm that processes the payroll for  millions of American workers, and studied who

04:04 still had a job, month after month. The AI impact was real.

04:09 Just now where people expected it.

04:11 The results showed that workers aged 22 to 25  in software and customer support had dropped

04:16 about 13% since late 2022. Workers over  30 in the same roles remained stable or

04:22 actually grew. It was the people just walking  in the door that were at risk of an AI cull.

04:27 Some don’t get in the door at all.

04:29 Revelio Labs, which tracks hiring across the  economy, counts roughly 35% fewer entry-level

04:35 postings since the start of 2023. Once  employers saw what the best models could do,

04:40 many stopped graduate hiring. That freeze only  surfaced in the payroll data a year or 2 later.

04:46 Brynjolfsson’s team found that when a company  used AI to take over a task completely,

04:51 employment among younger workers fell.  When AI was used to make a person faster,

04:55 employment remained stable, and sometimes grew.

04:58 Same technology, opposite result.

05:00 Everything comes down to one decision:

05:02 does a company use AI to replace  a worker, or to back one up?

05:05 Near the bottom of the pay  scale, replacement is winning.

05:08 Salesforce froze much of its junior  hiring for a stretch and credited its

05:12 own AI for work graduates used  to do. Goldman Sachs economists

05:16 found the results. The big names  weren’t even pretending anymore.

05:19 But not every bet paid off.

05:21 Klarna, the buy-now-pay-later company, spent a  year bragging that its chatbot did the work of

05:26 hundreds of agents and that it had stopped hiring  people. They later admitted the bot gave “lower

05:32 quality” service and started hiring humans back.  But some companies didn’t see that as a reason

05:36 to slow down. They saw it as a reason to aim  lower… and the contractor was in the cross hairs.

05:42 An MIT report on AI in business found that AI  is wiping out outsourced and contract roles,

05:47 not full-time staff. In mid-2025, the  data-labeling firm Scale AI laid off 200

05:53 staff and cut ties with 500 contractors.  That same report put the share of jobs

05:57 AI can already do at roughly 3% today,  and saw it climbing over the longer run.

06:02 Graduates weren’t losing out  to people with a better resume.

06:05 They were losing out period. There was not job.

06:09 By early 2026, nearly half of employed Gen Z said  AI's risks at work now outweigh its benefits,

06:14 a jump of 11 percentage points in just one year.  And when they're handed the same piece of work,

06:20 69% overwhelmingly trust the human version over  the AI one. An entire generation now spends its

06:26 days training the technology that's replacing  the jobs they're trying to build careers in.

06:31 The lost jobs are easy enough to measure. But the resentment isn't just about money.

06:35 In July 2024, all it took was a power surge  across northern Virginia for nearly 60 data

06:40 centers to drop off the grid. Roughly 1,500  megawatts of demand vanished instantly.

06:45 Operators scrambled to get the surge under  control before it took down anything else.

06:49 For a few seconds, the densest data-center  hub in the country just wasn’t there.

06:54 Virginia holds more of these  buildings than anywhere else,

06:57 and by 2023 they were already drawing about  26% of the state’s electricity. That’s why

07:02 one voltage swing could shock the whole grid. Each of those buildings runs hot. One question

07:08 to a chatbot burns about 2.9 watt-hours,  that’s roughly 10 times a normal web search.

07:13 On its own, it’s nothing. But nobody asks just one question.

07:17 Multiply it by billions of questions a day, every  day, in warehouses that never switch off, and it

07:22 becomes 183 terawatt-hours a year. That’s about  4% of all the power the country burns. That's

07:28 already 540 kilowatt-hours running in your name  every year, whether you've ever touched a chatbot

07:34 or not. And the forecasts are only going up, as  high as 17% of the nation's electricity by 2030.

07:41 More than 40% of the power fuelling the data  centres comes from natural gas. Before the decade

07:46 is out, these buildings are set to burn more  electricity than the entire country uses to make

07:50 its steel, cement, aluminum, and chemicals… Combined.

07:54 A high-voltage line takes up to 8 years to build,  meaning a fifth of these data center projects are

07:59 about to run straight into a power shortage.  To cover the expense of these extra lines,

08:04 utilities are going to regulators to demand  more money from regular consumers. This means

08:09 your monthly expenses are going up by 2030 just to  keep the lights on at a server farm down the road.

08:15 You didn't leave your lights on or  crank up your AC, but your money

08:18 is bleeding out anyway to power the  massive cooling fans of a tech giant.

08:22 Researchers at Carnegie Mellon estimate  it could push the average American

08:26 power bill up about 8% by 2030, and in the  worst-hit parts of Virginia, north of 25%.

08:33 There simply isn’t enough  energy or money to fund it.

08:36 So, some companies got tired of waiting.

08:38 Instead of waiting years for the power  grid to catch up, they built their own

08:42 power plants beside the data centers. And  one company took that idea to the extreme.

08:47 To power Colossus, the supercomputer  training Elon Musk's Grok chatbot,

08:51 xAI deployed a fleet of gas turbines in  South Memphis.The entire site was up and

08:56 running in under 122 days, a project that  would normally take years. By the time the

09:01 Southern Environmental Law Center flew thermal  drones overhead, it counted around 35 turbines,

09:06 most of them without air permits. Just downwind sits Boxtown,

09:10 a neighborhood that has spent decades  surrounded by refineries and chemical plants.

09:14 Residents began showing up at public hearings  describing a rotten-egg smell in the air and

09:19 children wheezing through the night. Memphis  already earns an "F" for ozone pollution from

09:24 the American Lung Association, and Boxtown's  cancer risk is about 4 times the national average.

09:29 Then researchers at the University of Tennessee  analyzed satellite data for TIME and found peak

09:34 nitrogen dioxide levels near the site had jumped  roughly 79% compared with before xAI arrived.

09:41 The turbines were labelled as temporary,

09:43 a workaround that allowed them to keep running  and bypass the regulations. Lawsuits followed,

09:48 but by the time the case moved forward, the  servers had already been running for a year.

09:52 Power isn't the only resource  these data centers consume.

09:55 In Newton County, Georgia, about  an hour and a half east of Atlanta,

09:59 Beverly and Jeff Morris live 1,000 feet (305  meters) from a Meta data center. Their house

10:04 runs on a private well, which means their  drinking water comes straight out of the

10:07 ground. It worked fine for years, right up  until Meta broke ground next door in 2018.

10:13 A few months after construction began,  the water pressure slowed to a trickle,

10:17 then stopped altogether. When it eventually  came back, it was brown and murky. Beverly

10:22 Morris told the New York Times she was afraid  to drink the water coming from her own tap.

10:26 The neighboring data center uses roughly  500,000 gallons every day, nearly a tenth

10:31 of all the water Newton County pumps. County  projections show demand outpacing supply by 2030,

10:37 while residents face water bills  expected to jump 33% in just 2 years,

10:41 compared with the usual 2% increase. A Meta  funded study said the company’s operations

10:46 probably aren't to blame and has invested more  than $4.5 million in local schools and nonprofits.

10:52 Private wells like the Morrises' fall  outside the federal Safe Drinking Water Act,

10:57 so Meta didn’t break any laws. The Environmental  Protection Agency is powerless, so Meta keeps

11:02 pulling water to cool the chips. And these hubs are insatiable.

11:07 A 2023 study by UC Riverside and the University  of Texas found that training one model, GPT-3, ran

11:13 through about 5.4 million liters of fresh water…  before the public ever typed a word. The same

11:20 researchers found that a short back-and-forth,  around 100 words, consumes close to a full bottle.

11:25 One Google data center in Papillion, Nebraska,  went through about 1.5 billion liters in 2024,

11:31 more than 600 Olympic pools, and it’s one site  among thousands. That daily draw dwarfs the

11:37 one-time cost of training. Nationally, data  centers used over 60 billion liters in 2023,

11:42 and the World Resources Institute expects AI  to pass a trillion gallons a year by 2030.

11:47 In August 2025, Tucson’s city council  voted 7 to 0 to reject Project Blue,

11:53 an Amazon-linked data-center campus  that would have drained millions of

11:56 gallons of city water in the middle of a  desert. Residents had packed the chamber

12:01 for weeks under a banner that read  No Desert Data Center. For one night,

12:05 it looked like a regular city could tell a  tech giant no, and actually make it stick.

12:10 It didn’t end there.

12:11 The developer already owned land just outside  the city limits and kept building anyway. Then,

12:16 in the spring of 2026, the contractor was  caught drawing enough Tucson water to supply

12:21 5 households for a year. The city shut it  off. Mayor, Regina Romero, has been writing

12:26 ordinances to guard against the next data  center, because there’s always a next one.

12:31 Tucson wasn’t alone.

12:32 In The Dalles, Oregon, a Google plant ended up  using close to a quarter of the entire town’s

12:37 water. The company fought to keep those numbers  hidden from the public through court orders.

12:41 Newer facilities can cool with air or  closed-loop systems that use almost no

12:46 local water. Microsoft has already converted  2 Arizona sites to do exactly that. But the

12:51 biggest water users aren't the new builds,  they're the older data centers. The ones

12:55 still sucking up millions of gallons  instead of returning it to the river.

12:58 So while families shorten their showers  and wait until dark to water the lawn,

13:02 the data center down the road keeps pulling  water at full capacity, every hour, every night.

13:07 Jobs. Electricity. Water. Three separate  battles happening in different parts of

13:11 the country. But they all lead back  to the exact same business model.

13:14 In 2024 alone, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Meta  spent more than $200 billion building the data

13:20 centers behind AI, up over 60% in a single year.  Management consultancy firm McKinsey expects $5.2

13:27 trillion to be funnelled into them by 2030. That  money buys the land, the power, and the water.

13:33 But there’s one more thing it buys. Something  nobody signs off on: the writing, art,

13:38 and code scraped off the open internet  to train the models in the first place.

13:42 To the companies, that’s an investment  in the platform of the century. To the

13:46 creatives whose work fed it, it  looks different. Their work was

13:50 harvested for free, then rented  back to everyone by the month.

13:54 Not one of them was asked.  Not one of them got paid.

13:57 Publishers and authors have sued in waves arguing  their work was stolen and used to train AI without

14:02 permission. The courts still haven't decided  where the legal line is, and so far none of

14:06 it has been ruled illegal. But AI is built on  other people's writing, powered by other people's

14:12 electricity, cooled with other people's water… Then sold back to those same people as progress.

14:17 Now, Americans are starting to notice. The  companies insist the costs are temporary.

14:21 Google and Microsoft both promise they'll return  more water than they use by 2030 and keep shifting

14:27 to cleaner energy. But if you've already lost  your job, your power bill just went up, or your

14:32 town's water is running low, a promise four years  from now doesn't feel like much of an answer.

14:36 Between May 2024 and March 2025, that anger  blocked or delayed about $64 billion in

14:43 data-center projects nationwide, according  to Data Center Watch. In Virginia alone,

14:48 42 separate groups were working  to slow or stop new ones.

14:51 What nobody agrees on is what to do about it.

14:54 No one is demanding an outright  ban. No one is cheering it on.

14:58 There’s just a country caught between  needing the tool and resenting it.

15:02 Most of these fights end the same  way. A council denies the water,

15:05 the way Tucson did. The county next door sells  the land. A state commission signs off on the

15:11 power. The building goes up anyway, trading its  thirst for water for a heavier pull on the grid.

15:16 Residents keep learning the same lesson: the  project can almost always route around them.

15:20 This was never about whether AI would  arrive.That was inevitable. It was about

15:24 whether anyone still had the power to stop it. By the time we started asking that question,

15:29 the answer was already no. It’s not just ordinary Americans

15:32 who are losing faith in AI. The people building  it are too. Watch Why AI Researchers Are Quitting

15:38 and Panicking on the Way Out to find out why the  industry is collapsing. Or click on this video.

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 A man is sitting in front of his computer mindlessly scrolling down his Facebook news

00:04 feed.

00:05 He’s been feeling a bit insecure since losing his job and getting dumped by his girlfriend,

00:09 so it’s his good fortune on this particular dark day that he comes across one of those

00:13 bunkum posts that say, “If you can correctly answer these questions you have a genius-level

00:19 IQ.”

00:20 Lo and behold, like his friends before him, he scores 10 out of 10 and is rewarded with

00:24 the knowledge that he’s a genius with an IQ of over 160.

00:28 He seems blissfully unaware that most 10-year olds could get those questions right.

00:32 Nonetheless, he’s not too bright and so he shares his results, which is exactly what

00:36 the creators of the post wanted him to do.

00:39 Poor guy, if he had a higher IQ, he might be savvier to the manipulative guff that does

00:43 the rounds on social media.

00:44 Ok, so this guy knew the capital city of France and he understood that the chemical formula

00:49 for water is H2O.

00:51 He even knew that Earth was the third rock from the sun.

00:55 We hate to burst his bubble here, but that doesn’t mean he has a high IQ, far from

00:58 it.

00:59 You can’t base IQ on the ability to answer a handful of easy general knowledge questions.

01:03 There are even games of “spot of the difference” surfacing on Facebook these days, stating

01:07 that if you can spot the 10 differences you have an IQ of 180 or over.

01:13 Before we tell you how you can easily improve your own IQ, you need to know a few things

01:17 about what IQ actually means.

01:20 Its full name is intelligence quotient.

01:22 Such standardized tests have been around since the late 19th century, with their purpose

01:26 being to help judge a person’s intelligence.

01:29 Sometimes the tests were given to see if a person’s background, often a child, affects

01:33 their intelligence.

01:34 For example, does poverty affect IQ, or does bloodline make a difference?

01:38 During the First World War, the American Army gave new recruits such intelligence tests

01:42 so it could try and judge what a person could or couldn’t do.

01:45 It still does that now.

01:47 Later, industry and education started using such tests.

01:50 There are lots of different IQ tests, but if you’ve ever taken one that has a vast

01:54 number of questions and gives you a headache, you’ll know that to get a lot of questions

01:58 right you’ll need to be good at a few things.

02:01 Those are usually arithmetic, abstract reasoning, logic, vocabulary, and spatial reasoning.

02:06 Other tests focus more on memory.

02:08 The average IQ is around 100.

02:10 If you score over 145, you are in the top 0.1 percentile.

02:15 If you get below 70 you are in the bottom 2.1 percentile.

02:17 We shouldn’t have to say it, but if you can spot a missing cat paw on a sketch it

02:22 has no bearing whatsoever on your IQ.

02:24 In fact, if you fell for that test it would likely mean that your reasoning faculties

02:28 are not top-notch.

02:29 It’s not easy scoring well past 100.

02:32 Singapore citizens have the highest average IQ in the world at 108.

02:36 China is 105.

02:37 Switzerland is the highest European nation at an average of 102.

02:41 Canada is the highest in the Americas at an average of 99.

02:44 The U.S. average is 98.

02:46 The UK average is 100.

02:48 Brazil is just 87.

02:49 India, 81.

02:50 South Africa, 77.

02:52 Don’t fear if you did a test and were below average, because between 85 and 115 is considered

02:58 in the normal range.

02:59 There are different kinds of intelligence, too.

03:01 No doubt a gifted computer programmer would score high in a general IQ test, but someone

03:06 who’d grown up farming in a hill tribe in South East Asia would likely score low.

03:10 Ask that programmer to survive up in those hills and for all his intelligence, he’d

03:14 likely fail.

03:15 All the same, if that farmer had an IQ higher than his peers he might be faster than them

03:20 deducing tricky problems on the farm.

03:22 You might have an average IQ and still write a novel or a historical piece of nonfiction

03:26 that will be read for centuries to come because your insights were outstanding.

03:30 There are also plenty of people with genius-level IQs who struggle to get a job.

03:34 Still, a high IQ overall is an indicator of success.

03:38 Although social class is way more important when it comes to making it in life.

03:42 Success also often depends on the environment you grew up in.

03:45 You might only have an average intelligence but were schooled at Eton, where British political

03:49 leaders and other ruthless capitalists often cut their teeth.

03:52 You could have a high intelligence in Britain but were schooled at a place nicknamed the

03:56 “Zoo” and grew up with selfish parents that at best acknowledged your existence when

04:00 feeding you your meager daily ration of baked beans on toast.

04:03 But if you had parents that instilled in you self-confidence, perseverance, self-awareness,

04:08 open-mindedness, creative thinking, critical thinking- well, that could work out well,

04:12 even if you are poor.

04:13 There are so many factors when it comes to success, including having lady luck on your

04:17 side, but in general, a high IQ is better than a low IQ when it comes to getting by

04:22 in the world of work.

04:23 But again, we must point out the environment you grew up in.

04:26 Poverty and trauma is a serious issue that should never be overlooked when considering

04:31 intelligence.

04:32 For centuries the wealthy folks in the world have looked down on the poor for their alleged

04:35 low intelligence, calling them names like white trash.

04:38 It’s not as if those rich folks were born with big brains.

04:41 Their success was simply down to where they were born, in some cases at least.

04:45 Before we get to the teaching part of the video, let’s look at some examples of high

04:48 IQs in the real world.

04:51 You have an American man named Richard Rosner.

04:53 His IQ is off the charts.

04:55 He’s scored 190 on some tests.

04:57 He’s had some strange jobs, too, at one time working as a nude model and another time

05:01 working as a bouncer.

05:02 Then there’s the Greek man, Evangelos Katsioulis.

05:05 With an IQ of around 198, he’s said to have one of the highest IQs in the entire world.

05:10 He currently works as a psychiatrist in Greece and is also the founder of the World Intelligence

05:15 Network.

05:16 The South Korean/Japanese man named Sho Yano started college at the young age of nine and

05:20 had a Ph.D. by the time he was 21.

05:22 His IQ is an astounding 200.

05:24 This former child genius now works in child neurology.

05:28 The Guinness Book of Records once had an American woman named Marilyn vos Savant as having the

05:33 highest IQ.

05:34 She once scored 228 on an IQ test, although some people have questioned the formula used

05:39 on that test.

05:40 Still, she’s a genius, there’s no doubt about that.

05:42 These people seemed to do well in life, giving strength to the theory that high IQ leads

05:47 to success.

05:48 But what about the American guy named Nathan Leopold?

05:51 He had an IQ of around 200, but he ended up in prison for committing murder.

05:55 He thought he was so darn clever that he could commit the crime of the century and get away

05:59 with it, but he was wrong.

06:00 At a young age, he was obsessed with German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche’s theory

06:04 of the “Superman”.

06:05 It seems a lot of people who take this route end up in dark places, including Mr. Hitler.

06:10 Perhaps humility is a sign of intelligence, too.

06:12 By the way, Nietzsche hated nationalism and he certainly was not an anti-Semite, but some

06:17 people don’t have the intelligence to see that.

06:20 Ok, so some of you might already know you have a high IQ because you’ve taken the

06:24 tests or you were dubbed a child genius after getting your physics degree at age 12.

06:28 But, we are guessing that most of you watching this are average when it comes to IQ.

06:33 The question is, would it help you to have a higher IQ?

06:35 The answer to that depends on what you want in life and what you think a high IQ will

06:39 get you.

06:40 We had a look at a study that was undertaken to try and compare certain IQs with various

06:44 jobs.

06:45 That doesn’t mean that all workers of one job will have an IQ close to other workers

06:48 in that job, but some occupations on average seem to be filled with higher or lower IQs.

06:53 Janitors, for instance, were at the lower end of the scale with an average IQ spanning

06:57 from about 75 to 110.

06:59 Auto mechanics ranged from 75 to 118.

07:02 High school teachers from 92 to 126, and at the top of the scale were college professors.

07:07 They scored on average from the high 90s to over 130.

07:11 Physicians scored ever higher, from 106 to over 130.

07:14 What this means of course is you can be an auto mechanic or a janitor with the same IQ

07:18 as a college professor, but in general, if you work as a professor or a doctor, your

07:22 IQ will likely be higher than that of a janitor.

07:24 From what we can see, a lot of the high-paying jobs employ people with higher IQs.

07:28 If you want a higher paying job, then, maybe improving your IQ couldn’t hurt.

07:32 You’d think that just by taking lots and lots of tests, you’d be able to improve

07:35 your IQ score.

07:36 That’s actually debatable.

07:37 It might work, it might not.

07:39 There’s a saying that goes, “The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and

07:43 over again, but expecting different results.”

07:45 This maxim is often attributed to Albert Einstein, but he never said it.

07:49 The saying is kind of true, though.

07:51 If you want to improve at something it’s better to explore different avenues as to

07:54 the problem you want to solve, in this case, your IQ score.

07:58 One thing that has seen positive results in doing just that is working on your memory.

08:02 According to studies we found, a better memory can help you to attain a higher standard of

08:06 something called, “fluid intelligence.”

08:08 You need good fluid intelligence to attain a high IQ score because it relates to solving

08:12 problems on your feet, meaning you don’t have the key to the problem but you can figure

08:16 it out.

08:17 That’s what a real IQ test will have in wait for you; lots of tricky problems you

08:21 haven’t seen before.

08:22 During one study, participants all had to take tests relating to their fluid intelligence.

08:26 But, some people took the tests without any memory training and others had some memory

08:30 training.

08:31 By memory, we mean, working memory, which refers to the memory you use for temporary

08:35 tasks.

08:36 If we say the words, sheep, ghost, Steve Jobs, Ukraine, blue, incredible, and we tell you

08:41 to repeat that to us in 10 seconds, you’re using your working memory.

08:45 In the tests in the study, each time someone was asked to remember something, there was

08:49 never any pattern.

08:50 Each test was different, making the person think on their feet.

08:53 There was no key to the puzzle.

08:54 Each time they had to adapt to a different test.

08:56 This in fact was training their brains, and as you know, being able to think on your feet

09:00 is good for IQ tests.

09:02 Once those people were good at solving the memory questions, they were asked to take

09:05 the fluid memory test, as were the people in the study that hadn’t done the memory

09:09 tests.

09:10 What was the outcome?

09:11 The researchers said that those who’d taken the memory tests showed a striking difference

09:15 in how they fared with the fluid intelligence test.

09:18 Their conclusion was: “Our findings are of general significance

09:20 because they provide evidence for enhancement of fluid intelligence by cognitive training

09:25 different from training the test itself.”

09:27 By different, they mean you don’t have to train at an IQ test to necessarily become

09:32 better at it.

09:33 You can just improve your working memory.

09:34 To do this yourself, just go online and find working memory tests.

09:38 There are tons of them.

09:39 The researchers said their work was remarkable because it has always been thought that fluid

09:44 intelligence wasn’t something that could be improved.

09:46 It was previously thought to be innate, unchangeable, but it isn’t.

09:50 We suggest you take an IQ test before you do this and see what score you get.

09:54 Then do the memory tests and do them until you see some improvement.

09:57 After that, take the IQ test again, or one that is similar, and then see what score you

10:01 get.

10:02 If the researchers are right, you might just see an improvement.

10:05 The brain’s elastic, or what people often say, a muscle, so don’t go thinking you

10:09 can’t improve.

10:10 You can.

10:11 So, even though you might think you need to be going online and doing lots of IQ tests,

10:15 it’s working memory improvement that will get you ahead.

10:18 If you’ve done IQ tests, you’ll also know a lot of questions relate to spatial awareness.

10:23 That can be putting shapes in the right place.

10:25 Believe it or not, just by doing jigsaw puzzles you can improve upon this.

10:29 You can also play games where objects are put in a certain place, then removed, and

10:33 subsequently, the person has to tell someone to put the object back in the right place

10:37 with words.

10:38 Like the star of the Netflix series, “The Queen’s Gambit”, you could also imagine

10:41 playing chess in your head.

10:43 This will train what’s called, “Spatial Cognition.”

10:45 There are other games you can play that might help you to solve problems on an IQ test,

10:49 as long as they are problem-solving games.

10:52 Take Scrabble for instance, in that game you not only have to create the highest-scoring

10:56 words but you have to place a word in a sometimes-complex grid of letters.

11:00 You use something called your executive functions when you play games like Scrabble or similar

11:05 games.

11:06 These functions are what you need to solve challenges that are sometimes not anticipated.

11:09 Again, you have to think on your feet, and if you play such games, you can improve your

11:13 fluid intelligence.

11:15 Many games that ask you to think outside the box to attain a good score could help you

11:19 improve your IQ score.

11:20 When doing these tests, you can’t rely on old habits, and you can’t just be impulsive,

11:25 you need this ability to look at things from all angles.

11:28 We found another study relating to the improvement of fluid intelligence, called, “Multi-modal

11:32 fitness and cognitive training to enhance fluid intelligence.”

11:36 That’s a bit of a mouthful.

11:37 In layman's terms, it means doing different stuff to train your brain to solve problems

11:41 you might not have seen before.

11:43 They took 424 healthy adults and split them up.

11:47 Some did just fitness training.

11:48 Others did fitness along with cognitive training.

11:51 Others did those two but with some added meditation.

11:54 The last group did nothing.

11:55 The long and short of this was the people that did the training were better at visuospatial

11:59 reasoning, which means moving objects around and knowing where things should go.

12:03 Those people then performed better on fluid intelligence tests.

12:07 So, like those study participants, you could do the same.

12:10 Try and keep fit; play some cognitive games online, and maybe even practice some mindfulness.

12:14 There’s no solid proof that things like learning a second language or reading books

12:18 will help you improve your IQ score, but learning a new language does make you think about how

12:23 language is constructed.

12:25 This might help you with the verbal reasoning part of the test.

12:27 As for reading books, well, you should try it.

12:29 It’s massively underrated, and the more you read, the less likely you’ll end up

12:33 playing spot the difference so you can bask in the warmth of having a completely unsubstantiated

12:38 high IQ score.

12:39 We’ll finish with a real quote from Einstein, something very relevant to you getting a better

12:43 brain, “One should not pursue goals that are easily achieved.

12:47 One must develop an instinct for what one can just barely achieve through one's greatest

12:51 efforts.”

12:52 Now you need to watch, “How To ACTUALLY Learn Anything (The Feynman Technique)”.

12:56 Or, have a look at, “Scientifically Proven Best Ways to Study.”

00:00 Hour 0 April 25, 1986.

00:03 Chernobyl power plant, located about 2 miles (3km)  from Pripyat, a small town in northern Ukraine.

00:09 At just before midnight the engineer-mechanic  Alexander Yuvchenko clocks on for his nightshift,

00:14 a shift that will go down on record as one of  the most controversial few hours in history,

00:18 creating a panic that will take over the planet.

00:21 The mood among the workers is joyful.  It’s a beautiful night after a sunny day

00:24 and the May Day holiday is just around the corner. At home sleeping in his small apartment is his

00:29 wife Natasha, and his two-year-old son, Kirill.  The family is well taken of, and although Natasha

00:35 has some misgivings about the safety of nuclear  power, only recently those fears were diminished

00:39 when she heard a Soviet official on TV saying  nuclear meltdowns just don’t happen, or, if they

00:44 do, he said there might be one every 10,000 years. In just over 24 hours from now, people who Natasha

00:50 knows will be out in the street looking into the  sky at a dazzling laser beam shooting up to the

00:54 stars. At exactly the same time, her husband  will be in a party of four men who are exposed

00:59 to deadly amounts of radiation after being sent  to assess damage at Chernobyl’s reactor number 4.

01:05 Three of them will die in excruciating pain,  their bodies destroyed from within. Alexander

01:10 will survive because he doesn’t enter the reactor  hall but only holds a door for his friends.

01:15 The arm and leg and shoulder that he uses  will later turn black. He’ll tell Natasha

01:19 with what he thinks could be his dying  words that he’s been turned into a mutant.

01:23 Alexander will see things the communist government  will want to keep secret. Death by radiation is

25:14 His eyes, nose, and most of his face  hurts, but then after a couple of days,

25:18 he and the other men all start to  feel pretty good. As you already know,

25:21 this doesn’t mean they are good. One day he’s in pain again and he

25:25 pulls back his bedsheets to see massive ulcers  and necrotic skin on his shoulder, hip, and calf,

25:30 all the bits exposed when he held that door open.  He is turning black and feels like he’s a monster,

25:35 telling himself he looks like  some kind of radioactive mutant.

25:38 Luckily for him, his body accepts the skin grafts,  and blood transfusions and bone marrow transplants

25:43 do the rest. His arm is in really bad shape and  will stay in bandages for years. In the hospital,

25:48 ever so often someone walks in the room and  tells him another of his colleagues is dead.

25:53 One of them first goes blind, and then the  infection in his blood finishes him off. For

25:57 two months, Alexander lies in bed close to death  thinking about when it will be his turn to die.

26:03 He will later be awarded medals for  his bravery, but once he’s better,

26:06 he’ll keep his Chernobyl experience mostly to  himself. For many years to come, people in this

26:10 part of the world will cross the street if they  see a Chernobyl survivor walking toward them.

26:15 These people, not educated about  radiation, wrongly assume the

26:18 survivors are still contaminated. This  fear has devesting consequences.

26:27 Chernobyl, in fact, will make much of the world  wrongly over-estimate the dangers of producing

26:31 nuclear power. This will go on for decades and  is still a factor in some people’s minds today

26:36 when they think about nuclear energy. What or who is to blame for the disaster

26:40 is the question that the Soviets and  many other countries will be asking

26:43 for some time to come. The investigations at the  start will mostly blame human error rather than

26:49 technical error and pick out a few names to  shame and send to prison, such as Mr. Dyatlo.

26:54 Sure, he messed up a bit, as did others at  the plant, but the fault lies in many people,

26:59 going right up to the top brass  in the Communist government.

27:02 1 year later It's now 1987 and Legasov is very

27:07 ill from radiation poisoning and is in and out of  hospital all the time. He knows he’s going to die,

27:12 so he records himself on tape telling the whole  truth about how and why this disaster happened.

27:17 Part of the tape goes: “The Chernobyl disaster is an apotheosis,

27:21 the pinnacle of all the mismanagement that has  been carried out for decades in our country…

27:25 When one looks at the chain of events, why  someone acted in this way and another in that way,

27:29 and so on, it is impossible to point to  a single culprit, an initiator of all

27:33 the unpleasant events that led to the crime.  Because it is a chain that links to itself.”

27:38 He finishes off by warning that as he speaks,  the Soviet Union does not have safe nuclear power

27:43 plants, not because the production of energy is  dangerous in itself, but because too many mistakes

27:48 have been made and too many corners have been cut.  He says when you can’t hold the state accountable

27:53 then the state is broken. 2 years later

27:56 In 1988, the day after the second anniversary of  the accident, he is found dead in his apartment.

28:01 Shcherbina, who had become a close friend,  said, “Valery was too great, I loved him

28:05 more than all the people I knew, he gave all of  himself to work, to Chernobyl. He burnt out.”

28:10 Of the 237 people that suffered acute radiation  sickness, 31 died within a couple of months. The

28:16 amount of people that died from cancer due  to radiation poisoning reached around 4,000,

28:21 and many more survived cancer. Still,  the health effects of the disaster

28:24 have been argued about for many years. As for reactor 4, it was covered with a

28:28 giant steel and concrete building called  the sarcophagus containment structure.

28:33 An Exclusion Zone was formed, covering an  area of around 1,000 sq. miles (2,600 km2) of

28:37 Ukraine. Over the years, the town of  Pripyat became home to life again,

28:41 but of the wild animal kind, not the human kind.

28:44 20 years later As for all those pet

28:46 dogs and cats, they were killed by special  teams not long after the disaster became

28:50 worldwide knowledge. Some may have survived,  though, because in the years to come, dogs in

28:55 the town will be seen alongside wolves, brown  bears, dear, badgers, lynx, bison, and moose.

29:01 In 20,000 years, the town of Pripyat might be  safe again for humans to go and live there.

29:06 You can visit now, but experts recommend you  don’t eat the wild mushrooms or other plants

29:10 you can find there, and wear something you’re  prepared to throw away later. Radiation sucks,

29:14 but we can’t live without it. Now you need to watch,

29:17 “What If There Was A Nuclear War Between  the US and Russia?” Or, have a look at,

29:21 “Man Receives Highest Dose of Nuclear  Radiation - This Is What Happened To Him.”

  • Video ID: 4EPW0Ht7XCc

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Wall Street is panicking. And the problem started 6,000 miles away.

00:04 In the summer of 2026, more than 320,000 South  Korean investors saw their accounts liquidated

00:10 in a matter of hours. Why?

00:13 Because the world's most profitable company  just did something it hasn't done in 20 years.

00:17 Alphabet, Google’s parent company, burned  $5.9 billion in a single quarter. All on AI.

00:24 Big Tech's AI obsession isn't an unlimitless cash  machine… it's a value-destroying black hole. When

00:31 Seoul stops trading, New York is next. And you’ll be in the fallout.

00:35 For the last 5 years, the US Nasdaq 100 and  the South Korean stock market, the Kospi,

00:41 barely paid attention to each other.  The 60 day rolling correlation average,

00:45 how they move over time, stood at 0.16. It  was pretty much background noise. By mid-2026,

00:52 it exploded, climbing to between 0.46 and 0.50. In  other words, the two markets are moving together.

01:00 And it all comes down to one thing. AI.

01:03 South Korea builds the hardware that  keeps the US tech bubble intact.

01:07 Every night, while Wall Street sleeps, companies  like Samsung and SK Hynix open for trading. Their

01:12 earnings, their guidance, their panic, all of it  lands on trading screens of American investors

01:18 when they finish their coffee. When U.S. traders  see major dips in Asia’s hardware supplies,

01:23 it dictates their own behavior. If those  companies are in trouble, it sets off a

01:27 chain reaction that impacts companies like  Alphabet, who are trying - and failing - to

01:32 reap the benefits of AI infrastructure projects. Korea’s stock exchange is a monitor for the

01:36 health of the entire AI sector. And that monitor just flatlined.

01:41 Behind it all, is Google’s $5.9 billion cash burn. It exposes a circular illusion. A closed loop

01:48 where tech giants manufacture their own  demand. Nvidia makes the physical chips

01:52 that power nearly every major AI system on  the planet. In 2025, Nvidia invested $100

01:58 billion into OpenAI. OpenAI used a large  chunk of that money to buy Nvidia’s chips.

02:04 The cash goes out, and the  cash comes right back in.

02:07 Nvidia’s revenue looks strong. OpenAI looks  well-capitalized. Valuations go up. But the

02:13 closed loop means they don't even need paying  customers to make the balance sheet look good.

02:18 That’s the important part for  investors and shareholders.

02:21 They see cash inflow and outflow, and they see  confidence in AI systems, making them more likely

02:26 to invest their own money into similar companies.  That same problem isn’t solely in investment, but

02:32 in the timing of the returns. Unlike “traditional”  investments where people would expect to see

02:37 returns in a year or 2, many AI investors believe  that the real payoff is 3 or even 5 years away.

02:44 That “hype” leads to the second part  of why AI investment is so rampant.

02:48 FOMO. Investors want to get their foot in

02:51 the door early. If they don’t, someone else ends  up reaping the rewards. And that can be millions.

02:56 Nvidia isn’t alone in running this playbook.  Microsoft poured billions into OpenAI,

03:01 and that money flowed straight back to Microsoft  in the form of cloud computing contracts. It’s

03:06 the same loop under different branding. But Google’s cash burn is what happens when

03:10 a company tries to compete in that environment  without relying on circular deals. They try to

03:15 absorb the cost of either building infrastructure  or getting the necessary server load. Alphabet

03:20 managed to spend $44.9 billion in just three  months. The entire premise was that it was

03:26 banking on its own sustained growth to cover it. It was a record quarter for Alphabet. Revenue

03:31 hit $119.8 billion, up 24%. Operating income  climbed 30%. So Google took those profits and

03:39 chose to burn billions in cash. The alternative is  losing the AI race to Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon,

03:45 who are all on their own AI spending spree. It’s not just one company making a gamble on AI.

03:51 Every major player in the AI race is  using some kind of cover-up to spend

03:55 more but report that it’s spending less. If  it pays off, then it’s hailed as a perfect

04:00 strategy. A calculated gamble that came in. But  while all that cash was disappearing into data

04:05 centers, a second story was unfolding. And it made things in Korea much worse.

04:10 A report surfaced that a homegrown  Chinese company, based in Shanghai,

04:14 was building its own deep ultraviolet  lithography machines. The very equipment

04:18 used to manufacture advanced semiconductors. According to the report, the company is planning

04:23 to build 5 of these machines in 2026 and 20  more the following year. Most of the components

04:28 are sourced domestically, with only a handful of  parts still coming from Japan. 2 weeks later, the

04:33 company was named: Shanghai Aishengna Electronic  Technology Group, also known as Aishengna. And

04:39 it turned out to be majority state-owned. The news sent shockwaves through the markets.

04:44 The existing manufacturing was almost monopolized  by ASML, based in the Netherlands. It’s the

04:49 dominant supplier of both deep ultraviolet,  or DUV, and extreme ultraviolet, or EUV,

04:55 lithography machines. These are tools that  actually etch circuits onto chips at a scale

05:00 measured in nanometers. Out of the two, DUV  is considered less technologically impressive,

05:05 but it still delivers results. But ASML has been barred from

05:09 selling its most advanced EUV systems to  China. Even if Aishengna makes the less

05:13 advanced version domestically, it means China  is suddenly free from the imposed export ban

05:18 that kept its huge industrial potential in check. When the report of the Aishengna's existence went

05:23 out, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix share prices  went down by more than 10% in a single session.

05:29 Tokyo Electron and TSMC dropped alongside them. The fear wasn’t abstract.

05:34 For years, the assumption was that IP  restrictions and export controls kept

05:38 China years behind on the equipment needed to  make advanced chips. Analysts estimated that

05:43 gap at 7 to 10 years. But the market immediately  reacted to the possibility that China might close

05:48 that gap much faster than expected. But there’s another side to this.

05:52 One that has executives worrying. For years, Chinese firms have offered

05:56 lucrative signing bonuses to entice engineers  away from Samsung and other Korean chipmakers.

06:01 They have been importing decades of institutional  knowledge one hire at a time. Lee Byung-chul,

06:06 a Sejong Institute research fellow, has stated  that Samsung and SK Hynix DRAM technology has

06:12 already been leaked to China. He also believes  that a separate attempt to leak HBM packaging

06:17 technology was caught before it got out. That’s only half of the problem

06:21 A civil war is erupting in  South Korea’s tech industry.

06:24 Samsung is watching its chip engineers - the  brains behind the hardware - walk out the front

06:29 door to join SK Hynix. The insane AI profits  have been weaponized with eye-watering bonus

06:34 packages of up to $500,000 being offered to  poach employees. The company that’s supposed

06:40 to be defending Korea’s semiconductor edge  against China is completely helpless as its

06:45 own talent signs up with a domestic rival. It’s not illegal and it isn’t new.

06:50 Corporate espionage, a talent war, and a Chinese  domestic lithography program are now threatening

06:55 South Korea’s AI industry. And the global AI  market relies on a country with no backup plan.

07:01 If cheap Chinese alternatives start chipping away  at this monopoly, the entire financial foundation

07:05 built by American AI giants collapses. But China isn’t stopping there.

07:10 It has another option. It can flood the  global market with cheap chips to crush

07:15 South Korea. Or, it can ban chip exports  entirely, fund their own AI industry,

07:20 and steal a market of over a billion people. For an industry running on pure speculation,

07:25 that’s a massive problem. Because AI isn’t a finished product.

07:29 Back in 2023, Alphabet’s chairman John Hennessy  told Reuters that a single exchange with a

07:34 large language model costs 10 times more than a  traditional search. When the numbers were run,

07:39 the added cost of AI searches could run to $6  billion a year. Google says those per-query costs

07:45 have fallen sharply since, as much as 33 times  less, as hardware and models get more efficient.

07:51 But this just leads to another problem. Reduced costs mean that the product

07:55 gets used more often. That means burning through

07:58 more resources. It’s an example of Jevons  paradox: as technology becomes more efficient,

08:03 we don't save resources, we just use them more. In 2025, Google’s own environmental report

08:09 admitted its emissions had surged by 50%  compared to 2019, before the AI trend started.

08:15 Tech giants are burning the world to  build a product that has no clear purpose.

08:20 According to a S&P Global Market Intelligence  survey, 42% of companies abandoned most of their

08:25 AI initiatives in 2025. That’s more than double  the 17% recorded the year before. On average,

08:31 organizations scrapped nearly half of their AI  proof-of-concept projects before the projects ever

08:36 reached production. Budgets got approved. Pilots  got built. Demos got applause in the boardroom.

08:42 Then… nothing shipped. This pattern has a precedent: IBM.

08:47 IBM spent years and billions of dollars  building Watson Health into what was supposed

08:52 to be a revolution in AI-powered medicine. It was  supposed to read scans faster than radiologists,

08:57 and cross-reference treatment options. Instead,  the project was sold off in pieces in 2022 before

09:03 mainstream AI LLMs grabbed the public’s attention. Watson Health failed because, despite having solid

09:09 results in testing, no company could see how it  would make them money. IBM also mandated that

09:14 any prospective buyer abandon its existing  tech stack and adopt Watson’s, essentially

09:19 pigeonholing themselves for one solution. The trillion dollar valuations are all resting

09:24 on a lie. The uncontrollable growth is based  on investments leading to more investments.

09:28 It’s a corporate carousel. So who actually eats the

09:32 loss when the leverage begins to unravel? Remember those Korean retail investors and

09:36 those 360,000 liquidated accounts? Well, 62% of  them belonged to people under 35. These were young

09:43 people who borrowed money because the market had  been rising in a way that felt less like investing

09:48 and more like a game everyone was winning. When  the leverage snapped back, it snapped back on

09:53 people with the least capacity to absorb it. Some  of them are now left owing brokers more money than

09:58 the positions were ever worth. This affects America too.

10:01 A large share of ordinary retirement savings,  the kind sitting in index funds and 401(k)s,

10:06 is concentrated in the same AI-heavy companies  burning cash at record rates. When you contribute

10:12 to a retirement account without picking  individual stocks, a portion of that money

10:16 is flowing into the AI ambitions of a small  group of companies, whether you like it or not.

10:20 Passive investing was supposed to be the safe,  boring choice after the dot-com crash. The 2008

10:26 housing crash taught a generation not to gamble  on individual names. Instead, the index itself

10:32 became the concentrated bet. Then there are pension funds.

10:35 Public-sector retirement systems – the  accounts backing teachers, municipal workers,

10:39 and union pensioners – have been increasing their  exposure to the same AI-concentrated indices.

10:44 These are some of the most consequential and least  visible fault lines sitting inside this entire

10:50 trade. The upside from AI spending, if it ever  fully materializes, gets captured by the companies

10:56 making the bets and the executives holding the  stock options. If the bet goes wrong instead,

11:01 the losses land on people who never had a say in  the decision and can least afford to take the hit.

11:07 That’s the part that gets ignored  every time this story gets told in

11:10 terms of stock tickers and index points. A crash isn’t just numbers on a screen.

11:15 It’s a transfer of risk. One  passed from the people who chose

11:18 to take it, to the people who didn’t. The worst part? It’s not the first time.

11:23 In August 2024, Japan’s Nikkei and Topix indexes  plunged more than 12% in a single session,

11:30 the steepest one-day drop since 1987. The  trigger was a surprise rate hike from the

11:35 Bank of Japan that sent the yen surging. It forced  a violent unwind of the so-called “carry trade,”

11:41 where investors had been borrowing cheap  yen to fund bets on assets like American

11:45 tech stocks. When the yen strengthened, those  investors had to sell to cover their positions,

11:50 which pushed the yen higher still, triggering  more forced selling. On the same day,

11:54 Korea’s Kospi dropped more than  8% and briefly halted trading.

11:58 Go back further, 25 years to the dot-com  bubble, the parallel gets sharper.

12:03 At the peak of that boom, the top 20 companies  in the S&P 500 made up 38% of the index’s total

12:09 value. In the 5 years before the crash, the Nasdaq  had climbed 572%, pulling in investors who’d never

12:16 bought a stock before. When the crash came,  the Nasdaq fell 78% over the space of 2 years,

12:22 wiping out more than $5 trillion in market value.  It didn’t reclaim its old high for 15 years.

12:28 Today, the top 20 companies in the S&P 500 account  for more than half the index’s total value,

12:34 with roughly 10 of them tied directly to AI  and semiconductors. The reasoning investors

12:39 give for holding on sounds almost identical  to 2000. There are no meaningful earnings yet,

12:44 but there’s untapped potential in AI. And the  companies investing in them are big on FOMO.

12:50 There is one big difference this time. During the dot-com crash, the infrastructure

12:54 that got built, the fiber-optic cable  laid by companies that went bankrupt,

12:59 didn’t disappear. Cheap, abandoned fiber ended  up carrying the internet traffic of the next 2

13:04 decades. Someone paid pennies on the dollar for  that fiber and built real businesses on top of it.

13:09 But AI infrastructure doesn’t  leave that kind of gift behind.

13:12 The chips inside these data centers physically  degrade within 1 to 3 years, even losing most

13:17 of their economic value the moment the next  generation of hardware ships. After 3 years,

13:22 a data center is full of outdated chips and has  ruined the local environment by soaking up water,

13:27 emitting noise and pollution, and devastating the  local real-estate market. If the AI bet doesn’t

13:32 pay off, that data center is as good as scrap. The AI-era doesn’t leave a legacy. It ends with

13:38 sky high debt, and a pile of useless  tech that no one will want in 5 years.

13:43 Put these two stories side by  side, and it gets uncomfortable.

13:46 In 2024, we saw how quickly a currency move on  the other side of the world can force a same-day,

13:51 double-digit selloff in Seoul. The year 2000  showed what happens when an entire market

13:56 convinces itself that potential is the same thing  as profit, right up until the moment it isn’t.

14:01 2026’s crash carries pieces of the leverage and  the speed of 2024 while having the concentration

14:07 and the mispriced potential of 2000. And this  time it’s unfolding when the two markets most

14:12 linked to it, Korea’s chipmakers and America’s  AI giants, are more tightly bound together

14:17 than at any point in the last 5 years. The question that actually matters isn’t

14:22 whether this ends. Bubbles always end.

14:25 The question is who’s still standing when the  leverage finally runs out of places to hide,

14:29 and who gets handed the bill  they never agreed to pay.

14:32 And China might be ready to pick up the pieces.  To learn more, watch “What China Understands About

14:38 AI That the US Doesn’t” to see how it’s ready to  shake up the tech sector. Or click on this video.

00:04 So let's look a little more closely

00:06 at aperture settings, which in fact is

00:08 a discussion on, really, what we call depth of field.

00:12 Depth of field is about what is in focus

00:15 and what is not in focus in your picture.

00:18 Your aperture setting on your lens

00:21 sets the size of your aperture.

00:24 Or maybe it's easier to think of it as a hole.

00:27 The size of that hole determines how much of your image

00:31 is in focus.

00:33 When you set your lens to the largest aperture

00:36 that your lens offers, we say that your lens is wide open.

00:40 And in that wide open setting is what

00:44 you see in your view finder.

00:46 If you want to see what is in focus through your viewfinder,

00:50 that is, if you set your aperture, let's say, at F/32,

00:54 you'll have to press the 'Preview' button

00:56 to see what will be in focus.

00:58 By pressing the 'Preview', the aperture will close down

01:02 to your chosen F-Stop, and you'll see a darkened image

01:05 in your viewfinder.

01:07 It's another reason why I use the software.

01:09 Remember, in the software's Live View,

01:12 we see the image with the chosen aperture on the screen much

01:17 easier than seeing a darkened image

01:19 and trying to figure out what's in focus.

01:22 There's no need to press a 'Preview'

01:23 button when you use software.

01:26 So in our situation, two eight is the largest aperture

01:30 in this particular 105 lens.

01:33 We call it F-stop 2.8 , or F / 2.8 .

01:37 Notice that the number is actually written as F over 2.8

01:42 .

01:43 When we set the diaphragm to those numbers written

01:46 on the lens, the numbers in fact represent fractions

01:50 and for that reason F over two eight

01:53 is larger in terms of size of the aperture than, let's say,

01:58 F over 4.

01:59 And F4 is larger than five six, and so on.

02:04 This can be a little confusing, but if you

02:06 think in terms of fractions, it will make more sense.

02:10 So these are the settings we'll look at in this exercise.

02:13 You'll see more potential settings on your lens.

02:16 But for our purposes here, these should

02:19 be enough to make the point about focus changes.

02:22 We'll stay with these five.

02:24 Okay now here is the image I made of our music box at F/4.

02:28 Take a hard look at what is in focus and what is not.

02:32 Not very much in the foreground and background, and so we

02:36 say this image has a narrow depth of field.

02:39 Not a whole lot is in focus.

02:41 Now at 5.6, here is the image again.

02:45 Let's compare the two.

02:47 We're seeing very slight changes in focus.

02:51 That's what we're looking for.

02:53 Take a hard look what's in focus.

02:55 And now we'll go to F/8.

02:57 And comparing F/8 to five six, little by little,

03:01 more of the image is coming into focus.

03:04 You should stop the video and give the two a careful look.

03:08 Notice the turning mechanism a tad more in focus in F8

03:12 and a tad more as well in the screws and everything else

03:15 in that object plane.

03:18 We'll go to the next F-stop, F/11

03:22 and we'll compare to the previous image, F/8.

03:25 And again, you should stop the video to make the comparison.

03:29 And just to move things along a bit,

03:31 we'll just go right to F/32.

03:33 Look at how small the aperture is.

03:36 And look at how so much more of the image

03:39 is in focus compared to the previous.

03:42 Now to drive home the point even further,

03:45 let's compare F/32 with F/4.

03:48 So you really see a significant change.

03:51 That's what these observations are about.

03:54 We're seeing how focus or depth of field

03:57 changes more and more, get's into focus, as we close down,

04:02 or stop down the aperture to the smaller fraction

04:06 settings on your lens.

04:09 But remember, as we close the aperture

04:12 to smaller settings like F/32, we also

04:16 decrease the amount of light we let into the camera.

04:19 We're not getting the right exposure

04:23 until we compensate by increasing the amount of time

04:28 the shutter is open.

04:30 For example, when I change from one second [clicking sound]

04:34 to two seconds [clicking sound], I'm

04:39 keeping the shutter open twice as long, allowing

04:43 more light into the camera.

04:45 The longer the shutter is open, the longer

04:48 we permit the light to enter the camera

04:51 and to be read by the sensor, compensating

04:54 for the small aperture setting.

docs.text:
00:00 Facebook's parent company, Meta, has, to put  it mildly, not been having a very good year.

00:05 It has splat effectively all of its free cash flow  and then some into competing in the AI race only

00:10 to end up coming a convincing fifth place. It has  now accumulated more than half a trillion dollars

00:16 in offbalance sheet debt. Its other side projects  have been all but abandoned, and it's been hit by

00:20 several lawsuits that could all potentially set up  a precedent that would simply make their business

00:24 nonviable. Earlier this year, they were forced to  pay $2.1 million in damages to a single victim for

00:30 the mental health damage they had caused her.  Now, $2.1 million alone is barely a drop in

00:35 the bucket for a company like Meta, but it did  set the standard for thousands of similar cases

00:40 that people are bringing against the platform,  and that many drops can quickly add up. Also,

00:45 given how much attention that case got, there are  now naturally even more people lining up to sue

00:49 these companies. In addition to this, Meta has  also been forced to pay over a billion dollars

00:54 in two separate state cases. And just last  week, it went to court again for a potential

00:59 $1.4 trillion case brought against them by dozens  of states for platform features alleged to have

01:04 been specifically and unlawfully targeting users  under 13 without proper parental consent. That is,

01:09 as of the time of making this video, more than  the entire company is worth and many times more

01:14 than the business has in actual assets. So even  in the much more likely outcome of a fractional

01:20 settlement in this case, that alone could still  render them insolvent when considering all of

01:24 the other financial commitments they have tied  themselves to, which of course raises the question

01:28 of would the government actually let that happen.  Well, yeah. So about 2 hours before we posted

01:34 this video yesterday, we got an answer to this  question. No, the government did not let this

01:40 happen. The company was allowed to settle for just  under $17 billion. But we will get back to this

01:45 later on. Even if you are rightfully skeptical  about this company actually being held responsible

01:50 here, these are still risks that are compounding  on one another. Risks that the market has clearly

01:55 already priced in. Meta stock is down almost  25% over the last 12 months. At the same time,

02:00 the Magnificent 7 as a whole is up by over 30%.  Now, this is normally the part of the intro where

02:06 I say that, well, at least they still have a very  stable core business of harvesting our attention

02:10 and selling it to advertisers, right? But even  in this most basic part of their operation,

02:15 there are a number of problems just under the  surface that are each seriously worth addressing

02:20 if they are going to survive. And I guess just  for a bit of fun, it's also worth asking what
