00:00 With all the talk of reckless money printing, hyperinflation and debasement of currencies

00:04 around the world today, it sounds reasonable to have some kind of backup plan ready to

00:09 replace regular currencies should the need arise.

00:12 Now of course there are crypto “currencies” and they are great as alternative investment

00:16 vehicles, but their high transaction fees and slow processing times make them extremely

00:21 unsuitable to replace something like the American dollar, in whatever form it may take.

00:26 This is all really frustrating because a nations currency is supposed to serve the people of

00:30 the nation and it does genuinely seem like in recent years this role has mutated into

00:35 bending the economy to the whim of policy makers… who may not always have the best

00:39 ideas.

00:40 If only YOU had access to the control panel, you could stop all of this reckless money

00:44 printing (that according to some top economists and financiers, is driving us towards hyperinflation

00:50 Armageddon).

00:51 This begs the question, how could you create your own currency?

00:55 And how could an obscure old video game give us the answer to this question.

01:00 So it’s time to literally learn how money works as we look into the steps an individual

01:04 or a group could take to create a currency with the same functionality and recognition

01:09 as a those created by governments around the world.

01:12 So to get started we need to properly understand what a currency must do, to be a viable replacement

01:17 for lets say the US dollar.

01:20 For starters it must be easy to use and widely accepted.

01:24 So you need to make sure almost everybody within a desired region or as part of a desired

01:28 community is willing to accept this in exchange for the things they have to offer, be that

01:32 goods, services or their labor to an employer.

01:35 It must also be easy to use.

01:37 You want people to be able to exchange this currency quickly and easily with one another

01:42 either by handing over some kind of designation of this currency or by setting up software

01:46 to handle these transfers, which is obviously the more modern solution.

01:50 It must also remain fairly stable in pricing.

01:53 The value of a “currency” appreciating thousands of percent within a year might be

01:57 heralded as a victory in crypto communities, but for real currencies this is what we call

02:02 hyper-deflation which is a real thing, and in many ways is way way worse than hyperinflation.

02:09 A steak dinner should cost approximately the same units of your currency one year to the

02:13 next.

02:14 Minor variations are fine but anything more than 10% either way per years and you don’t

02:19 have a currency you have a vehicle for rampant speculation.

02:23 Finally as an added bonus it should be fairly cheap to use.

02:27 This has a little asterisk next to it because technically this is just part of being easy

02:31 to use, but it is easier to think of as it’s own little category.

02:35 Your currency should be cheap to store, transport and transfer.

02:39 That means you should probably avoid things like heavy metals which have historically

02:42 been popular but are not great on the cheapness front.

02:46 To this point you will also want to make sure your currency can be digitized, because if

02:50 you want it to be compatible with all of the other legit currencies in the world then this

02:54 is how the vast majority of trade back and forth between these currencies is made.

02:58 Now if you are still thinking “ooh oohh a crypto currency can do all of these things”,

03:03 you might not be wrong, but there are certainly better options.

03:08 Almost all crypto currencies work a blockchain, which is just a technical way of saying a

03:12 public record shared between everybody in the network.

03:15 This is great for making the system decentralised but it also tends to make it very cumbersome

03:20 because you are basically processing transactions via committee.

03:24 There are people that can explain the computer sciency stuff behind this much better than

03:27 me but basically crypto currencies get pretty mediocre scores across the board in all of

03:32 these categories.

03:33 And yes yes I know, before the enthusiasts blow up the comment section, there are plenty

03:38 of different coin designs that shift around these stats a bit but ultimately they still

03:42 do away with the thing that inspired this whole process in the first place – control.

03:48 Decentralisation is great in theory, but if you are going to all of the effort to float

03:52 your own currency you want to be one with your finger on the money printer button.

03:57 So a more traditional system is probably better here.

04:01 Fortunately this is also far easier to create.

04:04 You could print out paper rectangles but even easier still is just digit’s on a computer.

04:10 So here is how you should actually go about doing that.

04:13 First you want to create a secure database that is able to record and adjust who owns

04:17 how much money.

04:18 This will effectively be a glorified excel spreadsheet, and you might be surprised to

04:23 learn that most modern bank keep records of bank balances in this way.

04:27 Now you can add utilities to this database system like the ability for people to easily

04:31 update their own accounts by sending or receiving this money, and of course you will need a

04:35 secure way to host this this database.

04:38 All of this is fairly easy to pull off with modern database software and web hosting services

04:42 like AWS or Microsoft Azure, even someone with the most basic understanding of database

04:47 systems could pull this off no problem at all.

04:50 The difficulty is in actually getting people to care about these digits.

04:55 If I offered to move a billion How Money Works dollars into your account in exchange for

04:59 your house, you would be pretty stupid to take that deal because basically nobody else

05:04 would be willing to exchange those dollars for anything else.

05:07 But consider this, lets say you set this whole system up and then create a two way exchange

05:12 where you will convert 1 american dollar for 1 how money works dollar and 1 how money works

05:16 dollar back for an American dollar.

05:18 Well suddenly this means that your digits in the database do have value, because if

05:22 someone has some in their designated account then they can just transfer them for American

05:27 dollars.

05:28 Now if I offered you a billion How Money Works dollars for your house you would be more than

05:32 happy to take that deal because you could just transfer this money into American dollars.

05:37 This is of course assuming that you were confident that the exchange could honor this transaction.

05:41 So at this point the value of your currency is determined by what you say it is exchangeable

05:45 for, and the confidence people have in you being able to honour this exchange.

05:49 For an individual that confidence might be a hard thing to build, but for a large well

05:53 known institution it shouldn’t be too difficult at all.

05:57 In fact what I have described here in this system is basically a casino.

06:02 In a casino, Individuals will willingly trade in real dollars for plastic chips confident

06:07 in the fact that they can later be traded back for an equal amount of real dollars.

06:11 Infact patrons of casinos can be very confident of this exchangeability because casinos are

06:16 legally required to keep enough cash on hand to pay out all of the chips that they have

06:20 in circulation.

06:21 But the thing is these poker chips are not reaaaallllyyy a currency.

06:26 There is nothing that a market participant can purchase with these chips apart from entires

06:29 in games of chance, their value is not propped up by their exchangeability for another currency,

06:35 their value relies EXCLUSIVELY on their exchangeability with another currency.

06:40 In fact one of the best examples of a currency that was not made by a regular government

06:44 is PED from the video game Entropia Universe, a video game that uses a currency that is

06:49 also exchangeable for real world dollars.

06:52 Just like our hypothetical how money works dollars or casino chips, this currency is

06:57 exchangeable back and forth for a fixed rate.

06:59 The game developers will exchange 1 American dollar for 10 PED and likewise they will also

07:05 exchange 10 PED for 1 American dollar.

07:08 Now for this reason this video game has often been compared to a casino, where engaging

07:12 in the activities of the game are basically like playing hands of blackjack, now this

07:17 isn’t entirely unfair, but there is one big difference especially as it relates to

07:22 the currency.

07:23 While casino chips basically have no value outside of the money they can be exchanged

07:26 for, PED does actually have some value as a stand alone unit of exchange.

07:31 For example, if you wanted to buy a house in Germany, you would need to pay for that

07:35 house in euros.

07:36 If you want to buy land in this video game you will need to pay for it in PED.

07:40 Both of these currencies have value not only because they can be exchanged for other currencies,

07:45 but because they can be used to buy goods within their own markets.

07:48 For what it’s worth some real estate investments within this game have actually generated higher

07:53 returns than real estate investments within Germany, so make of that what you will.

07:58 So for all intents and purposes Mindark the developers of this video game have effectively

08:03 created their own currency, soooo if you want to make YOUR own currecency just follow their

08:09 steps.

08:10 Create the technical infrastructure to facilitate electronic funds transfers (basically that

08:14 glorified excel spreadsheet we made earlier)

08:17 Establish an exchange with the reputation to always be able to exchange this new currency

08:20 back and forth for another currency.

08:23 And then create a market where your new currency is the only one accepted to purchase things

08:27 that people really do value.

08:29 Now the last problem that you would face is that your new currency is still ultimately

08:32 pegged to some other currency because of this exchange.

08:35 No matter what happens nobody is going to trade in their American dollars for less than

08:39 one how money works dollar, and nobody is going to exchange a how money works dollar

08:43 for less than 1 american dollar because why would they?

08:47 If either side got a worse offer they would just go to the exchange and get this 1 for

08:51 1 deal.

08:52 This means that after all of this effort your currency will still suffer the same kind of

08:56 hyperinflation that people are fearing the US dollar will.

08:59 The solution to this is to slowly but surely widen the spread that you offer at this exchange.

09:04 Start off at 1 to 1, but over time work to a system where you will offer only 50 how

09:08 money cents for every 1 American dollar, and likewise will only offer 50 us cents for every

09:14 how money works dollar.

09:16 At this point people might go this exchange rate sucks, I am going to deal with other

09:20 people that want to exchange this currency and get a better price closer to the middle.

09:25 This is how you “float” a currency, and make its foreign exchange value purely determined

09:29 by market forces.

09:31 This means if the value of the USD really does tank over night your new currency will

09:36 be immune from that impact just so long as people still see value in the market your

09:39 currency facilitiates.

09:41 Now maintaining that value will be the big challenge at this point.

16:20 multi-billionaire co-founder and former CEO of  Apollo Capital Management, one of the largest

16:25 private equity firms in the world. An interesting  but totally irrelevant little connection is that

16:30 Apollo Capital Management shares the same New York  office building with another private equity firm,

16:34 Sycamore Partners. Sycamore Partners acquired  the holding company, The Limited, in 2017,

16:40 which is the parent company of Victoria  Secret. This means absolutely nothing,

16:44 but it is a warning that when you start looking  at financial documents for 2 months straight,

16:47 you do start seeing connections everywhere.  Anyway, Leon Black similarly was noted as

16:53 having a close personal relationship with Epstein,  even making him one of the trustees of his family

16:57 foundation as far back as 1997. As far as major  financial dealings go, Black allegedly paid at

17:03 least $158 million to Epstein for financial  services between 2012 and 2017, according to

17:09 an ongoing investigation by the Senate Finance  Committee. That is more than $30 million a year.

17:15 Black's payments to Epstein potentially raise even  more eyebrows because of the simple reality that

17:19 he himself is a highly sophisticated financier  and was the head of a major investment firm. So,

17:25 what did he need Epstein for? Now, to play devil's  advocate here, this alone isn't actually that

17:31 unusual. Most major financial figures tend to keep  their personal finances somewhere separate from

17:36 their own firm for privacy, flexibility, and risk  mitigation. It's kind of like how doctors don't

17:41 go for a checkup at their own clinic. What was  unusual, though, is how much Black was paying for

17:46 seemingly boilerplate financial advice. In the  worst case scenario, a clear explanation would

17:51 be that these were veiled ways to give money  to Epstein for quid-pro-quo services that uh

17:56 went beyond just finance. Now, even if that wasn't  true, another explanation is that Epstein's fees

18:02 were so high because he was pursuing aggressive  tax mitigation strategies and was acting as a

18:06 conduit to the tax havens that he was clearly  comfortable working in. In fact, his firm itself,

18:11 later were branded from J. Epstein and Company  to the Financial Trust Company used his infamous

18:16 islands as a headquarters to claim economic  development tax incentives in the Virgin Islands,

18:20 meaning that on all of these fees, he was  paying an effective tax rate of just 4%. Less

18:25 than a tenth of what he would be paying if he was  similarly set up in New York. Now, Les Wexner and

18:30 Leon Black were by far his largest known clients.  But despite some early reports, new information

18:35 has revealed that they weren't his only clients.  In total, his firm received an additional $118

18:40 million in traceable fees from individuals like  Elizabeth Johnson of the Johnson and Johnson

18:45 family fortune and the hedge fund Highbridge  Capital. A report by Forbes pieced all of these

18:49 together and found that in total, as far as we  know, Epstein's firm brought in over $488 million

18:55 in fees for questionable financial services. If  we were just tracking the source of his wealth,

19:00 these payments, as suspicious as they were,  combined with some modest investment returns,

19:04 should pretty much explain it, right? Well, not  quite. According to the very will and testament

19:10 that outlets are basing his estimated net worth  off of, only around half of his wealth was

19:14 actually invested in cash flow generating assets.  And this also isn't accounting for the fact

19:19 that several of his major investments completely  imploded, taking out a major share of his fortune

19:23 with it. He did have some successful private  investments such as Carbine, a communications

19:28 technology company that he was an early investor  in alongside other luminaries like Peter Teal. But

19:33 this company only saw significant growth after  he was already dead, so it didn't contribute

19:37 significantly to his 2019 net worth. Additionally,  his firm had staff and operational expenses. It is

19:44 still unclear how many people Epstein had working  for him, but we do know that in order to qualify

19:49 for his tax exemptions, he employed 11 full-time  staff in the Virgin Islands, which was confirmed

19:53 by a public audit that is still available online.  Now, that is not a lot of manpower for the type

19:59 of business he was reportedly doing. But this was  in addition to an unknown number of staff in his

20:04 New York offices. All of these investment losses  and business overhead costs money to maintain,

20:10 which means it isn't as simple as $488 million  in fees, equating to $488 million directly

20:16 landing in Epstein's wallet. This is also ignoring  potentially the biggest unaccounted for variable,

20:21 which is that his lifestyle was obviously  deplorable, but it was also not cheap.

20:26 frequent private jet travel, property taxes, and  upkeep on a hundreds of millions of dollars worth

20:30 of real estate, and personal expenditures all  amounted to several million dollars a year on the

20:34 low end. On top of this is one of his biggest  personal expenses of all, which was lawyers.

20:40 According to court records, Epson engaged with  more than 75 lawyers over the course of his life,

20:44 including major names like Alan Dersowitz, who  charged several thousand an hour for his services.

20:49 Adding it all up, it is possible that over the  roughly 30 years he was in business for himself,

20:54 he could have very easily spent as much money  as was coming in through these traceable revenue

20:58 sources, which means to amass this wealth, he was  either getting investment returns from somewhere

21:02 that hasn't been revealed yet, or he had other  sources of revenue. This sounds bad, but it

21:08 potentially gets worse. Now, this part is verging  on potentially conspiratorial, but so far in this

21:13 video, we've been working off the same number that  most news outlets have been working off of, the

21:18 $577 million detailed in his will. But that was  written while he was in prison, and it was done 2

21:24 days before his death. It is possible that someone  who was comfortable carrying a fake passport and

21:29 slipping in and out of international deals kept  some assets outside of the typical financial

21:34 system in the event that he had the opportunity  to make a run for it. Now, back to what we know.

21:38 The Senate Finance Committee has reported that  Epstein's company accounts held with several

21:42 major Western banks had over $1.9 billion worth  of direct transactions flowing between them, well

21:48 above the $488 million in fees that have already  been well documented. These transactions also

21:54 linked the currently sanctioned Russian banks,  putting further question marks over who Epstein's

21:58 clients were and what they were really paying for.  Unfortunately, until further details are released

22:04 and or more pressure is put on these banks to  hand over information, that is all we do know

22:08 for now. Offshore financial dealings are already  hard to track. So then add on a man who obviously

22:14 wanted to keep most of his business a wonderful  secret and then add the literal opakqueness of

22:18 the publicly released information and we may  not ever truly know the full extent of even

22:23 simple stuff like the man's personal finances.  Now the comments tell me that I am always a bit

22:28 too negative about these things. So, if there  is some good news that might come from this,

22:32 it is a demonstration of just how widespread the  network of shadowy offshore business deals really

22:37 is. A majority of the activity in these places is  just from people trying to avoid taxes. But with

22:43 very little oversight by design, it's not a good  look when that is the best possible outcome. But

22:48 if for some reason you want to set up one of  these offshore shell companies for yourself,

22:51 go and watch one of the first videos I ever made  here on YouTube to make sure you're at least going

22:55 to be doing it right. And don't forget to like  and subscribe to keep on learning how money works.

00:00 You have decided to go on a hunger strike. You  vow not to eat a single thing for days or even

00:04 weeks if you can last that long. The worst part  is that as each day goes by, things will get

00:09 worse and worse. By the time you reach the end,  you will be a husk of the person you once were.

00:13 The day you stop eating.

00:15 You take your final bite of a delicious meal. This  will be the last food you will eat for weeks. The

00:20 food is broken down into small pieces in your  mouth by your teeth. Spit and saliva lubricate

00:25 the chewed-up food so that it’s easier for you  to consume. When you swallow, your throat muscles

00:29 expand and contract, pushing the food down into  your stomach. This process is called peristalsis

00:34 and is what allows you to swallow even if you are  upsidedown. Ironically it is also the process that

00:39 enables you to throw up when it’s done in reverse.  Once the food reaches your stomach, the acids in

00:43 it break down your food into its basic components,  one of the most important of which is glucose.

00:48 Glucose is the sugar molecule that your  body uses to produce energy. It’s arguably

00:52 the most important molecule you ingest while  eating. There are other important nutrients

00:56 and vitamins your body gets from your food,  but the main goal is to break down anything

01:00 you put into your mouth into glucose so that  the mitochondria in your cells can use it to

01:05 make energy. If this does not happen, you  will die. In the days to come, it will be

01:10 glucose that your body craves. Everything else  is inconsequential, as you will soon find out.

01:14 The food sitting in your stomach is torn  apart by the acid contained within it. Some

01:18 of the molecules diffuse through your stomach  lining and into your bloodstream. Others are

01:22 released into your intestines, where they will  travel through around 20 feet of tubes. It’s

01:27 here that the majority of the nutrients from  your food are absorbed into the bloodstream,

01:31 and the waste is carried to your bowels to be  pooped out. Digestion can take hours to complete,

01:36 which means once you stop eating, you will not  feel the effects of starvation for some time.

01:40 6 hours after you stop eating.

01:42 Your body has now broken down all of the food  from your last meal. Some of the nutrients are

01:46 still in your bloodstream but in lower numbers  than they were while your food was still being

01:50 digested. However, the glucose from that  meal is almost completely used up. This is

01:54 when your brain starts sending signals  to your body that make you feel hungry.

01:58 Hunger is your body telling you it needs  more glucose to make energy. Really it’s

02:02 just your brain’s way of tricking you into  eating more food so it can make more energy.

02:05 But since you’ve decided to stop eating  altogether, these signals go unanswered.

02:10 It is at this point you might start to become  irritable or what has become known as hangry. Many

02:14 people have a shift in their mood when they get  hungry. Your brain is signaling your stomach to

02:18 make hormones such as ghrelin which stimulates the  feelings of hunger. Ghrelin can also make you feel

02:23 anxious, which is one of the reasons you become  irritable and grouchy when you are hungry. After

02:27 several hours of not eating, people will not want  to be around you. You might have a short temper,

02:31 experience mood swings, and heightened emotions,  all because your body is craving more glucose.

02:36 1 day after you stop eating.

02:38 You wake up after a good night's sleep. Biological  changes have started to occur within your body.

02:43 The surprising thing is you may feel like  you have more energy now than you did the

02:46 day before. While you slept, your body tried  to conserve energy, and now that you’re awake,

02:51 it’s pulling whatever glucose is left out  of your bloodstream to keep your body going.

02:54 It has been a full 24 hours since your last meal,  which means your body quickly goes from feeling

02:59 good to sluggish and miserable. The energy you  conserved is slowly being sapped from you. You

03:04 drink a lot of water to keep yourself hydrated  because although you can survive for weeks without

03:08 food, you would be dead within days if you become  dehydrated. You have sworn off juices and soda,

03:13 so you will not be replenishing your glucose  supply that way, and although the water

03:17 quenches your thirst, it will never provide  you with the energy you need to stay alive.

03:21 You carry on and complete your daily activities.  That night as you look at your bed, it manifests

03:26 into a hot, juicy, cheeseburger right before your  eyes. It’s just your mind playing tricks on you

03:31 because you are so hungry, but it seems so real  at the time. This will become a common occurrence

03:36 as you drift in and out of consciousness in the  days to come. Not eating will begin to mess with

03:41 your mind in ways that you can’t possibly imagine,  and in the end, it might just make you go crazy.

03:45 Your hunger strike continues, and you  go to bed with a grumbling stomach and

03:49 a brain that is screaming at you to  eat something. In the coming days,

03:52 your body will take drastic  measures to keep you alive.

03:54 2 days after you stop eating.

03:56 The glucose in your body is now  completely gone. You enter ketosis,

04:00 which is when the liver produces ketone  bodies that can be broken down and used

04:04 for energy. Although glucose is the most  desirable molecule for energy production,

04:08 it’s not the only one. The brain will use ketone  bodies as a replacement in dier situations. There

04:13 is a lag time between the depletion of glucose  in the blood and the breaking down of your body’s

04:17 energy-storing molecules such as carbohydrates  and fats. During this transition time,

04:22 the ketone bodies are a vital resource your  brain uses to maintain its basic functions.

04:27 When the liver is producing ketone bodies, it  signals the beginning of what will become a

04:31 very destructive process for other parts of your  body. As your internal systems try to keep vital

04:36 organs functioning, they will break down anything  and everything to keep you alive. Once the ketone

04:40 bodies are all gone, things start to get even  worse. Your body has to resort to destroying

04:45 itself to generate more energy. And all of this  destruction will come with some dire consequences.

04:49 3 days after you stop eating.

04:52 Your body is in full-blown starvation mode at this  point and begins feeding on itself. Whenever you

04:57 eat, some of the nutrients you ingest such as  carbohydrates, fats, and proteins are stored

05:02 in your tissue. This is the reason why your  weight increases if you eat too much food

05:06 on a regular basis. However, now that you are  starving, your body takes these energy stores

05:10 and starts to break them down. Carbohydrates and  fats are the first macronutrients to be used.

05:14 The most common location where fats and  carbohydrates are stored is in the abdominal

05:19 region. However, they can be found throughout the  body. As they are broken down, you lose weight,

05:23 and your BMI decreases. Carbohydrates are made up  of complex sugars. Enzymes in your body break them

05:29 down into components that are easier to use.  Many carbohydrates contain glucose molecules,

05:33 which are stripped and quickly  used up by your starving body.

05:36 The fatty acids that are broken down contain  acetyl CoA. This molecule can be used by your

05:41 cells to generate energy. Acetyl CoA does  not contain as much energy as glucose,

05:46 but in this situation, your  body doesn’t care where the

05:48 energy is coming from as long as there is  enough to carry out basic life functions.

05:52 Your metabolism slows immensely, and you  feel tired all of the time. It’s at this

05:56 point that your organs begin to shrink.  This is another step your body takes to

06:00 lower the amount of energy required to  keep things running. At the same time,

06:03 your body temperature drops,  which also helps conserve energy.

06:06 All of these changes can be dangerous and are  clear signs that your body is starving. In any

06:11 other circumstance, you would eat a huge meal to  replenish the nutrients and stored energy that is

06:15 being lost. But since this is not an option, you  power through the pain and exhaustion. You find

06:20 it hard to move around even for short periods  of time, and keeping your eyes open is a chore.

06:25 The most dangerous effect of starvation  is that your brain is not receiving the

06:29 glucose it needs to run smoothly. If  the brain shuts down, it’s game over;

06:33 you die. The brain cannot use fatty acids and  other energy stores as efficiently as glucose,

06:38 so it monopolizes any remaining glucose in your  system. On average, your brain uses around 120

06:44 grams of glucose every day. This is a significant  amount of your daily sugar intake, which is why

06:49 if you don’t eat enough, your brain will signal  that you are still hungry. Now that you are not

06:53 consuming any new sugars, all the energy your  brain requires must come from the body itself.

06:57 Things go haywire as your body is broken  down to keep you alive. Your blood pressure

07:02 drops, and your heart rate slows. These  are countermeasures to try and reduce

07:05 energy needs. From here on out, every  day that passes without food entering

07:09 your body will cause even more serious  damage to occur. In the coming days,

07:13 your body will do some pretty miraculous things to  keep you going, but eventually, it will shut down.

07:18 5 days after you stop eating.

07:20 Your body is now in a constant state of feeling  threatened. You haven’t eaten in almost a week,

07:24 so you begin to act more like a cornered  wild animal than a rational human. Your

07:28 brain can’t function properly, so animalistic  instincts take over, and you are driven only

07:32 by the will to survive. This means you might  become aggressive or aggravated more quickly.

07:37 Around this time, non-essential organs begin  to shut down. Your body is trying to conserve

07:41 as many resources as possible to keep the  brain going. The digestive system is one

07:45 of the first organ systems to be shut down  as it hasn’t been used in days. However,

07:49 there are some nasty side effects that  develop as a result of this occurring.

07:52 Once the digestive and excretory systems start  to lose energy and cells due to starvation,

07:57 they cause a build-up of excess water in  your body. As a result, you begin to have

08:02 diarrhea. Even though you may be drinking water  constantly, this can still have life-threatening

08:06 consequences. As the liquid explodes out  of your bowels, nutrients come out with it.

08:10 There is no way for your body to separate the  vital nutrients from the waste being excreted.

08:15 With even less nutrients available now, the  brain becomes more and more strained. Your

08:19 brain cells begin to die, and brain matter  loss escalates. This is especially dangerous

08:24 for brains that are still developing. Children  and young adults affected by starvation could

08:28 end up with permanent neurological impairment  even if they eventually start eating a healthy

08:32 diet again. It’s true that since the  brain is more plastic during development,

08:36 it might be able to repair itself,  but the danger of causing irreparable

08:39 damage to the nervous system due  to starvation is a real concern.

08:42 7 days after you stop eating.

08:44 Your body has used up its energy stores of  carbohydrates and fats. It’s now starting

08:49 to break down your own proteins in a last-ditch  effort to generate energy. This is when things

08:54 get really bad. Once your body starts breaking  down proteins, death is not too far away. You are

08:59 literally tearing apart your own muscles in  order to keep the brain going. Unfortunately,

09:04 this is at the expense of other  vital organs, including your heart.

09:07 You could start to develop convulsions  or disrupted heart rhythms. You are

09:10 also becoming weaker and more toxins  are building up in your body as your

09:14 kidneys and liver begin to shut down. The  brain tries to conserve as much energy as

09:17 possible by reducing the amount of glucose it  requires, but it still needs to send signals

09:22 to the rest of the body to keep things  functioning. Long-term starvation can

09:26 cause you to experience hallucinations  and fade in and out of consciousness.

09:30 The process of breaking down proteins into amino  acids and small amounts of glucose helps the body

09:35 initially, but it will only be a matter of  days until a major system fails and you die.

09:39 10 days after you stop eating.

09:41 You are cold all of the time. You can barely lift  your head off the ground, let alone stand up. Your

09:46 eyes have become super sensitive to light, so you  have to sit in the shade or in a dark room just to

09:51 prevent a throbbing headache from developing. You  start to cough as you feel yourself getting sick.

09:55 You have become much more susceptible to  disease without the necessary resources

09:59 or energy to make antibodies. Your  immune system has become compromised,

10:03 and even if you are just lying in  isolation as you suffer through starvation,

10:07 it’s only a matter of time until you  are attacked by a harmful pathogen.

10:10 When this happens, your body will not have  the energy or nutrients it requires to fight

10:14 off the infection. Your white blood cell  count is low. The antibody proteins your

10:18 immune system would normally develop cannot be  made due to a lack of resources. Much of the

10:23 protein in your body has already been broken  down and repurposed as an energy source;

10:27 there just isn’t enough left over to generate  the components needed to defeat the pathogen.

10:31 If you are lucky, you might receive medical  interventions before the disease kills you.

10:36 But this will do nothing if you don’t get food  into your system. Chances are that even if you

10:40 do catch a cold after close to two weeks without  eating, it will be starvation that causes your

10:45 body to shut down and not the illness.

14 days after you stop eating.

10:49 Your teeth begin to decay. Even if you decided  to eat something, you’re not sure you would be

10:53 able to chew and swallow it. You feel so weak that  you are almost positive that if you fall asleep,

10:58 you won’t wake up. Your bones have become brittle  and seem as if they will snap if you move. All you

11:03 can do is lay on your back and stare into the  darkness. Your body has broken down every store

11:07 of energy it can find. Your muscles have been  torn apart, and your bones have lost density.

11:12 21 days after you stop eating.

11:14 When you shift your head, you find hair all  over your pillow. Your bones are pressed up

11:18 against your skin as there is practically  no more muscle or fat left on your entire

11:22 body. You are nothing more than a  skeleton with skin wrapped around

11:25 it. Breathing becomes a chore. Your  heart begins to shut down. Your brain

11:29 can no longer generate the energy it needs  to send signals throughout your body. You

11:33 take in your final breath before your nervous  system becomes completely inactive and you die.

11:37 However, you are lucky. Someone is about to rescue  you from dying of starvation. Unfortunately,

11:42 this is easier said than done. Your body  is just a shell of what it once was. If

11:47 you are not reintroduced to food properly, you  will still end up dying. First, doctors must

11:51 give you a thorough medical exam to figure out  the best course of action to save your life.

11:54 Day 1 of the recovery process.

11:56 It’s likely you will be given antibiotics to try  and fight off any infections or harmful bacteria

12:01 that have found their way into your body. Since  your immune system has been all but destroyed,

12:05 pathogens are running rampant throughout  your system. You are hooked to an IV to

12:09 make sure you get the fluids you need to say  hydrated. In the solution are electrolytes,

12:13 nutrients, and, most importantly, glucose. The  life-saving substance flows into your body,

12:18 and your brain starts using it to  reactivate long inert muscles and organs.

12:22 Day 2 of the recovery process.

12:24 You might be given soft foods full of nutrients,  such as peanut butter paste. If you are able to

12:29 drink on your own, skim milk could be one of  the fluids that doctors ask you to consume.

12:33 Both are high in vitamins and minerals and will  help your body begin the recovery process. You

12:37 would not be able to eat solid foods as you  would be too weak. If you try to eat too much,

12:41 too quickly, you will make yourself  sick and throw it all up. This would

12:45 obviously defeat the purpose of  trying to eat in the first place.

12:47 Day 3 of the recovery process.

12:49 You are monitored for any swelling that  might occur as a result of introducing

12:53 food back into your system. The doctors  also check your heart as people who are

12:57 brought back from starvation often develop  cardiovascular problems as the heart muscles

13:01 have become so weak that they struggle to move  blood around the body. Even if you are pumped

13:05 full of glucose and nutrients, it won’t  matter if they can’t get to your brain.

13:08 Your diet will eventually return to  normal. But during the recovery process,

13:12 you will be eating boiled vegetables along  with other supplements. Your protein intake

13:16 will remain relatively low until your  body becomes stronger. And even though

13:20 you would think that you should be dumping  sugar into your system to generate energy,

13:23 this is not the case. Your cells would  not be able to use up all of the sugar,

13:27 which could lead to glucose resistance  that could develop into Type-2 diabetes.

13:31 Recovery from starvation is possible with the help  of medical professionals, but it’s highly likely

13:36 your body will sustain long-term damage from  the ordeal. Your heart might not fully recover,

13:40 and you may need to be put on blood pressure  medication. Your cognitive functions could be

13:45 impaired for the foreseeable future, and there may  be irreparable damage to organs within your body.

13:49 The amount of time you would survive without  eating varies depending on your body type,

13:53 weight, age, how active you are, and your  hydration levels. Some people only survive

13:58 a week without eating, while others can  survive 21 days. This tends to be the

14:03 normal time range people can last without food,  but there are some who can survive much longer.

14:07 How much longer, you ask? We are  talking months without anything to eat.

14:11 Mahatma Gandhi survived for 21 days while only  sipping water during one of his non-violent

14:16 protests for India’s independence.  There have also been accounts of

14:19 people on hunger strikes that have lasted  up to 40 days. This may seem incredible,

14:23 but it actually has been done a number  of times. Several studies have recorded

14:27 people on hunger strikes exceeding a  month without food. That being said,

14:30 the longest someone has ever gone without solid  food is so astonishing it will blow your mind.

14:34 According to the Guinness Book of World Records,  Angus Barbieri lasted for over a year without any

14:40 solid food. In June of 1965, Angus stopped  eating any food and only drank tea, coffee,

14:46 water, and soda while at Maryfield Hospital in  Dundee, Scotland. He was also given supplemental

14:51 vitamins to help keep his body going. In July of  1966, 382 days after starting his no-food diet,

14:57 Angus had his first real food in over a year.  He went from weighing 472 pounds to 178 pounds.

15:04 This was a special circumstance as  doctors were present to monitor him,

15:08 and he was given supplemental vitamins, but  382 days is an extremely long time to go

15:13 without any solid food. In cases where people  go on hunger strikes for long periods of time,

15:18 they are likely drinking water and  have access to other supplements.

15:21 Also, life expectancy due to starvation is  drastically different when it is by choice

15:25 rather than in a survival situation. If you found  yourself trapped on a deserted island with no food

15:30 and only water, it’s highly improbable that you  would make it past two weeks before dying. This is

15:35 because you would already be in survival mode,  which would dump adrenaline into your system

15:39 and cause you to start using your glucose much  quicker than if you actively chose to stop eating.

15:44 There is also some evidence to suggest that  females are able to last longer without food

15:48 than males. This has not been definitively  proven because an experiment to gather these

15:53 results would be highly unethical. But  women tend to have a higher percentage

15:56 of stored body fat than men. This means  that their body has more resources to pull

16:00 from before needing to tear apart proteins  to generate energy. The longer a body can

16:04 go before it runs out of carbohydrates and  fats, the longer the person will survive.

16:08 That being said, if you ever do find yourself in  a situation where you are in danger of starving,

16:12 there are a few things you can do to extend your  life expectancy. In the best of circumstances,

16:16 you will need to drink a lot of water and  make sure you don’t become dehydrated.

16:20 Dehydration will kill you much quicker than  starvation ever could. To conserve energy,

16:24 you should move as little as  possible and try to remain calm.

16:27 The faster your heart is beating, the more  energy you are using. The quicker you deplete

16:31 your glucose levels, the sooner your body will  start consuming itself to generate the energy it

16:35 needs to keep you alive. Your body is using the  least amount of energy while you are sleeping,

16:39 so resting is your best course of action to  extend the amount of time you can go without food.

16:44 The bottom line is that if you have the choice  between eating or going on a hunger strike,

16:48 it’s best to just keep eating. Starvation can have  long-term effects that you may never recover from.

16:54 Now watch “What Happens To Your Body If You Never

16:56 Move.” Or check out “What Does it  Actually Feel Like to be Shot.”

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: What Caused the Roman Empire to Collapse
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: What Caused the Roman Empire to Collapse
  • Video ID: 5tilhR0C6DY
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 The Roman Empire seemed unbeatable at  its peak - one of the largest empires

00:04 the world has ever seen. It fended off  all of its military foes. It built a

00:08 complex administrative state that ruled  regions from Egypt, to Spain, to England,

00:12 and as far east as modern-day Iraq. At its  height, it seemed like it would rule forever.

00:17 And today, it’s a distant memory.

00:20 Why did the Roman Empire ultimately fall?  Did it meet an enemy too powerful to fend

00:24 off? Was it undone by internal conflict? Or did  it simply stretch itself too thin? The answer

00:30 isn’t any one of those - and the empire’s  downfall happened over hundreds of years.

00:34 To find the truth of the Roman Empire’s fall,  we have to go back to how it became an empire

00:38 in the first place - because initially, it was a  Republic with far less territory. The Republic had

00:43 taken over from the previously flawed monarchy,  but the people seemed to be calling out for a

00:48 more unified government. One man was more than  willing to answer that call - Julius Caesar,

00:53 the man appointed perpetual dictator  of Rome in the mid-first century BCE.

00:57 He started consolidating power, becoming  a popular and effective ruler who won many

01:02 military campaigns - and many of his rivals  realized he had no intention of giving up

01:06 his newfound power. The elites of Rome  assassinated him, setting off one of the

01:10 biggest political crises in Roman history.  Civil wars kicked off as many people sought

01:15 to claim power - and in the end the wars saw  Octavian, the adopted son of Caesar, take power.

01:21 He continued his father’s legacy, conquering  nearby territories including Egypt - ending

01:26 that country’s Hellenistic era. Soon, he  was more powerful than his father ever was,

01:30 and the Roman senate responded accordingly.  They granted him the title of Augustus,

01:34 allowed him to rule in perpetuity, and soon no one  would dare challenge his power. The plotters who

01:40 feared Caesar’s role as dictator had accidentally  crafted the rise of Rome’s first Emperor.

01:46 And he wouldn’t be the last.

01:47 From then, Rome would not only become  another monarchy ruled by a series of

01:51 hereditary leaders both good and bad, but  it would develop a hunger for conquest that

01:56 would envelop a large part of Europe and  parts of Asia and Africa. While Italy would

02:00 continue to serve as the center of the  empire, the other territories would be

02:03 organized into provinces - each administered  by a local governor with drastically different

02:08 approaches to leadership. The empire would  soon be so large that it would be impossible

02:12 for one leader to maintain full control over every  territory, which meant the provinces would still

02:17 maintain some level of autonomy - as long as they  paid their taxes and didn’t cause any problems

02:22 that would arouse the ire of the Emperor.  And the system seemed to be working - the

02:26 empire was stable enough that the next two  centuries became largely known as “Pax Romana”.

02:31 But under the surface, trouble was brewing.

02:33 During the first century CE, religious conflict  started brewing under the surface. The Roman

02:38 Empire largely worshipped the traditional pantheon  - led by Jupiter and heavily tied to the Greek

02:43 pantheon led by Zeus. This polytheistic faith  was characterized by ornate temples dedicated

02:49 to the individual Gods and a wild lore that  made the Gods seem rather petty and human.

02:53 Jupiter’s dalliances with human women, and gods  taking revenge for the most petty grievances,

02:59 were both common staples of the faith in those  days - and then came Christianity. Spinning

03:04 out of the teachings of the Jewish Rabbi  known as Jesus and his eventual crucifixion

03:08 by the Roman authorities, this new Abrahamic  faith was based of the often-persecuted faith

03:13 of Judaism - and largely received the same  treatment in the early days. While some of

03:18 the more dramatic stories like early Christians  being fed to lions have no historical backing,

03:22 the Roman Empire saw new faiths  as a threat to the establishment.

03:26 But religions aren’t easy to kill.

03:28 The conflict stayed under the radar and  Christianity was mostly a small faith

03:32 during those early years, and a wise emperor  would have likely focused on maintaining the

03:36 empire’s stability rather than persecuting  heathens. But when you have a monarchy,

03:41 you’re often relying on the whims of birth  order and genetics - and in the year 177,

03:45 Rome’s luck ran out. The new Emperor, Commodus,  would soon become infamous for this exact reason.

03:51 The youngest Emperor ever at the age of  fifteen, his rule was dictated by his

03:55 emotions which led to recklessness. A teenager  making bad decisions when given too much power?

04:00 Perish the thought! As her was inheriting  the Empire built by many of his predecessors,

04:05 it was hard for him to screw up the larger things  - but back in Rome, he wasted no time throwing

04:10 things into chaos. He was known for his fickle and  dictatorial leadership style, as well as his love

04:15 of the gladiator matches in the Colosseum. He  would even participate in duels himself - which

04:19 largely meant anyone who faced off against him  would probably be expected to die quietly. He

04:24 built a cult of personality around himself,  and his reign was so chaotic that he would

04:29 eventually be immortalized by Joaquin Phoenix as  a villain in the Oscar-winning movie Gladiator.

04:33 And his reign ended as it began - with chaos.

04:37 Commodus was assassinated by a wrestler in  the Roman baths after fifteen years in charge,

04:41 and things would only get more chaotic  from there. The Roman Senate declared

04:45 him a public enemy and tore down  his statues, and he was succeeded

04:48 by a new Emperor - in what would become  known as the Year of the Five Emperors.

04:52 It was 193 CE, and civil war ensued. The next  emperor would be assassinated only three months

04:58 after taking office, his successor would  essentially pay off the guards to let him

05:01 become Emperor, and he would be ousted and  executed only weeks later. The chaos would

05:06 only die down when two emperors, Septimus Severus  and Clodius Albinus, ruled simultaneously despite

05:12 both considering the other to be a threat.  Rome’s political climate was in complete chaos.

05:17 And soon, people outside would start noticing.

05:19 Many of the provinces of Rome had been  semi-autonomous for a long time and

05:23 had developed their own cultures. So as the  Roman state spiraled into chaos, they started

05:27 to wonder - why not just make it official? As  the Romans struggled through a series of weak,

05:32 crazy, and inconsequential Emperors -  often in quick succession - territories

05:36 started to break away at an increasing rate.  First came the self-declared Gallic Empire,

05:40 which took most of the territory of  modern-day France and England with it.

05:44 Then came the Palmyrene Empire, which was led  by Queen Zenobia and took over much of Egypt

05:49 and the eastern coast of the Mediterranean -  including the many key sites in the Holy Land.

05:54 It was the biggest crisis in Rome’s history  - but it would bring many changes with it.

05:58 A series of three Emperors in the third  century would bring this crisis to the

06:02 end - but the Roman Empire that emerged from  it would not be the same. First was Aurelian,

06:06 who only reigned for five years  but had a huge impact. At the time,

06:10 the diminished Roman military was under attack  by Barbarian tribes and internal strife,

06:13 and it seemed like the Empire’s days might be  nearing an end. But Aurelian had risen through

06:18 the ranks of the military and knew its workings  well, and under his reign he fended off the

06:22 attacking tribes and conquered both the Palmyrene  Empire and the Gallic Empire. He surrounded Rome

06:27 with mighty walls, abandoned provinces that  were too much trouble to keep, and improved

06:31 Rome’s economy. Under his short tenure, Rome  started to look more like it did at its peak.

06:35 His successors would build on his work.

06:37 Diocletian would reign for twenty years and was  also a military veteran, but most of the military

06:42 work had been completed already. He would focus  his efforts on improving the empire’s stability,

06:47 which included creating a system of regional  courts that would give the empire more control

06:51 over its far-flung provinces. While the empire  had reclaimed the territory lost to the breakaway

06:56 provinces, Diocletian started expanding once  again - and by the end of his twenty years,

07:00 he became the first Roman emperor to abdicate  his position voluntarily, retiring to his palace.

07:06 But his successor might have  had an even bigger impact.

07:09 The thirty-one year run of Constantine the  Great would be among the most successful in

07:13 the empire’s history. He introduced a new  currency, expanded the empire’s territory,

07:18 and reorganized the army to be more effective.  But his most significant change was his conversion

07:23 to Christianity - reportedly spurred on by him  seeing a cross in the sky. As the Roman Emperor

07:28 converted, so did many of the citizens of Rome,  igniting Christianity’s rise to becoming a world

07:33 power religion. At the end of his reign,  the empire’s territory was near its peak,

07:36 expanding as far east as Byzantium. After his  death, Constantine left the empire to his sons,

07:41 starting a new dynasty which would rule over  Rome. The Roman Empire looked as healthy as ever,

07:46 and many people assumed that this was  the beginning of a new golden age.

07:50 So how could things go so very wrong?

07:53 The year was 337 CE when Constantine passed  away, and while Constantine’s reign had been

07:59 full of successes, there was trouble lurking  under the surface. His embrace of Christianity

08:03 had given the Church massive power in Rome, and  although many supported him in this decision,

08:08 there were some who didn’t wish for the empire to  fall under the grasps of Christianity. Enemies of

08:13 the state were executed, and their estates  were given to those he favored. The military

08:16 was paid well, but soon the soldiers seemed  to be engaging in blatant corruption. But the

08:20 empire was still the greatest power in the world,  and it was hard to imagine anyone challenging it.

08:24 But empire’s aren’t immune from internal strife.

08:27 In the aftermath of the death of Constantine,  the throne of the empire was once again open

08:31 for contest, and this era led to many conflicts  over who would take control. His sons initially

08:36 ruled jointly, but chaos would follow and  Rome would be plunged into civil war. Many

08:41 territories were taken over by local leaders,  with territories going back and forth at the

08:45 whims of military victories. Despite this,  the core of the empire was unchallenged,

08:49 and by 379 a new emperor named Theodosius had  risen. A proven general, he would become one

08:55 of Rome’s greatest military leaders and  would put an end to this era of strife.

08:58 But far greater threats were  brewing beyond the borders of Rome.

09:02 As far-reaching as Rome’s borders were at the  time, it was hard to believe that a nomadic people

09:07 from a continent away would throw the whole thing  into chaos. But the Huns were no ordinary nomads.

09:12 Fierce warriors, they had been making inroads into  Asia and Eastern Europe - and where they went,

09:17 people fled. Their mass takeover of territory led  the local Gothic tribes to flee towards the Roman

09:23 Empire. Suddenly, the Romans had a huge influx  of barbarian warriors fleeing across their border

09:27 - and Rome’s lack of management in their border  states came back to haunt them. A well-organized

09:32 government may have been able to resettle these  new residents and incorporate them into the

09:36 Roman state - even using their warrior smarts  to reinvigorate the military. Unfortunately,

09:41 the corrupt local officials instead chose to  exploit them, assuming they weren’t a threat.

09:45 They would be proven very wrong.

09:47 Now the Romans had a large number of outside  warriors within their borders. These guests

09:52 had seen Roman hospitality was lacking, and  they quickly took up arms. They were joined

09:56 by other tribesmen heading over the  border, and what started as a refugee

10:00 crisis quickly turned into a guerilla war. While  Rome had a superior military force, it was also

10:05 spread out and concentrated in the cities, and the  forces that were sent to confront the Goths found

10:10 the invaders fought much harder than expected. The  elites felt very little of this crisis - they were

10:15 kept safe in their walled cities - but across  the massive expanses of the Roman countryside,

10:19 the Goths quickly gained territory and claimed the  land of former Roman subjects across the Balkans.

10:24 And Theodosius may have neglected  this problem a bit too much.

10:28 The Emperor may have restored Rome’s  military in some ways, but the coffers

10:32 were still looking kind of bare after decades  of patronage under his predecessors. He raised

10:37 taxes to confront the barbarians - and was met  with rebellions from the people he ruled over.

10:41 He also cracked down on other faiths, doubling  down on Constantine’s embrace of Christianity,

10:45 and even persecuted believers of other  variants of Christianity. Soon he was

10:49 facing new rebellions in the west seeking to  end his rule, with rebel leader Magnus Maximus

10:54 declaring himself emperor in 383 and taking over  the territory of Gaul. This led to significant

11:00 losses in territory and troops until Maximus  made a failed attempt at defeating Rome itself

11:05 and was ultimately defeated in 388. Rome once  again became the greatest power on the planet.

11:10 But soon this would all change.

11:12 By 395 CE, Theodosius I would die, leaving behind  him a weakened army and no clear successor. His

11:19 two sons would each claim the empire, but neither  was a capable leader - leaving their ministers to

11:23 essentially take charge of the situation. Rather  than go to another brutal civil war only a decade

11:28 after the last, the two halves of the empire  essentially went their own separate ways - one

11:32 emperor, Arcadius, took the eastern Roman Empire,  which would become known as the Byzantine Empire

11:37 in the future, while the other son, Honorius,  would take the western part including Rome itself.

11:42 It was the biggest loss of territory for Rome yet  - and this time, there would be no going back.

11:47 The Byzantine Empire would endure, lasting  for another thousand years with a power

11:51 base in the city of Constantinople - but  it would never reach the world-defining

11:55 power of the Roman Empire. As for Rome, it  still ruled much of Europe - but its days

12:00 were drawing short. Without the massive  territory now owned by the Byzantines,

12:04 administering the empire was much more  manageable - but it also meant the massive

12:08 barbarian invasions were harder to control. The  leader of the Huns, Attila, was one of the most

12:13 feared military leaders of all time - and now  he placed his full attention on taking Rome.

12:18 It would be a death of a thousand  cuts for the Roman Empire.

12:21 Over the next eighty years, the Roman Empire dealt  with brutal attacks from the Huns on their fringes

12:26 and the Gothic population throughout the empire.  The Roman military was a shadow of what it used

12:30 to be, and it frequently found itself in retreat.  The territory of the empire shrunk piece by piece,

12:35 and Rome started to look less like a powerful  empire and more like a city in decline. Some

12:40 leaders would manage to restore the military’s  strength, but none would get it back to the level

12:43 where it could reclaim significant amounts of  territory. The empire would limp along until 476,

12:49 where one ambitious king decided it  was time to strike the final blow.

12:53 His name was Odoacer - and the  mostly-forgotten figure may have

12:56 been one of the most important people in history.

12:58 The last Emperor of Rome, Romulus  Augustulus, had a mighty name but

13:04 was only a sixteen year old boy when Odoacer  invaded. The barbarian king, surprisingly,

13:09 dealt kindly with the young king as he sacked  Rome - accepting his surrender and allowing the

13:13 boy to remain alive. He sent him away to live  with relatives, even granting him a pension,

13:17 before declaring himself the ruler of Italy.  Probably the most dramatic firing from a first

13:22 job a teenager had ever experienced! But now, the  Roman Empire was over - or was it? That depends on

13:28 how you define it, because Odoacer now ruled what  was left of it - but he was considered a foreign

13:32 occupier. The Roman Senate didn’t consider him a  legitimate Roman ruler and instead transferred the

13:37 seal of Rome to the eastern empire. And so the  greatest empire in history passed into legend.

13:42 Or did it?

13:43 The Roman empire as a government was no more,  but its greatest institution still remained - the

13:48 Roman Catholic Church. It was still in its  infancy, less than five hundred years old,

13:51 but its faith had spread very quickly and would  soon grow its roots in most of Europe. As the

13:56 Church spread, so did its power - and for  the best part of the next thousand years,

14:00 it would be the de facto government in much  of Europe. Even kings would answer to it,

14:04 and few would challenge the Pope’s  power until Henry VIII would start

14:08 his own religion when the Church  wouldn’t let him get divorced. So,

14:11 while the Roman Empire did not control Europe  anymore, the Church’s legacy far outlive it.

14:16 But why did the empire actually fall?

14:18 There is no one reason why the Roman Empire  crumbled, but many factors played a role - few

14:23 bigger than the collapse of its military. Rome’s  army was once the most powerful in the world,

14:27 and it attracted the best with good pay. But as  the empire’s coffers declined, it soon struggled

14:32 to recruit new troops effectively. This led  to Emperors filing out the ranks with foreign

14:36 mercenaries, who neither had the skills nor the  loyalty of previous armies. Many even came from

14:41 the invading armies they were fighting, and the  effectiveness of their fighting forces suffered.

14:45 They tried to make up for the personnel  problem - but that just made things worse.

14:49 Many emperors consistently overspent on  the military, but that didn’t make it any

14:53 easier to manage. The huge territory they  had to govern made it near impossible to

14:57 communicate effectively, and with no e-mail  or teams groups to share important memos,

15:01 it was often a matter of weeks or months before  key changes in policy were communicated. As the

15:06 empire got larger and larger, this became a  bigger problem - and soon the empire was more

15:10 focused on protecting its key cities than  effectively managing its whole territory.

15:14 But inside Rome itself, things  weren’t doing much better.

15:17 One of the biggest problems with Rome in its last  days was the lack of strong leadership - right up

15:22 to the top. Being Roman Emperor was not a  great job. Given that it was an appointed

15:26 position that came with near-unlimited power,  a lot of people wanted it - and that meant that

15:31 getting the job came with massive risks. At one  point between the second and third centuries,

15:35 over twenty men held the title in less than  75 years - and the most common way to be fired

15:40 from this job was with a knife between  your ribs. Turns out Julius Caesar was a

15:44 trendsetter. When an Emperor did manage  to hold onto power for years, there was

15:48 a good chance they would essentially turn the  empire into their own personal patronage mill,

15:52 appointing their allies to powerful positions. And  the Emperor’s bodyguards, the Praetorian Guard,

15:57 would often take matters into their own hands and  assassinate emperors when they became more trouble

16:02 than they were worth. With a government like this,  is it any wonder that the empire began crumbling?

16:06 All of these factors came together,  spelling the end of the Roman Empire.

16:09 For centuries, the Roman Empire had  been unchallenged on a military level.

16:13 Their expeditions would face little to no  opposition, and their army could largely

16:17 sweep into a territory and take it over as  they pleased. Conquering new territories often

16:21 meant having to build new infrastructure that  would increase quality of life in the region

16:25 in some way as well as enforcing the rule  of the Roman Empire on its newly acquired

16:29 citizens. So the army wound up being more of  an enforcement arm of the Roman government,

16:33 and it was no longer prepared to deal with  major military conflict. So when outsiders

16:37 such as the Goths came calling after being  pushed out of their territory by the Huns,

16:41 the Roman military wasn’t forimdable  enough to maintain its borders.

16:44 And it all came down to one fatal mistake.

16:47 If the military was well-prepared for this  invasion, the odds are they could have defeated

16:51 the Goth armies and defended their territory. They  were better trained and had superior weaponry than

16:55 the Goths. But once the Goths had managed to  enter the fringes of the empire, it was going to

16:59 be much harder to displace them without a major  military operation. The Romans ultimately chose

17:05 the worst option of all - they didn’t aggressively  repel the Goth invaders and defend their borders,

17:09 but they also didn’t welcome them into the empire  and take advantage of this new manpower like they

17:14 could have. Instead, they exploited them and hired  them while never letting them develop any loyalty

17:19 to the empire. This led to constant civil wars  and small military skirmishes, growing tension,

17:24 and a slow but sure loss of territory. And  it all could have been avoided if the Empire

17:29 coordinate a better response to the Goths seeking  refuge within the borders of the Roman Empire.

17:33 Want to learn more about the end  of empires? Watch “Real Reason

17:36 Ancient Egyptians Went Extinct”,  or check out this video instead.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: 16 Most Disturbing Videos From Pentagon UFO Release
