docs.text:
• Title: 16 Most Disturbing Videos From Pentagon UFO Release
  • Video ID: 6dPNiN5nf0E
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 The Pentagon just dropped its first UFO files and  it includes over 160 documents and never before

00:06 seen videos of unexplained aerial phenomena…  And some of the footage genuinely looks hard

00:11 to explain 16.

00:14 We’ll begin with one of the  shortest clips in the entire batch,

00:17 lasting just 5 seconds. Blink and you’ll  miss a dark, cigar-shaped object shooting

00:22 across the frame from the left to right. According to the Pentagon’s description,

00:26 this video was captured by an infrared sensor  aboard a U.S. military platform in May, 2022.

00:32 It was submitted to the All-domain Anomaly  Resolution Office (AARO) by U.S. Central

00:37 Command, with a report suggesting  it could be a “possible missile.”

00:41 When the footage is slowed down, that  explanation actually starts to make sense.

00:45 The shape is long and narrow, closely matching  a missile, especially as it was filmed over the

00:50 Middle East. At the same time, UFO supporters  point out that the military doesn’t usually

00:55 submit footage like this to AARO unless there’s  at least some uncertainty about what it is.

01:00 In other words, the fact it was  even flagged suggests it wasn’t

01:04 immediately and confidently identified. So, there’s a chance it could have been

01:08 something else.. 15.

01:10 The next video lasts just over a minute in total. It was also captured by US Central Command at some

01:16 point in 2020 and shared with the AARO. It’s worth noting the original reporter

01:21 made an edit, pausing the footage at the  10-second mark. They also added a note

01:26 highlighting a “small thermal signature” near  the top of the frame, shown as a white orb.

01:31 Beyond that, no other changes  were made to the footage.

01:34 After the pause, the video follows the orb as  it seems to weave from side to side through

01:38 the sky at a relatively slow speed. At times, it  disappears behind redacted sections of the frame,

01:44 and the operator cycles through different contrast  and zoom settings. Despite this, no clear details

01:49 ever actually emerge. The object just looks like  a small sphere of light, with no distinctive

01:54 features or characteristics whatsoever. Many of the videos in the UFO files are

01:59 similar to this one, captured on cameras that  weren’t designed for high-resolution recording.

02:03 On the one hand, those who believe in aliens  could argue that this may very well be some

02:08 sort of craft from another galaxy, due to  its unusual movements and unclear shape. But

02:13 skeptics just as easily point out that this  UAP could be anything from a weather balloon

02:18 to a random piece of airborne debris, like a  wedding lantern drifting away on the breeze.

02:24 14. Many of the declassified

02:26 videos take place above bodies of water, just like  PR29. This was captured over the Gulf of Oman in

02:32 2024 and submitted to AARO by US Northern Command. It’s a short clip at just 21 seconds. But it comes

02:39 with a separate mission report describing “an  object with a vertical pole or bar attached to

02:45 the bottom” that seemed to be skimming  just above the surface of the water.

02:49 The person submitting the report also suggests  that the UAP might actually be a reflection of

02:53 something moving beneath the water’s surface.  That would explain its speed and behavior.

02:58 The Pentagon itself describes the anomaly  as an “inverted teardrop” that stays mostly

03:03 centered in the sensor’s field of view  throughout the clip. It moves in a clean,

03:07 straight line across the frame, with a clear  rod-like extension sticking out from its base.

03:12 UFO enthusiasts argue that this could be an  example of a so-called ‘jellyfish UFO. There

03:17 have been other sightings of this type  of unidentified aircraft in the past.

03:21 But naysayers think it’s more likely some sort  of balloon, or even a bunch of balloons tied

03:26 together. They add that the object only  seems to be going so fast because of the

03:30 way that the video was filmed, creating a  well-documented visual phenomenon called

03:34 the ‘parallax effect,’ which can distort  the way we see and interpret moving images.

03:39 What do you think? 13.

03:41 The next video was captured in North America  and was submitted by the Department of the Army.

03:45 It’s almost 2 minutes in length and is one of the  most recent files, having been captured in 2026.

03:51 The opening frames show a camera locked onto  some sort of object, which seems to be a drone.

03:56 Suddenly, a white heat signature darts across  the screen from the right side to the left.

04:01 The camera quickly readjusts,  trying to track the anomaly,

04:04 adjusting its field of view in the process. At this point, two distinct heat-like spheres

04:09 come into view, apparently connected to a single  body as they move together in sync. For nearly

04:14 2 minutes, the camera tracks the anomaly,  zooming in and out, making the spheres appear

04:18 to shift in size as the perspective changes. Analysts studying the footage have noticed what

04:23 seems to be some sort of exhaust plume trailing  behind the object. That may hint at the true

04:28 identity of the anomaly. Experts  argue that it’s some sort of plane,

04:32 leaving a visible trail behind. The next video, however, isn’t quite

04:36 as conclusive. 12.

04:38 At more than 5 minutes in length, PR44  is longer than most of the other videos

04:43 released by the Pentagon. It was filed by the US

04:46 Central Command and captured in 2020 in an  undisclosed location in the Arabian Gulf.

04:51 While there’s no oral or written description  of this incident, the Pentagon has provided a

04:55 detailed commentary. The first 30 seconds  are pretty uneventful, but after that,

04:59 an unidentified object appears. The camera  then tracks the anomaly for around 3 minutes,

05:04 keeping it generally in the center of the frame  while adjusting both contrast and zoom levels.

05:09 Eventually, the camera stops tracking  the UAP, which then leaves the frame.

05:13 The length of this video has drawn attention,  with some analysts arguing it wouldn’t have been

05:18 tracked that long unless the operator thought  it was genuinely unusual or worth monitoring.

05:24 Others point out that even with zoom and contrast  adjustments, the footage never really sharpens.

05:29 It just remains a vague white orb, leaving plenty  of room for more mundane explanations like a drone

05:34 or balloon. 11.

05:37 Next, let’s take a look at what the Pentagon  has labeled PR36. It’s another unresolved

05:42 UAP captured by an infrared sensor  aboard a US military platform at some

05:47 point in 2020, somewhere in the Middle East. The video was accompanied by a written report,

05:51 which mentioned a “solid white object  making erratic movements above the water.”

05:56 The footage is heavily redacted, with large  black boxes obscuring much of the on-screen

06:00 action. However, we can still make out some  sort of anomaly entering the frame from the

06:04 left side after 5 seconds. The object looks like a

06:08 small white egg-shaped orb. The operator shifts between

06:11 camera settings and seems to lose sight of the  object for a moment, before locking back onto it.

06:16 For nearly 2 minutes, the UAP drifts through  the sky while the camera struggles to keep

06:21 it centered. Its speed and direction are  hard to pin down, since the operator is

06:25 constantly panning and adjusting to follow it. As the clip goes on, the operator zooms in,

06:30 making the object appear larger until it drifts  out of the top of the frame and the video ends.

06:35 UFO researchers say its shape is unusual,  with no clear wings, fins, or visible

06:40 propulsion. There’s nothing that matches the  characteristics of a conventional aircraft.

06:45 Skeptics, though, note there’s a long list of  possibilities, from balloons and lanterns to

06:50 satellites, drones, and other airborne objects  that can easily look unfamiliar on camera.

06:55 10.

06:56 File PR26 was recorded in October 2023,  somewhere around the United Arab Emirates.

07:02 It consists of 43 seconds of footage, with  a separate PDF file confirming that a UAP

07:08 of some description was spotted during a mission. The clip shows a small white mass speeding toward

07:13 the left side of the frame as the camera  struggles to keep up with it. Eventually,

07:17 the camera stops tracking the object,  which darts off out of the picture.

07:21 Analysts have slowed the footage down  and zoomed in to get a better look.

07:25 Some describe it as a mass of orbs. Others  note that it has a bird-like appearance,

07:30 with clear wing-like features and even a tail,  which becomes particularly clear when zoomed in.

07:35 As a result, opinions on this  particular clip are mixed.

07:38 Some say that it most likely was a bird or even  a fixed-wing drone. Others say it could have been

07:43 some sort of advanced, aerodynamically designed  alien craft, attempting to evade detection.

07:49 9. Next, another

07:51 very brief clip with another of those ‘blink and  you’ll miss it’ moments, but still one that the US

07:56 military felt was interesting enough to share. The clip itself, labeled PR31 and captured in

08:01 Syria in 2024, shows an aerial view of some  sort of structure, which could be a residence

08:07 or even potentially a military building. The video is only 5 seconds in length,

08:11 and it’s the first second that actually  matters. It shows a strange visual anomaly

08:16 darting erratically across the top of the  screen, before disappearing from view.

08:20 The anomaly is described by the Pentagon as  “multicolored,” though the original reporter

08:25 claimed it was more of a “misshapen  and uneven ball of white light.” They

08:29 added that a kind of “light/glare halo  effect” was produced as it passed by.

08:33 Skeptics have been quick to write this video off  as little more than lens flare. That might be the

08:38 most logical explanation of what happened here. At the same time, people argue that lens flares

08:43 usually have a more predictable pattern  of movement. This one, however, seems to

08:47 move up and down before it leaves the frame,  which could suggest that there's more to it.

08:51 Interestingly, the incident was also captured in  two more of the videos released by the Pentagon,

08:55 files PR32 and PR33. They both show the  same object but from different angles.

09:02 In video PR32, we also see a strange  flare-like phenomenon, with a curved,

09:07 almost halo-like beam of light at the  top of the video before fading from view.

09:11 PR33, meanwhile, shows the anomaly from above. For a split second, two irregular orange shapes

09:17 flash over the background,  then vanish just as quickly.

09:20 It might be easy enough for skeptics to explain  away one visual anomaly. But three separate visual

09:26 phenomena captured on three separate cameras  all at the exact same moment is slightly harder

09:31 to explain. Some UFO fans argued that this could  have been some sort of ultra-fast craft speeding

09:37 through the area. 8.

09:39 Another of the videos that has sparked debate  online is file PR35, which relates to an

09:44 unresolved UAP report from Greece in October 2023. An accompanying mission report described the sight

09:50 of a “small and circular” UAP that was  flying close to the surface of the ocean.

09:55 We see the unidentified object just a couple  of seconds into the video as it speeds along,

10:00 seemingly in a straight line. It’s worth  noting that the view here is from above,

10:04 looking down onto the sea. There are  other objects that come into frame,

10:08 which may be boats or other kinds of crafts. The anomaly, however, appears to be moving far

10:13 too fast to be any sort of naval vessel. It moves quickly toward the coastline,

10:17 but as the view shifts from water to  land, it becomes impossible to track.

10:21 Several other clips in the files show objects  that suddenly fade or disappear mid-frame,

10:26 almost as if they just drop out of view.  Again,the grainy footage fails to give any

10:30 clear details of the anomaly in question. So it’s  difficult to know exactly what we’re seeing here.

10:34 Skeptics argue that this could be any number  of man-made items. UFO enthusiasts point to

10:40 its rapid rate of travel, plus the strange way  it disappears from view, as evidence to support

10:45 their arguments that it might be something more. Many have also noted how this object is first

10:49 seen over water, which is also the case for many  of the other anomalies caught on camera in the

10:54 other files. 7.

10:56 Another mysterious object can be seen in video  PR28, which was reportedly captured over Greece

11:02 in January 2024. It’s a relatively short video,  but quite interesting, for a number of reasons.

11:08 For starters, the video was accompanied by a  separate mission report file which described

11:12 seeing some sort of “diamond-shaped” entity. They  added that it was moving at a speed of 434 knots,

11:18 or 500 miles per hour (804 kph). Perhaps the most interesting part

11:21 was that the object was only detectable  via a short-wave infrared (SWIR) sensor.

11:26 In the first 10 seconds, the screen is split  between electro-optical and SWIR views.

11:31 A faint area of contrast then appears near  the center of the split frame. It quickly

11:36 switches to full-screen SWIR, revealing an  “inverted teardrop” shape with a “vertically

11:41 linear trailing mass” hanging below it. Just before the minute mark of the video,

11:46 the operator tries to shift  to a visible spectrum view,

11:49 but the object vanishes. When they transition back  to SWIR, they are unable to locate the object.

11:54 It literally vanishes in mid-air. Some commentators have argued that this object

11:58 could be some sort of cluster of balloons, but  there are a couple of clear flaws in that theory.

12:03 Firstly, the report notes that this  object was moving extremely fast.

12:07 Second, the fact that it only showed  up on the SWIR screen suggests that

12:10 it wasn’t a normal physical object that  could easily be seen with the naked eye.

12:14 UFO enthusiasts argue it could be another  example of a ‘jellyfish’ style spacecraft.

12:20 Next, the one video that gives us arguably the  clearest look at a potential ‘flying saucer.’

12:25 6. Only 2 of the videos released

12:28 in the UFO files are listed as having taken  place in North America, and PR45 is one of them.

12:33 This particular video was reportedly  captured in the Southern United States,

12:37 home to a lot of famous US sightings in  places like Texas, Georgia, and Florida.

12:42 This video was submitted by the Department of  the Air Force and is just under a minute long.

12:46 It was captured in 2020 and shows a  targeting reticle locking onto what

12:50 first appears to be a ball of light, similar  to the objects the other clips seen so far.

12:55 The sensor narrows its field of view, zooming  in on the area of contrast to give us a

13:00 clearer look as it grows in size and detail. The most fascinating moment comes at the end,

13:05 when the small white dot suddenly appears  much larger, almost like the classic “flying

13:10 saucer” from older sci-fi films. AARO notes this change in size is

13:15 most likely just perspective, as the  US platform gets closer to the object.

13:19 In either case, the shape we see before  the anomaly exits the frame is strange.

13:24 It doesn’t appear to resemble any  known aircraft and has invited a lot

13:28 of speculation and discussion online  about what this object actually is.

13:32 5. Most of

13:33 the Pentagon’s UFO files show little more than  small white orbs or vague shapes moving across

13:39 the frame at speed. In many cases, they could  just as easily be drones, birds, or balloons.

13:44 This one, however, is a little different. File PR47 was submitted by the US

13:49 Indo-Pacific Command and captured  in 2023 somewhere around Japan.

13:53 It lasts for almost 2 minutes, and while not  much happens in the clip, it’s still triggered

13:58 plenty of discussion online. It’s all down to  the strange nature of the anomaly involved.

14:03 The Pentagon describes it as being made  up of “three distinct areas of contrast”

14:07 which “appear to maintain a fixed position  and orientation relative to one another.”

14:12 The video begins with a  vague shape in the distance.

14:15 A few seconds later, the camera zooms in and  the full nature of the anomaly is revealed:

14:20 what seemed to be one shape actually  appears to be three distinct rings

14:24 of light that seem to be connected. As the Pentagon’s description states, the

14:28 shapes maintain a fixed position and orientation  to one another, meaning that they all move as one,

14:34 and the camera tracks the anomaly for some  time before the video comes to a sudden end.

14:38 While skeptics have been able to explain most  of the videos, there hasn’t been any clear,

14:42 conclusive explanation for this one. Some say the rings might just be some

14:46 sort of visual distortion caused by lights on  an aircraft or a drone. But those who believe

14:51 in extraterrestrials argue that the appearance of  this anomaly is one of the best pieces of evidence

14:56 for alien life in the entire batch of files. And, as the next video proves, this wasn’t

15:01 the only example of a strangely shaped  object that left viewers mystified.

15:06 4. The next video was also captured and

15:08 submitted by the US Indo-Pacific Command, this  time in the East China Sea, sometime in 2024.

15:14 It’s one of the shorter clips in  the set, lasting just 10 seconds.

15:18 Again, it revolves around an anomalous  entity that doesn’t really move around

15:21 during the video itself but has a very bizarre  appearance. One that analysts have struggled

15:26 to come up with a rational explanation for. The Pentagon describes this anomaly as “a

15:30 football-shaped body with three radial  projections: one oriented vertically,

15:35 and two oriented downward at a 45-degree angle  relative to the major axis of the main mass.”

15:41 There does appear to be a larger central mass,  with two protrusions extending from the base

15:46 and another rising vertically from the rear. Analysts noted that the anomaly almost seems

15:51 to be pulsing, with wave-like movements. Some  have even described it as ‘organic’ in nature.

15:57 They believe it could be some sort of  gravity-bending spacecraft, turning the laws

16:00 of physics upside down with its very existence. From a more skeptical perspective, this could

16:05 just be a small aircraft or drone filmed  at an awkward angle. It would naturally

16:10 distort its shape and make it look unusual.  In that case, the “radial projections” are

16:14 probably just wings or stabilising fins,  rather than anything unusual or unknown.

16:19 As with the rest of the videos, there’s no way to  be entirely sure on what this anomaly actually is.

16:24 That's what makes it an ‘anomaly’. But  it’s one of the stranger-looking entities

16:29 captured on camera and shared with the public. CBS News Pentagon reporter Eleanor Watson even

16:34 included this clip in her personal list of the  six most interesting videos of the entire file

16:39 release. 3.

16:40 File PR34 was captured by a US military  platform in 2023, somewhere around

16:45 Greece. It was submitted to AARO by US Central  Command, along with a detailed mission report.

16:51 In that report, an unidentified object  is described as traveling at speeds of

16:55 “approximately 80 miles per hour” (129  kph) close to the surface of the ocean,

16:58 while “making multiple 90-degree turns.” Some of the internet’s biggest UAP and UFO experts

17:04 and analysts have called this one of, if not the  most impressive videos in the entire set of files.

17:10 It’s not hard to see why. It runs for almost three minutes,

17:13 and things kick off right away as a small  object appears in the bottom-left of the frame.

17:18 It then snaps into a sharp 90-degree turn,  darting left while still moving at high speed.

17:23 It then appears to come to a sudden  stop before turning back on itself.

17:27 In the seconds that follow, we see the object  continue to move across the screen, going left

17:31 then right and up and down. It continuously stops  and readjusts its flight path in unexpected ways.

17:37 The camera locks onto the object, which  then stops its erratic movement and

17:41 continues in a straight line for a while  before suddenly disappearing from view.

17:44 Skeptics suggest the sharp turns, sudden  directional changes and consistent speed

17:49 could indicate a drone. Others, however, say  that the object’s behavior, combined with the

17:54 way it seems to vanish in mid-air, suggest  that it could be something otherworldly.

17:59 Next, let’s talk about a video that a former  US Navy Admiral called “absolutely remarkable.”

18:04 2. PR48 is a 1 minute

18:07 and 39-second clip captured by an infrared sensor  on board a US military platform. It was recorded

18:13 at some point in 2024, at what seems to be a  wind farm, somewhere in the Indo-Pacific region.

18:18 The Pentagon’s description for this video  is quite brief, noting the appearance of

18:22 an “area of contrast,” far from the camera  that shows up as a faint glowing white orb.

18:28 What stands out here isn’t how  it looks… but how it moves.

18:31 The tiny orb flies through the wind farm,  weaving between the turbines at what seems

18:35 to be a high speed. Eventually it reaches  the end and then turns back on itself.

18:39 Former Rear Admiral Timothy Gallaudet  told reporters that this video “can’t be

18:43 explained,” but that hasn’t stopped online  analysts from attempting to unpack it.

18:48 Those on the skeptic side argued that  the object could easily be a drone,

18:51 and the internet is littered with examples of  people piloting their drones through wind farms.

18:56 However, analysts quickly countered that  argument. They point out that turbines or

19:00 windmills in offshore wind farms typically  have to be spaced at least several hundred

19:04 feet apart from one another. This object passes  from one turbine to the next at great speeds.

19:09 Some have estimated that it may even be  moving faster than the speed of sound,

19:13 which would be far beyond the  capacities of any commercial drone.

19:16 So, what’s the real explanation here? Well, some analysts have dug deeper

19:20 into the video, stabilizing it  and analyzing it frame by frame.

19:24 They claim the speed and erratic movement  are most likely an optical illusion caused

19:28 by how the footage was recorded. In their  opinion the object is actually travelling

19:32 in a fairly straight line and sits much farther  away from the turbines than it actually appears.

19:38 1. Now we come

19:40 to one of the strangest video of the entire batch  and the one that stands out the most: file PR38.

19:46 It was reportedly captured by  an infrared sensor back in 2013.

19:50 No oral or written description was provided,  but the Pentagon has added its own summary

19:55 of the scene. It describes how something  resembling “an eight-pointed star with arms

19:59 of alternating length” appears on the screen  early into the almost 2-minute-long video.

20:04 As the clip progresses, the strange star shape  moves in unusual patterns across the screen. At

20:10 times, it seems to slowly drift one way before  suddenly taking a sharp turn in a different

20:15 direction. The Pentagon’s report also notes that  the shape appears to have its own visible trail.

20:20 Halfway through the video, a second, much larger  shape appears on screen. It drifts in and out of

20:25 view a couple of times before disappearing. Soon after, the eight-pointed star eventually

20:29 speeds off the top of the  frame before the video ends.

20:32 This video generated a lot of excitement and  debate online following the files’ release.

20:37 Some viewers were understandably disturbed by  the sight of such a strange shape that appears

20:41 to move around in unnatural patterns. However, eagle-eyed analysts soon came

20:45 up with a logical explanation for the entire  video. According to them, what we’re seeing

20:50 isn’t an advanced alien spacecraft, but  a parachute flare used in conflict zones.

20:55 The flares are launched into the air and drift  down slowly under small parachutes. Because they

21:00 burn extremely hot, infrared cameras often  distort them into “starburst” shapes due to

21:05 thermal blooming, which matches what we see in  the footage. This could also explain the second

21:09 object, which looks just like a parachute. Due to the flares being lightweight,

21:13 they’re easily affected by the  wind. That would also explain why

21:16 the star seems veer around in random directions. As with the other clips, there might be a rational

21:22 explanation, but there’s just enough ambiguity  to keep people questioning what they’re seeing.

21:27 It leaves the bigger question hanging: are  we truly alone in a vast, empty universe,

21:31 or is there something else out there? The next release of files may

21:35 bring more answers… or more questions. And if these sightings already seem unsettling,

21:40 some of the most disturbing encounters of all  involve highly classified sites. Find out more in

21:45 ‘Military Can’t Explain These UFOs at US & Russian  Nuclear Weapons Sites.’ Or watch this instead.

00:00 Chinese cars are cheap, unsafe death  traps. That’s why they’re banned in the US.

00:05 That’s what you’ve been told.  It’s not the full story.

00:08 The reality is less about safety and  more about protecting a trillion-dollar

00:12 auto industry. A $12,000 EV with top  safety ratings wouldn’t just compete,

00:17 it would blow up the entire US car market  overnight. Detroit would be bankrupted.

00:22 So the US has built one of the most  aggressive protectionist barriers in

00:26 modern history to keep them out. The result  is a financial ‘iron curtain’ that will trap

00:31 the middle classes in record high auto loans,  averaging $767 per month for the next 6 years.

00:37 And that’s not even the worst part. Because, while American families are

00:41 worrying about how they’re going to cover the  cost of their family SUV, the country’s automotive

00:45 industry is preparing for something bigger. A digital ‘Pearl Harbor’ where every car on

00:50 the highway simply stops moving.

00:53 and The Kill Switch The American driveway

00:54 has become a financial crime scene. The average transaction price for a

00:58 new vehicle has crossed the $50,000 mark. If  you want a truck or an SUV, you often have

01:03 to pay significantly more than that. A Ford F-150 Raptor can cost around

01:07 $80,000. A fully loaded 2026 Chevy Suburban  High Country can hit into six figures. Even

01:14 more mainstream family vehicles come with  price tags of around $40 to $60,000… and

01:18 that’s before financing even comes into play. Because the vast majority of people can’t afford

01:23 to buy a new car outright. Instead, they opt  to pay for it through loans and leases. And

01:29 those financing options come with interest  rates, which can dramatically increase the

01:33 overall price you pay for the car you drive. By late 2025, the average new car payment

01:38 reached a jaw-dropping $767 per month. Many buyers are stretching their loans and

01:44 lease agreements out as long as they possibly can,  sometimes as far as 72, 84, or even 96 months. All

01:52 to keep the rates semi-affordable. 96 months is 8 years.

01:57 That means some Americans are financing their  vehicles for almost an entire decade, because

02:01 they have no other option. Car finance plans are  literally outlasting marriages, in some cases.

02:07 It’s the younger generations  who are being hit the hardest.

02:09 Statistics show that Gen Z drivers, aged  between 18 and 28, have reached an auto loan

02:14 delinquency rate of 7.5%. That’s significantly  higher than the national average of 5.1%.

02:21 That’s the highest level of borrower  distress seen in over a decade.

02:25 To give you some idea of just how bad the  situation has become: Take every single delinquent

02:30 car currently moving toward repossession or  already in default. Park them bumper-to-bumper,

02:35 and you’d have an unbroken line of steel  stretching from New York City to Los Angeles.

02:40 The effects of this will be felt for  decades to come. Millions of young

02:44 Americans are forced to watch their credit  scores plummet and their financial futures

02:48 break down before they’ve barely even taken  their first steps into the professional world.

02:53 The reason so many have been bound to these  multi-year loans for vehicles they can barely

02:57 afford is because they haven’t been given any  other option. They’ve been led to believe that

03:02 no other option exists. But it does.

03:04 The alternative is out there. On the other side of the world.

03:08 In China, the automotive industry is almost  like a parallel universe when compared to

03:13 its American counterpart. There, vehicles  – electric vehicles, to be precise – are

03:17 available for incredibly low prices. In 2023, one of China’s top car brands,

03:22 BYD, launched the Seagull. An electric hatchback that

03:26 retails for less than $10,000 domestically  and is available for around $20,000 in

03:31 international markets, like Mexico and Europe. This isn’t some stripped-down, barebones vehicle.

03:36 It’s a modern, sophisticated car, boasting  fast charging times, proven safety systems,

03:42 and a range of up to 250 miles (402 km). And you could buy 5 of these cars for

03:47 the same price you’d have to spend  on a single average American SUV.

03:50 Even the international prices, which  come with the added costs of tariffs,

03:54 shipping, and dealer margins, the cost  is still significantly cheaper than

03:58 what you’d pay in the US. So why isn’t it available?

04:01 Well, the US government would argue that modern  electric vehicles are vastly different from

04:06 conventional cars. They’re not just made up of  motors, brakes, and transmissions. They’re kitted

04:10 out with advanced electronic equipment, including  cameras, sensors, microphones, and telematics.

04:15 They’re ‘smartphones on wheels.’ And that scares the US government.

04:20 They believe the remote connectivity could  be exploited by China – or other foreign

04:24 agents – to spy on American citizens or  disrupt the country’s infrastructure.

04:28 The government imagines a fearful future  scenario in which Beijing has the power

04:32 to push some sort of ‘kill switch’ and instantly  disable millions of vehicles on America’s roads.

04:37 So, American consumers find themselves lumbered  with life-altering debt, forced to buy vehicles

04:42 that drain their bank accounts for years on  end. Meanwhile, the vastly more affordable

04:47 alternative is regarded by Washington as  some sort of terrifying weapon of war.

04:51 How did this happen? How did a consumer

04:53 product designed for the daily commute become  classified as a threat to national security?

04:58 In 2024, the United States

05:00 government imposed an eye-watering 100%  tariff on Chinese electric vehicles.

05:06 100%. It was a

05:07 complete economic blockade. A dramatic doubling  of the cost of these cars for American buyers.

05:12 The intention was clear. Deliberately make China’s  EVs instantly unviable in the American market.

05:18 Because if one of those cars costs around  $20,000 normally, this 100 percent tariff

05:23 adds $10,000 to its wholesale cost basis. The  price tag becomes $30,000. All of a sudden,

05:29 a car that would have seemed remarkably cheap and  attractive starts to look out of reach for some.

05:34 In other words, it’s doomed to fail. Meanwhile, the American brands

05:38 continue to monopolize the market. Imagine stepping into your local grocery store to

05:42 see that the price of a loaf of bread had suddenly  spiked by 50%. And imagine that the government

05:48 says it imposed that price change to protect  your local bakery, which charges $15 a loaf.

05:53 That’s effectively what happened here. And the speed and intensity of this

05:57 decision revealed how terrified Washington  was of these cheap Chinese cars. Because

06:01 it’s not normal trade policy to impose such  extreme tariffs on foreign products. 100%

06:07 tariffs are generally regarded as ‘extreme  measures,’ reserved for genuine emergencies.

06:12 But according to Washington,  this was an emergency.

06:15 The government argued that it would be detrimental  to allow such low-cost cars into the market. Its

06:20 argument centered on the idea that China provided  extremely high levels of subsidies and other state

06:25 support to its automotive companies. There’s some truth to that.

06:29 Beijing did subsidize its EV industry, quite  aggressively. It spent years and huge amounts

06:34 of money building up the infrastructure  needed to power its EV revolution. That

06:38 included battery manufacturing plants  and industrial scale charging systems.

06:42 But here’s the part that Washington glossed over. The US also heavily subsidizes its auto industry.

06:49 It provides literally billions of dollars’ worth  of subsidies through the Inflation Reduction

06:54 Act (IRA). There’s massive manufacturing  grants for the big dogs of the industry,

06:59 like Ford and GM. There’s also up to $7,500 in tax  credits for consumers who buy domestically-made

07:06 vehicles. The big auto firms received enormous  and low interest loans to help them invest in

07:11 EV technologies. It effectively shifted the  risk of the EV transition away from these

07:16 companies and onto the American taxpayers. So, while the government was criticizing

07:21 China over subsidies, it was guilty  of doing the exact same thing.

07:25 It was never about “Subsidies are bad.” It was always “China’s subsidies

07:30 could threaten our subsidies.” So we come to the frightening truth.

07:34 The end of free market capitalism  in the American automotive sector.

07:37 It’s no longer a battle between brands to see  which ones deliver the most efficient engineering.

07:42 Or who can optimize their manufacturing to produce  the very best cars at the very best prices.

07:47 It’s something much uglier. A market manipulated by the American government.

07:51 Washington is picking and choosing the  ‘winners’ of its automotive industry.

07:55 It’s building financial fortresses  around them to keep everyone else out.

07:59 It makes false claims about ‘fair  play’ and ‘safety.’ But ultimately,

08:02 the only reason the tariff exists is  to make sure American consumers can

08:06 only buy EVs subsidized by Washington. But if it's not about fair competition,

08:11 who actually demanded this 100% wall?

08:14 Think of the American automotive industry and  3 big names immediately come to mind: General

08:20 Motors, Ford, and Stellantis, the parent company  of well known brands like Chrysler and Jeep.

08:25 Together, they represent the ‘Empire’ of Detroit.  For decades, they dominated the auto market. They

08:31 shaped the face of suburban America, controlled  the roads, and impacted entire regional economies.

08:37 As they grew bigger and wealthier,  their power grew with them.

08:40 Before long, they weren’t just impacting towns and  cities, but entire states. This in turn increased

08:45 their political influence in DC. As time went by,  these companies used their influence and wealth to

08:51 rewrite the rules of the American auto market  in ways that would make them even more money.

08:56 That meant a gradual shift away from  affordable passenger cars towards larger,

09:00 heavier, and more luxurious vehicles. It happened slowly. But as the years passed,

09:05 certain kinds of cars began to vanish  from the nation’s roads. Small sedans

09:09 and compact hatchbacks disappeared,  along with other entry-level vehicles

09:13 that are common in other countries around the  world. The ‘Big Three’ shifted towards larger

09:17 vehicles with larger profit margins. As far as their bottom lines were

09:21 concerned, this shift made a lot of sense. Companies like Ford make far more money selling

09:26 full-size pickup trucks and premium SUVs than  they ever would selling simple family hatchbacks.

09:32 By focusing more on these high-margin vehicles  and phasing out the smaller alternatives,

09:36 they left buyers with fewer and fewer options.  Eventually, they reached the stage they’d always

09:40 dreamed of: everyone had to buy a $50,000 car  if they wanted to get from point A to point B.

09:46 But this entire model – and the very  survival of the Big Three firms – was

09:50 dependent on ensuring that no cheaper  competitors were able to enter the market.

09:54 There could be no other affordable  option for the American public.

09:58 Then, along came Chinese EV manufacturers,  offering vehicles like the Seagull s, all

10:04 for low price tags of around $12,000. America’s auto industry can’t compete with that.

10:10 The Big Three weren’t going to let that happen. So, they started to leverage that power they’d

10:15 amassed in Washington over the years. They used  every weapon in their arsenal and every trick

10:19 in their playbook to preserve the status quo.  It ultimately boiled down to pouring massive

10:24 amounts of money into lobbying efforts aimed at  the likes of senate subcommittees and executive

10:29 policymakers. Their objective was clear. Keep China out.

10:33 To do that, they framed Chinese EVs not just as an  economic challenge, but as an industrial invasion.

10:39 One that America needed to defend itself against. They warned of a ‘Solar Panel-style’ collapse of

10:44 the automotive industry, reminding lawmakers of  how cheap Chinese solar panel systems entered

10:48 the US market. Local brands were undercut and the  domestic solar sector was effectively wiped out.

10:54 They said the exact same situation would happen  in the automotive industry. But on an even larger

10:59 scale. Assembly lines that had been running  for decades in Detroit and elsewhere would

11:03 go dark and millions of jobs would be lost. But Detroit couldn’t just come out and say “We

11:09 don’t want those cheap Chinese cars coming  here, because we can’t compete with them.”

11:12 They needed a more concrete and convincing  argument. Something that would really

11:16 resonate with the public. And they found it.

11:19 Ask the average American what they

11:21 think about Chinese cars, and many would  undoubtedly bring up the topic of safety.

11:25 They might talk about how Chinese companies  “cut corners.” They might mention the “dangerous

11:30 batteries” that can blow up at any time. Or  even the lack of “rigorous security tests.”.

11:34 Some would even describe  Chinese cars as “death traps.”

11:37 These ideas and stereotypes are deeply  ingrained in the American media landscape

11:42 and the wider public perception  of Beijing’s automotive industry.

11:45 And there’s a reason for that. But it’s not the one you’ve been led to believe.

11:49 Sure, there were early catastrophic failures  like zero star crash tests and cabin collapses

11:55 in 2005. But it’s also the result of years  of propaganda and brainwashing campaigns,

12:01 bought and paid for by Detroit automotive giants. For years, Ford, GM, and others built and spread

12:07 the narrative that China’s cars were unsafe.  It was an incredibly useful narrative for them.

12:12 Fear is a powerful force. If people were frightened of

12:15 Chinese vehicles, they’d never want to buy one. What’s more, they’d more happily agree to pay a

12:20 significantly higher price for cars with a “Made  in the USA” sticker on the back. That extra $20 or

12:26 $30,000 was the cost of keeping their family safe. Suddenly, companies like Ford looked noble and

12:32 honorable. They were going the extra mile  to protect their drivers and passengers.

12:36 Chinese firms were painted as the evil,  money-hungry ones, shunning safety in

12:41 favor of cheaper and easier manufacture. That all falls apart when you look closer.

12:46 The myth of the “dangerous Chinese car” was  well and truly shattered when vehicles like

12:50 the BYD Dolphin and Atto 3 entered the highly  regulated European market. If they really were

12:56 deathtraps on wheels, they’d have zero chance  of being sold in places like France and Germany.

13:01 If the stereotypes were true, these cars  would fail the European New Car Assessment

13:06 Program (NCAP). It’s one of the most comprehensive  vehicle safety checks in the entire world.

13:12 They didn’t. They passed with flying colors.

13:15 Both the Dolphin and the Atto 3 earned 5-star  NCAP safety ratings. They either matched or

13:21 even exceeded the scores of some of  America’s best-rated vehicles, like

13:24 the Ford Mustang Mach-E and the Tesla Model 3. As far as ‘exploding batteries’ were concerned…

13:30 That myth got busted, too. BYD’s own ‘Blade Battery’ easily passed the

13:34 industry standard ‘nail penetration test’. It’s  designed to simulate the type of damage that can

13:39 cause batteries to suddenly burst into flames. The Chinese manufacturer even shared footage

13:44 online showing nails entering its battery  cells, without them catching fire. It was

13:48 a feat that many of the Western world’s  NMC batteries were unable to replicate.

13:53 The vehicles passed test after test and  met one safety standard after another.

13:58 The “unsafe Chinese car” narrative fell apart. That’s not to say that Chinese cars are perfect,

14:04 or that none of them have any safety concerns  whatsoever. There are always areas of improvement.

14:10 But what the tests revealed was that Chinese  cars were no more dangerous than American ones.

14:15 In many aspects they were even safer. With the safety myth destroyed,

14:19 the government needed a new, unassailable  reason to keep these cars out of the US.

14:23 Enter, the Trojan Horse.

14:25 As the economic and safety-related  arguments began to crumble,

14:28 Washington orchestrated a swift and surprising  pivot in an even more extreme direction.

14:33 It began to argue that Chinese cars  were a threat to national security.

14:37 While that might sound ludicrous, DC’s  argument was put together in a cold and

14:41 calculated fashion. It leveraged decades of public  indoctrination and widely-held fears about China,

14:46 its ruling communist party, and the threat  it posed to the American way of life.

14:51 The groundwork was laid in 2024. The US  Department of Commerce (DOC) carried out

14:56 an investigation into the so-called ‘systemic  risks’ posed by connected vehicles originating

15:01 in China and other countries that could be  classed as adversaries of the United States.

15:06 The findings of that investigation were alarming. The DOC explained in excruciating detail how

15:12 modern vehicles could be mobilized  into platforms of cyber warfare.

15:16 The investigators theorized a nightmare  scenario, a kind of ‘Digital Pearl Harbor,’

15:21 in which Beijing would hold the power to disrupt  American society on an unprecedented scale.

15:26 Let’s say tensions ramp up in the South  China Sea. The long awaited Chinese

15:30 invasion of Taiwan begins. At that very same moment,

15:33 in the United States, hundreds of thousands  or even millions of American citizens sit

15:38 behind the wheels of their Chinese EVs. To ensure that America doesn’t interfere

15:42 with its immediate invasion plans, China’s  intelligence agency could deploy a malicious

15:46 over the air software payload to  every single one of those vehicles.

15:50 Programmed to bypass the usual systems, the  payload would be immediately downloaded and

15:54 installed in each car. Within seconds, they would  become utterly and entirely immobile. Steering

15:59 systems would lock up. Electronic parking brakes  would engage. Power inverters would shut down.

16:04 Drivers would lose control of their cars before  they knew what was going on. In the blink of

16:08 an eye, countless vehicles traveling across  highways like the I-95 or the labyrinth-like

16:13 arteries of Downtown Manhattan would seize up. All  frozen by some invisible but all-powerful force.

16:19 It would be catastrophic infrastructure paralysis. There would be accidents. Injuries. Deaths.

16:24 Destruction. Emergency services would struggle  to respond. Shipping corridors would be choked

16:29 and impassable. Logistics would collapse. The domestic economy would collapse.

16:33 It might sound exaggerated.  But the technology exists.

16:36 Cars today are fitted with complex webs  of electronic control units and networking

16:41 devices. They have the power to collect  and share countless pieces of data, every

16:45 single second. They rely on software to control  every core feature and functionality, from the

16:51 steering assist to the power distribution system. And, ultimately, the brands that make these cars

16:56 hold the power to control exactly how they work. They’re the ones that can make and deploy

17:01 important firmware updates. So it’s not all that crazy to

17:04 imagine how that sort of power could be  used in a dangerous or destructive way.

17:09 And once that idea is out there, DC has the  justification it needs to effectively ban

17:13 these vehicles. The Big Three get what  they want while building a narrative

17:16 that this is all for the public good. But tariffs only apply to cars shipped

17:20 from China. So what happens when the  cars are being built right next door?

17:24 With the tariff wall in place,

17:26 it looked like the US government had won. It had made it all but impossible for Beijing

17:30 to bring its EVs into the American market and  have even a slight chance of competing with the

17:35 likes of Ford and General Motors. At least, that’s how it seemed.

17:38 But China wasn’t going to give up that easily.  It didn’t take long for Beijing’s strategies

17:42 to spot a loophole. They realized that the  100% tariffs applied based on strict Country

17:48 of Origin rules for manufacturing and major  components. That meant assembling cars in Mexico

17:53 only bypasses taxes if enough parts are made  locally, not just by avoiding Chinese ports.

18:00 So, if it can make and export them from somewhere  much closer to home for the American consumer,

18:05 then those tariffs would, in effect, be nullified. So, the big Chinese brands, like BYD and MG,

18:10 started to look south, to Mexico. They made plans and quickly put them

18:14 into action. They agreed land deals and  broke ground on brand new, multi-billion

18:18 dollar automotive manufacturing plants on Mexican  soil… just a short distance from the US border.

18:23 From a business perspective,  it was a stroke of genius.

18:26 Mexico is already a major  automotive manufacturing hub.

18:29 It has reasonably cheap labor and a proven  track record of shipping vehicles into the US.

18:34 From a legal perspective, the  move made a lot of sense too.

18:37 It was a calculated play on China’s part  to bypass the legal architecture of the

18:41 United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, or  USMCA, the modern-day successor to NAFTA.

18:47 According to the provisions set out in the USMCA,  any automobile manufactured in one of the three

18:52 signatory nations can cross the borders of  the other nations duty-free. But it has to

18:57 follow certain rules and requirements. Each vehicle must derive 75% of its

19:02 components and structural value from  North American labor and materials.

19:06 By bringing its manufacturing infrastructure to  Mexico, making use of local steel, and relying on

19:11 Mexican assembly workers, Beijing was confident  it could easily pass the 75% restriction.

19:17 The cars from “Chinese imports”  to “North American products.”

19:20 It was like China had found a secret  backdoor into the American market.

19:24 And if its plan worked, it would soon be able  to make vehicles like the BYD Seagull in Mexico,

19:29 transport them over the border and into Texas.  All while paying zero taxes in the process.

19:34 Again, the US was desperate  to stop this from happening.

19:37 A desperate scramble broke out in the Office of  the United States Trade Representative (USTR).

19:42 Washington diplomats reached out to their Mexican  counterparts and argued if these Chinese ‘Trojan

19:47 Horses’ entered their territory, they’d be in  direct violation of the spirit of the USMCA.

19:52 They even threatened to deploy  aggressive measures in response.

19:56 This included the possible invocation of the  USMCA’s “Sunset Clause,” which could lead to the

20:01 entire agreement being torn apart. It would have  disastrous consequences for the Mexican economy.

20:06 Mexico relented. Its government began

20:09 pulling back some of the incentives it had  previously offered to Chinese auto firms.

20:12 Suddenly it was trickier and harder for them  to set up their facilities inside the country.

20:17 While some of those companies announced  that they were pausing their Mexican plans,

20:20 others went ahead with the expansion. The  future remains increasingly uncertain,

20:24 with a very real possibility that more Chinese  auto plants will inevitably appear in Mexico.

20:29 But even if the cars are assembled in Mexico,  the software that powers them will still be

20:34 controlled in Shenzhen. Which brings us to the

20:36 root cause of the entire ban.

20:38 Trade disputes, corporate lobbying, and public  relations campaigns are all just background noise.

20:43 The deepest and darkest underlying cause of the  industrial conflict is down to geopolitical drama.

20:49 We’re witnessing a dramatic, generational,  and irreversible shift on the global stage:

20:54 the gradual but definitive decoupling  of the United States and China.

20:58 Both nations have had their disagreements  over the years. But they’ve tended to put

21:01 those issues to one side to enjoy the  benefits of globalized trade. Consumer

21:05 goods are able to flow easily across oceans  and beyond borders based purely on the rules

21:10 of supply and demand. Political posturing  or disagreements are pushed to the side.

21:14 Until now. It’s being replaced

21:16 by something very different. An era in which  the world’s great powers aren’t interested.

21:21 They want competition. In this new age, the humble

21:24 automobile has undergone a profound  transformation. It has turned from a

21:28 mechanical product into a software-defined asset. The cars of today are networked sensor arrays,

21:33 operating within physical and digital boundaries  dictated by their manufacturer. And state powers

21:39 support and subsidize those manufacturers. Whoever controls the software and operating

21:44 systems of those vehicles ultimately holds a  significant amount of leverage over their users.

21:49 That reveals a frightening truth. Automotive companies today,

21:52 no matter whether they’re American, Chinese, or  European, all have the power to remotely ‘brick’

21:57 vehicles from across the globe. And the repercussions are huge.

22:01 Let’s say a consumer defaults on their car’s  lease, or a vehicle is reported as stolen. The

22:05 corporation behind it can simply issue a command  from hundreds or even thousands of miles away,

22:10 and bring it to a sudden stop. With the  click of a mouse or the tap of a screen,

22:14 these companies can turn $50,000 vehicles  into immobile blocks of plastic and metal.

22:19 The infrastructure is there. It’s integrated into  every new EV as it rolls off the assembly lines.

22:25 This is the genuine threat facing America. According to Chinese law, all domestic

22:30 corporate entities and citizens are  legally obligated to support, assist,

22:33 and cooperate with national intelligence efforts. If a car company like BYD or Geely is contacted

22:39 by the CCP and asked to share access to  its networks of real-time location data,

22:44 camera feeds, interior recordings, or even  remote vehicle control systems… it can’t refuse.

22:50 It has to comply. This potentially puts

22:52 the Chinese government in charge of millions  of vehicles in dozens of countries worldwide.

22:57 It’s the ‘Digital Pearl Harbor’ scenario… But worse.

23:00 China doesn’t just have the power to shut down  these vehicles as and when it wants, it could also

23:05 turn them into intelligence gathering assets. The  cars could harvest everything from biometrics to

23:10 acoustic data from their customers. It’s easy to  imagine how such immense power might be misused.

23:16 It is an unprecedented threat that no  sovereign superpower can possibly allow.

23:20 So, Washington’s ban on China’s vehicles isn’t  the product of paranoia, after all. Nor is it

23:25 entirely about keeping the market in the hands of  the biggest domestic brands. It is, at its core,

23:30 a national security decision. It’s about the US locking the

23:33 gates against a potentially existential threat. So far, it’s succeeded. But at what cost? Because,

23:39 in blocking out these vehicles, we may  have sabotaged our future, in the process. The climate crisis.

23:45 Net zero. Renewable energy.

23:47 For years now, and with increasing  regularity, the American public has

23:50 heard these terms repeated ad nauseam by  politicians and policymakers. They’ve been

23:55 lectured about the perils of global warming and  the importance of shifting away from fossil fuels.

23:59 Yet, at the highest levels, in the  halls of power itself, the American

24:03 political machine has operated in a blatantly  hypocritical and contradictory way. It’s saying

24:08 one thing but doing the exact opposite. Policymakers say that they’re committed

24:12 to these ambitious environmental frameworks  and the concept of ‘Net Zero’ by 2050. They

24:18 share plans for mass-scale adoption of  electric vehicles to help ‘decarbonize’

24:22 the transportation sector and slash emissions. Yet their decisions paint a different story.

24:28 When those same people were confronted  with a choice between achieving their

24:31 eco-friendly goals and maintaining some sort of  nebulous protectionist posture against China…

24:36 They chose the latter. Without a moment of hesitation.

24:40 They erected a tariff wall and, in doing  so, they didn’t just ban Chinese cars,

24:45 they systematically outlawed the world’s most  efficient supply of clean energy transport.

24:50 That wouldn’t matter so much if the US was  already on the way towards matching China’s

24:54 EV infrastructure. But it’s not.

24:56 It’s miles behind. Research models suggest that

24:59 Washington policies, restrictions on affordable  imports, and raw material constraints are slowing

25:04 electric vehicle adoption in the United States. As  a result, the projected timeline for reaching 50%

25:09 electric vehicle adoption in new passenger vehicle  sales has been pushed back from 2034 to 2039.

25:16 With the rate the climate crisis is evolving,  5 years isn’t a small period of time.

25:20 It’s enormous. And it’ll have

25:22 massive consequences for the environment. During that time, millions more internal

25:26 combustion engines will be made, sold, and  driven along American roads. They will burn

25:31 through billions of gallons of fossil fuels  and pump metric tons of carbon dioxide and

25:36 pollutants into the atmosphere. The hypocrisy is transparent.

25:40 The state says it wants to save the planet,  but has made it impossible for citizens to

25:45 buy the affordable vehicles required to do so. Just because they happen to come from China.

25:50 The fact is, if Chinese cars were allowed  into the market, people would buy them. That

25:54 would be better for the well-being of the  planet. Instead, people are instead faced

25:58 with a choice between conventional SUVs  or even more expensive American EVs.

26:03 They don’t have the financial luxury to afford  these expensive models. So the negative effects

26:07 of fossil fuel cars continue to perpetuate. In banning the $12,000 EV, the US government

26:13 has turned the green transition from a mass-market  movement into a luxury lifestyle statement. It’s

26:19 reserved exclusively for the upper middle class. The average American consumer is told to do their

26:24 bit, while actively being priced out of the  opportunity. They’re forced to stand on the

26:28 sidelines and watch the world burn. They have become the ultimate

26:32 casualty in a war they never wanted.

26:34 The United States has made a definitive  choice that will resonate for years to come.

26:39 Washington had the opportunity to push an  affordable ‘Green Revolution’. One that would

26:43 unite the global economy. Instead, it’s decided  to shut its gates, lock its doors, and develop a

26:48 high cost, high debt, fortress economy. The era of the affordable American

26:53 car is well and truly over. It has been liquidated part by part.

26:57 In its place sits a new system. One with a $25,000 price floor that is manipulated

27:02 to keep average Americans stuck in endless cycles  of high-interest loans, over and over again.

27:08 A new Iron Curtain has fallen across the  global industrial landscape. Yet unlike

27:12 the political barrier of the 20th century, the  new curtain is made of very different materials.

27:17 Like 100% tariffs used to shield monopolies  from competition. Trade restrictions turned

27:22 into geopolitical weapons to block the global  integration of manufacturing and supply chains.

27:27 And software kill switches built into everyday  products that allow governments to use them as

27:32 instruments of political power. Behind all of this is you.

27:35 The American consumer. The middle and working

27:38 classes have been isolated, locked into  economic systems that leech their wages.

27:43 They’re blocked from accessing more innovative  and eco-friendly alternatives. They’re denied

27:47 the ability to reduce their personal carbon  footprints. They’re monitored continuously

27:51 by technologies that are more suited to  serving national security agendas than

27:55 making their lives easier. This is the true reality

27:58 of the global economy today. Cheap Chinese cars weren’t kept out of America to

28:02 save you. They were kept out to preserve a system  of corporate survival and geopolitical dominance.

28:08 And you were left to pick up the bill. Chinese electric vehicles aren't the only

28:16 rising competition, and a rapidly changing  automotive landscape. Discover what's really
