00:00 We’re back with even more insane conspiracy  theories! Some might have seemed to be wild

00:05 and even totally implausible at one time, and some  even spent years totally obscured from the public,

00:10 but all of these were eventually revealed – at  least in part – to be true! And some of them are

00:15 even stranger than fiction, from shady government  scandals to aliens buried out in the desert,

00:21 to ghosts at sea that started a war, and  even a secretive meeting between some of

00:25 the wealthiest people in the world – that  involved strange rituals in front of a big

00:30 stone owl?! These are the Insane Conspiracy  Theories That Turned Out to be True, Part Two!

00:36 Let’s start with one that seems so obvious  that it would almost be more surprising if

00:40 it weren’t true, and that’s the theory that  the government is watching your every move.

00:44 It’s hardly an overstatement to say that,  in our modern, technology-driven world,

00:48 you’re never more than a few feet from a camera,  whether it’s part of a closed circuit system or

00:52 even those that are found near roads designed  to catch speeding drivers. But think about how

00:57 many other places you’d find a camera; your  smartphone’s got multiple, and your laptop or

01:02 PC will likely have a webcam, to name just a few.  What’s stopping the government from using these

01:07 devices to spy on you? Well, actually, nothing –  in fact, it’s completely legal for them to do so.

01:13 Mass surveillance is hardly a new innovation, as  dystopian as the concept might feel. In the United

01:19 States alone, there exist multiple federal law  enforcement and intelligence agencies that serve

01:23 the function of conducting surveillance over the  population, like the National Security Agency,

01:29 the Federal Bureau of Investigation, and the  Central Intelligence Agency. While this is

01:33 often done in the name of security, to protect  the public from the threat of acts of terrorism,

01:38 surveillance on this scale is also a tool used  to silence political dissent, often by targeting

01:43 particular individuals and organizations. Although it generally requires exploiting

01:48 software security vulnerabilities, the government  can technically use cameras in your devices to spy

01:53 on you. The FBI even has access to technology  that can remotely access webcams without

01:58 triggering the light that indicates the camera  is active – and they’ve been able to do this for

02:04 years! Remote activation tools – known by the  fitting acronym RATs – are a form of spyware

02:09 that the FBI uses for criminal investigations.  ‘Ratting’ is reportedly only done sparingly,

02:15 but it’s hardly reassuring knowing that they  can watch us without us being able to even tell.

02:20 In 2013, a former contractor who had worked for  the NSA leaked documents that exposed some of

02:25 the extensive surveillance programs  conducted by the NSA, FBI, and CIA.

02:30 The now infamous Edward Snowden revealed that  massive swathes of data had been gathered

02:34 by these agencies from sources, including  social media websites and email exchanges,

02:40 in order to form comprehensive profiles of  US citizens based on their online activity.

02:44 The leaks also highlighted the potential for  governments to remotely access the cameras

02:48 and microphones of personal electronic devices  for these purposes. So, it’s not just hackers,

02:54 stalkers, and other cyber criminals to be wary of  when you’re perusing the internet; the government

02:59 could be keeping an eye on you, too. After all,  having your own FBI agent watching you has long

03:04 been a running joke online, featured in various  memes. Ours is called Jonathon, and even though we

03:09 can’t see him, we know he can see us – unsettling! From one tale of shady governmental overreach to

03:16 an attempt to suppress political opposition  that became so infamous, that its name has

03:20 been immortalized in the conspiracy theory  hall of fame. It was 1972, and the several

03:26 month-long build-up towards the next presidential  election was already underway, with Republican

03:31 President Richard Nixon running against Democrat  candidate George McGovern. Little did the public

03:36 know that a discovery was about to be made  that threatened to upend the entire election

03:40 process. And the President himself knew about it. Several months before the election, Frank Wills,

03:46 a security guard working at an office, apartment,  and hotel complex in Washington DC, discovered

03:51 that various locks around the complex had been  tampered with. Suspecting a possible break-in,

03:56 Wills called the police, who arrived and  apprehended five burglars who had forced

04:01 an entry into the offices of the Democratic  National Committee. But this wasn’t about a

04:05 score because these weren’t ordinary burglars.  While inside, they had intended to steal several

04:10 important campaign documents and attempted  to plant bugs to listen in on phone lines.

04:15 Upon investigation, it was discovered that  four of these five men were former agents

04:19 of the Central Intelligence Agency and had been  involved in actions taken against Cuban leader

04:24 Fidel Castro. At the time, though, the press  reported that the attempted burglars were Cubans,

04:29 despite only three of them having Cuban  heritage. The fifth was a security chief

04:33 for the Committee to Re-Elect the President, or  CREEP for short. They had conspired with a former

04:39 FBI agent who was a counsel for CREEP, as well as  another high-ranking CIA officer who’d recently

04:45 been appointed to the staff of the White House. As this tangled web began to unravel, it seemed to

04:50 point to one man being at the center: President  Nixon himself. He made aggressive attempts to

04:55 cover up the scandal and was believed to have  even hired the five men in the first place. But

04:59 this did little to prevent journalists from The  Washington Post from uncovering his role in the

05:03 conspiracy. This botched attempt at an act of  blatant political sabotage was what ultimately led

05:08 to the downfall of the Nixon administration, with  almost seventy people being impeached as a result.

05:14 Nixon resigned from office in 1974 since Congress  couldn’t impeach him if he were to step down;

05:20 thus, he avoided facing criminal charges. The  scandal would eventually be named after the

05:24 hotel it started in: the Watergate complex. The  Watergate Scandal forever changed US politics,

05:31 leading many Americans to think more  critically about their leaders – after all,

05:34 if the President could use his power to attempt to  cover up something like this and get away with it,

05:39 then it didn’t exactly smack of being trustworthy. As if mass surveillance and an administration

05:44 trying to snuff out its opposition secretly  weren’t enough government overreach for you,

05:48 there’s an arguably darker conspiracy theory  that turned out to be true. One that might have

05:53 led to thousands of Americans being poisoned…  by the government! A while ago, an alarming

05:58 factoid was circulating on the Internet that,  in 1926, the federal government had poisoned

06:03 alcohol in an effort to discourage the public from  drinking during Prohibition. This was, of course,

06:08 a real thing – well, Prohibition was, anyway – as  between 1920 and 1933, it became illegal to sell,

06:15 produce or even transport alcoholic beverages. But  naturally, this didn’t stop people from buying,

06:20 drinking, and often making their own booze. According to the claim, though, the government

06:24 added poisonous substances to alcohol as a way  to crack down on the number of people drinking

06:28 it. Apparently, this event caused an estimated ten  thousand deaths before Prohibition was eventually

06:34 ended in 1933. But the truth is a little more  nuanced. The government wasn’t exactly sneaking

06:39 into black market distilleries and emptying  barrels marked with a skull and crossbones

06:44 into the booze like a cartoonish supervillain. In actuality, when the 18th Amendment was passed,

06:50 bringing Prohibition into effect, this led to  regulatory agencies encouraging measures to make

06:55 alcohol used for industrial purposes undrinkable  by adding lethal chemicals like methyl alcohol

07:01 or wood alcohol to grain alcohol, making it  poisonous. This wasn’t done to any alcohol that

07:07 was intended for human consumption. Still, one of  the ways that criminals tried to make money during

07:11 Prohibition was by producing their own illegal  booze to sell on the black market – and can you

07:17 guess what they stole to use as a key ingredient?  Yep, the now-tainted industrial alcohol. While

07:23 the government didn’t set out to purposely kill  drinkers, it did seek to stop making industrial

07:27 alcohol just so darn tasty to drink, leading to  a number of alcohol poisoning deaths from those

07:33 who bought booze from less than stellar brewers. From bad booze to Big Tobacco: did big cigarette

07:38 companies really try to cover up the fact that  smoking can kill? It seems almost quaint that

07:43 anyone would try to lie about that, especially if  you’re used to seeing the often graphic ‘Smoking

07:48 Kills’ PSAs on TV and similarly unpleasant  warnings on packs of cigarettes to dissuade

07:53 people from buying them. Or so that the  companies making them can at least say

07:57 they’re being honest about it. But back at the  beginning of the 1950s, new evidence was emerging

08:01 that seemed to show an indisputable link between  smoking cigarettes and developing lung cancer.

08:07 Naturally, people knowing your product  is deadly can be pretty bad for business;

08:11 never mind the moral and ethical implications of  slowly killing your consumers, tobacco companies

08:16 had their bottom lines to worry about! As  a result, they released A Frank Statement

08:21 to Cigarette Smokers in January of 1954, an  advertisement campaign designed to dispute the

08:26 recent scientific studies that linked smoking  with its dangerous effects on people's health.

08:31 The tobacco industry’s campaign was intended  to cast uncertainty on the recent scientific

08:36 findings and not only sway consumer opinions on  smoking but also undermine efforts by regulatory

08:41 bodies to impose better guidelines on cigarette  companies. These then could have led to better

08:47 standards and practices, potentially even making  cigarettes less addictive and thus reducing the

08:52 risk of causing further cases of lung cancer. The entire industry spent decades using PR

08:58 strategies to knowingly deny the link between  smoking and its serious negative health impacts,

09:03 including refuting the scientific evidence that  connected smoking with increased lung cancer cases

09:08 in the USA and UK, misleading consumers into  believing their products actually had benefits

09:13 to their health. Refuted the potential harms of  inhaling secondhand smoke, claimed that nicotine

09:18 wasn’t addictive, and large cigarette corporations  even established organizations designed to produce

09:23 their own research that specifically aligned  with the claims they made. All while knowing

09:28 that smoking does kill, in the interest of  protecting their profits over public health.

09:32 From no smoke without fire -or potentially fatal  illness- to suspicions of a conspiracy within

09:37 the world of sports. Accusations of cheating,  bribery and rigging have been present in every

09:43 major league for every sport in history,  from football and basketball to even the

09:47 boring stuff like fishing. But if hidden weights  and frozen supermarket fish fillets stashed in

09:52 prize catches prove anything, it’s that sometimes  these accusations are warranted. This was revealed

09:58 to be the case with the Black Sox Scandal. In a pivotal championship bout of the 1919

10:02 World Series, American League champs, the Chicago  White Sox, were playing the Cincinnati Reds,

10:08 champions of the National League. Over  the course of a best-of-nine series,

10:11 the Cincinnati Reds beat the White Sox five to  three, crowning them the winners of that year’s

10:16 World Series. But almost immediately after, rumors  of an organized conspiracy among members of the

10:21 Chicago White Sox began spreading. Eight players  in particular were accused: the two pitchers,

10:27 Eddie Cicotte and Claude ‘Lefty’ Williams, the  team’s first baseman, Arnold ‘Chick’ Gandil;

10:32 shortstop Charles ‘Swede’ Risberg, the Sox’s third  baseman George ‘Buck’ Weaver, two outfielders

10:38 including power hitter ‘Shoeless Joe’ Jackson  and Oscar ‘Happy’ Felsch, as well as an infielder

10:43 named Fred McMullin. And yes, those are some of  the best 1920s nicknames we’ve ever heard too.

10:49 Although the suspicions of a conspiracy among  these players died down as the following year’s

10:53 season started, in September of 1920, a grand  jury began to investigate the allegations,

10:59 particularly as they pertained to gamblers  invading the sport of baseball. Four of the

11:03 accused players – Eddie Cicotte, Lefty Williams,  Happy Felsch and Shoeless Joe Jackson – admitted

11:10 that they threw the 1919 World Series in exchange  for bribes. Court records suggest that the players

11:16 received between seventy and a hundred  thousand dollars for the loss; however,

11:19 following a public trial in 1921, the indicted  players were acquitted thanks to insufficient

11:24 evidence. Suspiciously, the original confessions  from the players had disappeared from the grand

11:29 jury’s files. All eight of the now dubbed  ‘Black Sox’ were subsequently banned for life

11:35 from continuing to play professional baseball. Jumping from the Black Sox Scandal to Operation

11:40 Snow White, did a crazed cult really try to  scrub any unfavorable reports about them by

11:45 sending out thousands of undercover agents  to infiltrate government agencies? Well,

11:49 if you know anything about the Church of  Scientology, their questionable belief system,

11:53 and their -allegedly- abusive practices, then this  might not come as much of a surprise. We’re not

11:58 looking to sully the good name of Mr. Tom Cruise  here at The Infographics Show, but if you’re

12:03 -allegedly- part of a cult that -allegedly- has  a torture chamber out in the California desert,

12:08 then maybe it is not surprising that your  ex-wife, Katie Holmes, and her daughter would

12:12 start to think twice before hanging out with you. During the seventies, the largest infiltration of

12:17 the United States government in history  took place. However, rather than coming

12:20 from outside forces like opposing nations  or even an invasion of body snatchers,

12:25 it came from within the US. Covert agents from the  Church of Scientology enacted what became known

12:30 as Operation Snow White, wherein they installed  wiretaps, stole documents, and used various other

12:36 criminal means in an attempt to destroy anything  bad about them and their founder, L. Ron Hubbard,

12:41 on record. You know, the exact kind of thing  you do if your organization is entirely

12:46 trustworthy and has nothing to hide, right? Gaining access to the likes of the IRS,

12:51 the DEA, foreign embassies, and a total of 136  government agencies, these Scientology agents’

12:57 other primary goal was to protect the Church’s tax  exemption status in order to avoid them having to

13:03 pay millions in taxes. The US government wasn’t  about to stand for this, however and retaliated by

13:09 sending 156 of their own agents on organized raids  of various locations linked with Scientologists,

13:15 uncovering evidence of the cult’s illegal actions  against the government, as well as other entities

13:20 they perceived as enemies of the Church. In  December of 1979, eleven high-ranking figures

13:26 within the Scientology cult, including L. Ron  Hubbard’s wife, Mary Sue Hubbard, were arrested

13:31 and received five-year prison sentences. Hubbard  himself managed to evade facing legal consequences

13:37 for Operation Snow White; however, he would end up  spending the remainder of his life in hiding from

13:42 the authorities, considered to be an ‘unindicted  co-conspirator’ for his hand in having members of

13:47 his cult infiltrating the US government. From the weird things Scientologists do

13:51 to some of the weird things Scientologists would  probably believe, what’s all this about evidence

13:56 of extraterrestrials being buried in a desert  somewhere in New Mexico? Believe it or not,

14:01 this one is completely real. The video game  adaptation of E.T. the Extra Terrestrial for the

14:06 Atari 2600 was so infamously bad that it’s widely  considered to be the worst video game of all time.

14:12 The game was such a commercial failure that  Atari took drastic measures, burying hundreds

14:17 of thousands of unsold game cartridges in  a landfill in New Mexico. The total number,

14:22 as verified by Atari officials, was around  seven hundred thousand E.T.s discarded in the

14:27 mass burial site until 2014, when the New Mexico  government, alongside companies like Microsoft,

14:32 worked to excavate a fraction of the abandoned  alien life – around thirteen hundred cartridges.

14:38 Okay, you’ve got us; we cheated a little with  that one. You were probably expecting us to talk

14:42 about actual buried aliens. In New Mexico, of all  places? As if that would ever happen! But, indeed,

14:47 little green or grey men and flying saucers have  long been a mainstay of conspiracy theories. For

14:53 several decades, the idea of these outlandish  theories ever being proven to be true seemed

14:58 beyond the realm of possibilities, no matter how  many The X-Files posters in college dorm rooms

15:03 urged us to believe that the truth is out there. That is, until in 2023, NASA released information

15:10 pertaining to their findings on what they called  Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena or UAPs. Moving

15:16 away from the popularised UFO – or Unidentified  Flying Object – the UAP acronym used to refer

15:22 exclusively to Unidentified Aerial Phenomena but  was broadened to a more general term for objects

15:28 detected in the air, sea or in space that defy  an easy explanation. NASA publicly outlined how

15:34 it would be researching possible incidents  of UAPs and vowed to be more transparent

15:38 with information to the public. Most interesting of all, though,

15:41 was the conclusion of their report, that there  was “no reason to conclude” that aliens were

15:46 behind the hundreds of UAP sightings that NASA  had already investigated. But even though the

15:51 report didn’t confirm that extraterrestrial  life exists, NASA still has yet to deny that

15:56 alien technology is potentially zipping around  in Earth’s atmosphere. We don’t know about you,

16:01 dear viewer, but we here at the Infographics Show  want to believe – life from other planets is more

16:06 like the aliens in Close Encounters of the Third  Kind than the Xenomorphs from the Alien franchise.

16:12 Taking a step away from invaders to our planet  to look at a US invasion of another country that

16:17 could have been launched based on a complete  fabrication… one involving ghosts? The Gulf of

16:22 Tonkin Incident began on the 2nd of August,  1964. It was an unprovoked attack by North

16:27 Vietnamese torpedo boats against a pair of US  Navy destroyers, the USS Maddox and Turner Joy

16:34 of the Seventh Fleet. The crew of the Maddox, who  had been involved in an intelligence gathering

16:38 mission, found they were being approached  by North Vietnamese torpedo boats and fired

16:43 warning shots. The torpedo boats returned  fire; a firefight broke out between them.

16:48 After calling in air support from a nearby  aircraft carrier, the Maddox could ward off

16:52 the attacking boats, and the Turner Joy was sent  to provide reinforcements. Then, two days later,

16:57 the US intercepted North Vietnamese communications  that led them to believe another attack on their

17:02 destroyers was being planned. Or at  least, that was the story presented

17:05 to Congress by the National Security Agency… On a stormy night, both the USS Maddox and Turner

17:11 Joy were reportedly tracking multiple unidentified  vessels that were rapidly approaching their

17:15 positions, coming from different directions,  and that these boats were somehow impossible

17:20 to lock onto. Still, both ships fired upon what  they thought were more torpedo boats and called

17:26 in more air support. Yet, planes flying at low  altitudes could see no signs of enemy ships.

17:31 Still, the seemingly ghostly vessels and unproven  attacks led Congress to pass the Gulf of Tonkin

17:35 Resolution, which opened the floodgates for  the direct involvement of the US military in

17:40 the Vietnam War. However, there was a striking  lack of evidence that the allegedly unprovoked

17:44 attacks even happened. The ‘Tonkin ghosts’  were thought to have been false radar images,

17:50 with North Vietnam’s military commander, Vo Nguyen  Giap, revealing that there had never been an

17:55 attack on August 4th. It had all been an excuse by  President Lyndon B. Johnson’s administration for

18:00 the US to expand its war against North Vietnam. The Gulf of Tonkin Incident was hardly the only

18:05 maritime incident that officials went  to great lengths to cover up. One that

18:09 occurred in 1989 actually led to the deaths  of forty-seven US Navy crewmen, with the Navy

18:14 attempting to use thinly veiled homophobia to  smear one of the victims who lost his life.

18:20 Aboard the battleship the USS Iowa, in the  Caribbean Sea, off the coast of Puerto Rico,

18:25 a live fire exercise went drastically wrong. An  explosion occurred in the number two sixteen-inch

18:30 gun turret, emanating from the center gun  room. The blast was so devastating that it

18:34 not only damaged the gun turret itself  but, far worse, it claimed the lives of

18:38 forty-seven crewmen. Naturally, following the  incident, exactly what went wrong had to be

18:43 determined. But of the multiple investigations  launched into the USS Iowa turret explosion,

18:48 their conclusions seemed to conflict dramatically. According to the Navy, one of the crew members who

18:53 had died in the explosion aboard the Iowa had been  directly responsible and had deliberately caused

18:58 the blast that killed his fellow crew members.  They claimed, and later leaked to the media, that

19:03 Gunner's Mate 2nd Class Clayton Hartwig had been  in a romantic relationship with another sailor and

19:09 had then caused the explosion in the gun turret  when their relationship had soured. However,

19:13 there was no evidence that this had even happened  or that Hartwig was gay in the first place. Their

19:18 investigation seemed to be just trying to  implicate gay people in the deaths of multiple

19:23 people for no reason. Stay classy, US Navy. When the media and the victims' families disputed

19:28 the Navy’s findings, and the US Senate and House  Armed Services Committee held inquiries into these

19:33 conclusions, the Government Accountability Office,  with the help of Sandia National Laboratories were

19:38 then asked to conduct their own investigation. Did  they uncover some secret plot by a gay crewman to

19:43 enact an explosive murder self-destruction?  Of course they didn’t. Instead, a technical

19:48 examination revealed that an excess of powder bags  used in the gun turret’s breech had been rammed in

19:53 at a higher speed than it was designed for. The  powder had then ignited during loading, resulting

19:59 in the explosion. The Navy even conducted a  test proving that an excess of powder was more

20:04 likely to blame for the disastrous detonation. These new findings prompted the US Navy to reopen

20:09 the investigation; however they still refused  to accept accountability for any wrongdoing,

20:13 despite the reports from the GAO and Sandia. They  never apologized to Hartwig’s family and instead

20:19 closed the investigation, saying that the cause of  the explosion couldn’t be accurately determined.

20:23 That last conspiracy about lies told  by the military got a little dour,

20:27 but don’t worry – this next one might  be just as bad! It’s about a harrowing

20:31 testimony before Congress that described some  truly heinous actions and that was instrumental

20:36 in launching another armed conflict. How much  do you want to bet it was completely made up?

20:41 On the 10th of October, 1990, a fifteen-year-old  girl identified only as Nayirah gave a tearful

20:47 testimony to Congress. In it, she recounted  witnessing firsthand Iraqi soldiers taking

20:51 fifteen babies out of incubators in a Kuwaiti  hospital. The soldiers reportedly then left the

20:57 newborn children on the ground to die. This had  been following the invasion of Kuwait by Iraq,

21:02 which marked the beginning of the Gulf War. Nayirah’s testimony was widely publicised,

21:06 and we do mean widely. It aired on 700 TV stations  across the USA, with then-President George Bush

21:12 Sr. repeating the story almost verbatim at  least ten times in the weeks following. All

21:18 to sway public opinion in favour of the Gulf War,  justifying the US’s position in backing Kuwait.

21:24 Stop us when you figure out the twist of this one… The testimony by Nayirah was completely falsified.

21:29 Although it hadn’t been revealed to the  public, her full name was Nayirah Al-Sabah,

21:33 the daughter of the Kuwaiti ambassador  to the United States, Saud Al-Sabah. Her

21:38 falsified testimony had been orchestrated by an  American public relations firm, Hill & Knowlton,

21:43 as part of the Citizens for a Free Kuwait campaign  on behalf of the Kuwaiti government. The CIA had

21:48 even requested that Nayirah receive acting  lessons before she testified before Congress.

21:53 Amnesty International initially corroborated  the story about the supposed killings,

21:58 but it was later discovered that, while some  patients – including prematurely born babies – did

22:03 die when Kuwait nurses and doctors fled during  the Iraqi invasion, the troops had at no point

22:08 stolen hospital incubators or intentionally left  children to die. In response to the findings,

22:13 there were subsequent accusations made against the  Bush administration for attempting to manipulate

22:18 the international human rights movement  through the use of atrocity propaganda.

22:22 As you’ve no doubt learned throughout this video,  and the last part, the United States government

22:27 is pretty much the undefeated world champion  regarding conspiracies and cover-ups. What can

22:31 we say? It’s something we’re just so darn good at!  Ready for another one? Of course you are! Let’s

22:36 turn the clock back a few decades; the fifties and  sixties were a crazy time for conspiracy theories;

22:41 in fact, you could argue that much of the public  fascination with conspiracies came into its own.

22:46 Exposing the top secret things the government  doesn’t want you to know became something of

22:50 a national pastime, and one of the craziest  of all was codenamed Operation Northwoods.

22:56 In 1962, officials within the US Department of  Defence had proposed a false flag operation that

23:01 would see the Central Intelligence Agency carrying  out acts of terrorism… against American citizens

23:06 on American soil.. Additionally on the hit list  were military bases in Miami and Washington,

23:12 along with plans to destroy US ships as well as  refugee boats coming into the States. There were

23:17 talks of hijacking planes and planting phony  evidence to implicate someone else in these

23:22 various acts of terror. The big question is why  would the US government want to attack Americans?

23:28 To make them afraid of Communism. Oh, of course. A few years earlier, in 1959, Fidel Castro had

23:34 come to power in Cuba. He allowed communists  to form part of his new government, improving

23:39 relations between Cuba and the Soviet Union.  Given the Cold War between the USA and USSR,

23:44 Castro created concern among some within the  US government and military. So, the goal of

23:49 Operation Northwoods was to carry out attacks  on innocent American civilians, as well as kill

23:54 Cuban refugees, all while pinning these attacks  on Castro and implicating the Cuban government.

23:59 Ultimately, they wanted to paint a false image of  the Cuban leader and misinform the American public

24:04 in the hopes it would encourage the sentiment  that the US should wage war against Cuba.

24:08 Perhaps most terrifyingly of all, Operation  Northwoods was actually authorized by the

24:13 Joint Chiefs of Staff, meaning the US almost  came dangerously close to carrying out terror

24:18 attacks on its own people in order to  pin their deaths on Cuba. Fortunately,

24:22 the operation was ultimately rejected by President  John F Kennedy. Of all the things he’s remembered

24:27 for, using his power to stop this absolutely  heinous craziness was definitely one of his

24:32 better decisions, so thanks for that one JFK! When the government isn’t at the heart of

24:36 conspiracies, it’s normally a nebulous, vaguely  defined secret society secretly controlling the

24:42 world through nefarious means. And the moment you  hear someone arguing that such a group exists,

24:47 be wary! Unfortunately, a lot of conspiracy  theories that center around a shadowy organization

24:51 like the Illuminati are usually just used by  bigots to justify their very blatant and virulent

24:57 antisemitic and racist worldviews. The people who  are really up to some shady dealings are the rich

25:03 and powerful, especially big businessmen and CEOs.  In particular, the members of the Bohemian Club.

25:09 Every July since 1872, some of the world's  wealthiest, most powerful and most influential

25:14 figures head to a 2,700-acre campground in  California. This is the Bohemian Club, an elite,

25:20 invite-only social club initially founded in San  Francisco. And on the surface, they’ve got all

25:25 the things that’ll raise your eyebrows, from  a reported history of mysterious ceremonies,

25:29 a top-secret guest list that’s previously  included presidents, wealthy businessmen,

25:33 and military officials, and a weird stone  owl statue on their retreat in Sonoma County.

25:39 For years, the secrecy surrounding the  tight-lipped club and their getaways to

25:42 Bohemian Grove in Monte Rio, California, has  fanned the flames of many conspiracy theories.

25:48 Most of the stories revolve around the performance  of pagan rituals and worship of that big stone

25:53 owl that reportedly plays voice recordings of  Walter Cronkite, who served as the anchorman

25:58 for CBS Evening News for nineteen years and  was also a Bohemian Club member. While this all

26:03 sounds like it could just be wild speculation  by conspiracy theorists, the club’s existence

26:08 has been proven by several news organizations. Founded in 1892, the Bohemian Club was started

26:13 by an all-male collection of artists, writers,  lawyers, actors, and journalists from the San

26:18 Francisco Examiner, all sharing interests in arts  and culture. It quickly received attention – and

26:24 then funding – from wealthy businessmen, and  since its inception, the club has expanded

26:29 to include the likes of Clint Eastwood, Henry  Kissinger, and even Presidents Richard Nixon

26:33 and Ronald Reagan. Even in the modern day,  the Bohemian Club maintains a reputation

26:38 for having predominantly the richest and most  politically conservative men in the United States.

26:43 However, they weren’t all gathering around an  owl to perform human sacrifices or coordinate

26:48 their efforts to maintain control  of the world. Since its founding,

26:51 the Bohemian Club has held regular gatherings  for members, allowing them to socialize, drink,

26:56 and enjoy theatrical and musical performances.  They inhabited various temporary locations in

27:01 their early decades before establishing  a permanent headquarters in the 1930s,

27:05 over on Taylor Street in downtown San Francisco. They also host an annual summer retreat to

27:10 Bohemian Grove, which is when things tend  to get weird. Robed figures are reported

27:15 to sacrifice an effigy to banish all the  worries of the gathered members. From there,

27:19 things just tend to descend into a lot of  drunken debauchery – really, the Bohemian

27:23 Club is just an excuse for some of the wealthiest  figures to act like a group of stereotypical frat

27:28 guys. What happens in between is still a question  many conspiracy theorists and people alike ask.

27:33 Want to know more? Check out  “Insane Conspiracy Theories

27:36 That Turned Out to be True.”  Or watch this video instead!

14:00 electricians around a 32% premium over traditional  construction work with specialized electricians

14:05 in Northern Virginia and Texas commanding up to  $280,000 a year. Obviously, that is an amazing

14:11 opportunity for those guys and nobody is going to  begrudge them for cashing in while they can. But

14:16 the businesses building houses and factories are  having to compete on price for the same people.

14:21 A cost that will eventually need to be passed  along through higher housing or goods costs,

14:24 respectively. The country is already short  around 300,000 electricians. And in Texas,

14:30 home builders say competition for them is delaying  housing construction by a couple of months. Now,

14:35 all of this is obviously not great, but one of  the biggest problems with fixing it is that the

14:40 cure is going to hurt almost as much as the  illness. The logical first step would be to

14:45 end the war in Iran and at the very least provide  clarity on tariffs. But we have tried that about

14:51 30 times now. The most recent second signing  of the Treaty of Versailles is certainly the

14:56 most noteworthy step towards bringing the war  to a close, albeit with significant concessions

15:01 from America. But it should also be noted that  even if this peace deal does stick this time,

15:06 Hormuse tolls may still continue. They will just  be called environmental fees instead of tolls,

15:11 which it must be emphasized is exactly the  same thing. Although maybe it's better for

15:15 Auron's ESG credentials. So, in the meantime,  while all of that is still getting worked out,

15:20 this is going to fall on the Fed that really only  has two tools at their disposal. Sucking money out

15:25 of circulation or raising the interest rates. But  these have their own problems. If we raise rates,

15:32 that means investors can get better returns  by just parking their money somewhere safe,

15:36 which might tempt a few more people to cash out  on an already very frothy investment market. Why

15:41 risk being on the wrong side of a bubble when the  30-year Treasury will pay you over 5%, effectively

15:47 guaranteed more than it has paid at any point  since 2007? Maybe the market will offer better

15:53 returns, but even the most optimistic investors  are seeing the warning signs. This is especially

15:58 risky right now because there's going to be an  even greater demand for cash as three IPOs and

16:03 a major capital raise come from SpaceX, OpenAI,  Anthropic, and Google. SpaceX, which listed this

16:09 week, raised $75 billion at a $1.75 trillion  valuation, which made it the largest IPO in

16:15 history. OpenAI confidentially filed for its own  IPO just days before that listing at a valuation

16:21 of over $850 billion. And Enthropic has already  filed for its own at over a trillion. Google has

16:28 also announced plans to raise up to $80 billion in  new equity, which is kind of the thing that mega

16:33 caps basically never do, but it's been forced into  continue funding its data center expansion. These

16:38 companies are all going to be holding their hand  out at the same time as the government is holding

16:42 its handout, offering better rates than almost  any time in the past 20 years for the privilege.

16:47 If the Fed raises rates or pulls money out of  the market, there is going to be even less cash

16:51 to go around amongst these hungry, hungry hippos.  This is why the market reacted so badly to this

16:57 week's inflation announcement. In theory, higher  inflation should actually be good for the market.

17:02 Because people will naturally want to put their  money into real businesses as a hedge against the

17:06 declining value of the dollar. But because there  is so much demand for cash, any sign that interest

17:11 rates are going to tempt people to lock that  cash up is really scary. An even more perverse

17:16 sign of the same paradox is that the market is now  really afraid of good jobs reports. Last Friday,

17:22 payrolls came in at almost double what forecasters  expected, which was the third month in a row,

17:27 the number has beaten consensus. Stocks and bonds  both sold off because traders immediately started

17:33 pricing in rate hikes. In a normal economy, lots  of people getting new jobs should be a good sign

17:38 for businesses like the ones listed on the stock  market, right? More people with jobs means money

17:43 to spend, as well as being an indication  that companies are confident enough to hire.

17:48 But we aren't a normal market at the moment.  Valuations are stretched so far that it would

17:53 take decades of good consumer spending to  pay back a lot of the values we are seeing,

17:57 which is such a long time horizon that it has  basically become irrelevant. So what is actually

18:03 happening is that good jobs numbers remove the one  excuse that the Fed could hold up to lower rates

18:07 or at least leave them alone. The Fed has a triple  mandate to maintain stable prices, stable rates,

18:13 and maximum employment. If employment is  apparently really good and prices are going up,

18:18 then in theory they have no choice but to raise  interest rates. The brand new Fed chair, Kevin

18:23 Walsh, who was only sworn in a few weeks ago,  completed his first ever policy meeting in the

18:27 big chair last week with exactly that combination  sitting on the table. Now, we have already made

18:32 another video on why those job numbers may not  actually be all they really seem in reality. So,

18:37 I will leave a link to that below instead of  going over it all again. But the point is that

18:41 as long as the job numbers look good, at least  on paper, and the inflation numbers look bad,

18:46 interest rates are likely to increase. But okay,  this is about inflation, not the stock market. So,

18:52 for the sake of this video, who cares? Current  stocks are overwhelmingly owned by wealthy people

18:57 who can theoretically afford the loss. According  to the Fed's own distributional accounts,

19:02 the wealthiest 10% of households hold around 87%  of household-owned corporate equities, and the top

19:08 1% alone holds about half. However, those wealthy  people are the ones currently doing a large share

19:14 of the spending. By Moody's estimates, the top  10% of earners now account for almost half of

19:19 all consumer spending, which is the highest share  in records going back to 1989. A booming stock

19:24 market makes these people feel good. And when they  see big numbers in their Schwab account, they are

19:28 more likely to splurge on goods and services that  provide opportunities to every other household.

19:33 But if Green Line does not go up, that could  knock out the last leg that has been holding up

19:38 our economy for a long time now. Both companies  and wealthy households would stop spending on

19:43 capex and luxuries, respectively, eliminating the  biggest growth sectors of the economy, potentially

19:49 causing an employment crisis just as bad, if not  worse, than the cost of living crisis. Okay, so

19:54 what if we just let inflation run hot? Well, that  has its problems, too, even beyond just higher

19:59 prices. The US dollar is already under stress  as the global reserve currency. Something that

20:04 buys us extraordinary privilege in international  markets both for imports and for debt. The dollar

20:09 share of global foreign exchange reserves  has slipped to its lowest level in roughly

20:13 three decades of IMF records. And the dollar  index briefly broke below 97 earlier this year,

20:19 back to lows it hadn't seen in years before the  war sent everything scrambling back into dollars.

20:24 If our dollar inflates away, we will start to  lose that privilege. Now, a cheaper dollar does

20:29 make American exports more competitive, which is  why some people in Washington have openly argued

20:34 for one, but that math works a lot better when  one of our biggest imports isn't suddenly around

20:38 40% more expensive than it was a year ago. Also,  we are still a massive net importer of goods and

20:44 services that will get relatively more expensive  if our dollar gets weaker, compounding the problem

20:48 of prices on shelves. In the short term, if wages  are adjusted upwards, it may help smooth things

20:53 over for a little while. But realistically, it  will just leave wage earners further behind on

20:58 already significant cost of living pressures.  Long-term, it would significantly undermine the

21:03 easy capital we have been blessed with over the  last 80 years. Our debt has always been a burden

21:08 to carry, and keeping it manageable relies on  being able to grow faster than the debt does,

21:13 while simultaneously doing everything we can to  carry the weight responsibly. Right now, that

21:18 debt is just shy of $40 trillion, and it grew by  about $3 trillion over the past year. The economy

21:24 underneath it managed less than two. The interest  alone is costing around a trillion a year. At the

21:30 same time, we are doing a lot of things that are  shifting that weight around while simultaneously

21:33 shooting ourselves in both feet. Now, one ray of  hope in these numbers is that out of everything,

21:38 cars are getting cheaper. New vehicle prices  fell again in this report as manufacturers have

21:43 undermined their own market in some of the dumbest  ways possible. So, go and watch this video next

21:47 to find out how. And don't forget to like and  subscribe to keep on learning how money works.

docs.text:
00:00 Your 8GB RAM laptop is already on borrowed time. By the end of 2026, it could struggle to run the

00:06 basic security systems of  a modern operating system.

00:09 Not because it’s broken, but because  the rules of computing are changing.

00:13 Behind the scenes, tech giants are racing  to secure massive amounts of memory for AI,

00:18 while everyday consumers are left  fighting over outdated hardware.

00:21 Millions of machines could become obsolete  because the future was built without them.

00:25 The next computer upgrade won’t be about  getting faster… it’ll be about staying alive.

00:30 When you buy a smartphone, a tablet, a laptop,  or a computer, you expect it to work. Sure,

00:34 it won’t last forever. And you know that cheaper  products might not be as efficient, but you spend

00:39 money on these products thinking that they’ll for  at least a few years before you need to find a

00:44 replacement. It’s not an unreasonable expectation.  One that consumers across the world have been able

00:49 to enjoy for generations. Then AI came along.

00:53 And everything changed. As AI’s tendrils extend across industries

00:57 and infiltrate almost every facet of modern life,  the lifespans of standard computers are dropping

01:02 quickly. In homes and offices around the world  there are hundreds of millions of laptops and

01:06 desktop devices that are less than 2 years old. They look good. Their keyboards aren’t fading.

01:11 The displays are crisp. They boot up in a  matter of seconds. Yet beneath their sleek

01:15 exteriors, a death sentence has been issued. The countdown clocking is about to hit zero.

01:20 The numbers highlight the problem. There are  around 2 billion machines in use today. They’re

01:25 used by people from all walks of life, for all  manner of tasks, both personal and professional.

01:30 Without them, lives would fall apart. Yet the majority of those devices - more

01:34 than 1.3 billion - are missing  the Neural Processing Units (NPUs)

01:39 or the base amount of system memory required  to complete local, next-generation AI tasks.

01:44 Those are the same tasks that tech companies  are forcing on us. The tasks that are about to

01:49 become essential, not optional, for anyone  who wants to browse the internet and use

01:53 the software they’ve relied on for decades. The entire baseline of functional computing

01:57 has shifted. Forever.

01:59 It’s like waking up and finding that 3 lanes  of a 4 lane highway have been permanently

02:03 barricaded and are now exclusively reserved for  a convoy of corporate VIPs. The rest of us are

02:09 forced to battle it out over a single, crumbling  lane, trapped in a bottleneck that never ends.

02:14 That’s what’s happening in the  consumer computer market in 2026.

02:17 And there’s nothing you can do about it. You didn’t make a mistake. You didn’t buy

02:21 broken hardware or download a system-destroying  virus, yet your device has been shut off from the

02:26 future of the internet. There was no warning, no  compensation, and no mercy. It all boils down to

02:32 something relatively simple… Memory.

02:34 That all-important component that has rapidly  become one of the most valuable technological

02:39 resources on the planet. As AI has become  more prominent, the world’s largest tech

02:44 companies have started spending huge amounts of  money on powerful AI infrastructure to run it.

02:49 Memory is a vital piece of that infrastructure.  Brands like OpenAI, Microsoft, Google,

02:54 and Amazon are buying it in droves. The impact of this record-setting RAM

02:58 investment can be seen and felt in the pockets  of millions of consumers the world over.

03:02 Take the smartphone market. For years, this  sector has followed a familiar pattern. Each year,

03:07 the big brands release their latest devices.  Each time, they promise incremental improvements:

03:12 a faster processor, a better display, or a  stronger camera. This is how they have justified

03:17 their price hikes and encouraged users to abandon  their old models in favor of the latest releases.

03:22 But smartphones - just like laptops and computers  - require RAM to function. The AI boom has sent

03:28 the cost of memory soaring to never-before-seen  highs. This has impacted the “Bill of Materials”,

03:34 or BOM, for a smartphone released in 2026. A BOM is a list of all the materials and

03:39 components that go into a device, along with  the raw costs of those materials. In 2022,

03:45 memory made up a small part of the overall cost.  Since then, however, it has dramatically risen,

03:51 to the point where memory now accounts for almost  60% of the BOM in phones worth $400 or less.

03:57 Even in mid-range devices, the BOM cost  of memory has risen to around 40% as RAM

04:03 effectively becomes a luxury good. This leave smartphone manufacturers

04:07 in a difficult position. They need to give people a

04:09 reason to buy their latest devices, but are  having to spend far more to make them. They

04:14 can’t pass all of those costs onto the consumer  by raising the price of the devices themselves.

04:19 People have budgets. Not many are willing to hand  over an extra few hundred dollars for a phone that

04:24 is more or less the same as last year’s model. So, they opt for a different tactic.

04:29 A tactic that revolves around minimizing  manufacturing costs by cutting corners

04:34 as subtly as possible. They swap out camera  sensors for smaller and simpler alternatives.

04:38 They make the phone’s frame from  a cheaper, less durable material.

04:42 They trade the battery for one with a shorter  lifespan, but is more affordable to source.

04:47 They actively make their devices worse,  using cheaper parts and materials to make

04:51 changes that most people won’t notice right  away. On their own, any one of these changes

04:55 would be almost invisible to the consumer. Together, they become a kind of hidden tax.

05:00 The spiraling costs of money have to be accounted  for, somehow. So, even as the product gets worse,

05:05 the price tag stays the same. The customer absorbs  the added cost of RAM and ends up with an inferior

05:11 phone. They might not realize that until a year  or two down the line when it starts freezing or

05:16 failing and they’re forced to buy another. It’s not just affecting smartphones.

05:20 It’s happening all across the tech sector.  Tablets, laptops, gaming PCs, and everything in

05:25 between. The brands that make these products are  no longer just competing with each other for RAM.

05:30 They’re competing with something bigger. Enormous, insatiable beasts that eat up

05:35 energy and computing power far faster, and in  far greater quantities, than anything the world

05:40 has ever seen before. AI data centers.

05:43 These windowless, concrete building are lined  with hyper-efficient cooling towers that pump

05:47 vast plumes of steam into the atmosphere. And  inside each one are rows upon rows of servers.

05:53 Each server is filled with thousands of AI  accelerators, or GPUs, running round-the-clock,

05:58 carrying out the complex mathematical computations  required to train and run machine learning models.

06:04 All of those accelerators rely on RAM to function. With every passing month, more of these data

06:09 centers are springing up around the  world. And they’re getting bigger.

06:12 It’s the physical embodiment of the AI arms race. It doesn’t stop. It continues to hurtle forward

06:17 at breakneck speed. There is a constant,  unrelenting push towards the next big thing:

06:22 the next model, the next leap in intelligence,  the next stage of digital evolution. The only

06:26 way to achieve any of those objectives is growth. Bigger data centers. More servers. More power.

06:32 More memory. Companies like Microsoft, Meta, and

06:35 Alphabet want to dominate the market, and release  the AI tools that millions or even billions of

06:39 people want to pay for. To do that, they have to  stay one step ahead of their rivals. Because in a

06:45 race as ruthless as this, even a tiniest setback  can spiral into a multi-billion dollar loss.

06:50 They have no choice but to purchase all the memory  they can afford as quickly as humanly possible.

06:55 And that’s exactly what they’re doing. The numbers speak for themselves.

06:58 Meta, Microsoft, Amazon, and Alphabet,  are set to allocate $725 billion

07:03 in combined capital expenditure towards their  AI ambitions in 2026 alone. It’s a huge amount

07:09 of money and it’s only going to increase. Experts estimate the combined CapEx for

07:14 the biggest AI brands will reach a whopping $1.2  trillion in 2027, rising to $1.4 trillion in 2028.

07:21 Compare that sort of spending with people  just trying to buy a new device. Like a

07:25 family looking for a new computer or a student  on a tight budget, searching for a laptop they

07:30 can carry around campus. Around the world, there  are millions of people in the market for a new

07:34 computer. But the prices they pay are no longer  influenced by conventional supply and demand.

07:39 Instead, they’re being controlled  by a handful of mega-corporations.

07:43 The technological elite are leveraging  their almost infinite cash reserves

07:47 to outbid the consumer market for silicon chips.  They’re buying up global factory capacity,

07:52 leaving retail brands - and their  customers - to fight over the scraps.

07:56 This is the brutal truth of the AI arms race. It’s not just about companies competing with

08:00 one another to get ahead of the game  and release the next big AI asset.

08:04 It’s about those same companies carrying out a  violent assault on the consumer computer market.

08:09 And the worst part of all is  that there’s no end in sight.

08:13 This isn’t a temporary shortage. It’s not a blip.

08:16 Things aren’t going to simply sort  themselves out and get back on track.

08:19 AI only moves in one direction: models are  only going to get smarter and more demanding.

08:24 They are going to hoover up resources year after  year. As long as that continues, these companies

08:29 will keep on consuming memory in record-setting  amounts, leaving everyone else in the dust.

08:33 The scale of their greed is only getting worse. Because these companies don’t accept the classic

08:38 kind of RAM you’d find in an everyday  laptop or an entry-level smartphone.

08:43 They want the best of the best:  High Bandwidth Memory, or HBM.

08:47 HBM produces incredible speeds by stacking  multiple memory chips together, creating a level

08:52 of performance far beyond traditional RAM. The  gap between advanced AI enterprise systems, like

08:57 NVIDIA H100s clusters, and the 8GB of DDR5 memory  found in a typical consumer laptop is massive.

09:05 The best HBM products score at least 50  times higher on performance benchmarks

09:09 compared to regular RAM. It’s like having  a supersonic fifth-generation fighter jet

09:14 racing against a toddler on a plastic tricycle. This has created a new technological hierarchy.

09:20 The largest companies can process trillions  of data points in fractions of a second,

09:25 while everyday users are left with  machines that struggle with basic AI tasks.

09:29 That’s why HBM has become the backbone of  modern AI processors and supercomputers.

09:34 But in technology, every  breakthrough comes with a cost.

09:37 For HBM, that cost is measured in silicon. Producing a single gigabyte of HBM for AI systems

09:43 requires around 3 times more silicon capacity  than making standard DDR5 memory. So when a

09:49 factory shifts its focus toward HBM to chase the  AI boom, regular RAM production gets squeezed.

09:56 These two markets can’t grow side by side. Every piece of silicon dedicated to high-end

10:01 AI memory is silicon that can’t be used to make  RAM for millions of everyday devices like laptops,

10:07 phones, and tablets. The result is a brutal  trade-off: the AI industry is consuming the

10:12 resources that powered the consumer market. And when you look at the profits involved,

10:16 it’s easy to understand why memory manufacturers  are choosing to chase the HBM orders.

10:22 In today’s market conditions, manufacturers can  easily have operating margins in excess of 50%.

10:28 Some are even being forecast to see  their margins rise close to 80%.

10:33 That’s a massive difference compared to the  much slimmer margins these same companies

10:36 had to cope with when making regular  RAM before the AI boom really began.

10:41 The problem is, this isn’t a market with  dozens of companies making different choices.

10:46 The global memory industry is controlled by 3  giants: Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron. Together,

10:53 they produce around 93% of all memory chips. That gives them enormous control over where

10:58 the industry goes. And they’re choosing  the path that makes them the most money.

11:03 They can cater to a small, elite market,  rather than worrying about pleasing the masses.

11:07 Even when their CEOs acknowledge the shortfalls  in the DDR markets, they’ve continued to pour

11:12 resources into expanding HBM production. Their loyalties lie with Big Tech.

11:17 Of course, they won’t admit  that they’re “abandoning” the

11:20 general public or leaving millions of  consumers to fight for scraps. Instead,

11:24 they talk about “diversifying” their product  lineup or “expanding” into emerging markets.

11:29 It’s boring business speak to cover up  the consequences of their decisions.

11:33 But no matter how much they dress it up, the end  result is the same: the HBM market gets bigger

11:39 and richer, all at the expense of the DDR market. The likes of Meta and Microsoft get the massive

11:44 stacks of chips they need to build bigger  data centers and train their AI models.

11:49 Families, students, and struggling  professionals have to make do with less.

11:52 This isn’t a supply chain hiccup or “Act of God.” It’s not some evil masterplan, either.

11:58 It’s a cold, calculated, and entirely legal  corporate strategy, driven by the oldest and

12:03 purest bedrock of the business world: The pursuit of profit.

12:06 During the final quarter of 2025, SK Hynix saw  a 66% increase in revenue compared to the same

12:12 period a year earlier. Operating profits also  surged by 137% over the same span of time.

12:19 It was a similar story at  the other big memory firms.

12:22 They didn’t go all-in on HBM and starve  the DDR market entirely, but they made a

12:27 big enough investment to send their profits - and  shareholder satisfaction rates - to record levels.

12:32 The ugly by-product of this strategy, however,  is a ruthless reallocation of global resources

12:38 away from the working and middle classes. While the market evolves to optimize yields

12:42 for every single square millimeter of silicon  in existence, a memory famine has swept across

12:47 large parts of the world. And, in the wake  of that famine, a frightening new world is

12:51 beginning to emerge. A divided reality.

12:54 A digital caste system. A world in which two

12:57 contrasting extremes exist in a state of chaos. On the one hand, there are hyper advanced AI

13:03 systems, training on never-ending sets  of data, chewing through resources.

13:07 As these systems grow smarter and stronger,  their capabilities increase exponentially,

13:11 to the point where almost no task is impossible. At the other end of the spectrum sits the

13:16 consumers. You.

13:18 The everyday people who are looking for  devices that let them do the things they

13:21 need but are increasingly being made to pay  higher prices for lower quality machines.

13:26 To make matters worse, most of these  machines aren’t just falling slightly behind,

13:31 they’re heading toward obsolescence. AI is being  pushed into everyday devices and workplaces.

13:36 That leaves millions of people with basic  laptops and mid-range PCs that can’t keep

13:41 up with the wave of AI-powered apps and operating  systems. So, they’ll be left with only one option.

13:46 The cloud. The same cloud owned and operated by

13:49 those very same mega-corps. The same cloud they  power with all the silicon and other computing

13:54 components they steal from the rest of the world. People will either buy an expensive

13:59 AI-ready machine, or pay tech giants  monthly just to use basic features.

14:03 That’s the future we’re moving toward. It’s not just about big tech using billion dollar

14:07 budgets to dominate the market. It’s about turning  one-time purchases into endless subscriptions.

14:12 It’s a slow shift toward “digital serfdom,”  where people no longer truly own their computers.

14:17 Instead, they become portals for accessing  services and renting digital lives from the

14:21 same companies that built the system. These are the harrowing consequences

14:25 of the AI boom. The tech giants are  only going to become more powerful,

14:29 while the people gradually lose whatever  control, choice, and freedom they once had.

14:34 They told you AI would transform the  world and unlock opportunities for all.

14:38 They just forgot to mention the price  you’d have to pay for that transformation.

14:42 Now people are starting to see the real  cost… and it’s already too late to stop it.

14:46 The AI bubble is growing and affecting us daily.  But is it sustainable? Watch $115 Billion Burn

14:53 Rate. The AI Bubble Just POPPED to find out  where it all ends. Or click on this video.

00:00 It was called the war to end all wars.

00:03 Unfortunately, World War I didn’t deliver on that promise.

00:06 It was however the first time in the history of planet Earth that nations from around the

00:10 world fought in a single war.

00:12 It started with an assassination and a series of questionable decisions.

00:16 We can point fingers and play the blame game, but really there is no single person or country

00:21 that holds all of the responsibility.

00:23 Could the war that killed millions have been prevented?

00:26 Most definitely.

00:27 Let’s take a look at what caused the Great War, explore how it could have been prevented,

00:32 and learn how to not repeat the mistakes of the past.

00:35 World War I lasted from 1914 to 1918 and included countries in Europe, Russia, the United States,

00:42 and countries in the Middle East.

00:44 The two main sides of the war were the Central Powers which consisted of Germany, Austria-Hungary,

00:48 Italy, the Ottoman Empire, and Bulgaria, who fought against the Allied Powers of France,

00:54 Britain, Russia, Portugal and Japan.

00:57 Later in the war the United States would also join the side of the Allies.

01:00 But what happened?

01:01 Why did all of these nations get involved in one of the most disastrous wars in history?

01:06 Let’s explore the mechanisms and missteps that led to the first World War.

01:10 Although there were many players in World War 1, the conflict started with Serbia and

01:15 Austria-Hungary.

01:16 The Serbian government was eager to claim more territory for the nation.

01:20 Serbia was already in a state of aggression due to the Balkan Wars that ended just a year

01:24 before the start of World War I.

01:26 After the Balkan War, Serbian nationalists wanted to liberate the South Slavs of Austria-Hungary,

01:32 thus unifying the Slavic peoples under one nation.

01:35 This extreme nationalism led to the assissnation of the Archduke Franz Ferdinand who was heir

01:40 to the Astro-Hungarian Empire.

01:42 At 11:15 AM on June 28, 1914 Franz Ferdinand and his wife, Sophie, duchess of Hohenberg,

01:49 were shot to death in Sarajevo, Bosnia by Gavrilo Princip.

01:53 Princip was a Serbian extremist who had connections to a secret society called the Black Hand.

01:57 The assaisnation was the match that ignited the first world war, however, there were many

02:02 other factors that led to the powderkeg that would explode.

02:06 Should the assassination of Franz Ferdinand have led to an all out War?

02:09 Probably not.

02:10 There is more to the story here.

02:12 In the shadows lurked Kaiser Wilhelm II, who may be as much to blame as Gavrilo Princip

02:17 in starting World War I. Wilhelm II was the leader of Germany and he was diabolical.

02:23 Kaiser Wilhelm II wanted a strong Germany that dominated Europe both economically and

02:28 militarily in strength.

02:29 He did not want Russia or Great Britain to have more influence and power than he did.

02:34 Therefore, Wilhelm II allied himself, and Germany, with Austria-Hungary.

02:38 He knew that if Austria-Hungary went to war with Serbia, then Russia would come to Serbia’s

02:43 aid.

02:44 This would drag Russia's ally France into the conflict.

02:46 We will examine later why Wilhelm wanted this war to happen so badly.

02:50 Kaiser Wilhelm II secretly funded Austria-Hungary in their endeavor to suppress Serbia.

02:55 He allowed Germany to give Austria-Hungary a carte blanche, or “blank check.”

03:00 Basically Germany would fund the war effort using their wealthy economy to ensure Austria-Hungary

03:05 came out on top.

03:06 With the assassination of their heir, and the backing of Germany, Austria-Hungary felt

03:10 empowered to start their war with Serbia.

03:13 They sent Serbia an ultimatum with such harsh terms that it was impossible to accept.

03:18 There was only one alternative.

03:20 War.

03:21 But there was more to the story.

03:22 The decisions of Austria-Hungary and Germany were clearly geared towards war.

03:26 It is undeniable that World War I started because of these aggressive decisions.

03:30 But could the whole conflict have been avoided if other countries had made better decisions?

03:35 Were there strings being pulled behind the scenes by the countries on both sides of the

03:39 war?

03:40 Let’s find out.

03:41 First let’s take a look at the Triple Entente nations, which consisted of a secret pact

03:45 between Great Britain, France, and Russia.

03:47 Could any of these nations have secretly wanted a world war to heighten their power?

03:51 Could there have been a secret plot by the Allies to set up a war they would eventually

03:55 win?

03:56 Russia is, and always has been, a large, powerful nation.

04:00 What could Russia gain from a war against the Triple Alliance of Germany, Austria-Hungary,

04:04 and Italy?

04:05 At first glance Russia’s role in World War I seems to be based around supporting their

04:10 ally of Serbia.

04:11 But as we look closer it seems that Russia’s alliance only played a superficial role in

04:16 their decisions to go to war.

04:18 In fact Russia barely even tried to find a diplomatic solution to prevent this conflict.

04:22 Instead, they immediately started to deploy troops and ramp up military production once

04:27 Austria-Hungary showed aggression towards Serbia.

04:29 It would seem Russia had no intentions on working out the conflict diplomatically.

04:34 History shows it was Russia, not Germany, that mobilized its military first.

04:39 Russia may have wanted war to claim more territory and power for the nation.

04:43 But there was another player on the Triple Entente side who may have played a behind

04:47 the scenes role of starting World War I. France did not make any outwardly aggressive moves

04:52 in the months that led to the outbreak of war, but they were making secret strategic

04:57 moves.

04:58 France may be the only reason that Russia prepared for war in the first place.

05:02 During talks of what was to be done about the Central Powers, France offered Russia

05:06 its own blank cheque.

05:07 The stipulation was that Russia would help Europeanise the Austrian-Hungry Empire.

05:12 France had an idea of what this part of the world should look like, and rather than entering

05:16 directly into conflict, they funded the Russian military to start a war that they could benefit

05:21 from.

05:22 France encouraged Russia’s aggression towards Austria-Hungary and Germany.

05:25 French leaders seemed not to like the idea of having the powerful nation of Germany right

05:29 next door.

05:30 If Germany was focused on fighting Russia on the Eastern front, it would provide France

05:35 with the opportunity to either protect itself, or launch an uncontested invasion into Germany

05:41 from the western front.

05:42 It would seem that things did not play out exactly as France predicted because of Germany’s

05:46 deployment of troops to fight on both the Russian and French fronts simultaneously.

05:51 If the shady actions of France leading up to the start of World War I surprised you

05:55 then what Great Britain did may shock you even more.

05:58 Britain was a dominant force in colonization and had control of the seas with their powerful

06:02 Navy.

06:03 Would they benefit from an all out war in Europe?

06:06 Germany was becoming powerful, both economically and militarily.

06:09 Britain knew that this was a threat to their empire.

06:12 In the eyes of Great Britain’s leaders the world wasn’t big enough for both a German

06:16 empire and British empire.

06:18 If Germany continued on the path it was headed, Britain’s global dominance of the seas and

06:22 financial system would be threatened, and perhaps lost.

06:25 This was unacceptable to the leaders of Great Britain.

06:29 These notions of loss of dominance may have driven Great Britain to stay out of diplomatic

06:33 talks, and instead encourage Russian aggression.

06:36 It would seem that at the time Great Britain had an inferiority complex when it came to

06:40 Germany.

06:41 They had failed to meditate during the Balkan Wars and they refused to meditate during the

06:45 lead up to World War I.

06:46 The thought process may have been that the more conflicts Germany was a part of, the

06:50 more likely they were to be weakened.

06:52 Great Britain had clearly won the naval arm race by 1910, it just seemed that it wasn’t

06:57 enough.

06:58 They were still living in fear of Germany’s threats.

07:01 And it would appear rightfully so as history showed over the next several decades.

07:04 It needs to be said that if Great Britain wanted to prevent war, they should have contributed

07:09 to the mediation discussions.

07:11 The fact that they actively avoided the mediations shows Britain may have had other motives.

07:15 Especially if war meant a weakened Germany.

07:18 History is written by the victors.

07:20 Therefore, history textbooks tend to attribute most of, if not all of, the blame for World

07:24 War I to Austria-Hungary and Germany.

07:27 You have to wonder who would be blamed if the outcome of the war was reversed.

07:31 We discussed how the nations of the Triple Entente were by no means free of blame for

07:35 the start of this conflict.

07:36 But let’s take a closer look at the motives and actions of the Triple Alliance, which

07:40 was the secret pact between Germany, Austria-Hungary, and Italy.

07:44 Let’s find out if they really are to blame like so many textbooks say.

07:48 Other than retaliation, what was Austria-Hungary after?

07:51 In a word, territory.

07:53 Austria-Hungary wanted to add more land and people to its already large empire.

07:57 More land equals more resources, and more men for their military.

08:01 Austria-Hungary had its sights set on Serbia for a while.

08:04 The assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand allowed them the perfect opportunity to make

08:09 their dreams of taking over Serbian lands a reality.

08:12 Austria-Hungary’s desires were made clear when they offered an obscene ultimatum to

08:16 Serbia.

08:17 The ultimatum itself was delivered on July 23, 1914.

08:21 It required Serbia to accept an Austro-Hungarian inquiry into the assassination of Archduke

08:26 Ferdinand.

08:27 The inquiry would be conducted solely by Austria-Hungarian investigators.

08:31 Serbia also needed to suppress all anti-Austrian propaganda and eliminate any terrorist or

08:36 extremist organizations within its borders.

08:39 The leaders of Austria-Hungary demanded that an answer to the ultimatum be sent within

08:43 48 hours.

08:44 However, the ambassador to Serbia delivered the ultimatum and immediately left the country

08:48 to return back to Austria-Hungary.

08:50 He already knew what was going to happen next.

08:52 There was no way that Serbia would accept the ultimatum.

08:55 This meant war.

08:56 The ultimatum served one purpose.

08:58 Austria-Hungary knew Serbia would never accept their terms, but they also knew if they attacked

09:02 without warning it would make Serbia look like the victim.

09:06 By sending the ultimatum it pushed the burden of avoiding war onto the Serbian government.

09:10 This way Austria-Hungary created the illusion of giving Serbia a chance to stop the war.

09:16 When they didn’t, Serbia would look like the bad guy.

09:19 But the ridiculous ultimatum did not stand up to the test of history, and Austria-Hungary

09:23 is still seen as the aggressors.

09:26 Really what it came down to was that Austria-Hungary wanted to control more territory in the Balkan

09:30 region.

09:31 They needed a reason to go to war with Serbia to secure that land and they found it in the

09:36 assassination of their Archduke.

09:38 Was the assassination a reason to conduct an all out war?

09:41 Probably not, but it was sufficient enough reason for the Austria-Hungary government

09:45 at the time.

09:46 However, none of this would have been possible without one key player.

09:49 I am sure you can guess what is coming next.

09:52 Germany.

09:53 In the eyes of many historians Germany is to blame for the first world war.

09:57 Why was Germany considered the most responsible in a conflict that they did not directly start?

10:02 It is mostly because they alone had the power to stop the war between Austria-Hungary and

10:07 Serbia.

10:08 All they needed to do was withdraw their blank cheque, and Austria-Hungary would not have

10:12 had the financial ability to support a war with Serbia.

10:15 This would have kept Austria-Hungary in check and they would never have issued their ultimatum.

10:20 Germany also knew that if Austria-Hungary went to war with Serbia, Russia and France

10:24 would both get pulled in.

10:25 It was almost as if Germany needed to find a way to declare war on their competitors

10:29 in the region without doing it themselves.

10:32 Germany could never just outright declare war on the other nations or they would risk

10:35 unifying the entire continent of Europe against them.

10:39 But by strategically destabilizing the Balkans they could gode Russia, and therefore France,

10:44 into a war with their ally, thus allowing Germany to start a war to suit their needs.

10:49 The other reason that Germany wanted war was because it had peaked as a nation.

10:53 If Germany allowed the rest of Europe to catch up they would lose power and prestige.

10:57 This upset no one more than Kaiser Wilhelm II, who was an angry militaristic autocrat.

11:02 He believed that he was predestined by God to lead his country to greatness.

11:06 He hated diplomats and maintained that the only way to ensure Germany's spot of power

11:11 was through war.

11:12 He knew it was now or never if Germany was going to become the predominant world power.

11:17 When a power hungry autocrat is in charge of one of the world’s most wealthy and armed

11:21 nations there is only one outcome.

11:23 War.

11:24 In the end World War I was caused by many different factors and countries.

11:27 There is not just one person or nation to blame.

11:30 However, some are more responsible than others.

11:33 If the leaders of Europe were less hungry for power, and more willing to sit down and

11:37 negotiate, the war could have been avoided.

11:39 Make no mistake, World War I was not unavoidable.

11:42 But the leaders in charge saw war as a desirable outcome, or were forced into it by allies.

11:47 A situation that would repeat itself again 21 years later.

11:51 If you are interested in more World War I information check out 50 Insane World War

11:56 1 Facts That Will Shock You!

11:58 Or if you want to know how World War I and World War II stack up watch World War 1 VS
