docs.text:
00:00 So, you’ve committed a crime.

00:02 Save the reasons for your next appeal, because you’ve already been tried, convicted, and

00:06 sentenced to a term in prison.

00:07 The question now is which prison you’ll be sentenced to – state or federal prison.

00:12 Aren’t all prisons created equal, you wonder?

00:14 Well, there I’m afraid, you’d be terribly wrong.

00:16 We’re going to tell you about all the differences between state and federal prisons.

00:20 What they are, what gets you admitted, what the general experience is like inside, and

00:25 which one you’d prefer to serve your sentence in.

00:27 First, let’s take a look at state prisons.

00:29 These are, as the name suggests, government prisons run by the state in which they’re

00:33 located.

00:34 Referred to as “State Penitentiaries” in Pennsylvania and most Southern states,

00:38 these jails are intended for criminals who committed minor to major crimes within a single

00:43 state.

00:44 They’re tried by state judges, in state courts.

00:46 And the care of state prisoners and the maintenance of the prisons themselves are funded by taxpayers

00:51 within the given state.

00:52 State prisons also make up the grand majority of prison facilities in the United States,

00:56 as state crimes are significantly more common than federal.

01:00 To give you some perspective, there are 122 federal prisons operated by the Bureau of

01:05 Prisons in the United States.

01:06 For comparison, there are 1,719 state prisons.

01:11 Between them, they manage 1,518,559 inmates.

01:15 1,328,599 of these are state prison inmates.

01:21 State prisons also more commonly offer the possibility of parole, and – on average

01:25 – have lower sentences than their federal counterparts.

01:28 The exact workings of a state prison can sometimes vary from state to state, and these prisons

01:33 are significantly more likely to admit violent criminals – such as murderers, sex criminals,

01:38 and people found guilty of most gun-related offenses.

01:41 In spite of this, state prisons generally have a lower standard of security than federal

01:45 prisons.

01:46 Some state prisons are even run by private companies contracted by the state authorities,

01:50 because the problem of overcrowding in state prisons has required the intervention of outside

01:55 help.

01:56 There are three different types of state prison facility: Minor, Medium, and Maximum-security

02:00 prisons.

02:01 Some of these prisons even have the facilities to execute prisoners, in states that still

02:05 practice Capital Punishment like Texas and North Carolina.

02:08 Due to their overpopulation problems, these prisons are often underfunded, understaffed,

02:12 and pretty dangerous.

02:14 Getting hundreds or even thousands of violent offenders together in poor living conditions

02:18 is a recipe for disaster.

02:20 Prison mortality rates and suicides have been on the uptick since 2010, and prison riots

02:24 are also a constant risk.

02:26 Recently, tensions boiled over at the Mississippi State Penitentiary in Parchman, Mississippi.

02:31 Brutal gang violence broke out, killing five inmates and allowing a further two to escape.

02:37 Conditions in these state jails are often shoddy – with filthy cells and low-quality

02:40 cafeteria meals.

02:42 The ACLU has even presented lawsuits against state prisons on the grounds of inhumane treatment,

02:47 physical and sexual violence, and racial discrimination.

02:51 Because 20% of all US prison inmates are convicted for drug offences – and the grand majority

02:56 of these inmates end up in state prisons – state prison populations are often disproportionately

03:00 made up of minorities.

03:01 This, in turn, is because mass drug incarceration disproportionately targets minorities to begin

03:07 with.

03:08 Non-violent drug offenders end up shoulder to shoulder with violent criminals, creating

03:11 huge risks to their safety.

03:13 This is only the tip of the iceberg in terms of the horrific conditions faced in a lot

03:18 of state prisons, particularly in the South.

03:20 The civil rights division of the Justice Department investigated a number of state prisons in

03:24 Alabama and their findings were deeply disturbing: Prisoners left face-down, dead in their cells,

03:30 for so long that their faces rotted and flattened.

03:33 There was other evidence that prisoners had been tied up and tortured for days on end.

03:37 Attacks included a prisoner being doused with shaving cream so dangerously hot that it left

03:42 the prisoner with second-degree chemical burns.

03:44 And a prisoner having industrial bleach poured onto their skin, before being beaten senseless

03:49 with a broom handle.

03:50 According to Justice Department reports, some Alabama state prisons have murder rates at

03:55 eight times the national average.

03:57 The lack of funding also means that security standards have slipped, with prisoners sneaking

04:01 in contraband like drugs and improvised weapons.

04:04 These same Justice Department reports have reported rudimentary improvised knives, guns,

04:08 hammers, and even small swords.

04:11 Sexual violence also runs rife in many state prisons, with guards underqualified or simply

04:16 unwilling to intervene and help.

04:18 In order to make up for being understaffed, state prisons often force guards to work gruelling

04:22 hours for very little pay.

04:24 Fusing exhausted, understaffed prison guards with frustrated, overcrowded and often violent

04:28 prisoners creates a dangerous powder keg.

04:31 Federal investigators described the violations of prisoners Eighth Amendment Rights as “severe,

04:36 systemic, and exacerbated.”

04:38 Even the most well-staffed prisons often only operate with seventy-five percent of the staff

04:43 necessary to properly run the facilities and attend to the prisoners.

04:47 Many state prisons are basically an accident waiting to happen, and the staff of these

04:51 prisons are rarely able to contain the results of these accidents.

04:54 Even worse, with very little state government oversight, corrupt and poorly-trained prison

04:59 guards are often responsible for the violence and abuse.

05:02 State prisons are often criticised for their collaboration with private prison companies,

05:06 such as the Corrections Corporation of America and the GEO Group, Inc.

05:09 The stated objective of State Prisons is to rehabilitate inmates and reintroduce them

05:14 into society.

05:15 However, through prison violence and gang activity, prisoners admitted for non-violent

05:19 offences often end up being transformed into hardcore crooks.

05:23 While this could easily seem like an accidental result of the previously mentioned understaffing

05:27 and mismanagement issues, there have been accusations of a profit motivation.

05:31 Because these private prison companies receive government subsidies based on the number of

05:35 inmates housed, these companies benefit from large inmate populations and high recidivism

05:41 rates.

05:42 So, if you’re unlucky enough to get sent to a state prison, you better hope it’s

05:45 a short term and that you’ve got an excellent attorney.

05:49 Because you’re at risk of experiencing dehumanising and unsanitary conditions, violence from both

05:53 other prisoners and the guards, and the damaging effects of gang activity.

05:58 Government oversight bodies like the Department of Justice and activist groups like the Equal

06:02 Justice Initiatives have campaigned for state prison reform, in order to end mass incarceration

06:07 and improve the treatment of prisoners.

06:09 But until these groups win their hard-fought battles for justice, state prisons are probably

06:14 going to remain horrible places to be.

06:16 This brings us to the other subject of today’s video: Federal prisons.

06:20 What exactly is a federal prison?

06:22 Well, the clue is in the name.

06:24 Established under the Hoover administration in the 1930s, Federal prisons are reserved

06:28 for criminals who’ve broken federal laws – such as one or more of the following examples.

06:33 Crimes taking place on federal land or crimes committed against federal officers.

06:37 A crime involving the crossing of state lines.

06:39 Immigrations and customs violations.

06:41 And a grand majority of financial crimes, like fraud, embezzlement, and identity theft.

06:47 Violations of federal law tend to be less violent than state crimes, and this difference

06:51 is also often reflected in the facilities themselves.

06:54 Federal prisons are run by the Federal Bureau of Prisons (or BOP), a government body under

06:58 the Department of Justice.

07:00 The BOP is typically allocated a yearly budget of around $6.5 billion.

07:05 Divided between the Bureau’s fewer than 200 facilities, this results in far better

07:09 funding for each facility than their state-run counterparts.

07:12 This often results in better-quality buildings, living conditions, training programs, and

07:17 food.

07:18 Despite having fewer inmates to process than state prisons, there are five main types of

07:21 federal prison facility rather than three, mostly divided by the level of security.

07:26 There are minimum security federal prisons, referred to by the BOP as Federal Prison Camps.

07:31 These are for prisoners judged to pose no risk of escape or danger to public safety.

07:36 These are the facilities often referred to as “Club Fed” – as prison goes, these

07:40 are about as easy-going as you get.

07:42 Larry Levine, director of the Wall Street Prison Consultants – an organisation that

07:46 helps future inmates from the financial industry adjust to their impending imprisonment – compared

07:51 the experience to junior college.

07:54 Prisoners are hosted in dormitories rather than cells, and the ratio of guards to inmates

07:58 is low.

07:59 While it isn’t exactly a day spa, it’s far from the terrifying environment of an

08:02 Alabama State Prison.

08:04 For Federal Prison Camp inmates, the biggest threat is the soul-crushing boredom of the

08:08 daily routine.

08:10 Low security federal prisons are similar, but with slightly stronger security precautions

08:14 – such as double-fenced perimeters.

08:16 Prisoners are still housed in dormitories and cubicles rather than cells.

08:20 Medium security federal prisons, on the other hand, do have largely cell-based living facilities.

08:25 They also have higher security and a greater number of guards.

08:27 High security federal prison institutions – also referred to as United States Penitentiaries

08:32 – are the closest to state prisons in terms of control over their inmates.

08:36 These prisons are reserved for the most violent criminals, and criminals with the highest

08:40 probability of escape attempts.

08:42 Examples include violent political criminals, murderers, and high-level members of organised

08:47 crime.

08:48 There are also some Federal Corrections Complexes, wherein two different federal prison facilities

08:52 work closely together, despite having different security levels.

08:56 These facilities pool resources in order to better achieve their respective missions.

08:59 It’s a level of cooperation and coordination not found in state prisons.

09:04 Lower-end security facilities also have smaller facilities nearby, referred to as Satellite

09:08 Prison Camps, that use inmate labour and work programs to support the main institution.

09:13 Despite state prison’s stated intention to rehabilitate inmates and re-introduce them

09:18 into society, Federal prison seems a lot better equipped for successfully rehabilitating its

09:23 inmates.

09:24 But the differences between these two institutions don’t stop there.

09:27 On average, sentences served in federal prison tend to be longer than their state counterparts.

09:31 This is both because federal prisoners tend to have a narrower spectrum of crimes – most

09:35 of which are typically more severe – and because these crimes tend to have higher mandatory

09:39 minimums.

09:40 People convicted for federal crimes are also a lot less likely to be offered probation.

09:45 Compared to the disproportionate number of minorities imprisoned in state prisons, the

09:49 populations of federal prisons are disproportionately white.

09:51 Out of a total of around 190,000 inmates, 59% of the federal prison population is white

09:57 and only 38% is African-American.

09:59 Whereas, in state prisons, these stats are a lot more even.

10:04 Almost 50% of the inmates in federal prisons have been convicted of drug-related offenses,

10:08 such as production and trafficking.

10:10 The rest is largely white-collar crime.

10:12 Unlike criminals sentenced to state prisons, federal criminals aren’t always admitted

10:15 to a prison in the state where they’re convicted.

10:18 People convicted of federal crimes can be housed in any federal prison facility in the

10:22 country.

10:23 Federal criminals convicted of white-collar crimes – if not judged to be a flight risk

10:27 – can even self-report to their prison facility on the first day of their sentence.

10:31 People in state prisons are likely to spend the duration of their trial in a local jail.

10:35 While federal prisons do have violent inmates, violence within the prisons themselves is

10:39 a less frequent issue because these prisons aren’t as overcrowded.

10:43 Unlike most state prisons, federal inmates are often moved from facility to facility

10:46 as needed.

10:47 Federal facilities work closely with the US Marshall service, who handle tracking and

10:51 transporting federal inmates across the country.

10:54 Federal inmates that become violent or repeatedly break prison rules may be transferred to a

10:58 higher security federal prison.

11:00 Though the facility is more likely to put a troublesome inmate in solitary confinement

11:04 before resorting to these costlier methods.

11:07 Compared to the overcrowded, brutal conditions of state prisons, medium, lower, and minimum

11:11 security federal prisons also regularly offer a wide range of recreational activities.

11:16 In the prison yard, inmates may have access to sports like tennis, bocce ball, and volleyball

11:21 to maintain physical fitness.

11:23 Inside the building, there are often gymnasiums with basketball, exercise, and wellness facilities.

11:28 Many federal prisons also offer arts and crafts classes, allowing inmates to develop skills

11:32 like painting, crochet, and leather-craft.

11:35 If you’re lucky, you may also have access to televisions and computers with closed-network

11:39 internet connection.

11:41 Federal prisons also offer rec rooms where inmates can interact and let off steam.

11:45 While these facilities have been known to help reduce prison violence – and keep inmates

11:49 in a more relaxed, cooperative mindset – this must feel almost like a cruel joke to non-violent

11:54 drug offenders left for dead in overcrowded, underfunded state prisons.

11:58 But hey, nobody ever said prison was fair.

12:00 So, if you plan on committing a major crime sometime soon, you should probably do yourself

12:04 a favour and keep it federal.

12:06 Especially if you live in Alabama.

12:08 Thanks for watching this video.

12:09 We don’t think you should commit any crimes, because when you’re in jail, you can’t

12:14 watch videos like “What Actually Happens If You Get Beat Up In Prison?” and “How

12:17 To Survive In Prison?”

12:19 We’ve got your watch history on maximum-security lockdown.

00:00 For just the third time in history, women now  outnumber men in the workforce. Or at least that's

00:05 the story. As of 2 months ago, this gap stood at  around 100,000 more jobs held by women. And last

00:11 month, that difference grew to 150,000, which  in the grand scheme of things of the national

00:16 workforce is basically a rounding error. But the  fact that this is so close at all is a sign of

00:23 some major changes in the labor market that have  really only been seen before in 2008 and 2019.

00:29 So, you know, maybe not a good sign. Now, by  itself, there's absolutely nothing wrong with

00:35 this. Some women want a career and some  men want to be stay-at-home parents. So,

00:39 if these non-traditional gender roles become more  accepted and end up splitting the workforce almost

00:44 perfectly 50/50, that is basically the perfect  outcome, right? Except, of course, that's not

00:50 what's actually happening here. Besides the small  little inconvenient detail that every news outlet

00:55 reporting on this issue so far has either been  maliciously or incompetently misunderstanding

01:00 what the data actually means, there is still  a much bigger issue. For a number of reasons,

01:06 this kind of statistical reversal is not really  an indication of women getting ahead or even men

01:10 falling behind. It's instead normally the sign of  some relatively serious issues across the entire

01:16 job market. Which means it's only fair to ask if  the same thing is happening here again. Women now

01:22 outnumber men in the workforce, helping fuel the  rise of the stayathome boyfriend. I've been a stay

01:28 at home dad for 13 years, and I've been a stay  at home dad for approximately 8 years. Officially

01:33 became a stay-at-home dad. Men are missing from  the American workforce. New government data shows

01:38 more men are out, more women are in, many of them  working in fields traditionally dominated by guys.

01:44 A record number of people in the US have more than  one job. That's according to the Labor Department.

01:49 and women appear to be leading that trend. Okay,  so I guess the first thing we need to get out

01:54 of the way is how is this claim even possibly  true? Anybody who even takes a cursory glance

02:00 at the actual numbers might see some pretty  obvious problems with this statement. Sure,

02:05 the labor force participation rate for men has  infamously been falling for a long time now, and

02:09 the participation rate for women is much closer to  its all-time peak. But there is still a 10% point

02:16 difference between them in favor of men. According  to the most recent BLS data, 66.8% of men aed 16

02:23 and over were participating in the labor force,  while only 56.6% of women were. Now, to be fair,

02:29 participating in the labor force does include  people who are looking for work, but not actually

02:34 holding down a job. It takes everybody in these  groups and divides them by the total population,

02:39 outside of a few narrow exceptions, which we will  discuss later. But even if somehow unemployment

02:44 only applied to men, that still wouldn't explain  the disconnect between these numbers and this

02:48 claim. If we wanted to make it even more simple,  we can just look at the BLS's own data and see

02:54 plain as day that in June of this year, there were  84.9 million men employed in this country and only

02:59 77.4 million employed women. So, uh, when these  articles said that women now outnumber men in the

03:05 workforce, what they actually meant was, well, men  still outnumbered women by more than 7 million.

03:11 So, this raises the pretty obvious question of,  were they just straight up lying? Well, no. They

03:17 were doing something much worse. They were either  misunderstanding or outright misrepresenting the

03:22 data. The government effectively runs two separate  job surveys every month. One asks businesses how

03:28 many names were on their payrolls and the  other asks actual households who is working.

03:33 What has actually flipped slightly in favor  of women, is the number of payroll jobs held

03:37 by these genders, which might sound like exactly  the same thing as the number of people employed,

03:42 but it isn't because people can have multiple  jobs. And holding down multiple jobs is quite

03:47 common as a bit of foreshadowing, especially  when they are struggling to get by. All right,

03:52 to show you what I mean here, take 10 men  and 10 women. Two people from each group are

03:56 retired. Three of the women and one of the men are  stay-at-home parents. And sure, for good measure,

04:01 let's say one of the men is out of work entirely.  That leaves five working women and six working

04:06 men, which is actually roughly indicative of the  actual US population, where men do still indeed

04:11 outnumber women in the workforce. But now, let's  say that these two women and one of these men pick

04:16 up an extra job to help pay their bills. Well,  now between the two groups, men have claimed seven

04:22 jobs and women have also claimed seven jobs. So  even though there were more men employed, both men

04:27 and women are working in the same number of jobs,  which is again basically exactly what is happening

04:32 here. Women are statistically more likely to hold  multiple separate jobs. Partially because they

04:37 tend to favor flexible schedules that can work  around other commitments, but also because they

04:41 are over represented in fields that run on shift  work, and they typically just have less stable

04:46 employment, especially if they are moving into  the workforce involuntarily. Men on the other hand

04:51 are also more likely to have more work without a  typical payroll because they are running a small

04:55 personal business as a sole proprietorship and  well yeah also because they are over represented

05:00 in gig work. This still counts as having a job  obviously but doesn't count as a regular payroll

05:06 because of course in contract work like this there  is no payroll. The point is the payroll number

05:11 just isn't counting what these reporters think  it is counting. And look, the misrepresentation

05:16 of this statistic is really disappointing for  two separate reasons. The first is that a lot

05:21 of these articles just took a cool sounding data  point, failed completely to explain what it meant,

05:25 and used it entirely to justify whatever story  they already wanted to write. In just a beautiful

05:30 encapsulation of everything wrong with reporting  these days, one outlet used the data to declare

05:35 the manchild stay-at-home boyfriend an official  economic trend. And another outlet used the same

05:40 figure to support that men were all becoming  communists. Again, maybe you personally agree

05:45 with one and or both of these ideas, but the point  is this figure, while it sounds cool, isn't saying

05:51 what they think it is saying. It's not great,  but it gets worse. Because, well, the second

05:56 reason this is so disappointing is that even with  a proper understanding of what this data actually

06:01 means, it's still really important. Men do still  technically outnumber women in the workforce.

06:06 But this payroll reversal is a real statistical  phenomenon and one that has really only shown up

06:11 in not the greatest of economic times. So I guess  it's worth asking why is this happening now? Well,

06:18 a few reasons. The first one is honestly that  well yeah, even though it's not yet a majority,

06:24 more men really just are choosing to stay at home.  The trend of the stay-at-home dad is much more

06:29 socially accepted today than it was even just  a decade ago. And by Pew's most recent count,

06:33 dads make up almost one in five of America's  stay-at-home parents. Women have also had a

06:38 higher rate of university attainment than men  for a while now. As of last year, nearly half

06:43 of all employed women held a bachelor's degree or  higher compared to about 42% of employed men. So,

06:48 it stands to reason that a lot of them would  choose to actually put that degree to work by

06:52 well, working while their partner stayed home. For  what it's worth, as a personal anecdote, my wife

06:58 makes more than I do as she works a real job and  I have fallen into the prototypical 21st century

07:04 insufferable influencer/trophy husband role.  Now, obviously, that is the best case scenario

07:09 to explain this trend. But let's be honest, most  households these days really need two people

07:14 generating an income in order to survive. And  yeah, in twothirds of married couples with kids,

07:19 both parents already work. So another major driver  is that a lot of these men have started opting out

07:25 of these traditional commitments including the  workforce entirely. This means that in order to

07:30 survive they either rely on their parents, their  partner, government benefits or some combination

07:34 of all three. For young men this group has been  given the name neat not in education, employment

07:40 or training. A classification that now covers  roughly 1 in 10 young men. Among young adults,

07:47 20% of men are still living in a parents home  compared to 15% of women. We have already made

07:52 a whole video about the causes of these trends.  And the TLDDR is that it has largely been the

07:57 result of people effectively seeing that they will  never get ahead through traditional employment. If

08:02 working 40 hours a week provides no meaningful  benefit over just sitting at home, then a lot of

08:06 people who are falling behind are making the  logical decision to fall behind in comfort.

08:11 Now, this has impacted men more so than women,  partially because of the traditional expectations

08:16 that are placed on men to be the breadwinners.  But again, already a whole video about that.

08:21 Even still, this is a long slow drift that has  been playing out over decades. The share of prime

08:27 working age men participating in the workforce  peaked all the way back in 1954, and it has been

08:32 sliding lower across most of the decades since.  So a slow multi-deade slide at the same time that

08:37 women were entering the workforce in mass due  to a combination of necessity and empowerment

08:42 did help to close the gap. But what it can explain  is the very steep flip that just happened and has

08:48 only happened two other times in history. So it's  time to learn how money works to find out why this

08:53 badly misrepresented statistic might legitimately  be a recession indicator. This video is sponsored

08:59 by Monarch. If you have ever tried to track  your money across multiple apps and accounts,

09:03 you know how easy it is to lose sight of the big  picture. Monarch is a private ad-free personal

09:08 finance platform that syncs all your accounts from  13,000 plus institutions into one clean dashboard.

09:14 What I like about Monarch is that it does not  make you try to obsess over every transaction.

09:19 It separates your fixed and flexible spending,  keeps everything organized with your own rules and

09:23 categories, and when something unusual happens,  it explains what changed in plain English.

09:28 you stay aware without being overwhelmed. My  partner and I actually use the shared view for

09:32 our monthly check-ins. We both see the same  dashboard, the same goals, the same recurring

09:37 bills. It has cut out most of the awkward money  conversations because there are no surprises.

09:42 Monarch also tracks your net worth over time and  gives you clear payoff timelines for savings and

09:46 paying down debt, so you can see whether you  are actually making progress instead of just

09:50 hoping you are. And because you are the customer  and not the product, Monarch is completely adree

09:55 with bank level encryption. No ads, no data  selling. Try Monarch for yourself. Scan the QR

10:01 code on screen or use the link in the description  and use code HMW50 to get 50% off your first year.

10:11 Okay, so women entering the workforce and men  opting out of it has helped to narrow this gap

10:16 over the years, but a full inversion is usually  the sign of something going not quite right in

10:20 the wider economy. So, the second big pressure  flipping these scales is that women typically

10:25 have roles that are more secure in an economic  downturn, especially in fields like healthcare.

10:30 According to Indeed's hiring lab, America added  1.2 million new jobs between 2024 and early 2026,

10:37 with 2/3 of those being new jobs going to  women. That was largely because basically

10:41 all of our recent workforce growth has been in  healthcare. as our country slowly transitions

10:46 into being a giant glorified age care facility  with a little bit of data center construction

10:50 tacked on the side. That is barely even an  exaggeration. By the way, over the last 12 months,

10:55 healthcare and social assistance added more  jobs than the entire American economy did on net

11:00 because everything else combined actually shrank.  Care jobs are also much harder to hand over to

11:05 the clankers or layoff in a downturn. And there  are more people getting older and more reliant

11:09 on that care every single year. People over the  age 65 now outnumber children in 11 of 50 states,

11:16 up from just three in 2020. And that's after  CO did a bit of statistical trimming. So yeah,

11:22 there's plenty of positions available to people  looking after the elderly and sick. Again,

11:27 we have already done that video. But on the other  hand, something like construction, which is still

11:32 about 89% male, is incredibly cyclical. If the  economy isn't building, there just naturally isn't

11:38 stable demand for that work. Now, of course, men  can have healthcare jobs, too, but nursing, admin,

11:44 and care work are heavily female-dominated  fields. Registered nurses, for example,

11:48 are still about 87% women. Doctors are closer to  a 60/40 split in favor of men, but they only make

11:54 up a small share of the healthcare workforce.  About 1 million physicians, spread across more

11:59 than 80 million healthcare jobs. Additionally,  statistically speaking, healthcare jobs also tend

12:04 to be shiftbased. And it's much more likely for a  nurse to pick up shifts at two or three different

12:08 facilities, each with its own payroll, than it is  for an engineer to somehow work at three separate

12:13 firms. This again means that women are likely to  hold more payrolls without there actually being

12:18 more women working. Now, as for the wider effects  on the workforce, the reality is that women have

12:22 spent decades being actively encouraged to go  take on roles in typically male-dominated fields

12:27 like engineering, finance, or even the trades. But  there has never really been an equivalent push for

12:32 men to move into typically female dominated fields  like nursing, primary care, social work, or early

12:37 childhood learning. Betsy Stevenson, an economist  at the University of Michigan, said in an

12:42 interview that we have to help men understand that  they can do caregiving roles and stay masculine.

12:47 Now, this is a noble ambition and all, but there  are a few reasons for the split, and one of them

12:52 is simply that these fields don't typically pay  as much. Laura Oric, an economic researcher,

12:57 put it as plainly as an economist can. if you're  seeing a shift towards more female employment, all

13:02 else equal, you would see a shift towards lower  wages. Now, as a quick little interlude, this

13:07 isn't always true, and a lot of healthcare rules  pay extremely well, even outside of the ones that

13:12 require medical school. But even still, for better  or worse, men have been apprehensive about making

13:17 that move. Although, as a side note, the men who  do go into these fields often enjoy a good amount

13:22 of job security and some suspiciously fast career  progression. Sociologists have been calling this

13:27 the glass escalator for more than 30 years. And  male registered nurses today earn about 25% more

13:33 per week than their female colleagues. Part of it  is just a practical reality. A lot of this work is

13:38 quite physically demanding. So having a bigger  guy around to do the literal heavy lifting is

13:43 genuinely useful in many of these settings. Even  still though, despite this very interesting little

13:48 tangent, most people don't go into healthcare  or age support for the paycheck, and men are

13:52 typically more financially focused when picking  a career path. And well, to play devil's advocate

13:57 once again, the third reason that women are  holding more jobs than men is just desperation.

14:02 In a traditional single-income family, if the  breadwinning man of the household loses his

14:07 job in one of those more precarious fields, his  wife or girlfriend might need to go out and take

14:11 on a job where they would typically have been a  stay-at-home spouse. Economists literally call

14:16 this the added worker effect. Studies tracking  laid-off workers found that a wife picking up

14:20 extra work ends up covering about a quarter of  her husband's lost income. In plain English, as an

14:26 example, say you lost a decent job and your wife  goes from staying at home to a part-time role at

14:31 the local clinic, plus a weekend shift somewhere  else while you look for a new primary job. Your

14:36 household budget is still going to be in serious  trouble. But on paper, your family just went from

14:41 one payroll to two. This is pretty much what  we saw in 2008 when men bore almost 80% of the

14:47 recession's early job losses thanks to their over  representation in construction and manufacturing.

14:52 The same thing happened again at the end of 2019  as the result of slowly losing traditional jobs in

14:56 manufacturing and mining and replacing them with  more female dominated service roles. Stevenson,

15:02 the same professor from a minute ago, told NPR  back then that she felt very strongly that women

15:06 would still hold the majority a year later.  Of course, a couple months later we were hit

15:10 with the pandemic which had a bigger impact  on service fields instead, which meant that

15:14 uh that prediction did not age well. So yeah,  as much as it would be nice to say that this is

15:20 a statistic of empowered girl bosses or even  a story of lazy dudes who would rather smoke

15:24 cones and play video games, the actual story  is that the workforce is getting shafted. But

15:29 certain corners of the workforce are getting  shafted slightly less. Someone holding one job

15:33 is usually in a much better position than someone  juggling four of them. Because in most fields,

15:38 the only reason to do that is that one or two  jobs just isn't enough to survive on. The Fed's

15:43 own researchers profiled this group and found that  they average almost 50 hours a week of work across

15:47 their jobs and that for the first time ever about  half of them have college degrees. It sounds bad,

15:53 but it gets worse. Remember when I said about 10  minutes ago that the labor force counts all people

15:58 looking for or actively engaged in work outside  of a few narrow exceptions? Well, there is one

16:03 other statistical anomaly that men in particular  generally turn to in hard economic times. The

16:08 military. Despite being a very real job, the BLS  does not count active duty military personnel as

16:15 part of the regular workforce. And despite getting  a paycheck, their payrolls don't count either.

16:19 Typically, when people, and especially young  men, can't find work anywhere else, the military

16:24 is happy to welcome them with open arms and a  steady wage. And well, yep, as of 2 months ago,

16:29 military recruitment has actually hit a 15-year  high. Every single military branch met or beat its

16:35 goal last year, and the army filled this year's  entire quota about 4 months early. Now, I suppose

16:40 it's possible that young people are just feeling  really patriotic about our on-again, off-again

16:45 special military operation in Iran. But it's  also possible that people are signing up because

16:49 it's the easiest way left to get some financial  stability. The Pentagon's own compensation reviews

16:55 literally treat the civilian job market as a core  recruiting variable. where finding a job gets

16:59 harder for you. Enlistment gets easier for them.  Now, I know this probably isn't a shock to you,

17:04 and even the Army is honestly pretty open about  this. Their own director of market intelligence,

17:09 yes, the Army has one of those, explained the  recent recruiting boom by pointing out that

17:14 job openings have been falling and that we're  postured well to compete in that arena. This

17:18 means that there is a statistically meaningful  group of men out there holding down what are

17:22 effectively payroll jobs that just don't get  captured in this comparison. And yes, of course,

17:27 before the comments say it, there are women in the  military as well, but it is a very male-dominated

17:32 employer. Women make up about 18% of the 1.3  million people on active duty. If these jobs

17:38 were counted normally by the BLS, men would still  comfortably claim more payrolls than women by some

17:44 margin. So, yeah, these claims are wrong. They're  wrong for bad reasons. And even by the narrow

17:49 definition that they are correct, it's really not  the good news or the particular brand of bad news

17:54 they are trying to sell. It's all a little bit  dumb, but it gets even dumber because even in the

18:00 industry that started this whole layoff trend, the  companies driving the cuts have ended up hiring

18:04 back the exact same jobs all over again. So, go  and watch this video next to find out what all

18:10 of this was actually for. And don't forget to like  and subscribe to keep on learning how money works.

00:00 Today we’re going to talk about the darker aspects of war.

00:03 Yes, war is dark enough in itself, but as you’ll know from some of our other shows

00:07 many despicable things happen in war behind what we might call closed doors.

00:12 We only need to look at the Nazi doctor, Josef Mengele, who conducted experiments on people

00:18 that make your stomach churn.

00:20 We might also look at the Nazi ‘Death Marches”, the massacres, the genocides, the torture

00:24 of prisoners and prisoners literally being worked to death.

00:28 These things all happened during the Second World War, as did biological warfare and the

00:33 testing of deadly agents on those captured by certain militaries.

00:36 But today we’ll focus on just one matter of total depravity during that war, in this

00:41 episode of the Infographics Show, The Horror of Unit 731.

00:45 Unit 731 was the brainchild of the Imperial Japanese Army during World War II.

00:50 It was a biological and chemical warfare research unit that conducted experiments on prisoners

00:55 with the aim of developing deadly weapons.

00:57 It’s written that at its base in China – remember the Japanese were at war with China – around

01:02 3,000 men, women, and children were tested on.

01:05 Most of these we are told were Chinese, but some of them were from the Allied Nations,

01:10 the Soviet Union, Korea and Mongolia.

01:12 The unit lasted until the end of the war in 1945 and it’s written that it had ample

01:17 funding from the Japanese government.

01:19 Ok, so this unit was developing dastardly weapons and it needed to test those weapons

01:23 on people first.

01:25 But other tests were also done, related to trying to understand what the human body could

01:29 endure.

01:30 That way the Japanese military might better understand what its own soldiers could go

01:34 through.

01:35 The Cold One of the things many soldiers had to put

01:37 up with during the war was cold, and cold did kill a lot of people.

01:42 At Unit 731 they wanted to understand just how cold someone could get and still survive.

01:47 The website Unit731.org tells us, “Some human test subjects were taken outside during

01:53 the harsh winter until their limbs froze off for the doctors to experiment how best to

01:57 treat frostbite.”

01:59 The New York Times, which had testimonies from people who had seen the horrors of this

02:02 unit, wrote that these people would be taken outside and guards would throw water on them

02:07 until they saw the victim had frostbite.

02:09 Sometimes, wrote the newspaper, the guard would hit the arm of the prisoner with a stick

02:13 and if he heard something like a wood-against-wood sound he knew the arm was totally frozen.

02:18 What happened next is the doctors would use various methods to try and unfreeze the arm

02:22 or other body part.

02:24 Sometimes the prisoner would be left alone to unfreeze, sometimes warm water would be

02:28 thrown on him or her and sometimes much warmer water.

02:32 The Japanese doctors, according to The Times, concluded that water over 100 degrees fahrenheit

02:36 but never more than 122 degrees fahrenheit worked the best.

02:41 Vivisection The Japanese military also wanted to know

02:43 how best to treat disease and injuries, but we are told that to do this they would often

02:48 use live prisoners to operate on.

02:50 It’s said that some of these prisoners would be deliberately given a disease, and then

02:54 the doctors would open up the body of the patient without any kind of anesthesia.

02:57 They wanted to look at the effects of the disease before the body began decomposing,

03:01 and that’s why they kept the subjects alive.

03:05 These people were called marutas, or logs.

03:07 The New York Times, with testimony from a former surgeon, said they just wanted to know

03:11 what had happened inside.

03:13 That man told the Times, “I cut him open from the chest to the stomach, and he screamed

03:18 terribly, and his face was all twisted in agony.

03:20 He made this unimaginable sound, he was screaming so horribly.

03:24 But then finally he stopped.

03:26 This was all in a day's work for the surgeons, but it really left an impression on me because

03:30 it was my first time.”

03:32 Testing Pathogens One of the major experiments at Unit 731 was

03:36 to test how certain pathogens, including cholera or anthrax, would affect a number of people

03:42 if they were exposed to the pathogens.

03:43 They didn’t just do this inside the camp, but also did what they called field testing.

03:48 This was done by dropping the pathogens on small communities in China.

03:52 They wanted to see if they could cause an outbreak of disease.

03:55 We are told some of these experiments were successful, so the Japanese then had the idea

03:59 to carry these pathogens to the United States in what were called balloon bombs.

04:03 It’s written that the Japanese did send about 200 balloons to the U.S. but these failed

04:08 for the most part, only leading to the death of seven people.

04:11 They also had a plan to drop plague-infected fleas on San Diego by using Kamikaze pilots.

04:18 Testing Weapons The Japanese also wanted to test weapons that

04:21 they could use on the battlefield, and this included regular weapons but also toxic gases.

04:26 To do this prisoners would be taken out to a field and tied to a spot with a stake.

04:30 The soldiers would then start testing, which sometimes just meant shooting guns at the

04:34 target, and other times throwing grenades at certain distances to see how effective

04:38 they were.

04:39 The bodies of the victims would then be analyzed so the Japanese knew exactly what damage their

04:44 weapons could do.

04:45 We are told that in one experiment gas was fired at the tied-up prisoners, but the wind

04:49 changed direction and it sent the Japanese soldiers running.

04:53 It’s also said that the soldiers would occasionally test their flamethrowers on the prisoners.

04:57 The pressure chamber and spinning While Japanese people who had worked in the

05:01 camp later recalled how many parts of prisoners could be seen in jars all over the camp, it’s

05:06 not always known how those people died.

05:08 Perhaps one of the worst deaths was the pressure chamber.

05:10 We are told that prisoners would be placed inside a pressure chamber, sometimes alongside

05:14 another prisoner, and the pressure would be turned up until basically the prisoners’

05:19 eyes popped and they eventually died.

05:21 If that wasn’t horrific enough, other prisoners would be literally spun to death so that the

05:26 military could test centrifugal forces.

05:28 Operations The Japanese also wanted to have better surgeons,

05:32 and those surgeons needed subjects to work on.

05:34 One report found tells us how one subject was given an appendectomy.

05:38 After that, his arm was removed and after that he received a tracheotomy.

05:42 This all took about 90 minutes and when the doctors were done, they just killed that patient.

05:47 The man who did these surgeries was at the time a student doctor.

05:50 He told the media that he’d had no idea what to expect when he was told he was going

05:54 to China to practice surgeries.

05:57 Spreading syphilis This is the testimony from a worker at Unit

06:00 731: “Infection of venereal disease by injection was abandoned, and the researchers started

06:06 forcing the prisoners into sexual acts with each other.”

06:09 It’s said that if the pair refused, they would be shot.

06:11 At other times children were infected with the disease.

06:14 The reason this happened was so those infected prisoners could be vivisected at various stages

06:18 of the disease and the doctors at the camp could better understand how it affected a

06:23 person’s organs during that stage of infection.

06:26 Forced pregnancy It’s said that female prisoners would be

06:29 made pregnant by force so that the doctors could understand if disease was passed to

06:33 the child.

06:34 They also wanted to know what damage a disease may have caused to the woman’s reproductive

06:38 organs during pregnancy.

06:39 It’s said the guards would just take women and do this, even to those already injured

06:44 from other experiments.

06:45 While many children were thought to have been born on the camp, it’s said that none survived.

06:50 One former soldier said this sometime later, “Of course there were experiments on children.

06:54 But probably their fathers were spies.”

06:57 For a long time this unit was not talked about, but The Guardian reported in 2018 that Japan

07:02 released lots of information from its national archives relating to Unit 731.

07:07 Prior to this, much of what we knew was only based on testimonies.

07:10 No one has denied what we have talked about today did not happen, but there are more reports

07:15 that tell us smaller experiments also happened.

07:18 These included people being exposed to dangerous levels of radiation, being injected with the

07:22 blood from animals, being injected with sea water and also being burned alive.

07:27 It’s said during the war the Americans knew about the camp and after they granted immunity

07:32 to the physicians of Unit 731 if they shared all their findings with the U.S. military

07:36 as some of those findings might be useful and the U.S. didn’t want the Soviets getting

07:40 hold of the research.

07:42 We will leave you with a comment made by a former Unit 731 worker when he was contacted

07:47 some years later.

07:48 “I don't want to think about Unit 731.

07:50 Fifty years have passed since the war.

07:52 Please let me remain silent.”

07:54 Do you think anything like this could happen again?

07:57 How do you think people could do to this other human beings?

08:00 Tell us in the comments.

08:01 Also, be sure to check out our other video Could You Survive the Stanford Prison Experiment.

08:05 Thanks for watching, and as always, don’t forget to like, share and subscribe.

08:09 See you next time.

00:00 I know it's not going to come as a shock to any  of you watching when I say that the healthcare

00:04 industry in America is incredibly broken.  We spend almost double most other advanced

00:09 economies and yet we have measurably  worse outcomes, lower life expectancy,

00:13 higher infant mortality, more easily preventable  deaths, far lower early intervention methods,

00:18 not to mention the general stress that goes along  with the trip to the hospital, which means a lot

00:23 of people just don't go until it's too late. Now  again, I know none of this is shocking to you,

00:29 but these frictions, failures, and financial  incentives have all become so ingrained into a

00:34 system that has in turn become so ingrained into  our country that it raises a rather concerning

00:39 question. Would it even be possible to unfuck the  health care system without destroying the economy

00:45 in the process? The USA is the largest market in  the world thanks to the disproportionate share of

00:51 our economy dedicated to consumer spending. This  is a statistic that even I have highlighted here

00:56 before on this channel because it makes us look  like we just love buying overpriced trucks and

01:01 useless consumer junk. And while maybe that's  still true, if you remove healthcare spending

01:05 from this equation, we are actually right in line  with most other pure countries. Put another way,

01:10 if we actually demolish the health care system and  built something somewhat efficient in its place,

01:15 we would cut out as much as 10% of our GDP. Now,  10% of our entire economic output going towards

01:21 spinning the wheels of medical bureaucracy isn't  great. But this broken window still represents

01:26 millions of jobs, not to mention a lot of our  financial system. They might contribute nothing

01:31 outside of justifying their own existence. But  now that they are there, they are extremely hard

01:36 to remove. Now, I know what you might be  thinking. Just because something is hard

01:41 doesn't mean we shouldn't do it. And even for the  people who don't believe in socialized medicine,

01:45 the bureaucratic bloat in healthcare is still a  problem. But it's also important to realize that

01:49 no policy maker wants to preside over millions of  lost jobs, even if it would fix one of the biggest

01:55 ongoing burdens on the nation. Oh yeah, and one  last thing. Before all of you non-Americans start

02:01 feeling too smug about the rock and a hard place  we have wedged ourselves into, it's probably worth

02:06 exploring how we have exported this issue across  the world to the point where there is a pretty

02:10 good chance we are making your health outcomes  worse as well. I think what's happening today is

02:15 actually quite important which is is a reflection  of the uh sprawling bureaucracy that's actually

02:20 making America sick. Families have to check their  bank account before seeing a doctor. The result

02:26 is that manageable conditions go untreated until  they become emergencies which is worse of course

02:33 for the patient. Younger Americans die earlier  than young people in other developed countries.

02:39 That statistics drags down the overall American  life expectancy. American men ranked last among

02:45 the 17 countries in that study. Women, by the way,  were second to last. Now, before we get into it,

02:52 I think a bit of context is in order. About 5  years ago, I was personally very much a part of

02:57 the problem in this industry. I worked as an  investment banker specializing in businesses

03:02 operating specifically in healthcare. The scale of  the regulations and business activity that takes

03:07 place in the system between you and your medical  career was big enough that several firms could

03:12 specialize in just serving these companies.  The fact that several investment banks can

03:16 be kept afloat just off the fees they charge as a  middleman on transactions between other middlemen

03:21 in the medical industry should give you a sense  of just how much bloat has been piled onto the

03:25 end goal of treating illness. In fact, the broken  incentives, lobbying, anti-competitive business

03:31 practices, and simple entrenched interest was  part of the reason why I started this channel

03:34 to begin with. It's easy and honestly a little bit  cathartic to anthropomorphize the players in this

03:40 game and group them into heroes and villains.  But to get a good understanding of the problem,

03:44 it's a lot more productive to follow the simple  conflicting incentives that have log jammed the

03:48 system so badly that it's basically impossible  to get things done without stepping on someone

03:52 else's toes. So in the interest of fairness, I  want to start with the doctors themselves because

03:57 of course typically they get much less blame than  something like an insurance company because well

04:02 you know they actually achieve something but they  still have incentives of their own and bodies that

04:07 lobby aggressively to protect those interests.  Becoming a doctor and especially a specialist

04:12 takes a long time and puts most students into a  massive amount of debt. According to the AAMC,

04:18 the median medical student was graduating  $25,000 in debt. And that's accounting for

04:23 some people who were able to get a scholarship or  had parents to fund their education. For students

04:28 going the private college route, that number can  be as high as $400,000. To compensate for these

04:33 immense upfront costs and several years  of loss earnings compared to their peers,

04:36 it's always been the expectation that American  doctors are paid extremely well. And on average,

04:42 they are. Physicians in America are  paid on average almost double that

04:45 of other OECD countries and even extremely  high-income outliers like Switzerland. Oh,

04:51 and as something of foreshadowing, you might have  noticed that Canada is right up there with us. But

04:55 more on that later. In a lot of other countries,  being a doctor is still a prestigious and highly

05:00 respected job. But it doesn't come with nearly the  same expectation of earnings. And in America, this

05:06 wasn't by mistake either. The American Medical  Association, which represents physicians, has

05:11 lobbyed Congress relentlessly to limit residency  positions for students graduating from medical

05:15 school. The Medicare graduate medical education  funding has remained more or less intact since

05:20 1997. But during that same time, we have added  70 million people to our population. This has all

05:25 limited the supply of doctors to the point where  the AAMC estimates that we will have 139,000 fewer

05:31 physicians than we need by 2033 as our population  continues to age. But on the demand side,

05:36 there has been just as much meddling. One of the  other big pushes by the AMA is to make sure that

05:42 there are lots of things that can only legally be  done by a doctor, even when they could be done by

05:46 a nurse practitioner, a physician assistant, or  a non-fysician specialist, like an occupational

05:51 therapist for a lot of this work. Now, of course,  something like brain surgery should probably

05:56 require a specialist to be present, but a lot of  the tasks that legally only doctors can perform

06:01 really aren't that important or that sensitive.  One of the most egregious examples of this scope

06:05 creep is the amount of time that doctors spend  justifying routine prescriptions and procedures

06:09 to health insurance providers. Now, despite being  some more foreshadowing about how bureaucracy

06:14 creates bureaucracy, even if this was all totally  necessary, most of this work is simple data entry,

06:19 which could easily be done by a trained  receptionist. But because only doctors are deemed

06:24 worthy of these specific tasks, they have to spend  their valuable time filling out online forms,

06:28 a cost which is ultimately passed along to their  patients. America has by far the highest medical

06:33 administration cost per capita anywhere in the  world. We spend more than triple the runner up

06:38 which is Germany and bureaucratic administration  is basically their cultural identity. Mandated

06:43 inefficiency is just one of the causes. A simple  combination of bottlenecking the number of doctors

06:48 entering the field and then wasting their time  once they are there means that their hours become

06:52 extremely valuable. Medical schools have realized  this which means they can charge more. And even

06:58 the doctors themselves who largely do just want  to help people aren't going to turn down a far

07:02 higher than average income because they need it  to pay off their far higher than average debt.

07:07 The same goes for things like indemnity insurance,  licensing, and training. All of these things can

07:11 be expensive because doctors are paid well. But  doctors need to be paid well because everything

07:15 they do to maintain their professional  standings is expensive. But all right,

07:20 so far all of this is still only counting the  groups that do still largely want to help people.

07:25 And of course, these little inefficiencies  have snowballed into something much larger.

07:29 There are fewer than a million direct patient  care physicians in America, but over 20 million

07:34 people employed by the healthcare industry  in total, with an alarming share doing very

07:38 little in the way of actually caring for anybody's  health. So, it's time to learn how money works to

07:43 find out how it got this bad and why it's become  almost impossible to undo. If you've ever looked

07:48 at a system like healthcare and wondered why it  never seems to change, then this free report from

07:53 HubSpot called Industries Right for Disruption is  exactly what you should read next. It breaks down

07:57 the industries that are most overdue for major  change and explains what's holding them back.

08:01 This report covers everything from healthcare and  education to real estate and insurance. Basically,

08:06 the sectors where outdated business models and  regulation have created massive inefficiencies.

08:10 If you've ever looked at an industry and thought,  "How has nobody fixed this yet?" This report digs

08:15 into exactly that. My favorite section is the  breakdown of what makes an industry disruptible

08:19 in the first place. Things like high customer  frustration, fragmented incumbents, and regulatory

08:24 modes that are starting to crack. It's the kind of  framework that actually changes how you evaluate

08:28 opportunities. Whether you're looking to build  something in one of these spaces, or just want

08:33 to understand where the biggest shifts are coming,  this is worth bookmarking. This resource was made

08:37 by HubSpot, who's sponsoring this video. Download  it for free at the link in my description and see

08:42 what sectors are next. Okay, so another group that  is often overlooked in this whole equation are

08:47 the hospitals themselves. Like a lot of things in  the economy, hospitals and practices have become

08:52 another entrenched strain on the system simply  because of how consolidated they have become.

08:57 Medical groups have become so dominant in certain  areas that patients effectively have no other

09:01 options if they want a certain procedure outside  of traveling several hours. At the same time,

09:06 the number of doctors that run their own private  practice has been consistently shrinking as

09:10 the industry pressure has pushed doctors into  these collective health systems. Oh, and well,

09:15 you know, I had to bring it up eventually. But the  Government Accountability Office has also pointed

09:20 out the role of private equity in strategically  buying up regional medical practices to create

09:25 local monopolies on care. Now, anti-competitive  practices are nothing new in any industry anymore.

09:30 The FTC has been infamously flaccid with their  enforcement for the last 45 years. But the medical

09:36 industry in particular gets away with a lot more  than it should for two specific reasons. The first

09:41 is that healthcare is complicated. The average  regulator hasn't been to medical school to argue

09:45 against industry groups claiming that a merger  is necessary for patient outcomes. The second

09:50 is that the actual costs that come out of these  mergers are extraordinarily opaque. Of course,

09:55 public enemy number one in this whole game are  the private insurance companies. And don't worry,

09:59 we will get to them soon enough. But a lot of  these combined groups have become so large that

10:03 not even insurance providers can push back against  their market power. If a hospital system has a

10:09 monopoly over a critical medical service in an  area, people will change their insurance if their

10:13 current insurance provider doesn't cover that  network. Large insurers do have more negotiating

10:18 power than individual payers. But if a hospital  is the only game in town, there really isn't much

10:23 they can do. This consolidation has also pushed  insurers into all or nothing contracts where large

10:28 health systems will require insurers to include  all their facilities in their coverage, including

10:33 the expensive ones, or else they won't provide  access to any of them. Now, obviously, health

10:38 insurers aren't the victim here. But in certain  areas, this does prevent them from making a

10:42 narrower network of providers just offering basic  services for a potentially more cost-effective

10:47 plan. All or nothing contracts also incentivize  hospitals to provide services that may not have

10:52 been demanded. even by the massively distorted  market since they are being strongarmed into

10:57 covering it anyway. Even for services provided to  patients on Medicare, there are logical incentives

11:03 that push up prices. One of the key groups that  decide how much a medical service should cost

11:07 Medicare is the Specialty Society Relative Value  Scale Update Committee. A bit of a mouthful,

11:13 so it's normally called Ruck. This is a group of  31 physicians who volunteer to provide guidance on

11:18 how to value a physician's work for computing  healthcare prices. Now, naturally, a group of

11:22 physicians would like to say that physicians  are worth quite a lot. But this group is also

11:27 overwhelmingly made up of specialists, creating  a bias that overvalues specialist procedures over

11:32 simple primary care. Now, the reason why this  is important is because the prices this group

11:37 lays out are almost always adopted by Medicare.  And the prices adopted by Medicare act as a price

11:42 floor template for the rest of the industry as  a whole with various built-in markups. Honestly,

11:47 it's not too dissimilar to how government  treasuries determine the rates that people

11:51 pay on their home loans and credit cards. All  of these conflicting groups obviously create

11:55 a lot of friction in an already very complex  industry, which also allows for other groups

12:00 to cash in in ways that are harder to notice with  everything else going on. Pharmaceutical companies

12:05 make roughly 40% of their global revenue here in  America, even though we have 4% of the world's

12:10 population. It's no secret that we massively  overpay for medicine. But within this whole mess,

12:16 who's going to notice? The US market has become  so lucrative that we have effectively subsidized

12:21 R&D for the rest of the world because selling a  new drug to Americans is so profitable that every

12:26 other country can basically just break even.  And then of course, boxing this whole thing in

12:31 are health insurance companies, which may get some  push back from some of the big health care groups,

12:35 but can still ultimately pass everything along  to regular consumers in costs that are usually

12:40 obfiscated by employer healthare plans. These guys  keep everything out of sight and out of mind for

12:45 most people until they actually need to deal with  it. And then of course they have an incentive to

12:50 delay, deny, and defend. Even if it did function  without this log jam of conflicting interests,

12:55 healthcare is never going to be a normal market.  The information asymmetry is huge. The groups

13:00 paying the bills are rarely the ones receiving  the support. Prices are borderline impossible

13:05 to find. And even if you could get access to  this information and actually understand it,

13:09 you can't shop around while you're dying. Now,  it certainly doesn't help that the regulators who

13:15 should be in there trying to direct this traffic  jam towards something slightly more functional

13:19 are being paid off by these various parties to let  them get a little bit further ahead in traffic at

13:24 the expense of making it impossible to fix the  system as a whole. According to Open Secrets,

13:29 the healthc care sector is the number one lobbying  spender in the country, spending almost 3/4 of a

13:34 billion dollars in 2024 alone, just at the  federal level. But now, the thing is, this

13:40 has been going on for so long that even if it was  completely fixed and ironed out tomorrow, there is

13:44 too much built up in it. Every one of these groups  employs tens of thousands of people to negotiate,

13:49 coordinate, lobby, market to, or just plain old  sue all of the other groups. Each and every one

13:55 of these groups is just trying to serve their  own self-interest, but none of those interests

13:59 are aligned. And the group that is consistently  made to compromise is the patient right in the

14:04 middle of everything with the least understanding  and negotiating power. Another slightly darker

14:09 visual metaphor is that often rats will get their  tails caught together. And as they run to try and

14:14 free themselves, they only end up pulling the knot  tighter. Collectively, this administrative bloat

14:19 built to service the administrative bloat is one  of the largest employers in the country and at

14:24 least up until recently has been one of the only  industries safe from layoffs. If we could snap our

14:29 fingers tomorrow and replace our healthcare system  with something like what exists in Australia,

14:33 we would lose 7 12% of our economic uh  productivity and shed millions of these

14:39 jobs. It's also worth noting that Australia's  system is not exactly an unfair comparison.

14:45 They also have very well-compensated doctors  on average. They have extremely good health

14:49 outcomes and rely on a blended system of private  health insurance and public Medicare. Either way,

14:54 this would be a larger hit to both of these  numbers than the global financial crisis. However,

15:00 that doesn't mean it's not worth trying because  over time, this problem is only getting worse. The

15:06 size of the healthcare industry has consistently  been growing faster than the size of the overall

15:10 economy. By 2033, the Centers for Medicare and  Medicaid Services predicts that more than 1/5if of

15:16 our entire economy will be dedicated to healthcare  and the apparatus that is built up around it.

15:20 But just like healthcare has slowly grown on the  economy, it can also slowly be disassembled over

15:26 time as well. Simple things like antitrust  enforcement, proper lobbying, regulation,

15:30 and more transparency will at the very least deal  with the elements that are intentionally trying to

15:35 pile more logs into the log jam. We may lose some  jobs like internal auditors for the legal firms,

15:40 servicing the investment banks, managing the deals  between market information providers, giving leads

15:45 to pharmaceutical sales businesses that sell  third-party generic substitutes to regional

15:49 healthcare groups. But that's just measuring  the uh downsides. One of the biggest hurdles

15:54 to skilled professionals starting businesses of  their own is losing the healthcare security that

15:59 comes along with being a skilled professional.  Removing one of the biggest obstacles to genuine

16:03 business development in the long term would be  far healthier for the economy than piling another

16:08 layer of administration on top of our health  care system. Finally, it might also solve what

16:12 some consider to be one of the most existential  problems in the world. We aren't having enough

16:17 babies. But when a visit to the hospital can be  bankrupting, maybe this shouldn't be too shocking,

16:22 especially to the same group of people who want  to replace us all with AI anyway. But go and watch

16:27 this video next to find out why they still really  want you to have a child anyway. because it gets

16:32 really weird. There was a lot more to talk about  in this video which I will be writing a newsletter

16:36 on in my totally free newsletter compounded daily.  So, make sure to sign up for that if you want to

16:41 learn about it more. And don't forget to like and  subscribe to keep on learning how money works.
