00:00 A planet-killing asteroid could  already be hurtling toward Earth…

00:03 and we might not see it until it’s too late. Despite the idea of 24/7 sky monitoring,

00:09 there are still blind spots. And that’s  exactly where something catastrophic

00:12 could come from. Objects can slip past our  detection networks depending on their angle

00:16 of approach,especially steep “above the plane”  trajectories no one is continuously watching.

00:22 It’s happened before… and it will happen again. We got lucky once.

00:26 Next time, we might not. Humans have built systems

00:28 designed to watch the sky for anything coming our  way. Constant surveillance. Precision tracking.

00:33 The ability to map the paths of objects moving  millions of miles through space. And if something

00:38 looks dangerous, in theory, we can respond. For decades, that idea has given billions

00:43 of people a quiet sense of security. That idea is fundamentally flawed.

00:48 On September 9th 2017 an interstellar  object slingshotted past the Sun.

00:52 The cigar-shaped structure, estimated at around  a quarter of a mile (400 meters) in length,

00:56 travelled at almost 196,000 miles per hour  (315,431 kph). Just over a month later,

01:01 it made its closest approach to Earth. And nobody saw it.

01:05 It wasn’t until October 19 that  the object was detected. By then,

01:09 it had already spent years in our vast solar  system and was already on its way towards the

01:13 exit. Weeks had passed with this large, anomalous  object speeding through our solar system unseen.

01:18 This object was later named ‘Oumuamua.  It passed through the solar system and

01:22 left again without impact. Now imagine the same kind of

01:26 arrival… but with something actually locked  onto Earth. A massive hunk of rock and metal,

01:31 moving straight through space toward us and  nothing in our satellite networks, telescopes,

01:36 or monitoring systems picks it up in time. Not until it’s already too late.

01:40 If it happened once, it can happen again. How did we miss it?

01:44 Simp;e. We weren’t looking in the right places. Not because we didn’t want to, but because we

01:49 weren’t able to. It turns out that even  the most advanced observatories on Earth,

01:54 like Pan-STARRS and the Vera C.  Rubin Observatory, have blind spots.

01:59 In other words, the planetary defence systems  we count on… aren’t as reliable as they seem.

02:04 They’re designed to map objects  moving across the full 3D dome of

02:07 the night sky. But there are regions  they struggle to watch clearly,

02:11 especially the bright, sun-facing areas  where detection becomes far harder.

02:15 It was from that same abyss that ‘Oumuamua  emerged, ‘dropping into’ our system from

02:20 above. By the time we understood what  we had seen, it was already gone.

02:24 It proved we’re vulnerable. So, if we’re blind to this

02:27 part of our solar system, why haven’t we  simply sent probes to take a look for us?

02:31 To understand how humanity became so worryingly  blind to this enormous existential vulnerability,

02:37 we have to go back to the  birth of our solar system.

02:39 4.5 billion years ago, it was little more  than a flattened disk of gas and dust,

02:45 spinning wildly in the deep darkness of  space. It was collapsing, reshaping itself

02:49 under gravity. As it contracted, it didn’t just  fall inward, it spun faster. Collisions built

02:55 structure. Small grains became larger bodies. At the center of it all, the future Sun.

03:01 The result was a single shared orbital plane: a  cosmic “disc” everything would eventually follow.

03:07 Every planet and asteroid were into the same  general lane of motion. And that structure shaped

03:12 how we see everything around our solar system. For thousands of years, mankind watched the night

03:17 sky and tracked the movements of the stars.  And because our planet moves along a flat,

03:22 ecliptic plane, all the other planets appear to  move in narrow, predictable paths across the sky.

03:27 In short, we grew up in a world where everything  happened along the same horizontal axis, which

03:31 embedded a kind of ‘two dimensional bias’ into our  collective consciousness. And that bias persisted

03:37 right up to the time when we finally invented the  type of technology we needed to build high-power

03:43 telescopes and send rockets into space. We still operated outside the

03:47 intense glare of the Sun. We sent our most advanced

03:50 probes outside that glare, where they  could function safely and consistently.

03:55 We built our detection and planetary defense  systems with a heavy bias toward the ecliptic

03:59 plane, because that’s where most comets,  asteroids, and debris were expected to

04:04 emerge from. We built, in effect, a 2D  surveillance system in a 3D universe.

04:09 It all traces back to those ancient laws of  physics that shaped the architecture of our

04:13 solar system. It defined the orbits of planets  and the limits of where we looked. But the void

04:18 above and below was outside that limit. But this isn’t a mere psychological bias

04:23 that we can easily overcome; it’s a physical  barrier that demands an immense amount of

04:27 energy for rockets to break through. In the field of space exploration,

04:31 distance and speed aren’t necessarily  the most important metrics. Instead,

04:35 numerous theories and projections are built  around a measurement known as Delta-V.

04:40 It’s arguably the only metric that  matters. It measures the total change

04:44 in velocity a spacecraft is capable of producing. It’s sometimes referred to as the ‘fuel budget’

04:49 or ‘range’ of a rocket. Every maneuver in space,  whether it be launching from Earth, landing on

04:54 the moon, or adjusting from one orbital trajectory  to another, demands a certain amount of Delta-V.

05:00 We’ve built rockets and probes with enough delta-v  to explore the solar system, and even leave it. So

05:05 why is it so difficult to send them in a different  direction and map the space above and below us?

05:11 It all comes down to one thing. ‘Gravity Prison.’

05:15 When a rocket takes off from the Earth’s surface,  it inherits the Earth’s orbital velocity,

05:19 traveling around the Sun at a rate approaching  19 miles per second (30 kilometers a second).

05:23 That powerful forward momentum is helpful when  you want to travel to another location along the

05:28 same plane, somewhere like Mars, for example.  If we want to send a rocket to the outer edges

05:33 of the solar system, past Pluto, it would  only need an additional Delta-V of around 10

05:38 miles per second (16 kilometers per second). It’s because the rocket or probe is

05:41 benefiting from the Earth’s orbit. It’s already moving the right way,

05:45 but just needs a relatively small  push to move further across the plane.

05:49 If we want to turn a corner, however, and  move out of that ecliptic plane, then that

05:53 means a much greater amount of energy. To pull off a maneuver like that,

05:57 you can’t rely on Earth’s orbit. You  have to fight against it, canceling out

06:00 that horizontal momentum while accelerating the  spacecraft in a completely different direction.

06:05 Because of this, the estimated amount of  Delta-V required to achieve a 90-degree

06:10 solar polar orbit is approximately 20 miles  per second (32 kilometers per second).

06:14 Double the amount of energy needed to  get past Pluto and exit the solar system.

06:18 It’s like launching a rocket from Earth,  pushing it to maximum speed, and then

06:22 trying to stop it instantly by slamming into  a wall at 67,000 miles per hour. (107,826 kph)

06:27 That kind of maneuver is beyond what our  current propulsion systems are built to handle.

06:32 This is the Gravity Prison. The laws of orbital mechanics and the pull of our

06:36 planet effectively lock us into a flat, horizontal  corridor that’s almost impossible to escape.

06:42 Almost. Because, despite

06:43 this massive barrier, NASA actually managed  to send one probe out of the plane in 1990.

06:49 What it found broke our understanding of the Sun. NASA called its 1990 probe Ulysses and

06:54 it represented something unprecedented. A blind and daring leap into the unknown.

06:59 Because engineers couldn’t rely on conventional  chemical propulsion alone to conquer the Delta-V

07:04 barrier, they had to get creative. Ulysses was  launched towards Jupiter. The gas giant’s huge

07:09 gravitational field slingshotted the probe out  of the ecliptic plane and into a high-inclination

07:15 polar orbit around the Sun. Somehow, it worked.

07:18 The data started pouring in. And it defied every expectation.

07:22 Before the Ulysses mission, the scientific  community operated according to a rigid belief

07:26 in something called the Parker spiral model. It  dictates that the Sun’s magnetic field twists

07:32 into a neat spiral-like structure as it extends  across the solar system. According to this model,

07:37 the solar poles were relatively quiet and orderly  regions where magnetic lines returned to the star.

07:43 Ulysses revealed that our polar  magnetic fields are unwound and chaotic.

07:48 Far from following a precise, predictable  pattern, the lines are wildly disorganized

07:53 and entirely unpredictable. This suggests that  all of our established mathematical models of

07:57 solar physics weren’t just a little ‘off’. They were missing 50% of the picture.

08:03 In an instant, entire theories and formulas fell  apart. Everything we thought we knew about the

08:08 most important star of all had to be rewritten. The drama didn’t end there.

08:12 The environment that Ulysses encountered above the  Sun was almost unimaginably violent. Solar winds

08:18 reached speeds of around 466 to 497 miles per  second (750 to 800 kilometers a second). That’s

08:23 almost double the winds  found at the solar equator.

08:25 It was the equivalent of passing from  a breezy day at the beach to a Category

08:30 5 hurricane simply by changing latitude. The space above us was not some peaceful,

08:35 empty, uninteresting void. It was a torrent of  energetic chaos, a whirlwind of magnetic violence,

08:41 far beyond our wildest expectations. The swift solar winds of the poles

08:45 were only the beginning. As scientists scrambled to

08:48 analyze the new data, they realized that this was  just one part of a much larger systemic crisis:

08:54 the space above us isn’t just unstable. It’s crushing our entire solar system.

08:59 For generations, space agencies presented a clear  visual model of our solar system and its position

09:04 in the wider galaxy. We were told that our  world and the planets that share the surrounding

09:09 space travel through the universe inside a  stable, symmetrical, bubble-shaped shield.

09:14 The heliosphere. It was a reassuring concept.

09:17 We didn’t have to worry about world-ending  catastrophes and interstellar radiation,

09:22 because there was always this vast invisible  force-field to keep us safe. That model isn’t

09:27 exactly wrong. But it misses something vital:  our so-called shield is under immense pressure.

09:32 And the cracks are already starting to show. In recent years, data gathered by deep space

09:37 probes and interstellar satellites has revealed  that the cosmic architecture we depend on is being

09:42 forcefully altered. Professor Merav Opher, one  of the world’s leading astrophysicists, famously

09:47 concluded that while ‘sphere’ may be a part of its  name, the heliosphere is anything but spherical.

09:52 It’s more like a flat croissant. A flat croissant that is constantly being

09:57 crushed and warped by intense magnetic pressure,  leaving dangerously thin spots at the poles.

10:02 In other words, Earth’s protective  magnetic field bends, stretches,

10:06 and shifts over time. It’s not a secure bunker  or impenetrable barrier. It’s more like a

10:11 plastic tent with a sagging roof, struggling to  withstand the weight raining down from above.

10:16 The fragility of our situation was highlighted  in 2009. NASA’s Interstellar Boundary Explorer

10:21 satellite, or IBEX, turned towards the  edges of our system and saw something

10:26 humanity had never seen before. The so-called IBEX Ribbon.

10:30 A massive, mysterious structure made up of  enhanced energetic atom emissions, spanning across

10:35 the sky. Containing particle densities that are 2  to 3 times higher than surrounding space, the IBEX

10:41 Ribbon acts like a kind of ‘magnetic mirror’  which reflects escaped solar wind particles

10:46 right back into the core of the solar system. It’s like a glowing neon fence surrounding our

10:51 entire solar system. We had no idea it was even  there until 2009. But that same energetic ribbon

10:57 extends right through the high-latitude  polar regions of our dynamic shield.

11:01 That same barrier, meant to protect us from the  lethal radiation of outer space, isn’t fixed. It

11:06 shifts and flexes at its edges over time. Because  we’ve been so busy looking out across our own flat

11:12 2D plane, we’ve had no way of knowing about it,  and no way of tracking its changes over time.

11:18 In fact, the only way to monitor the highly active  poles required an extreme gravitational maneuver.

11:24 All of the problems outlined so far  boil down to one underlying cause:

11:28 the conservation of angular momentum. It’s that very same physical law that

11:33 formed our solar system and gave our  planet life that blinds us today.

11:37 It’s a true case of cosmic irony. Billions of years ago, it was the conservation of

11:41 angular momentum that helped the early condensing  chaos of the solar system flatten and extend

11:47 outwards into a life-sustaining disk. A miracle of  physics that paved the way for life as we know it.

11:53 Without that flattening, the Earth wouldn’t  have formed. It wouldn’t have begun to follow

11:57 that perfectly precise and stable circular  orbit it has to follow to sustain life..

12:02 The flat ecliptic plane - the end  result of angular momentum - is the

12:06 only reason we exist at all. Yet that same law of physics

12:10 now traps us in a gravity wall prison. If humanity truly wants to set up an early

12:14 warning or defense system above the solar system  to scan for signs of the next ‘Oumuamua, it can’t

12:20 fight the rules of physics. It has to use them to  its advantage. In real terms, that means the only

12:25 option is to slingshot us where we want to go. If we can survive it, that is.

12:30 One way we’re ever getting out into the abyss  relies on a high-stakes orbital strategy called

12:34 the Oberth Maneuver, otherwise known as  a Powered Flyby. It’s an extremely risky

12:39 orbital technique in which a spacecraft allows  itself to fall inside a gravity well. It waits

12:44 until the very last moment - at the lowest  point of that well - to fire its engines.

12:49 This, in turn, takes advantage  of the so-called Oberth effect,

12:53 which states firing a rocket’s engines at high  velocity produces far more kinetic energy than

12:58 doing so at lower speeds. If we can’t achieve  enough Delta-V through conventional propulsion,

13:03 this becomes our only remaining option. We have to literally make a

13:07 spacecraft fall into the sun. As it falls deeper and deeper,

13:11 it will accelerate to an extreme speed, activating  its on-board propulsion systems at the very nadir

13:16 of its orbit. This would give it a boost that  might just be big enough to send it slingshotting

13:21 out of the ecliptic plane. It’s an extreme maneuver.

13:24 At that distance from the Sun, no  conventional spacecraft would survive.

13:28 Even our strongest current heat shields would melt  in an instant. The spacecraft would be subjected

13:33 to a thermal bombardment it would have no hope of  withstanding. And with no shields to guard them,

13:38 all of the sensors, cameras, communications  systems, and other components required to collect

13:43 and send data back to Earth would be vaporized. In short, this desperate ‘jailbreak’ gamble

13:49 requires technology we don’t have yet. Until then, we’re sitting ducks.

13:53 A potentially world-ending threat could be  somewhere in space right now, speeding towards us.

13:58 The world’s leading space agencies  spend vast amounts of time and

14:01 resources on planetary defense initiatives. They scan the stars for signs of Potentially

14:06 Hazardous Asteroids (PHAs) with an estimated  diameter larger than 460 feet (140 meters) and

14:12 an orbit that brings them within 4.64 million  miles (7.48 million km) of the Earth’s path.

14:17 There are thousands of known  PHAs in existence today.

14:20 There could be countless  others we don’t yet know about.

14:23 Less than 1% of known PHAs have an  inclination greater than 45 degrees.

14:29 The interstellar void - the vast regions above  and below our solar system - doesn’t follow the

14:34 same flat plane we live in. ‘Oumuamua wasn’t a one-off.

14:37 It was a warning shot. It was the wider universe sending a message that

14:41 we aren’t as safe as we’ve been led to believe.  The space that surrounds us is much greater - and

14:46 more dangerous - than we ever could have imagined. Since ‘Oumuamua’s arrival, much has changed

14:51 in the way we observe the universe. We retuned software algorithms for the

14:55 upcoming Vera Rubin Observatory, approving an  ESA Comet Interceptor mission and scanning the

15:01 skies to specifically chase the next object. A potential planet killer might already be on

15:06 its way, set to descend through the thin,  flaking layers of our crushed croissant

15:10 shield. It might past the blind spots of  the Pan-STARRS and other observatories,

15:14 ready to catch us all entirely off guard. It won’t announce itself.

15:18 And it won’t follow the rules we want it to. Our survival depends on mapping the full 3D

15:23 sphere of our origin, breaking past the Delta-V  barrier, using gravity assists, and looking

15:29 above and below, not just across the plane. Until then, we’re relying on telescopes,

15:34 surveys, and deflection physics to keep us  safe from the one impact we never see coming.

15:39 And that only works… until it doesn’t. There’s little we can do if a planet

15:44 killer is already on its way. Watch “The  Last 60 Minutes Before Asteroid Impacts with

15:48 Earth” to see what those final moments would  actually look like. Or click on this video.

00:00 8 am. April 2, 1912. The magisterial ship the  Titanic leaves the Belfast dock for sea trials.

00:06 Thousands of people have come to watch,

00:08 waving their handkerchiefs in the  air and shouting “Rule Britannia”.

00:12 Some of them chase the ship down the  slipway as she slowly moves away.

00:15 Not one of them could ever expect  that such a behemoth of a vessel

00:19 would end up at the bottom of the icy-cold ocean,  dragging countless people to the depths with it.

00:24 April 10, 1912. On a cold morning, Captain  Edward John Smith arrives at the Southampton dock

00:30 where his crew has been sleeping  on the Titanic through the night.

00:33 Smith is a confident man, and proud of  British shipbuilding expertise. Prior to

00:37 his heading the Titanic he’d told a reporter: “Whatever happens, there will be time enough

00:41 before the vessel sinks to save the life of  every person on board. I will go a bit further.

00:45 I will say that I cannot imagine any condition  that would cause the vessel to founder.”

00:49 Oh, how wrong could he be! We’ll talk  a lot about this guy as things go on.

00:53 Later in the morning, Fifth Officer Harold  Lowe and Sixth Officer James Moody are there

00:58 to supervise a lifeboat drill, unfortunately,  the only one that would happen on the Titanic.

01:02 As midday approaches, the passengers arrive:  rich, poor, and something in between. The ship

01:07 can take 2,453 passengers: 833 in first class,  614 in second class, and 1,006 in third class,

01:16 but there will only be about 2,200  passengers on board when the thing goes down.

01:20 The wealthy board from one entrance and the poor  at another entrance. Those with meager means are

01:25 the third-class passengers, who on arrival are  checked for an eye disease called trachoma.

01:30 The USA doesn’t want these folks, but only  one person it seems is turned away. Lucky him!

01:35 About a third of third-class, dreaming of a new  life in the US, are not native English speakers.

01:40 Their basic cabins reflect their status,  or class, as the British like to call it.

01:44 These are people who will suffer the worst,  screaming in their native tongues as they slide

01:48 down the deck of a ship turning upwards towards  the sky. Some are Bulgarian, Syrian, Italian,

01:54 Swedish, and Russian; some are even Chinese,  even though the Chinese Exclusion Act in the US

01:59 means Chinese laborers aren’t  welcome in the country.

02:02 The first-class passengers enter their  beautiful cabins. These are the bankers,

02:06 businessmen, military leaders, socialites,  athletes, American millionaires,

02:10 and the ever-snooty British aristocracy.

02:12 This is the who’s who of wealthy society,

02:14 and many have arrived with personal  nurses, valets, chefs, and chauffeurs.

02:18 On the ship, they’ll enjoy Turkish  baths, a gymnasium, a squash court,

02:22 a saltwater swimming pool, and even first-class  kennels for their beloved pooches. For their trip,

02:27 and ultimately their death, some of them have  paid around 90,000 bucks in today’s money.

25:44 But even worse, because the ship goes down  with so much force that it takes tables,

25:48 chairs and huge chunks of timber and steel down  with it. A lot of the debris comes right back up,

25:54 and does so with some speed, killing the swimmers  on impact. It’s likely they’ll die anyway, with

26:00 −2 °C (28 °F) water being enough to finish most  people off in a few minutes. That’s if the shock

26:05 of being submerged hasn’t already killed them. Many swimmers die between 15 and 30 minutes in the

26:10 water, their bodies going into cardiac arrest.  Only 13 of them are fished out by lifeboats,

26:15 even though if all the boats go back  500 people can be helped. It’s anyone’s

26:19 guess how many folks could be saved, but  that some people needlessly died is true.

26:24 As they float through the water in the  darkness, the survivors hear shouts of anger,

26:28 cries of distress, screams of pain, sounds they  will never forget. One of the survivors will

26:32 later sum up what he hears, saying, it was “a  dismal moaning sound which I won't ever forget;

26:37 it came from those poor people who were  floating around, calling for help. It

26:41 was horrifying, mysterious, supernatural.” At times the lifeboats float past a person.

26:46 Its occupants apologize for not helping  the swimmer, but rather than become upset,

26:49 the swimmer just says, “I understand”  and “good luck and God bless you.”

26:53 But as they float on, they hear one man,  perhaps the last man, shout, “My God!

26:57 My God!” As he freezes his voice loses hope until  all that is left is silence. That’s all there

27:03 is after a while: stiff bodies and silence. But one guy who does survive for a long time

27:08 in the water is the Titanic’s  chief baker, Charles Joughin.

27:11 Prior to the sinking of the Titanic, he  drinks more whiskey than is humanly possible,

27:16 having just turned down the offer to get in  lifeboat 10. Right before he heads for his drink,

27:20 he persuades reluctant women to get in the boats. When he emerges on the deck, most people have

27:24 gone, so he throws a bunch of chairs in  the ocean to use as floatation devices,

27:28 but then he changes his mind. He grabs  hold of something and in his own words,

27:32 goes down with the ship as if it is an elevator. He miraculously treads water for about two

27:37 hours, and maybe because of that booze he just  drank, he doesn’t even feel cold. When there’s

27:42 some daylight, he spots a boat. It’s Lightoller’s  boat, but Lightoller denies him a place. Joughin

27:47 holds on to the boat anyway, and then when he  sees another boat, he swims over and gets on that.

27:51 How he survives is anyone’s guess, but later when  asked later he’ll put it down to the whiskey.

27:56 Whatever the case was, he will be known as  the last surviving person on the Titanic.

27:59 He was a tough old boot, that’s for sure. Nonetheless, don’t go thinking booze will stop you

28:04 from getting hypothermia. It actually makes things  worse, so we can’t explain how Joughin survived so

28:09 long when others died in a matter of minutes.  He didn’t panic, which counts for something.

28:14 The first sound heard by the survivors is that of  the approaching Carpathia at around 3.30 am. By 4,

28:20 people are being pulled from the boats, most of  them alive, but more than a few already dead.

28:24 Those with the strength climb onto the ship,  while others are hoisted up with ropes. More

28:28 than 1,500 have died. 706 live to tell the tale. At 8.30 am, the Californian scouts the area

28:34 looking for survivors, but of course there  are none. The others are taken to New York

28:38 City where they’ll arrive on April 18 to  huge crowds and hordes of journalists.

28:42 Some of the surviving crew are interviewed,

28:44 but what really happened on that ship is  something they’re too traumatized to talk about.

28:48 Many questions are later asked, one,  of course, is why so few lifeboats,

28:52 but even with the mass grief and global  outrage, no one is ever really held accountable.

28:56 An act of God is blamed, but we now know  that human error was more to the point.

29:01 Perhaps one of the best artifacts  from the wreckage is a watch that

29:04 was pulled out of the water. That’s because  it stopped when its owner drowned: 2.28 am.

29:09 In 1985, the wreckage was found  12,500 feet (3,800 meters) underwater,

29:13 around 370 nautical miles (690  kilometers) off the coast of Newfoundland.

29:17 The two parts are still now separated  by about 2,000 feet (600 meters).

29:20 It’s the rich and famous whose names we remember,  so we guess the classes on that boat are separated

29:26 even in death, but we remember you third-class  victims: Mrs. Johanna Persdotter Ahlin,

29:31 Mr. Karl Ivar Sven Berglund, Mr. Liudevit Cor,  Miss Kate Conolly, Mr. Lee Bing, and Mr. Fang

29:39 Lang, Mr. Husayn Mahmūd Husayn Ibrāhīm. Ok, we can’t go through all the poor folks

29:44 that died, and to be honest, about 100  of them were buried in unmarked graves.

29:48 But you get the picture. Many of them were  immediately forgotten, while the media and

29:52 public mourned for just a few known names. At  least the fish understood those dead people were

29:56 all the same in the bigger scheme of things. Now you need to watch a video about an equally

30:00 horrific tragedy, “Creepy Reason Nobody Talks  About The Deadliest Ship Disaster In History.”

30:05 Or, have a look at “What If The Earth  Stopped Spinning - Minute By Minute.”

00:00 The biggest issue in 20 years will be population collapse.

00:04 So we're looking at the Chinese running out of people.

00:07 Within ten years.

00:08 The population collapse in developed countries is precipitous.

00:13 A demographic earthquake is going to destroy our economies.

00:17 Fewer workers, fewer ideas, higher taxes to fund more pensioners, slower growth.

00:22 By now, you've probably heard all the doom and gloom

00:24 arguments, perhaps even on this very channel.

00:27 But what if we wait?

00:29 What if I was wrong?

00:31 What if the historical evidence actually tells us that collapsing

00:34 birthrates, paradoxically, are good for the economy?

00:39 Because they force companies to innovate?

00:42 That's exactly the premise of a new paper by Nobel Prize winning economist Darren

00:46 Asamoah and coauthors that has been going econo viral on X.

00:53 In this paper, he studies some of the biggest fertility

00:56 collapses of all time China, Japan and South Korea.

00:59 And they found that these coincided with growth miracles, not disasters.

01:06 In fact, it turns out that countries with the lowest fertility rates back

01:09 in 1950 turned out to grow faster

01:12 over the next 70 years than countries that still had lots of babies.

01:17 In other words, if we look at history, it seems like collapsing birthrates

01:21 are not that bad and may even be good for the economy.

01:25 But does that encouraging evidence actually apply

01:28 to our coming demographic doom story?

01:31 Before we can find out, let's quickly review

01:33 the standard story the global economy faces demographic doom.

01:38 All right.

01:38 As I see it, there are essentially two parts to this story

01:42 about why a rapidly aging society is bad news for the economy.

01:46 The first is simple.

01:47 Far fewer workers will have to support a lot of pensioners.

01:51 The economy GDP is simply a measure of all goods and services produced.

01:56 If you rapidly reduce the number of people who make stuff versus

02:00 those that are retired, and of course you should expect

02:03 economic growth to slow down rapidly.

02:06 Yes. Slow down.

02:08 Because the thing is, economic growth is not just hours worked.

02:12 It's also how productively these hours are used.

02:15 So far, even a rapidly aging economy like Japan

02:19 has been able to grow by getting more productive.

02:21 However, sadly, the second part of the doom and gloom story

02:25 predicts that as fewer babies are born, workers will be less productive

02:29 because there will be less innovation for two reasons.

02:33 Reason number one young workers are uniquely innovative.

02:36 Fewer babies today mean fewer entrepreneurs and inventors tomorrow.

02:40 After all, beyond the fact that older workers tend to start fewer

02:44 high growth startups, aging workforces create massive bottlenecks.

02:50 That is when senior employees hold onto key positions for longer and longer.

02:54 They prevent younger talent from acquiring the management

02:58 and business skills needed to succeed.

03:01 Therefore, economists like doctor Fatih Garan

03:04 argue that roughly half of the decline in U.S.

03:08 startup activity since the 1980s can be explained

03:12 purely by fewer young Americans entering the workforce.

03:15 Second, when a population is growing rapidly,

03:18 there is a big prize for those who innovate.

03:21 Put yourself in the shoes of an ambitious software entrepreneur.

03:24 Competing with established giants requires immense upfront investments.

03:30 If the population is growing, so does your future customer base,

03:34 making it worth the risk to build new products.

03:37 But in a country facing demographic decline, where the pool

03:40 of potential business clients shrinks year after year,

03:44 the price for innovation might simply not be big enough anymore to justify

03:48 spending so many years on researching and trying potential new products.

03:53 So in summary, the standard narrative is twofold.

03:56 One. Fewer babies means fewer workers, means

03:59 less supply of goods and services simple to fewer young people.

04:03 And a falling population means less innovation.

04:06 And together, these two trends spell certain doom for the economy.

04:10 But that is just a theory.

04:12 And a theory must always answer to evidence.

04:16 And according to some Moghalu and his coauthors,

04:18 the evidence does not support this story at all.

04:21 Yes, aging

04:22 will reduce the number of workers, but rather than becoming less innovative,

04:26 they believe a reduced workforce will make

04:29 economies more innovative, not less.

04:32 And crucially, this positive effect will be stronger

04:36 than the negative effect of having fewer workers, at least.

04:40 This happened clearly when people least expected it

04:43 during a time of war or war, and its unexpected blessings.

04:49 It's 1809 and Britain is at war with France for control of the world.

04:53 The Royal Navy soon runs short of sailors,

04:57 so every captain suddenly has to find his own crew however he can,

05:01 looking for volunteers, taking men of passing merchant ships and,

05:05 crucially, recruiting many unexperienced farmers and workers off the coast.

05:10 In this case, the Navy recruited mostly farm men from coastal regions.

05:15 Of course close to the deep waters where the biggest warships could anchor.

05:20 Therefore, these regions last prime working age males to fight the French,

05:24 and this caused, of course, labor shortages and as a consequence,

05:28 those that stayed behind could, in theory ask a higher wage.

05:32 As economists Joachim von and his colleagues show, that is exactly

05:36 what happened.

05:37 The higher the recruitment in an area, the higher the wage.

05:40 Agricultural servants on annual contracts and day laborers got.

05:45 Okay, that makes sense.

05:46 This turned out to be a crucial factor behind the mechanization of British farms,

05:53 a shift that many point out

05:54 as the peak starter for the Industrial Revolution in Britain.

05:58 Already back in the 1780s.

06:00 Andrew Maxwell had built the first threshing machine,

06:04 but it was expensive and somewhat unreliable.

06:08 So for two decades it had only made sense

06:10 in northern England, where wages were already fairly high.

06:14 In southern England, it was cheaper to hire a man to do the work instead.

06:18 However, as labor became more expensive due to war, recruitment

06:22 machines essentially became cheaper compared to labor.

06:27 So machines, of course, ended up showing up exactly in places

06:30 that had an higher number of men recruited to fight in the war against France.

06:36 Hence, for these regions, paradoxically,

06:39 losing young workers was the opposite of a catastrophe.

06:42 Instead, it became an incentive to innovate

06:45 simply because labor was getting too expensive.

06:48 And this is what the standard doom story misses.

06:52 More pessimistic economists like Professor Charles Goodhart

06:56 do stress that fewer workers will likely cause wages to rise, causing inflation.

07:01 That's a bad thing, but they typically do not stress so much

07:05 that this could be a major boost to innovation, because higher wages

07:09 force firms to innovate, which ultimately makes remaining workers

07:14 more productive, causing the economy to grow.

07:17 But this happened more than 200 years ago, and it's just a single case study.

07:22 Of course, as a moghalu and his coauthors present way more evidence in the paper

07:27 specifically on how the past 70 years of falling birth rates affected economies.

07:32 To answer this question, Asim Moghalu and his coauthors compared

07:36 70 years of birth rate and GDP data across more than a hundred countries.

07:42 So a lot of data. Very impressive.

07:45 As you can see here, their findings are clear.

07:47 Lower birth rates in 1950 correlate with higher GDP growth.

07:52 But of course, this in itself does not prove the innovation story.

07:56 Therefore, the researchers dug deeper.

07:59 After tracking millions

08:00 of battered records worldwide, they found a striking pattern.

08:05 As you can see here in these graphs, the higher the birth rate

08:08 in 1950, the fewer patents were filed.

08:12 So by implication, countries with fewer birth rates actually innovate more.

08:18 Which again contradicts the standard story.

08:20 And crucially, these inventions did not just sit

08:23 on shelves collecting dust in patent offices.

08:27 They transformed real world economies.

08:30 Reading our graph again, we see that countries with more births

08:34 in 1950s went on to export significantly

08:38 fewer high tech products in the decades that followed.

08:41 In other words, low birth countries exported more high tech products.

08:47 They were more innovative.

08:49 This provides an additional layer to the economic miracles of both dependent China.

08:53 Both nations started out exporting cheap, simple goods to Western markets

08:57 and quickly moved up the ladder into advanced,

09:00 sophisticated industries like robotics, electronics and high tech manufacturing.

09:05 As their birth rate collapsed.

09:07 Of course, while many factors drove this transition from industrial policy

09:11 to global trade demand, the things that we often discuss

09:14 on the channel the urgent need to replace a shrinking

09:17 younger generation of workers was potentially an underrated factor.

09:22 So history so far contradicts actually the main doom

09:25 and gloom narrative of demographic decline.

09:28 Fewer workers do not automatically mean less innovation, on the contrary.

09:33 Countries facing labor scarcity have often adapted technology

09:37 to compensate for missing heads, making the average worker

09:40 significantly more productive in the process.

09:43 Does this mean that the standard pessimistic story is entirely wrong,

09:47 and that falling fertility rates will simply make us all richer?

09:51 Sadly, no.

09:52 Because this time may actually be different.

09:56 After all, the present does not have to be like the past.

09:59 And in this case, I think there are two main weaknesses

10:02 in the new positive story presented by Professor Acemoglu and his coauthors.

10:08 First, fertility rates in the 1950s

10:10 were very different to our current rates that are ultra low.

10:14 In 1950, the country with the lowest fertility rate

10:17 on Earth was Austria, and it was still at 2.0.

10:22 That's very close to the replacement level needed to hold the population steady.

10:26 Today, South Korea is at 0.8.

10:29 If you hold that for a generation, the next generation will be 38%

10:33 smaller than last.

10:34 And this isn't just a projection.

10:36 It's already happening.

10:37 Korea was delivering around 650,000 babies a year at the start of the 1990s,

10:42 but last year it was closer to 230,000.

10:46 Those 1980s and 1990s babies are the engineers

10:50 designing chips at Samsung right now.

10:52 But the classrooms behind them are two thirds empty.

10:56 Sure, some of those remaining students will still grow up to become

11:00 brilliant engineers and creative inventors.

11:03 But it's hard to believe that such a massive collapse in the talent pool,

11:08 something we have not seen before, will not lead to less innovation overall.

11:12 That's the scary math of ultra low fertility.

11:15 It gets worse over time, driving population decline

11:18 faster than anything we've seen in human history.

11:22 We simply did not have this dynamic back in 1950, when virtually

11:26 every country on earth was sitting well above the replacement level.

11:30 Now, the second weakness in a similar story is that he just looks at falling

11:34 birth rates.

11:35 Yes, that is a trend that has been happening for a long time.

11:39 However, what I'm worried about is actually the ratio

11:41 of pensioners compared to active workers.

11:45 More specifically, what I'm worried about is the changing dependency ratio.

11:49 That is, those who do not work, that depend on those who work.

11:52 You see, while you may say how strange that

11:55 falling birth rates coincided with an economic miracle,

11:59 I would instead look at the dependency ratio of both kids

12:03 and old people in the 1950s, all the way up to the 20 tens.

12:07 The dependency ratio was actually falling fast

12:10 in China and Korea, but now it's starting to rise.

12:14 That is a very different trend.

12:16 Some demographic researchers call the times of falling

12:19 dependency ratios a positive demographic dividend for a reason.

12:24 Having two young kids myself, I can definitely tell you

12:26 that I became far less willing to take massive entrepreneurial risks

12:31 since I became a dad.

12:33 So the fact that falling birth rates, a period of demographic dividend

12:37 coincided with a productivity boom does not surprise me at all.

12:41 But now, with more elderly people to take care of,

12:44 the world is heading into a period of reverse demographic dividend today,

12:49 which is fundamentally different than the period

12:51 a small group studied in his paper.

12:53 So, in conclusion, where I and other economists wrong about

12:58 warning for the economic consequences, the doom story of more and more pensioners

13:03 with fewer workers to depend on.

13:06 Perhaps, but I was not fully convinced by this paper.

13:11 I think that the simple fact that so many people

13:13 stop working while the remaining workers have to pay for their pensions presents

13:17 a huge, never before seen risk to the global economy.

13:22 But the paper we discuss today did make me more hopeful

13:27 that rather than gray economies becoming

13:30 less innovative, rising workers shortages

13:33 could actually force them to become more innovative.

13:37 Just like what happened in southern England during the war with France,

13:41 which I surely would have expected would have been negative for the economy,

13:45 the way I see it.

13:46 Each of these three effects can be true at the same time.

13:50 The question that really matters is which effects will be stronger.

13:54 Sadly, historical economic research cannot yet answer that question

13:59 because a new wave and falling population levels.

14:03 That is simply something that we have never seen before.

14:08 But that's my take.

00:00 AI was supposed to kick off a

00:01 white-collar purge, but the reality is

00:04 different. In Fortune 500 boardrooms

00:05 across the country, thousands of AI

00:07 agents are being shut down. Not because

00:10 they didn't work, [music] but because

00:11 they're a legal timebomb. The narrative

00:14 is that tech giants are spending

00:16 everything to win an AI arms race, but

00:18 the reality is much messier. They're

00:20 stripping the liability out of their

00:22 systems while pouring billions into the

00:24 buildout. And when the dust settles,

00:27 someone [music] still has to pay for it.

00:29 The US Interstate Highway system is

00:31 48,000 mi long. It took 35 years to

00:34 build and cost $630 billion in today's

00:37 money. It is, by any measure, one of the

00:39 most consequential infrastructure

00:40 investments in human history. Meanwhile,

00:42 Big Tech is spending $725 [music]

00:45 billion in 2026 on AI infrastructure

00:48 alone. That number has more than doubled

00:50 in just 2 years and is projected to keep

00:53 climbing into the trillions by 2030. In

00:55 fact, Goldman Sachs [music] now

00:56 estimates that the total AI

00:58 infrastructure bill between now and 2031

01:00 will exceed $7.61 trillion. For that

01:04 kind of money, you'd expect a

01:05 revolution. What these companies are

01:07 getting right now is cents on the

01:08 dollar. The entire global AI services

01:10 market in 2025 generated around $25

01:13 billion against hundreds of billions of

01:15 infrastructure spending. When a Chinese

01:17 startup called DeepSeek revealed in

01:19 January 2025 that it had built a

01:21 competitive AI model using Nvidia's

01:23 [music] lower-end chips for under $6

01:25 million, it seemed almost impossible,

01:27 but it still shook the market, wiping

01:30 out around $590 billion from Nvidia's

01:32 market cap in a single day.

01:34 >> [music]

01:34 >> It was the largest single-day loss in US

01:37 stock market history. DeepSeek, far from

01:39 breaking AI, merely raised the question

01:41 every investor had asked himself,

01:42 [music]

01:43 "What exactly are we paying for?" The

01:45 companies spending this money don't just

01:47 have it lying around. They are borrowing

01:48 it. While Alphabet quadrupled its

01:50 long-term debt in 2025 to $46.5 billion,

01:54 the five biggest tech companies issued

01:56 $108 billion in new bonds last year

01:59 alone. Bank of America now estimates

02:01 that AI CapEx now consumes 95% of

02:04 operating cash flows after dividends.

02:06 >> [music]

02:06 >> Amazon is projecting a 95% decline in

02:09 free cash flow thanks to its AI

02:10 build-out costs. They are in essence

02:13 mortgaging their present against a

02:14 future that hasn't shown up yet. The

02:17 gamble is genuinely alarming. If it were

02:19 startups chasing hype, that would be one

02:21 thing. These are the most sophisticated

02:23 capital allocators on the earth. When

02:25 they spend like this, they either know

02:27 something the rest of us don't or

02:28 they're caught up in something they

02:29 [music] can't stop without admitting

02:31 they were wrong. Either way, something

02:33 has broken. To understand what, you have

02:35 to go [music] back to the moment a

02:37 grieving man in Vancouver asked an

02:39 airline chatbot a simple question and

02:41 changed [music] corporate legal history

02:43 forever. On the day his grandmother

02:45 died, Jake Moffatt opened his laptop and

02:47 went to Air Canada's [music] website to

02:49 book a flight from Vancouver to Toronto.

02:51 He had one question, did the airline

02:53 offer bereavement fares? And could

02:55 [music] he apply for one after the fact?

02:57 He asked the chatbot and it said yes. It

02:59 told him to submit his request within 90

03:01 days of purchase and the discount would

03:03 be retroactively applied. So, Moffatt

03:05 booked the ticket, flew to Toronto, came

03:07 home, and then filed the request like

03:09 he'd been [music] told, and Air Canada

03:11 denied it. Their actual policy, as it

03:13 turns out, required bereavement fare

03:15 requests to be made before [music]

03:17 travel. The AI chatbot had simply made

03:19 up a policy that didn't exist, stated it

03:21 with complete confidence, and sent a

03:23 grieving man to buy a full-price ticket

03:25 based on a lie. So, Moffatt sued. And

03:28 what happened next is the reason every

03:30 corporate lawyer in America now has an

03:32 opinion about chatbots. Air Canada's

03:34 legal defense was [music] interesting.

03:36 They argued it could not be held liable

03:38 for information provided by its chatbot

03:40 because the chatbot was, quote, "a

03:42 separate legal entity responsible for

03:44 its own actions." They had deployed a

03:46 piece of software to represent their

03:47 company, and when that software caused

03:49 harm, their position was essentially,

03:52 "Don't look at us. Tribunal member

03:54 Christopher Rivers was not impressed.

03:56 While a chatbot has an interactive

03:57 component, he wrote, it is still just a

03:59 part of Air Canada's website. It should

04:01 be obvious to Air Canada that it is

04:04 responsible for all the information on

04:05 its website. [music] It makes no

04:07 difference whether the information comes

04:08 from a static page or a chatbot. Air

04:11 Canada was ordered to pay 812 Canadian

04:13 dollars, and in perspective, that amount

04:15 is trivial. The precedent was not.

04:18 [music] That ruling landed in February

04:20 2024. What followed was a corporate

04:22 panic that never made headlines,

04:24 >> [music]

04:24 >> but could be seen in the risk sections

04:26 of SEC filings. In 2020, 4% of public

04:29 companies mentioned AI as a material

04:32 risk in their annual filings.

04:33 >> [music]

04:33 >> By 2024, that number was 43%. Among the

04:37 Fortune 500 specifically, 56% now list

04:40 AI as a formal risk factor. Among media

04:42 and entertainment companies, it's 92%.

04:45 The SEC itself has been sending

04:47 enforcement letters demanding more

04:48 specific disclosures, backed by 8.2

04:51 billion dollars in financial remedies in

04:53 the [music] year 2024 alone. Climate

04:55 change took decades to achieve similar

04:57 disclosure penetration across corporate

04:59 America. AI did it in three years. What

05:02 the Air Canada ruling established is

05:04 that whatever your AI says to a

05:06 customer, you said it. You can't

05:08 outsource the liability to the software

05:10 you employ. You can't just point at the

05:12 machine and then look innocent. You are

05:14 the machine. For a technology that can't

05:16 guarantee it won't make things up,

05:18 [music] that ruling created an absolute

05:20 certainty. Deploy AI at scale and

05:22 eventually liability follows. The bigger

05:25 question is will there be anyone left to

05:27 cover the bill? In July 2024, research

05:29 and advisory firm Gartner predicted that

05:31 at least 30% of enterprise gen AI

05:34 projects [music]

05:34 would be abandoned after proof of

05:36 concept by the end of 2025. By April

05:39 2026, they had to revise their original

05:41 estimate. [music] It turns out that it

05:42 was actually more like 40% of enterprise

05:45 AI projects launched in the previous

05:47 [music] two years that would be scrapped

05:49 before they ever shipped. Separately,

05:50 Gartner now predicts that over 40% of

05:53 agentic AI projects, the next generation

05:55 of AI tools companies are currently

05:57 betting on, will be canceled by the end

05:59 of 2027. [music]

06:00 The graveyard keeps growing. S&P Global

06:02 Market Intelligence put some finer

06:04 numbers on it. The average organization

06:06 scrapped [music] 46% of AI proof of

06:08 concepts before reaching production. Of

06:10 the projects initiated, only 48% make it

06:13 to production with an average of 8

06:15 months between prototype and launch.

06:17 That is 8 months of engineering hours,

06:19 infrastructure [music] costs, and

06:20 executive attention on a coin flip

06:22 chance of shipping anything at the end

06:24 of it. McKinsey, another consulting

06:26 firm, [music] surveyed organizations

06:27 globally in late 2025 and they found

06:30 that 88% use AI in at least one business

06:33 function. If that sounds like [music] a

06:35 success story, it's not. Only 39%

06:38 reported any measurable impact on

06:40 earnings. At most, 61% reported no

06:42 meaningful financial impact on their

06:44 business whatsoever. Roughly six in 10

06:47 companies [music] have plugged AI into

06:48 their operations and can't point to a

06:50 measurable return it's made [music]

06:52 them. The reasons are familiar enough

06:53 that Gartner has named them outright.

06:55 Poor data quality, weak risk [music]

06:57 controls, rising costs, and unclear

06:59 business value. Each project costs

07:01 between 5 and 20 million dollars to

07:03 build and deploy. Multiply that across

07:06 thousands of Fortune 500 initiatives and

07:08 you're looking at tens of billions of

07:10 dollars buried in the corporate

07:11 graveyard. It gets even [music] worse

07:13 for Big Tech. A 2024 Deloitte survey

07:15 found that 47% of enterprise AI users

07:18 admitted [music] to making at least one

07:20 major business decision based on the

07:22 content AI had simply invented. In other

07:24 words, nearly half had already trusted a

07:27 hallucination with real-world [music]

07:28 consequences.

07:29 Granted, things have evolved a lot since

07:31 2024. The efficiency revolution is still

07:34 an aspirational possibility as agentic

07:36 [music]

07:37 AI improves, but you wouldn't be human

07:39 if you who wondered why the flaws you've

07:41 seen firsthand [music] seem absent from

07:43 the market's calculations. There's a

07:45 particular breed of corporate fear that

07:47 shows up where you would least expect

07:49 it, insurance contracts. Basically, if

07:52 the people whose entire business model

07:53 depends on their ability to correctly

07:55 [music] price risk deem something

07:57 uninsurable, that is usually a huge red

08:00 flag. In January 2026, the Insurance

08:03 Services Office introduced new

08:04 exclusions targeting generative AI.

08:07 Essentially, if generative AI causes the

08:10 damage, don't assume you're covered. New

08:12 policy language began excluding claims

08:14 tied to AI-generated text, images,

08:17 audio, video, and code. That is every

08:20 large language model ever built. The

08:22 chatbots, the AI copilots, the

08:24 autonomous agents, all of them circled

08:26 with black ink and excluded from the

08:28 policies that cover 82% of US

08:30 businesses. [music]

08:31 In 2024 and 2025, insurers have been

08:34 narrowing AI coverage in existing

08:35 policies [music]

08:36 by tightening up language and adding

08:38 exclusions. WR Berkeley introduced an

08:41 absolute AI exclusion across directors

08:43 and officers, errors and omissions, and

08:45 fiduciary liability lines. AIG [music]

08:48 saw that and they said, "Well, we'll

08:50 have more of the same." Great American

08:52 Insurance followed. Chubb, Travelers,

08:54 Berkshire Hathaway received state

08:56 regulatory approval for their own

08:57 exclusions. [music] State regulators

08:59 have been approving more than 80% of

09:01 those requests. The industry has seen

09:03 this movie before. A decade ago, cyber

09:05 insurance went through an identical

09:07 cycle. There was invisible coverage

09:09 until claims mounted and then came the

09:11 exclusions. Eventually, standalone

09:13 products emerged at premiums most

09:15 companies couldn't stomach.

09:16 >> [music]

09:17 >> The AI liability market is speed running

09:19 the same cycle. Insurance companies are

09:21 not moral actors. They do not [music]

09:23 exclude things because they find them

09:25 distasteful. They exclude them because

09:27 the numbers don't work. They tried to

09:29 price in AI liability throughout 2024

09:32 and 2025, and 42% of insurers reported

09:35 tracking no AI risk metrics at all. When

09:38 you can't measure risk, you can't price

09:40 it.

09:40 >> [music]

09:41 >> And when you can't price it, you exclude

09:43 it. The legal system said, "Whatever

09:45 your AI does, you did it." The insurance

09:48 industry said, "And we won't be covering

09:52 running public-facing AI deployment

09:54 holding the entire liability themselves,

10:18 sheets like assets, and venture

11:07 nobody was buying at the rate anyone

11:10 projected. Thousands of companies

11:12 weighing up where to sell the cards at a

11:13 loss. It is the difference between

11:15 making payroll and not making payroll.

11:18 This signals a deeper problem about the

11:19 infrastructure thesis [music] that

11:21 justified the entire buildout. The

11:23 argument was always that compute was

11:24 scarce. [music] That scarcity created

11:26 value, and whoever controlled the most

11:28 compute would win out in the AI race.

11:32 building a model competitive with GPT-4

11:37 catering. The telecom industry learned

• Title: You NEED to STOP Using Meta Right NOW. The Collapse JUST Began.
