docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 In his 20s, he was the  untouchable God of social media,

00:03 a tech industry rockstar who turned  everything he touched into gold.

00:06 But Mark Zuckerberg’s luck has turned.

00:08 Now 42, he lost over $70 billion dollars  on a bad bet that the Metaverse would be

00:13 the future. He’s tanked his reputation with  increasingly controversial personal dealings,

00:18 and now, the platforms that built  his fortune are being smothered

00:21 under the relentless growth of AI slop content.

00:24 On paper, he’s as successful as he’s ever  been, with a $1.6 trillion market cap for

00:29 Meta Platforms Inc. as of late 2025, but the  ground is secretly collapsing under his feet.

00:35 The problem is… he might just take the  whole internet as we know it with him.

00:39 Inside the corporate structure of Meta, that “God  of social media” thing is a lot more literal than

00:44 you might expect. While Zuck only has 13% to 14%  of the stock locked down, he can still control the

00:50 whole company with an iron fist. It’s all thanks  to the ingenious mechanism of Dual-Class Shares,

00:55 which is basically a division of first and  second class shareholders. In a single class

00:59 share system, one share is one vote, whoever owns  the most has inordinate control over the company.

01:05 But in a Dual-Class Share system, some shares have  a higher vote rating and others.And in Meta, an

01:10 inordinate amount of those juiced up shares just  happened to be inside Zuck’s 13% to 14% holdings.

01:17 That’s because he’s got the Class B shares,  reserved for founders and insiders, which can

01:21 each count for up to 10 or more votes compared  to the Class A shares, sold to consumer grade

01:26 investors out on the stock market. He’s got 60%  percent voting power over the company thanks to

01:32 his Class B share hoard. The remainder are diluted  enough that one other person or entity couldn’t

01:37 ever hope to veto him, especially given you only  need a majority of 1% to swing a vote your way.

01:43 Even the company’s 2 top institutional  shareholders, the Vanguard Group and BlackRock,

01:48 only hold around 8.5% and 7.5% each. Most of  those are the far weaker Class A shares. These

01:55 kings of the private equity world still need to  bow to the almighty Zuck while on Meta territory.

02:00 So, what does Zuckerberg do with  his absolute control over his

02:04 industry-dominating company? Well, he turns  his company into a laboratory for some of the

02:09 riskiest corporate and technological  experiments the world has ever known…

02:12 Including the absolute disaster  that is “The Metaverse”.

02:16 It was a whole new virtual reality  where we’d do everything from shop

02:20 to socialize to work behind headsets and  digital avatars. Zuck had a reason to be

02:25 confident. But this wasn’t the first  time that a major move from Facebook

02:29 had disastrous and wide-reaching  ramifications for the whole internet.

02:33 Facebook was one of the major drivers  behind the internet phenomenon called

02:36 “Pivot to Video”. By touting the incredible  impressions of their short form video platform,

02:41 Facebook sparked a mass cull of internet writing  jobs. That one move effectively killed written

02:47 articles on the internet. It all happened in 2015,  when Zuck’s word was so strong in the corporate

02:52 world that his claims about Facebook’s  impressions didn’t even need to be true.

02:56 Facebook was sued for lying about  its metrics, or at the very least,

03:00 seriously miscalculating them. In order  to woo advertisers, whose money controls

03:04 everything on the internet, he claimed  not only huge view numbers but impressive

03:08 view durations. The actual average they  counted for these extended duration views?

03:13 Anything over 3 seconds.

03:16 Everyone had been duped… but it didn’t matter.

03:18 Facebook was still on top and  they’d practically murdered an

03:21 entire internet industry over some fudged stats.

03:24 Who’s to say that lightning couldn’t strike  twice for Zuck, and have him kill social media

03:29 as we know it and replace it with his very  own private Matrix? He was so certain that

03:33 this would be a win that in 2021, the Facebook  Company officially changed its name to Meta.

03:38 But would all this hype actually take the  Metaverse from science fiction to science fact?

03:43 The heart of Zuck’s most painful losses here is  Meta’s “Reality Labs” division. Originally the VR

03:48 company “Oculus” founded by Palmer Luckey in 2012,  Facebook would acquire the business in 2014 for

03:54 $400 million in cash and 23.1 million common  shares, valued at $1.6 billion. In 2020,

04:03 Oculus was rolled into the emerging  division of Facebook Reality Labs,

04:06 the research and development squad who would  build the architecture of the Metaverse.

04:10 Except that isn’t how any  of this played out at all.

04:14 While exact numbers differ depending on the  accounting, most sources agree that the Reality

04:18 Labs have had to swallow at least a brutal $73  billion in losses since being founded. That’s

04:24 “Billion”, with a “B.” In late 2025, Zuck  seemed to notice how much trouble he was in,

04:29 and cut 30% of Metaverse funding to  reallocate to more profitable ventures.

04:34 With 3.5 billion monthly users across all of  its apps and platforms - Facebook, Instagram,

04:38 WhatsApp, and more - Zuck had every reason to  think he could pull this off. It doesn’t matter

04:43 that for most people, high-end VR is prohibitively  expensive and a barrier to mass adoption. Nor did

04:49 it matter that the graphics on their Metaverse  platform, “Meta Horizon Worlds”, looked about 10

04:54 to 15 years behind the current standard. When it  shipped, none of the avatar characters had legs.

05:00 But that didn’t matter.

05:01 The common tech industry motto is “move fast and  break things”, it’s practically become a cliche.

05:06 The person who coined the phrase was actually  Mark Zuckerberg himself. It’s a way of saying,

05:11 “Barrel in and worry about the consequences  later”. It’s the exact mentality that kept

05:15 the Reality Labs team moving forward  despite all the evidence pointing to

05:18 their task being completely fruitless in the  long run. Instead of profits, the attempt at

05:23 a Metaverse spawned countless mocking memes.  Comparisons to the previous tech that everyone

05:27 insisted would be world-changing,  NFTs and the Blockchain, were rife.

05:32 The irony of Zuckerberg’s humiliating Metaverse  failure is that partial metaverses have existed

05:36 for years. They still run successfully  today in places like Second Life, VR Chat,

05:41 MMORPGs like World of Warcraft, and even  Fortnite in its non-combat modes. Ultimately,

05:47 Facebook was late to the party, and lost so  many billions for breaking the fundamental rule

05:51 of good business: Only make products that  fill a need your customers actually have.

05:57 And really, not enough people want to have

05:59 to wear a VR headset to clock  in at work or go to the bank.

06:03 It’s almost hard to believe but back in 2004, when  it was first founded, the intention was to make

06:08 Facebook “cool.” It started on American college  campuses before anywhere else, running on pure

06:14 FOMO. Anyone who was anyone was encouraged to join  up so they wouldn’t be left behind by their friend

06:19 group. This method worked wonders, leading to the  website logging over a billion users in 2012. Even

06:25 as recently as 2024, it’s got a genuinely  phenomenal 98% brand recognition rating.

06:31 But this picture gets a lot less rosy when you  look at the stats for members of Gen Z. 17% of

06:37 the general population says they love Facebook  and plan on continuing using the product,

06:42 but on these metrics for Gen Z, it’s only 3%.  Facebook isn’t the exciting platform anymore,

06:48 with 45% of Gen Z users saying that they  mainly keep it just to keep up with relatives.

06:53 BrandVue Media found that in 2023, 3 out of  4 Gen Z users would be happy to give it up.

06:59 So, what does this mean for the future of Meta?

07:01 It’s a little more complex than you think. Gen Z  on the whole are moving away from social media,

07:06 with the old guards like Facebook being  the hardest hit. But where are they all

07:11 going? Gen Z aren’t kids anymore,  a lot of them are in their 20's,

07:14 and Gen Alpha is slowly becoming the most  lucrative market. The kings of social media

07:18 for Gen Z and Alpha are, of course, TikTok… and  Instagram, which has a 38% audience usage rate.

07:25 So it seems the younger generations  are running straight out of one of

07:28 Mark Zuckerberg’s hands… and into the other.

07:31 But in the long run, the trends seem to  be working against the Meta Products,

07:34 as Gen Alpha largely prefers video-first apps  like TikTok and YouTube. According to Axios,

07:39 social media burnout is leading to an increase  in members of Gen Z blocking apps and buying

07:45 “dumbphones” that don’t give them connections  to apps. Could the same social media world that

07:49 Facebook invented be the atmosphere that  eventually chokes out their own user base?

07:54 But with a serial entrepreneur like  Mark Zuckerberg, even alienating your

07:58 former core demo and experiencing an  almost $100 billion failure is just

08:03 a setback. What he needed was another  pivot, another technology that he could

08:07 push all his chips forward onto and hope  that being a high roller would pay off.

08:12 And as luck would have it, the world  provided him with that technology.

08:15 In early 2026, Zuck said some now  infamous words on an earnings call:

08:20 “Soon, you'll open our apps, and you'll  have an AI that understands you, and…

08:24 show you great content or even generate  great personalized content for you.”

08:28 The word “Great” here is doing  some incredibly heavy lifting.

08:33 You’ve seen the images and videos, the ones that  feel like something straight out of a fever dream:

08:38 Jesus Christ floating underwater, his body made of  shrimps and lobsters amalgamated into a monster.

08:44 Thousands of comments underneath these  images all read “Amen.” In another video,

08:49 Jesus pushes Satan in a wheelchair off  of the side of a cliff. Buff humanoid

08:53 cats save babies that have fallen off the  Golden Gate Bridge. And in an aquarium,

08:58 a gleeful woman watches a disgusting  human-seal-monster swim around.

09:02 This is the kind of insane AI slop  that’s infested Meta services like

09:06 Facebook and Instagram. It’s gotten so bad

09:08 that there’s a whole “rFacebookAISlop”  subreddit with almost 200,000 members.

09:13 While AI slop is rife thanks to AI being  the shareholder-friendly buzzword across

09:17 the tech industry, few CEOs have  embraced it as enthusiastically as

09:21 Mark Zuckerberg… Just like he previously  embraced the Metaverse. He called it the

09:26 “Third Phase” of social media. What does that  mean, and what was the first and second phase?

09:30 Zuck himself had the answers.

09:32 “First was when all content was from  friends, family, and accounts that you

09:36 followed directly. The second was when we  added all of the creator content. Now as AI

09:41 makes it easier to create and remix content…  we'll see an explosion of new media formats

09:45 that are more immersive and interactive, and  only possible because of advances in AI.”

09:50 Clearly the proof is in the pudding,  because this stuff is absolutely everywhere.

09:54 These pages aren’t all surreal and silly, some  of them are genuinely extremely disturbing.

10:00 Take Anita Kumari, an Instagram account that  specializes in the spreading of “misery porn”

10:05 content: Skeletal, impoverished people  starving to death, being eaten by bugs,

10:10 or dying in the midst of disaster or  disease. All of them are fully AI generated,

10:15 with well over 100,000 followers.  The whole point is to exploit the

10:19 audience’s emotions to get engagement,  and the scariest part is… it works.

10:23 A popular subgenre of this kind of AI slop is the  “Birthday Cake”. This will often show a diseased,

10:29 emaciated, and even disfigured person,  usually a child, a war vet or an old woman,

10:34 carrying a birthday cake. There will often be  the heartstring-tugging message that nobody

10:38 came to their birthday party, so won’t you  wish them a happy birthday in the comments?

10:43 There are videos that use unspeakable racial  stereotypes that we can’t even describe here,

10:48 let alone show any footage of. Fake videos  of massive explosions, natural disasters,

10:53 murders, police shootings, terrorist attacks.  The most messed up thing is, if you find yourself

10:58 watching in horror as these videos unfold,  you’re only going to be shown more of them.

11:02 According to Facebook’s vice president of product,  Jagjit Chawla, “If you… are interested in a piece

11:07 of content which happens to be AI-generated, the  recommendations algorithm will determine that,

11:12 over time, you are interested in this topic and  content. If you are not into it… and if you have

11:17 given us signals that this is not for you,  that algorithm will respond appropriately...”

11:21 The only way you can really show that it’s  “not for you” is to scroll away as quickly as

11:26 possible. But, by the time you’ve stuck around  long enough to figure out what’s going on,

11:30 it’s already gotten the algorithmic hook into you.

11:33 If Facebook is drowning in AI slop content,

11:35 then what caused a leak to spring in  its previously pretty reliable hull?

11:39 It might not surprise you to hear that  the call is coming from inside the house.

11:44 Facebook and its own incentive structures are  the ones behind the slopocalypse. Thanks to

11:49 Facebook’s Creator Bonus Program, engagement can  equate to cold, hard cash for the posters. But

11:55 it’s at rates that most influencers on YouTube  and TikTok wouldn’t consider worth the effort.

11:59 When you factor in currency conversion, and  the low overhead of creating this slop content,

12:04 it can be a huge passive income generator  for people in places like Pakistan, India,

12:09 Vietnam, Thailand, and Indonesia.  The process has been industrialized,

12:13 with different monetized accounts posting dozens  of Shrimp Christs and wounded veterans every

12:18 single day. Sometimes they rack up views in the  millions from real users and rampant bot swarms.

12:24 Not only is industrializing slop  posting becoming a cottage industry,

12:27 teaching people how to start their own slop  machines for money is a thriving business,

12:32 too. The tools and tutorials are being sold  online to anyone who wants to start posting.

12:36 They give aspiring posters the means to  avoid spam detection systems on the site

12:41 and consistently produce viral content that’s  worked for other, similar spammers in the past.

12:46 The result is a problem that  keeps propagating itself,

12:49 making Facebook more unpleasant  and unusable bit by bit.

12:52 The slop problem from both content creators  and audience bots on Facebook has gotten so

12:57 bad that it’s fed into an increasingly popular  movement called “Dead Internet Theory”. It’s the

13:03 existentially terrifying idea that the internet  is becoming less and less a place for living,

13:08 human users. Instead, it’s more a hive of  “Dead Zones” populated by bots interacting

13:13 with each other, not even realizing that  what they’re talking to isn’t human.

13:18 Media researcher and AI expert Thomas  Sommeror said of the proliferation effect,

13:22 “Just as Jesus was supposedly the  messenger for God, Shrimp Jesus is

13:26 the messenger for the fatal system [we've]  maneuvered ourselves into. Decoupled,

13:31 proliferated, and in a state  of exponential metastasis.”

13:34 Metastasis really is the key word here, because  AI is the cancer spreading through Facebook,

13:39 rotting it away from within.  And it isn’t just content,

13:42 AI on Facebook is also replacing the  social component of social networking,

13:46 with the option to generate an AI response to  group posts by tagging @MetaAI. The AI will also

13:52 step in if the original post included a question  and this question wasn’t answered by anyone within

13:58 an hour. It’s like Facebook groups are now  haunted by these staring digital ghosts. And

14:03 this isn’t some conspiracy theory, it’s what top  employees of Meta have said proudly and publicly.

14:09 Connor Hayes, vice-president of  product for generative AI at Meta,

14:12 said, “We expect these AIs to actually,  over time, exist on our platforms,

14:17 kind of in the same way that accounts  do ... They'll have bios and profile

14:20 pictures and be able to generate and share  content powered by AI on the platform.”

14:24 This all started back in late 2023, with a  collection of celebrity AI chatbots including

14:30 Snoop Dogg and Mr. Beast, and everyone  absolutely hated it. So much so that in

14:35 July 2024, Facebook scrapped the idea of  officially licensed celebrity chatbots,

14:39 and instead opened an AI Studio for their  userbase to create their own AI chatbots.

14:44 This also quickly got out of control.

14:47 Despite Facebook insisting on stringent  moderation for its Chatbots, user generated

14:52 Chatbots were every bit as bizarre and  sinister as the slop content started

14:56 showing up. Bots were called Adolf Hitler,  Jesus Christ, and of course, Taylor Swift.

15:01 Before the Facebook and Instagram moderation  teams took them down, if you messaged Taylor

15:05 Swift - spelled “Taylor Swif” to get around  restrictions - she would first reply,

15:10 “Hey there, music lovers! I’m Taylor Swift, and  I’m thrilled to share my latest album with you.

15:15 Let’s get this musical journey started!”  She exchanged over 2000 different messages

15:19 with users before being taken down.  Jesus was even more egregious, saying,

15:23 “Peace be with you. I am Jesus Christ, the Son of  God. How may I guide you on your journey today?”

15:28 But these are extremely small time compared to  some of the more highly used AIs on Facebook.

15:33 Some of the top ones at the height of  the application’s popularity in early

15:36 2025 were "Astrologer AI”, which boasted  over 6 million messages with people in

15:42 January of that year. Second most popular was  “Step Sis Sarah”, which had around 2 million.

15:47 Meta creating and then immediately needing to  roll back its AI tools after massive consumer

15:52 backlash has continued with another  high profile incident in July of 2026.

15:57 Meta published its “Muse Image” tool, a new  generative AI feature that, among other things,

16:02 would allow users to utilize and  alter the photo content of users

16:05 on Facebook and Instagram. In other words, if  someone wanted to use your profile picture,

16:10 or the photos on your marriage announcement,  your vacation photos, or the memorial post

16:14 for a relative to make their own AI generated  content, Muse Image would allow them to do it.

16:19 With zero friction.

16:21 After all, that’s not your content  anymore. You put it on a Meta platform,

16:25 so it belongs to Meta. All Instagram  users were opted in by default.

16:29 It feels a million miles away from  Facebook’s original mission statement,

16:33 of providing a way for friends to connect online  and stay up to date with each other’s lives. But

16:37 Meta has consistently said that going so all-in  on AI is the only way for them to keep up with

16:43 their competitors in the social media space.  But it’s going to have some nasty consequences

16:47 for their bottom line in the long run… even if  shareholders love it in the immediate future.

16:52 There are two key differences between real and AI  users on Facebook and Instagram. These differences

16:57 are a huge problem for Mark Zuckerberg  and everyone else at Meta: Number one,

17:01 companies don’t want to pay to advertise to AI  users on either of these platforms. Number two,

17:07 no companies will be interested in purchasing  the personal data of AI users on either site,

17:11 too. So as AI begins to outnumber human beings,

17:15 you see Facebook’s business model collapse  like a house eaten from the inside by termites.

17:20 And the problems seem to be as much  from the inside out as the outside.

17:24 Leaks from Meta’s new Applied AI division  seem to show that the employees working

17:28 there are utterly miserable, and aren’t seeing  larger benefits to their work. Quotes include,

17:33 “it's literally a gulag”, you have  “zero purpose in life all of a sudden,

17:38 you barely interact with anyone”, and  “you just have these tasks every week.”

17:42 It’s hard to even express how much money Meta is  sinking into AI development. In 2026 alone, it’s

17:47 forecasting between $125 billion and $145 billion  on AI capital expenditures. That’s 88% higher than

17:56 2025 even measuring from the midpoint between  the two figures, and the equivalent to over half

18:02 of Zuck’s $231 billion net worth. But in July of  2026, Zuck admitted that the spectacular results

18:09 he’d hoped for his AI spending hadn’t come into  fruition yet. Meta’s stock dropped 5% as a result.

18:15 In early 2026, they “streamlined”, laying  off around 8,000 employees, around 10% of

18:21 their workforce, while moving another 7,000  into that new AI division. And what do they

18:26 have to show for it so far outside of exciting  the shareholders? Products like Muse Image,

18:31 that everyone hates so much that the backlash  immediately sends them back to the drawing board.

18:35 Tristia Hennessey, a senior strategist  at Portland-based Evolve Solutions Group,

18:40 said, “If you think you're rolling out AI  responsibly, you better be thinking beyond

18:44 the best possible use case. Meta/Instagram's  fiasco with their Muse tool had real-life

18:49 consequences… Serious financial and health  consequences for hundreds of people. And it

18:54 was all legal… There's no protection for victims.  If you think you're safe, you're being naive.”

18:59 But who’s really being naive  here, and who’s really in danger?

19:03 Anyone who’s been following the activities of  Mark Zuckerberg and his companies will be able

19:07 to tell you a laundry list of awful things  they’ve all been involved with. On the more

19:12 minor end, knowing that Instagram has horrific  effects on the mental healths of teen users,

19:17 Facebook conducting psychological tests on 700,000  unconsenting participants in 2012. They were also

19:23 fined over $5 billion by the Federal Trade  Commission for violations of user privacy.

19:28 And on the more severe end, it  gets a lot darker than that.

19:32 In 2020, Sophie Zhang, a former Facebook  data scientist, blew the whistle that

19:36 the company allowed foreign nations to  interfere in elections by manipulating

19:41 data on the platform. This would track  with Facebook’s own part in the meddling

19:44 in domestic elections. It was implicated  in the Cambridge Analytica scandal that

19:49 used vast swathes of Facebook user data to  craft manipulative political ad campaigns,

19:54 and its refusal to fact check posts made on  the platform by politicians in election season.

19:59 All of that pales in comparison to the  worst thing Facebook has ever done:

20:04 Stoking the fires of hatred that led  to the Rohingya massacre in Myanmar,

20:08 a literal modern day genocide. How could something  like that possibly happen? Part of it is buried

20:14 in the code of Facebook itself: It wants to  keep you on the platform as long as possible,

20:18 so the content that gets engagement gets  boosted… even if that content is baying

20:23 for the blood of a persecuted minority  group and pretexting horrifying bloodshed.

20:28 But evidence found by Amnesty International  suggests that the whole truth might actually

20:32 be even worse than irresponsible,  amoral code. Facebook was warned,

20:36 multiple times, about the hate  it was stoking and did nothing,

20:40 probably fearing it would affect their bottom  line. They refused calls to hire local content

20:45 moderators who could spot and control the  rampant hate speech, and when the massacre

20:49 unfolded in 2017, over 700,000 Rohingya  had to flee truly nightmarish violence.

20:55 Pat de Brún, researcher and adviser on artificial  intelligence and human rights at Amnesty, said,

21:00 “These algorithms are really dangerous  to our human rights… what happened to

21:04 the Rohingya and Facebook's role in that  specific conflict risks happening again,

21:08 in many different contexts across the  world. The company has shown itself

16:52 fishing lure. At that point, the

16:54 question is obvious. Has the jackpot

16:56 grown so large that the machine is now

16:58 actually a good bet? And the answer is

17:00 maybe. But unless you know the hidden

17:02 probability of hitting that progressive,

17:04 you can't prove it from your side of the

17:05 glass. The way to think about it is that

17:07 every extra dollar above the reset value

17:10 adds expected value to each eligible

17:12 spin, but only in proportion to the

17:14 chance of actually winning it. If the

17:16 jackpot is $75,000 above reset, then

17:18 your chance of hitting it is one in

17:20 100,000. That extra meter value is still

17:22 meaningful. But if the chance is 1 in 10

17:24 million, it's mostly casino wallpaper.

17:26 At some sufficiently gigantic jackpot, a

17:29 progressive can actually become positive

17:30 expectation, meaning that over a large

17:32 number of plays, the math would favor

17:34 the player. But that does not mean that

17:36 you are more likely than not to win. You

17:38 may still lose almost every single spin.

17:41 It just means the rare hit has become

17:42 large enough to compensate for all the

17:44 losing spins in between. Few of us would

17:46 be wise to ride that train to its

17:48 ultimate destination. If you have

17:50 comments or questions about today's

17:51 episode, please leave them in the

17:53 comments section below cuz I do try to

17:54 read them all. And then every Friday on

17:56 Shop Talk on the Dave's Attic channel,

17:58 we answer and discuss all the best user

18:00 insights and questions. Check it out.

18:01 I'll throw a link up here. So give it a

18:03 subscription if you happen to enjoy an

18:05 episode. If you found today's episode to

18:07 be interesting or entertaining, remember

18:08 that I'm mostly in this for the subs and

18:10 likes. So I'd be honored if you would

18:11 consider leaving me one of each before

18:12 you go today. And in the meantime, and

18:14 in between time, I will see you next

18:16 time right here in Dave's Garage.

docs.text:
00:00 We’ve been told pandemics are biological  accidents that take years to emerge.

00:05 But what if that’s wrong? New evidence suggests

00:08 something far more unsettling. The next  global killer is already out there,

00:12 waiting and it’s pre-programmed  to hijack your cells right now.

00:15 What if there was never a missing  link in COVID’s origin story?

00:19 Not because of a conspiracy. But because  the virus may never have needed to evolve

00:23 to infect us in the first place. It was born with the master key.

00:27 And if that's true, we're not waiting  for the next pandemic to evolve…

00:31 we're waiting for it to arrive.

00:33 From the very first day of existence, humanity  has had to navigate a biological minefield.

00:37 We knew that there were viruses out there,  invisible to the naked eye. We knew they had

00:42 the potential to wreak havoc inside our bodies  and even bring our lives to an early end.

00:46 We thought we had a certain level of safety. For years - generations, even - public health

00:52 policies, vaccine strategies, and  pandemic response systems were all

00:55 based on a single and important assumption.  That there is a buffer between us and the

01:00 viruses that could potentially wipe us all out. We believed that microbes essentially followed a

01:05 pre-programmed, step-by-step route. First, those viruses would spread

01:08 through that animal population before  eventually jumping into another species,

01:12 like a pangolin, a pig or maybe a civet. And that's where things began to change.

01:17 Inside these new hosts, the  virus would start changing.

01:20 Each infection created new copies. Each new  copy was another chance for a mistake. Another

01:25 mutation. Most went nowhere. But over time,  those mutations could stack up. And eventually,

01:30 the virus might stumble onto the exact  tools it needed to infect humans.

01:35 That’s when we’d need to worry. Once they gained the ability to infect humans,

01:38 they could spread from person to person. As they  moved through the population, they could trigger

01:43 powerful immune responses that make us sick. At  best, that means pain, fever, and discomfort.

01:48 At worst, it can cost lives. Scientists called this buffer the species barrier.

01:53 It was the idea that animal viruses couldn't  simply jump into humans. Before making that leap,

01:58 they were thought to need months, years, or even  decades of evolution inside animal populations.

02:03 It was like a key that still needed to be  filed down before it could fit the unique

02:07 ‘lock’ of the human body. And that mattered.

02:10 It suggested there was distance between us and the  world's most dangerous viruses.The species barrier

02:16 wasn't just a scientific concept. It became a kind of safety net.

02:20 A belief that we’d have a window to  spot a virus spreading through animal

02:23 populations. To track how it was changing  and stop it before it ever reached up.

02:28 But what if that window never existed? What if the virus was already

02:32 loaded and ready to fire? Recent research reveals that the evolutionary

02:36 barrier model may not be anywhere near as concrete  as we thought. Because if viruses need to mutate

02:41 to infect us, then how did the deadliest  outbreaks in history skip this step entirely?

02:47 To understand the implications

02:48 of this biosecurity blind spot, we have  to go back to one of the worst pandemics

02:53 the Earth has ever seen: the Spanish Flu. In just 2 years, it infected roughly a third

02:57 of the world's population and killed tens of  millions of people. It was a uniquely deadly

03:02 strain of H1N1 influenza and it unleashed  chaos on a scale the world had never seen.

03:08 In the decades that followed, scientists  worked to understand exactly how it happened.

03:12 They traced its path and developed  a model for how pandemics spread.

03:16 For nearly a century, we  thought that model was correct.

03:19 The pandemic was portrayed as a slow-motion  disaster. A chain of events that unfolded over

03:24 years, not months. If there had been a warning  window, the tragedy could have been avoided.

03:29 But that narrative was shattered  around the turn of the millennium.

03:32 Scientists exhumed and analyzed the bodies of  Spanish Flu victims from an Inuit community

03:37 in Brevig Mission, Alaska. The bodies had  been perfectly preserved in the permafrost,

03:42 allowing the researchers to extract samples  of the viral RNA. They were then able to

03:46 effectively reconstruct the virus using  modern genomic sequencing techniques.

03:50 That’s when they uncovered the truth. A truth that rewrote the rulebook

03:54 on how viruses operated. It turned out that the 1918

03:58 H1N1 virus hadn’t spent years mutating in pigs  before making the leap into human populations.

04:04 It was believed to have started as an avian  virus, originating in birds. And somewhere

04:08 along the way, it developed something important:  a ‘human-ready’ Hemagglutinin (HA) protein that

04:14 was already capable of binding to human cells. In other words, the virus already had the ‘key’

04:20 it needed to unlock the doors of the human body. At the very moment of spillover as it passed from

04:25 wild bird populations into humans, it didn’t  need to undergo any sort of rapid mutation.

04:30 It didn’t need to multiply to develop the  tools it needed to launch a global pandemic.

04:35 It was a ‘plug and play’  biological weapon found in nature.

04:38 And that completely defied  everything the scientific

04:41 community had believed about this virus. It called into question the idea of a long

04:45 warning window and the so-called  evolutionary barrier itself.

04:49 But every virus is different. They  mutate and move in different ways.

04:52 With that in mind, scientists were  left with one crucial question:

04:56 was 1918 just a bizarre historical fluke?  A once-in-a-lifetime example of a virus

05:01 breaking convention or is nature mass-producing  these ‘plug and play’ weapons as we speak?

05:06 In 2021, a team of researchers

05:08 discovered something that shattered everything  we believed about how viruses operate.

05:12 It was at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic,  caused by the SARS‑CoV‑2 strain of coronavirus.

05:18 There were a lot of different theories  about how that particular virus began and

05:22 crossed from animals into humans. Several  studies pointed toward bat populations.

05:27 So, the researchers set out to see if  they could find that ‘missing link’.

05:30 They explored the limestone  caves of Laos in Southeast Asia,

05:33 collecting samples from various bat species  and taking them back to the lab for analysis.

05:38 They uncovered a group of wild bat coronaviruses.  Three in particular - named BANAL-52, BANAL-103,

05:45 and BANAL-236 - stood out due to their  distinctive genomic similarities to SARS-CoV-2.

05:51 Further analysis showed that all 3  of them had a specific spike protein

05:55 that was actually able to attach itself  to the ACE2 receptors of human cells.

06:00 ACE2 receptors act like entry points on the  surface of our cells. Think of them as locks

06:05 and the spike protein are the key viruses use  to open them and gain entry into the body.

06:10 All these viruses possessed the necessary key. But that’s not all.

06:14 Using advanced techniques like binding  measurements and computer simulations,

06:18 researchers found something unexpected. The 3  bat viruses behaved almost identically to the

06:23 original Wuhan strain of SARS-CoV-2.  In some cases, they were even better

06:27 at attaching to human cells, giving the body  almost no chance of preventing an infection.

06:32 One of them, BANAL-236, showed clear evidence  of being able to multiply inside human cells.

06:38 These viruses - found far from  urban centers - were, in some ways,

06:42 better equipped to infect humans than the strain  that was, at the same time, shutting down society.

06:48 Then it got worse. Unlike SARS-CoV-2, none of

06:51 the wild viruses possessed a Furin Cleavage Site,  or FCS. This is a unique molecular structure that

06:57 allows viruses to easily fuse with human cells. At the time, COVID-19 skeptics argued that the

07:03 presence of an FCS was proof that SARS-CoV-2  must have been modified in a laboratory. It’s

07:09 such a rare feature in nature. It was the ‘smoking gun,’

07:13 But the wild viruses proved that Mother Nature  was already producing pre-programmed viral

07:18 strains that could, in theory, bypass the  species barrier. Humans could be infected

07:22 far more easily than expected. All without  the slow, step-by-step evolutionary process

07:27 scientists had long assumed was necessary. And if nature is building these human-optimized

07:32 keys in the middle of the jungle,  what happens when they find a lock?

07:36 Middle East respiratory syndrome-related

07:38 coronavirus, otherwise known as MERS-CoV, is  one of the most lethal pathogens on the planet

07:43 This virus causes a condition called MERS, and  can produce a range of symptoms, from fevers and

07:48 coughs to respiratory difficulties and diarrhea. The first case was identified in 2012 in Saudi

07:53 Arabia. Several thousand more have occurred  since then, with an approximately 35% fatality

07:59 rate. There have been several notable outbreaks,  including one in South Korea in 2015, though most

08:05 cases have been isolated to the Arabian Peninsula. Studies have found that humans are typically

08:10 infected with MERS-CoV via contact with camels. If we follow conventional epidemiological models,

08:16 then the virus found in those camels  should be notably different from the

08:19 one found in the cells of dying human  patients. It should show clear evidence

08:24 of countless mutations that enabled it to pass  from one species to the other. The very changes

08:29 that allowed it to survive in the human body. This would confirm the ‘intermediate host’ theory.

08:34 That’s not what the data shows. When researchers used genomic

08:38 sequencing techniques to map out the MERS-CoV  viruses found in both humans and camels,

08:43 they discovered a disturbing fact:  the two are almost exactly the same.

08:48 To be more precise, they’re 99.9% identical. They’re not distant relatives,

08:54 but biological mirror images. That means that this virus doesn’t

08:57 need any sort of learning or adaptation period  to bridge the gap from one species to the other.

09:02 There isn’t some vast chasm separating the  two, but a tiny, almost imperceptible 0.1% gap.

09:09 The virus can simply cross the species barrier,  using the exact same architecture it relies on

09:14 to infect livestock and other animal populations. It’s a fully functional, completely compatible,

09:20 and capable invader. A microscopic  weapon of mass destruction that is

09:24 more adaptable than we ever thought possible. The implications of this are terrifying from a

09:29 biosecurity standpoint. This discovery suggests  that virologists may have been working on flawed

09:34 information for years. They have been looking  for the wrong warning signs, following unreliable

09:40 models, and allowing society to sleepwalk  its way towards another biological crisis.

09:45 If animal-based viruses like MERS-CoV are  already identical to the human-killing versions,

09:50 then how many more of them are out there,  just waiting to kick off the next pandemic?

09:54 By the early 2020s, we knew that

09:56 there were viruses that could move from animals to  humans far faster than anticipated. Scientists had

10:02 proved that this was the case with the  likes of the Spanish Flu and MERS-CoV.

10:06 But they were still seen by  many as outliers or anomalies.

10:09 Then, a groundbreaking 2024 study arrived.  It showed that these alleged anomalies might

10:14 be part of a larger and deeply worrying trend. The study was carried out by researchers at the

10:19 Bloom Lab at the Fred Hutch Cancer Center,  led by evolutionary biologist Jesse Bloom.

10:24 It was designed to put the evolutionary  barrier hypothesis to the ultimate test.

10:29 They wanted to know whether viruses actually  need time to adapt when they jump into humans,

10:34 or whether they might already be  capable of doing it from the start.

10:37 To do this, the team didn’t just focus  on a single outbreak or viral strain.

10:41 Instead, they analyzed large genomic  datasets to understand how they behave

10:46 at a molecular level. They used a technique  called deep mutational scanning to study

10:51 specific viral proteins in detail. Their  analysis covered a wide range of viruses,

10:56 including influenza, SARS-CoV-2, HIV, and Zika. This allowed them to map out how thousands of

11:03 potential mutations might affect a virus’  ability to evade antibodies and infect cells.

11:08 First, the researchers had to create  so-called ‘pseudoviruses’. These were

11:12 safe versions of real pathogens that were able  to enter cells but unable to replicate. This

11:17 eliminated the multiple risks associated with  working with live, dangerous viral strains.

11:22 They were then able to genetically  engineer the viral proteins to make

11:25 their own mutations, exploring. It was similar  to the ways a viral cell might change or adapt

11:30 to increase its infectivity and ability to survive  in different hosts and environments. The variants

11:35 were then tested and researchers measured how  well they resisted antibodies and how tightly

11:40 they attached themselves to host cells. The data pointed in one direction.

11:44 Some of the deadliest pandemics  in human history had zero

11:47 adaptation time during their initial outbreaks. In other words, when these strains first entered

11:53 the human population, they didn’t immediately need  to evolve to become more effective at infecting us

11:58 or evading the immune system. They didn’t need to.

12:01 They were already capable of doing that. This exposes a truly systemic flaw in global

12:07 health surveillance and security. Scientific communities and virology

12:10 initiatives like the USAID PREDICT program  have believed that we should be looking for

12:15 viruses in the wild that are ‘beginning to  evolve’ human-like traits. The ones that

12:20 could pave the way towards widespread infections. Meanwhile, more ‘generalist’ viruses that are able

12:24 to infect multiple species have historically been  viewed as ‘lower-risk’. That’s because they don’t

12:29 appear to be optimized for human transmission. This research has turned those beliefs upside

12:34 down. It suggests that by the time a virus begins  to evolve human traits it is already too late.

12:40 The pandemic has already started.

12:42 Studies seem to suggest that there could be a  number of viruses out there in the wild today,

12:47 just waiting for human hosts to come  along. The one factor that seemed to be

12:51 working in humanity’s favor was that these viral  strains were confined to places far from human

12:56 populations. They appeared to exist primarily  in jungles, caves, and other remote ecosystems.

13:01 If that was true, then it explained  why global pandemics had seemingly

13:05 been once-in-a-century events. People simply  weren’t coming into contact with these viruses.

13:10 The evolutionary barrier model may have been  shattered, but a new ‘geographic barrier’ seemed

13:15 to have emerged. The actual physical distance  between human populations and infected animals

13:20 helps us to stay relatively safe. That was the theory.

13:24 Researchers made yet another frightening discovery  which sent scientific communities back to the

13:29 drawing board to reassess their understanding of  viral biology. They found that people are actually

13:34 encountering these kinds of viruses. All the time.

13:38 A study was carried out involving almost  700 subjects from rural communities in

13:42 Myanmar. They were screened for signs  of sarbecoviruses: specific sorts of

13:47 coronaviruses that mostly infect bats and  have the potential to cross over into humans.

13:52 The study found that 12.1% of the people possessed  antibodies for these viruses. That meant they had

13:58 been exposed to them at some point in the past. People were significantly more likely to test

14:03 positive if they worked in industries that  involved spending time outdoors or handling

14:07 raw materials. This included activities like  logging, hunting, and harvesting forest products.

14:12 It was an important finding. On average, over 1 in 10 people in these parts of

14:17 the world have been infected by wild viruses. Most  of it appears linked to bats, with some evidence

14:23 also pointing to pangolins. But when you check  official public health records from these same

14:28 areas, you won’t find reports of major outbreaks.  There’s no unexpected spikes in atypical

14:33 infections, no sudden lockdowns or quarantines. But the clues are all there.

14:37 They’re hidden in the blood of these individuals. Those clues are the remnants of the silent ‘test

14:42 fires’ of weapons that haven’t  yet been fully triggered.

14:45 The old explanations of how viruses work have  been well and truly obliterated by this stage.

14:51 Humans aren’t as special as we were led to  believe. Not in the eyes of viruses, in any case.

14:55 We’re just the next step in the chain. Viruses  already have everything they need to infect us,

15:00 and they’re actively doing so, albeit in  places that don’t dominate the headlines.

15:05 If everything we’ve seen so far is accurate,  then humanity’s days must be numbered.

15:10 Evidence suggests that mankind has been

15:12 lucky to survive this far with so many  potentially deadly viruses circulating

15:16 in nature. Fortunately, there’s one thing that  has been working in our favor, this entire time.

15:22 Our last line of defense. A biological safeguard that

15:25 has helped keep humanity alive for generations.  One that has allowed us to survive pandemics

15:30 that killed tens of millions. It’s called the Interferon response.

15:34 And it acts like the body’s built-in firewall. When a human-ready virus enters the body,

15:38 the data suggests it has no trouble binding to  receptors and entering cells. It already carries

15:43 the key it needs to unlock those biological locks.  That’s the easy part. Because the moment it enters

15:49 the body, something else begins. An invisible countdown.

15:52 If the virus doesn’t move fast enough, it won’t  have the freedom it needs to replicate and spread.

15:57 Instead, it’ll be killed out in a matter of hours. This is where the Interferon response comes in.

16:02 Interferons are a group of signaling proteins,  also known as cytokines. They’re produced by

16:08 the body in response to the presence of foreign  microbes, like viruses and bacteria. As their name

16:13 suggests, Interferons are designed to interfere  with these invaders. They slow them down,

16:18 disrupt their replication, and make it  harder for them to take hold in the body.

16:22 They do this in various ways, including  actively degrading viral RNA and alerting

16:27 other cells to defend themselves against the  coming threat. Studies show that the majority

16:31 of wild viruses are entirely neutralized  by this initial cellular counter-attack.

16:36 Even though the viruses have the key to pass the  front door, they soon discover that the house is

16:41 equipped with a state of the art security system. Because for viruses, the real challenge isn’t

16:45 just getting inside the body or even entering  cells. It’s surviving long enough to replicate.

16:51 To multiply fast enough to gain control  before the immune system shuts them down.

16:56 This is the only thing that’s saving us from  a perpetual state of pandemic emergency.

17:01 The warning window depends on the virus itself.  Some viruses mutate quickly, allowing them to

17:05 weaken or evade interferon responses. Others are  stopped earlier. It also depends on the body’s own

17:11 ability to detect the invasion fast enough. To sound the alarm.

17:15 And activate its defenses  before the virus can spread.

17:18 This is why those 1 in 10 people in the rural  villages of Myanmar have those antibodies.

17:22 Yes, their systems were invaded by wild  viruses from bats and other creatures,

17:27 but it didn’t trigger a massive outbreak or  society-halting pandemic. Their bodies were able

17:32 to respond in time and their Interferons  did the job they were designed to do.

17:36 The enemy was effectively eliminated  just inside the castle gates.

17:40 But why is nature building these  human-ready keys in the first place

17:43 if we aren’t the primary target?

17:45 It’s clear humanity has been following  a fundamental misunderstanding

17:49 of viral evolution for generations. We have spent decades believing that viruses

17:53 have to adapt to us because we’re so different and  distinct compared to other animals. Humanity has

17:59 represented the ultimate prize for these microbes,  the pinnacle of their evolutionary pathways.

18:04 The data tells a very different story. It shows that the most successful viral

18:08 strains in history - like the 1918 Spanish Flu  and SARS-CoV-2 COVID-19 - didn’t show any major

18:15 signs of recent human adaptation. These were what virologists

18:18 refer to as ‘generalist’ viruses. They didn’t evolve in the wilderness or mutate

18:23 in dense jungles. They weren’t pre-programmed to  infect and kill humans specifically. They didn’t

18:28 even require years of random mutations  to reach their ‘human-ready’ forms.

18:32 They simply evolved over time to survive in  high-density, multi-species environments.

18:36 They learned to thrive in places where bats,  birds, rodents, primates, and other creatures were

18:41 present. That gives them an enormous advantage. viruses spread more easily when they aren’t

18:46 limited to a single species. These viruses  effectively come with their very own skeleton keys

18:51 that allow them to go almost anywhere they please.  In other words, people aren’t the targets. They’re

18:56 not the end goals or ultimate objectives. They’re just collateral damage.

19:00 This is what makes the next  pandemic an invisible inevitability.

19:04 The hardware is already there. And it’s fully compatible

19:06 with the human operating system. When nature is creating its own biological

19:10 weapons, humanity isn’t sitting on the sidelines.  And when things go wrong, it has consequences.

19:16 Discover the horrifying truth in “Viruses That  Were Actually Lab Leaks”. Or watch this video.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: What Happens When a Shipping Container Falls Off a Ship
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: What Happens When a Shipping Container Falls Off a Ship
  • Video ID: SpXCOlrCgfM

  • Views: Unknown

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 In 2018, a cargo ship battling 30 foot (9 meter)  waves off North Carolina lost 70 containers in a

00:06 storm. One carried 6,000 pounds (2,721 kg) of  sulfuric acid, a compound capable of causing

00:11 severe chemical burns and even blindness. Only 4 were ever recovered.

00:16 The shipping industry says almost 1,500  containers fell overboard in 2025.

00:21 The NOAA says it's closer to 10,000. That  difference exists because of a loophole

00:27 almost nobody outside the industry knows about. So why do Lego bricks and Garfield phones keep

00:32 washing up on beaches? And  if they're wrong about the

00:35 containers... what else are they not telling us? In 1997, in the English town of Bigbury Bay,

00:40 dragons began invading the beach.  The ship, the Tokio Express,

00:44 was making the long sea journey from Rotterdam  to New York when a storm hit. Nearly 5 million

00:50 Lego pieces fell into the ocean and washed up  beaches in Cornwall for almost 30 years now.

00:56 It’s expected people will be finding Lego  dragons and octopuses for decades still to come.

01:01 It sounds fun, but there’s a downside.

01:04 In 2013, a woman in Galveston,  Texas, found a black Lego octopus

01:08 at a local beach that experts think  may have come from this original spill,

01:12 thousands of miles away. MBARI researcher Josi  Taylor has said, “Although the effects of one

01:18 container may seem small, the thousands of  shipping containers lost on the seafloor

01:22 each year could eventually become a significant  source of pollution for deep-sea ecosystems.”

01:27 There’s been an incident where containers  carrying around 2,000 computer monitors

01:32 fell into the ocean, never to be seen again.  Another incident caused thousands of Nike

01:37 shoes to wash up on beaches all across  the globe. Marlboro Cigarettes became

01:42 an infestation on Dorset beaches, chow  mein noodle cups in Northern California,

01:46 and even hockey gloves in Alaska. The  Svendborg Maersk experienced one of if

01:51 not the worst container loss catastrophes of all  time, losing 520 containers in a single voyage.

01:58 But there’s a hidden danger to these  floating refrigerated containers.

02:02 They can be like natural torpedoes.

02:05 A floating shipping container is small  enough to not register as a concern on radar,

02:09 big enough to completely rip open  the hull on a mid-sized boat.

02:13 Enough of these things out in the water and  the whole ocean becomes a minefield across

02:17 popular international shipping routes.  But why is this happening so frequently?

02:22 The obvious answer is storms. But  that’s just part of the problem.

02:25 The real answer is much more complicated. The answer is a mix of corporate incentives...

02:31 and the brutal physics of moving  floating skyscrapers across an ocean.

02:35 The bigger the vessel, the greater  the chance of containers falling off.

02:39 Shipping companies will always  demand bigger and bigger vessels,

02:42 because they can carry more containers in a  single trip. That means maximising profit.

02:47 So just how big are these vessels?

02:49 One of the largest cargo ships available  is appropriately called the Ultra Large

02:53 Container Vessel, or U.L.C.V. These are  generally over 1,300 feet (396 meters) long,

02:58 or taller than the Chrysler building in New York  if it was stood up end to end. It was a ship

03:03 like this that famously blocked the opening  in the Suez Canal, holding up global trade.

03:08 But the more weight is on a single vessel, the  less agile it is, especially when moving at high

03:13 speeds. Getting a ship across the world’s oceans  is a masterclass in understanding and control of

03:18 physics, and especially in stormy waters, careful  maintenance of weight distribution is key.

03:23 But these vessels are carrying tens  of thousands of containers at a time,

03:27 they’re effectively floating skyscrapers. No  human can possibly fully control them when

03:32 the water starts getting choppy. This creates the  problem of roll, where this huge weight of tightly

03:38 packed carriers can skid across the deck of the  ship when it’s being buffeted from side to side.

03:43 When the cargo rolls hard and far enough, it’s  almost impossible to stop some of it from going

03:48 over the side. Much like long haul truckers,  because of the demands of corporate overhead,

03:53 the workers on these vessels are  pushed to the absolute limit.

03:56 When you push people to the  limit, mistakes are inevitable.

03:59 According to NTI.Com, “Incorrect or  inadequate securing can significantly

04:04 reduce the stability of a container stack.  Combine this with the motion of a vessel on

04:08 the ocean and you have a high exposure  to containers falling from the vessel.”

04:12 And how hard these situations are to control  start to make sense when you understand just

04:17 how small some of the crews are. For context,  one of these Ultra Large Container Vessels,

04:22 carrying over 20,000 shipping containers,  can be crewed by as few as 25 people.

04:28 And the increasing size of these ships  has another dangerous side effect

04:32 Parametric Rolling.

04:33 The ship's design actually works  against it. As one wave lifts the bow,

04:37 the next suddenly drops it, sending the entire  vessel into violent rolling. Containers begin

04:43 shifting thousands of tons at a time. Once  that starts, losing cargo is almost inevitable…

04:48 And there's virtually nothing  the crew can do to stop it.

04:51 Every vessel has its Container Securing  Manual, or CSM, which will have exact

04:56 specifications for safe weight and height of  cargo. But these hard and fast safety rules are

05:01 often treated like guidelines when weighed  against the potential that profit brings.

05:05 Regulations are put in place to avoid  the dreaded scenario of “Stack Collapse”,

05:10 which is the number one cause of  more severe container loss incidents.

05:14 Simply put, the higher you stack, the  greater chance the containers will tumble…

05:18 No matter how well they’re secured.

05:20 And of course, there’s always speed.

05:22 Time is money, and that’s as true in  shipping as it is in any other industry,

05:26 if not more so. Especially when some of those  shipping containers are lugging perishable goods.

05:31 That’s why ships are incentivized to go as  fast as they can, even though this is one

05:35 of the biggest factors that put ships at risk of  container loss. The quicker a job is completed,

05:40 the more jobs can be completed, so the pressure  from the top will always be full throttle.

05:45 In order to avoid red tape, it’s  not uncommon for shippers to lie

05:48 in official documents about the actual  weight being shipped in these containers.

05:52 When the MSC NAPOLI lost 100 containers in a  single incident back in 2007, the UK’s Marine

05:58 Accident Investigation Branch discovered that  the weight of 137 of the 660 containers on deck

06:05 differed by more than three tonnes from the  declared weight. This meant that in total,

06:10 the ship’s cargo load was 312 tonnes  heavier in actuality than it was on paper.

06:16 It was an accident waiting to happen.

06:18 There’s a reason container losses are so much  worse than the shipping industry is reporting.

06:22 Companies and their clients are under no legal  obligation to publicize container loss at sea.

06:27 It’d be a complete nightmare to legislate,

06:30 given that these ships are constantly  passing through international jurisdictions.

06:33 You also have to understand that it goes  against the interests of shipping companies,

06:38 who are in tight competition with one another,  to draw attention to their container losses.

06:43 Despite the ecological impact, for  most international shipping companies,

06:46 container losses are little more than a  rounding error on their balance sheets.

06:50 The shipping industry largely only  considers container loss a "catastrophic

06:53 event” if 50 or more containers go  missing during a single incident.

06:57 How many ships are losing 30 to  40 containers on every voyage,

07:01 and simply don’t feel the  impulse to report these losses?

07:04 In the words of Gavin Spencer, the head of  insurance at Parsyl, a company that focuses

07:08 on risk management in the supply chain,  “No one reports fully transparent figures…

07:12 That would be a bit like airlines  declaring how many bags they lose.”

07:16 A lot of the time, the companies don’t need to  take an actual financial hit for their lost cargo

07:20 thanks to something called General Average.  This maritime law dictates that the cost of

07:25 cargo jettisoned knowingly from the ship will be  split between the captain and crew on that ship,

07:31 not the people they take their orders from.

07:33 It’s the perfect system…

07:35 For corporate abuse.

07:36 And the true scale of this abuse  is almost impossible to measure.

07:40 There’s no universal, internationally-recognized  metric for taking full account of lost shipping

07:45 containers and the reasons behind them.  Different nations and shipping companies

07:49 all keep their own versions that are almost  impossible to factor into some grand,

07:53 unifying model that gets at the heart of the  corruption. But independent watchdogs have

07:57 estimated that the number of containers lost  at sea in 2025 is almost triple the average.

08:03 And it’s getting worse.

08:05 Even before you get into the structural issues  behind why so many of them go overboard in the

08:10 first place, there are so many other problems.  Most of these general purpose containers are

08:16 shells made out of solid steel either  20 or 40 feet (6 - 13 meters) long.

08:19 When you factor in cargo weight if  non-buoyant, one of these is going

08:24 straight to the ocean floor any time they go  overboard. These containers rust over years,

08:29 releasing toxic iron oxide and heavy  metals into the surrounding water.

08:33 Containers with buoyant cargo or interior foam  wall insulation can be even more of a nightmare.

08:38 That’s because the currents inevitably start  carrying them inland while they break down,

08:42 spreading the toxic footprint  of the spillage further.

08:45 The containers still break  down, even when on the move.

08:48 When they do, their cargo spreads far and wide.

08:51 These are the ones that are most often responsible  for waterlogged goods ending up on otherwise

08:55 pristine beaches and untouched ecosystems.  Since that foam is a synthetic polymer,

09:00 you get that added bonus of plastic  pollution regardless of the contents.

09:04 There’s an estimated 75 to 199 million  tonnes of plastic in the ocean as it stands,

09:10 with experts predicting that this  could rise to catastrophic levels.

09:13 By 2040, it could infect every ocean ecosystem  on earth if something isn’t done about all this.

09:18 Incidentally, some oceanographers claim  that there could be as many as 12,000

09:22 unclaimed shipping containers  rusting away on the ocean floor.

09:26 Marine biologist Andrew DeVogelaere  of California’s Monterey Bay National

09:30 Marine Sanctuary has said, “Just because  it may seem ‘out of sight, out of mind,’

09:34 doesn’t mean there aren’t vast environmental  consequences. We are leaving time capsules on the

09:38 bottom of the sea of everything we buy and sell —  sitting down there for maybe hundreds of years.”

09:44 That makes it extremely dangerous.

09:46 All of these lost shipping containers  feels like a glaring alarm bell for

09:49 an even bigger problem that we’ve  been hiding from for far too long.

09:53 The devastating impact global shipping  has on the environment, and human health.

09:57 There isn’t a major nation on earth that doesn’t  have its economy enmeshed deeply in shipping.

10:02 90% of the world’s international goods arrive by  ship. That rises to 95% when you’re just looking

10:08 at the US. It has over 360 ports that receive  millions of tons of goods every year. But even

10:13 that is dwarfed by the over a billion metric tons  of greenhouse gases these ships are releasing.

10:18 According to OceanConvervancy.Org, if the world’s  ships were a nation, they’d be the sixth largest

10:24 polluter on earth. Shipping alone is responsible  for 3% of all carbon emissions on earth.

10:29 Zoom in on just two major American ports:  Los Angeles and Long Beach, which account

10:34 for 40% of all the goods that pass through the  US by sea. They also produce 100 tons of smog,

10:40 not per year, but per day. That’s more than the  absolute maximum of emissions that six million

10:45 cars can produce across Southern California in the  same time period. And if you’re one of the nearly

10:51 39 million people who live near ports in the  US, this should terrify you. No matter how clean

10:56 you’re living you’re being exposed to air that’s  like smoking a whole pack of cigarettes every day.

11:01 Your health, your life, is forfeit here  for the sake of the shipping industry.They

11:05 have the American economy over a barrel, and  your lungs are considered acceptable losses.

11:10 As recently as 2024, some reports have suggested  that emissions from the global shipping industry

11:15 are responsible for 250,000 premature deaths  and 6 million childhood asthma cases each year.

11:22 And when you look under the water, at the complex  ecosystems that allow all life on earth to exist,

11:27 you see an even grimmer picture when it comes to  the impact shipping has on the only planet that

11:32 we can call home. The constant low-frequency  noises of huge cargo ships passing through

11:36 the water creates an underwater noise pollution  nightmare that can disrupt the communication of

11:41 everything from fish to whales. Ballast water  discharge can completely screw up the delicate

11:46 biodiversity of ocean environments by introducing  invasive species from other parts of the ocean.

11:51 Spillages, microplastics, and chemical runoff can  bleach whole reefs and kill thousands of fish.

11:57 But will anything be done about this,

11:59 when in 2023, there was 1.5 tons of  annual shipping per every person on earth?

12:05 It’s unlikely.

12:06 Even if companies and governments are blinded  by the endless dollars in global shipping,

12:10 we have every reason to be worried about  what’s happening to the ocean here: The ocean

12:14 covers over 70% of our planet’s surfaces, and is  responsible for regulating heat across the globe,

12:20 in addition to creating half the oxygen we need  and absorbing 30% of global carbon emissions.

12:26 Nearly 10% of the global population, that’s 680  million people, live in low-lying coastal areas.

12:33 Sire, it’s easy to grin about weird objects  washing up on beaches, but these communities

12:38 are also on the chopping block when it comes  to natural disasters and rising sea levels.

12:42 Exactly the problem that global shipping  is making worse every single day.

12:46 And you’re not safe from the ramifications  of this if you live inland. 37% of the

12:50 human population lives within 62  miles (100 km) of a coastline.

12:53 As one concerning United Nations article  put it, “Humanity’s future depends on

12:58 protecting the rapidly changing ocean.”  Marine food is a $90 billion industry,

13:03 121 million people engage in recreational fishing  globally. Marine food makes up around 20% of all

13:09 protein that humanity consumes. If those  ecosystems drop out from under our feet,

13:14 expect to see consequences ranging from  extreme price hikes to mass starvation

13:19 that kills tens if not hundreds  of millions of people worldwide.

13:23 It’s a serious, and catastrophic, problem.

13:25 And the cruel irony of all this?

13:27 It’s actually going to make the  shipping container problem worse.

13:31 One of the major factors in shipping  mishaps that send containers into our oceans

13:35 are the brutal weather patterns of the Pacific  Ocean. Man-made changes in weather are worsening,

13:40 with us now experiencing the strongest Northern  Pacific winds since 1948. That just compounds

13:46 with increased shipping traffic as demand  rises in an increasingly connected world.

13:50 An investigation by the New Yorker also  stressed the sinister Black Box nature of

13:54 the shipping container world. Most crews  on cargo ships will have no idea what’s

13:59 in the containers they’re carrying. Neither will  border patrol and the people working at customs.

14:04 A single shipping container can hold 5,000  individual boxes. A single ship can offload

14:09 9,000 containers within hours. It’s almost  impossible to inspect more than a fraction

14:13 of the world’s shipping containers. It’s a boon to  drug cartels, human traffickers, and terrorists.

14:19 And a logistical nightmare for  the people paid to inspect them.

14:23 That’s exactly what the ever-growing  problem of overboard ships is…

14:27 A nightmare.

14:28 The question we don’t even know the answer  to is, “How do we wake up from this one?”

14:33 Want to know more about the weird quirks of  international sailing? Now check out “Why

14:37 are Cruise Ships Registered in Liberia (and Other  Weird Cruise Ship Facts)”, or watch this instead!

17:13 and if it doesn't do well, it can cause  serious problems. Copying a video is easy.

17:18 It comes with some guarantee of success. That's  the exact reason why I've decided to mix things up

17:23 and steal the Smoothie King's talking points and  thumbnail for this video. Now, hopefully it goes

17:27 without saying that I am joking. I will always  leave a link in the description below and we

17:31 mostly discuss different things. But the point  is this clearly happens everywhere on YouTube

17:36 as people just naturally follow basic incentives.  The same is true 10 times over for video games.

17:42 Any game that does well is going to be copied  by dozens of people with tools that make basic

17:46 game design relatively simple. This is  especially the case with people porting

17:49 paid indie games into Roblox for free with  inbuilt microtransactions. Last summer,

17:54 Peak, one of Steam's bestselling games of the  month, got cloned on Roblox almost immediately.

17:59 The copy pulled in 6 million visits in about two  weeks, monetized with Roblox own microtransaction

18:04 system, while the studio that actually made the  game got nothing. The game developers said that

18:09 they would rather you pirate their game than play  the microtransaction riddled Roblox slop ripoff,

18:14 which is a sentence an actual game studio felt  the need to post in 2025. Roblox is running

18:19 132 million daily users and 31 billion hours of  engagement every quarter, which the same Matthew

18:25 Ball from earlier estimates is about the same  engagement as Steam, PlayStation, and Fortnite

18:29 combined. Now, obviously, this is bad. But the  point is for large studios, it further means that

18:35 they need to make games with some kind of mode  around them to defend against obvious ripoffs.

18:39 And the easiest one is to make something too  complex to copy and then integrate recognizable

18:44 IP in addition to some guarantee of players  being around for consistent online multiplayer.

18:48 Now, it sounds bad, but it gets worse because  this has literally already happened before.

18:54 The last time this industry drowned itself  in cheap copies of whatever it was selling,

18:57 it was 1983 and the American home video game  market fell by around 97% in 2 years. So, yeah,

19:04 I'm not exactly going to feel bad for the big  gaming companies. They have made plenty of their

19:08 own mistakes and have leaned into anti-consumer  practices to compensate for their own failing.

19:12 But it's not been an easy time to be a game studio  either. Now, if you want to see this whole dynamic

00:00 America is losing its smartest people. By the  numbers alone, 80% of postoc researchers now

01:48 But the thing is, none of this has really  changed. We still have all of the systems

01:54 alongside the good and bad that comes with them.  What has changed, though, is that despite the

01:59 chance to make a lot more money, smart people  from across the world aren't coming in nearly

02:08 have are moving out. It doesn't sound great, but  perhaps this could all mean more opportunities and

02:25 Americans are leaving the United States at record  levels in large part because of divisive politics

02:30 and an affordability crisis. A poll from the  journal Nature earlier this year found that 75% of

02:37 researchers in the US are considering leaving the  country. We've lost more than 15,000 scientists

02:48 in powerful lowcost Chinese AI models are sending  shock waves through Washington and Silicon Valley

02:54 as Chinese companies continue to narrow the  AI gap despite vast differences in computing

02:59 power and financial resources. Okay, so obviously  the most pressing question would be to ask why is

03:05 this happening? Or rather, why is it happening  now? And well, yeah, while it would be easy to

03:11 blame everything on the current state of America,  it's worth at least acknowledging that most other

03:15 countries are dealing with their own problems as  well. And in the grand scheme of things, we still

03:19 have it pretty good. Especially for people at the  top of their respective field. And yet, people who

03:24 theoretically have the qualifications to live and  work almost anywhere they want are still reversing

03:29 a very long-standing trend of gravitating to  the USA. And they are doing it for two reasons.

03:34 The first is that despite spending hundreds of  billions of dollars on R&D every year, we are very

03:44 path to return on investment. The private sector  now funds about 3/4 of all American research and

03:50 development. And even amongst what's left, federal  agencies only fund around 40% of the country's

03:55 basic research. The problem this creates is that  private for-profit companies have no incentive

04:00 to fund the risky foundational work that doesn't  have a clear path to making well a profit. This

04:06 means something like climate science, which might  actually stand in the way of corporate profits,

04:15 budget request for the National Ocean and  Atmospheric Administration proposed exactly 0 for

04:20 climate research, which would theoretically impact  the ocean and the atmosphere. At the same time,

04:27 for comparison, the EU set aside almost 5 billion  of its current 2-year research budget just for

04:56 especially in less profitable fields of science,  less and less of that money is in the USA. Now,

05:10 Well, we will get to that assumption, but even  if it was completely true, it would still be

17:21 But the trend is not our friend and these fields  naturally compound on themselves. But this also

17:27 raises a pretty fair question. Is this actually a  problem? Sure, we have attracted a lot of talent

17:33 at every level of this pyramid from overseas for  a long time. But we also have a lot of very smart

17:38 people right here at home. The acceptance rates at  top colleges, research firms, grants, and jobs in

19:15 pouring money into facilitating the reversal.  Its flagship recruitment effort, a program it

19:20 has never officially announced, reportedly offers  returning researchers signing bonuses that can

19:24 reach $700,000 plus help buying a home. So even in  the complete absence of any sinister intentions,

19:31 normal students just following the best available  opportunities for themselves could easily end up

19:35 on this path. And this is genuinely causing some  big hits. The founder of Moonshot AI, Yong Jerene,

19:42 got his PhD at Carnegie Melon. And well, his Kimmy  models are kind of moonshotting our domestic AIs

19:48 at the moment, which even though we may not like  it, is a major component of our economy. Now, it's

19:53 happening outside of AI, too. The mathematician  Jangi Tong, famous for a landmark proof about the

19:59 gaps between prime numbers, left UC Santa Barbara  last year for a university in Guanghou. Now,

20:04 I really can't tell you what the right answer is  here. And for every argument about furthering a

20:08 rival science, there is a counter-argument about  international students overcontributing to the

20:12 funding of these educational institutions in the  first place. They poured about $43 billion into

20:17 the US economy last year alone. But genuinely, I'd  be interested to see your guys' thoughts in the

20:22 comments. I can't see that going badly. For what  it's worth, if this really is an adversarial zero

20:27 sum game, then well, we are still taking more  smart people from them than they are from us.

20:33 What's more is that if we really wanted  to avoid this dilemma in the first place,

20:36 we should probably double down on K through2  education for the domestic talent pipeline,

20:40 but that's a whole different video. The point is  on either side of this debate, we should probably

20:45 be trying really hard to reduce the exodus of  the talent that is already here. This is also,

20:50 let's be honest, a very emotional argument where  it's all too easy to dismiss one side as racist

20:55 for raising legitimate concerns, and it's also  very easy for actual racist ideas to piggyback

21:00 on some valid criticism. The unfortunate reality  is that companies know this and they know the

21:06 emotions of this debate will make for a great  get out of jail free card. So go watch this
