00:00

00:02 PROFESSOR: Trees are about the most basic data structure

00:05 that you're ever going to come across.

00:07 They pervade computer science and other subjects.

00:09 So let's talk about them.

00:11 And the simplest definition of a tree

00:13 is that a tree is a connected graph with no cycles.

00:16 In this setting we're talking about simple graphs, and trees

00:20 with undirected edges.

00:22 Well, in order to make sense of that,

00:24 we better have a definition of a cycle.

00:26 There's a picture of a typical tree,

00:28 but to be precise, what's a cycle in a simple graph?

00:32 Well, it's a closed walk of length greater than 2

00:35 that doesn't cross itself.

00:37 So the not crossing itself is the standard definition

00:40 of a cycle that we were using in a directed graph.

00:43 It simply means that it's a path, except that the beginning

00:47 and end vertex are the same.

00:48 So it looks like you start someplace at v,

00:52 and then you go around to a and to w,

00:54 and it's all distinct vertices as you go around in this path.

00:58 Except that the path ends where it

01:00 starts at v, which is what keeps it from being a path

01:02 and makes it a cycle.

01:04 Now, the length greater than 2 is

01:05 what is the difference between the definition of cycle

01:08 [? between ?] simple graphs and directed graphs.

01:12 And in a directed graph, it's perfectly possible

01:14 to have a self-loop of length, 1,

01:17 that is an interesting and important kind of cycle

01:19 to have.

01:19 But we forbid them in simple graphs,

01:22 because there's no way to avoid having a cycle of length 2,

01:26 because you always have the ability

01:28 to go back and forth across an edge-- that's not interesting.

01:31 And so we don't consider that to be a cycle.

01:34 A cycle, then, has to be of length greater than 2.

01:37 It also rules out the cycle of length 0,

01:40 which you get by taking a vertex all by itself.

01:43 OK, with that technical definition,

01:45 we now know what a cycle is in the simple graph,

01:47 and we understand the definition of tree.

01:50 Here are some more pictures of trees--

01:52 simple graphs with no cycles.

01:55 Now, they really come up all the time.

01:58 And why is that?

01:58 Well, there are family trees, which

02:00 you may be familiar with-- where you're

02:02 drawing a picture of the descendants of a given person,

02:06 and they keep branching out in a tree structure,

02:09 as traditionally displayed.

02:13 There are search trees, which come up all the time

02:15 in computer science, where you branch on the answer

02:18 to some question, which tells you which way to search next.

02:21 There are game trees, which we've already

02:22 discussed in this class, which are used

02:24 to define games and strategies.

02:26 There are parse trees, that come up in compiler technology,

02:31 and in language theory.

02:33 And there are spanning trees, which we're going

02:35 to be talking about some today.

02:38 Now, in addition to these places where trees come up,

02:42 there are a lot of different kinds of trees.

02:44 There's rooted trees, where there's some designated

02:46 vertex called the root, and you think

02:48 of getting to all the other vertices from the root.

02:54 There are ordered trees, where when you're at a given vertex,

02:57 there's a distinct order in which the exit

03:04 edges from a vertex-- there's a first one, and a second one,

03:07 and a third one, or a left one, and a next, left, most, and so

03:10 on, so that there is an order in which you

03:12 can choose to leave the vertex.

03:15 There are a binary trees, in which

03:17 each vertex has two ways out exactly-- or no ways out

03:22 if it's a so-called leaf.

03:24 And then there are a complete trees, whose definition

03:28 is not important to us, because we're not

03:30 going to consider any of these.

03:31 There's also, by the way, directed trees in which edges

03:35 have a direction, as in a [? di-graph ?] tree.

03:38 But we're not considering any of these.

03:40 We're going to focus on so-called pure trees, which

03:43 are unordered, unrooted, undirected,

03:46 and that's what we're talking about.

03:48 So let's examine some more properties

03:50 of trees and equivalent definitions of trees.

03:52 It will be important for theoretical reasons

03:55 and convenience to know lots of different characterizations

03:58 of trees.

03:58 So we're starting off with a definition which says,

04:01 it's a connected simple graph with no cycles,

04:05 but there's other ways to characterize it.

04:08 So an edge in a simple graph is called a cut edge,

04:11 if, when you remove it from the graph,

04:15 two vertices that used to be connected--

04:17 that is used to have a path between them--

04:19 cease to have a path between them.

04:21 So here's a simple graph illustration.

04:24 And that edge, e, is a cut edge, because if I delete it, then

04:29 there are now two components.

04:31 There used to be two vertices-- actually any

04:34 of the vertices here used to be connected

04:36 to any of the vertices there via that edge.

04:38 But once I've deleted that edge, all of those

04:41 vertices here and there that used to be connected no longer

04:44 are.

04:44 So that makes e a cut edge.

04:47 f is not a cut edge.

04:48 Because even if I delete f, there

04:51 is, in fact, still a path from every vertex

04:54 to every other vertex here, so that f is not

04:56 disconnecting anything.

04:57

05:00 And as I say, it's still connected after you delete it.

05:03 So now we get a simple way to characterize trees

05:06 in terms of cut edges-- because an edge is not a cut edge if

05:11 and only if it's on a cycle.

05:12 If you think about that, if it's on a cycle,

05:15 and you cut an edge out of a cycle,

05:18 then everything on the cycle is still

05:19 connected by going the other way around the cycle that

05:22 doesn't use that edge.

05:24 And if it's not on a cycle, then, in fact,

05:27 you can think through that deleting it

05:29 means that there's not going to be two paths between two

05:35 things at its endpoints.

05:37 And so it will separate them.

05:41 OK, so another way, then, to define

05:44 a tree is to say a tree is a connected graph where

05:47 every edge is a cut edge-- that is

05:50 as soon as you cut any edge out of a tree

05:52 it stops being connected.

05:55 That yields another way to say that something

05:58 is a tree-- a tree is a simple graph that is connected

06:02 and is edge-minimal, which, again,

06:04 means that if you remove any edge,

06:07 it stops having that property of being connected.

06:10 So its an edge-minimal connected graph.

06:12 That's kind of the reason why trees are so important,

06:14 because if you're trying to figure out a way

06:17 to get a whole bunch of things-- a whole bunch of vertices--

06:19 connected, a tree is going to have

06:22 the minimum number of edges that are sufficient to get them all

06:25 connected.

06:26 If you think about different nodes in a network that

06:30 need to communicate with each other,

06:32 and you want to know how many direct connections that there

06:34 have to be between these communication

06:37 centers in order for everybody to talk to everybody else,

06:40 the answer is-- it's got to be a tree on n vertices.

06:44 And a tree on n vertices is going

06:45 to have exactly n minus 1 edges.

06:48 So that gives you still another equivalent definition

06:51 of a tree.

06:52 A tree is a connected graph that has n vertices,

06:55 and n minus 1 edges.

06:57

06:59 A kind of dual way to think about it

07:01 is that a tree is an acyclic graph that

07:08 has as many edges as it possibly could

07:10 without having any cycles.

07:12 So typically, an acyclic graph might not be connected,

07:16 but as long as it's not connected,

07:17 you can keep adding edges that will connect things up

07:20 without creating cycles.

07:22 But the minute you get a tree, so

07:24 that everything is connected, you can't add another edge.

07:27 So an edge maximal acyclic graph is still another way

07:31 to characterize trees.

07:33 And maybe the most useful way is to say

07:36 that a graph, in which there is a unique path between any two

07:40 vertices, is a tree.

07:43 So of course, if there is a unique path-- in particular,

07:45 there's a path, so all the vertices have to be connected.

07:48 But what makes it a tree is that there aren't two different ways

07:51 to connect between two vertices, because as soon as there

07:54 were there would be a cycle.

07:56 And those are some of the basic ways that trees

08:00 can be formulated equivalently.

08:03 And in fact, there's lots more, but this is enough for today.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Why Alexander The Great Is The Single Most Important Man In History

• Title: Why Alexander The Great Is The Single Most Important Man In History
  • Video ID: a2a4oR0ZUYE
  • Published: Unknown

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 It is said that he was born from Zeus himself, a demi-god in the flesh.

00:04 He tamed an unbreakable wild stallion that full-grown men feared to approach at the age

00:08 of 12, and that horse would carry him to military victory after military victory until his untimely

00:14 death at the age of 32.

00:16 He was tutored by one of the ancient world's greatest thinkers.

00:18 His name says it all- Alexander The Great.

00:21 But how much about Alexander is really true, and what's fiction?

00:25 And ultimately, with a whopping zero instagram followers, can we truly say he was all that

00:30 great?

00:31 Haters and historians alike will tell you that Alexander the Great was born in 356 BC

00:35 to the Macedonian king Phillip II and his wife, Olympias.

00:38 A true Greek however knows that Alexander was actually the love child of Zeus himself,

00:43 who had a nasty habit of popping down to earth and taking various animal shapes to con women

00:48 into sleeping with him.

00:49 In many ways, Zeus was the original frat boy.

00:52 Alexander's father was already an impressive figure - a brilliant military leader and politician

00:57 both.

00:58 Through force of arms and political maneuvering, he turned Macedonia into a military and cultural

01:02 power house- which was a pretty impressive feat because in the ancient world, Macedonia

01:06 was basically the backwoods of Greece.

01:09 Phillip's ambitions though weren't limited to his strengthening of Macedonia, and he

01:12 had a dream that would be handed down to his son, Alexander- to conquer the mighty empire

01:18 of Persia.

01:19 To date, Persia had been a world superpower, premier in many fields of science and philosophy,

01:24 it was backed by a formidable military which tried again and again to destroy the stubborn,

01:28 and defiant, Greeks.

01:29 To dream of conquering this mighty nation was to put it lightly, a very optimistic dream.

01:35 At the age of 13, Alexander was personally tutored by Aristotle, a man so famous that

01:40 even if you know nothing about his teachings, you definitely recognize the name.

01:44 One of the ancient world's greatest minds, Aristotle fostered a curiosity in the young

01:48 prince, and sharpened an already formidable intellect.

01:51 Alexander learned philosophy, medicine, politics, and art from Aristotle- and also that he should

01:56 treat non-Greeks as if they were slaves.

01:58 Thankfully, when Alexander would begin his military conquests later in life, he would

02:02 discard this belief, and this would help establish his mighty, if short lived empire.

02:07 In 340 BC, Philip went off to attack Byzantium, and left the young Alexander in charge of

02:12 things at home.

02:13 Alexander used the opportunity to prove that even though he was just a teenager, he was

02:17 destined to be a great leader, and gathered the army for a successful attack against the

02:21 Maedi - a people who lived in what is now the southeastern Baltics.

02:25 Two years later Philip returned home, determined to unite Greece under one banner, and went

02:30 to war against a coalition of Greek city-states led by Thebes and Athens.

02:34 In that battle Alexander led the cavalry to a triumphant defeat of the legendary Sacred

02:39 Band of Thebes, a fighting force made up of 150 pairs of lovers.

02:43 This victory catapulted an already popular Alexander to new heights of popularity with

02:48 the Macedonian military.

02:50 Alexander would need that popularity too, as a year later Philip divorced Alexander's

02:54 mother, and then in a feast to celebrate his new marriage, Philip got into a fight with

02:58 Alexander over his new wife.

03:00 Alexander and his mother fled for fear of their lives, though Philip and Alexander were

03:04 soon reconciled and he was allowed to return home.

03:07 When Philip was assassinated shortly after though, Alexander was not the clear heir to

03:11 the throne, and he rallied the support of the military to help him kill his potential

03:15 rivals.

03:16 Solidifying his grip over Greece, Alexander then attended an assembly of Greek city-states

03:20 which had already been called for by his father.

03:23 The Greeks were finally going to make good on the ancient dream of conquering Persia,

03:27 and the assembly unanimously voted to make Alexander supreme commander of Greek forces.

03:32 Before crushing Greece's ancient rival though, he needed to secure the Greek peninsula.

03:37 Alexander spent some time bringing wayward city-states into the fold- often by military

03:41 force- as well as waging campaigns against the Thracians to the north.

03:44 While in battle though, rumors of his death circulated back in Greece, and the city-state

03:49 of Thebes used the opportunity to revolt.

03:51 As many other Greek city-states favored Thebes over Alexander, support for the fledgling

03:55 rebellion flowed in- especially from Athens.

03:59 Upon hearing of the brewing revolt, Alexander forced a hard march on his troops, traveling

04:03 an astounding 240 miles (386 km) in just two weeks to the gates of Thebes.

04:07 The Thebans however refused to rejoin Alexander and he was forced to lay siege to the city,

04:12 ultimately burning it to the ground and selling off any survivors into slavery.

04:15 With the rest of the city-states terrified at the treatment of Thebes, they quickly fell

04:19 in line, and in an act of generosity which would earn him some favor with the Greeks,

04:24 he forgave Athens' betrayal.

04:26 Leaving behind three garrisons, Alexander was now free to take on Persia.

04:30 By comparison, Greece was tiny versus mighty Persia, but Alexander was confident that his

04:34 men were better trained and equipped.

04:36 His superior troops would outweigh Persia's superior numbers.

04:39 That theory would be put to the test in 333 BC, when Alexander's forces met with a massive

04:44 Pesian army led by the new king, Darius III.

04:48 Alexander's belief that his superior troops could win out over superior numbers was well-founded.

04:53 The Persians had largely become complacent in the last century, and their military forces

04:57 suffered from a noticeable lack of discipline- as well as a lack of cavalry.

05:02 Alexander by comparison fielded an army comprised of archers, javelin throwers, infantry, and

05:06 heavy cavalry.

05:07 His mastery of what was in that day combined arms warfare saw him utterly crush the Persian

05:12 forces laid out against him.

05:14 With defeat inevitable, the Persian king fled the battlefield with the few forces that he

05:18 could muster into a hasty withdrawal.

05:20 Darius III was so hasty in his retreat that he even left behind his own wife and family,

05:24 and his mother was so ashamed of him that she disowned him publicly and adopted Alexander

05:29 as her own son.

05:30 This gesture would be paramount to Alexander's cementing of his grip on what was formerly

05:34 the Persian empire.

05:36 Over the next few years Alexander would continue his push east and south, striking deep into

05:40 the Persian empire and taking Egypt.

05:42 Time and again Darius sued for peace, and Alexander rejected each overture.

05:46 At last, he forced a confrontation with Persia's king at Gaugamela in 331 BC, and faced off

05:52 against another large Persian force.

05:54 The fighting was intense, each side knowing they were fighting for total victory and the

05:58 fate of Persia.

06:00 Ultimately though, Alexander's forces would be triumphant, and once more Darius fled the

06:03 battle.

06:04 This time though, his own men caught and killed him for his cowardice.

06:08 Alexander however proved to be honorable, and upon finding Darius' body, he gave the

06:12 former Persian king a royal funeral.

06:14 Some sources also state that he punished the murderers for daring to strike down their

06:18 king.

06:19 With Darius dead, Alexander was free to claim the throne of Persia for himself- except another

06:23 Persian leader, Bessus, had already claimed the throne for himself.

06:26 This would prove to be what historians call, a slight miscalculation.

06:31 Alexander's forces pursued Bessus and his army until finally Bessus' own troops captured

06:35 him and handed him over to the Greeks.

06:37 Bessus was tortured and then killed, and Alexander was finally king of Persia.

06:41 The empire that had threatened Greece for centuries was now at last, itself a Greek

06:45 territory.

06:46 In order to secure his hold on Persia, Alexander granted large amounts of freedom to Persian

06:50 territories, even allowing them to govern themselves in exchange for loyalty to him.

06:54 He did not force conversions of Persian culture or religion, the way most rulers did back

06:59 in his day, and instead actually adopted many Persian customs for himself.

07:03 This made him very popular with the Persians, although it made him just as unpopular with

07:07 his own Macedonian troops.

07:09 One of his generals and close friends, drunkenly insulted Alexander's adoption of Persian culture,

07:14 and in a fit of rage, Alexander killed him.

07:17 This proved to further drive a wedge between him and his native Macedonians.

07:21 Feeling that further conquests would help stabilize his political situation, and further

07:25 feeding his appetite for glory, Alexander rallied his forces once more and marched on

07:30 India.

07:31 Many tribes surrendered to Alexander without a fight, and in exchange he once more granted

07:35 them many freedoms that other conquerors wouldn’t have given them.

07:38 In 326 BC though, Alexander faced King Porus of Paurava, whose army was less experienced

07:43 but packed a superweapon- the war elephant.

07:46 Initially the war elephants sowed fear and devastation upon Alexander's army, but the

07:50 big beasts were vulnerable to Alexander's lightning-fast cavalry.

07:54 The elephants were brought down and Alexander secured defeat.

07:57 His troops though, completely exhausted, refused to continue with Alexander's plan to push

08:01 further into India and seize all of it.

08:04 Instead, Alexander wisely chose to let his troops rest.

08:07 Though the Greeks had been enriched greatly off Persia's vast wealth, they resented the

08:11 Persians after centuries of warfare.

08:13 Knowing he would never hold on to his new empire unless he could unite the two sides,

08:17 he forced the mass marriage of his Greek officers to Persian princesses, hoping that their sons

08:22 and daughters would be explicitly loyal to him.

08:25 This move turned out to be even more unpopular, and many Greeks threatened to mutiny until

08:29 Alexander replaced them with Persian officers and soldiers.

08:32 Not wanting to be left out of future spoils, his troops backed off their threats to mutiny,

08:37 and in an attempt at reconciliation, Alexander threw a fantastic banquet for all and returned

08:42 all military titles and honors to the mutinous officers.

08:45 Alexander’s conquest of Persia and forays into India helped spread Greek culture and

08:49 influence across the ancient world, as well as bringing some of the best of Persian thinking

08:54 to the Greek world.

08:55 The unity that his conquests had brought to two of the greatest people of the ancient

08:59 world would spur the Hellenistic age, and Alexander founded many of the ancient world's

09:03 most important centers of cultural and scientific development.

09:06 Among many of his accomplishments was the setting of a silver standard for currency,

09:10 which facilitated trade all across his former empire.

09:13 His liberating of huge amounts of wealth from the former Persian empire's treasury also

09:17 greatly boosted trade and wealth across the Mediterranean, and a period of prosperity

09:22 settled over the region.

09:23 Alexander's empire proved to be short-lived though, following his mysterious death at

09:27 the age of 32 made him one of history's shortest-lived rulers.

09:31 Some believe that he was poisoned by a political rival- of which he had many both on the Greek

09:36 and the Persian side.

09:37 Others though believe that he died due to malaria which he contracted during his travels

09:41 in India.

09:42 Whatever the cause of his death, Alexander proved to be the only thing holding the fragile

09:45 empire he had created together, and following his passing it immediately began to fall apart

09:50 at the seams.

09:51 His generals began to war amongst themselves in a bid to become the new supreme ruler.

09:56 Ultimately it's unknown if Alexander could have really held his empire together even

09:59 if he had lived.

10:00 His conquests had brought together many disparate peoples under one banner, most of them who

10:04 did not share a common culture.

10:06 Even while alive his empire strained and groaned under the pressure of revolution, and it was

10:11 only his political shrewdness along with savagery against his political enemies that kept it

10:16 together while alive.

10:17 How long this could have lasted though remains in doubt, and ultimately it's likely even

10:21 if he had not died from disease or poison, it would have eventually imploded anyways.

10:26 For more crazy stories about history’s world leaders go watch “Genghis Khan - Greatest

10:30 Conqueror Ever” And as always don't forget to like, share, and subscribe for more great

10:35 content!

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Why Gen Z DON'T WANT Kids

• Title: Why Gen Z DON'T WANT Kids
  • Video ID: aPyFM0Cav4M

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 We’re constantly told that Gen Z is  the most selfish generation in history.

00:04 Instead of starting a family, they spend  their time and money on TikTok, travel,

00:08 and skincare. But the truth is much  darker than they’d have you believe.

00:12 By 2050, the working-age population in  countries like South Korea is projected

00:17 to shrink by 35%. But it’s not  because the youth are selfish…

00:22 because they’re rational. Gen Z is  practicing extreme risk management.

00:27 They are the first generation to realize  they’ve been recruited into an economy that’s

00:30 about to go bust. Their refusal to have  kids is the only leverage they have left.

00:35 Gen Z is staring down some terrifying 2050  projections. The global working-age population,

00:40 especially in rich countries, is drastically  shrinking. In Europe, the working-age group

00:45 will decline by 10% to 53%, just over half the  population. In parts of southern and eastern

00:51 Europe, the decline will be much more dramatic.  The working-age share of the population will

00:56 plummet by over 20% in countries like Greece,  Portugal, Bulgaria, Romania, and Hungary.

01:01 What does that mean for the young  people living there? A lot more

01:05 pensions to support, and a totally broken economy.

01:08 For every senior in Europe today, there are an  average of 3 working-age people. That means there

01:13 are enough people working to keep the economy  going or literally taking care of the retirees.

01:18 But by 2050? That ratio will go down to  less than 2 working-age people per senior.

01:24 That’s a huge issue.

01:25 Europe won’t even experience the worst  of it. That would be South Korea,

01:29 which had a record-low fertility rate of 0.72 in  2023/2024. It’s a record low in its own history

01:37 and the world’s at. The working-age population  there is going to contract by 50% by 2070.

01:43 That’s like a company losing half its staff while

01:46 its obligations for elderly  care grow significantly.

01:49 It’s a demographic death spiral.

01:51 Because 2070 is not that far off.  Most of Gen Z will be in their 60s

01:55 and thinking about or actively  in retirement. Theoretically.

01:59 Because in countries like the UK, half  of Gen Z already thinks state pensions

02:03 won’t exist anymore by the time they’ll  need them. Some of the young adults who

02:07 do think they’ll have pensions believe they  probably won’t see them until at least 75.

02:12 So they’re squirreling away as much  as they can … which is not much.

02:16 How in the world are they going  to raise kids on top of that?

02:19 This is the world Gen Z has grown up in. The  population is collapsing, and the youth are

02:24 being handed the bill… and the blame. But  if the consequences are this apocalyptic,

02:29 why are our leaders blaming the victims  instead of fixing the actual problem?

02:33 Because it turns out, it’s easier to  just blame an entire group than accept

02:38 that you have destroyed the system that  was supposed to support their future.

02:42 It’s generational gaslighting.

02:44 Everywhere you turn, from newspapers  and websites to political statements,

02:48 the narrative for Gen Z is clear: they’re  “selfish”. All they do is travel, go to brunch,

02:53 and buy whatever TikTok tells them to buy.  Instead of settling down and having children,

02:57 they’re booking a retreat  in Bali and making content.

03:01 Leaders of every type have made their  position clear. Pope Francis said,

03:05 “today…we see a form of selfishness. We  see that some people do not want to have

03:09 a child.”. J.D. Vance said the nation  was now run by “childless cat ladies”.

03:14 The media is no better.

03:16 FOX news commentator, Ashley St. Clair,  described Gen Z as people who “just want

03:20 to pursue pleasure and drinking all  night and going to Beyonce concerts.

03:24 It’s this pursuit of self-pleasure in replace  [sic] of fulfillment and having a family.”

03:29 But is that really what the generation is all  about? More importantly, is that really the

03:34 reason they’re not having children? Or  is something much more serious at play?

03:38 Sociologists and researchers looking at  the bigger picture don’t agree with these

03:42 assessments of Gen Z. They think the  issue is much larger than selfishness.

03:46 In fact, one university director’s study  found that most Americans in their teens

03:50 and 20s still want to have children, two in  fact. In almost every survey of people that

03:56 age, they rarely find more than 20%  overall who want to remain childless.

04:00 However, most of these young adults  want to hit certain milestones first,

04:04 whether it’s paying off student debt or  owning their own house. When they enter the

04:08 job market and have to support themselves, they  quickly find that their dreams of a debt-free,

04:13 home-owning, kid-filled existence  may be financially impossible.

04:17 As family demographer Dr. Karen Guzzo says,  “it’s not about being selfish and saying,

04:22 ‘I’m not having kids because I want to sleep  in all the time. When fertility rates are down…

04:26 that’s because people don’t feel like they  have a future that they feel confident in.”

04:31 That’s partly because work looks so  much different now than it did when

04:34 boomers had 2.5 kids and a white picket  fence. Gen Z, as well as millennials,

04:39 are increasingly reliant on  the gig economy for work.

04:42 A 2025 survey found that 43% of Gen Z  workers take part in the gig economy,

04:48 way more than any previous generation. While  the perks of gig work may seem enticing,

04:52 the reality is often not  what it’s cracked up to be.

04:55 Especially if you’re trying to become  financially stable enough to have a child.

04:59 Gig work is, as the name would imply, unsteady.  You never know exactly what you’re going to be

05:04 earning next year. Making financial planning for  a child anywhere from difficult to impossible.

05:09 With some specialized exceptions, gig work  also isn’t really financially rewarding even

05:14 at its best. The same survey found that  median earnings for Gen Z gig workers in

05:19 the U.S. were $32,000. If you live in the  U.S., you may recognize that number as not

05:25 a whole lot to live off of. If you live  in a major city, it sounds 5 times worse.

05:30 To get an idea of how bad it is, the median  income for full-time, year-round workers

05:34 in the US was just under $63,400. Almost  double what most people make as gig workers.

05:41 That makes most freelancers too financially  strapped to even think of things like daycare,

05:46 which averages $1,400 per  month across the U.S.. But

05:49 it can easily run up to $3,000  in high cost of living cities.

05:53 To top it all off, gig workers usually don’t get  one huge financial relief that most boomers got:

05:59 company-provided healthcare. Making medical

06:01 coverage a further out of pocket  expense for almost half of Gen Z.

06:05 Since the average costs of pregnancy, birth,

06:07 and post-partum care alone are over  $20,000 in the U.S., having a kid

06:12 could literally be the difference between  being able to pay rent and being homeless.

06:17 So the generation has adjusted  accordingly… and logically.

06:20 Deloitte found that more than half of Gen Z  - 55%, to be exact - and 52% of millennials

06:26 are delaying major life decisions because of  their financial situation. These decisions

06:31 include marriage, having kids, starting  a business or pursuing further education.

06:35 Putting this all down to Gen Z being  “selfish” is a distraction from the

06:39 systemic failure that has robbed them of  their job security, chances of home ownership,

06:44 and future earnings. And history actually  proves the fault doesn’t lie with Gen Z.

06:49 Because they’re not actually the first generation

06:51 to stop having kids in the face  of extreme financial distress…

06:54 Enter the “Silent Generation”.  Children of the Great Depression.

06:58 During the 1930s, birth rates plummeted. While

07:01 people had been hovering at close to  3.0 children per couple in the 1920s,

07:06 during the Great Depression they  fell all the way down to 2.1 in 1936.

07:11 Things are obviously not as bad now as  they were during the Great Depression.

07:14 The Misery Index for an average  Gen Z 25-year-old today is 8-10%,

07:20 while the Silent Generation during the Great  Depression found themselves around 25%. But

07:24 the feeling of being “trapped”, of having no  faith in a healthy financial future, is similar.

07:30 The Population Reference Bureau looked  through the data and confirmed that

07:33 birth rates have almost always been an  economic indicator; not a cultural one.

07:38 When people can’t afford tomorrow, they don’t  create life today. When the economy for young

07:43 people stagnates, people stop having  kids. Sociological research backs up the

07:47 viewpoint that Gen Z views childbearing not as a  milestone, but as a financial existential threat.

07:53 However, there still is something a little  off about the comparison to the 1930s. The

07:57 Great Depression came after a shocking stock  market crash. But today, the stock market is

08:02 booming. Turn on the news, and you’ll hear about  the Dow Jones setting new records every so often.

08:08 So if the economy appears to be thriving,

08:10 but Gen Z and millennials aren’t reaping  its rewards…where is all that money going?

08:15 It’s mostly been hoarded by the older generations.

08:18 A big component of boomers’ financial stability  was their high rate of home ownership. By 1980,

08:24 the oldest boomers had turned 34;  half of them were already homeowners.

08:28 Almost 40 years later? Only 39% of  those aged 25-34 owned their own home.

08:34 And for most who haven’t  already attained that goal,

08:36 the prospect of ever buying their own  property seems like a far-off dream.

08:41 No wonder. Since 1970, the average house  has cost 2.4 times the average income. In

08:46 2024? It costs 6 times the average income.  As anyone who has seen a two-bedroom dump

08:52 being advertised for a million dollars  in the Tri-state area can attest to.

08:56 That means that in 1970, boomers only needed  to set aside around 2 years of salary to buy

09:00 their dream starter home. While today, Gen  Z better get a full-time job and somehow

09:06 save almost 8 years of that total gross  income if they ever want to own a home.

09:11 It’s clearly an impossible feat.

09:13 That’s made obvious by the fact that the  average age of first home ownership in

09:17 Europe has climbed up to over 31 years old. In  the US, it’s up to 40. Most people are already

09:23 shopping for reading glasses by the time they  can get a house in their name. Couples who

09:27 want a home to raise their kids in? They don’t  have a lot of fertile years left at that point.

09:32 It’s not just a housing problem either.  Every dollar Gen Z has in their hands

09:35 isn't as strong as it was. In fact, since 1970,  the U.S. has lost 88% of its purchasing power.

09:42 What does this translate to?

09:44 Someone shopping for their weekly  groceries today will end up paying

09:47 $100 to buy the exact same calories a  boomer would have bought for $13 in 1970.

09:53 Add this to the fact that young people are  holding less money and assets than ever,

09:58 and the picture starts looking really bleak.

10:01 In 2019, the Federal Reserve found that  millennials, while making up about a

10:05 quarter of the population, held only 3%  of the country’s wealth. Even by 2025,

10:10 Gen Z and millennials combined only held  just over 10% of the country’s wealth.

10:16 Even the Silent Generation, the same people born  before 1946 and raised during the Depression,

10:22 meaning most are either dead or retired in 2025…  hold more wealth than young people: over 12%.

10:29 OK, but maybe older generations hold more wealth  now because they’re older and saved it up?

10:34 No. Turns out, when boomers were in their 30s,  they held 21% of the nation’s wealth. That’s

10:40 over double what two generations hold now.  If the entire economy is 100 slices of pizza,

10:47 boomers easily got 21 before they even turned 35,

10:50 while millennials and Gen Z are  fighting to the death for ten.

10:54 The system priced out the future for  young people; so Gen Z responded by

10:58 canceling the family altogether. While  boomers got a fair chance to save up,

11:02 invest in a house, and in their future life,  Gen Z is barely keeping their head above water.

11:08 To make matters worse, housing and inflation may

11:11 have destroyed this generation’s present…a  new technology just destroyed their future.

11:16 “Where do you want to be in five years?” The  answer for most of Gen Z is staying afloat.

11:23 The introduction of AI to a job market  already stacked against its youngest

11:26 entrants has put many long-term career  plans into question. Almost 43% of Gen

11:31 Z workers have adjusted their career  plans because of worries about AI.

11:35 It’s not just that Gen Z can’t predict their  income for the next year; at this point,

11:40 they don’t even know if they’ll have a job or  the career path they studied and worked for.

11:45 One third of employers admitted they will use  AI to replace entry-level jobs. The ones that

11:50 would put Gen Z on the career ladder.  Many employers who responded worked at

11:54 Fortune 500 companies, the firms with some  of the biggest impact on the labor market.

11:59 Getting a college degree in this job market won’t  do much for most young workers except put them in

12:04 debt. The most affected sector is technology. More  than two thirds of Gen Z workers think a college

12:09 degree won’t protect them from AI-related  job loss. For those who think fewer college

12:14 degrees and more manual labor is the answer: the  second most affected sector is manufacturing.

12:20 And AI-related job loss is not a far-off  problem. 39% of executives admitted that

12:25 they have already laid off workers because  of AI. Even though more than half of them

12:30 say they regret it, it still creates a  completely unstable work environment.

12:34 With all this unpredictability in  the labor market, how are any of

12:38 them supposed to commit to financially  providing for a child for 18 years?

12:42 It’s like being asked to sign a 20-year  mortgage while standing on a trapdoor.

12:47 In response, governments are panicking  and throwing money at the problem. But

12:50 these programs are almost all failing.  Because while they may be well-intended,

12:55 they’re not getting to the heart of the issue.

12:57 Government subsidies can’t fix birth  rates. They can make life and finances

13:01 for parents a little easier. They can  help people who have already decided

13:04 they’re somewhat stable enough to  have kids. But for most of Gen Z,

13:08 subsidies aren’t going to help much at all. The  primary example of this is the Nordic model.

13:13 Despite massive, family-friendly subsidies,

13:15 and some of the most generous  parental leave programs in the world,

13:18 Nordic countries like Norway and Finland have  seen fertility rates drop to historic lows.

13:23 In 2024, Nordic fertility rates ranged from 1.25

13:27 children per woman in Finland  to 1.91 in the Faroe Islands,

13:31 according to the Nordic Statistics Database. In  rich countries, women need to have an average of

13:36 2.1 children to achieve stable replacement of the  population. Most of the Nordics are nowhere near.

13:43 Despite the fact that the subsidies and  regulations for parents are generous. Sweden

13:47 allows couples to take off 480 days of paid  parental leave. That’s more than 15 months.

13:53 If your child gets seriously sick,  you can get another 120 days off.

13:58 The fertility rate in Sweden? 1.4.

14:00 Because all the subsidies in the world can’t  fix the instability young couples feel,

14:05 and the rocky future they see ahead of them.

14:07 One Swedish professor put it perfectly:

14:09 “if those who are young adults - 29  and under - have kids, they are not

14:13 in a good economic position so it’s not very  strange that they don’t want to have kids.”

14:18 In Denmark, one survey found that the  percentage of young people who want

14:21 to have 2 to 3 kids in 2021 is exactly  the same as it was in 1970. The reason

14:27 they’re not having them? As one young woman  says, “I think it would be irresponsible”.

14:32 What’s shocking about these countries  isn’t just the fertility rate;

14:36 it’s how fast it’s fallen. Since 2010,

14:39 while the overall EU fertility rate fell by just  over 10%, in Finland, it dropped by a third.

14:45 This proves that financial incentives  alone do not offset the deeper issue.

14:50 The problem isn’t just peoples’  financial situation. It’s a form

14:53 of “structural hopelessness”.  Asset inflation that makes

14:57 life milestones - including marriage  and kids - seem absolutely hopeless.

15:01 If free money doesn’t make people want kids,

15:03 what is the actual root cause  keeping a lot of Gen Z childless?

15:08 Turns out, the system isn’t  really fixing the demographic

15:11 crisis…because the system is the one  that caused it in the first place.

15:14 Governments all over the world have spent the  last 40 years prioritizing the asset values,

15:19 housing equity, and pensions of the  oldest generations. And it’s been at

15:23 the direct expense of the purchasing  power and stability of the young.

15:27 In the UK, for example, studies found that boomers

15:30 were “net beneficiaries of the welfare  state - they will get more in benefits

15:34 than they have paid in tax”. The younger  generations will be net contributors.

15:38 A lot of this is because of the “grey vote”.  The co-founder of the Intergenerational

15:43 Foundation says, “the older generation  have more voting power…they lobby more,

15:48 the MPs and the policy makers are  more likely to be baby boomers so

15:52 [young people’s] interests tend  to be treated as less important.”

15:55 After benefitting from the state their whole  life due to tax cuts and generous pensions,

15:59 to name a few, boomers are now  in charge and making the rules.

16:03 Which are made to protect them and their  wealth at the expense of younger people.

16:08 While working-age benefits in the UK - and  across much of the Global North - are being cut,

16:12 the government decided to protect state pensions  by guaranteeing an annual rise of 2.5% - minimum.

16:19 Which seems odd. As many of these  pensioners have more assets and

16:23 wealth than most. But even those who are  well-off receive government handouts.

16:27 Retirees in the US receive, on average, 6 times  more government money than young people. That

16:32 added up to $2.7 trillion in 2025. While they  hold the most wealth and assets of any generation.

16:40 Young people are literally seeing  their potential wealth stolen out

16:43 from under them. While their future gets  destroyed in front of their very eyes.

16:47 State governments have massively  cut back on college subsidies,

16:51 while the cost - and necessity - of a degree  has skyrocketed. In 1975, when boomers were

16:57 graduating, states subsidized 60% of college  tuition. In the 2010s, this was down to 34%.

17:04 In 1960, 2% of a parent’s spending  went to childcare and education.

17:08 Fast forward to 2013. That share is  now 18%. Higher educational costs,

17:14 daycare costs and the necessity of 2  working parents, and insanely expensive

17:18 healthcare costs all add up. And those  numbers are only getting worse over time.

17:23 Gen Z is being asked to hand over one fifth  of wealth they don’t have to raise a kid,

17:28 while wealthy boomers continue to receive  government protection and handouts.

17:32 The social contract was broken by the very leaders  who are now calling Gen Z selfish. They forgot

17:37 to plant the trees for their grandchildren,  opting to chop them down for firewood instead.

17:43 So what happens when a generation  refuses to participate in a broken game?

17:47 Gen Z running away from having kids is not  the tragedy of selfishness that media and

17:52 leaders often depict it as; but an act of  quiet rebellion against a broken system.

17:57 They are simply refusing to bring life into  what they view as a “liquidation sale”.

18:02 Every indication shows that Gen Z  wants kids. But to actually have them,

18:06 they need some sense of stability  and actual hope for the future.

18:09 Until governments around the world decide to  seriously invest in the future of their youth,

18:13 create affordable housing, and allow real  hope to return to a generation that can’t

18:18 even imagine a good future for itself right now,  the birth rate trend will continue to collapse.

18:23 And unlike the Silent Generation? There  may be no coming back from it this time.

18:27 It seems like a lot of the issues lie at  the feet of one generation. And they’re

18:31 not getting any younger. Watch “THIS Will  Happen After Baby Boomer Generation Dies

18:36 Off” to find out what the future might look like  for Millennials and Gen Z. Or click on this video.

docs.text:
00:00 It was July 9, 1958, and an earthquake on the Fairweather Fault in the Alaska Panhandle

00:05 rattled for about one minute.

00:07 It was the strongest in Alaska for 60 years, and could be felt as far as Seattle.

00:11 The quake sent around 82 million tons of rock in the waters of Lituya Bay.

00:16 All that rock hitting the water was like an asteroid impact, and the result was the world’s

00:20 tallest mega-tsunami, measuring something like 1720 feet (524 meters).

00:25 The giant mass of a wave continued down the bay, taking with it any vegetation on the

00:30 mountainside.

00:31 That monster destroyed everything in its path.

00:33 One man and his son were sleeping in a boat in that bay as all this happened.

00:37 Through the skin of their teeth they survived, but others weren't so lucky.

00:41 Howard Ulrich and his eight-year old son named Sonny had been catching some Zs on their boat,

00:45 the Edrie, when the earthquake happened.

00:47 (Credit: geology.com https://geology.com/records/biggest-tsunami.shtml).

00:48 They had been out salmon fishing throughout the day and had retired to their bunks.

00:51 Just after 10 pm their bunks started shaking, almost knocking the two guys onto the floor.

00:55 Howard had no idea what had happened, so he got up and went on to the deck.

01:00 The boat was still shaking violently from side-to-side.

01:03 Suddenly there was an eerie calm for about 2 1/2 minutes, and what followed almost knocked

01:07 Howard off his feet.

01:08 He heard a crashing sound that was deafening, which was the rocks hitting the water in the

01:12 bay.

01:13 His son joined him on the deck.

01:14 They both looked into the distance down the bay, and on each side they saw the mountains

01:18 shuddering, sending snow flying high into the air.

01:21 Suddenly the two witnessed a wave coming towards them, so large they could hardly believe their

01:26 eyes!

01:27 As the wave approached though, it became smaller..

01:28 Still, it was racing down the bay at about 120 mph (193 km/hr), taking out trees on the

01:33 mountainside, plucking hundreds from their roots in a matter of seconds.

01:37 Howard now knew this was no time for standing around and admiring the power of nature.

01:42 There was no way this wave was going to stop before it hit their small boat.

01:47 Howard told Sonny to put on his life preserver and start praying to God Almighty.

01:51 There was not much he could do to steer the boat out of the way since it was anchored,

01:55 but he managed to turn on the engine and steer the boat so it was facing the oncoming wave.

01:59 Had he had not done that, the two might not have survived.

02:02 Howard dropped the anchor as low as it could go and his last words on the radio were, “Mayday,

02:07 Mayday.

02:08 This is the Edrie in Lituya Bay.

02:10 All hell has busted loose in here.

02:11 I think we’ve had it.

02:13 Good-bye.”

02:14 The wave was now 1720 feet when it was close enough for Howard to really see what was coming,

02:19 but receded to just 100 feet high as it neared.

02:22 When it finally reached them the wave was only around 50 to 75 feet high, but that was

02:27 enough to snap that anchor chain like it was nothing but a fishing line.

02:31 The boat rose high into the air, riding the wave.

02:34 With such force Howard believed the boat would be thrown to the land and smashed to pieces,

02:39 but that didn’t happen.

02:40 Once they were over the crest of the wave there was more danger, because the choppy

02:43 waters were full of debris that the wave had taken with it.

02:46 The two weren’t out of trouble yet, and little did they know, others were in danger,

02:51 too.

02:52 Unfortunately, not everyone was as fortunate as Howard and Sonny and managed to ride the

02:55 mega-tsunami.

02:56 Some would succumb to the giant wave.

02:58 There were two other boats in the bay on that historic day, a boat owned by Bill and Vi

03:03 Swanson named Badger, and a boat named Sumore owned by another couple, Orville and Mickey

03:08 Wagner.

03:09 Both these couples were actually friends and prior to the incident had waved across the

03:12 water and said hello.

03:13 When Bill Swanson felt the swaying of his boat he too got up to see what was happening.

03:17 He later described what he saw next was, “like a big load of rocks spilling out of a dump

03:22 truck.”

03:23 That might have been an understatement, because the rocks that hit the water would have weighed

03:26 as much as 240 Empire State Buildings.

03:29 The Swanson’s boat was lifted even higher when it was hit by the wave.

03:33 In Bill’s own words, he said, “We went away up over the trees, and I looked down

03:38 on rocks as big as an ordinary house as we crossed the spit.

03:42 We were away up above them.

03:43 It felt like we were in a tin can and somebody was shaking it.”

03:46 Looking down at the trees, Bill believed he was at least 80 feet in the air when on the

03:50 crest of the wave.

03:52 That crest broke and the Badger landed quite close to the shoreline.

03:55 The boat soon began to sink and suddenly trees and other debris flooded into it.

03:59 Bill was hit in the chest and broke a couple of ribs, but both he and his wife didn’t

04:02 go under.

04:03 The couple, still in their underwear, quickly got in their small dingy.

10:59 platforms. They knew their apps could

11:01 contribute to anxiety, depression, and

11:05 those risks while prioritizing profits.

11:07 The recent history verdict underscores

11:09 the consequences of those decisions. If

11:12 you or your child spent years growing up

11:14 on social media and experienced serious

11:16 mental health struggles, you should hear

11:18 this. Morgan and Morgan is stepping up

11:31 into the video. By 2025, he had become a

11:56 relationship with Celeste was becoming

11:58 increasingly volatile and dangerous.

12:01 Court filings reportedly describe

12:07 increasingly unhappy with the

12:09 relationship. In one text message cited

12:11 by prosecutors, Celeste allegedly told

12:13 David, "All we do is have and hang out.

12:26 constructing around her. The prosecution

12:29 argues that tensions escalated

12:45 endorsement opportunities were about to

13:01 charge. According to the timeline laid

13:03 out by investigators, David allegedly

14:00 blood while dismemberment occurred

14:40 was found. The sheer carelessness

14:42 investigators described throughout the

14:44 entire alleged cleanup has led many

14:47 observers to speculate about David's

14:49 mental state during the crime and

14:51 aftermath. Prosecutors claim he never

14:53 properly disposed of the remains, never

14:55 thoroughly cleaned the garage, never

14:58 removed crucial forensic evidence, and

15:00 continued driving the Tesla while the

15:04 vehicle's front trunk alongside air

15:06 fresheners meant to mask the

15:10 abandoned the vehicle entirely rather

15:12 than destroying it. Even more bizarrely,

15:15 court filings reportedly state that

15:46 fully clarified publicly. The autopsy

15:49 findings only intensified the public

15:51 horror surrounding the case. Medical

15:53 examiners reportedly concluded that

15:55 Celeste died from stab wounds causing

15:58 catastrophic blood loss. Her remains

16:00 showed evidence of dismemberment and two

16:02 fingers were missing entirely. her left

16:04 ring finger and her pinky. Internet

16:07 users quickly linked that detail to a

16:29 tested negative, preliminary screens

16:31 reportedly turned presumptive positives

16:33 for MDMA, methamphetamine, and

16:36 benzoazipines. Experts cautioned that

16:38 decomposition can complicate toxicology

16:41 interpretation significantly, especially

16:43 because post-mortem fermentation can

16:46 naturally produce ethanol inside the

16:48 body. Still, some observers speculated

16:50 that Celeste may have been drugged

16:52 before the attack, though no definitive

16:54 public conclusion has yet confirmed that

16:57 theory. As prosecutors continued

16:59 building their case, investigators also

17:01 began examining the role of people

17:03 surrounding David. Private investigators

17:06 publicly suggested he believed someone

17:08 may have assisted with moving or

17:10 dismembering the body, arguing that it

17:12 would have been extremely difficult for

17:14 one person to handle alone. He also

17:16 alleged that some individuals close to

17:18 David may have received money in

17:20 exchange for silence or cooperation,

17:22 though those claims remain unproven

17:24 publicly at this stage. Meanwhile,

17:27 additional scrutiny fell on David's

17:29 management team and professional

17:30 associates after reports emerged that

17:33 warnings about his relationship with

17:34 Celeste had allegedly been sent directly

17:36 to people working around him. According

17:39 to private investigators, an email

17:41 warning management that David might be

17:43 connected to a missing 13-year-old was

17:45 forwarded internally rather than

17:47 immediately reported to law enforcement.

17:50 Although simply receiving an email does

17:52 not prove criminal knowledge, critics

17:54 argue it demonstrates how many

17:56 opportunities existed for someone to

17:58 intervene before the situation escalated

18:00 into murder. There is one last strange

18:03 footnote to all of this. After the raid,

18:05 David broke his lease and cleared out of

18:08 that Hollywood Hills home, the same

18:10 house where prosecutors say Celeste

18:12 spent time before she died and where

18:14 investigators searched the garage. Crews

18:16 were photographed hauling everything

18:18 out. And then earlier this year, right

18:21 around the time he was finally arrested,

18:23 the house quietly went back up for rent.

18:26 A fully furnished Hollywood Hills home

18:28 with a private pool around $4,000 ft,

18:31 listed at just under $24,000 a month and

18:34 marketed as a peaceful luxury escape.

18:37 Whoever signs that lease next probably

18:39 has no idea what's alleged to have

18:41 happened in that garage. Ultimately,

18:44 this case with David seems pretty cut

18:46 and dry when all the details are laid

18:47 out. David had exhibited psychopathic

18:50 tendencies and a fascination with gore

18:52 even at a young age and clearly had

18:55 issues for his entire life. He somehow

18:57 got away with allegedly gy old all while

19:00 being at the height of his fame. It

19:02 almost seems that when he allegedly

19:04 murdered Celeste, he wanted to be caught

19:07 as Tony Soprano calls it. He got

19:09 cowboyis.

19:10 >> People do that [ __ ] they want to get

19:11 caught.

19:12 >> Oh, I WANT TO GET CAUGHT.

19:13 >> YEAH, YOU WANT TO GET CAUGHT. I'VE SEEN

19:14 IT BEFORE. THAT'S [ __ ] COWBOYIS. or

19:16 wanting to be seen as tough or however

19:18 you want to say it by other people. He

19:20 seemingly left clues like the Riddler

19:22 throughout his music videos. And the

19:24 fact he barely even disposed of the

19:26 evidence that he allegedly left behind

19:29 is proof that not only was he insane,

19:31 but he was stupid, too. David has

19:34 officially been charged with firstdegree

19:36 murder with special circumstances,

19:38 including lying in weight, murder

19:40 committed for financial gain, and murder

19:42 of a witness to an investigation. He was

19:45 also charged with lewd sex acts with a

19:47 person under four is old and the

19:49 mutilation of a human body. Since being

19:52 charged, he has pleaded not guilty and

19:54 is being represented by a Hollywood

19:56 legal powerhouse, Blair Burke, the same

19:59 attorney that Harvey Weinstein hired

20:01 back in 2017. The case isn't over yet,

20:04 but if I were a betting man, I would

20:06 guess that he will most likely be

20:08 spending the rest of his life in jail.

20:10 He might even be facing the death

20:12 penalty, although that is a slim chance.

20:15 At the end of the day, even if

20:17 prosecutors took a slightly long time to

20:19 gather all the evidence, it was for a

20:21 good reason, and they made as airtight

20:23 of a case as possible to try and ensure

20:26 that he won't be going anywhere anytime

20:28 soon.

00:10 [MUSIC PLAYING]

00:13

00:31 GUOLONG: Good morning, students.

00:33 STUDENTS: Good morning, Mr. Su.

00:35 GUOLONG: Can anyone tell me the answer, please?

00:38 STUDENTS: I can!

00:39 GUOLONG: Is everything clear?

00:40 STUDENTS: Yes, perfectly clear.

00:44 GUOLONG: Are there any other questions?

00:46 STUDENTS: No, no questions.

00:49 GUOLONG: I will see you on Tuesday.

00:51 STUDENTS: Thank you.

00:52 [APPLAUSE]

00:55 NARRATOR: Wait a minute.

00:57 That's not what happens in real life.

01:01 Actual MIT undergraduates often come to class

01:04 on three hours of sleep.

01:06 GUOLONG: Can anyone tell me the answer, please?

01:09 NARRATOR: Sometimes they're afraid to volunteer

01:11 what might be the wrong answer.

01:13 GUOLONG: [INAUDIBLE] lecture by considering a simple example.

01:16 NARRATOR: They're not always paying attention.

01:19 STUDENT: What?

01:22 NARRATOR: And they might not understand what

01:23 you thought you explained well.

01:26 GUOLONG: Is everything clear?

01:27 STUDENTS: Not really.

01:30 NARRATOR: So how can you be a successful TA at MIT?

01:34 Try thinking of your class as a popular website

01:37 that visitors come back to again and again.

01:40 What makes a website user-friendly?

01:42 CAROL: User-friendly to me means that in order

01:46 to complete the task at hand, the website is designed

01:49 in a way that's logical.

01:50 CHANDLER: Yeah.

01:51 I feel like format, just a clean, simple format

01:55 is really nice.

01:56 ADRIAN: It's not cluttered and messy.

01:58 BILLY: The most important things for a user-friendly website

02:01 is a clear interface, simple categories, and a search

02:05 option.

02:06 ADRIAN: And accessible language.

02:08 CHANDLER: So being able to find things very efficiently

02:10 and quickly is definitely pretty important.

02:13 ADRIAN: I think it's more user-friendly when

02:15 you can actually understand what they want you to do

02:18 and where things are.

02:20 CAROL: Being able to find the right things

02:23 in a way that's easy.

02:24 NARRATOR: In other words, a user-friendly website.

02:26 GUOLONG: Should be the designed with a thinking that

02:32 to make the user feel happy and easy, instead

02:35 of making the computer engineers to feel happy and easy.

02:40 NARRATOR: What if the engineer is a teacher

02:42 and the user a student?

02:45 ADRIAN: The main principle of accessibility

02:48 should be the same.

02:49 CHANDLER: A website should be simple, clean,

02:51 and also, like, should have where

02:53 you want to go right away.

02:54 And a teacher should be able to judge where the students need,

02:57 what the students need to where the students want

02:59 to go and adapt in that way.

03:00 BILLY: I guess like the Search button would be asking the TA

03:03 or asking the professor for more information.

03:06 ADRIAN: It's not necessarily that everyone

03:09 is going to be your friend.

03:11 But it's more about being easy to understand.

03:16 BILLY: In terms of having a clear interface, just

03:19 a simple structure of the class, something

03:21 that students can expect, like the lectures go the same way,

03:25 the recitation go the same way, and something

03:28 that students can expect.

03:29 NARRATOR: So organization and predictability

03:32 are key to the user-friendly class.

03:34 CAROL: Planning that way in a logical session, where

03:38 you, like, review things that are necessary

03:40 and then going into problem, practice problems,

03:43 and then going over what were the right answers,

03:47 I thought that was, like, pretty user-friendly for a student.

03:49 Because it was a good review and then good practice.

03:53 So it was, like, logical.

03:54 TA: For today's recitation, we're going to do--

03:56 NARRATOR: The TA acts as a guide for the students.

04:00 BILLY: It's important to, well, explain the learning objectives

04:05 of the class early on.

04:06 CHANDLER: Have just, like, an air of confidence

04:08 and be able to direct the recitation.

04:10 BILLY: A very big expectation in a recitation is for the TA

04:14 to provide us with the big picture of the concepts.

04:18 NARRATOR: The TA is approachable and supportive.

04:21 ADRIAN: You need to feel that you can approach them and ask

04:25 questions without any problem.

04:27 NARRATOR: And knowledgeable.

04:29 CAROL: The most important thing for a TA

04:31 is that they have to have a very solid understanding of what's

04:36 going on in the material.

04:38 NARRATOR: But is knowledge enough?

04:40 BILLY: Unfortunately, it's not enough to simply

04:42 be knowledgeable about the subject.

04:44 It's the way you present it, the way you communicate it.

04:46 CHANDLER: They're all very smart.

04:47 I know they all know what they're talking about.

04:49 So it's just how they can communicate that to us.

04:52 NARRATOR: So what is good communication

04:54 in the user-friendly classroom?

04:55 CHANDLER: The biggest thing that came across my mind

04:58 was definitely, like, how they answered questions

05:00 and the feedback they got the students

05:02 and how they responded to that.

05:03 ADRIAN: It's not the same when they read a paper,

05:06 and they just write the problem in the board

05:09 and solve the problem than explaining,

05:11 why is it going like this?

05:12 Or why is it working like this?

05:14 CAROL: I think just a willingness to clarify

05:17 is very, very important.

05:19 BILLY: Being patient and being able to explain

05:22 the same concept in different ways.

05:23 ADRIAN: And they can actually explain it to you

05:25 at a basic undergrad level.

05:29 NARRATOR: In the next videos, we will learn communication skills

05:32 and strategies to meet students' expectations

05:35 and create a user-friendly classroom.

docs.text:
00:00 If you are watching a YouTube channel  dedicated to finance and business,

00:03 I am almost 100% confident that you have watched  Wolf of Wall Street at least a dozen times.

00:08 It’s an amazing movie that’s gone on to inspire a  generation of douchey sales bros around the world.

00:14 But there is one line that still  makes me angry 7 years later.

00:18 …

00:36 No no no, I WAS FOLLOWING! It does matter! I even  had my notepad and pen out ready to take notes.

00:43 Yeah well if you were anything like me you  might have been thinking the same thing.

00:47 But that’s fine. The real Jordan Belfort  himself said that the movie was only

00:50 loosely based of the book he wrote and that  book was only loosely based off of reality.

00:55 There were a lot of things intentionally left  out of the book because if they were left in

00:59 they could be could be  considered proceeds of crime.

01:02 Similarly there were lot’s of things left  out of the movie because Martin Scorsese

01:06 specialists in chronicling the rise  and fall of organized crime figures,

01:10 not analyzing fraudulent stock market activity.

01:13 But that’s ok cause you guys have me,  so it’s time to learn How Money Works

01:17 to lift the hood on Straton Oakmonts  questionable operations and find out

01:21 how it let Mr Belfort rake in “almost” a  million dollars a week in ill gotten gains.

01:26 As always I would like to thank my channel members  and patrons on patreon for making it possible

01:31 for me make a de-monetized video about literal  financial fraud. If you want to make more video’s

01:35 like this possible please consider supporting  the channel on either of these platforms…

01:40 Jordan Belfort’s career really picked up when  he was laid off from his job at L.F Rothschild,

01:45 a New York based stockbrokerage.

01:47 Back before the 2000’s buying stocks was  not as simple as going online and typing

01:51 in a ticker symbol. People would actually  call a real living person (a stockbroker)

01:56 and give them instructions on what  stocks to buy and what stocks to sell.

01:59 Oh well actually, more often than not it  would actually work the other way around,

02:02 the stockbroker would call their clients  and tell them what to buy and sell.

02:07 The same was true of getting information. Here  in 2021 if you want to know what the price of

02:12 GME is all you need to do is plug it into google  and hey there it is. Back in the 80’s you either

02:18 needed to wait for tomorrows paper, or call  your broker to see what the market was up to.

02:22 Now as Matthew McConaughey  so insightfully points out,

02:26 nobody, I don’t care if your Warren Buffet  or if your jimmy buffet, nobody knows if a

02:30 stock is going to go up, down, sideways or in  trucking circles, least of all stockbrokers.

02:35 So why did they do this then?

02:37 …

02:45 Yeah that’s right, they earned significant  commissions by processing these trades.

02:50 These days we are used to zero commission brokers,  but that hasn’t always been the case. In the 90’s

02:55 it wasn’t unusual for trades to cost as much as  2% of the total value of the assets being traded.

03:00 A stock broker would normally  get 1% of that and the firm the

03:04 stock broker worked for would get the other 1%.

03:06 …

03:07 Jordan Belfort would later go  on to work at investor center,

03:10 in reality Jordan actually worked  for a series of companies like this,

03:13 but what the movie portrays is pretty  indicative of these types of operations.

03:18 These are what is called “over  the counter” brokerages which are

03:21 very different from the exchange  brokerages like L.F Rothschild.

03:24 Exchange brokerages facilitate  trades on public exchanges.

03:28 They would have a team of actual people down  on the floor of the NYSE calling out trades

03:32 on behalf of the stock brokers in their office  who would be relaying trades from their clients.

03:37 As we had seen this system was still susceptible  to unscrupulous behavior ( mainly in the form

03:42 of stock brokers driving their clients to  make as many trades as possible to drive

03:45 up their commissions) but the exchange  had some level of control over all the

03:49 players in this game to make sure  things didn’t get too out of hand.

03:53 If the exchange decided that a particular  stock broker, or a particular stock broking

03:57 company was acting in a way that was  detrimental to the exchanges reputation

04:01 they reserved the right to kick them off the  trading floor. This would destroy the stock

04:05 brokerage because if they can’t make  trades, they don’t have a business.

04:09 Exchanges also heavily regulate what companies  are allowed to be listed on their exchanges.

04:14 They audit financial statements, conduct  background checks on the management, and

04:17 make sure that the company CEO’s mother doesn’t  pick up the phone when you call their head office.

04:22 Over the counter firms are different. They  do not utilize the services of an exchange,

04:27 and because of this they do away with a lot of  the regulation and oversight that comes with them.

04:32 Companies can approach these over the  counter firms directly and say hey,

04:36 I need 1 million dollars in funding to conduct R&D

04:38 on a new piece of radar tech that has  both military and civilian applications.

04:43 The stock firm will say sure, but we keep  50% of all of the money we raise for you.

04:48 At best these companies are just desperate  for funding to get their idea off the ground,

04:53 at worst they are also looking to defraud  investors using any money they raise.

04:57 One other thing is that 50%  number was just a bit of Hollywood

05:01 magic. The OTC brokers were likely only  making about 10 – 20% on these trades.

05:06 Either way, it should be clear to see  that any company that needs to offer a 20%

05:10 cut to a stockbroker just to raise money  is probably not worth investing in,

05:15 and that is why Jordan Belfort,  and his colleague’s resorted to

05:18 high pressure sales tactics  on unsophisticated investors.

05:21 Jordan eventually founded Stratton Oakmont,  a subsidiary of Stratton Securities, which

05:26 was a small time dealer that could trade both  over the counter and exchange listed companies.

05:30 Belfort and his co-founders, Brian Blake and  Danny Porush (portrayed as Donnie Azoff in

05:35 the 2013 film) later bought out the entire firm  and started to change how things would be run.

05:40 Belfort had been making  good money by, as he put it…

05:44 …

05:48 But he had grander ambitions.

05:50 He went on to hire a team of brokers who would all  aggressively pitch whatever stock he told them to.

05:55 Before giving this order he  would call up unaffiliated,

05:58 but trustworthy connections who would buy up a  large amount of stock in a small value company,

06:02 preferably one with less than a one  hundred million dollar market cap.

06:06 Once his connections (affectionately called rat  holes) owned a big enough portion of the company,

06:11 he would instruct all of the  brokers on his sales floor to

06:13 go out and sell the stock to whoever would buy it.

06:16 The buying frenzy would drive  up the price which would have

06:18 the convenient side effect of making  it easier to sell to new investors

06:22 “this stock has doubled in value this week”  “get in now or you’re going to miss out”.

06:27 Once the price of the stock had  reached a certain level Jordan

06:30 would instruct his rat holes to start selling.

06:32 While this was happening Jordan's company would  make it incredibly difficult for their regular

06:37 clients to sell off the stock, brokers  would be instructed to not answer phone

06:41 calls from investors looking to sell, or  just to intentionally lose trade orders.

06:45 This gave the rat holes time to exit  their positions, and as soon as regular

06:49 investors could start selling their  own stock the price would collapse.

06:52 The rat holes would then give the money they made

06:54 to Belfort while keeping a  small cut for themselves.

06:58 This scheme was taken to new heights when  Stratton Oakmont started taking companies public.

07:02 An Initial Public Offering is when a company  is first listed on a public exchange.

07:07 There are lots of rules and regulations involved  in this process but the advantage to the business

07:11 at the end of the day is that it becomes much  easier to raise capital from public markets.

07:16 Businesses will hire an underwriting firm  to guide them through the process and assume

07:20 some of the risk of the whole operation. The  underwriting firm will then be responsible

07:24 for making sure the IPO is successful. A  successful IPO really just means all of

07:29 the shares that the company wants to sell,  get sold at or above the agreed upon price.

07:34 Normally companies will go to investment  banks to do their underwriting, but in

07:38 it’s prime Stratton Oakmont managed to court  a few companies to use their services instead.

07:44 You might have thought that the re-introduction  of public exchanges into the mix would have slowed

07:48 down Belfort’s scheming. There was a reason he  traded in over the counter stocks in the first

07:52 place, and that was to avoid the regulation and  scrutiny that comes with these public markets.

07:57 But Jordan didn’t let that stand in his way,

08:00 in fact he developed a system to get  the best out of both of these systems.

08:04 Jordan would instruct his ratholes to buy up stock  in a company that he was about to take public.

08:08 The company would then debut on a  public market and he would instruct

08:12 his army of brokers to sell the  IPO stock to all of their contacts.

08:15 This would drive up the price of  the stock just like it did before,

08:19 but this time because it was  listed on a public market,

08:21 it would attract the attention of other investors  who didn’t even know who Stratton Oakmont was.

08:26 People would just hear the  news that some IPO was up 50%

08:29 at open and they would want to get in on  that action. The rat holes could then use

08:34 this buying mania to silently sell their  stocks netting them a very healthy profit.

08:38 Jordan effectively combined the  unregulated environment of over

08:41 the counter operations with the  inherent trust investors had in

08:45 publicly traded stock to create  the ultimate money making scam.

08:49 and that’s how you make…

08:50 …

08:54 For those of you who haven’t connected the dots  yet, this is what is called a “pump and dump”

08:59 and it was the mechanism by  which Belfort made millions.

09:03 For a while it actually looked like these  schemes were becoming a thing of the past.

09:07 Online stock trading platforms and  easy access to market information

09:10 meant that investors were no longer exposed to  brokers who would hype up some small cap company.

09:16 Unfortunately the rise of loosely regulated  crypto markets has meant that pump and dump

09:20 schemes are back with a vengeance. The  only difference is today the coked-up

09:24 stockbrokers have been swapped out for  discord communities and gaming influencers,

09:28 and penny stocks have been replaced  with dumb trucking meme coins.

09:31 …

09:32 Another important part of the movie was how Jordan  hid his money once he had made it. I don’t have

09:37 time to go into that in this video but fortunately  I actually made an entire video on exactly how you

09:42 could do this if you ever found yourself in the  possession of a large pile of ill gotten gains.

09:46 So go and watch that video if you think that’s  something that’s likely to happen to you.

09:51 As always a special thank you to my  channel members and patrons on Patreon

09:54 for making it possible for everybody  to keep on learning How Money Works.
