docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Ads You See Online Are Now Police Surveillance
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: Ads You See Online Are Now Police Surveillance
  • Video ID: cq36YXrfyJE
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Everyone knows the police need a  warrant to track your movements.

00:03 That's the Fourth Amendment... right?  Not anymore. Because the app you

00:07 checked for tomorrow's forecast just sold the  government a map of everywhere you've been…

00:11 Including where you slept last night. Ben Renick, a world-renowned exotic

00:16 snake breeder, was found dead in his  Missouri reptile facility in 2017,

00:20 a pool of blood surrounding. Police thought one  of his prized snakes had attacked and killed him.

00:26 Until they looked closer. They found a shell casing.

00:29 With few leads, investigators turned to a  surveillance tool that harvests location data

00:34 from popular phone apps. They searched for every  phone that was near the property at the time of

00:38 the murder. One device stood out. The babysitter’s.

00:42 Investigators spent weeks reconstructing its  movements… all without a warrant or its owner's

00:47 knowledge. To track her, police didn't need  a judge's approval. They just needed access

00:52 to an ad-tech database and a subscription  that reportedly starts at $7,500 a year.

00:59 Except… she was totally innocent. Right now, somewhere in America,

01:03 a detective can open a web browser, draw a box on  a map, choose a date, and click "Search." Seconds

01:09 later, they'll see every phone that entered  that area and up to 90 days of where those

01:13 phones traveled afterward. All thanks to Fog Reveal.

01:17 It’s a product of a Virginia  company called Fog Data Science,

01:20 founded by 2 former senior officials  from the Department of Homeland Security.

01:24 Their platform pulls location data from  the advertising systems embedded in the

01:28 apps you use for navigation, shopping rewards,

01:31 and local weather. It then feeds  it all into a searchable database.

01:35 Law enforcement agencies can log in and find  out which phones were inside their perimeter

01:39 of interest on a specific date, using what  the tool calls a “pattern of life analysis.”

01:45 The phrase came straight from the intelligence  community. It’s the same methodology that the

01:49 NSA uses to profile terrorism suspects. By 2022, investigative reporters at the Associated

01:55 Press and the Electronic Frontier Foundation had  uncovered the scope of the program through Freedom

02:00 of Information Act requests. Fog Data Science  had sold around 40 contracts to law enforcement

02:05 agencies across the country. The list included  state highway patrols, county sheriffs, municipal

02:10 police departments, and federal agencies. Some smaller departments share access with

02:15 neighboring jurisdictions to split  the cost. It’s a tool that can track

02:18 a quarter of a billion devices for less  than the cost of a used police cruiser.

02:23 And Missouri wasn't an exception.

02:25 When nurse Sydney Sutherland disappeared while  jogging outside Newport, Arkansas in 2020,

02:30 her phone was found in a ditch and  police had almost nothing to go on.

02:34 A local prosecutor shared his agency's Fog  Reveal access with the U.S. Marshals Service,

02:38 and investigators used the tool to identify  which devices had been in the area when

02:43 Sutherland was last seen. That data helped  lead to the arrest of a local farmer for

02:47 her assault and murder. Fog’s use was not  documented anywhere in the court record.

02:52 That’s the part that should stop you cold.

In two separate investigations, a surveillance

02:57 tool was used to identify suspects. In neither  case was its existence disclosed to the defense.

03:03 Bennett Cyphers, a senior adviser at the EFF  who led the public records investigation,

03:08 described it as "a mass surveillance program  on a budget." He noted there had been no

03:13 previous record of companies selling this kind of  granular data directly to local law enforcement.

03:18 "We're seeing counties with less than 100,000  people," he said, "where the sheriff is using

03:22 this extremely high-tech… invasive, secretive  surveillance tool to chase down local crime."

03:28 Fog Reveal is different from the  surveillance tools you’re probably

03:31 imagining. It doesn’t tap cell towers,  go to Apple or Google or your carrier,

03:36 or require a subpoena or any contact with  the company that made your phone to work.

03:40 The data it uses was never officially  collected by law enforcement at all.

03:45 Instead, it was collected by the  apps people freely use. That data

03:48 is then sold to brokers for the highest  bid, aggregated and repackaged until it

03:54 lands in a web portal that a county  sheriff can access from a laptop.

03:57 The broker sitting at the center of  that supply chain is called Venntel,

04:01 a subsidiary of a company called  Gravy Analytics. Venntel's confirmed

04:05 government clients include the IRS,  the Department of Homeland Security,

04:09 Immigration and Customs Enforcement,  Customs and Border Protection, the DEA,

04:13 and the FBI. Venntel claims to source its data  from over 80,000 different apps. The developers

04:19 of most of those apps almost certainly have no  idea where their users' location data ends up.

04:25 Which is problematic.

04:27 How is any of this legal? The  Fourth Amendment is supposed to

04:30 protect you from exactly this kind of  warrantless government surveillance.

04:34 Yet here we are.

04:35 The Fourth Amendment says the government  can’t search your private life without a

04:39 warrant. That’s the deal. Police need  probable cause, a judge’s signature,

04:44 and a specific description of what  they’re looking for to get in the door.

04:48 It’s been that way since 1791.

04:51 So how, you ask, is a company selling your  location history to federal agencies without

04:55 any of that? How does that not violate the most  foundational privacy protection in American law?

05:01 Easy. They make the data disappear from  the Constitution before they take it.

05:05 Here’s how it works. The moment you share  your information with a third party app,

05:10 bank, or phone company, the law says  you've voluntarily surrendered your

05:14 reasonable expectation of privacy in it. Not  to that company specifically… to everyone.

05:20 Including the government.

05:21 Once it's in someone else's hands, the  Fourth Amendment stops following it. The

05:25 government doesn't need a warrant  to get it from the third party,

05:28 because legally it's not your information anymore.

05:31 You gave it away; you assumed the risk.

05:34 This is what’s known as Third-Party Doctrine,

05:36 and it’s been the law since the 1970s.  If you thought the Supreme Court invented

05:41 the enabling of mass surveillance after a  mass terror event like 9/11, you’re wrong.

05:46 It actually came out of a mundane robbery case in  Baltimore in 1976 where the suspect kept calling

05:52 his victim afterward to threaten her. Police  wanted to prove it was him, so they went to the

05:57 phone company and asked them to record which  numbers he was dialing from his home phone.

06:02 They had no warrant, and the court said that was  fine. The suspect, they argued, had voluntarily

06:07 shared those numbers with the phone company by  dialing them. Therefore, he had no reasonable

06:12 expectation they'd stay private. But the logic the  Court used was so broad, so cleanly transferable,

06:19 that it became the master key for nearly every  form of digital surveillance that followed.

06:24 Supreme Court Justice Thurgood Marshall  saw it coming in his dissent to this case.

06:28 He warned that the ruling gave the  government unchecked power to monitor

06:32 patterns of association. He was outvoted  5 to 3, and largely ignored for 4 decades.

06:38 Then in 2018, the Supreme Court blinked.

06:40 Then, in 2018, the Supreme Court  heard a case called Carpenter v.

06:44 United States. It centered on a string of armed  robberies in Detroit. In a 5 to 4 decision,

06:49 the Court ruled that police violated the  Fourth Amendment by collecting 127 days

06:54 of a suspect's cell phone records  from his carrier without a warrant.

06:58 Chief Justice John Roberts wrote that tracking  a phone amounted to "near perfect surveillance,

07:03 as if it had attached an ankle monitor to the  phone's user." He said it gave the government

07:08 a window into a person's "familial, political,  professional, religious, and sexual associations."

07:13 It had to stop.

07:15 Privacy advocates celebrated his stance.

07:17 The government more broadly  just took notes and nodded.

07:20 Carpenter v. United States protected location  data held by your cell carrier, the company whose

07:25 towers your phone pings just by being switched on.  That narrow category of data now needs a warrant.

07:32 Everything else is still wide open.

07:34 That includes every piece of location data you  hand to an app, which then sells it to a broker,

07:40 who sells it to another broker,  who sells it to the government.

07:43 That entire chain powers Fog Reveal as well as  Venntel's confirmed clients at ICE, the DEA,

07:48 and the FBI. It currently sits in the  gap Carpenter deliberately didn't close.

07:53 When you tapped “allow” on that  Weather App’s location prompt,

07:57 you shared your data with a third party. And  the Third-Party Doctrine took things from

08:01 there. The Constitution stopped following your  location at the exact moment you let an app see

08:06 it. What the government buys from brokers is,  legally speaking, data you already gave away.

08:12 Kevin Metcalf, the Arkansas prosecutor who  used Fog Reveal in the Sydney Sutherland

08:16 case said people need to decide whether  they want "all this free technology."

08:21 His position is that you can't have free  apps and privacy. You need to pick one.

08:26 What he left out is that nobody taught  you that was the choice. Have you ever

08:30 seen a disclosure that said, “tap Allow,  and law enforcement agencies can purchase

08:34 a 90-day map of your movements without  ever speaking to a judge.” Of course not.

08:39 You got a push notification, and you  tapped yes. That was the transaction.

08:44 Here’s something worth knowing about the internet

08:45 advertising business. It all started as  a pretty sensible concept. Back then,

08:50 mass surveillance operations were still  just a remote Orwellian pipe dream.

08:54 If you were reading a fishing website in 1998,  you got fishing ads. Advertisers matched the

09:00 ad to the content. It was a surefire way to reach  someone who was actually interested in your wares,

09:05 and at that point, your identity  was irrelevant to that transaction.

09:08 Nobody needed to know who you  were. All they needed to know

09:12 is where you were reading.

Then the smartphone arrived.

09:15 The moment a GPS-enabled computer  went into everyone’s pocket,

09:19 someone in an office somewhere had the  thought we didn’t know we were dreading:

09:23 What if the ad didn’t follow the  content? What if it followed the person?

09:28 Because location, it turned out, was the most  important thing about you. Even more than your

09:33 search history, or your purchase history,  or anything you consciously typed into a

09:37 box. It is the one thing that gets transmitted  even if a service is disabled on a smartphone.

09:43 Where you go tells a story about who you are  that you’d never volunteer to a stranger. It

09:48 shows where you sleep, where you pray,  whether you’re at an oncologist or a

09:52 divorce attorney or a methadone clinic.  It shows your politics, your vices,

09:57 your health, your relationships, all  in ways you’d never openly verbalize.

10:01 Advertisers figured this out fast.

10:03 And they built an industry around it.

10:05 The technical name for what they built is  a Software Development Kit, or SDK. It’s a

10:10 small package of code that app developers can  drop into their apps, usually in exchange for

10:15 revenue sharing. You've never seen it and  the app developer often barely thinks about

10:19 it. But every time you open an app with one  embedded, it wakes up and starts harvesting.

10:24 It notes your device's advertising ID, records  your location, timestamps it, and sends it

10:29 upstream to whoever owns the SDK. Eventually, a  government contractor is waiting to collect it.

10:35 Martin Gundersen, a journalist at Norway's  national broadcaster NRK, decided in 2020 to

10:40 find out exactly how this worked in practice.  He installed a navigation app from a company

10:44 called Sygic and an app called Funny Weather on  an Android phone, granting them both location

10:49 permissions. Then, using Europe's GDPR privacy  law, which gives citizens the right to know who

10:54 holds their data, filed access requests with  every company he could find in the chain.

10:59 What came back was a map of a supply chain nobody  had ever fully traced before. Sygic sent his data

11:04 to a broker called Predicio. Predicio sold it  to Gravy Analytics. Gravy Analytics passed it

11:10 to its subsidiary Venntel. Venntel informed  Gundersen that his data had been shared with

11:14 their customers, who use it for purposes including  "federal law enforcement and national security."

11:20 They declined to say which agencies specifically.

11:23 Gundersen did a simple Google search of his own  name and address. He found himself immediately.

11:28 The data Venntel held on him was just a device  ID and just over 75,400 location records.

11:35 Anyone with access to that data  and a search engine could have

11:39 identified him in about 30 seconds.

11:41 The developer of Funny Weather, when contacted  by NRK, said they weren’t familiar with Venntel

11:46 and wouldn’t comment on their practices.  Sygic said they couldn't confirm their

11:50 data had been involved. None of the apps had  mentioned Venntel anywhere in their privacy

11:54 policies. The people who built the apps had  no idea where their users' data ended up.

11:59 That’s the smartphone trap.

12:01 A single app doesn’t tend to be malicious  in isolation. The developers are still

12:05 trying to build something useful  and make money while they do it.

12:08 So they drop in an SDK, agree to some  terms they don't fully read either,

12:12 and move on. The data leaves their  hands and enters a supply chain so

12:16 long and so opaque that nobody in  the middle knows where it ends up.

12:20 The person at the fishing website at  least understood they were looking

12:23 at a fishing ad. You have no idea that  the navigation app you used to find a

12:28 parking spot 3 months ago helped a government  contractor build a file on your movements.

12:33 When ads stopped selling products,  they started selling lives.

12:36 Today, your life is worth  just a fraction of a cent.

12:39 Every time an ad loads on your phone, something  happens. Something that takes about as long as

12:44 a camera flash to finish. Your device sends out a  packet of data, something known as a bid request,

12:49 to an advertising exchange. That packet contains  information about you. It knows what app you’re

12:54 using, what you were looking at on that app,  and where you were when you were looking at it.

12:58 The exchange broadcasts that packet simultaneously  to hundreds, sometimes thousands, of companies.

13:04 Each of those companies decides in a fraction  of a second whether to bid to show you an ad.

13:09 One of them wins, so their ad loads, and  usually you scroll past it without looking.

13:15 Every company that received that packet,  including all the ones who lost the bid,

13:19 already had your data. They received  it the moment the broadcast went out.

13:23 There are, according to the advertising  industry’s own documentation, “no technical

13:28 measures” to control what happens to  that data once it’s been broadcast.

13:31 The losing bidders are not required  to delete it, and most of them don’t.

13:36 This system is called Real-Time Bidding, and  it runs behind every ad on every app and every

13:41 website you visit. The Irish Council for Civil  Liberties, or ICCL, spent 30 days analyzing it

13:46 and published their findings in 2022. The  headline number claimed that the average

13:51 American has their online activity and location  exposed 747 times per day by the RTB industry.

13:58 That’s once every 2 minutes  during your waking hours.

14:02 If every bid request were a text message, your  phone would be physically unusable. And that

14:07 figure, the ICCL notes, is a conservative  estimate. It excludes Facebook and Amazon,

14:12 whose RTB operations they couldn't fully measure.

14:15 To understand the scale of who receives that data,

14:18 consider that Google alone allows almost 4,700  companies to receive RTB data about people in

14:25 the United States. Microsoft’s ad platform  sends data to over 1,600 companies. It’s a

14:31 $117 billion industry. Those numbers are  just the ones those 2 companies admit to,

14:37 not the total count of companies in the  RTB system as a whole. The ICCL estimates

14:43 that across the U.S., location and behavioral  data is broadcast 107 trillion times per year.

14:49 Consider who is on the receiving end of all  of that, since it’s not only advertisers.

14:54 In January 2025, a hacker  breached Gravy Analytics,

14:58 the government contractor selling location  data to ICE, the DEA, and the FBI.

15:02 The hacker claimed to have stolen 17  terabytes of data and posted samples on

15:06 a Russian cybercrime forum to prove it.  Researchers who analyzed those samples

15:10 found precise location records for devices  that had been inside military installations

15:16 including Fort Bragg. Devices near the  White House, the Kremlin, the Vatican.

15:20 The same surveillance infrastructure that  a data broker built to sell shoe ads had

15:25 assembled one of the most comprehensive  maps of human movement on earth,

15:29 including the movements of American  military personnel and government

15:32 officials. They stored it on servers  that a single stolen key could unlock.

15:37 A former employee at a location data firm  that sells to U.S. law enforcement said,

15:41 "I don't think people understand  just to what degree your location

15:45 tells you everything you need to know about  someone's life; just how invasive that is."

15:50 The people running these  companies understood it just fine.

15:54 That was the whole point.

15:55 The free apps populating your phone are data  collection terminals that also happen to show

16:00 you a rain forecast or see what live events  are occurring in your city that weekend.

16:04 The brokers who buy the end product  - your data - tell you not to worry,

16:08 because none of it has your name on it. It’s  all anonymous, they claim. It’s completely safe.

16:13 That is technically true and functionally  meaningless. We’ve known that since 2013.

16:19 That year, MIT researchers published  a study in Nature Scientific Reports

16:23 analyzing 15 months of mobility data from 1.5  million people. The names were all stripped;

16:28 the date contained only device IDs and locations.

16:31 They wanted to know how much information  you'd actually need to identify someone

16:35 from a supposedly anonymous dataset. With 4 data  points - 4 approximate locations at 4 approximate

16:42 times - it was generally enough to identify  95% of the 1.5 million people in the dataset.

16:49 The researchers concluded bluntly  that “even coarse datasets provide

16:52 little anonymity,” which was at  the time only slightly alarming.

16:56 Law enforcement knew that.

16:58 A St. Louis County officer, after a Fog  Reveal briefing, wrote in an internal email:

17:02 "There is no (personal information) linked to  the (ad ID). But if we are good at what we do,

17:08 we should be able to figure out the owner."  One EFF attorney called it child's play.

17:12 The method they use is called dwell time  analysis. If a device consistently appears

17:17 at the same address between 10pm and 7am,  it sleeps there. That's the home address.

17:22 If you cross-reference a public  property record or voter roll,

17:25 you have a name. Suddenly that "anonymous"  device just became an all-seeing eye

17:30 providing a known address and 90 days of  movement history for any given person.

17:35 Fog's own marketing materials  describe the service's ability to

17:38 identify "where the device owner sleeps,  works, studies, worships, and associates.”

17:44 It’s basically a company casually dismantling  its own anonymity claim in a sales brochure.

17:49 The most striking demonstration of how  powerful this technology is didn't come

17:53 from law enforcement. It came from a small  Catholic media outlet called The Pillar.

17:58 In 2021, it bought commercially available location  data from a broker and hired an independent

18:03 analytics firm. The dataset contained no names.  Yet investigators were still able to identify

18:08 Monsignor Jeffrey Burrill, the general secretary  of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops,

18:14 essentially the top administrator  of the American Catholic Church.

18:18 The data showed his device emitting signals  from Grindr on a near-daily basis over 2 years,

18:24 at his office, his residence, and  during official church events in

18:27 other cities. Burrill resigned the  day before the story was published.

18:32 All it took was a media outlet with a data  broker subscription to out the highest-ranking

18:36 administrator in American Catholicism using  the same ecosystem that sells him ads.

18:41 At this point, nobody could blame you for  reaching for your phone and turning something off.

18:46 You probably remember all  those little prompts that said,

18:48 “Ask App Not to track” you mindlessly  accepted, feeling vaguely righteous inside.

18:53 In April 2021, Apple launched App Tracking  Transparency, or ATT, an initiative that

18:59 required every App to ask your permission before  tracking you across other apps and websites. Most

19:04 people said no when the prompt came up, and  for a while that looked like a genuine win.

19:09 For 6 weeks.

19:10 Fingerprinting was the first workaround. Instead  of using the advertising ID Apple was blocking,

19:16 trackers began assembling device profiles of  dozens of data points that ATT didn’t cover.

19:21 This included screen dimensions, GPU specs,  CPU core count, installed fonts, battery level.

19:27 Combine enough of them and you've built a unique

19:29 identifier that works just about as well  as the one Apple blocked. One vendor was

19:34 caught telling clients in writing that  it could still reach more than 95% of

19:37 iOS users this way. Apple's own policy banned  fingerprinting, but Apple didn't enforce it.

19:43 Oxford researchers studying ATT’s real-world  impact found apps computing fingerprint-derived

19:49 identifiers through server-side code specifically  to evade Apple’s on-device enforcement.

19:54 App Tracking Transparency targets cross-app  tracking via the advertising identifier,

19:59 so it has no effect on the bid request broadcast  that fires every time an ad loads. You know,

20:05 the one sending your location  data to thousands of companies.

20:08 That system operates at the network  level. Apple's prompt never came near it.

20:13 The underlying villain in all this  is the smartphone app business model

20:16 itself. Free apps need revenue. Revenue  means behavioral data. Behavioral data

20:21 is worth more with location. The entire  economic logic of the free internet is

20:25 built on harvesting human movement. No single  opt-out prompt, no corporate privacy gesture,

20:30 changes that logic. The machine is too big, too  distributed, and too profitable to stop itself.

20:36 You can’t turn it off, because the  system was never designed to let you.

20:40 Right now, you’re generating roughly 747  location data broadcasts per day. Over a year,

20:45 that’s more than 272,000 data  points mapping your movements.

20:50 Every one of those data points  exists in a database somewhere,

20:53 attached to a device ID that any competent  investigator can trace back to you in minutes.

20:58 Now imagine one of those points  places your phone near a crime scene.

21:02 You could have been innocently driving past. You  could have been stopping for gas. The geofence

21:07 warrant, a court order compelling tech companies  to hand over every device that appeared in a

21:11 defined area at a defined time. It has become  a standard investigative tool these days.

21:16 A Florida man was swept into a 2019 burglary  investigation because he regularly cycled

21:21 past the scene for exercise. A Virginia federal  judge found that police had violated the rights

21:26 of innocent people by collecting their data  in a robbery investigation dragnet. In 2024,

21:32 the Fifth Circuit ruled geofence  warrants unconstitutional. The

21:35 Fourth Circuit ruled they're fine.  However, in June 2026, the Supreme

21:39 Court decided that law enforcement’s  use of ‘geofence warrant’ was a search.

21:43 But it's a system working exactly as the  business model intended. The consumers are

21:48 generating a permanent, detailed, commercially  available record of where every person with a

21:53 smartphone has been. And it’s for sale  to anyone with a budget and a use case.

21:57 Your iPhone costs around $1,000. Your data  plan runs $50 to $80 a month. Over 2 years,

22:03 you've spent roughly $2,200 to carry,

22:06 power, and maintain the surveillance  infrastructure being used to track you.

22:10 That $7,500 Fog Reveal subscription  that law enforcement uses means you

22:15 are subsidizing your own surveillance at a loss.

22:18 Two things can fix this. A federal law requiring a

22:21 warrant before any government agency  purchases commercial location data,

22:25 and a comprehensive data privacy framework  that treats meaningful consent as something

22:29 more than a push notification you tapped at  7am before heading out on your morning jog.

22:34 Neither exists yet. Congress has been  introduced to versions of both for years,

22:39 but neither has passed. Until one does,  the deal is simple. You bought the phone.

22:44 You pay the bill. And 747 times a day,  it tells someone exactly where you are.

22:49 And if you think that's bad, you probably  don’t need us to tell you that your phone

22:53 was deliberately engineered to  make sure you never put it down.

22:56 If your smartphone is constantly tracking  you, it's tempting to want something a

23:00 little... dumber. No phone does that better  than the Nokia 3310. Watch The Indestructible

23:06 Phone That Destroyed Its Own Company to  discover its story. Or click on this video.

01:23 basic logic gates are the fundamental

01:25 building blocks of digital circuits

01:27 there are electronic circuits that

01:28 perform a logical operation on one or

01:31 more binary inputs to produce a single

01:33 binary output which can be either one or

01:35 zero

01:36 there are several types of basic logic

01:37 gates each with its own specific logic

01:39 function let's take a look at them the

01:42 or gate imagine you have two smoke

01:46 when either one is tripped and they

01:48 should keep alarming if both are tripped

01:50 of course in that case you'd want an or

01:52 gate an or gate takes two or more signal

01:55 inputs and produces an output signal if

01:56 either of the input signals is high or

01:58 both if all the inputs are low then the

02:01 output is also low

02:03 and gate an and gate takes two or more

02:06 signals and produces an output signal

02:08 only if all the input signals are high

02:10 otherwise the output is low

02:12 not gate a not gate also known commonly

02:16 as an inverter has a single input and

02:18 produces the opposite value at its

02:20 output that is if the input is high the

02:22 output is low and if the input is low

02:23 the output is high just the opposite

02:25 nand gate a nand gate is a combination

02:28 of an and gate and a not gate it

02:31 produces the opposite output of an and

02:33 gate meaning that the output is low only

02:35 when the input signals are high and it's

02:37 high for any other input combination nor

02:39 gate a nor gate is a combination of an

02:51 now in addition to the basic logic gates

02:56 that can perform more complex logical

02:58 operations here's just a few quick

03:00 examples the xor gate an xor gate also

03:04 known as an exclusive or gate takes two

03:06 input signals and produces a high output

03:08 if the two input signals are different

03:10 if the two inputs are the same then the

03:12 output is low you can think of it as any

03:17 xnor gate an ex nor gate also known as

03:25 the two input signals are the same and a

03:27 low output if the inputs are different

03:28 so if the two inputs match the result is

03:31 true

03:32 buffer a buffer is a logic gate that has

03:35 a single input and a single output the

03:37 output of the buffer is the same as its

03:39 input with no logical operation

03:40 performed buffers are often used to

03:42 amplify or transmit signals without

03:44 changing their logical State

03:46 multiplexer a multiplexer or mux for

03:49 short is a logic gate that has multiple

03:51 inputs but just a single output it

03:53 selects one of the inputs to pass

03:55 through to the output based on a set of

03:56 control signals d multiplexer a d

03:59 multiplexer or demux for short is the

04:02 opposite of a multiplexer it has a

04:04 single input but multiple outputs and it

04:06 selects one of the outputs to receive

04:07 the input signal based on the set of

04:09 control signals the gates can have more

04:11 than just two inputs and they do still

04:13 roughly what you'd expect so a four

04:15 input or gauge turns on when any

04:17 combination of its inputs is turned on

04:18 except for all off in an and gate with

04:38 by combining these basic logic gates in

04:40 various ways you can create digital

04:42 circuits that Implement a wide range of

04:44 complex functions such as arithmetic

04:45 operations memory storage and decision

04:47 making fpga is also typically include a

04:50 number of input output i o blocks that

04:52 allow you to connect the fpga to

04:54 external devices such as sensors

04:55 displays and other digital circuits the

04:58 i o blocks can be configured to support

05:00 a variety of different interfaces such

05:04 of the main benefits of using an fpga is

05:07 that it allows you to implement custom

05:08 digital circuits that are tailored to

05:10 your specific needs without the need to

05:12 design and actually fabricate a custom

05:13 chip this can be useful in a variety of

05:18 Hardware Designs implementing custom

05:21 building high performance Computing

05:23 systems

05:26 entire chip in Silicon known as an Asic

05:28 for application specific integrated

05:30 circuit as an example think of a chip

05:32 like the video chip in a Commodore 64.

05:34 you're going to produce millions of them

05:36 so in the long run it's cheaper to

05:38 produce an Asic because while an fpga

05:39 could be programmed to do the job at

05:48 comparative handful of MRI machines for

05:54 fpga likely makes more sense

05:56 it's the same deal with the space and

05:58 defense Industries wherever money meets

06:00 the need for a quick iteration or

06:01 turnaround you're likely to find fpgas

06:04 in use

06:05 however fpgas can be more complex to

06:07 work with than other types of

06:08 programmable logic devices such as

06:10 microcontrollers or Digital Signal

06:12 processors

06:13 it's because they require specialized

06:14 tools and knowledge of digital logic

06:16 design to use effectively

06:18 additionally fpgas are typically more

06:21 expensive than other types of

06:22 programmable logic devices which makes

06:23 them less accessible for hobbyists or

06:25 DIY projects

06:27 so what about microcontrollers why would

06:30 you choose an fpga instead of a

06:32 microcontroller well fpga's and

06:34 microcontrollers are both types of

06:35 programmable devices but they have

06:37 different strengths and weaknesses and

06:38 are suited for different types of

06:40 applications

06:41 microcontrollers are typically optimized

06:43 for executing a set of predefined

06:45 instructions or firmware that controls

06:47 the behavior of the device they

06:49 typically have a small amount of on-chip

06:50 memory and peripherals such as perhaps

06:52 timers interrupts and communication

06:54 interfaces which makes them well suited

06:56 for a wide range of embedded systems

06:58 applications such as controlling Motors

07:00 collecting sensor data or interfacing

07:02 with external devices

07:04 fpgas on the other hand are designed to

07:07 be highly configurable and customizable

07:08 allowing you to create custom digital

07:10 circuits that are tailored to your

07:12 specific needs they're typically used in

07:15 applications that require high

07:16 performance Computing or Digital Signal

07:18 processing such as image or audio

07:19 processing cryptography or network

07:21 processing fpgas can also be used to

07:24 implement custom Hardware accelerators

07:26 for specific tasks such as crypto

07:28 machine learning or artificial

07:29 intelligence algorithms

07:31 one of the key advantages of fpga's over

07:34 microcontrollers is their flexibility

07:36 fpgas can be reprogrammed or

07:38 reconfigured multiple times allowing you

07:40 to quickly iterate and modify your

07:42 digital circuit designs without having

07:43 to create new physical circuits or

07:45 boards so if your satellite isn't doing

07:47 what you want you can reprogram it in

07:49 place both on the bench before and on

07:52 the Fly after launch this can be a major

07:54 advantage in applications where rapid

07:56 prototyping or development is important

07:58 another advantage of fpgas is their high

08:01 performance because fpgas can be

08:03 customized to implement specific digital

08:05 circuit functionality they can often

08:07 outperform general purpose

08:08 microcontrollers or dsps for certain

08:10 tasks they are also highly parallel

08:13 which means they can perform multiple

08:14 operations simultaneously making them

08:17 well suited for applications require

08:18 high-speed processing of large amounts

08:21 of data consider the case where the CPU

08:23 wants to check if any of eight gpio

08:25 lines are triggered it might have to

08:27 issue a separate interrupt and I O

08:29 instruction plus a comparison eight

08:31 times to get the answer whereas an fpga

08:33 can do it in a single clock cycle with a

08:35 large or gate it seems that for most any

08:38 task that you can express in an fpga it

08:40 will likely be the faster solution

08:43 overall the choice between an fpga and a

08:45 microcontroller depends on the specific

08:47 requirements of your application if you

08:49 need a general purpose device that can

08:50 execute predefined instructions a

08:52 microcontroller will be the best choice

08:54 but if you need a highly configurable

08:56 device that can be customized to

08:57 implement specific digital circuit

08:59 functionality the fpga is likely the

09:01 better option

09:05 it with a configuration file that

09:06 specifies the desired circuit design

09:08 functionality this configuration file is

09:11 typically loaded onto the fpega each

09:13 time the device is powered on or reset

09:15 they start up blank

09:17 fpgas have what is called a

09:19 configuration memory that stores the

09:21 configuration file this memory is

09:23 typically implemented using a type of

09:25 non-volatile memory called flash memory

09:27 now in volatile memory retains its

09:29 contents even when powered off making it

09:31 the ideal choice for storing the fpga

09:33 configuration file

09:34 it can be self-contained within the fpga

09:36 or more commonly live as an external

09:38 chip on the board when the fpga is

09:41 powered on or reset it reads the

09:43 configuration file from the flash memory

09:44 and uses the configure the digital

09:46 circuit functionality and then once the

09:48 fpga is configured it behaves as if it

09:50 were just a physical digital circuit

09:52 implementing the desired functionality

09:54 the role of a flash memory is critical

09:56 in the fpga configuration process

09:58 without a valid configuration file in

10:01 flash memory the fpga will not be able

10:02 to operate correctly because it would

10:04 remain effectively blank Additionally

10:07 the flash memory must be fast enough to

10:09 enable the fpga to read the

10:10 configuration file quickly and

10:11 efficiently so it boots promptly

10:14 because the fpga configuration file is

10:16 stored in non-volatile memory it can be

10:18 programmed or reprogrammed multiple

10:20 times without the need for a physical

10:21 circuit board or chip in fact in most

10:25 designs the fpga is programmed from

10:27 scratch using the configuration file

10:28 stored in the flash memory every time

10:30 the chip boots so to completely modify

10:32 the fpga you're really just rewriting

10:34 the configuration in the flash storage

10:36 and then rebooting this allows you to

10:38 quickly iterate and modify your digital

10:39 circuit designs without having to create

10:41 new physical circuits or boards

10:44 to program an fpga you typically use a

10:46 hardware description language such as

10:51 logic functionality your Hardware

45:29 With a Cessna 172, for example, it's around 55 knots.

45:35 And you want to look at your airspeed indicator. Because if you just feel yourself, you might notice that much lower, like 40 knots,

45:44 that the plane has already taken off. You're already floating. You're flying. And you might be very excited about that.

45:50 And you might want to just pull back on your yoke to take off. Well, you won't be able to sustain flight.

45:59 And so this is what why ground effect is really important is that you can kind of float over the ground

46:05 because you're so close to the ground that the ground is blocking some of the effects of the air.

46:10 And so what you want to do is really make sure that you continue your ground roll, continue.

46:15 Even if you're a little bit airborne, stay close to the ground until your airspeed comes up to that rotate speed, so in this case, 55 knots,

46:23 and then you pull back on your yoke to take off.

46:29 So again, so when does ground effect happen? When you're close to the ground-- when you're within one wing span of the ground

46:37 So let's talk a little bit about stability. And we'll start by just talking about the three axes of flight.

46:44 So there is a longitudinal axis, which

46:49 is basically from the nose to the tail of your airplane. And there's a lateral axis, which

46:56 is from wingtip to wingtip and then vertical going straight through the plane.

47:01 So you have the ability to control all three of those axes. So the elevator, which I keep talking about is like your yoke

47:10 where you push it forward or you pull it back, that allows you to pitch the airplane. So pitch nose up, pitch nose down--

47:17 that's you controlling the back part of this tail, the elevator, which allows you to have

47:25 motion in this direction, so pitch nose down. So you might hear that a lot. In case you're getting close to stalling

47:32 because your angle of attack is getting too high, they might say, nose down or pitch nose down.

47:39 You also have ailerons, which are out on the side of your wings.

47:44 And those ailerons control the roll. So that's rolling along the longitudinal axis.

47:50 And then your rudder, which is at the back of the tail,

47:57 the vertical part of the tail-- that controls yaw. So this is called yaw, this type of motion.

48:03 So when you're turning, you actually kind of do a roll and yaw usually to enact a turn.

48:10 There are some cases where you actually

48:16 want to have adverse yaw or you actually--

48:21 adverse yaw means basically you're using the yaw direction in maybe the opposite direction at which

48:27 you're trying to turn with the roll or other angles of your plane. And so this just talks about an adverse yaw

48:37 is when you're not turning the rudder in the same direction that you're using your aileron.

48:44 And so this is where you talk about coordinated flight or uncoordinated flight. When you're actually in an airplane, the rudder or the yaw

48:53 is controlled by your feet. So you have feet pedals that control the rudder.

48:58 And the yoke that you're holding onto or a joystick that you're holding onto front and back

49:04 controls the pitch. And then turning it like in the steering wheel of a car

49:10 is only controlling the roll. So you actually also use your feet for that third direction of the yaw.

49:17 So just talking about stability in general,

49:24 this isn't going to dive into a whole diffy q discussion or anything. But just in general, something that's stable--

49:31 so it's just talking about like a little bowl if you have a ball in a bowl, even if the ball gets jostled

49:36 around, it'll return to the center point. Unstable would be the opposite. So if you have a convex surface, then if the ball moves

49:44 even just a little bit, it'll really get moved out of control. So the reason that we talk about this

49:51 is basically when you're flying in an airplane, and you're talking about stable aircraft,

49:56 for example, the reason I really love flying a Cessna 172, even

50:02 though it's kind of the training airplane, is that the-- as people call it, it flies itself.

50:07 So if you notice the plane's doing something weird and turning, almost the best thing you can do is just let go.

50:13 And the controls will normalize, and then the plane will fly straight and level, which is really great.

50:19 There are other types of aircraft that are inherently unstable. So we have Minachi and Oxsana over here

50:26 who do aerobatic flights. And Mark will be talking about that tomorrow.

50:31 So that's where you actually want an airplane that's not so stable so that you can cause it to do all kinds of crazy maneuvers and turns

50:39 and twists very easily. You pretty much can't get a Cessna to do that. It really wants to fly straight and level.

50:51 So then there are also other aspects that can affect stability, such as your center of gravity,

50:56 so how you load the airplane. We'll have a specific lecture that just talks about weight and balance.

51:03 But one thing to keep in mind is that as people sit in your airplane or as you put bags

51:08 in the baggage compartment, you're loading the airplane. And so if you have too much weight aft of the CG

51:15 or behind the center of gravity, you can cause the plane to basically go like this, which isn't very helpful when you're flying.

51:22 If you have things a little too forward, it actually pushes the nose down. In general, the nose down is a little bit

51:29 more stable from the perspective of lift and getting air to fly over.

51:34 You don't want something that keeps trying to stall whenever you let go of it.

51:39 And then similarly, you can talk about the stability in the lateral direction in the roll direction.

51:47 And some of these things like swept-back wings like you see on a jet can affect that type of stability.

51:54 And then finally, there's stability

51:59 about the vertical axes. Generally, this is going to be kind of fixed for the given

52:05 aircraft that you're in. But you can affect it as you design an aircraft. So we started talking about stall already.

52:13 So when you have your angle of attack past its so-called critical angle of attack,

52:21 it can cause the air to basically no longer be able to flow over the top and no longer be able to effectively

52:28 deflect air down. And so the air kind of separates. And you can stall.

52:34 So it's really important to know that you can actually stall at any airspeed.

52:40 Even with full power, you can stall. In fact, one of the maneuvers you'll have to do in order to get your pilot's license

52:46 is a power on stall. So you can stall both where your engine is idle,

52:52 like you're coming in for a landing, and you get too steep, but you can also stall with full power.

52:58 And you just made your angle go too steep. So it's really affecting that critical angle of attack.

53:06 And again, once you have that angle of attack too steep, then there's a very significant loss of lift, which is not good

53:12 when you're flying an airplane. So when can you stall?

53:20 At any airspeed and any power setting, and it's really based on the angle of attack.

53:29 So if you-- yes, go ahead. AUDIENCE: So what happens after the end of the graph? Does it just plunge zero?

53:35 Is it not like any solution? Like why does it stall? TINA SRIVASTAVA: Yeah, basically, it's

53:40 not generating any lift. Right. You can see this like with a paper airplane.

53:46 Sometimes, if you-- it kind of stops and kind of crashes. We'll see how Minachi's paper airplane does here.

53:52 Well, that one-- I definitely had a low angle of attack, so it flew very well.

54:00 Let's see if I can get it to stall or if it's too stable of an airplane.

54:07 That one-- basically, after it stalled, it basically went nose down, which is good. It has a little extra paper folding at the front

54:14 so that the nose will go down. But it's really bad basically. If you stall, it can go that way.

54:22 The other thing that can happen after you stall a lot usually is you can enter a spin, which

54:28 is actually the next case. So this is when you're uncoordinated in your stall.

54:35 So what I mean by uncoordinated? So that's what I was just talking about before, where your roll and your yaw are not

54:42 going in the same direction. And here you can have a situation where both of the wings have stalled.

54:48 So the airflow has separated over both of the wings. But one may be more stalled than the other.

54:54 And it causes the airplane to have a very, very hazardous condition or an intentional condition

55:02 if you're Oxsana over there, and you're trying to spin your airplane to do a fancy trick.

55:08 This is very dangerous close to the ground. As you'll hear, you only intentionally

55:13 do this in certain types of aircraft when you're wearing parachutes in certain airspace when you're very high above the ground.

55:19 You don't want to do this. And in fact, if you're just getting your private pilot's license or your PPL, you're not going

55:27 to practice a spin because it's pretty dangerous thing to do in many aircraft. But you do have to learn about it

55:34 and make sure you don't get into a spin.

55:39 So let's talk a little bit about maneuvering flight. So basically, that means when you

55:44 were flying straight and level, that's kind of when you're at an equilibrium where your lift and your weight kind of cancel out.

55:50 And the plane's just going straight and level at the same altitude. But climbing is when your lift temporarily exceeds the weight

55:58 so you can actually climb. So once you are in a steady climb, then you can actually still have your forces be in equilibrium.

56:06 So remember f equals ma. So a is acceleration, which is a change in velocity.

56:12 So if you're not changing your velocity, and you're just in a steady climb, then you're also not accelerating.

56:18 Now, this is a little bit complicated,

56:24 so I will say this is a little bit tricky. There is a tendency for these airplanes to turn left.

56:33 And there are actually multiple things that contribute to this left-turning tendency.

56:39 And when you're in an airplane flying, you might hear your instructor say right rudder.

56:45 And it is really to counteract some of these left-turning tendencies. So we're going to break them down and talk about them.

56:53 But this can be a very in-depth subject, so I will definitely refer to the PHAK, which

56:58 is the Pilot Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge. Chapter 5 goes into all of these.

57:04 So the first one is torque. So basically, the thing is when you're-- if you're sitting

57:10 in the airplane, and you're looking forward at your propeller, most US engines actually have

57:17 the propeller rotating clockwise. So and you can see that arrow that says action.

57:22 That's the propeller rotating clockwise. And so because of Newton, we know for every action,

57:30 there's an equal and opposite reaction. So because the propeller is turning to the right, the whole airplane is trying to roll to the left.

57:37 So that is the first left-turning tendency. Before we move to the next one, are there any questions

57:43 on this left-turning tendency?

57:50 Great. So the next one is p-factor, which is an asymmetrical thrust.

57:57 This happens when the airplane has a high angle of attack, so either when it's climbing or in this condition called

58:04 slow flight, which is where it's kind of an uncomfortable thing. You have to do this in your flight training.

58:10 So basically, you have your power setting pretty high, but you've kind of pitched the airplane up.

58:16 And so you're not getting as much airflow over your control surfaces like your ailerons and your elevator.

58:23 So they call your controls mushy. So it's hard to kind of coordinate your airplane. But you kind of sit in that environment

58:30 to basically understand how it's difficult to control the airplane in that environment. So if you're pitched up, and you have a-- so you have a high

58:36 angle of attack, and you're either climbing or in slow flight, you have this tendency where the--

58:43 because you're angled to the wind, the right propeller blade, which is descending,

58:49 is kind of cutting into the air as it's coming in. So it's actually generating more thrust,

58:54 whereas the ascending left propeller blade, so the propeller blade that's going up on the left side

59:01 is kind of coming away from the wind that's coming at it. And so it's not generating as much thrust

59:07 as the right propeller blade. So that causes the center of thrust to move towards the right.

59:13 And that creates a little bit of a yaw tendency of the airplane.

59:19 Does that make sense? Great.

59:24 Lot of head nods. P-factor was one that both Phillip and I spent quite a bit of time getting our heads around.

59:30 And Professor Hansman helped us out there. So another one is called the corkscrew effect.

59:38 Sometimes, it's called slipstream or spiraling slipstream. It basically has to do with the fact

59:45 that that propeller remember is just kind of like a wing that's spinning around.

59:51 And so it's basically pushing the air back.

59:57 And since the propeller is spinning around, that air that's coming back from the propeller

60:02 is spinning around the airplane. And as it spins around, when it comes up to the back,

60:09 it pushes on the vertical stabilizer, that tail piece, and causes the plane also to do a left yaw.

60:18 Does that make sense? Some good head nods.

60:24 Yes. AUDIENCE: Why doesn't it also cause it to roll? TINA SRIVASTAVA: Why doesn't it also cause it to roll

60:30 was the question. And it could, especially if it's hitting the wing.

60:36 But in general, what we've seen is that it can depend on whether you're in a high wing or low wing. But the biggest thing that it sort of hits is here.

60:44 Now, in general, when you get to a left yaw, you sort of kind of roll. These are connected angles.

60:52 But I think just what we've observed is primarily that the air, when it hits the vertical stabilizer, is the biggest surface that's

61:00 kind of pushing it and the angle that it's at. So if you sum it all together, yes. I'm actually quite confident you'll get some roll,

61:06 but the biggest thing that you notice is the yaw.

61:13 So let's see if we understood p-factor as well as we think we did.

61:36 A, B, or C? AUDIENCE: A. TINA SRIVASTAVA: A. Good job. I actually have my little hint there that the B is actually

61:43 talking about torque, which is a different left-turning tendency. And then finally, we're going to talk a little bit

61:50 about gyroscopic precession. It's a little bit complicated if you're not

61:56 familiar with the gyroscope. But when Phillip talks to you about all the different controls in your airplane,

62:01 you'll have to learn about gyroscopes all over again in a little bit. But in general, what do you need to know about a gyroscope?

62:08 What is a gyroscope? A gyroscope is something you can hold. It's spinning. You can play with them.

62:14 What they allow you to do is have rigidity in space. And they also have this concept of precession.

62:20 And precession is basically that the resultant action of a spinning rotor when a deflecting force is applied

62:28 happens 90 degrees ahead of that rotation. And so because of that, you can consider that the--

62:38 you have the propeller spinning, and that causes this gyroscopic precession.

62:43 And that basically causes 90 degrees out of that sink is this force which causes

62:49 a yawing movement, a pitching and a yawing in this case.

62:58 Once we talk more about gyroscopes and how they work, you'll also learn different flight controls

63:05 that you look at in the plane, leverage these gyroscopes. And we'll come back and circle back

63:10 to making sure we understand the key fundamentals of gyroscopes. Yes. AUDIENCE: So why is p-factor a left-turning tendency

63:17 and not a pitch up tendency? TINA SRIVASTAVA: Sure. So let's go back to p-factor.

63:27 So what we're talking about is the difference in the center of thrust. So the thrust, when you're straight and level,

63:35 the thrust is just forward. But what we're seeing is that when the right blade,

63:41 because when you're in a high angle of attack, the right blade is generating more thrust than the left blade.

63:47 So the center of thrust is slightly to the right. So that is why because it's to the right and not up or down.

63:54 Up or down would cause a pitch up or down. But since it's to the right, that's why it's causing the yaw action.

64:01 AUDIENCE: So it is not 90 degrees ahead because of precession. TINA SRIVASTAVA: So precession is separate.

64:07 It is generating its own factors and dynamics. So both of these things are acting at the same time.

64:14 So precession does in fact affect pitch just like you correctly recognized. But this is an additional factor that's

64:22 happening is that since the center of thrust is actually moved to the right, it's causing the yawing.

64:28 Did that answer your question? AUDIENCE: No, but that's OK. TINA SRIVASTAVA: You want to chime in, Phillip? AUDIENCE: It's an external force, as opposed to generating

64:35 by the propeller. PHILLIP GREENSPUN: It's a little bit tough. I think, yeah, we should table it and refer you

64:43 to that physics book See How It Flies, which has some of it. But the one thing I would add on p-factor

64:48 is another thing to keep in mind is whether the propeller is advancing or retreating

64:56 into the wind. So if you think about it, when the airplane is level, the propeller is not moving relative to the oncoming wind.

65:08 But if you tilt the airplane up, as the propeller goes down, it's actually advancing into the wind

65:15 and getting a little bit of an efficiency boost that way. Whereas when it's coming up, it's going from the front of the airplane towards the back

65:21 of the airplane. So it's retreating TINA SRIVASTAVA: Yeah, so what Phillip's describing is why the right propeller blade is generating more thrust

65:29 than the left propeller blade, which is what's moving the center of thrust. So I think the real thing to answer your question

65:36 is that there's more than one effect happening simultaneously. Yeah, so the-- PHILLIP GREENSPUN: I'm not sure that you

65:42 get gyroscopic precession from that action here because it's generating lift by pushing air.

65:50 I'm not sure that all the thrust really has to go through, for p-factor at least,

65:57 through the center of the spinning propeller. Also, I know in helicopters, the physics 101 answer

66:06 is 90 degrees. But the real answer for engineering it is 72 degrees.

66:11 So it does get complicated. Fortunately, it's beyond the scope of what the FAA tests you on because they themselves, I'm sure,

66:19 don't understand it fully. TINA SRIVASTAVA: Yeah. How about we come back after we've talked about gyroscopes in excruciating detail and then we have a set of terminology

66:27 to talk about, let's come back to discussing that more. Thanks. AUDIENCE: I have a simple question for you maybe.

66:34 TINA SRIVASTAVA: Yes. AUDIENCE: Just to help me remember, why is it called p-factor? What is the p for? TINA SRIVASTAVA: Power or propeller.

66:40 So the p is referring to that propeller,

66:46 right propeller more than the left. It also usually happens when you're at a higher power.

66:52 So some flight instructors like you to think about when you have higher power in the airplane,

66:58 you need to put on more right rudder to counteract that left-turning tendency. PHILLIP GREENSPUN: We're a little bit behind.

67:04 Should we take our bathroom break now and then-- TINA SRIVASTAVA: I'm actually almost done, so I think we can finish there.

67:11 So one thing is to talk-- so we talked about with climbing flight, f equals ma.

67:17 So once you're done changing the velocity, and you don't have a change in velocity, your forces are in equilibrium.

67:23 So the same is the case with a descending flight. When you're actually turning, your forces

67:30 are not in equilibrium because you're having this change in velocity. And so you actually have a number of changes happening.

67:40 And it's basically considered accelerated flight, which is same as when you're driving if you're turning.

67:46 So when you're flying, when you're doing a turn, you're accelerating because you're constantly changing the direction of your velocity.

67:54 You also have load factor, which we'll get into in more detail when we talk about performance

67:59 of an aircraft and how the load affects your performance. But another thing to think about back

68:05 when we were talking about that zero gravity flight and a plane flying in a parabolic trajectory or a roller

68:11 coaster when you're at the top. But when you're at the bottom of the roller coaster, you really feel like you're being pressed down

68:17 into your seat. In fact, when we run that zero gravity flight,

68:22 although at the top, we had 30 seconds of weightlessness so we could do our experiments, when you go to the bottom of the parabola,

68:29 you basically get 2G or twice what you normally feel. And so you have to kind of lay down and let that happen

68:35 before you come up again. And so when you think about load factor, just think about you being at the bottom

68:40 of your roller coaster and really feeling a kind of twice that force on you.

68:46 And then just to kind of end, we want to talk about most of the time we're talking about the planes

68:52 that you'd be flying, but another type of aircraft altogether is a blended wing body aircraft.

68:58 So just like this is one example of that. So what it means is that that fuselage

69:04 or that kind of tube in the middle that you sit in is blended into the wings so that the whole body is

69:11 generating more lift because the whole surface is kind of designed that way. It's really kind of cool.

69:17 And from an aerodynamic perspective, it's got a much better lift to drag ratio

69:22 because the whole thing is really deflecting the air molecules downward and generating

69:27 that lift. So I just asked kind of a thought question. If this is so much better, it's more efficient of an aircraft

69:35 and aerodynamically has much better properties, why do you-- it actually-- we've also found that it's

69:41 better in terms of fuel efficiency because it has less drag and more lift. Why do you think that JetBlue and American Airlines

69:49 don't fly aircraft that look like this? AUDIENCE: They don't have routes with a thousand passengers.

69:55 TINA SRIVASTAVA: They don't have routes with a thousand passengers? Well, you could make a smaller blended wing body aircraft.

70:02 Yes. AUDIENCE: Passengers like windows. TINA SRIVASTAVA: Passengers like windows. That's actually a big--

70:07 it's a big reason truthfully. Yes. AUDIENCE: It's very different from what's currently made,

70:13 so the development would be expensive and risky. TINA SRIVASTAVA: So it's very different from what's currently made. And then you said so the development

70:18 would be very risky. Actually, I think it's more than just the development. Because it's different from what's currently made,

70:24 the entire infrastructure supports the current format of an airplane with a tube and wings.

70:30 So we're talking about airports, jet bridges, the way that people load food carts onto a plane,

70:38 the way that passengers get on and off, the fact the passengers don't have as many windows on this type of aircraft.

70:43 It's unfortunately that whole infrastructure that surrounds it that is a big contributing factor to why,

70:49 even though there's a better design, why we don't move towards that. So this was a big, big thing for me

70:55 when I was an undergrad at MIT aero-astro. I'm thinking I'm going to design the next best amazing airplane.

71:02 But even if you do design the next best amazing airplane, it may not be widely deployed because

71:08 of these other infrastructure aspects, which really got me into systems engineering. But enough with that thought exercise.

71:15 For time, we'll just summarize what did we learn today. So we talked about how does an airplane generate lift?

71:21 And we talked about different factors that affect lift. We also discussed that lift is very hard to calculate.

71:26 And so we experimentally measure a lot of aspects of it. And we discussed the different forces on an airplane--

71:34 stability, and kind of this left-turning tendencies, and some of the different aircraft configurations.

71:40 So are there any questions about that? PHILLIP GREENSPUN: Yeah, Tina, what do you think about let's do questions, let's take a bathroom break, and then--

71:47 TINA SRIVASTAVA: Yeah, so you can think about it. PHILLIP GREENSPUN: People with questions talk. I'm going to call the pizza people and give them my credit card.
