00:00 Europe's economic map is being redrawn. For 70 years, the heart of

00:04 Europe’s economy beat in Berlin. Now that heart is being surgically removed

00:08 and transplanted 300 miles (483 km) to the east. In 2023, while German industrial production fell

00:14 by up to 2%, Poland absorbed a  flood of German manufacturing,

00:18 pushing its economy toward the $1 trillion mark. Defying Brussels and rejecting Western European

00:24 rules, Poland is pulling off one of the most  dramatic industrial shifts in modern history.

00:29 This isn't a catch-up story. It's a takeover.

00:32 In September 2025, Poland hit a milestone once  reserved for the world’s economic giants. Its

00:38 GDP had surpassed $1 trillion, putting it in the  same league as the United States, Germany, France,

00:43 the United Kingdom, China, and Japan. At first glance, Poland doesn’t

00:48 seem to fit in that list. It looks like an outlier.

00:51 An anomaly. This, after all, is the same nation that sat

00:54 behind the Iron Curtain just a few decades ago. A  country that certainly wasn’t known as an economic

01:00 powerhouse when it entered the European Union in  2004. It was more associated with cheap labor,

01:05 rather than any sort of domestic industrial might. Yet here it is, with a trillion dollar economy

01:11 and ever increasing influence not just  in Europe, but on the global stage.

01:15 And at the very same time Poland  is rising, its neighbor, Germany,

01:19 is suffering a dramatic decline. The contrast between the

01:22 two countries is striking. For decades, Germany was Europe’s

01:25 undisputed industrial powerhouse. It dominated  manufacturing and built a global reputation for

01:30 producing everything from luxury automobiles to  advanced industrial machinery. Germany wasn't

01:36 just Europe’s largest economy. It was the motor  that kept the entire European project running.

01:41 But in 2023, that motor started to sputter. Industrial production rates fell

01:46 by approximately 1.5 to 2%. Then came the so-called Mittelstand Exodus.

01:52 One of the reasons why Germany has been so  successful over the years is its vast network

01:56 of successful small to mid-sized businesses,  known collectively as the Mittelstand.

02:01 They may not get the attention as bigger brands  and Fortune 500 firms, but these companies are

02:06 often world leaders in their specific niche  markets. But together, they make up a massive

02:11 part of Germany’s economic strength. Between 2023 and 2024, however,

02:15 a staggering 32% of the country’s Mittelstand  manufacturers reported plans to move production

02:21 out of Germany. The Rhine-Ruhr valley - the  forge of Germany’s economic foundations - is

02:26 being hollowed out, one company at a time. And they’re not moving to China or the US.

02:31 They’re not going far, at all, in fact. Just over the eastern border, into Poland.

02:35 German appliance giant, Miele has moved its  washing machine production out of Germany

02:39 to a facility in Ksawerow, Poland. Heating company  Viessman poured €200 million into a new heat pump

02:46 production plant in Legnica, while winding down  its operations in longstanding German hubs.

02:51 These aren't one-off occurrences. They're part of a much bigger trend.

02:55 The wealth that funded the post-war  European project is drifting eastwards,

02:59 and it didn’t happen overnight; this is  the culmination of a 30-year master plan

03:03 that started from absolute zero. The dawn of the 1990s brought about the

03:07 end of one massive chapter in Polish history,  and the start of something completely new.

03:12 Back then, the country had almost nothing.  Its very survival hung in the balance.

03:16 The collapse of communism delivered  widespread chaos. Factories closed,

03:20 jobs were lost and entire industries vanished  overnight. Poland’s new leadership was left to

03:25 pick up the pieces and make sense of the mess. A lot of countries would have struggled

03:29 to get through it. But Poland had a plan.

03:32 One that had the potential to either ruin the  country completely, or put it on the path to a

03:36 far better and brighter future. The Balcerowicz Plan.

03:40 Known as Shock Therapy, it was a high-stakes  survival plan built around rapid, sweeping

03:45 economic reforms. In the span of a single day,  price controls were lifted, subsidies to state

03:50 industries were cut, the currency was devalued,  and Poland opened itself to international trade.

03:56 It was an economic shockwave that tore down  the old system and forced a new one into place.

04:01 Its impact was immediate… And severe.

04:04 Unemployment, which hadn’t really even  existed as a concept under communism,

04:08 skyrocketed. Millions of people found themselves  without jobs and living standards plummeted.

04:13 The state safety net was falling apart.  National income plunged by 22%. Industrial

04:18 production dropped by 25%. Inflation soared. But beyond the pain and the struggle,

04:24 an economic revolution was taking place.. Since the state had stopped bailing out

04:28 businesses that weren’t working, old monopolies  died out. In their place emerged a new private

04:33 sector with the potential to rival any in Europe. Lean, hungry, and with everything to prove,

04:38 new businesses rose out of the ashes. Since  they were operating in strict constraints,

04:42 Polish entrepreneurs designed their companies  to be resilient, cost-effective, and flexible.

04:47 It set them up for success not just in the  short-term, but for generations to come.

04:51 Once the dust had started to settle, Poland  had laid the foundations for decades of

04:55 economic expansion. And time would prove that the  Balcerowicz Plan was the right one, after all.

05:01 In 1990, Poland’s nominal GDP stood at  $65 billion. Now, it’s over $1 trillion.

05:08 It has grown more than 15 times  larger in under 4 decades.

05:11 Most other European nations can’t match that.

05:14 And Shock Therapy didn’t just stabilize  the currency and revive the economy.

05:17 It created a new generation of workers and  entrepreneurs with a desire to succeed.

05:22 For the first time in decades, hard work,  innovation, and risk-taking were rewarded.

05:27 All they needed was the infrastructure…  and they found someone else to pay for it.

05:32 Poland had put the pieces in place for  long-term success, but it still needed

05:36 to link them together. It needed roads, rail,  logistics networks, and other infrastructure.

05:41 All of that costs money. Poland didn’t want to foot

05:44 the bill by itself. So, it got more than a  little help from its wealthy Western neighbors.

05:48 In 2004, it entered the EU. At the time, this was widely

05:52 seen as a generous gesture from the West.  Wealthier nations like France, Germany, and

05:56 the United Kingdom were extending a helping hand  to the struggling countries of Eastern Europe.

06:01 Warsaw, however, saw the situation  through a different lens.

06:04 It was a momentous occasion. A sign of Europe  growing stronger and neighboring nations

06:09 wanting to help and support one another. But it was also a golden opportunity.

06:13 An opportunity to execute the biggest wealth  transfer in the history of the European

06:17 continent. Over two decades, Poland absorbed an  astonishing €161.6 billion from the EU budget.

06:25 That's enough to build more than 100 copies of  the world's tallest building, the Burj Khalifa.

06:30 The scale was staggering. Tens of billions of  dollars were flooding into Poland every year. But

06:35 getting the money was just part one of the plan. Poland had to spend it correctly.

06:39 Other EU member states had mismanaged their  EU funds, and continue to do so. Poland had

06:45 no intention of making the same mistakes. It  weaponised the war chest it had been given,

06:49 directing massive portions into all-important  agricultural and infrastructure developments.

06:54 In the following years, Poland  constructed a web of highways, roads,

06:57 and high-speed rail corridors that completely  rewrote the logistical maps of Central Europe.

07:02 In 2004, the country had just 450 miles (720  kilometers) of highways and expressways. By 2024,

07:08 it had over 3,100 miles (4,989 km). The roads  and rail lines weren’t laid out randomly;

07:14 every inch was carefully calculated  and optimized for efficiency.

07:18 Bit by bit, Poland built an enormous geopolitical  trap that the Western world never saw coming.

07:23 As the country’s infrastructure improved,  multinational corporations faced a new choice.

07:28 They could stay in Western Europe and deal with  rising costs and strained transport networks.

07:32 Or they could “near-shore” their operations  to Poland and take advantage of lower costs,

07:37 EU-funded infrastructure, and  a rapidly expanding workforce.

07:41 The EU’s Western leaders didn’t even see the  impending crisis unfolding in front of them.

07:45 They thought that by funding Poland’s  development, they were creating a reliable

07:49 and even submissive economic partner. They  expected nothing but political obedience in

07:54 exchange for those tens of billions of Euros. Warsaw, meanwhile, was using the West’s cash

07:59 to rip away its industrial dominance. And once the infrastructure was in place,

08:03 Warsaw was ready to reinforce it with something  that would cement its status not as a bit-player

08:08 on the European stage, but a headline act. In February 2022, another seismic shift

08:14 struck the European continent. Poland was, once  again, ready to make the most of the change.

08:19 Russian tanks and troops  crossed the border into Ukraine,

08:21 signaling the start of a years-long war. The  effects would ripple far beyond the battlefield,

08:26 impacting politics and economies around the globe. For decades, countries like Germany treated

08:31 defense as a low priority. Military  budgets were scaled back while budgets

08:35 were ploughed into social welfare projects. Warsaw, however, went the opposite way.

08:39 It funneled large amounts of its national budget  into defense. By 2024, its military spending had

08:45 surged to a historic 4.12% of its GDP. That is the  highest percentage in the entire NATO alliance.

08:52 Proportionately speaking, it’s  double that of Germany and France.

08:56 It’s even higher than the biggest military  superpower of them all, the United States,

09:00 which was around 3.4% of GDP at the time. Once again, Poland wasn’t just throwing

09:06 that money around or spending at random. It was investing in some of the finest

09:09 military hardware on the planet: South  Korean K2 Black Panther main battle tanks,

09:14 hundreds of K9 Thunder self-propelled  howitzers, and dozens of FA-50 fighter jets.

09:20 By the time Poland’s purchases are finished in  2030, the country will have more main battle tanks

09:24 than the UK, Germany, France and Italy combined. It’s pulling off the most aggressive military

09:30 buildup since the Cold War. But that’s not all.

09:33 Poland isn’t just buying tanks and shipping  them in. It has signed “Offset” deals with

09:37 South Korea to secure the technology and  know-how to build the tanks on its own soil.

09:42 Today, hundreds of tanks and howitzers are  rolling off production lines inside Poland.

09:47 And with the war in Ukraine, the country  has also become a vital logistics hub for

09:50 US and NATO forces. Since 2022, countless  tons of weapons, ammunition, and supplies

09:56 have flowed through Poland, and the country has  benefited from a massive geopolitical shield.

10:01 By making itself a reliable transit corridor,  while building one of the continent’s strongest

10:05 armies, Poland gained importance. The US, the  UK, France, Germany, and other Western powers

10:11 can’t afford for this country to fail. So, they’ll do whatever it

10:14 takes to defend and protect it. And with American military backing secured,

10:19 Poland gained the ultimate  leverage to force the EU’s hand.

10:22 For years, there was a narrative  among Western media regarding

10:25 Poland’s place on the European stage. It was seen as a pariah state. A “problem child.”

10:31 Some of Warsaw’s more outspoken leaders were  regularly condemned in the European Parliament.

10:35 Brussels often invoked various articles and  EU rights to punish and penalize Poland.

10:40 The country was repeatedly fined and threatened.  For a time, it looked like Warsaw would have to

10:45 eventually bend the knee and toe the line. But the war changed everything.

10:49 The country was vital for Europe’s survival.  So it became harder for Brussels to threaten

10:53 or intimidate. While Western leaders continued to  argue over abstract articles and the rule of law,

10:59 Warsaw was focused on what mattered:  using its newfound status as the

11:03 “Ukraine Logistics Hub” to its advantage. The turning point came in early 2024.

11:08 For months, the European Commission  had kept €137 billion worth of funds

11:13 that were intended for Poland on ice. It was a  game-changing amount of cash, completely frozen

11:18 and used as a financial chokehold to  pile pressure on the country’s leaders.

11:23 But Warsaw didn’t blink. It continued to do what it had always done:

11:27 strengthening its infrastructure, beefing up its  borders, improving its defenses, and making itself

11:32 more valuable for the continental cause. It shifted political course,

11:36 committing to restore judicial independence and  resetting relations with the European Union.

11:41 Poland’s mission paid off. The EU eventually gave in,

11:44 unblocking the entire €137 billion package,  including approximately €60 billion in Recovery

11:51 and Resilience Facility (RRF) funds. It was a complete capitulation by

11:56 the EU establishment. And a  remarkable victory for Poland.

12:00 It had overturned the odds, gaming the system to  enjoy an enormous injection of Western capital.

12:06 All while maintaining a solid and  stable stance of sovereign defiance.

12:09 By this point, Poland had attained the  very summit of its strategic leverage.

12:13 It was strong economically and militarily,  and it had beaten the West at its own game.

12:18 But while Warsaw’s leaders celebrated, they  didn’t realize that they were losing a battle

12:22 that couldn’t be fought with tanks or subsidies. Another long-standing narrative has also persisted

12:28 around Poland as the years have gone by. It claims that the country is some sort of

12:32 conservative cultural fortress. A nation that  has effectively sealed its borders against

12:37 the demographic shifts that are occurring  elsewhere across the European continent.

12:40 Warsaw’s leaders have pushed this myth,  repeatedly stating that they will never

12:44 adopt the immigration-oriented models of  places like Germany and the United Kingdom.

12:49 But the data says something completely different. In 2022, it issued over 700,000 first residence

12:56 permits to non-EU citizens. For 6 years  running, Warsaw issued more work permits

13:01 to non-EU nationals than any other EU member,  including Germany and France. Poland claims to

13:07 be some sort of bastion of anti-immigration  policy, yet imports more foreign labor

13:12 than the countries its leaders like to criticize. Hundreds of thousands of workers have been brought

13:16 in from all over the globe, including countries  like India, Uzbekistan, and the Philippines.

13:21 Why? Because

13:22 it was the only way that Poland would survive. The country’s growth came at a cost. Eventually,

13:28 it found itself with businesses  that were on the verge of booming,

13:31 but a massive lack of labor to power them. The  country’s unemployment rate had dropped to one of

13:36 the lowest levels in Europe. But there were still  too many jobs and not enough people to fill them.

13:40 To prevent a catastrophic economic collapse, the  state flipped its immigration stance on its head.

13:46 It funneled hundreds of thousands of  foreign workers into logistics hubs,

13:49 manufacturing plants, and critical industries. But it was never a permanent solution.

13:54 In fact, importing labor is merely a stop-gap  measure for a much darker, permanent crisis

13:59 looming over this trillion dollar economy. What Poland really wanted was to have more

14:04 home-grown workers to fill roles and power  its continued economic expansion. There was

14:08 just one problem: the country was heading  straight for a dramatic demographic cliff.

14:13 In 2016, Warsaw launched  the “Family 500+” program.

14:17 It offered a monthly tax-free cash benefit of  500 Zloty, around $130, to families for every

14:24 child they had. It was an aggressive measure  to encourage Polish people to have more kids.

14:29 It was leveled up in 2024,  becoming the 800+ program,

14:33 with a new and improved monthly  payment of 800 Zloty, almost $220.

14:38 The Polish government went all-in. They hoped  this would be enough to reverse its nation’s

14:42 demographic decline. It wasn’t.

14:45 The pro-family program certainly helped countless  Polish people, easing child poverty and making it

14:50 easier for households to put food on the table.  But it didn’t improve the number of babies being

14:54 born. By 2023, Poland’s fertility rate  had fallen to 1.16 children per woman.

15:00 The trend continued in 2024, with the  rate dropping even lower, to just 1.11.

15:05 It was the lowest in all of Europe and the lowest  in Poland since the end of the Second World War.

15:10 It’s nowhere near the recognized  “replacement level” rate of 2.1

15:14 deemed necessary for any population to remain  stable without having to rely on immigration.

15:19 Warsaw learned that money alone  can’t solve its demographic decline.

15:23 The causes run deeper. They’re structural,  shaped by social change in Poland.

15:27 And those same changes are  tied to its economic boom.

15:30 Because as Poland surged swiftly towards  its trillion dollar economy, a housing

15:34 crisis emerged in the country’s big urban centers. In cities like Warsaw and Krakow, average property

15:40 prices haven’t just risen, they’ve soared.  For a young Polish couple just starting off,

15:45 even a simple one-bedroom apartment feels out of  reach. This has forced millions of people into

15:50 rental insecurity or massive mortgages. When people don’t know where they’ll be

15:54 living next year, or if they can even  make their next mortgage payment,

15:58 starting a family is rarely their top priority. At the very same time, Poland is also sprinting

16:02 headfirst into a deadly environmental trap. The country’s industrial surge was fueled

16:07 by fossil fuels. Poland still relies  heavily on coal for around 50% of its

16:11 electrical energy. That means it has the most  carbon-intensive power grid in all of Europe.

16:16 Poland’s reliance on fossil fuels means a  ticking clock is looming over the country.

16:21 The EU is pushing ahead with strict climate  targets that will force member states to cut

16:25 emissions quickly. That means Poland will have to  shut down large parts of its coal infrastructure,

16:30 setting off a chain reaction through its economy. Higher energy prices. A weaker cost advantage.

16:35 And a country that may no longer look  as attractive to global manufacturers.

16:39 Its exports will suffer and its  revenue streams will be squeezed.

16:42 If it dares to defy the EU’s rules, it could face  devastating border tariffs that would undermine

16:47 its position inside the single market. In short, Warsaw is speeding straight

16:51 into a brick wall, and it may not have enough  time to slow down before the collision comes.

16:56 Even with the challenges ahead. Poland has  succeeded in changing the face of Europe.

17:00 The continental map has been redrawn.  The historical architecture that saw

17:04 the Western powers exert control  for generations has been smashed.

17:08 While the old guard of Paris and Berlin was busy  with bureaucracy and political polarization,

17:13 Poland wasn’t just rewriting the  rulebook. It was inventing its own,

17:17 and in doing so, it was dragging the  continent’s center of gravity to the east.

17:21 Poland is no longer an emerging market. It’s  no longer a subservient, peripheral partner.

17:27 It’s the new face of 21st century Europe. Warsaw exploited the EU’s financial structures

17:31 to build its own world-class  infrastructure. It offered a

17:34 more profitable and attractive alternative to  the corporations of the German Mittelstand.

17:39 Even when war came to its doorstep, it made all  the right moves to capitalize on the situation.

17:44 It is a heavily armed, highly industrialized  powerhouse, and it reached that point not by

17:49 conforming to the classic Western liberal  playbook, but by charting its own course.

17:53 And that very course could be the  one that wins the 21st century,

17:57 if - and only if - Poland can survive  its ongoing demographic collapse.

18:01 The country stands on a precipice. It has become a  European superpower. It has fortified its borders.

18:06 It has gained enormous influence  and respect on the world stage.

18:09 It has achieved what once seemed impossible. The only question left is can it hold on?

18:15 Poland’s ambitious moves couldn’t come at a more  important moment. As tensions rise across Europe,

18:20 every major power is keeping a close eye on  Russia. Watch “What Will Actually Happen if

18:24 Russia Invades Poland” to see how a Russian  advance would play out. Or click on this video.

docs.text:
00:00 AI was supposed to kick off a white

00:02 collar purge, but the reality is

00:04 different. In Fortune 500 boardrooms

00:06 across the country, thousands of AI

00:08 agents are being shut down. Not because

00:10 they didn't work, but because they're a

00:12 legal time bomb. The narrative is that

00:14 tech giants are spending everything to

00:17 win an AI arms race. But the reality is

00:19 much messier. They're stripping the

00:21 liability out of their systems while

00:23 pouring billions into the buildout. And

00:25 when the dust settles, someone still has

00:28 to pay for it. The US interstate highway

00:30 system is 48,000 mi long. It took 35

00:33 years to build and cost $630 billion in

00:36 today's money. It is by any measure one

00:39 of the most consequential infrastructure

00:40 investments in human history. Meanwhile,

00:43 big tech is spending $725 billion in

00:46 2026 on AI infrastructure alone. That

00:49 number has more than doubled in just 2

00:51 years and is projected to keep climbing

00:53 into the trillions by 2030. In fact,

00:56 Goldman Sachs now estimates that the

00:57 total AI infrastructure bill between now

00:59 and 2031 will exceed $7.61 trillion. For

01:04 that kind of money, you'd expect a

01:05 revolution. What these companies are

01:07 getting right now is cents on the

01:08 dollar. The entire global AI services

01:10 market in 2025 generated around $25

01:13 billion against hundreds of billions of

01:15 infrastructure spending. When a Chinese

01:17 startup called Deepseek revealed in

01:19 January 2025 that it had built a

01:21 competitive AI model using Nvidia's

01:23 lower-end chips for under $6 million, it

01:26 seemed almost impossible. But it still

01:28 shook the market, wiping out around $590

01:31 billion from Nvidia's market cap in a

01:33 single day. It was the largest single

01:36 day loss in US stock market history.

01:38 Deepseek, far from breaking AI, merely

01:41 raised the question every investor had

01:42 asked himself. What exactly are we

01:44 paying for? The companies spending this

01:46 money don't just have it lying around.

01:48 They are borrowing it. While Alphabet

01:50 quadrupled its long-term debt in 2025 to

01:52 46.5 billion, the five biggest tech

01:55 companies issued $18 billion in new

01:58 bonds last year alone. Bank of America

02:00 now estimates that AI Capex now consumes

02:03 95% of operating cash flows after

02:05 dividends. Amazon is projecting a 95%

02:08 decline in free cash flow thanks to its

02:10 AI buildout costs. They are in essence

02:13 mortgaging their present against a

02:15 future that hasn't shown up yet. The

02:17 gamble is genuinely alarming. If it were

02:20 startups chasing hype, that would be one

02:21 thing. These are the most sophisticated

02:23 capital allocators on the earth. When

02:25 they spend like this, they either know

02:27 something the rest of us don't, or

02:28 they're caught up in something they

02:30 can't stop without admitting they were

02:32 wrong. Either way, something has broken.

02:34 To understand what, you have to go back

02:36 to the moment a grieving man in

02:38 Vancouver asked an airline chatbot a

02:40 simple question and changed corporate

02:42 legal history forever. On the day his

02:44 grandmother died, Jake Moffett opened

02:47 his laptop and went to Air Canada's

02:48 website to book a flight from Vancouver

02:50 to Toronto. He had one question. Did the

02:53 airline offer bereavement fairs and

02:55 could he apply for one after the fact?

02:57 He asked the chatbot and it said yes. It

02:59 told him to submit his request within 90

03:01 days of purchase, and the discount would

03:03 be retroactively applied. So, Moffett

03:05 booked the ticket, flew to Toronto, came

03:08 home, and then filed the request like

03:09 he'd been told, and Air Canada denied

03:12 it. Their actual policy, as it turns

03:14 out, required bereavement fair requests

03:16 to be made before travel. The AI chatbot

03:19 had simply made up a policy that didn't

03:20 exist, stated it with complete

03:22 confidence, and sent a grieving man to

03:24 buy a full price ticket based on a lie.

03:27 So Moffett sued. And what happened next

03:29 is the reason every corporate lawyer in

03:31 America now has an opinion about

03:33 chatbots. Air Canada's legal defense was

03:35 interesting. They argued it could not be

03:37 held liable for information provided by

03:39 its chatbot because the chatbot was

03:42 quote a separate legal entity

03:43 responsible for its own actions. They

03:45 had deployed a piece of software to

03:47 represent their company. And when that

03:49 software caused harm, their position was

03:51 essentially don't look at us. Tribunal

03:54 member Christopher Rivers was not

03:55 impressed. While a chatbot has an

03:57 interactive component, he wrote, "It is

03:59 still just a part of Air Canada's

04:00 website, it should be obvious to Air

04:02 Canada that it is responsible for all

04:05 the information on its website. It makes

04:07 no difference whether the information

04:08 comes from a static page or a chatbot."

04:11 Air Canada was ordered to pay $812

04:13 Canadian, and in perspective, that

04:15 amount is trivial. The precedent was

04:18 not. That ruling landed in February

04:20 2024. What followed was a corporate

04:22 panic that never made headlines, but

04:25 could be seen in the risk sections of

04:27 SEC filings. In 2020, 4% of public

04:30 companies mentioned AI as a material

04:32 risk in their annual filings. By 2024,

04:35 that number was 43%. Among the Fortune

04:37 500 specifically, 56% now lists AI as a

04:41 formal risk factor. Among media and

04:43 entertainment companies, it's 92%. The

04:45 SEC itself has been sending enforcement

04:47 letters demanding more specific

04:49 disclosures backed by $ 8.2 billion in

04:52 financial remedies in the year 2024

04:54 alone. Climate change took decades to

04:56 achieve similar disclosure penetration

04:58 across corporate America. AI did it in 3

05:01 years. What the Air Canada ruling

05:03 established is that whatever your AI

05:05 says to a customer, you said it. You

05:08 can't outsource the liability to the

05:10 software you employ. You can't just

05:12 point at the machine and then look

05:13 innocent. You are the machine. For a

05:16 technology that can't guarantee it won't

05:17 make things up, that ruling created an

05:19 absolute certainty. Deploy AI at scale

05:22 and eventually liability follows. The

05:25 bigger question is, will there be anyone

05:27 left to cover the bill? In July 2024,

05:29 research and advisory firm Gartner

05:31 predicted that at least 30% of

05:33 enterprise gen AI projects would be

05:35 abandoned after proof of concept by the

05:37 end of 2025. By April 2026, they had to

05:40 revise their original estimate. It turns

05:42 out that it was actually more like 40%

05:44 of enterprise AI projects launched in

05:46 the previous 2 years that would be

05:48 scrapped before they ever shipped.

05:50 Separately, Gartner now predicts that

05:52 over 40% of Agentic AI projects, the

05:55 next generation of AI tools companies

05:56 are currently betting on, will be

05:58 cancelled by the end of 2027. The

06:00 graveyard keeps growing. S&P Global

06:02 Market Intelligence put some finer

06:04 numbers on it. The average organization

06:06 scrapped 46% of AI proof of concepts

06:09 before reaching production. Of the

06:11 projects initiated, only 48% make it to

06:13 production with an average of eight

06:15 months between prototype and launch.

06:17 That is eight months of engineering

06:19 hours, infrastructure costs, and

06:20 executive attention on a coin flip

06:22 chance of shipping anything at the end

06:24 of it. McKenzie, another consulting

06:26 firm, surveyed organizations globally in

06:28 late 2025, and they found that 88% use

06:31 AI in at least one business function. If

06:34 that sounds like a success story, it's

06:36 not. Only 39% reported any measurable

06:39 impact on earnings. At most, 61%

06:42 reported no meaningful financial impact

06:44 on their business whatsoever. Roughly

06:46 six in 10 companies have plugged AI into

06:48 their operations and can't point to a

06:51 measurable return it's made them. The

06:52 reasons are familiar enough that Gardner

06:54 has named them outright. Poor data

06:56 quality, weak risk controls, rising

06:58 costs, and unclear business value. Each

07:01 project costs between $5 and $20 million

07:03 to build and deploy. Multiply that

07:06 across thousands of Fortune 500

07:07 initiatives and you're looking at tens

07:09 of billions of dollars buried in the

07:11 corporate graveyard. It gets even worse

07:13 for big tech. A 2024 Deote survey found

07:16 that 47% of enterprise AI users admitted

07:19 to making at least one major business

07:21 decision based on the content AI had

07:23 simply invented. In other words, nearly

07:25 half had already trusted a hallucination

07:27 with realworld consequences. Granted,

07:30 things have evolved a lot since 2024.

07:32 The efficiency revolution is still an

07:34 aspirational possibility as Agentic AI

07:37 improves. But you wouldn't be human if

07:40 you hadn't wondered why the flaws you've

07:41 seen firsthand seem absent from the

07:44 market's calculations. There's a

07:46 particular breed of corporate fear that

07:47 shows up where you would least expect

07:49 it. Insurance contracts. Basically, if

07:52 the people whose entire business model

07:54 depends on their ability to correctly

07:55 price risk deem something uninsurable,

07:59 that is usually a huge red flag. In

08:01 January 2026, the Insurance Services

08:03 Office introduced new exclusions

08:06 targeting generative AI. Essentially, if

08:08 generative AI causes the damage, don't

08:11 assume you're covered. New policy

08:13 language began excluding claims tied to

08:15 AI generated text, images, audio, video,

08:18 and code. That is every large language

08:21 model ever built. the chat bots, the AI

08:23 co-pilots, the autonomous agents, all of

08:25 them circled with black ink and excluded

08:28 from the policies that cover 82% of US

08:30 businesses. In 2024 and 25, insurers had

08:34 been narrowing AI coverage in existing

08:36 policies by tightening up language and

08:38 adding exclusions. WR Berkeley

08:40 introduced an absolute AI exclusion

08:42 across directors and officers, errors

08:45 and omissions, and fiduciary liability

08:47 lines. AIG saw that and they said,

08:49 "Well, we'll have more of the same."

08:51 Great American Insurance followed. Chub,

08:53 Travelers, Bergkshire Hathaway received

08:56 state regulatory approval for their own

08:58 exclusions. State regulators have been

09:00 approving more than 80% of those

09:01 requests. The industry has seen this

09:03 movie before. A decade ago, cyber

09:06 insurance went through an identical

09:07 cycle. There was invisible coverage

09:09 until claims mounted and then came the

09:11 exclusions. Eventually, standalone

09:13 products emerged at premiums most

09:15 companies couldn't stomach. The AI

09:17 liability market is speedr running the

09:19 same cycle. Insurance companies are not

09:22 moral actors. They do not exclude things

09:24 because they find them distasteful. They

09:26 exclude them because the numbers don't

09:28 work. They tried to price in AI

09:30 liability throughout 2024 and 2025. And

09:33 42% of insurers reported tracking no AI

09:36 risk metrics at all. When you can't

09:38 measure risk, you can't price it. And

09:41 when you can't price it, you exclude it.

09:44 The legal system said, "Whatever your AI

09:46 does, you did it." the insurance

09:48 industry said, "And we won't be covering

09:50 that." Which left every company still

09:52 running public-f facing AI deployment,

09:54 holding the entire liability themselves,

09:56 all on hardware that was simultaneously

09:58 losing most of its value. In the summer

10:00 of 2023, if you wanted to rent a single

10:02 Nvidia H100 GPU, a foundational chip in

10:05 the inception of the AI arms race, you

10:08 were paying between $7 and $10 an hour.

10:10 To buy one outright on the secondary

10:12 market, you were looking at $40,000 to

10:14 $50,000 per card. Startups were putting

10:17 H100s on their balance sheets like

10:19 assets, and venture capitalists were

10:20 asking portfolio companies how many they

10:22 had on their books. Nvidia's market cap

10:25 soon passed the $1 trillion threshold,

10:27 and it kept rising. In February 2026, it

10:30 hit 5 trillion. The H100 was, for a

10:33 brief, dizzying moment the most

10:35 strategically valuable piece of hardware

10:37 on the Earth. Today, you can rent one

10:39 for $2 an hour. In June 2025, AWS cut

10:42 H100 pricing by 45% overnight. The

10:46 secondary market collapsed right behind

10:47 it. GPUs that had sold for as much as 50

10:50 grand during the AI boom were suddenly

10:52 worth less than half that. Entire H100

10:55 server systems that once cost more than

10:56 $350,000

10:58 were now trading for a fraction of their

11:00 peak value. Over 300 new GPU cloud

11:03 providers entered the market in 2025

11:05 alone. All of them selling capacity that

11:08 nobody was buying at the rate anyone

11:10 projected. Thousands of companies

11:12 weighing up where to sell the cards at a

11:14 loss. It is the difference between

11:16 making payroll and not making payroll.

11:18 This signals a deeper problem about the

11:20 infrastructure thesis that justified the

11:22 entire buildout. The argument was always

11:24 that compute was scarce. That scarcity

11:26 created value and whoever controlled the

196:04 then it signed a second giant deal with

196:06 Amazon worth tens of billions more. This

196:09 isn't a company spending money because

196:10 it's found a profitable business model.

196:12 It's spending money because it needs

196:14 more compute to keep the AI race going.

196:17 In April 2026, Microsoft and OpenAI

196:19 rewrote their partnership and the new

196:21 terms set OpenAI loose. Its Microsoft

196:24 license stopped being exclusive, so it

196:26 can now run on any cloud it likes. It's

196:29 even building its own chip with

196:30 Broadcom. Suddenly, OpenAI bought itself

196:33 more room to move and with it control of

196:36 the layer that everything now depends

196:37 on. We've seen versions of this before.

196:40 Ride hailing kept fairs below cost until

196:42 subsidies faded and prices rose.

196:45 Streaming did the same thing with

196:46 content. But AI is harder to escape. If

196:49 a ride gets expensive, you just switch

196:51 apps. If a subscription changes, you

196:53 cancel it. But if your product is built

196:55 on top of a model, you don't switch, you

196:58 rebuild. Most companies can't rebuild

197:00 fast enough because they didn't just

197:02 build on the system they built into it.

197:04 Large-scale AI systems run on physical

197:07 infrastructure with hard power limits. A

197:09 training cluster with around 20,000

197:11 Nvidia H100 GPUs pulls about 20 megawws

197:15 nonstop. A smaller cluster of 10,000

197:17 chips runs somewhere between 10 and 15

197:20 megawatt. To put that into context,

197:22 that's enough to power 15,000 average

197:24 American homes all at once, day and

197:26 night. And that's just a single cluster.

197:29 The biggest companies run multiple

197:30 versions of them. Every answer you pull

197:32 out of one of those systems draws power

197:34 off the grid. It also wears down chips

197:37 that cost tens of thousands of dollars

197:39 each and age out within months. 20,000

197:42 of them can run past half a billion

197:44 dollars in hardware alone. The moment

197:46 they switch on, they begin losing value.

197:48 For a while, engineers tried to push

197:50 costs down, and for a while, it worked.

197:53 But you can't just write code that beats

197:55 the laws of physics. Power costs money.

197:57 A chip wears out in its own time, no

197:59 matter how clever the software around it

198:01 is. The numbers reflect that grim

198:03 reality. These clusters have to be

198:05 running almost every hour because an

198:07 idle chip means a loss. Tech firms pay

198:10 rising power bills. They write off the

198:12 hardware fast because the next chip

198:14 makes the current generation look

198:15 obsolete. Put all of that against what

198:17 providers actually charge and the charge

198:20 does not come close. It was never

198:22 supposed to. The low price was bait.

198:24 These companies are not bleeding cash by

198:26 accident. They are doing it on purpose.

198:28 Investor money has filled in the gap

198:30 between costs and price. But that gap

198:32 keeps widening. That cheap price tag is

198:35 actually just an illusion. Cash can push

198:37 the price below cost. But the power bill

198:40 doesn't change. When the investor money

198:42 runs out, there's only one option left.

198:44 The price charged to the customer who

198:46 can't leave. That's why AI companies try

198:49 almost everything except charging what

198:51 it actually costs. The workarounds buy

198:53 some time, but they distort the market.

198:56 When an AI company that builds the model

198:58 also decides to sell it directly to

199:00 customers, the effects show up quickly.

199:02 The clearest example is a company called

199:04 Jasper. It built an AI writing tool

199:06 directly on OpenAI's models and for a

199:09 while it was a successful business.

199:11 Revenue climbed past $120 million.

199:13 Investors valued it at $1.5 billion and

199:17 more than 100,000 customers signed up.

199:19 Then ChatGpt arrived and it was

199:22 virtually free. It did much of the same

199:24 work for a fraction of the price.

199:25 Jasper's growth suddenly went in

199:27 reverse. By 2025, its revenue had fallen

199:30 to around $88 million. The company

199:32 survived, but by pushing hard into

199:34 corporate marketing and finding firmer

199:36 ground. It's a bit like a building full

199:38 of chefs. Each one rents a small kitchen

199:41 upstairs and cooks for their customers.

199:43 And then one morning, the landlord opens

199:44 his own restaurant in the lobby. It's

199:46 the same dishes but given away for free

199:48 and using the same recipes that he

199:50 learned by watching his tenants work. If

199:53 your only advantage is access to a model

199:55 owned by somebody else, you don't really

199:57 have an advantage at all. Not when the

199:59 model's owner just decides to compete

200:01 directly. It's a move known as

200:02 sherlocking. It comes from an old Apple

200:05 habit of swallowing up the best features

200:07 of other apps into its own software. The

200:10 provider watches how people use the

200:11 tools built on it and then finds the

200:14 most valuable uses and folds them in.

200:16 The original maker is quickly undercut

200:18 and out of business. A startup spends

200:20 years polishing its prompts and

200:22 workflows. Soon that work shows up

200:24 inside the platform copied for free. Its

200:27 edge evaporates, its pricing power

200:29 follows, and its biggest contracts slip

200:31 from must-have to maybe. And this is why

200:34 relying on a single vendor has climbed

200:36 the list of corporate fears. It used to

200:39 look like a smart fast choice. After

200:41 Jasper, it looks more like a loaded gun

200:43 left on the table. But eating your own

200:45 customers still doesn't balance the

200:47 books. All you gain is a smaller group

200:49 of rivals. So, the providers try

200:51 something else. A move that doesn't

200:53 touch the companies on top at all. It

200:55 touches the product itself. On the

200:57 surface, token prices keep falling and

200:59 every press release calls it progress.

201:01 But beneath those announcements,

201:03 something might be happening to the

201:04 thing you actually pay for. A large,

201:06 smart, expensive model can be diluted

201:08 into a smaller and cheaper one.

201:10 Shrinking a model can be fair, useful

201:12 engineering done only to protect profit,

201:15 it becomes a swap, and it has the same

201:17 label, but the product is thinner. The

201:20 new version is tuned to stay just good

201:22 enough that you don't cancel. Yet, it is

201:24 cheap enough to save a fortune across

201:25 billions of prompts. The decline rarely

201:27 is visible itself. The model forgets

201:30 just a little bit sooner, reasons a

201:32 little less deeply, and dresses up its

201:34 guesses as creativity. Because the price

201:36 keeps dropping, people see the whole

201:38 thing as a win. Frontier models are

201:40 still growing, and shrinking them into

201:42 highly capable systems represents

201:44 massive technological processes. But

201:46 that steady drift towards smaller and

201:48 cheaper points the other way. It hints

201:50 that the numbers never really added up.

201:52 Time is the only thing this really buys.

201:54 the hostage contracts, the sherlocking,

201:57 the shrinking of the models. None of

201:59 this is a real plan to solve the issue

202:01 because the problem lies elsewhere.

202:03 Software was supposed to be the perfect

202:05 business. You build it once, you sell it

202:07 a million times, and each extra copy

202:09 costs you almost nothing. That promise

202:11 built 20 years of sky-high valuations.

202:14 It's baked into every pitch that called

202:15 AI the next great software story.

202:18 Silicone shattered all of that. Thanks

202:20 to all the costs associated with AI,

202:22 OpenAI's margin was close to 33%. A

202:25 healthy software business operates at 70

202:27 to 80%. So, OpenAI got desperate. It

202:31 began selling ads inside Chat GPT. The

202:34 pilot launched in February 2026. Within

202:36 6 weeks, it was on pace to make $100

202:38 million a year with over 600 advertisers

202:41 on board. Sam Alman had spent years

202:43 calling ads a last resort. Now, the most

202:46 famous AI company on Earth is renting

202:48 out your attention. Rival company

202:50 Anthropic mocked the move. But mockery

202:52 doesn't cover a $25 billion bill. HSBC

202:56 analysts have estimated that OpenAI will

202:58 need $27 billion in fresh funding by

203:01 2030 to cover data center and compute

203:03 costs. Sam Alman, meanwhile, has

203:05 promised $100 billion in revenue by

203:08 2027. The gap between those figures

203:11 keeps widening. What comes in and goes

203:13 out are moving on very different

203:15 trajectories. In late 2025, Altman said

203:18 OpenAI had lined up about 1.4 trillion

203:21 in compute deals over 8 years. The

203:23 company made roughly $13 billion that

203:26 year. One investor questioned the

203:28 numbers on a podcast, which led to

203:29 Altman offering to buy his shares. Just

203:32 months in, in early 2026, the plan

203:34 changed again. OpenAI told investors the

203:37 real target was closer to $600 billion.

203:40 Even the scale of the ambition had to be

203:42 rewritten. When a plan is revised

203:44 downward by more than half, it stops

203:47 looking like strategy and starts looking

203:48 like constraint. Patience is beginning

203:51 to run thin. The latest funding terms

203:53 require a clear path to profitability,

203:55 something the cheap access era never had

203:57 to prove. The timeline is tightening as

203:59 well. With an IPO insight, OpenAI can't

204:02 afford more losses. Public investors

204:04 want profit, not promises. Neither is

204:07 falling fast to save the current

204:08 business model. No amount of code

204:10 removes the need to run massive clusters

204:12 of hardware that must be replaced long

204:14 before they've paid for themselves. The

204:16 industry assumes software margins would

204:18 eventually outrun infrastructure costs,

204:20 but so far that hasn't happened. That

204:22 leaves a simple constraint. Keep prices

204:24 low and burn through cash faster than it

204:26 returns or raise prices and bleed users

204:29 who made the system valuable in the

204:31 first place. Either path arrives in the

204:33 same outcome. The only uncertainty left

204:35 is how many players are still in the

204:37 game when it does. When the prices

204:39 reset, the companies still standing will

204:41 be the ones that control their own

204:42 models. There's already an alternative

204:44 emerging. Open models can be downloaded

204:47 and run on hardware users control.

204:49 Meta's Llama is freely available.

204:51 DeepSeek has shown that capable models

204:53 can be trained at a fraction of the

204:54 expected cost. They are good enough to

204:56 run a real business on. Whole teams

204:59 already run them on their own servers

205:01 with no outside key and no surprise

205:03 invoice. The trade is straightforward.

205:05 Customers take on the headache of

205:07 running the software and the headache of

205:08 running the hardware, but they stop

205:10 being held hostage. At scale, this can

205:12 be considerably cheaper than renting

205:14 models and infrastructure. But there is

205:16 a bigger advantage. Customers have

205:18 control. They own their data. They

205:21 decide when the model changes. The great

205:23 shutout is already beginning. The

205:25 smallest rappers will fold quickly after

205:27 the first real price change. Mid-sized

205:29 firms will scramble for tools and

205:31 engineers they should have hired

205:32 earlier. And at the top end, only the

205:34 biggest players will end up running

205:36 serious models on their own. For

205:37 everyone, it stopped being about saving

205:39 money. It's about staying alive. Leaning

205:42 onto a single provider for your core

205:44 income is a massive risk. One decision

205:46 in someone else's office can cut you off

205:48 completely. The companies moving fastest

205:50 are already building their own clusters

205:52 and tuning open models on their private

205:54 data. They're pulling their most

205:56 sensitive work back in-house. Owning

205:58 also means a bill you can predict.

206:00 Renting means a number that can leap in

206:02 any given month. Owning means a cost you

206:05 can plan around for years. For most

206:06 businesses, that beats any discount. A

206:09 split is forming and within a few years,

206:10 it'll be obvious to see. On one side

206:13 will be the companies that treated cheap

206:14 tokens as a permanent gift. They built

206:17 their whole cost structure on top of

206:18 them. They are the tenants and they will

206:20 learn the lease was never really theirs.

206:23 On the other side are the companies that

206:24 treated the cheap years like a window.

206:26 They used it to get started and figure

206:28 out what worked. They were able to see

206:30 the escape route. The difference between

206:32 the two groups isn't money or talent.

206:34 It's timing. One side saw falling prices

206:36 and they assumed it would last. The

206:38 other saw borrowed time. Either you

206:40 control the hardware your business runs

206:42 on or you let a company that must

206:44 squeeze you set the price. Waiting

206:46 carries its own price. The longer

206:48 customers stay, the harder the eventual

206:49 fall. The cheapest moment to leave has

206:51 already passed. The next cheapest moment

206:53 is right now. Tokens were never getting

206:56 cheaper because the technology had set

206:57 itself free. They were cheap because

206:59 someone else was covering the bill and

207:01 that bill is due.

00:00 This week we'll be talking about probably one

00:06 of the most important aspects of photography, which is light.

00:10 As in photo-graphy [spoken phonetically],

00:12 writing or drawing with light.

00:15 It's a very content-rich conversation,

00:18 we're going to have, and could really, easily,

00:20 take up a full six-week course.

00:22 But for our purposes here, we're going

00:25 to give you something of an overview,

00:27 showing you various forms and characteristics

00:30 of some light sources.

00:32 We can't address every conceivable possibility.

00:35 But what we can do is tweak your curiosity, I hope,

00:39 so that you pay attention, very close attention, to what you're

00:43 seeing as you change your own light sources,

00:46 looking at the shadows for example.

00:49 How do they and they and the highlights

00:51 change as you move your light source?

00:54 And observe exactly what's going on when you make even

00:58 some very minimal changes.

00:59 Let's start with a very simple piece of equipment, a lightbox.

01:05 It's really easy to use when you're

01:07 working with transparent material,

01:09 just by placing your work directly

01:12 on top of the lightbox.

01:14 But you'll see also, later, it can

01:15 be also another general source of lighting.

01:19 So let's start with a picture of these two petri dishes

01:22 growing E. coli.

01:24 So that works.

01:26 In this image, we're seeing small pieces of colored plastic

01:30 shapes, about 3 millimeters across that are organizing,

01:34 or self-assembling at the interface

01:36 between two solutions.

01:38 They're becoming a flat assemblage at that interface.

01:42 And all I did was put the glass container

01:44 holding all the material on the lightbox.

01:48 And here, I'm making images of sugar crystals growing

01:52 on sticks.

01:53 You know, they serve you that sometimes

01:55 when you order a cup of coffee.

01:57 So here is one rendition on a lightbox of the sugar,

02:01 and what I decided to do for the next one

02:04 to simply invert the image, which we've seen before.

02:07 Here's a picture that I made a number of years ago,

02:10 which I still like.

02:11 It's a picture about light, a metaphor about light.

02:16 It was one of those lucky efforts

02:18 when I just set up a magnifier and the paper, [laughs]

02:21 and in about 30 seconds, I got the picture!

02:24 (Very unusual, by the way!) So the image

02:26 is intended to suggest a process of etching with light when

02:31 we talked about it in our book No Small Matter,

02:34 about nanoscience.

02:36 In this image of something I assume you recognize by now,

02:40 we see a different kind of lighting

02:42 that you've seen from previous images of the music box.

02:46 I shot from above with mostly daylight,

02:49 and then I turned on a little bit more

02:52 light from a Tungsten lamp above.

02:55 This is specific to this situation,

02:57 but you might find it helpful in yours.

03:01 Look what happens when you just simply click and turn

03:04 a light on.

03:05 From the light being off, to the light being on,

03:09 you'll see how the image drastically

03:11 changes by just adding an additional lamp

03:14 from above this fishing reel.

03:17 Yup [laugh], that's what it is, by the way,

03:19 it is a fishing reel placed in a translucent, green garbage can.

03:24 [laughs] I thought it was fun to see what kind of quality

03:27 I could get by shooting into a plastic, translucent garbage

03:31 can.

03:31 Very specific to say the least.

03:34 Again, just by adding one additional light -- this time,

03:38 inside the vacuum chamber I'm imaging ' we see what starts

03:43 as this kind of image, and becomes this image.

03:46 You'll see how it really changes with the simple addition

03:50 of just one light.

03:53 In this image of a triangular-shaped water drop --

03:57 it's actually an etched area on a surface onto which we placed

04:01 water ' you can see the reflection of the lamp

04:04 on the water drop.

04:06 We just directed a lamp onto the water.

04:10 That's considered direct lighting.

04:13 When I shine the lamp onto a card,

04:15 in this case, a gold card, the light then

04:18 bounced back onto the water drop and you'll

04:21 see a completely different quality of lighting.

04:24 This is called bounce lighting.

04:27 The bounce gives us diffuse lighting.

04:30 Let's compare the two.

04:31 Let's look at a quick test that I

04:35 made for us to see the difference between two

04:38 kinds of bounces.

04:40 In this case, the bounce lighting

04:42 will used as fill lighting.

04:44 We'll use a white card and then we'll fill with a mirror.

04:48 The main source of light is daylight from a window.

04:51 So, here's an image of the inside of the watch

04:53 that we've seen before, just with daylight

04:56 on an overcast day.

04:57 Here, I added a white card on the side of the watch

05:01 for a fill.

05:02 Here is a mirror reflecting the daylight, again, as a fill,

05:06 onto the watch.

05:09 Let's go back to the original 'just daylight'; then the card;

05:13 then the mirror; back to the watch alone;

05:18 then adding a card; then adding just the mirror.

05:23 Let's zoom in to see the subtle differences

05:26 in each of these cases.

05:28 Now depending on what your material is,

05:30 you might see much more dramatic changes.

05:33 But I encourage you to experiment with these ideas.

05:37 By the way, here's another image I

05:38 made, this time using both the card and the mirror as a fill.

05:43 Let's see them all together.

05:44

05:49 Light is all about shadows as well.

05:51 And it is quite remarkable how small changes can

05:54 change the shadow in images.

05:56 How a powerful direct light source

05:59 can produce a significant shadow, and that shadow does,

06:03 in this image, become a very strong compositional element.

06:09 Here's where I'm using the light on this wafer showing

06:15 In this particular image, I was playing around;

06:32 I actually like the first one better,

06:35 about using light in terms of making compositions.

06:40 In this image, I'm using a shadow

06:47 It's diffracting the light into different wavelengths.

06:53 in front of the light source.

06:55 See how the image looks without the card.

07:02 Here, we're trying to show something called the Marangoni

07:05 effect; you know, when you twirl a glass of wine we see some --

07:09 what some people call 'tears of wine'.

07:12 It's a complex phenomenon.

07:14 In this image, I tried for quite a

07:16 while to make an image depicting the Maragoni effect.

07:21 Not at all successful.

07:23 Finally, thinking that I should concentrate

07:26 on the glass, and the shadow that is being produced,

07:30 then I finally focused in on what is the Marangoni

07:35 effect on its own, as a shadow.

07:39 Now, for example, looking at this small assemblage, which

07:44 is about two centimeters across, I lit this with one light.

07:50 It's a monopoint, it's somewhat of a fiber optic source.

07:54 And you could see carefully, if you look at this image,

07:59 where does the light source come from,

08:02 and hopefully you will figure out that if the shadow is here,

08:07 then the light source has to be around here.

08:11 In this next one, I added a second light source

08:15 that not only lights the device as light to it,

08:19 but it also adds another shadow.

08:22 And in this next one, the second light source

08:26 has been altered in terms of its direction and the height

08:31 because the shadow that it casts is slightly longer and even

08:36 more so in this final image where

08:40 the light, the second light source,

08:42 is very low compared to where it was.

08:45 And you know that again because the shadow

08:48 is considerably longer.

08:50 Now, why bother looking at all this?

08:53 It really is, once again, learning

08:56 to see so that when you play with your own light sources

09:00 with your own devices, you're going

09:02 to pay not only great attention to lighting of your device,

09:08 but the shadows that the lighting will be producing.

09:12 It's important.

09:13 It might not seem that way at this point, but [laughs],

09:16 I promise you, it really is important.

docs.text:
00:00 You decided to go hiking alone.

00:02 All those days indoors were starting to make you go a little stir-crazy, and even though

00:06 a thick blanket of fog was creeping in, you knew you just had to get out.

00:10 The local forest had a nice hiking trail – the kind of place where you could really get lost

00:14 in your thoughts.

00:15 But as you trudge through the foggy woods, bordered on all sides by thickets of towering

00:19 ever-greens, you hear a strange crackling noise.

00:23 Then harsh, modulated whispers, hissing out numbers and words with no logical configuration.

00:29 Must be an old radio, you think, and keep walking.

00:32 Just then you hear a quiet rustling in the trees behind you, and then footsteps, even

00:36 though you would have sworn you were alone.

00:38 Then it’s that crackling again, and those nonsense words and numbers.

00:43 “SIXTEEN.

00:44 THREE.

00:45 WOMAN.

00:46 FOURTEEN.

00:47 RIP.

00:48 DISGUSTING.”

00:49 It was like two voices at once, saying the same thing at exactly the same time.

00:53 You feel the hair on the back of your neck bristle, then you turn and see it.

00:57 Your jaw gapes in horror.

00:59 It’s huge – forty feet tall, rail-thin, with mummified skin clinging tight to its

01:04 bones.

01:05 You look up, hoping to see the creature’s face, but there is no face.

01:08 Just two metal sirens grafted to a long pole of flesh.

01:12 Before you can even scream, its long, spindly hands are already wrapping around your face.

01:17 You’ve just fallen victim to Sirenhead.

01:19 Like its numerous creepypasta predecessors, such as the Slender Man, Smile Dog, and The

01:25 Rake, Sirenhead is a kind of online cryptid that has entangled the internet in its web

01:29 of fear.

01:30 Despite only first appearing in August of 2018, this frightening, faceless monster has

01:34 become a hub of internet folklore and content creation.

01:37 It’s captured the imagination of thousands, appearing in countless pieces of fan art and

01:42 even popular indie games.

01:43 But what exactly is Sirenhead?

01:45 Where did it come from?

01:47 How did it get so popular and widespread in the first place?

01:49 And, like the best of urban legends, is there a hint of frightening truth behind the fiction?

01:54 Let’s start from the point of inception.

01:56 Sirenhead is the creation of Canadian illustrator and master of horror Trevor Henderson, better

02:01 known by his online handle of SlimySwampGhost.

02:04 Henderson is internet horror royalty, and is also no stranger to creating horrifying

02:09 online cryptids.

02:10 In fact, he’s already made a number of other iconic internet boogeymen.

02:14 These include Cartoon Cat, a terrifying, homicidal feline demon.

02:18 The Smile Room, a toothy nightmare hidden inside an abandoned bowling alley.

02:22 And the Fetid King , a mysterious and frightening entity able to manipulate technology, to name

02:27 just a handful.

02:29 But Sirenhead is, by far, Henderson’s most beloved creation.

02:32 He first appeared in a post on Henderson’s Tumblr blog back on August 19th, 2018, with

02:37 this image.

02:38 In the photo, taken at a distance, we see the imposing figure of Sirenhead looming over

02:42 an old, abandoned graveyard.

02:44 If this wasn’t creepy enough for you, the photo came with the following terrifying caption:

02:48 “She was on vacation with her husband and they were scoping out graveyards on the way,

02:52 as you do, when she saw it.

02:54 Rising out of the old cemetery, big as an old – macabre - telephone pole.

02:58 Was this some kind of bizarre art piece the authorities hadn’t gotten wise to yet?

03:02 Even as she stepped out of the car, the megaphones on its “head” screeched to life.

03:06 “NINE.

03:07 EIGHTEEN.

03:08 ONE.

03:09 CHILD.

03:10 SEVENTEEN.

03:11 REMOVE.

03:12 VILE.”.

03:13 A buzzing, doubled voice screamed random words at her.

03:14 At this point, it jerked into motion, striding down the hill towards her.”

03:17 The tags under the picture include the words “found footage”, perhaps even suggesting

03:21 some underlying truth to the events depicted here.

03:24 That’s enough to give anyone the willies.

03:26 After Sirenhead made his debut, thousands of people chimed in in response, stating just

03:30 how scary and captivating they found this strange new creature.

03:33 Little by little, Henderson began to drip-feed more information about this monstrous creature

03:37 to the public via his twitter account.

03:39 Each tweet painted a slightly more detailed picture of the horrifying threat we were dealing

03:44 with here.

03:45 In his first Twitter thread on the subject, Henderson stated that Sirenhead is the static

03:49 physical form of an unfathomable supernatural entity.

03:52 A being truly beyond any limits of human understanding.

03:56 For example, it doesn’t have eyes, but can still see.

03:59 Its teeth – hidden in gaping, fleshy mouths inside the sirens – are biological, but

04:03 the creature doesn’t eat.

04:04 It uses its similarities to a telephone pole to camouflage itself and hunt humans like

04:09 an ambush predator.

04:10 While its Siren-head can play siren noises, it typically communicates in odd snippets

04:15 of music or words.

04:16 It can also record and play back other sounds, similar to the sport-hunting alien from The

04:21 Predator, and is able to manipulate other noise-emitting devices.

04:23 In other words, while it might seem, at face value, like a brainless monster, Sirenhead

04:28 is an intelligent and powerful supernatural force.

04:31 While it spends large periods of time inactive, it can move scarily fast when it needs to

04:35 – say, for example, when it’s chasing you down through the woods.

04:38 It also tends to avoid major population centres, preferring to stalk areas where victims won’t

04:43 have anyone to save them.

04:45 But, as you’ll soon find out, that doesn’t mean you’re any safer tucked away at home

04:48 in the burbs…

04:49 In the second Tweet about Sirenhead, Henderson shared a frightening image of the creature

04:54 lurking in someone’s backyard.

04:55 The caption indicated that Sirenhead was responsible for the disappearance of a family of four

05:00 in their own home.

05:01 They were gone without a trace, with the neighbours just reporting the patio door being left open

05:05 in their absence.

05:06 The quiet suburbs are actually one of Sirenhead’s favourite hunting grounds, as shown by the

05:10 next frightening found photo shared.

05:12 When Sirenhead abducted people on the seemingly innocent streets outside their own homes,

05:17 there were always three commonalities: It was always people walking the side streets

05:21 on their way home, it was always dark by the time people started wondering where they were,

05:25 and it was always past the time when the street lights come on.

05:28 The fact that Sirenhead can also perfectly disguise itself as a normal street lamp just

05:33 adds another dimension of terror to the creature.

05:35 How can you ever feel safe walking past street lamps in the dark again?

05:39 Sirenhead can appear almost anywhere dark, secluded, and depopulated, so you can never

05:44 let your guard down when you’re in one of these areas.

05:46 He’s been spotted everywhere from Yellowstone National Park in 2016 to a darkened country

05:51 lake to the parking lot of an unassuming motel, always causing unexplained paranormal activity

05:56 and disappearances in his wake.

05:59 Worse still – for all members of the human race who like living safe, comfortable lives

06:03 – it’s been hinted that Sirenhead is part of a far grander and more dangerous picture,

06:07 almost like a “hype man” for some other unnamed but presumably far more powerful and

06:12 dangerous entity.

06:13 It has also been said that the proper collective noun for a group of Sirenheads is a “static”,

06:18 implying that Sirenhead may not even be a singular being, but just one member of a whole

06:23 species of dangerous cryptids.

06:25 Though Henderson himself has mentioned that he sees Sirenhead as more of a manifestation

06:30 than simple animal, and it doesn’t therefore abide by the same set of physical rules that

06:34 creatures from our plane of existence are forced to conform to.

06:37 Because of this, the true extent of Sirenhead’s power is unknowable, especially considering

06:42 that so many who encounter it don’t seem to live to tell the tale.

06:46 Though as with any good urban legend, Sirenhead’s legend didn’t end with its creator.

06:50 Sirenhead quickly became a worldwide sensation thanks to an unlikely force: Online indie

06:55 video games.

06:56 Two video game artefacts featuring Sirenhead were made initially, one being a mod for the

07:00 game Fallout 4 called “Whispering Hills”, and another five-minute Sirenhead game developed

07:05 by indie games studio Modus Interactive.

07:08 While neither of these games were an immediate smash hit back in 2018, they found a second

07:12 life a couple years later after being picked up by a number of prominent YouTubers..

07:16 From here, Sirenhead’s popularity exploded to unprecedented levels.

07:20 He quickly became the subject of countless creepypasta short horror stories the world

07:24 over, as well as hundreds or even thousands of pieces of fan art.

07:28 People were also making home-made Sirenhead dolls and action figures, Lego sculptures

07:33 and even Halloween costumes Outside the gaming community, Sirenhead was

07:36 becoming the internet equivalent of a household name.

07:39 The creature had gained its own subreddit, where fans feverishly discuss theories and

07:43 ideas and share fan-made content.

07:45 In early 2020, Sirenhead also gained a huge boost in popularity from TikTok, after user

07:50 Alex Howard posted a frightening CGI video of Sirenhead lumbering across a town in the

07:55 horizon while sirens blared menacingly.

07:58 This ten second clip not only scared the bejeezus out of the internet, but was also insanely

08:04 memeable.

08:05 Variations of the video were used in everything from making fun of the strange name of Elon

08:09 Musk’s new baby, to one particularly creative version where Sirenhead dances to South Korean

08:14 hit single “Gangnam Style.”

08:15 So, let’s pump the breaks for a second.

08:17 You’re probably wondering: If Sirenhead is just some character made by an online horror

08:21 artist, what’s all the fuss about?

08:22 It’s not like he’s real, right?

08:24 Well, the answer to that question might be a little more complicated than you’d imagine.

08:28 To fully understand, we need to take a look at one of the most iconic internet urban legends

08:32 of all time: The Slender Man.

08:34 This dapper, faceless, internet boogeyman was created by Eric Knudsen in 2009, but quickly

08:39 spun into a phenomenon with a life of its own, as you can find out in one of our other

08:43 videos, “How A Meme (Slenderman) Became Real.”

08:46 The Slender Man’s immense popularity quickly made him a fixture of the internet’s public

08:50 consciousness, much like Sirenhead, with fan art, costumes, spin-off games and fan films.

08:55 The dark ending of the Slender Man saga was a near-fatal stabbing supposedly inspired

09:00 by the character in 2014, and a pretty lame movie adaptation four years later.

09:05 Why is all this relevant to Sirenhead?

09:07 Because, if you read quite literally any article about him, you’re more than likely to see

09:11 the phrase “the next slender man” pop up.

09:14 And this comparison isn’t without merit – as both have starkly similar points of

09:18 origins and trajectories into popularity.

09:20 The lines between fiction and reality become blurred, and in a metaphorical sense, when

09:25 enough people believe in the urban legend, to them it might as well be real.

09:29 In a more spooky, mystical, supernatural sense, characters like Sirenhead and the Slender

09:33 Man are often associated with the concept of “Tulpas” or “Thought-Forms.”

09:37 This is the idea in paranormal circles – and proponents of Tibetan mysticism – that one

09:42 can quite literally believe a being into autonomous existence through the sheer force of their

09:47 psychic energy.

09:48 When you believe in the idea of Tulpas, the concept of the internet’s collective fear

09:52 bringing Sirenhead to life on some level is a real and tangible concern.

09:56 Sure, it may seem like a far-fetched concept, but is it any more far-fetched than the idea

10:01 of being stalked by a forty-foot extra-dimensional zombie with a siren for a head on the way

10:05 home from work?

10:06 At the end of the day, regardless of what you believe, it can’t be denied that something

10:10 special and terrifying has been brought into the world with Sirenhead.

10:13 Is Sirenhead real?

10:15 Well, ultimately, he’s as real as any urban legend – whether it’s the man with the

10:18 hook hand, the killer in the back seat, or the man making sinister calls from inside

10:22 the house.

10:23 And like any great urban legend, Sirenhead is sure to feel a whole lot more real next

10:28 time you’re walking home alone at night, you hear a faint crackle somewhere in the

10:32 distance, and you could swear you saw something move in the corner of your eye…

10:36 Check out “Russian Sleep Experiment – EXPLAINED” and “How A Meme (Slenderman) Became Real”

10:40 for more on the spookiest corners of the world wide web.

10:43 If, of course, you’re brave enough…
