00:00 Everyone knows about World War  II, but you don’t know everything.

00:04 Here are fifty insane facts about  the largest war in human history.

00:08 #50. The War Before the War

00:10 In the 1930s, the world was still  scarred by the brutal First World War,

00:14 and few western nations didn’t want  any part of another future conflict.

00:17 But they wouldn’t have a choice - because the  future Axis Powers were already brewing plans.

00:22 Imperial Japan had been building its territory  for a while, and its biggest move came in the

00:26 Sino-Japanese War of 1937. This war between China  and Japan went on until the end of World War Two,

00:33 and raised many eyes around the world about  just how ambitious Japan actually was.

00:38 But it wasn’t the only Axis  power planning for wars.

00:41 #49. PR Offensive

00:43 Unlike Japan, Germany was in no state to  think about another war in the 1930s - not

00:48 that it stopped them. The devastating economic  fallout after their loss in the First World War

00:54 was used by the Nazis as a motivation. While  Hitler was rolling out the PR offensive to

00:58 the world with one hand, including hosting the  Olympics, the Nazi leader was also arming up.

01:03 The 1930s were a time of heavy investment  in the military for the Nazis - so when they

01:08 started their march against Europe, everyone was  surprised by just how powerful they had gotten.

01:13 But the Nazis weren’t originally called that.

01:15 #48. Damn…Nasos?

01:18 By now, the term Nazi has become shorthand around  the world for a force of pure evil. But when the

01:24 party first started pitching their gospel of hate,  they were simply called the National Socialist

01:28 party. “Nazis” wasn’t even their preferred  nickname - they called themselves the Nasos.

01:33 So where did the term “Nazi” come from?  It was coined by journalist Konrad Heiden,

01:38 who derived the nickname from a Bavarian word  that was a synonym for stupid or simple-minded.

01:43 Somehow, the Nazis didn’t notice.

01:45 But not everything about the  Nazis was originally evil.

01:48 #47. An Appropriated Symbol

01:51 As the Nazis waved it around Europe  and plastered it on their war machines,

01:54 the swastika became a symbol of evil. Everyone  was horrified - including those for whom it had a

01:59 very different meaning. Although it was usually  aligned differently, the swastika began as an

02:04 ancient religious symbol that got its name  from the Sanskrit word for a hooked cross.

02:08 It typically meant fertility and good fortune,  and was found in ancient civilizations around

02:13 the world from Greece to India. Many  of those who used it in religious rites

02:17 have since called for its removal due to  painful associations with the Nazi regime.

02:21 And as war grew closer, some  interesting experiments began.

02:25 #46. Unleash the Death Ray!

02:28 Robert Watson-Watt was a British engineer  who was a pioneer in radio technology,

02:32 and when word got around of a Nazi  death ray being built, people went to

02:36 him. Was it really possible to build a machine  that could down airplanes using radio waves?

02:40 Watson-Watt looked into it and determined  the answer was no - but his research wasn’t

02:44 all for nothing. In the late 1930s, Watson-Watt’s  research led to quantum leaps in radar technology,

02:50 which made it easier for British troops  to identify German planes and U-Boats.

02:54 But another technique to  avoid war didn’t go so well.

02:57 #45. Pinky Promise?

02:59 The governments of Europe  were desperate to avoid war,

03:02 so they made several concessions to Hitler. The  most significant were territorial concessions

03:06 out of Czechoslovakia - whose leadership was  not even invited to the peace summit! Hitler

03:11 promised to abide by the terms of the treaty -  up until the moment he didn’t. The last straw

03:15 was when he went ahead and invaded Poland,  crossing the red line Britain had set. That

03:20 was enough for Britain to declare war on  September 3rd, 1939, starting World War 2.

03:25 But did Britain itself have a hand in it?

03:28 #44. The Scapegoat?

03:29 For decades since, historians have debated the  legacy of then-Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain,

03:34 whose name has become synonymous with  surrender. His detractors say he gave

03:38 away the store to Hitler for no benefit.  His defenders say he was acting in good

03:43 faith and everyone in Europe was  taken aback by just how ruthless

03:46 Hitler was. But the verdict then was swift -  Chamberlain was ousted before the next general

03:50 election by his party and he was replaced  as Prime Minister by Winston Churchill.

03:54 But Hitler had been planning  for war long before that.

03:58 #43. The Dark Pact

04:00 Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin couldn’t have been  more different. One represented a fascist regime,

04:06 the other was the current leader of the  Communist revolutionaries who took over

04:09 Russia. But they had one thing in common - a  dislike for the democracies of Western Europe.

04:15 In the months before Hitler’s invasion of Poland,

04:17 the two countries signed a non-aggression  pact that detailed how they would divvy up

04:21 Eastern Europe. But like most things with  Hitler, it couldn’t be trusted for long.

04:25 But for the time being, the  war wasn’t much of a war.

04:28 #42. Overwhelmed

04:30 Poland fought hard at the start of the  war, but they were fighting two much

04:34 larger, better-equipped nations that  were determined to overrun them.

04:37 In September and October of 1939  alone, as the invasion began,

04:41 Poland saw its forces devastated. Not only  were 70,000 soldiers killed and more than half

04:46 a million taken captive, but the fight against  the Russians on the other front was just as bad.

04:51 The Poles lost 50,000 men on their eastern front,  while the Russians lost less than a thousand.

04:56 But surprisingly, not everyone  was united in how to respond.

05:00 #41. War or Not?

05:02 Britain declared war on Germany after the  invasion of Poland, but the front was far away

05:07 and the early moves of Britain were less than  inspiring. The Royal Air Force mostly dropped

05:11 propaganda leaflets over Germany in what  would become known as the Phoney War. Both

05:15 in Britain and in America - which was not  involved in the war yet - there were many

05:19 people who wanted no part of another  war and advocated for isolationism.

05:23 But it wasn’t all wins for  Germany and its allies right away.

05:27 #40. Defeat in the North

05:29 Russia was looking to expand its territory, and it  wasn’t long before they launched an invasion into

05:33 the neighboring country of Finland. This would  have given Russia a beachhead in Scandinavia and

05:38 a massive strategic advantage- but the Finns had  another idea. Their well-trained army knew the

05:43 snowy region and had some of the best snipers  in the world. It wasn’t long before the Soviets

05:48 were on the run. This invasion also led to  their expulsion from the League of Nations.

05:52 However, Soviet persistence would eventually  lead to Finland signing a peace settlement.

05:56 But the biggest front yet in  World War 2 was about to launch.

06:00 #39. Mon Dieu!

06:02 Hitler’s march across Europe concerned  his neighbors, but many of them thought

06:06 that he would eventually be satisfied.  Then in 1940 came a line that no one

06:10 could ignore - the invasion of France  as Hitler crossed the Maginot line.

06:14 German forces advanced into France through  Luxembourg and Belgium, overwhelming the

06:18 French troops and leading to mass evacuations.  It was the biggest German advance in the war yet,

06:23 as the Nazi troops used armored vehicles  and planes to gain territory in a hurry.

06:28 It led to one of the biggest  refugee crises in history.

06:31 #38. Chaos at Dunkirk

06:33 With the German troops advancing fast and many  British soldiers stationed in the north of France,

06:38 Allied command decided they had to evacuate - and  fast. There weren’t enough boats and the Army’s

06:42 capabilities were limited, especially with German  troops having trapped troops on the mainland.

06:47 The evacuation effort would eventually  be known as the Miracle of Dunkirk,

06:51 because over eight days over three  hundred thousand troops would be

06:54 evacuated on a fleet of over eight hundred  vessels - many of them civilian ships.

06:58 But the crisis was only beginning.

07:01 #37. The Flood

07:02 France, Belgium, and the Netherlands were  all invaded in 1940 and all fell quickly,

07:07 which led to a massive influx of  refugees fleeing Nazi tyranny.

07:11 Over eight million civilians fled their  home countries, seeking new homes in

07:15 allied or neutral nations - but many wound up in  displaced person camps and struggled to survive.

07:20 While conditions weren’t easy and overcrowding  was a problem in many places - especially with

07:24 the countries on war footing - some refugees were  eager to enlist and turn the tables on the Nazis.

07:29 And as the Nazis marched across Europe,  things on the home front weren’t any better.

07:34 #36. Holy War

07:36 Hitler was a narcissist, and the Nazi  dictator wanted to be praised everywhere.

07:40 Something that raised his ire was the fact  that Roman Catholic schools in Germany didn’t

07:44 have his picture on the wall. Who was this  “Jesus” guy that they kept everywhere instead?

07:49 Hitler’s persecution of Catholics intensified  in Germany, and eventually, he turned his eye

07:53 to the man in charge - Pope Pius XII, who in the  latter days of the war had issued condemnations of

07:58 Hitler. Hitler consulted with a General about  occupying Vatican City and killing the Pope,

08:03 but the General was so shocked he  tipped off the Italians instead.

08:06 There were few institutions the  Germans weren’t trying to destabilize.

08:10 #35. Money Money Money!

08:12 Hitler had an interest in weakening Britain’s  economy to make it harder for them to fight in

08:16 the war. In 1939, he came up with a scheme to  cause hyperinflation in his hated enemy with an

08:21 unlikely weapon - counterfeit cash. He enlisted  prisoners at a German concentration camp and

08:26 put them to work creating countless fake bills  of the British Pound - a whopping $132 million

08:32 worth in that day’s money, or over six billion  today. When introduced to the British economy,

08:37 it caused brief fluctuations but  not the total chaos he hoped for.

08:41 But not all of Hitler’s  schemes worked out for him.

08:44 #34. Shocking! Simply Shocking!

08:47 Hitler was obsessed with the purity of German  culture and cracked down on any expression

08:51 he deemed “degenerate”. Books were burned en  masse, and creators of art thought unpatriotic

08:56 were arrested. Connoisseurs of the arts were  displeased, so Hitler decided to shock everyone

09:01 by holding an exhibition of banned art, called  degenerate art. A massive collection of over

09:06 650 books, paintings, and sculptures were put on  display - and the public came en masse to stare,

09:12 far more than the number of people who  visited the approved Nazi art galleries.

09:15 It wasn’t the only time  Hitler embarrassed himself.

09:18 #33. The Perfect Baby?

09:21 Hitler was also fixated on  the purity of the German race,

09:24 plastering propaganda posters with images of  blonde, blue-eyed children. Which was ironic,

09:28 given that he was a dark-haired Austrian,  but no one was going to tell him that.

09:32 He even started a campaign in 1935 to find the  perfect Aryan baby as a symbol of the country.

09:37 His propaganda minister, Joseph Goebbels, was  put in charge of the search - and oddly chose

09:42 a brunette child whose photo was submitted to him  by Hans Ballin, a prominent photographer. Ballin

09:47 was an anti-Nazi activist who had submitted the  photo of a Jewish child as a way to sabotage the

09:52 Nazi campaign. It worked - a little too well,  as the girl’s family had to flee to Latvia.

09:57 Art had a powerful impact on those  campaigning against the Nazis.

10:01 #32. The Great Dictator

10:03 Across the Atlantic Ocean, the thought of  getting involved in World War II wasn’t

10:07 very popular. The United States had a strong  isolationist bent and many people campaigned

10:12 against any intervention. The news media  wasn’t covering many of Hitler’s atrocities,

10:16 and those trying to raise attention  didn’t have much luck. But there was

10:19 one exception - the legendary silent film star  Charlie Chaplin. The anti-Nazi activist had no

10:25 luck getting studios to fund his anti-Nazi  satire The Great Dictator, so he funded it

10:30 himself at great cost. Hitler was reportedly  not pleased to be portrayed as a buffoon.

10:35 But a far bigger name was working the other side.

10:38 #31. The Pilot

10:40 While the America First movement had a troubled  past, with many of its members coming from groups

10:44 that were initially loyal to Nazi Germany, the  isolationists found hope in a celebrity champion -

10:49 Charles Lindbergh, the famous pilot who was one of  the country’s most famous German-Americans. Many

10:54 people even tried to convince him to run against  President Franklin Delano Roosevelt in 1940,

10:59 with polls showing he was the Republican’s best  candidate. He eventually decided against a run.

11:04 A celebrity with no political experience  deciding to run for President? Crazy talk.

11:08 But the war was about to intensify  - and bring in new fronts.

11:12 #30. Take to the Skies

11:14 After the fall of France, Nazi Germany  turned their attention towards Britain.

11:18 A ground invasion would have been challenging  against the fortified island nation, so Hitler

11:22 focused on bombarding the British into surrender.  But that turned out to be more difficult than

11:26 expected - thanks to the Dowding System. Created  by RAF Commander in Chief Hugh Dowding, it set up

11:33 a reporting system that let the British respond  to air attacks faster. This would streamline

11:37 the process of passing information between the  ground and the air - and foiled many Nazi attacks.

11:42 But it couldn’t foil all of them.

11:44 #29. On the Run

11:46 As the Blitz hit London and other English cities,

11:49 everyone had a role to play to ensure their  survival. Many of the men went off to war,

11:53 while women were left to take on many of their  old responsibilities. As for the children, many

11:57 parents didn’t want them anywhere near the city.  One stray bomb could wipe out an entire family,

12:02 so parents frequently sent their children to  live in the countryside for the duration of the

12:06 bombing, with relatives if they had them - or  willing host families if they could find them.

12:10 This was famously the setup for the CS Lewis  novel The Lion, the Witch, and the Wardrobe.

12:15 But Britain looked like a heavy underdog at first.

12:18 #28. Outmatched

12:20 Britain had never fought an extensive air  war before, and its initial fleet wasn’t

12:24 the most impressive in the world. They had around  thirty-seven hundred planes in the RAF to start,

12:29 with less than half of them being high-speed  fighter aircraft. By comparison, the Luftwaffe

12:33 had almost forty-two hundred total aircraft,

12:36 including over a thousand fighter planes and  almost a thousand bombers. This allowed them

12:40 to hit Great Britain more frequently,  hoping to pound them into submission.

12:43 The reality, though, was rather different.

12:46 #27. The Victor

12:47 While the island nation suffered heavy losses,  including a single brutal day when they lost

12:52 thirty-nine aircraft and fourteen pilots,  Britain’s defense systems were far more

12:56 accurate than Germany’s attacks. Ultimately,  they survived the attack and persisted,

13:00 while Germany suffered far heavier losses  in the Battle of Britain. While the British

13:04 lost over 1,500 aircraft and over five hundred  aircrew, plus over a thousand other casualties,

13:09 the Axis forces lost hundreds more planes  and suffered over three thousand dead.

13:14 And the war was about to change again..

13:16 #26. New Fronts

13:18 It was the middle of 1941, and the German  bombing of Britain had failed to cause the

13:22 nation’s surrender. So naturally, the perfect  thing for Hitler to do was…open up a huge and

13:27 brutal new front in the war? On June 22, 1941,  German forces invaded the Soviet Union in what

13:34 would be known as Operation Barbossa. Why did  Hitler decide to take this risk, in what many

13:38 consider to be the biggest blunder of the  war? It was all about his obsession with

13:43 race - Russia had a lot of land, and Hitler  thought that it would be great real estate

13:46 to fill with German citizens instead  of the supposedly inferior Russians.

13:50 And it wasn’t the only time Hitler  picked a fight he didn’t need to.

13:53 #25. A Costly Declaration

13:56 It was the most famous moment of the war - a day  of infamy. The Japanese forces, looking to deter

14:01 the United States from interfering in their  conquests in the Pacific, had attacked Pearl

14:05 Harbor and devastated the United States Naval  Fleet. The US immediately declared war on Japan

14:10 in retaliation, and those advocating against war  switched their strategy to urging the US to stay

14:16 out of the European front. But they wouldn’t  have that chance, because almost immediately,

14:20 Germany declared war on the United States in  solidarity with its ally Japan. And just like

14:25 that, Hitler had made himself another enemy  that would arrive on the European battlefield.

14:29 US Soldiers were on their way - but fighting  wasn’t the only way to die in such a conflict.

14:34 #24. The First Casualty

14:36 Who was the first US soldier to die in World War  II? Surprisingly, it wasn’t in combat. His name

14:42 was Robert M. Losey, an Iowa native who worked  as an aeronautical meteorologist. He was serving

14:47 as a military attache in 1940 during the German  invasion of Norway. While working to evacuate

14:53 American diplomats from the country he was caught  up in a bombing raid, becoming the first American

14:58 soldier to die on the European front - over a year  and a half before the bombing of Pearl Harbor.

15:03 One unit of soldiers wore uniforms  that would cause a double-take.

15:06 #23. Wrong Uniform

15:09 The 45th Infantry Division  was as American as they came,

15:12 containing soldiers from Oklahoma, New Mexico,  Colorado, and Arizona. Those areas all had a

15:17 large Native American population, which  influenced the unit’s choice of uniform.

15:21 They all wore a pin that contained a proud  eagle - atop a swastika. The Nazi symbol was

15:26 a commonly-used symbol of good luck among Native  American groups and no one raised an eyebrow

15:31 until the 1930s. But there wouldn’t be any  unfortunate cases of mistaken identity when

15:35 the unit was deployed - by 1939 they had replaced  the symbol with a Native American Thunderbird.

15:41 It wasn’t the only pre-war symbol that changed.

15:44 #22. Hitler Loves Amerika?

15:46 Being the dictator of an empire comes with some  advantages - especially when you determine what’s

15:51 essential war spending. Hitler had secret  fortresses and compounds built for himself,

15:55 but he also traveled in style - on his own private  train. It was basically a mobile compound with a

16:01 conference room, a bedroom, and a dining room.  And its initial name? Amerika. Needless to say,

16:06 that became awkward by the time American  forces were the ones targeting the train,

16:10 and the name was eventually  changed to Brandenburg in 1943.

16:14 Some changes might seem…less essential.

16:17 #21. No Hamburgers Here

16:19 America is a melting pot, with multiple  generations of immigrants influencing

16:23 its culture - and its language. And as  the country went to war with Germany,

16:27 people were surprised to realize just  how many common words had German roots.

16:31 Probably the most common example?  The good old-fashioned hamburger,

16:34 which got a name change to “Liberty Steak” in  many locations. Of course, it was the same dish,

16:39 which made it all a little pointless.  Freedom fries to go with your liberty steak?

16:43 Food and drink could be oddly  important to the war effort.

16:46 #20. Gotta Have My Coke

16:48 During the war, US manufacturing  operations focused on the essentials.

16:52 They made sure the troops  had ammo, armor, supplies,

16:55 and…soda? The Coca-Cola Company’s signature drink  was beloved by the troops, and the company showed

17:00 its support for the boys in uniform by setting up  manufacturing plants in North Africa. This allowed

17:04 them to ship millions of bottles of Coke across  the Mediterranean to the soldiers - and helped

17:08 to improve the company’s image and cemented the  brand as a household name for years to come..

17:13 But the tide of battle was turning  - and it was getting bloody.

17:17 #19. The Worst Battle

17:19 Hitler had made a critical misjudgment when he  invaded Russia - Napoleon could have told him

17:23 that you never invade Russia! But neither side was  prepared for just how brutal that front would be.

17:28 The German forces were superior and were able  to inflict massive casualties on the Russians,

17:33 with the country suffering a shocking 21 million  casualties by the end of the war. But they were

17:37 fighting on their own turf, had superior numbers,  and inflicted massive pain on the Germans - with

17:43 eighty percent of German casualties in  the war coming from the Eastern Front.

17:46 And as the war turned against him,  Hitler became increasingly paranoid.

17:50 #18. Death in the Ranks

17:52 Hitler was surrounded by powerful people  who advised him on the war effort - but

17:56 he didn’t like the advice he was hearing. It  was very common for him to turn on people who

18:00 questioned him and cast them out of the party,  with even elite Nazi officials like Wernher Von

18:05 Braun finding themselves on the outs in  the last days of the war. Most famously,

18:09 he executed a shocking eighty-four  of his Generals over the course of

18:12 the war - although most of them were actually  plotting against him, and can you blame them?

18:17 Most famously, Hitler was  nearly killed by his own men.

18:21 #17. Operation Valkyrie

18:23 In the last year of the war, Hitler was becoming  increasingly erratic, and many of his military

18:27 inner circle believed he was actively  sabotaging the war effort. For one thing,

18:31 he kept on killing his own scientists. Led by  Claus Von Stauffenberg, a group of Nazi insiders

18:36 planned to kill Hitler with a bomb plot at his  secret compound. But a sudden change in seating

18:41 arrangements led to the bomb only injuring Hitler,  and most of the collaborators being executed. Even

18:47 his renowned General Erwin Rommel was caught up in  it, bringing a sudden end to his military career.

18:52 Some of Hitler’s plans were  just genuinely bizarre.

18:56 #16. Bugging England

18:58 In the early days of the war, the Nazis  were considering unconventional attacks

19:01 on their enemy - and one tactic was  smaller than usual, with more legs.

19:05 The Nazis looked at weaponizing the Colorado  Potato Beetle, a notorious pest of potato

19:10 crops. They would drop a mass number of the  bugs on British farmland, devastating their

19:15 food supplies and starving the island nation into  surrender. But the plan was ultimately dropped

19:19 for one reason - it wasn’t feasible to collect  the forty million bugs needed for the mission.

19:24 But there were some lines  even Hitler wouldn’t cross.

19:27 #15. Even Evil Has Standards

19:29 The Nazi scientists were hard at work  on deadly biological weapons, including

19:33 enhanced versions of Typhoid and Cholera. However,  when they presented them to the Nazi leader, he

19:38 didn’t approve and most of the projects never saw  the light of day. What offended him about these

19:43 plans? Hitler had no problem killing millions of  civilians - but he was also a World War I veteran,

19:48 and that war had brutal biological and chemical  warfare. Maybe it hit a little too close to home.

19:54 But far more powerful weapons were in development.

19:57 #14. The Nazi A-Bomb?

20:00 It was one of the most persistent rumors after  the war. Did the United States just barely beat

20:04 the Nazis to the Atom bomb? The answer is…not  really. The Nazis weren’t close to finishing a

20:09 nuclear weapon, but that didn’t mean they didn’t  make progress on weapons of mass destruction.

20:13 The Nazis had Uranium and the Japanese  could get closer to the US mainland,

20:17 so the plan was to hit the west coast with  a conventional bomb packed with uranium. But

20:22 the plan never came to fruition, and the German  uranium may have eventually wound up in US hands.

20:26 But across the ocean on the US  mainland, development was heating up.

20:30 #13. The Canadian Bomb?

20:33 Canada was ahead of the US  in the war in a lot of ways,

20:36 entering the Allied Powers while the US was  still neutral. They even had their own atom

20:40 bomb project with Britain, called the Tube  Allows project. It would eventually merge

20:44 with the United States Manhattan Project  to speed up development, with both sides

20:47 promising to share all their information. But  the US didn’t live up to its end of the deal,

20:51 and it would be another seven years before  Britain successfully developed their own bomb.

20:56 And ultimately, the first bomb  detonated wasn’t in combat.

20:59 #12. It’s a Go

21:01 The hope was that the nuclear bomb would  lead to the end of the war by delivering

21:04 a massive punch to the Axis powers. It took a  lot of money and manpower to build the bomb,

21:09 and the Allies wanted to be sure that  it would work before dropping it.

21:12 The first successful test actually took place  on US soil, at a testing range in a New Mexico

21:16 desert. It was a massive success - and it  horrified one of the men responsible for it,

21:21 as Oppenheimer quoted a line from a Hindu sacred  text - “I have become death, destroyer of worlds”.

21:27 But there was a twist to  the first two bombs dropped.

21:30 #11. Alike but Different

21:32 The first two nuclear bombs detonated in combat -  and the only ones so far - were nicknamed Fat Man

21:38 and Little Boy. But their size and designations  weren’t the only differences between these two

21:42 bombs. They actually used entirely different  mechanisms, with Little Boy being powered by

21:47 the fission of uranium-235, while Fat Man - which  was forty percent more powerful - used plutonium.

21:53 Now, let’s get into some truly  shocking facts about the war.

21:56 #10. The Good Hitler?

21:58 William Patrick Stuart-Houston was,  by all accounts, a normal British lad.

22:02 Growing up in Liverpool, he would eventually  immigrate to the United States and serve in

22:06 the US Navy. But he had a secret - his father’s  name was Alois Hitler Jr, Hitler’s half-brother.

22:13 Not only would he fight for the United  States against his mad uncle’s empire,

22:16 but he would be awarded the Purple Heart  after being wounded in combat - just

22:20 another noble German-American doing  his part against the Axis Powers.

22:24 The Nazis used all sorts of unusual  tactics to fund the war effort.

22:28 #9. Who Was Max Heiliger?

22:30 The main purpose behind the Nazi persecution of  the Jewish people was Hitler’s obsession with

22:34 race science, but the Nazis weren’t above  benefiting from it. They looted money,

22:39 gold, and jewelry from the Jews they arrested  and deported. But because many countries were

22:43 freezing the Nazis out of their banking  systems, the SS created a bank account

22:47 under the name Max Heiliger that would  allow them to transfer assets undetected.

22:52 But in some ways the threat of the  Nazi death machine outlasted the Nazis.

22:56 #8. Unholy Ground

22:58 The Bergen-Belsen concentration  camp was a brutal and deadly place

23:02 where countless people died. It wasn’t  an extermination camp like some,

23:06 but the rampant spread of disease and lack of  medical care led to many casualties - including

23:10 Anne Frank. When the camp was liberated in  1945, the plague Typhus was so widespread

23:15 that the Allies decided to burn the place  to the ground to contain the spread.

23:19 But amid the horror, there were heroes.

23:21 #7. The Saviors

23:23 Most countries that were invaded by the Nazis  quickly saw their Jewish community rounded up

23:27 and deported or killed. But not Denmark. Denmark  had quickly surrendered to the Nazis and allowed

23:32 themselves to be occupied, and the lack of  resistance meant the Nazis gave them more

23:36 autonomy. That gave them several years before  the Nazis began cracking down, and the Danes

23:40 were able to smuggle the vast majority of  their Jewish population to neutral Sweden.

23:44 But sometimes, all it takes is one good man.

23:47 #6. The Heroism of Sgt. Edmonds

23:50 The Nazis were notorious for violating  the laws governing prisoners of war,

23:54 especially when it came to Jewish soldiers.  When they captured American troops,

23:58 they would demand the Jews among them  be singled out so they could be taken

24:01 to concentration camps or killed. But they  hadn’t met Master Sergeant Roderick Edmonds.

24:06 When the Army man was ordered to identify the  Jews among the captured POWs, he boldly said

24:10 that they were all Jews. While this put the  entire unit at risk, the Nazis were scared off

24:15 by the threat of being prosecuted for war  crimes. Edmonds may have saved as many as

24:19 three hundred people and was eventually honored  as one of Israel’s Righteous Among the Nations.

24:23 Some facts of the war are hard to believe.

24:25 #5. The Old College Try

24:28 If any Bostonians were fighting the Nazis and saw  them on the march, they might get an odd sense of

24:33 deja vu. Why does the Nazi “Sieg Heil” march song  sound almost exactly like the Harvard fight song?

24:39 That’s because the composer actually  attended Harvard University - and amid

24:42 the Nazis’ many crimes, a little plagiarism  probably wasn’t high on anyone’s list.

24:46 For some people, the war went on and on.

24:49 #4. The Peace That Wasn’t

24:52 If the war hadn’t ended when it did due to the  collapse of Nazi Germany and the strikes on Japan,

24:56 it’s likely there would have been  a new front as the Soviet Union

25:00 invaded Japan. While this war never reached  the scale it could have, the two countries

25:04 were still at war - and still technically are.  A formal peace treaty was never signed between

25:09 the two of them - and negotiations fell apart in  2000 over some islands that Russia had seized.

25:14 But even amid the carnage, there was some hope.

25:17 #3. In the Blood

25:18 While World War II was the most  bloody war in human history,

25:22 it did have a higher number of soldiers who  actually came home after surviving serious

25:26 injuries. What set this war apart? It was the  advance in medical technology and one technique

25:31 in particular. Blood transfusions  had been around for a long time,

25:34 but they were consistently used in combat for the  first time in this war - and it saved many lives.

25:40 And in the fog of war, things got weird.

25:42 #2. The Parachuting Nazi

25:44 The year was 1941, and Germany was still  confident about victory. So confident,

25:49 in fact, that they sent one of their top men  into the UK to negotiate Britain’s surrender.

25:54 Rudolf Hess, Hitler’s deputy, parachuted into  Scotland intending to return a hero - and

25:58 instead was promptly arrested. He was kept as  a prisoner of war for the rest of the war until

26:02 he was sent to Nuremberg to answer for his  crimes, where he received a life sentence.

26:07 But the heroes of World War II  included some surprising names.

26:10 #1. The Big Guns

26:12 Is this a list of soldiers, or a marquee?  World War II had a massive draft,

26:17 and many of Hollywood’s most famous names  wound up strapping on their army greens.

26:21 Among the people who would later become  famous or took a break from the movies

26:25 included Walter Matthau, Peter Fonda,  David Niven, and Christopher Lee. One

26:30 name surprisingly absent? All-American cowboy John  Wayne, who was excused due to a football injury.

26:36 If you’re looking for more secrets  of the last days of the war,

26:39 check out “What Actually Happened to Nazi Leaders  After World War 2?” or watch this video instead.

docs.text:
00:03 Everyone has their own ways of preparing

00:05 for doomsday. Some people would rather

00:07 not think about it while the world burns

00:09 down around them. Others have a spot

00:11 reserved in one of the most luxurious

00:12 doomsday bunkers in the world. One

00:14 family in a small New England town is

00:16 stockpiling honeybees. And at the very

00:18 top of the planet in the frigid

00:19 temperatures of the Arctic, a select few

00:21 maintain a vault that could contain

00:23 humanity's last hope for survival. Let's

00:25 start with the best of the best, or at

00:27 least the richest of the rich. What do

00:29 the super rich get when they buy into

00:31 the Oppidum complex in the Czech

00:33 Republic? The answer is pretty much

00:35 anything they want. The architects of

00:37 the Oppidum have not only created a

00:39 doomsday shelter, but a doomsday

00:40 paradise. The complex sits in a quiet

00:43 valley protected by natural features and

00:45 a solid concrete wall. The walls are so

00:48 high that the only way to see inside of

00:49 the complex is by aerial view or

00:51 entering through one of the secret

00:53 entrances. The property itself is

00:54 323,000 square feet in size, but that

00:57 doesn't even count most of the living

00:59 space deep underground. There are plenty

01:01 of things to do on the surface of the

01:02 compound, but if the outside world is

01:04 irradiated from nuclear war or a super

01:06 volcano blocks the sun for hundreds of

01:08 years, the residents of Oppidum will

01:10 spend most of their time in the two

01:12 underground levels of this doomsday

01:13 community. Each of these levels is

01:15 77,500

01:17 square feet with 13-foot high ceilings.

01:19 So, how did the super rich prepare for

01:21 their doomsday scenario? By adding all

01:23 of the comforts they now enjoy to their

01:25 secure underground community at Oppidum.

01:28 To keep their clients comfortable and

01:29 ensure they have everything they would

01:31 ever need, Oppidum has added some key

01:33 components at their underground

01:34 facility. There's a garden that is grown

01:36 using artificial lights, which are

01:38 programmed to imitate the sun as closely

01:39 as possible. Of course, they need to

01:41 include a spa, a swimming pool, and a

01:43 library, but no doomsday shelter for the

01:46 super rich would be complete without

01:47 installing a theater complex complete

01:49 with every movie ever made. The

01:51 underground compound will also contain

01:53 the basics such as a medical facility

01:55 and all the necessary supplies to keep

01:57 the community healthy. But, it also

01:58 includes custom vaults, so the residents

02:00 can store their private art collections

02:02 and any other valuables they don't want

02:04 to lose during the end of the world.

02:05 There will also be a full-service

02:07 restaurant and a fully stocked wine

02:08 cellar to keep everyone happy and drunk.

02:11 The price tag for reserving a spot at

02:12 Albi Dume is not advertised, which means

02:14 you'd have to contact them directly to

02:16 find out. And if you have to ask the

02:18 price, you probably can't afford it.

02:20 Obviously, this is not how most people

02:22 prep for doomsday, but when you have a

02:23 ton of money, you can go all out

02:25 preparing for the end of the world.

02:26 However, there are people who do some

02:28 pretty insane things to prepare for

02:29 doomsday, even if they don't have a huge

02:31 budget. One former high school teacher

02:33 in Ontario named Bruce Beach came up

02:35 with an ingenious doomsday plan using

02:37 recycled school buses. He first started

02:39 planning for doomsday in the 1960s

02:41 during the Cuban Missile Crisis, but

02:42 even after we made it through the Cold

02:44 War, he continued to build onto his

02:46 doomsday plan. Beach found the best way

02:48 to utilize abandoned school buses from

02:49 the school district he worked at was to

02:51 repurpose them as a doomsday bunker. He

02:53 would purchase them from the town and

02:55 bury them underground. As Beach

02:56 collected more and more buses, he

02:58 connected them like Legos, forming a

03:00 labyrinth of tunnels. In the 1980s, he

03:02 finished his school bus shelter and

03:03 named it Ark II. The whole complex is

03:06 made up of 42 school buses that are

03:08 completely buried underground with a

03:09 secure opening to enter the doomsday

03:11 bunker. He was so proud of his

03:13 accomplishment, he even rented out his

03:14 school bus shelter to people to stay in

03:16 like an Airbnb. Ark II has a kitchen, a

03:19 shower, and several bedrooms. One unique

03:21 trait that Beach has that many doomsday

03:23 preppers don't is generosity. He even

03:25 has said that people have called him up

03:27 just to ask if they had a space in Ark

03:28 II for them if the world came to an end.

03:31 He always responded that he did. This

03:33 might be a uniquely Canadian trait as

03:35 it's very rare for someone to offer

03:36 shelter to others in their doomsday

03:38 shelter. One man in China is taking a

03:40 different approach using the Ark name.

03:42 Instead of reusing buses, he's taking a

03:43 page out of the Bible. Liu Qianghai has

03:46 spent $160,000

03:48 on materials to build up a ship

03:49 reminiscent of Noah's Ark. Except a

204:07 one crazy drug smuggler who thought

204:09 literal holy water would be the best

204:11 vector for his smuggling. This actually

204:13 happened in 2008 when customs caught

204:15 Warren Maynard, a 50-year-old New York

204:18 man, trying to sneak dozens of bottles

204:20 of ketamine-laced water that he claimed

204:22 was holy water. While he wasn't

204:25 technically right in that regard, a

204:27 bottle of water mixed with a powerful

204:28 hallucinogen certainly might make a

204:30 person feel like they're a little closer

204:32 to the almighty. He wasn't even the only

204:34 smuggler to use religion as a shield for

204:36 his sinister activities. In March 2020,

204:38 a Cincinnati customs and border patrol

204:40 team intercepted a collection of

204:42 religious paintings that just so

204:44 happened to contain 9.2 lb of meth with

204:47 a street value of $16,720.

204:50 Is nothing sacred anymore? And because

204:52 subtlety is dead, Bernardino

204:54 Garcia-Cordova, a drug trafficker also

204:56 known as the spider, imported a statue

204:59 of Jesus that was literally made from

205:01 $30,000 worth of cocaine. And this isn't

205:04 just a classy ornament for drug lords

205:06 who also happen to be devout Catholics.

205:08 DEA spokesperson Steven Robertson said

205:11 the statue could have been broken down

205:12 with water, sifted, and then strained to

205:15 get the all-too-precious powder into

205:17 street sale form. It's clear that if you

205:19 want to be successful in this field of

205:20 criminality, you got to use your head.

205:23 But there are right and wrong ways to

205:24 use your head, as two British women aged

205:26 17 and 25 found out when they engaged in

205:29 a hairbrained scheme to smuggle $220,000

205:32 worth of cocaine stitched to wigs. They

205:35 were apparently paid only 4,000 pounds

205:37 to be the mules in this scheme, which

205:39 probably wasn't worth the risk or the

205:41 many, many, many years in prison they

205:43 were likely handed after being caught by

205:45 the Jamaican authorities and sent back

205:47 to the UK. This seems to be a pretty

205:49 embarrassing way to go down, but at

205:51 least those two anonymous British drug

205:53 mules aren't alone. In 2011, a 12-person

205:55 drug ring was arrested in Philadelphia

205:58 for a more complex but still equally

206:00 stupid scheme. They were smuggling drugs

206:02 out of Panama by sewing the drug packets

206:04 into wigs and weaves before accepting

206:06 the packages in the US and passing the

206:09 drugs over to street-level dealers in

206:10 not one, not two, but three different

206:13 states. Of all the flaws in their plan,

206:15 a lack of ambition was not one of them.

206:18 Sometimes it isn't the quantity of drugs

206:20 smuggled that surprises you, but the

206:21 location. Fellas, we warn you, this one

206:25 is going to make you squirm. Two

206:26 different men, Antoine Banks in 2011 and

206:29 later Joshua Hair in 2016, were both

206:32 arrested for hiding tiny drug packets

206:34 under their foreskins. We here at The

206:36 Infographics Show are not entirely sure

206:38 that any kind of payment would be worth

206:40 going through that particular ordeal.

206:42 Let's get away from that nightmare as

206:44 soon as possible and instead talk about

206:46 horses. Don't worry, equestrians, we're

206:48 not going to tell you anyone's cutting

206:49 open horses. Well, not yet, anyway. In

206:52 this 2017 story of a deranged drug

206:54 distribution, customs seized 1.2 million

206:57 dollars worth of liquid meth that an

206:59 enterprising 31-year-old woman had

207:01 hidden in horse shampoo bottles. Do we

207:04 think this is a good idea? Neigh. Was

207:06 that too corny? Sorry. We'll show

207:08 ourselves out through the stable. If all

207:10 this has left you all feeling a little

207:11 disturbed, please take a second to rest.

207:13 How about a snack? Maybe some sweet

207:16 delicious strawberry jam. Just make sure

207:18 that the jam didn't come from this

207:19 particular shipment of jam that was

207:21 intercepted by Customs and Border Patrol

207:23 back in Arizona in 2016. A 51-year-old

207:27 trucker was caught with 6,500 lb of

207:29 contraband marijuana valued at $3.25

207:32 million

207:33 hidden inside vats of strawberry jam.

207:36 Yummy. Food products can be a common

207:39 vector for drug smuggling. In January

207:41 2017, a Southern Border Patrol bust

207:43 revealed huge quantities of cocaine

207:46 hidden in cans of tuna and corn. In

207:48 Melbourne, Australia, Customs agents

207:50 found 5 tons of ecstasy hidden in tins

207:53 disguised as canned tomatoes. But even

207:55 the fruits and vegetables themselves

207:56 aren't safe. The infamous Sinaloa drug

207:59 cartel has been known to stuff

208:00 plantains, cucumbers, and coconuts with

208:02 drugs. The same can be said of burritos,

208:05 chili peppers, fake carrots, soda cans,

208:07 candy, yams, and extremely unconvincing

208:10 packs of limes, which were actually just

208:12 printed photos of limes wrapped around

208:14 larger bricks of marijuana with a street

208:16 value of half a million dollars. Believe

208:19 us, this is a lot more appealing than

208:21 the Texas drug smugglers who hid

208:23 $459,000

208:24 worth of cocaine and marijuana in

208:26 barrels of grease. Talk about slipping

208:29 Customs. A similarly unappealing

208:31 smuggling scheme unfolded in Thailand,

208:33 where a popular variation of

208:35 methamphetamine known as yaba,

208:37 translated literally to crazy drug, has

208:39 taken the scene by storm. One of the

208:41 weirdest ways of smuggling yaba has been

208:43 hiding it in the bodies of dead bugs.

208:46 Though personally, we find ferrying

208:47 around shipments of dead bugs pretty

208:49 weird and suspicious in its own right.

208:51 Don't you agree? You think it's too

208:53 risky or too obvious to smuggle drugs

208:55 inside a car, but professional drug

208:57 smugglers still find bizarre and novel

208:59 ways to do it. One bust in early 2017

209:02 found a record-breaking $2 million worth

209:04 of methamphetamine in packs under the

209:06 dashboard of a Volkswagen Jetta. A white

209:09 sedan also had $1.3 million of cocaine

209:12 stashed in a secret compartment hidden

209:14 behind the license plate. And who could

209:16 forget the pickup truck that hid

209:18 $800,000 worth of marijuana in a secret

209:20 compartment beneath its flatbed. And

209:22 hey, just in case you were worried that

209:24 there was really really any part of a

209:25 vehicle that a drug smuggler couldn't

209:27 turn into a hiding place, a smuggler at

209:29 the Presidio border hid half a million

209:31 dollars in meth above the gas tank of a

209:33 1999 Mercedes-Benz. And now we

209:36 understand the true secret of being able

209:38 to afford a Mercedes-Benz. Wow. But not

209:41 every drug smuggler about town is

209:43 willing to settle for something that

209:44 mundane. Some drug lords truly want to

209:47 live up to their Bond villain media

209:48 image. One way of doing that is by

209:50 investing in a six-man drug smuggling

209:52 submarine, or drug marine, if you will.

209:55 The submarine, powered by diesel and

209:56 seized in Ecuador in 2010, was designed

209:59 to carry over 10 metric tons of drugs.

210:01 And while it may have been intercepted

210:03 and caught in the end, nobody could deny

210:05 it is incredibly theatrical. But what if

210:07 you want to go old school? We're talking

210:09 World War I old school. In Colombia,

210:12 there have been documented cases of

210:14 carrier pigeons being used to transport

210:16 small pouches of marijuana and crack.

210:18 Like sending wartime messages, but far

210:20 more illegal. How about we go even older

210:23 school? This time we're talking about

210:25 medieval old school. Catapults and

210:27 trebuchets are siege weapons used for

210:29 taking down castles, but drug cartels

210:31 have found a new purpose for them,

210:33 flinging marijuana buds across the

210:35 border so they can start their own

210:36 free-range weed farms in the US. It's

210:39 forced border agents to keep an eye on

210:40 the land around the fence for any

210:42 suspicious seedlings. Some people don't

210:44 care for the classics, though. They just

210:46 want to keep it cutting edge, such as

210:48 one anonymous drug smuggler who used a

210:50 drone to smuggle 13 pounds of meth

210:52 across the border between San Diego and

210:53 Tijuana, Mexico. Border Patrol

210:55 intercepted the drone pretty easily and

210:57 arrested the smuggler who'd later be

210:59 sentenced to 12 years in prison for his

211:01 trouble. Perhaps it's better to stick to

211:03 the classics and invest in a sturdy,

211:05 reliable trebuchet instead. It still

211:07 somehow gets crazier from here though.

211:10 You may remember such meme movies as the

211:12 2006 Samuel L. Jackson classic Snakes on

211:15 a Plane and the 2023 Elizabeth Banks

211:18 classic Cocaine Bear. But what if their

211:21 powers combined into snakes on a plane

211:23 on cocaine? Except this isn't a movie,

211:25 it was real and it happened in 1993 when

211:28 80 lb of cocaine was forced into the

211:30 bellies of 223 live snakes by drug

211:33 smugglers. Crazy antics ensued, the

211:35 snakes somehow escaped causing chaos

211:37 throughout the plane until one

211:39 quick-thinking cop escorting an

211:41 important witness to the stand was able

211:43 to take control of the situation and

211:45 scene. Snakes on a plane on cocaine

211:48 coming to your local cinemas next fall.

211:50 Unfortunately, the reality didn't follow

211:52 our little movie script. The snakes

211:54 actually all died from the trauma, much

211:56 like the bear that inspired Cocaine

211:58 Bear. But to a drug smuggler sometimes a

212:00 dead animal can be just as useful as a

212:02 live one. The Mexico City drug cartel

212:04 split a ton of cocaine between 20 dead

212:07 sharks which they then tried to sneak

212:09 into the United States. Much like the

212:11 dead bugs full of yaba back in Thailand.

212:14 We can't help but wonder if hiding

212:16 cocaine in a bizarre shipment of 20 dead

212:18 sharks might just draw too much unwanted

212:20 attention to your secret cargo. But hey,

212:23 we just make infotainment videos on

212:25 YouTube. Who are we to tell El Chapo how

212:27 to do his job? Just please don't send

212:29 any sicarios our way, okay? On the less

212:32 ambitious side of things, in 2007 some

212:35 small-time New Zealand criminals tried

212:36 to get drugs to their incarcerated

212:38 friends by shoving the drugs into dead

212:41 birds and throwing them over the prison

212:43 walls. In 2001, a A named Richard Reed

212:46 made going to the airport harder for all

212:48 of us when he tried and failed to

212:50 detonate a bomb inside a shoe while on

212:52 an airplane. But, it wasn't just Mr.

212:54 Reid's fault. The TSA soon got another

212:56 reason to check your smelly sneakers. A

212:58 man was busted at JFK in New York for

213:00 allegedly trying to smuggle cocaine in

213:02 his shoes. He had 4 lb of cocaine hidden

213:05 between six pairs of shoes in his

213:07 luggage. He was hoping to make $67,000

213:09 on this contraband, and instead all he

213:11 got was federal narcotics charges from

213:13 Homeland Security. High risk, no reward.

213:16 A northern Spanish gang of drug

213:18 traffickers took shoe smuggled drugs to

213:20 a whole new level by also throwing

213:22 counterfeiting on top. They created

213:24 high-quality knockoffs of Manolo Blahnik

213:27 stiletto shoes held together with

213:29 cocaine paste. Each pair of shoes sold

213:31 for $75,000,

213:33 which for those keeping track is more

213:35 than the previous guy at JFK Airport

213:37 stood to gain from all six of his

213:38 life-ruining cocaine shoes. In 2018,

213:41 Portuguese airport security couldn't

213:43 help but notice an unusually kicked-up

213:45 Brazilian man strolling through Lisbon

213:47 International Airport. Nobody will ever

213:49 know what was going through their heads

213:51 when they pulled that man aside and

213:52 asked him to drop his trousers and bare

213:54 his buttocks. But, in that moment they

213:56 uncovered a drug smuggler. He was hiding

213:59 a kilogram of cocaine inside a pair of

214:01 fake butt cheeks. That's a badonkadonk.

214:04 But, sometimes smugglers go even further

214:06 than that, such as a Colombian woman

214:09 arrested in Germany in 2016 whom customs

214:12 noticed had fresh scars beneath her

214:14 breasts. This turned out to be because

214:16 she was hiding a kilogram of cocaine

214:18 inside her breast implants. I guess you

214:20 could say we saved the breast for last.

214:23 Now, watch what happens to your body

214:25 when smoking weed or check out Devil's

214:27 Breath, world's scariest drug.

• Title: Modern Cyber Security Is DEAD. The $3300 BILLION Quantum COLLAPSE.

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Somewhere in secure vaults, encrypted  messages intercepted over the last decade

00:04 are being stored and cataloged. And the timer to unlock them

00:07 is heading toward zero. Most people assume their

00:10 encrypted data is safe forever. It isn't.  Intelligence agencies are harvesting it,

00:15 so they can decrypt it later. They’re just  waiting for a faster computer to read them.

00:20 If they're right, the fallout  won't stop at private messages.

00:23 The scenarios security experts worry about include  failing infrastructure, frozen financial markets,

00:29 and a world where passwords suddenly mean nothing. The most valuable data breach in history

00:33 hasn't happened… yet.

00:35 The threat of quantum computing  is a real threat to society.

00:39 These computers use the laws of quantum  mechanics to solve problems that would

00:42 take today's machines millions of years. And  theoretically they're exceptionally good at it.

00:47 In 2024, the Global Risk Institute surveyed  industry experts. They estimated a 19% to

00:52 34% chance that, by 2034, a quantum computer  powerful enough to break modern encryption

00:58 will exist. The day it does, the systems  protecting everything from bank transfers

01:03 to government networks become vulnerable. This is how it plays out when the clock hits zero.

01:08 At T-minus 0, the first thing to fail is identity. Every secure website, banking app,

01:14 software update, and VPN relies on digital  certificates. They’re essentially online ID

01:19 cards that prove something is who it claims to be. Right now, those certificates are protected by

01:24 encryption so strong that even the world's  fastest supercomputers would need longer

01:28 than the age of the universe to crack them. But a quantum computer would change that.

01:33 Suddenly, websites can be impersonated. A fake  software update could be sent to millions of

01:38 computers, and servers, and every one of them  would accept it as real. Messages seem to come

01:43 from trusted sources when they’re really spam. It’s all because trust on the internet is built in

01:48 layers. Breaking a single trusted authority  can affect a number of systems below it.

01:53 At T-plus 2 hours, the damage  reaches the physical world.

01:57 Much of the power grid still runs on decades-old  control systems built for an era when fake

02:02 commands weren't a realistic threat. Now those commands can be imitated.

02:06 Safety relays begin tripping, shutting down  substations and transmission lines in response

02:11 to instructions it believes are legitimate. Surges  begin to blow up substations. Grid operators are

02:17 plunged into a no-win situation.They’re forced to  choose between trusting systems they can no longer

02:22 verify or run everything by hand. That’s when the blackouts hit.

02:27 Cities go dark. Hospitals and  other critical infrastructure

02:30 are forced to rely on backup generators.  No software patch is bringing this back.

02:35 Recovery happens one section at a time. When the clock hits T-plus 12 hours,

02:41 money stops moving. The global financial system depends

02:44 on secure digital messages to verify transfers  between banks. Every day, the SWIFT system routes

02:50 around $5 trillion in transfers. That daily flow  is larger than the entire yearly output of Japan.

02:57 Now it has collapsed. Banks can’t be certain that

03:00 transfers are real. Trading floors freeze.  The paperwork that lets goods cross borders

03:05 stops clearing, and supply chains seize up.  No firm will take on risk it can’t verify.

03:10 In early 2026, researchers at Citi modeled  what would happen if just one of America's

03:15 5 largest banks lost access to the system  that moves money between institutions. A

03:21 single day attack could cost $2 trillion to  $3.3 trillion. That is a 10% to 17% drop in

03:28 US output. A loss that size does not clear in a  day. The country goes into a 6-month recession.

03:35 That’s just one bank. In a single day.

03:38 When T-plus 48 hours arrives,  the second shock comes with it.

03:42 For years, governments and intelligence agencies

03:44 have been gathering encrypted data that  remained locked behind security walls.

03:48 Those walls are gone. Archived emails, messages, documents,

03:52 and communications that were once deemed secure  suddenly become accessible. At the same time,

03:57 systems across factories, logistics, and  communications networks continue receiving

04:02 malicious updates. The internet has gone  into survival mode. Nothing can be trusted.

04:07 To most people, none of this looks like  cryptography. A card gets declined for

04:11 no obvious reason. Hospitals go back to  paperwork. Your banking app still works.

04:16 It just can't tell the difference between  your bank and someone pretending to be it.

04:20 That little padlock on the address bar was  doing far more than most people realized.

04:25 It was holding the internet together. This disaster doesn't begin the

04:28 day the quantum computer arrives. It happened years before that,

04:32 while nobody was paying attention.

04:34 In 2021, the NSA openly admitted that  adversaries were already harvesting

04:38 encrypted data. They were just waiting for the  key to open it. But they aren’t alone. Other

04:43 global intelligence agencies are doing the  same thing. No one wants to be left behind.

04:48 Every day, vast amounts of the world's data flow  through undersea cables stretching across oceans.

04:53 It’s a bottleneck of information and that  makes them the ideal place to capture it.

04:58 At this point, most people have the  same reaction: "Can't we just update the

05:02 encryption when quantum computers arrive?" That works for future data. But for the

05:07 information that’s already out there? It’s too late.

05:10 Anything intercepted today can be stored for years  and decrypted later. Once someone has a copy, you

05:16 don't get to take it back. That's what makes this  threat different from a normal cybersecurity flaw.

05:21 When a vulnerability is discovered, you patch it  and move on. But now, the data can be stolen first

05:26 and decrypted later. Which means the clock isn't  ticking from the day the quantum computer arrives.

05:32 It's ticking from the day  the information was sent.

05:35 The real prize isn’t the conversations in  your group chats. It’s state secrets, weapons

05:40 designs and financial arrangements. The things  that can become leverage in a few years time.

05:45 It’s a long term heist. Something that doesn’t  need to succeed immediately. Everything encrypted

05:50 today can be copied in bulk and stored. That changes everything.

05:54 Storage is getting cheaper. Keeping large  tranches of stolen data is no longer an issue.

05:59 For a state-level actor, keeping vast archives of  intercepted traffic costs almost nothing compared

06:04 to the value of what might be unlocked. So the strategy is simple.

06:08 Take everything now and  decide later what it’s worth.

06:11 No one outside those systems knows what  has already been collected. And there’s

06:15 no obvious way to tell. Because nothing  looks broken as the data is still there.

06:20 It just has an invisible copy somewhere else.

06:23 To find out why all this data

06:25 might be at risk, you have to understand  the lock that is supposed to protect it.

06:29 That lock depends on one  bizarre property of numbers.

06:33 Take two huge numbers and multiply  them together. A computer can do it

06:38 in a fraction of a second. But  when you start with the answer,

06:40 figuring out which two numbers created  it can take around 300 trillion years.

06:46 That’s what the security  of the internet relies on.

06:48 It's the reason why you can enter a credit card  number on a website and trust that nobody can

06:54 steal it. The same principle protects  your bank login, your private messages,

06:58 and the chip inside your passport. For decades,  it’s worked, because nothing could reverse that

07:03 answer fast enough to matter. But a quantum computer can.

07:06 There is a method, specifically designed for these  machines, called Shor's algorithm. It does the one

07:12 thing ordinary computers never could. It  finds hidden patterns inside those giant

07:16 numbers and uses them to reverse the process. The problem was something called qubits,

07:22 the quantum equivalent of the bits inside  a normal computer. Unlike ordinary bits,

07:26 qubits are incredibly fragile, and you  need huge numbers of them working together

07:31 to unlock a quantum computer's full power. Early estimates suggested you would need tens of

07:35 millions of qubits to threaten modern encryption.  Nobody had built more than a few hundred.

07:41 Then the estimates started to fall. In May 2025, a Google researcher showed

07:45 that the job might be done with fewer than 1  million qubits. That’s 20 times fewer than his

07:51 own estimate just 6 years earlier. Just one  year later, the figure dropped below 100,000.

07:57 None of this means the supercomputer exists  today. The best quantum chips on earth still run

08:02 somewhere between 100 and 1,000 usable qubits,  and they’re still fragile and error-prone.

08:07 IBM`s largest quantum computer holds just over  1,100 of them, still nowhere enough to break

08:13 encryption on the scale required. Building one  big and stable enough to break real encryption

08:18 could easily take another decade. But it’s getting closer.

08:22 Every piece of encrypted data sitting in those  vaults becomes exposed the moment the machine

08:27 arrives. Now, something drastic is happening. A race to rebuild the locks of the entire internet

08:32 before the ultimate codebreaker is finished.

08:35 Trying to crack encrypted data isn’t a new thing. It had been going on for years, long before most

08:41 people had heard the word quantum. But  while hackers tried to break the code,

08:45 a small group tried to replace it. For almost a decade, most of that work

08:48 ran out of a government lab in Maryland, an  agency called National Institute of Standards

08:53 and Technology, or NIST. The decisions made  there impact nearly every device you own.

08:58 NIST sets the standards that keep the modern  world running. When it approves a technology,

09:03 the world pays attention and adopts them. So when quantum computers threatened to

09:08 crack the locks protecting the internet,  there was one question: what replaces them?

09:13 The decision made by NIST analysts and researchers  would shape the security of billions of people.Get

09:18 it wrong, and everything from your bank  account to the power grid would be at risk.

09:22 In August 2024, after 8 years  of testing, they delivered.

09:26 NIST published the first encryption standards  built to survive a quantum computer:

09:30 one system to establish a secure connection,  another to prove that connection is authentic.

09:36 Their names aren’t exactly glamorous, ML-KEM and  ML-DSA, but what they represent is historic. For

09:44 the first time, the internet had locks designed  for a world where quantum computers exist.

09:49 The old encryption was a puzzle you cracked  by working backwards. The new kind is built

09:53 like a multi-dimensional geometric grid that’s  deliberately obscured by mathematical noise.

09:58 If you already hold the key, the path is  obvious. If you don’t, there is no shortcut.

10:03 The team then built a backup grounded in  a fundamentally different problem. This

10:07 ensures that even if the first is ever cracked,  the world wouldn’t have to start from scratch.

10:12 The biggest names in tech have already begun  swapping out their locks. Google switched the

10:16 new encryption inside Chrome. Apple rebuilt the  system behind iMessage around it. Cloudflare,

10:22 Amazon, and Signal have all made the move, in  most cases without their users noticing a thing.

10:27 Now governments are paying attention. A 2022 US law ordered every federal

10:32 agency to hunt down its old encryption and start  replacing it, with a hard deadline of 2035. The

10:38 finance world got the same message, with its  main security group telling banks to begin

10:42 the switch now rather than wait. But this comes with a warning.

10:46 A few years ago, one of the most promising  new methods, an algorithm called SIKE,

10:50 seemed to be rock solid. Then two researchers  broke it wide open. Not with a quantum computer,

10:56 but with an ordinary computer. It only took an hour.

11:00 The lesson was that no lock  stays unbreakable forever.

11:03 That's why the most advanced systems are  being redesigned around a different idea:

11:07 agility. When the next breakthrough arrives, they  want to swap out their encryption as easily as

11:12 changing a tire. It turns what could have been a  global emergency into a routine software update.

11:18 But inventing a better lock  was never the hard part.

11:21 The hard part is replacing the old one. Because the internet isn't a single machine.

11:25 It's billions of devices, millions  of servers, decades of software,

11:29 and infrastructure that was never designed  for a change this large. Every phone,

11:35 browser, bank, satellite, power plant, and  government system has to make the transition.

11:41 That’s where this starts to fall apart.

11:43 Changing the lock on one website is  simple. Changing it on everything,

11:44 all at once, is the largest forced  upgrade in the history of computing.

11:48 The US government alone expects to spend  $7.1 billion just to upgrade its civilian

11:53 systems. That number doesn’t include the  military and the intelligence agencies.

11:58 Spread the same job across every bank,  hospital, and power company on the planet,

12:02 and serious estimates climb past $1 trillion. The entire Y2K cleanup of the late 1990s,

12:09 by comparison, cost somewhere between $300  and $600 billion. This is bigger than that.

12:15 But money is the least of the problems.  The deeper issues are physical. The new

12:19 quantum-proof locks are larger and heavier than  the ones they replace. They use more memory,

12:24 more bandwidth, and more power. On a laptop  or a data-center server, nobody will notice.

12:29 The problem is everything else. A smart meter bolted to the side of a house.

12:33 A pacemaker in someone`s chest. A sensor on a  pipeline expected to run for 15 years on a single

12:39 battery. These were designed around the small,  light locks of today, with nothing to spare. Some

12:45 of them simply can’t carry the heavier locks. So the upgrades arrive unevenly.

12:50 The cloud can absorb most of the change  almost overnight. The edges of the network

12:54 can't. Billions of smaller devices humming  in the background are left behind. Many built

12:58 into infrastructure that's nearly impossible to  access without ripping it apart. So for years,

13:04 every system caught in the transition has to carry  both locks at once: the old one and the new one.

13:10 Many devices won't be upgraded at all. They'll keep running long after everyone

13:14 knows they're vulnerable. They’re just too  expensive to replace, too important to shut down.

13:19 It’s the start of a slow, spreading digital dark  age. Huge stretches of the world keep running

13:24 on locks everyone already knows are broken. And this is where the people in charge should be

13:28 panicking. While Western governments and companies  spend years replacing vulnerable systems,

13:33 one device at a time, their rivals are pursuing  a very different strategy. Instead of upgrading

13:38 the old network, they're building a new one. One  designed for a post-quantum world from the start.

13:44 And they're building it in space.

13:46 China has spent years working  on something the West mostly

13:50 ignored. Not better code, but physics itself. The approach is called quantum key distribution,

13:55 and it turns the whole problem on its head.  For decades, encryption has relied on a simple

14:00 assumption: that certain mathematical  puzzles are too difficult to solve.

14:04 But difficult isn't the same as impossible. A powerful enough computer could always change

14:09 the equation. Quantum key distribution  takes a different approach. Instead of

14:13 trusting a math problem, it trusts the laws  of physics. The encryption key is carried by

14:18 individual particles of light. And according  to quantum mechanics, the act of measuring

14:23 one of those particles inevitably disturbs it.  The moment anyone tries to intercept the key,

14:28 they leave evidence behind. A fingerprint. Eavesdropping gives itself away.

14:33 In March 2025, Chinese scientists used a satellite  called Jinan-1 to share one of these keys between

14:39 a station near Beijing and another near Cape Town,  South Africa, about 8,000 miles (12,875 km) apart.

14:45 On the ground, China has also built roughly  1,200 miles of dedicated quantum network

14:51 connecting secure sites between Beijing and  Shanghai. More satellites are already planned,

14:56 extending the system even further. So why doesn`t everyone simply switch

15:00 to physics and forget the software fix? Because this isn't a software upgrade.

15:04 A software upgrade is easy. Push an  update, and billions of devices can

15:08 switch to a new encryption standard overnight. Quantum key distribution doesn't work like that.

15:13 Its security comes from the physical world,  from photons traveling through specially

15:17 designed networks. It needs special hardware:  dedicated fiber lines or a direct link to a

15:23 satellite. You have to build it. That’s the difference.

15:26 A handful of nations will be able to protect  their most sensitive communications with the

15:31 laws of physics. Everyone else will remain  on the open internet, patching software,

15:35 upgrading systems, and hoping it works. Security becomes something you can

15:39 either afford or you can`t. And all of it traces back to a

15:43 single mistake made decades ago.

15:45 For half a century, digital security has depended  on a simple fact about computation. Some problems

15:51 are easy to do, but extremely difficult  to undo. We built the entire online world

15:56 on the faith that some doors were, for  all practical purposes, locked forever.

16:01 The mistake was believing  that would always be true.

16:04 Those problems were never genuinely impossible.  They were only impossible for the kind of computer

16:09 we knew how to build. A quantum computer is not  just a faster version of the machine on your

16:13 desk. It runs on entirely different rules, and on  these specific problems, those rules let it walk

16:19 straight through doors we thought were sealed. We mistook the limits of our own technology for

16:24 a law of nature. It was like building a city  on a fault line nobody knew existed. For years,

16:29 the ground felt perfectly solid. Until it moved.

16:33 And that's why no software update can fully  solve this problem. The new locks will help,

16:37 they might even protect us for decades. But  trust online was never permanent. The digital

16:42 world is changing… and when the foundations  change, you don't just replace the locks.

16:46 You rebuild the structure sitting on top of them. Because every password, every digital signature

16:51 depends on the same question: How do you prove  who you are when the old proofs no longer hold?

16:57 You don't.

16:58 The new digital world is already taking  shape and its first casualty is the

17:01 thing you use a dozen times a day: The password. It won’t be gone overnight, but it's something you

17:07 can no longer rely on by itself. What replaces it,  is something physical. A key you tap or plug in.

17:13 A fingerprint or a face. A hardware key you plug  in or tap against your phone. You can already see

17:19 the shift in passkeys, now rolling out across  Google, Apple, and other major platforms. The

17:24 proof of who you are is moving out of the cloud,  and back into the physical world you can touch. It

17:29 changes what attacks can reach in the first place. These systems are now reaching nationwide levels.

17:34 Countries are adopting old-fashioned analog  backups; deliberately simple machines that

17:39 can’t be hacked from thousands of miles away. Estonia, which runs nearly its entire government

17:44 online, already keeps full copies of its state  records on secure servers abroad and offline,

17:50 in what it calls a data embassy. Now,  other governments are copying the idea.

17:55 For the rest of us, the change will feel  small at first. An extra tap to log in. A

17:59 device you suddenly have to keep track of. It’s  an extra step in exchange for better security.

18:04 But it’s the end of something bigger. The internet we grew up with was built on a very

18:09 simple and generous assumption. That encrypted  meant private, and that anyone, anywhere, could

18:14 be trusted just enough to do business with. That  open, borderless, instant network doesn’t survive

18:20 beyond this. What takes its place is more guarded,  more broken up, more rooted in the physical world.

18:25 It trades convenience for survival. There’s no other choice.

18:29 The secrets locked away today will  keep being leaked, unlocked long after

18:33 we have forgotten about them. Some will be  worthless by then. Some will be essential.

18:38 There is a thin thread of hope in all of  this. We might be able to make a change

18:42 to the digital locks before the ultimate  quantum computer arrives. But the age of

18:46 taking digital trust for granted is over. Security shouldn’t be taken for granted.

18:49 From here on, privacy and proof aren’t the  default. They’re things we will need to build, on

18:54 purpose, into everything we make. The age when we  could assume the locks would simply hold is over.

18:57 The belief that the locks would  simply hold… no longer exists.

19:00 Despite all our best efforts, the online  world has always been vulnerable. But what

19:04 happens when those weaknesses are exploited  at a scale we’ve never seen before? Find out
