docs.text:
00:00 The 9/11 terror attacks scarred a  nation - and even decades later,

00:04 some things still don’t add  up. Like who knew about it?

00:07 Was there insider trading? And the  case of a strange disappearance...

00:11 Find out the answer to these mysteries and more

00:13 on this episode of The Infographics Show -  “Things About 9/11 That Don’t Make Sense”.

00:18 September 11th, 2001.

00:20 The world was shocked as coordinated  terror attacks hit the United States.

00:23 Members of Osama Bin Laden’s Al Qaeda terrorist  cult hijacked planes, using them as weapons

00:29 to hit high-profile targets.Two jets slammed  into the World Trade Center in New York City,

00:34 killing over 2,000 people and reducing the iconic  towers to rubble. A third plane hit the Pentagon,

00:39 killing hundreds. And a fourth - headed  for the Capitol Building - was brought

00:43 down in a Pennsylvania field by the  heroic actions of its passengers.

00:47 It was the deadliest terror attack in history.

00:49 Everyone knows someone who questions the official  story of 9/11. They usually have an elaborate rant

00:55 about how jet fuel can’t melt steel beams. And  when you question them on what actually happened,

01:00 they’ll tell you “The lizard people just  want us to think the towers blew up.” Those

01:05 conspiracies have been explored and debunked  many times over. But over twenty years later,

01:09 there’s still some things that just don’t  make sense about the horrifying day.

01:14 #9.

01:15 For one thing, the entire circumstances of the  attack seem surreal to those who grew up in its

01:20 aftermath. Unlike most terror attacks since, the  attack was extremely low-tech. The terrorists,

01:25 organized in groups of four or five,  boarded planes holding only box cutters.

01:30 They took the plane hostage, forced the  pilot to give up control or killed them,

01:34 and piloted the plane into its intended  target. It seems like a well-planned - if

01:39 simple - operation. But there’s one  thing that still raises some eyebrows.

01:43 Why did Mohammed Atta travel to Portland,  Maine the night before the attack?

01:48 On September 10th, 2001, Mohamed Atta picked  up his fellow hijacker Abdul-Azzia Al-Omari

01:54 at a hotel in Boston. From there, they drove a  rented car north to Portland - almost two hours

02:00 away. Surveillance footage captured the pair  checking into a Portland hotel that evening.

02:04 They were also seen making ATM withdrawals,  browsing the aisles of a local Wal-Mart,

02:08 and in the parking lot of a nearby Pizza Hut. Some believe Atta was conducting surveillance

02:13 detection, making sure no one was tailing him.  Others think it was a strategic move - security

02:17 at Portland’s airport may have been lighter than  Boston’s. Another theory was he was planning

02:22 for last-minute delays or meeting with an  unknown accomplice. Whatever the reason,

02:27 on the morning of September 11th, Atta boarded a  flight back to Boston. Once he landed, he received

02:32 a call from Marwan Al-Shehi, another 9/11 hijacker  - believed to be the green light for the attacks.

02:37 Atta would go on to hijack American Airlines  Flight 11, crashing it into the North Tower.

02:42 Despite years of investigation, Atta’s trip to  Portland remains one of the most mysterious pieces

02:47 of the 9/11 puzzle.

02:50 One of the scariest things about 9/11 was the  uncertainty in the immediate aftermath. Thousands

02:55 of people died - but very few bodies were found.  Almost all the casualties in New York and on the

03:00 planes were essentially vaporized, with their  families desperately seeking any evidence of

03:04 their loved ones’ so they could have some degree  of closure. Many disappeared without a trace.

03:10 One was Sneha Anne Phillip, an  Indian-American physician who

03:13 was last seen on September 10th  near her home in Lower Manhattan,

03:17 shopping at a department store. She  likely made her purchases and went home.

03:20 And then, no trace of her was ever seen again.

03:23 Unlike most of the 9/11 victims, there are no  reports of her being on-site, and no eye-witnesses

03:29 ever reported seeing her. Her family has reason  to believe she was there - she was a physician,

03:34 and may have gone to the World Trade Center to  offer medical assistance. But few of the doctors

03:38 who were on-site went into the towers themselves.  Instead, they were helping people who were injured

03:43 after escaping. And while people did die on  the ground due to falling debris and fires,

03:48 those were the bodies most likely to be recovered  intact. Multiple investigations by the NYPD and a

03:53 private investigation commissioned by  Phillip’s husband turned up nothing.

03:57 Which has led many people to  wonder - is everything as it seems?

04:01 Phillip had a troubled past before the events  of 9/11, being fired from her job at Cabrini

04:06 Medical Center due to tardiness and alcoholism.  She complained to police that an intern groped

04:11 her during a staff night out. The case would  later be dropped and Phillip was charged with

04:15 filing a false police report. It seemed like  her life was spiraling before the terror attack.

04:20 Could she have faked her  death or died in another way,

04:23 and it was completely ignored in  the chaos of the terror attack?

04:26 Her family has been suing to have her  officially confirmed as a victim of the

04:30 9/11 attacks, allowing her to be  honored officially. And in 2008,

04:34 an appeals court gave them their wish and  she was added to the Ground Zero Memorial.

04:39 That’s the legal outcome - but any hard  evidence remains painfully hard to come by.

04:43 And in the immediate aftermath, confusion reigned.

04:47 #7.

04:48 Osama Bin Laden and his Al Qaeda terror network  quickly claimed responsibility for the attacks,

04:53 and he became the world’s public enemy #1. But  he came from a very big family - the son of a

04:59 billionaire Saudi oil baron who had multiple  wives and 50 children. And he was considered

05:04 the black sheep - most of his family were  jet-setting businesspeople, with devoutly

05:08 Muslim beliefs. They had no affiliation to terror  groups and viewed Osama as a disgrace. In 2001,

05:14 the Bin Laden family was spread around  the world… including in the United States.

05:18 It was one of the strangest affairs that  took place in the days after the attacks.

05:22 Flights were grounded for two days, and strictly  regulated after that. And it would be several

05:28 weeks before one of the most controversial  flights to happen in that time was revealed.

05:32 On September 13th, twelve members of the  Bin Laden family who were in the U.S. were

05:37 put on a plane and evacuated back to  Saudi Arabia. When this was revealed,

05:41 it caused some outrage - why were the  relatives of our enemy being evacuated?

05:46 And many asked - why were they such a priority?

05:49 This was conspiracy fodder of the highest degree,  with some arguing it showed that the government

05:54 was in on the attacks or at least collaborating  with the Bin Laden family. But less conspiratorial

05:59 individuals said that most of the Bin Ladens  in the country were high school and college

06:03 students. And besides, money talks - reportedly  the evacuations were kick-started when one of

06:08 Bin Laden’s brothers sought help from the Saudi  Embassy. Saudi Arabia had good relations with

06:13 the Bush administration, thanks to their many oil  deals and geopolitical significance. The likely

06:18 scenario is that they were evacuated for their  protection due to fears of reprisals, but it

06:24 still raised some eyebrows - and the government  has been tight-lipped about it ever since.

06:28 But one figure might be at the center of it all.

06:31 #6.

06:32 The biggest question regarding 9/11 has  always been “who knew”? The most common

06:37 suspect has been George W. Bush. Many people  insist that the US President must have known

06:41 in advance and allowed the attacks to  happen so he would have an excuse for

06:45 war. There’s no evidence for that - but  his close ties to the Saudi government

06:49 continue to draw scrutiny. Almost all  the hijackers were from Saudi Arabia,

06:54 and so was one of the most mysterious figures  related to the attacks, Omar Al-Bayouni.

06:59 Did this Saudi intelligence  agent know what was coming?

07:02 Although of Egyptian descent, Al-Bayouni’s  family had settled in Saudi Arabia,

07:06 where he became a well-connected  figure with reported ties to the

07:09 Saudi government. He also reportedly had  close ties to known terrorist associates,

07:14 including helping two of the eventual  hijackers find housing in San Diego.

07:18 And by the time the attacks hit, he was gone.

07:21 He was in the UK pursuing a PhD when  the towers fell, and ten days later,

07:25 he was arrested in a joint US-British operation.  The evidence of his links to terrorist associates

07:30 was strong, including many phone calls to a  key Bin Laden associate, Ziyad Khaleel and

07:36 Saudi Ministry of Islamic Affairs cleric Fahad  al-Thumairy. Al-Thumairy denied knowing Bayoumi,

07:42 despite telephone records showing at least 60  calls between them. But the British weren’t

07:47 able to produce any hard evidence of his knowledge  or involvement, and they ultimately released him.

07:52 He would soon return to Saudi  Arabia…and disappear off the map

07:56 completely. His association with the  attack has never been fully proven,

07:59 but an FBI report indicates that they  believe there’s a better-than-even chance

08:04 he was a conspirator. But if anyone wants  answers, they’ll have to find him first.

08:09 But there’s one site on Ground Zero that  causes more controversy than any other.

08:13 #5.

08:14 In late 2000, two of the 9/11 hijackers -  Khalid Almihdhar and Nawaf Alhazmi - rented

08:20 a room in San Diego from a man who  was an undercover FBI informant.

08:25 The informant - whose identity has never  been released to the public - was a tested

08:29 asset for the Bureau. He prayed with the  two men and helped them adjust to life

08:33 in the U.S. - he even assisted one of them in  opening a bank account. But he never provided

08:38 their names to his FBI handler. And perhaps more  importantly, the handler never asked. At the time,

08:44 Almihdhar and Alhazmi were already persons  of interest to the CIA, having attended an

08:48 al-Qaeda summit in Malaysia just months earlier. The pair moved into the informant’s house in

08:53 September 2000. Almihdhar moved out six weeks  later, and Alhazmi left by the end of the

08:58 year. During that time, both men attended flight  school in preparation for the devastating attack.

09:03 It wasn’t until after the 9/11 attacks  that the informant recognized the names

09:07 being reported in the media. He called his  handler and revealed that the hijackers

09:11 had been his roommates. There’s no evidence he  intentionally concealed their identities - but

09:15 it still remains a glaring example of  miscommunication between intelligence agencies.

09:20 A CIA alert naming the two men as potential  terrorists had been issued on August 23,

09:26 2001. But by then, the opportunity was gone. As  one counterintelligence expert later queried, why

09:32 didn’t the agent ask more questions? Or at least  explore the possibility of recruiting new assets?

09:38 And it wasn’t the only  mystery that lingered on 9/11.

09:41 #4.

09:42 He’s called the “last person  killed in New York on 9/11”,

09:46 but he wasn’t a worker in the towers or a  first-responder. His name was Henryk Siwiak,

09:51 and he was a Polish immigrant minding his  own business in the Brooklyn neighborhood of

09:55 Bedford-Stuyvesant. A former Polish government  worker, he was visiting his sister in New York

10:00 and decided to get a job to send money back to  his family. While he didn’t speak much English,

10:04 he was a hard worker and managed to  get a job as a construction worker.

10:07 But on that fateful day, he  would meet a shocking end.

10:10 After his job site shut down for  the day after the terror attacks,

10:14 he walked across the Brooklyn Bridge and went to  interview for a job cleaning a local supermarket.

10:18 Through a series of miscommunications,  he was given the wrong directions for the

10:22 store address, and went to what was a fairly  dangerous, crime-ridden neighborhood. There,

10:27 eyewitnesses reported hearing an argument,  followed by some gunshots. Siwiak was found

10:32 on the pavement, bleeding out from  a fatal gunshot wound to the chest.

10:36 And over 20 years later, his  murder has never been solved.

10:40 Not surprisingly, this was mostly attributed  to one thing - the police were completely

10:44 occupied by the massive terror attack  in Manhattan. It left zero resources for

10:48 investigating a routine homicide. This has  led Siwiak’s case to gain extra notoriety,

10:53 but even in the best of times, a murder  where the murder weapon is never found

10:56 is extremely hard to solve. But there  were other odd factors to the killing,

11:01 such as the fact that no money was taken from  Siwiak. Did his killer think the mild-mannered

11:05 foreign man may have been involved with the  attack? The cold case is only getting colder.

11:10 And it’s far from the only false accusation  of involvement that has cropped up.

11:14 #3.

11:15 While some conspiracy theories relating to 9/11  are more outlandish - with people claiming the

11:20 towers were destroyed by explosives planted by the  government - most of them simply focus on who to

11:26 blame. In the immediate aftermath of the attacks,  a lot of suspects, including the U.S. government,

11:31 had fingers pointed at them. But in later years,  conspiracies focused on another target - Israel,

11:37 who were among the greatest enemies of Osama  Bin Laden. And people who insist they must

11:42 have been involved even point to some specific  targets - the so-called “Dancing Israelis”.

11:47 So what has made this theory stick around so long?

11:50 First off, there’s no evidence that anyone  else was involved in 9/11 besides Osama Bin

11:56 Laden and his network of terrorists - he  proudly took credit for the attacks. But

12:00 some people insist that a group of Israelis was  arrested near the towers a short time after 9/11,

12:06 reportedly laughing and celebrating the attacks.

12:09 There’s no evidence of how they were acting -  but a deep dive into government files did reveal

12:14 six Israeli nationals were arrested in lower  Manhattan, and later deported back to Israel.

12:19 It’s believed that the six men were  likely Israeli intelligence agents,

12:22 here collecting information on the attacks.  Israel viewed Al Qaeda as a serious security

12:27 threat at the time. Many countries likely  have spies in the country at all times,

12:31 and it only becomes a serious issue when they’re  trying to access secret or high-risk information.

12:36 But in the immediate aftermath of  9/11, security stepped up big time

12:40 and deported a lot of people who may  have been slipping under the radar.

12:44 And so they went back - leaving a trail  of decades-long conspiracies behind them.

12:49 But if there’s one question that’s been lingering  all these years, it’s this - did anyone know?

12:54 #2.

12:54 Some of the more outlandish conspiracy theories  claim that the attacks were masterminded in the

12:58 United States, but most simply allege that it  was allowed to proceed without being reported.

13:03 Some claim the government wanted to have an  excuse to start a war in the Middle East,

13:07 while others claim a massive insurance scam on the  World Trade Center. But no evidence has emerged of

13:12 advanced knowledge by the top power brokers at the  time - but it did emerge in a very unlikely place.

13:18 A high-school classroom.

13:20 It was September 6th, 2001, and English  teacher Antoinette DiLorenzo was greeting

13:25 a new year of students. Her class was  heavily composed of Pakistani immigrants,

13:29 and one of the boys made a disturbing comment  to his Bensonhurst classmates. He claimed that

13:34 the World Trade Center wouldn’t be standing  next week. She chalked it up to a bad-taste

13:39 teenage joke - but then watched in horror as  the prophecy came true. She quickly called

13:43 the authorities, and the FBI and NYPD  tracked the boy down to interrogate him.

13:48 So did this boy have advanced knowledge  of the world’s deadliest terror attack?

13:52 All these years later, we don’t have a clear  answer. The boy claimed he was only joking,

13:57 and his family backed him up - but the coincidence  was such that many people were dubious. The police

14:02 ultimately decided that it was just a case of  the world’s worst-timed joke and no charges

14:07 were ever filed. The most convincing  evidence was that none of the hijackers

14:11 involved in the attack were of Pakistani  background. Fifteen were from Saudi Arabia,

14:16 two were from the United Arab Emirates,  one from Lebanon, and one from Egypt.

14:21 That makes the connections needed for this random  boy to overhear talk about it much less likely.

14:26 But maybe the most bizarre story to  come out of 9/11 indicates that a

14:30 lot of people may have known - and  they made a lot of money off it.

14:35 #1.

14:36 Was there insider trading on 9/11?

14:38 It’s one of the biggest scourges of the insurance  world - people who have advance knowledge of an

14:43 event profiting off it by making trades on the  stock market. It’s what sent Martha Stewart to

14:48 prison, and many Senators faced allegations  of it during the Covid-19 pandemic. The most

14:53 common source of it is when people who work in a  specific company know that the company is about

14:57 to be sold or make a big announcement. They buy  or sell more shares while the price is right.

15:03 But would anyone sink so low as to profit  off a terror attack - and tell no one?

15:08 It was only a week after the attack  when The Times, a London-based paper,

15:12 announced that it was investigating whether  unusual trades happened as a result of advance

15:17 knowledge of the attacks. A massive number of  shares of insurance companies and airlines were

15:22 sold off before the attack, in countries  in Europe as well as Japan and the US.

15:27 This was especially high in the cases of United  Airlines and American Airlines - the two airlines

15:33 whose planes were used in the hijacking. In fact,  it was the highest amount of these stocks ever

15:37 traded on the Chicago Exchange - and the  investors who sold made millions off it.

15:42 The possibility of insider trading  was raised with the 9/11 commission,

15:46 and the fact-finders eventually found  explanations for the unusual trading.

15:50 Both the trading of United and American  shares, which happened on different days,

15:54 were linked to trading strategies  circulated by investment newsletters.

15:58 There was a thorough investigation by the SEC into  the American-based trades, and by intelligence

16:04 agencies into the foreign trades - but no evidence  of advance knowledge of the attack was found.

16:09 But that didn’t stop the digging.

16:11 As the post-9/11 era wore on, damaged hard  drives were discovered in the ruins of the

16:16 World Trade Center - which were transferred  to an elite data recovery company, Convar,

16:20 for retrieval. The German-based  company conducted an investigation

16:24 for US authorities into possible evidence  of criminal insider trading, and was able

16:29 to restore several hundred hard drives over  the next year. However, the 9/11 committee in

16:33 2003 stated that they had not received any  valuable information from the hard drives.

16:38 With no hard evidence of insider trading, much  of the discussion of the topic has turned on

16:43 speculation. As late as 2010, an independent  report claimed that there were at least thirteen

16:49 informed trades that would only make sense if  the investors knew something big was coming.

16:54 The international team of experts pointed to  an unusual increase in trading activity in the

16:58 days before the attacks. But with no hard  evidence, no one has ever been charged for

17:03 insider trading - and it’s likely they never  will. If someone did know and used it to make

17:08 money rather than dropping a dime, it would be the  biggest scandal in the financial sector’s history.

17:14 What do you think is the most overlooked  detail about 9/11? Share your thoughts below.

17:18 Want to know what happened in 9/11  on that fateful day? Check out “What

17:22 Happened Immediately After 9/11” for  all the grim details. And the good news

17:26 is…we got him. Watch “How SEAL Team Took  Down Osama Bin Laden (Minute by Minute)”

17:31 for the tale of the tape of how  the Al Qaeda leader met his end.

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 73 seconds after launch.

00:02 The Challenger space shuttle rises higher and  higher toward space. Its iconic white solid rocket

00:07 boosters roar as flames spew out the back of them.  The flight crew has continued to communicate with

00:12 launch control since lift-off. No one knows that  anything is wrong and that in the next second,

00:16 tragedy will strike. A fire rages along the  side of the right booster as fuel escapes

00:21 due to a compromised seal. In moments, the  supporting struts connecting the rockets to

00:26 the orange external fuel tank will experience a  catastrophic failure. The booster will slam into

00:31 the tank. The rocket fuel will ignite,  and there will be a massive explosion.

00:35 April 4, 1983: T minus 2 years and 9  months until the Challenger disaster.

00:41 “All systems go. Prepare for liftoff,” mission  control says over the intercom to the Challenger

00:46 flight crew. This will be the space shuttle's  maiden voyage. The boosters ignite, and the184

00:51 foot, 4.5-million-pound space shuttle thrusts  toward space. The first mission was a success,

00:57 and the Challenger space shuttle will end up  flying 6 more missions that year. The shuttle

01:01 is reliable, but every time it launches into  space and lands after re-entry, a toll is taken

01:06 on the spacecraft. Constant repairs need to be  made while old components are swapped out for

01:11 new ones. Engineers who work on the shuttle day  in and day out warn NASA that the stresses that

01:16 constant missions to space place on the space  shuttle may lead to tragedy in the future.

01:21 July 19, 1985 T minus 6 months  until the Challenger disaster.

01:26 “We are pleased to inform you that you have  been selected to become the first teacher

01:30 to go to space.” Christa McAuliffe can’t believe  the words she has just read. Several months ago,

01:36 she submitted her application to the  NASA Teacher in Space Project along with

01:41 11,000 other educators. Never in her wildest  dreams did she believe she would be chosen.

01:45 However, this letter confirms that she will, in  fact, be going to space and that she will be lucky

01:50 enough to share this incredible experience with  students across the country when she gets back.

01:55 McAuliffe teaches at Concord High  School in New Hampshire. When she

01:58 tells her colleagues the news, they  are elated. Her family, friends,

02:02 and students are all extremely happy for her.  As a part of the Teacher in Space Project,

02:06 she will conduct two lessons from orbit and embark  on a lecture series across the United States to

02:11 share her experience with students. This will  be done to highlight the importance of teachers

02:16 in the country and hopefully inspire students  to pursue careers in technology and science.

02:20 Over the next several months, McAuliffe  joins her fellow crewmates at Johnson

02:24 Space Center in Houston, Texas, where they  train and prepare for their coming mission.

02:28 Francis R. Scobee will be the commander  of the spacecraft. In April of 1984,

02:33 he piloted Challenger mission STS-41-C which  deployed a new satellite and repaired a damaged

02:39 satellite before returning to Earth. Since then,  he has been an instructor pilot for the Shuttle's

02:43 747 carrier aircraft. This will be his first  space command, and he couldn’t be more excited.

02:49 Piloting the mission will be Michael J. Smith.  He has flown 28 different types of civilian and

02:54 military aircraft and logged 4,867 hours  of flight time. Judith A. Resnik will be

03:00 one of the mission specialists on board.  Resnik had been part of Astronaut Group 8,

03:04 which was the first to include women on the  team. She has developed a variety of software

03:09 and procedures that are utilized throughout  NASA. She has been to space before aboard

03:13 the STS-41-D mission in August 1984. This was the  very first mission of the space shuttle Discovery.

03:19 Two other mission specialists are a  part of the Challenger crew as well.

03:22 Ronald E. McNair flew aboard Challenger in  February 1984 during mission STS-41-B. It

03:29 was on this mission that he became the second  African American man to fly in space. Ellison

03:33 S. Onizuka was the first Asian American  and the first person of Japanese origin

03:38 to reach space during his time aboard the  space shuttle Discovery during STS-51-C.

03:43 The final crew member aboard the upcoming  Challenger launch designated STS-51-L is

03:48 Gregory B. Jarvis. He’s the payload specialist.  This will be his first time in space, although

03:53 he had been slated to fly aboard a different  shuttle in April of 1985, but his spot was given

03:59 to U.S. senator Jake Garn instead. Then a similar  situation happened again in early January 1986

04:05 when U.S. representative Bill Nelson took his  place aboard another space shuttle. Now Jarvis

04:10 finally has the opportunity to reach space where  he can put his astronaut training to good use.

04:15 But like every other member of the crew, he will  never actually make it beyond Earth’s atmosphere.

04:20 January 22, 1986: T minus 6 days  until the Challenger disaster.

04:25 The Challenger crew eagerly awaits confirmation  of whether their mission is a go or not. A

04:30 high-ranking NASA officer enters the room with  a frown on his face. “Sorry about this crew,

04:35 but we’re going to have to delay your mission  until 61-C gets back. Their assignment ran into

04:39 delays, and their shuttle isn’t due to land  until tomorrow.” The Challenger crew looks

04:43 at one another in dismay. They are eager to  get going. Every mission to space is special,

04:48 and even for veteran astronauts,  it’s what they dream about doing

04:51 every night. It’s as if the stars are  beckoning them to reach for the unknown.

04:55 January 27, 1986: T minus 1 day  until the Challenger disaster.

05:01 Challenger mission STS-51-L is planned to have  an early morning lift-off the following day.

05:06 The astronauts toss and turn in their beds in  anticipation. A chill sweeps across Florida

05:11 as if foreshadowing the ominous events that  will happen in the coming hours. The launch

05:15 pad becomes covered in thick ice; the metals  that make up the space shuttle and boosters

05:20 contract slightly with the cold. As engineers  check the spacecraft over and over again to

05:24 make sure it’s in an acceptable condition for  launch, a disturbing realization surfaces.

05:29 “Sir, I want to reiterate that I am concerned  about the reliability of the seals in the

05:33 rockets,” an engineer explains to  his superior. For over two years,

05:37 the engineers and technicians that work  in the shuttle program have warned that

05:40 the space shuttles are being overused.  The crafts are sturdy and well made,

05:44 but every machine has its breaking point,  and it feels as if, after dozens of flights,

05:49 it’s only a matter of time before something  tragic happens. The NASA official acknowledges

05:53 the engineer's concern but does nothing  more. The launch will commence as scheduled,

05:58 regardless of the warnings voiced by the men  and women working directly with the spacecraft.

06:02 January 28, 1986: 9:00 a.m.: T minus 2 hours  and 38 minutes until the Challenger disaster.

06:09 The sun is rising higher and higher over the  Atlantic Ocean. A crowd gathers around Cape

06:14 Canaveral to watch the launch at Kennedy Space  Center scheduled for later that morning. There

06:18 are members of the press, local residents, and  people who have traveled from around the world

06:22 to watch the launch. Many are there to witness  the historic event of the first teacher to go

06:27 to space. Excitement and anticipation fill  the air. This will be the 25th space shuttle

06:32 launch and the 10th Challenger mission.  All other flights have been successful,

06:36 so there is no reason to suspect  today should be any different.

06:39 The astronauts don their suits and proceed  to their launch vehicle. They are greeted by

06:44 cheers as they step off their transport and  proceed towards the elevator that will carry

06:48 them to the cockpit of the Challenger.  Mission control in Houston prepares to

06:51 track and monitor the space shuttle's progress.  Telemetry coming in from hundreds of sensors is

06:56 recorded and double-checked to make sure that  Challenger is ready. The astronauts strap in,

07:01 and the shuttle door is sealed behind them.  The cockpit is quiet except for the sounds

07:05 of switches being engaged while Socbee and  Smith check the systems on board. There is

07:09 a sense of anxiousness, excitement, and pride  as the seven-person crew prepares for launch.

07:14 McAuliffe looks out the window directly  ahead of her at the blue sky. Just beyond

07:18 the atmosphere lies the edge of space. A bird  flies pasts; McAuliffe smiles. Soon she will

07:24 be doing something that only a handful  of people in all of history have done.

07:27 She checks her safety harness and leans  back in her seat, releasing a long sigh.

07:32 Besides the crew, the shuttle also  carries a Tracking and Data Relay

07:36 Satellite designated TDRS-B. Also in the  cargo bay is the Spartan Halley spacecraft,

07:41 which is designed to be released from Challenger  to study Halley’s Comet for two days while the

07:46 celestial object approaches the sun. The small  satellite will then be picked up by the Challenger

07:50 crew and brought back to Earth so scientists can  analyze the data it has collected. Tragically,

07:55 no one and nothing aboard Challenger will  survive to perform this series of tests.

07:59 January 28, 1986: 11:38: T  minus 10 seconds until launch.

08:06 Due to weather conditions, the launch  has been delayed yet again. However,

08:09 the atmosphere is beginning to  cooperate. The sky clears up,

08:12 and the wind clams. Commander Scobee and Pilot  Smith check their sensors and instruments one

08:17 last time as they prepare for the rockets to fire.  Mission control reaches the end of its countdown.

08:22 10. 9. 8. 7. 6. We have main engine  start. 4. 3. 2. 1 and liftoff.

08:32 Moments before the engines ignite and the space  shuttle rises, the solid rocket ignition command

08:38 is sent. The boosters roar to life. The space  shuttle and earth around the launchpad begin

08:42 to shake. The sound travels across the water and  reaches the bystanders watching the space shuttle

08:47 launch from miles away. Astronaut Judy Resnik is  heard over the intercom. “All right!” she yells.

08:52 Challenger Space Shuttle achieves liftoff.

08:55 After the rockets ignite eight 25-inch-long,  7-inch-wide exploding bolts fire. The Challenger

09:01 space shuttle is free to rise into the  sky. The deafening boom of the engines,

09:06 massive amounts of smoke, and intense heat roll  across the launch pad. A quarter of a second

09:11 after launch, sensors record the first vertical  motion of Challenger as it begins its ascent.

09:16 Unknown to anyone on board or at mission control,

09:18 an abnormal black smoke is seeping out of the  right solid rocket booster near the location of

09:24 one of the O-ring joints. This is the first sign  that something is about to go terribly wrong.

09:29 1 second after liftoff.

09:30 “Here we go!” Pilot Michael Smith  says over the intercom. As the space

09:35 shuttle proceeds toward the heavens, the  black smoke coming from the right rocket

09:38 seems to be slowing down.

3 seconds after liftoff.

09:41 Launch commentator Hugh Hariss has just finished  the countdown and pauses for a moment to watch.

09:46 He announces on NASA-SELECT television,  “Liftoff of the 25th space shuttle mission,

09:51 and it has cleared the tower." The  abnormal black smoke coming from

09:54 the bottom of the solid rocket booster  appears to have disappeared completely.

09:58 5 seconds after liftoff.

10:00 All systems go. There are no anomalies  detected by anyone at this point in the

10:04 launch. The three liquid-fueled main engines  on the back of the space shuttle are throttled

10:08 up from 90% to 104% thrust. Everything is  going according to plan. At mission control,

10:14 data processing systems engineer A.F. Algate  confirms liftoff. There is a cheer in the room

10:20 then everyone immediately goes back to monitoring  their stations. Suddenly, there is a data blackout

10:25 from the space shuttle. No one panics. This is to  be expected as the flames and structures around

10:30 the launch complex interfere with the radio  signals being sent to the antenna complex.

10:34 But there is one piece of data that is slightly  unnerving. “I’m reading the internal pressure

10:39 on the right-side booster to be 11.8 pounds  per square inch higher than normal,” one of

10:44 the technicians in mission control says. The  rocket is still within acceptable parameters,

10:48 but this initial data point will be used later on

10:51 to identify when the Challenger space  shuttle began to run into trouble.

10:54 8 seconds after liftoff.

10:56 Once Challenger is in the open air, Pilot  Smith begins a roll maneuver that puts the

11:01 crew in a heads down position so the top  of the space shuttle is pointing towards

11:04 the Earth and the bright orange external  fuel tank is towards the sky. "Houston,

11:08 Challenger. Roll program," Commander  Scobee says over the intercom.

11:12 "Roger roll, Challenger," Astronaut Dick  Covey says from mission control. "Good roll,

11:16 flight," Flight dynamics officer Brian  Perry confirms from the control room.

11:20 19 seconds after liftoff.

11:22 The Challenge space shuttle begins  to shake. There is a sudden violent

11:26 thrust to the side. The crew grits their  teeth as Michael Smith pulls on the flight

11:30 stick slightly. With the help of the NAV  system, the space shuttle realigns itself,

11:34 and Challenger is back on course. "Looks like  we've got a lot of wind here today,” says Smith

11:38 over the intercom. Commander Scobee confirms  the assessment. They begin throttling down the

11:42 three main engines of the space shuttle to 94%  thrust as planned at this point in the flight.

11:47 21 seconds after liftoff.

11:49 Challenger’s roll maneuver is completed,  and all systems confirm it is on the proper

11:54 trajectory to reach orbit. Commander  Scobee looks out the cockpit window,

11:57 hoping to get a glimpse of the land  below. "It's a little hard to see

12:00 out my window here,” he says. The  engines continue to throttle down.

12:04 28 seconds after liftoff.

12:06 "There's 10,000 feet, and Mach point  five,” Smith says over the intercom.

12:10 Challenger is now traveling at half the speed  of sound and is 10,000 feet above the surface

12:15 of the planet. It’s at this point that the  space shuttle begins reaching the region of

12:19 maximum aerodynamic pressure. Mission control  confirms that engines are throttling down to

12:24 94% and remind the flight crew that they will be  throttling down to 65% thrust in a few seconds.

12:29 35 seconds after liftoff.

12:31 Smith begins to throttle down the engines some  more. All data indicates that the shuttle’s

12:36 computer systems are making the proper adjustments  to deal with the wind shear. 5 seconds later,

12:40 Smith confirms that they have reached  Mach 1. Scobee adds that they are passing

12:45 19,000 feet in altitude.

45 seconds after liftoff.

12:48 There is a bright flash slightly behind the  space shuttle’s right wing. Moments later,

12:52 there is a second bright flash.

12:54 48 seconds after liftoff.

12:56 A third flash appears downstream  of Challenger's right wing.

12:59 The crew can’t see these ominous explosions,  but a 70-millimeter tracking camera captures

13:04 them as it zooms in on the shuttle for  a close-up view. Everyone who is viewing

13:08 the footage is baffled at what they are  witnessing. Suddenly an orange ball of

13:12 flames erupts from under the right wing. This  fireball is coming from the right booster.

13:16 The Challenger crew and mission control  have no idea that anything is wrong as

13:21 the space shuttle’s telemetry  all reads nominal. The fireball

13:24 from under the wing merges with the  flames of the solid rocket boosters.

13:27 58 seconds after liftoff.

13:29 Challenger accelerates past 1,539 miles per  hour or 2,477 kilometers per hour. It has an

13:37 altitude of 26,127 feet or 7,963.5 meters.  Scobee gives the command to throttle the

13:45 engines back as planned. Smith confirms the  command. Mission control confirms that the

13:50 three engines of the space shuttle  have throttled down to 65% thrust.

13:54 While this is happening, the tracking  camera on the ground observes the first

13:58 evidence that there is now something seriously  wrong with the right solid rocket booster. An

14:03 abnormal plume of smoke has begun pouring  out of the rocket. The Challenger crew has

14:07 no sensors in the cockpit that display the  performance of the solid rocket boosters and,

14:11 therefore, are unaware that  they are in serious danger.

14:14 A second later, Challenger passes through the  region of maximum aerodynamic pressure, which

14:19 pushes against the space shuttle and its boosters  with 720 pounds of pressure per square foot or

14:25 7,750 pounds per square meter. The plume of smoke  coming from the side of the booster intensifies.

14:31 Inside the booster itself, an O-ring has  disintegrated, the very same component

14:37 that engineers at NASA were warning would fail  if the space shuttle launches were not dialed

14:42 back. The O-ring on the booster was meant  to seal the joints between separate parts

14:45 of the rocket and prevent the leaking  of fluids and gasses from one chamber

14:49 to another. With the O-ring destroyed, fuel  is making its way through the booster and

14:54 igniting due to the intense heat of the flames.  A continuous inferno is expelled from the right

14:59 booster along the side furthest away from the  space shuttle. The windows in the cockpit give

15:03 Scobee and Smith limited visibility, and they  are not able to see the fire from the shuttle.

15:08 60 seconds after liftoff.

15:10 "Feel that mother go!" Smith says over the  intercom. Another member of the crew is heard

15:15 yelling with joy in the background. At that  moment, mission control receives data that

15:19 indicates the internal pressure in the right  side solid rocket booster has begun to drop.

15:24 It’s not known at the time, but this severe drop  in pressure is the result of the hole created by

15:28 the ignited fuel spewing out the side of  the rocket where the O-ring has failed.

15:33 The flames pouring out of the side of  the rocket begin to lick the fitting

15:36 attachments that couple the back end of the  booster to the external fuel tank on the

15:40 underside of the space shuttle. This starts  to degrade the integrity of the couplings.

15:44 62 seconds after liftoff.

15:46 Challenger shudders once again from high  wind speeds. The shuttle rolls slightly

15:51 to compensate as it passes 35,000 feet and  approaches Mach 1.5. The wind is worse than

15:57 predicted and stronger than any of the  previous 24 shuttle missions. However,

16:01 it’s still within acceptable limits, even if  it puts slightly more stress on the shuttle.

16:05 64 seconds after liftoff.

16:08 The flame in the right side booster changes shape  suddenly as the heat from the fire melts through

16:13 metal plating, and liquid hydrogen begins  to fuel the fire. The glow on the outside of

16:18 the booster intensifies. As the force of the  raging fire builds up, it begins to move the

16:22 engine nozzle in large arcs. This momentum  begins to shift the space shuttles course,

16:27 which the computer then adjusts for. The  right booster’s thrust levels are thrown

16:31 off due to the leaking fuel and fire burning  on the side. However, the NAV system manages

16:36 to compensate. Tremors vibrate through the  cockpit as the hydrogen fuel is ignited but

16:41 gets lost in the turbulence experienced due  to the massive acceleration and wind sheers.

16:46 66 seconds after liftoff.

16:48 "Throttle up, three at 104,” mission control says  over the com. Houston and the Challenger flight

16:53 crew are still unaware of the fire coming  out of the middle of the right booster,

16:57 and other than a drop in pressure, there is no  indication that there is a serious problem. The

17:01 fire outside of the shuttle spread further. The  flames creep toward the belly of the shuttle,

17:05 where the external liquid hydrogen tank  is located. The pressure inside the fuel

17:09 tank suddenly begins to drop, indicating that an  alarming amount of liquid hydrogen is leaking out.

17:15 The fuel tank gauge plummets inside the cockpit,

17:18 but Smith and Scobee don’t notice it as they  are focused on throttling up the engines and

17:22 preparing to disengage the boosters. Even if  either crewmember was looking at the fuel gauge,

17:27 the rapid dropping of pressure happened so  quickly that there was nothing they could have

17:31 done. The fuel tank can only be disengaged  when all other engines are turned off,

17:35 and the shuttle is in a benign aerodynamic  environment higher up in the atmosphere. If

17:40 they had disengaged the fuel tank to get away  from the leak at this stage, the Challenger

17:44 would have been forced into the fuel tank and  the still-burning solid rocket booster exhaust.

17:49 68 seconds after liftoff.

17:51 The fire spewing from the side of the  rocket connects to the exhaust plume.

17:55 The liquid oxygen propellant being fed into  the main engines of the space shuttle falls

17:59 drastically. Smith continues to throttle  up the engines to reach 104% thrust.

18:04 72 seconds after liftoff.

18:06 The back end of the right booster is ripped  away from the external fuel tank. The strut

18:11 that had been securing it has been compromised  and failed. The back end of the right booster is

18:16 now moving up and down relative to the space  shuttle and fuel tank. Another explosion,

18:20 likely from the stress and leaking  fuel, occurs higher up on the booster

18:24 near Challenger’s cabin. The flame near  the top of the booster grows rapidly,

18:28 creating an enormous fireball. The nozzles of  the engines on the back of the space shuttle

18:32 begin moving at a rate of 5 feet per second in  order to compensate for the unhinged booster.

18:37 The top of the right booster is  still connected to the fuel tank,

18:40 but the loose back end causes a burst  of lateral acceleration that jerks

18:44 the shuttle. The main engine pressure  decreases. Engine nozzle motion rates

18:48 are off the chart. Things are very, very bad.  Challenger sends its final navigation update.

18:54 73 seconds after liftoff.

18:56 “Uh oh…” Smith says. These will be the last words  uttered over the comms by any of the Challenger

19:02 crew. It’s not clear what Smith is referring  to, but it’s likely that several sensors begin

19:06 showing clear signs that something is wrong. The  fuel tank and loose booster begin breaking apart.

19:11 The shuttle jerks the opposite way it had moments  before. The right booster is now producing 100,000

19:17 pounds of thrust less than the left booster.  The unbalanced acceleration begins forcing

19:22 the right booster up into the liquid  oxygen section of the external fuel tank.

19:26 Liquid hydrogen and oxygen begin leaking out of  the external tank. A cloud of fuel accumulates

19:31 outside. The right-side booster pushes  further into the fuel tank and increases

19:36 the amount of liquid oxygen being expelled.  Milliseconds later, the inevitable happens.

19:40 There is a bright flash of light located between  the Challenger shuttle and the external fuel tank.

19:46 The leaking fuel has been ignited. The fireball  engulfs the space shuttle. There is a crackling

19:51 sound over the intercom as ground transmitters  search for a signal that is no longer there.

19:55 Another explosion occurs near the front of the  external fuel tank. This ignites the remainder of

20:00 the fuel inside the front section of the tank,  causing it to detonate. Challenger’s engines

20:05 redline and the computer initiates an emergency  shutdown. Main engine 3 goes first, followed by

20:11 number 1. The last telemetry signal from the space  shuttle is sent while it is being torn apart.

20:16 74 seconds after liftoff.

20:18 The radio signal from Challenger goes silent.

20:21 Another explosion occurs near the space shuttle's  nose. The cockpit with all seven members of the

20:26 crew is engulfed in flames as the rocket fuel  in the forward reaction control system ignites.

20:31 The debris of the destroyed shuttle continues  traveling upward at Mach 1.92, or approximately

20:36 twice the speed of sound. It reaches an altitude  of 46,000 feet or 14,021 meters. Challenger’s tail

20:43 emerges from the fireball around the same moment  that a wing can be seen. The fuselage and payload

20:48 bay are torn apart by the rush of air forced in  from the tail being ripped off, overpressurizing

20:53 the payload bay and breaking it apart from the  inside out. Wires and electrical cables flail

20:58 behind the fuselage like tentacles. The satellites  in the cargo bay are ejected into the air.

21:03 The crew cabin arcs out of the flames  and smoke. It seems to be intact,

21:07 although there is a gaping hole where it  used to be connected to the rest of the

21:11 shuttle. Some of the crew may still be alive and  awake, but when the Challenger is ripped apart,

21:15 all of the air is sucked out of the cockpit,  and a dramatic pressure drops results in

21:19 everyone passing out. For this mission, the  astronauts did not wear pressurized suits

21:24 during liftoff. As they slump in their seats  unconscious, oxygen deprivation settles in.

21:29 Any crewmember who is still alive will  suffocate within the next few minutes.

21:33 The two solid rocket boosters continue  to fly upwards at different angles,

21:37 now free from the struts that connected  them to the external fuel tank.

21:40 1 second after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

21:43 Mission control does not yet know that the  Challenger space shuttle has exploded. "One

21:48 minute 15 seconds. Velocity 2,900 feet per second.  Altitude nine nautical miles. Downrange distance

21:54 seven nautical miles," says Stephen Nesbitt,  the public affairs officer at mission control.

21:59 2 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:02 A parachute emerges from the carnage, giving  people hope. But as the tracking camera focuses,

22:07 it turns out to be the nose cap of the  right solid rocket booster. Smoke and

22:11 flaming debris arc outward from the blast.  The rocket boosters continue to fly upward,

22:15 leaving a corkscrew trail of smoke behind them.

22:18 15 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:21 "Flight, GC, we've had negative contact,  loss of downlink," says ground control

22:26 engineer N.R. Talbott. It’s at this  point that mission control is aware

22:29 something tragic has happened and  is trying to figure out exactly

22:32 what happened. They are informed that the  Challenger space shuttle has been lost.

22:36 36 seconds after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

22:39 A self-destruct signal is sent to the  rogue solid rocket boosters triggering

22:43 an emergency detonation. Both rockets explode  in a plume of black smoke. Debris falls back

22:48 towards the Earth. Without the weight  of the space shuttle and fuel tank,

22:51 there was no telling how far the rockets  would have gone before burning the last

22:55 of their fuel. They needed to be detonated  to eliminate the risk of them crashing back

22:59 to Earth in a populated area rather than in  the desolate waters of the Atlantic Ocean.

23:04 1 minute and 31 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

23:07 Multiple sources have now confirmed

23:10 that Challenger STS-51-L has been  lost. Rescue efforts are launched.

23:14 2 minutes and 11 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

23:18 The TV tracking camera spots the first pieces  of the space shuttle crashing into the ocean.

23:22 33 seconds later, the crew cabin slams into  the waves of the Atlantic at approximately 200

23:28 miles per hour or 322 kilometers per hour. At a  breaking force 200 times that of normal gravity,

23:34 the crew cabin disintegrates on impact and  sinks 100 feet to the bottom of the ocean.

23:39 For the next few minutes, debris continues to  splash down into the ocean east of Patrick Air

23:44 Force Base. A cloud of brown smoke lingers  over the surface of the water as a result

23:48 of the hydrazine rocket fuel that covered the  wreckage as it entered the ocean. Mission control

23:53 pinpoints the crash site as being approximately  28.64 degrees North and 80.28 degrees West.

23:59 5 minutes after the Challenger  space shuttle explodes.

24:02 The broadcast on NASA television has been  eerily quiet as everyone tries to take in

24:07 what just happened. The camera view switches  from the ocean back to the grandstand at

24:11 the press site. Observers stand with their  backs to the camera, looking up at the sky,

24:14 where a white cloud of smoke still lingers.  White wisps of haze extend from the explosion

24:19 site like weeping willow vines indicating  where burning debris fell from the sky.

24:23 8 minutes and 5 seconds after the  Challenger space shuttle explodes.

24:27 "This is mission control, Houston. We are  coordinating with recovery forces in the field.

24:31 Range safety equipment, recovery vehicles intended  for the recovery of the SRBs in the general area,"

24:36 says Stephen Nesbitt in a somber voice. The  only thing left to do is go through the data,

24:41 recover as much of the space shuttle as  possible, and determine what caused the

24:45 horrific accident that led to the loss of 7  people aboard the Challenger space shuttle.

24:49 March 7, 1986, 1 month and 10 days after  the Challenger space shuttle disaster.

24:54 The USS Preserver bobs up and down in  the dark waters of the Atlantic Ocean.

24:59 A dive team has just been deployed to  scout the hypothesized location of the

25:03 Challenger cabin. The divers locate  the wreckage that was the front of

25:06 the space shuttle and confirm that the  bodies of the crew are still inside.

25:09 The aftermath of the Challenger  space shuttle disaster.

25:12 All space shuttles are immediately grounded, and  any upcoming launches are canceled pending a full

25:18 investigation of what happened to the Challenger.  NASA and a group of men appointed by President

25:22 Ronald Regan, known as the Rogers Commission,  begin looking into the chain of events that led to

25:27 the loss of the space shuttle and its crew. It’s  concluded that the space shuttles are being pushed

25:31 too hard, and the concerns of engineers working on  the crafts are being ignored or overlooked. What

25:37 it came down to was that NASA has been trying  to accomplish too much with too little funding.

25:42 The investigation also determines that  the two rubber O-rings, which led to

25:46 the fuel leak in the right booster and eventual  catastrophic explosion of the external fuel tank,

25:50 were compromised by the severe cold from  the night before the launch. Unfortunately,

25:55 even if the crew had been aware of a problem  at liftoff, there would have been no way for

25:59 them to avoid the disastrous consequences.  The space shuttle wouldn’t have been able

26:03 to survive a high-speed separation even if it was  attempted before the external fuel tank exploded.

26:08 On June 6, the report is given to the President,  who determines Marshall Space Flight Center in

26:13 Huntsville, Alabama, Morton Thiokol Inc.,  and NASA as a whole are responsible for the

26:18 Challenger disaster. Marshall Space Flight  Center constructed the shuttle boosters,

26:22 engines, and tank, while Morton Thiokol  manufactured and built the booster motors.

26:27 It’s also uncovered during the investigation from  several engineers who testify that they expressed

26:32 concerns specifically about the O-rings and their  seals to their supervisors for at least two years

26:37 prior to the loss of the Challenger. The Rogers  Commission recommends that communication between

26:42 engineers and NASA management be tightened,  quality control procedures be improved,

26:46 and several more checkpoints be added  to the shuttle safety advisory panel.

26:50 On September 29, 1988, the space shuttle Discovery  launches with five veteran astronauts on board.

26:56 This is the first mission since the Challenger  disaster. The space shuttle program lasts for

27:01 23 more years. On July 8, 2011, Atlantis launches  from Cape Canaveral. It will be the 135th space

27:08 shuttle mission. Atlantis lands on Jul 21, 2011,  marking the official end of the space shuttle era.

27:14 Two space shuttles were lost during the 30  years that they were in use. On February 1,

27:19 2003, Space Shuttle Columbia disintegrated as  it reentered the atmosphere, and on January 28,

27:25 1986, Challenger exploded due to a faulty  O-ring. Both crafts held a crew of 7, all of

27:30 which were lost and all of which were heroes. Now watch “Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima and

27:35 Nagasaki (Minute by Minute)” Or check out “What  If USA Launched a Nuclear Bomb (Minute by Minute)”

docs.text:
00:00 It's Friday night, the end of a long  week, and you decide to have a drink…

00:04 maybe two or three. We've all been there.  But have you ever wondered what's really

00:09 happening to your body when you start  drinking alcohol? Today on the channel,

00:13 we’re exploring what happens to your body –  minute by minute – when you drink alcohol.

00:17 We’ll examine each of these concepts (backed  by science, of course) through the lens of our

00:21 character, Sarah. We’ll follow her on her night  out—and beyond—breaking down the changes in her

00:26 body from the very first sip of her cocktail.  Ready to see what happens? Let’s head to the bar.

00:32 It's 10:06 p.m., and Sarah takes her first sip of  a skinny margarita—her go-to drink after a long

00:37 work week. That tangy, sweet flavor aside, what's  going on inside? The alcohol, called ethanol,

00:43 is a small molecule absorbed rapidly. Within  minutes, it's traveling through her bloodstream.

00:48 The vibrant bar atmosphere surrounds Sarah.  The clinking of glasses, casual chatter,

00:53 and upbeat music fill the air. This sensory  overload usually feels a bit much for her,

00:58 but as the alcohol starts to take effect,  it blends into a pleasantly muted buzz.

01:03 A wave of warmth spreads through Sarah's body.  Alcohol acts as a vasodilator, expanding her blood

01:08 vessels and leading to a feeling of warmth.  However, this also means that her body loses

01:13 heat more quickly, explaining why some people  feel cold later in the night after drinking.

01:18 It’s 10:21 pm. What’s going on inside  Sarah’s body? Let's zoom in! We see the

01:24 alcohol molecules from Sarah's margarita begin  their journey. A small portion, about 20%, is

01:30 absorbed directly through the lining of her mouth,  entering her bloodstream almost immediately.

01:34 The rest of the margarita travels down her  esophagus and into her stomach. Here, another

01:39 small portion, about 20%, of the alcohol enters  the bloodstream through the stomach lining. Once

01:44 in the bloodstream, alcohol takes a whirlwind tour  of the body, impacting various organs, especially

01:50 the brain. This initial absorption can explain  why people feel the effects of alcohol so quickly.

01:55 The remaining alcohol continues to Sarah's  small intestine. The walls of the small

01:59 intestine are lined with tiny,  finger-like projections called

02:03 villi. These villi provide a huge surface  area to absorb nutrients… and alcohol.

02:08 The alcohol rapidly passes  through the villi and into

02:11 the network of blood vessels surrounding  the small intestine. Now it enters the

02:14 portal vein, which acts like a highway  transporting it directly to the liver.

02:19 The liver is bathed in a surge of alcohol-rich  blood. Keep in mind that while the liver is the

02:24 powerhouse of detoxification and will work  hard to break down the ethanol molecules,

02:29 its capacity is limited. It can only  process so much in any given time period.

02:34 When the liver can't keep up, the excess  alcohol continues to circulate throughout

02:37 Sarah's body via her bloodstream. This  is how alcohol ultimately reaches her

02:42 brain and other organs, causing the changes  we'll witness as Sarah's evening continues.

02:47 It's 10:39 pm, and with the first drink down,

02:50 Sarah is feeling a slight buzz.  Typically a pretty anxious person,

02:53 Sarah finds herself a bit less stressed.  Alcohol reduces activity in the amygdala,

02:58 the part of the brain associated with fear and  anxiety. But while this might feel good at the

03:03 moment, chronic reliance on alcohol for stress  relief can actually worsen anxiety over time.

03:08 Sarah leans back into her chair and takes a deep  breath. A sense of ease washes over her. The

03:14 worries that were nagging in her mind seemed  to fade into the background. This isn't just

03:19 her imagination; there's a biochemical reason  behind the shift. Alcohol acts as a depressant,

03:24 slowing down the activity of the  central nervous system. This means

03:28 that messages between Sarah's brain  cells are traveling a little slower

03:31 than usual. It's kind of like putting the  brakes on her usual whirlwind of thoughts.

03:36 As her thoughts quiet down, so does the  activity in her sympathetic nervous system,

03:40 which is responsible for our "fight-or-flight"  response. Her heart rate slows slightly,

03:45 her breathing becomes easier, and  any muscle tension she is holding .

03:50 A subtle change has come over Sarah’s  face. Her cheeks are slightly flushed,

03:53 and her eyes have a slight sparkle. This is  due to the blood vessel dilation we mentioned

03:58 earlier. As Sarah catches a glimpse of  herself in the mirror behind the bar,

04:01 she feels a little more attractive. This boost  in self-perception is a common effect of alcohol,

04:06 as it lowers inhibitions and can  temporarily increase self-confidence.

04:10 Alcohol affects the neurotransmitters in her  brain. It boosts the release of dopamine – the

04:15 "feel-good" chemical – making her feel  happier and more relaxed. Simultaneously,

04:20 alcohol suppresses glutamate, the brain's  primary excitatory neurotransmitter.

04:24 This slowdown is starting to slightly  impact her judgment and coordination.

04:29 Sarah’s usual social inhibitions start to fade,  and she starts talking to the guy next to her

04:34 at the bar. Conversation feels easy. Alcohol,  often known as a “social lubricant,” dampens

04:39 the activity in the prefrontal cortex of the  brain – the region responsible for judgment,

04:43 planning, and impulse control. This  makes it easier for Sarah to strike up

04:47 conversations with strangers and feel more  at ease in the social setting of the bar.

04:51 But it’s a delicate balance. While the  relaxation might feel nice at this point,

04:56 if Sarah continues drinking,  this effect will intensify,

04:59 potentially leading to poor judgment and impaired  decision-making further into her evening.

05:04 It's 10:55 pm, and with a second drink in  hand and almost finished, the alcohol level

05:10 in Sarah's blood is rising pretty rapidly. The  liver, our body's chemical processing plant,

05:15 is working hard to metabolize the alcohol. But  the liver can only handle about one standard

05:19 drink per hour. When it gets overwhelmed, excess  alcohol continues to circulate in the bloodstream.

05:25 Sarah swirls the remaining liquid in her  glass. The ice cubes clink hollowly with each

05:29 circle. She catches the bartender’s eye  and orders a third cocktail. The bar,

05:34 dim and tucked away, is starting  to blur a little around the edges.

05:37 It’s 11:16 pm, and Sarah has decided to buy a  round of shots for a group of strangers. While the

05:43 gesture feels generous at the moment, her impaired  judgment is making her less aware of the potential

05:48 financial strain of this decision. It also  increases the pace of her alcohol consumption.

05:53 Sarah is much more talkative than usual  and feels more and more confident. This is

05:58 because alcohol is further depressing the areas  in the brain associated with social anxiety and

06:03 judgment. However, her motor skills are also  starting to become increasingly impaired.

06:08 As the drinks keep coming, Sarah feels  more shifts. She senses a giddy lightness

06:13 she hasn't experienced in ages. Her  words, normally measured and precise,

06:17 tumble out in a stream, no  longer carefully filtered.

06:21 Sarah regales the bartender – a quiet, middle-aged  man named Pete – with stories about her demanding

06:27 boss, her disastrous dating life, and the  time she accidentally glued her fingers

06:32 together during a home improvement project.  It all comes spilling out, punctuated by

06:36 bouts of laughter that are just a touch too  loud for the subdued atmosphere of the bar.

06:41 The buzz that had been a pleasant hum  before is now a full-blown symphony

06:45 in Sarah’s head. Her movements  are becoming less deliberate,

06:48 her glass sloshing a bit as she sets it down,  a napkin fluttering to the floor unnoticed.

06:54 It’s 11:57 pm. When getting up to use the  restroom, Sarah accidentally bumps into a table,

06:59 almost knocking over someone else's drink.  She laughs it off and attributes it to

07:03 the dim lighting, but in reality, alcohol is  subtly affecting her coordination and balance.

07:08 Sarah’s blood alcohol concentration continues  to rise, affecting her vision, speech,

07:13 and balance. She’s continuing to experience  blurred vision and slurred speech. All of

07:17 this is due to the way alcohol continues to  disrupt communication between her brain cells.

07:22 The lights above the bar seem to pulse in rhythm  with her heartbeat. As she sips her next cocktail,

07:27 the world tilts just a touch. It seems funny  now that there is this lack of coordination,

07:32 as if someone else is in charge of her body.

07:34 Pete, the bartender, asks Sarah a question, which  she barely hears. She tries to respond, but her

07:39 words seem to trip over one another, a jumbled  mess that leaves a frustrated laugh in her throat.

07:44 At 12:32 am, with multiple cocktails and a shot in  her system, Sarah is definitely feeling drunk. Her

07:50 phone slips out of her hand as she tries to take  a selfie. It takes her several tries before she

07:55 manages to catch it. Her slower reflexes make  normally simple tasks slightly more difficult.

08:00 Sarah's appetite is starting to kick in. While  alcohol can temporarily increase appetite,

08:05 in the long run, it can disrupt hormones  that regulate hunger and fullness,

08:09 potentially leading to unhealthy eating habits.  Leptin suppresses appetite, while glucagon-like

08:14 peptide-1 (GLP-1) regulates food intake… and both  of these are inhibited when drinking alcohol.

08:21 She clumsily calls Pete over and orders  the enchiladas, but he informs her that

08:25 the kitchen is closed. She starts to  search on her phone for restaurants still

08:29 serving food and asks some of the other  patrons at the bar for recommendations. Then,

08:33 she stumbles next door to a slightly livelier  bar, where she orders another cocktail.

08:38 It’s 1:12 am, and Sarah has tried to maintain  her confident buzz and relaxed demeanor,

08:43 but she’s not feeling so hot. After drinking  far too much than her liver can handle,

08:47 she’s reeling from the effects. The upbeat music  she usually enjoys now feels too loud and chaotic.

08:53 She also misinterprets a friendly smile from  another bar patron as a flirtatious gesture.

08:58 Alcohol has altered her perception of  sound and social cues. When she tries

09:02 to flirt back and the stranger walks away,  Sarah feels a sweeping sense of rejection.

09:07 Coupled with an exaggerated emotional  state is a physical feeling of nausea,

09:11 and Sarah runs to the bathroom to vomit.  Throwing up is the body’s defense mechanism

09:16 for a variety of reasons. First, when the body  recognizes alcohol as a toxin and wants to get

09:21 rid of it as quickly as possible, vomiting  is one way to expel the excess alcohol.

09:26 Additionally, when your liver breaks down alcohol,  it produces a toxic byproduct called acetaldehyde.

09:31 If you drink too much, your liver can't process  the acetaldehyde fast enough, leading to a

09:32 buildup that makes you feel sick. Vomiting helps  your body get rid of some of the acetaldehyde.

09:32 Finally, alcohol directly irritates your  stomach lining. This irritation can lead

09:36 to nausea and vomiting, especially if you  drink a lot in a short period, like Sarah.

09:41 After a fellow patron helps hold Sarah’s  hair back as she throws up in the bathroom,

09:46 Sarah knows it’s time to go.  She gets a cab and heads home,

09:49 falling asleep in her clothes and  makeup on top of her comforter.

09:53 It’s 7:02 am, and Sarah wakes up with a  pounding headache and a hazy memory of

09:58 last night. That headache? It's partly  due to dehydration caused by alcohol,

10:03 which also greatly disrupted her sleep. After a  night of strange dreams and sweating profusely,

10:08 her body is still working to clear  the remaining alcohol from her system.

10:11 Alcohol's sleep disruption is a double-edged  sword. While drinking may help you fall asleep

10:16 initially, the quality of sleep is severely  compromised. REM sleep – crucial for memory

10:21 and emotional processing – is suppressed,  leaving you feeling groggy and unrested.

10:26 Sunlight pierces through a sliver  in Sarah’s blackout curtains,

10:29 a searing lance of pain across  her throbbing skull. She groans,

10:33 her head feeling as though it were filled  with angry wasps. Each movement sends fresh

10:37 waves of nausea through her body. Her stomach  churns, and her mouth is a desert landscape.

10:43 Dehydration is a major hangover culprit.  Alcohol acts as a diuretic, suppressing a

10:48 hormone called vasopressin, which regulates fluid  levels. Not only does this increase urination,

10:53 but paired with nausea and potential  vomiting, it can leave you dehydrated.

10:58 Fragments of the previous night  flickered back in painful flashes:

11:01 the laughter that turned too loud, the  spilled drinks, Pete's worried frown.

11:06 A wave of shame washes over Sarah. How  much had she drunk? What had she said?

11:11 Alcohol-induced memory blackouts are frighteningly  common. As blood alcohol concentration rises,

11:17 the hippocampus, the brain's memory  center, is impaired. Long-term memory

11:21 formation can be blocked, leaving you with  frustrating gaps in your recollection.

11:25 Sarah presses a shaking hand to  her temple. She would need to piece

11:29 together the night and retrace her steps—a  daunting task considering the state of her

11:33 brain. There was the lingering sense of having  done something reckless. She vaguely remembers

11:38 falling onto a table, and was that a  stranger holding her hair back while

11:42 she vomited in the bathroom? Everything  is just a little too foggy for her liking.

11:47 It’s 8:14 am, and after tossing and turning in bed  for a while, Sarah stumbles towards the kitchen,

11:52 each step a measured battle against the persistent  nausea. Her goal sits on the countertop – a tall,

11:58 frosted glass left out since the night before. She  fills it to the brim with icy water. Rehydration

12:04 is crucial to hangover recovery. Alcohol's  diuretic effect leaves you severely depleted,

12:09 throwing your electrolyte balance  off-kilter. Replenishing these

12:12 lost fluids can help ease symptoms  like headaches, fatigue, and nausea.

12:16 Alcohol also depletes vital nutrients, including  potassium, magnesium, and zinc. While water is

12:22 crucial, supplementing with electrolyte-rich  drinks or foods like bananas, sports drinks, or

12:27 broth can aid in restoring balance. Unfortunately,  there's no magical cure for a hangover. The body

12:34 simply needs time to metabolize the alcohol and  repair the damage. While rehydration and rest

12:39 are essential, the lingering effects  may well persist throughout the day.

12:43 So, does everyone’s body respond to alcohol  similarly? Or are there certain risk factors

12:48 Sarah has? While it's easy to assume that everyone  experiences a night of drinking the same way,

12:53 that's not true. While the immediate effects  of Sarah's drinks felt unpleasant enough,

12:58 there are hidden factors that might  make her especially vulnerable to

13:01 the longer-term effects of alcohol.  Let's examine some of those risks.

13:05 First, there’s the fact that Sarah’s a  female. Biology plays a big role here.

13:09 Women generally metabolize alcohol  slower than men, leading to a higher

13:13 concentration in their blood. They also tend  to have a higher percentage of body fat,

13:17 which means less water to dilute the alcohol,  making its impact stronger. These factors could

13:23 contribute to both negative short-term  and long-term consequences for Sarah.

13:27 What about weight? It’s true that a person  with a smaller body will feel the effects of

13:31 alcohol more strongly than someone with  a larger body, even if they consume the

13:35 same amount. This is because the alcohol is less  diluted in the bloodstream of someone smaller.

13:41 Next, there’s the factor of food intake  before and during drinking. In Sarah’s case,

13:45 she worked until 7:00 pm, then  went home, showered, got ready,

13:48 and went out… but skipped dinner, thinking she’d  get a bite sometime during the night. Not having

13:54 eaten beforehand was detrimental to her, and by  the time her appetite intensified later in the

13:59 night, the local kitchens were closed.  Drinking on an empty stomach accelerated

14:03 the absorption of alcohol into her bloodstream,  intensifying its impact on her brain and body.

14:08 There are also risk factors associated with  medications and other substances. It's vital

14:13 not to mix alcohol with anything else without  consulting a medical professional. Even common

14:18 over-the-counter medications or certain herbal  supplements can have dangerous interactions when

14:23 combined with alcohol, exacerbating the effects  of both. Sarah is on anti-anxiety medication,

14:29 which puts her at greater risk of feeling  the intense effects of excess alcohol.

14:33 It's crucial to remember that these  individual risk factors can compound

14:37 over time. The more frequently Sarah  drinks, and the more heavily she drinks,

14:41 the higher the risk of alcohol impacting her  health in the long run in a wide variety of ways.

14:47 While today’s hangover feels awful,  it's a short-term consequence of

14:50 Sarah's alcohol consumption. What's  more concerning is that repeated,

14:54 excessive alcohol use can put a strain on her  body, silently increasing her risk for serious,

14:59 chronic health problems over time.  Let's look at some of those risks.

15:03 First, there’s liver damage. Our liver takes  the brunt of processing the alcohol we drink.

15:08 It's resilient, but long-term, heavy drinking  can lead to a buildup of fat in the liver,

15:12 inflammation (hepatitis), and, eventually,  irreversible scarring known as cirrhosis. A

15:18 damaged liver can struggle to function properly,  which has widespread effects on the entire body,

15:23 from swelling known as edema to loss of menstrual  cycle to, possibly and eventually, cancer.

15:29 In fact, alcohol is a known carcinogen,  contributing to the development of several

15:34 types of cancer. The risk is associated with all  kinds of cancers, including those of the mouth,

15:39 throat, esophagus, liver, colon, and  breast. The more you drink and the

15:43 longer the duration of heavy drinking,  the higher your overall risk becomes.

15:48 Then, there’s potential heart disease. Chronic  alcohol consumption weakens the heart muscle and

15:52 disrupts its rhythm, increasing blood  pressure and making it harder to pump

15:57 blood efficiently. Over time, this raises the  risk of heart attack and stroke. Even light

16:01 to moderate drinking has been linked to a  slight increase in cardiovascular risks.

16:05 How about mental health? Alcohol and mental  health have a complex, two-way relationship.

16:11 For some people, drinking can become a way to numb  negative emotions or cope with stress. However,

16:17 chronic alcohol use can actually worsen  existing conditions like anxiety and

16:21 depression, even increasing the risk of  developing new mental health disorders.

16:26 These conditions can all develop insidiously.  Sarah might not immediately feel the impact

16:31 of chronic alcohol use, but if she has  regular occurrences of heavy drinking,

16:35 the damage might be silently accumulating  inside her body. Understanding these

16:39 risks highlights the importance of  responsible alcohol consumption.

16:43 Sometimes, the line between social drinking  and something more problematic can blur.

16:48 For some people, alcohol use can become  difficult to manage, leading to a condition

16:52 called Alcohol Use Disorder, or AUD. It's a  chronic, relapsing medical condition where

16:58 someone can't control their alcohol intake,  even when it causes significant harm.

17:04 Understanding the signs of AUD is  crucial. Let's break down some key

17:07 symptoms. Note that AUD comes in  varying degrees – mild, moderate,

17:11 or severe. These signs might be subtle at first  or only become noticeable during difficult times.

17:17 The first thing to look for is cravings – a strong  desire or compulsion to drink alcohol. Sarah might

17:23 find herself thinking about alcohol frequently,  and those thoughts may become hard to ignore.

17:28 Then, there’s the loss of control.  Having trouble limiting the amount

17:31 of alcohol consumed or the duration of  drinking episodes. For someone with AUD,

17:36 the intention of "just one drink"  might often spiral into several more.

17:40 Additionally, there’s the dependence factor.  This includes things like building a tolerance,

17:45 which means needing more alcohol to feel  the same effect, or experiencing withdrawal

17:50 symptoms like shakiness, nausea,  or insomnia when stopping drinking.

17:54 It's important to understand that AUD is  not a sign of weakness or a moral failing.

17:59 It's a complex disease influenced by a mix of  genetic predispositions, environmental factors,

18:05 and individual psychology. The earlier  someone with AUD seeks professional help,

18:10 the better their chances of successful recovery.

18:12 Now check out “What Happens To Your Body When You

18:15 Stop Drinking Alcohol.” Or  watch this video instead!

00:00 In October of 1347, 12 ships dropped anchor at a Sicilian port.
