00:14 boils that dripped blood and pus.

00:16 In horror, the Sicilian authorities demanded the ships set sail, but though they left,

00:22 the damage had already been done.

00:23 The Black Death was now in Europe and millions would die in what is considered one of the

00:28 greatest disasters in history.

00:30 Let’s explore how the bubonic plague wiped out at least a third of Europe’s population,

00:35 if not more, in this episode of the Infographics Show, What Made the Black Death so Deadly?

00:41 Europe was hit hard by the plague, but it was not hit first.

00:44 It was also not unaware of a disease that was already bringing widespread death and

00:48 destruction elsewhere.

00:50 Before the infested ships arrived in Sicily rumors of a frightful sickness devastating

00:55 the populations of first China and then India, Egypt, Persia, and Syria had spread near and

01:00 far.

01:01 While no one knew what caused it or why, it seemed to follow trade routes spanning the

01:06 Near and Far East.

01:08 Further, when it appeared, it was by all accounts unstoppable.

01:12 Those struck by the Black Death would begin to swell at the lymph nodes located in their

01:16 groin area or under arm regions.

01:18 The growths would soon develop into large blackish blue egg-sized lumps, or for the

01:23 even less fortunate, expand to the size of apples.

01:26 These would then fester and ooze various bodily fluids.

01:29 Beyond this, those with the disease could develop any combination of a series of additional

01:34 symptoms.

01:35 These included fever, pain, chills, sweating, upset stomach, and diarrhea.

01:40 Almost always, this was followed by death.

01:43 According to those who observed its effects first-hand, all it appeared to take was brief

01:47 physical contact with the clothing of someone who was sick to pass the disease on to another.

01:52 Though, some doctors claimed that it was the spirit leaving the body of the deceased that

01:56 infected others as it passed by.

01:59 Obviously, at this point in history the real methods of disease transmission were not yet

02:03 well understood.

02:04 Without understanding it, most were helpless to defend against it.

02:07 Few areas other than some islands cut off from the rest of Europe by the sea made it

02:12 through the pandemic plague-free.

02:14 The rest of the population was not so lucky.

02:16 The bacterium infiltrated virtually every European city’s defenses and many who appeared

02:21 perfectly healthy one day could be dead a few days later.

02:25 It was uncommon though possible for someone to survive a week or two before he or she

02:30 died.

02:31 Compounding problems further, those with the disease would typically be asymptomatic for

02:35 the first few days and so no one would be aware that they had caught it.

02:38 This meant that successfully isolating them from the rest of society at this point was

02:42 all but impossible.

02:44 Those who tried the next best thing to protect themselves by fleeing for the country were

02:48 not safe there either.

02:49 The plague decimated livestock as well and countless pigs, cows, chickens, goats, and

02:54 sheep who also died a brutal death.

02:57 This was such a problem that it led to a shortage of wool throughout the continent.

03:01 While many European areas had a death figure of around 30%, 90% of the Italian city of

03:07 Florence perished.

03:08 Sometimes, bodies of the deceased remained where they had died as there were not enough

03:12 people still living to bury them.

03:14 Thousands of French villages in addition to areas in other locations were left without

03:18 a single remaining soul.

03:20 The Black Death had mercilessly transformed them into ghost towns.

03:24 In some instances, nature eventually took over, and areas that people once called home

03:29 were re-claimed by surrounding forest.

03:31 It took aerial photography following the end of World War I to rediscover these locations

03:36 as places where men, women, and children once lived.

03:39 Most estimates place Europe’s death total between 50 and 70 million, or around thirty-some

03:44 percent, though the CDC claims it killed as much as 60% of the population, which is considerably

03:50 more.

03:51 World-wide estimates typically range from 155 to 200 million.

03:55 The world at the time was a mere 500 million people, so nearly half of all of its’ inhabitants,

04:01 or again according to some sources even more, were killed.

04:04 So how was it that the Black Death was able to spread so quickly and wipe out so many,

04:09 people and animals alike?

04:11 Well for one, as previously mentioned, there was little in the way of scientific knowledge

04:15 in the 1300s.

04:16 Not only did people not understand the plague’s causes or modes of transmission, but there

04:21 were also countless failures in how those in the medical field attempted to treat it.

04:26 It is true that Yersina pestis, the bacterium behind the Black Death, or bubonic plague,

04:30 is highly contagious.

04:32 It can also be spread in many ways, though obviously contaminated spirits aren’t one

04:37 of them.

04:38 Many believe that in its later stages it had the ability to morph into an airborne strain

04:42 that could be passed on to a new host via a simple sneeze or cough.

04:45 However, all strains, airborne or those in the more initial stages that are not, are

04:50 believed to have been transferred through flea or lice bites.

04:53 And many animals in addition to countryside livestock serve as hosts for the bacterium

04:58 and blood sucking pests.

04:59 Examples are things like squirrels, rabbits, chipmunks, and mice.

05:03 However, many in the scientific field have argued that by far the worst contributor to

05:07 the spread of the Black Death was the urban rat and its flea.

05:11 Part of the reason for this belief is that rats have been observed to develop symptoms

05:15 quite similar to those in people, and in cases of the modern-day plague many people with

05:19 the sickness had accompanying bites from fleas.

05:22 Recent outbreaks often follow what’s known as ‘rat falls’ as well, or when the rodents

05:27 die off in record amounts for whatever reason.

05:29 Thus, the most prevalent theory is that the Black Death all began when rats with the plague

05:34 died and their fleas then looked for more blood in another readily available source,

05:38 which would at times be human.

05:41 Upon being bitten by the contaminated flea this person would then be exposed to the deadly

05:45 bacteria.

05:46 Seemingly in support of this theory, ships during the mid-1300s were commonly infested

05:50 with the furry rodents who thrived in their dark.

05:53 moist environment.

05:54 And following the death ships’ arrival in Sicily the plague continued to spread further

05:58 following a trade route pattern, as it had previously in Asia, to other port locations

06:03 throughout Europe and as far down as North Africa.

06:06 However, more recently there have been some proposed tweaks to this rat-based theory.

06:11 As we just mentioned, the Black Death, after all, is not the only outbreak of the plague

06:15 in the world’s history.

06:16 There have been outbreaks before as well as after, and those that took place more recently

06:21 followed a different pattern entirely.

06:23 Europe’s black death spread much faster, and as far as historical records are concerned

06:27 there was no mention of a mass rat die-off in the days or months preceding it.

06:32 Now, some scientists suggest that it was human fleas and lice that were the true culprits

06:37 behind Europe’s version of the disease.

06:39 In this case fleas would bite infected people and then move on to others, one by one, who

06:43 happened to be in the nearby vicinity.

06:45 They describe the underlying mathematical model that a rat-flea spread follows is quite

06:49 different from a human-flea or lice one.

06:52 And, when information was plugged into simulations the human-flea model more closely matched

06:56 data from seven of nine plague-hit European cities.

07:00 Those with this newest evidence admit that the causes of the plague are surrounded by

07:04 ongoing controversy.

07:05 However, whether the fleas were of the human or rat variety, it is blood sucking pests

07:10 of one kind or another that likely passed it on successfully and so very quickly.

07:15 It also turns out that the Black Death may not have been causing mass devastation all

07:20 by itself.

07:21 When victims bodies were exhumed from mass graves in England anthrax spores were also

07:25 discovered along with them.

07:26 If anthrax was occurring at the same time as the plague this would definitely have made

07:31 things much worse.

07:33 Anthrax cannot only be passed by coming into contact with sweat, saliva, or tears but also

07:38 by mere skin contact.

07:40 In other words, at the time of the Black Death pandemic, people could have come down with

07:44 a life-threatening disease of one kind or another in pretty much every conceivable way.

07:49 It is possible anthrax and other diseases made people extra susceptible to the plague

07:53 due to already compromised immunity.

07:55 Also, it is possible that the body count of those claimed by the Black Death included

08:00 victims that actually died from anthrax or other diseases.

08:03 Beyond its quick transfer from host to host and the contributions of additional disease,

08:09 the way the Black Death was treated failed to help and may have actually helped kill

08:13 victims or spread it further unintentionally.

08:16 For example, at least initially, medical practitioners would do such things as perform bloodletting

08:20 on patients with the plague.

08:22 This is where they cut into veins or arteries in the necks or arms of those who were sick,

08:27 so that their blood flowed freely.

08:29 This procedure was nothing new and, in fact, dated back as far as to the times of ancient

08:34 Egypt and Greece.

08:35 Historical figures believed that to be healthy the body needed the right balance of blood,

08:39 phlegm, and bile.

08:41 Bloodletting was believed to correct a possible imbalance of too much blood which is what

08:45 caused the person to get sick.

08:48 Unfortunately, the procedure appeared to be as ineffective for the victims of the plague

08:51 as it was for Charles II or George Washington centuries later.

08:55 While Washington awoke with a sore throat and King Charles suffered a seizure, following

09:00 bloodletting treatment both died shortly thereafter.

09:03 Boil-lancing was another technique used as a form of treatment which was just how it

09:08 sounds.

09:09 Someone would essentially lance, or stick a pointy object, into the boils to drain them

09:13 of their gooey contents.

09:14 If this wasn’t done, they would only continue to grow larger and, in time.

09:18 poison their host due to the mass build-up of dead blood and pus.

09:22 Then again, popping them could also cause death due to toxic shock.

09:26 Beyond the patient likely dying, the boils contained highly contagious matter and possibly

09:30 spread the disease yet further.

09:32 Other methods such as the burning of various herbs or immersing the sick in vinegar or

09:36 rosewater were also, unsurprisingly, ineffective.

09:39 In time, after failure upon failure and in an attempt at self-preservation, many doctors

09:45 simply stopped accepting patients.

09:47 Even priests began refusing to perform last rites out of danger for their own safety.

09:52 Where man failed nature did little to help either.

09:55 Not only did people have little idea of how to handle the plague, but they were genetically

09:59 prone to succumbing to it.

10:01 Studies of the remains of the European population at the time determined that only 0.2% had

10:07 a gene that offered them any form of immunity.

10:10 The other 99.8% had none.

10:12 Since so many of those who were susceptible to the plague died from it, they did not pass

10:16 their genes on further to the following generations.

10:19 Many of those who did have the gene lived on to procreate.

10:22 This is why Caucasian Americans now have a 15% chance of having some resistance to the

10:27 disease.

10:28 This is pretty good news considering the modern form of the plague is still around today.

10:33 One encounter via the 12 so-called death ships would go on to wipe out men, women, and children

10:39 to such an extent that it would change the tide of history.

10:42 What do you think, was it passed on by human or rat fleas?

10:46 Let us know in the comments!

10:47 Also, be sure to check out our other video called Could the Black Death (The Plague)

10:51 Happen Again?!

10:52 Thanks for watching, and, as always, don’t forget to like, share, and

10:56 subscribe.

10:57 See you next time!

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: How EVE Online's Massive Virtual Wars Are Financed
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: How EVE Online's Massive Virtual Wars Are Financed
  • Video ID: m6j_UsGJnkQ
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 This is eve online, a massive  multiplayer online spaceship

00:03 game which is probably best know for two things.

00:07 Making headlines about it’s massive in game  conflicts involving tens of thousands of players

00:12 and it’s incredibly realistic in game financial  system which can make loosing a virtual spaceship

00:16 just as consequential as loosing a  phone or a car in the real world.

00:21 Countless magazines, and even much more successful  YouTube channels have talked about these two

00:25 factors individually, but where I think they get  really interesting is when they merge together.

00:31 For a game about spaceships set 21,000 years in  the future, EVE is surprisingly realistic, and

00:38 that realism extends to these massive  wars in the sense that they are expensive.

00:43 The in game currency called ISK has an approximate  exchange rate of about $6 per billion in game isk.

00:49 Although it must be mentioned that trading this  in game currency directly back or forth for real

00:53 life money is actually against the rules of the  game for now at least and will get you banned.

00:59 Even still, this shows that in game assets have a  very tangible real world value on the grey market,

01:05 so when you see headlines about trillions  of ISK been lost in these epic battles

01:10 it gives you an idea of just how expensive  it can be to wage entire wars in EVE Online.

01:15 But this all begs a bigger question…

01:17 Who or what funds these wars?

01:20 With a price tag of hundreds of thousands of  real world dollars and nothing but virtual

01:23 space pride in return, it doesn’t  sound like a very good deal… Right?

01:28 Well, it’s time to learn how space  money works, if you enjoy this video

01:32 please consider liking and subscribing for  new video’s like this one made every week.

01:37 Ok so there are three really interesting  and unique ways these major wars have been

01:41 funded over the past 2 decades that this game has  existed. But let’s start with the most basic one.

01:46 The game is home to a selection of  megacorporations that are run entirely

01:50 by players, similar in many ways to… guilds in  world of warcraft, only on a much larger scale.

01:56 Now the largest of these corporations effectively  run like nation states, they have defined borders,

02:01 a standing military, taxation, industry  and of course command structures.

02:07 These large institutions will inevitably but  heads with other similar entities over resources,

02:12 territory, or you know just for fun. At  the end of the day it is a video game

02:16 so the reasons to go to war can simply be to  entertain the members of these corporations.

02:21 Now what will normally happen is that the  individual participants in these wars will need

02:25 to provide their own combat ships, funded out  of the money they make in game themselves.

02:30 But if these ships are lost in battle the  mega corporations will pay to replace them.

02:34 They do this because ultimately they  will need manpower to win these wars.

02:38 Ensuring that people aren’t too afraid  of losing their ships will mean that

02:41 their players will keep on logging in and  yoloing into these devastating space battles.

02:46 Now these Ship Replacement Programs, or  SRP will most often be funded by the taxes

02:50 collected from these corporations  during times of relative peace.

02:54 The industrialist get given a safe and secure  piece of territory to conduct their business

02:58 and in turn they need to pay a portion of  their profits to a central authority which

03:03 will then fund a military program to maintain or  potentially even expand this protected territory.

03:09 Effectively it’s exactly the same as what happens  with every government ever in the real world.

03:14 Now this is fine in theory, but often times  these industrial entities don’t have the

03:19 capacity to wage war themselves. In these  circumstances they can call on mercenary

03:24 entities that do nothing but wage war  on other people’s behalf for a fee.

03:29 Again not overly dissimilar to what  happens from time to time in the real

03:32 world with military contract corporations like  academi performing a very similar function.

03:37 Now so far we have been looking at relatively  minor wars, the ones that might be a big deal

03:42 to the players of the game and s___posters  on R/EVE (Pronounced AR Slash EVE) but are

03:46 not exactly that remarkable to an  uninvolved onlooker like you or I.

03:50 But this all changed around 5 years ago.

03:53 You see EVE’s economy is so realistic and

03:56 so diverse that at one point there  were virtual casino’s in the game…

04:00 these were founded, funded and operated entirely  by regular players using the in game currency.

04:06 Of course, these casino’s generated massive  profits just like most of them do in the real

04:11 world. Now these in game profits were great  and all but there wasn’t much that they could

04:16 do with them on an individual level. That  kind of money could buy every spaceship

04:20 in the game many times over so they needed  something grander to put their money towards.

04:24 The logical answer was to sell the  in game money for real world money

04:28 whether it was allowed or not. Sure they  risked getting banned from a video game

04:33 but the collective total of ISK that these  casino’s generated was worth millions of dollars,

04:38 so that was a risk a lot of these  casino owners were willing to take.

04:44 This was especially convenient given  that the thousands of transactions the

04:47 casino’s handled daily were the perfect  cover from in game money laundering.

04:52 It was almost impossible to distinguish  between transactions that were legitimate

04:56 and those that weren’t. Again very  similar to casino’s in the real world

05:00 which are continually in the news for  being centre’s for money laundering.

05:03 However the more “honourable” casino owners,  decided to use their space dollars to buy

05:09 something not available on  the public market… Influence.

05:13 2016 kicked off the so called  Casino Wars, as the “I Want ISK”

05:17 Online Casino funded a coalition of player  corporations to wage war on the single most

05:21 powerful player corporation in the game which had  wronged the casino in a previous business deal.

05:27 In reality all of these other player  run organisations were looking for

05:31 any excuse to go to war in an attempt to bring  the “imperium” as it is known in check. They

05:37 simply lacked the financial backing to  undertake such a significant challenge.

05:41 But with the casino’s writing the cheques (as a  way to prove a point as to what happens when you

05:45 dishonour a business deal) one of the most  devastating wars in the game’s history was

05:49 enabled which in turn gave us the PC gamer  articles about spectacular space battles.

05:54 And yes, the finances behind it might  be a little bit less spectacular,

05:58 but that does not mean they  are any less interesting.

06:02 Now shortly following this war the developers

06:04 of EVE online decided to put an  end to these player run Casino’s.

06:07 Now they said they had their own reasons but  most players speculate it was a combination

06:12 of wanting to cut down on the trade of  in game money for real money, and also

06:16 as a response to player backlash over these  entities having too much power over the game.

06:21 What this meant was that in 2020 there  was a new funding model required.

06:26 The old belligerents from the casino  war were ready to go at it again,

06:30 only this time a few things were different.

06:33 For starters the casino’s were no more,  which meant that no side would have

06:37 limitless funding given to them. What’s more  is that 2020 was a year of working from home

06:42 with no options for entertainment besides sitting  in front of a computer playing video games.

06:47 This was all shaping up to create potentially  the largest conflict in the game’s history,

06:51 a conflict that would also be the most costly.

06:54 The most crucial battles during  this conflict were inevitably going

06:57 to be decided by who could bring more of the  largest ships in the game to bear, the titans.

07:02 These ships are extremely powerful, and were  at least up until recently extremely rare,

07:08 but changes in the game in recent years  had meant that the industrial powerhouses

07:12 could produce these once legendary  ship’s as if they were ford model t’s.

07:16 This didn’t mean they were  any less expensive however,

07:19 it just meant the powers that be had to bring  more of them to keep up with their opposition.

07:23 The side that had previously been funded  by the casino’s were happy to just fund

07:27 this war in the traditional way, using  the tax money they had collected over

07:30 the years of peace and prosperity  to foot the bill for these battles.

07:33 But the imperium had a better idea, they had  seen how finance had decided their fate in 2016,

07:40 and were keen to ensure they were  economically dominant going into

07:43 the war of 2020. So they once again  looked to reality for inspiration.

07:49 War bonds are often issued by governments  during periods of all out conflict.

07:53 This is because modern wars are  expensive, and raising taxes

07:57 is often impossible if the entire economy  has been dedicated towards the war effort.

08:02 So government bonds are issued so that people  can invest in their own nation’s victory.

08:08 The imperium did exactly this,  they sold off a series of bonds,

08:12 that would pay interest to their own members.

08:14 This was obviously great for the  imperium itself because it got the

08:18 much needed injection of capital it  needed to go off and fight the war,

08:21 but it was also great for the  members of the group as well.

08:24 Scams, and financial fraud are commonplace in eve

08:27 and there is no regulation around taking  someone’s stuff and never giving it back.

08:32 In fact these types of swindles are probably  the thing that eve is third best known for.

08:36 But while having a totally  unregulated financial system is

08:39 great for cool stories it’s  terrible for investing,

08:42 because well anything you invest can and likely  will just be stolen off you, so why bother.

08:48 These war bonds presented an  opportunity for players to

08:50 invest in an asset that didn’t have  quiet the same risk of being stolen.

08:55 For clarity, the imperium would be fully  within their right’s to turn around and

08:59 tell these investors to get stuffed, but the  hit to their entities reputation would likely

09:04 not be worth it, especially if they ever wanted  to sell war bonds again to fund future wars.

09:10 Now that doesn’t mean that these in game financial  instruments are totally without risk, if the

09:15 imperium get’s destroyed in this ongoing war,  well then, these bonds aren’t going to get paid.

09:20 In the real world analysts  call this sovereign risk,

09:24 and it’s no less important here as it  is in the land of internet spaceships.

09:28 But for now at least this war is still ongoing  and is likely to provide gaming magazines and

09:33 aspiring youtube channels alike many more  things to talk about, like the fact that

09:38 this games financial market predicted the short  squeeze on Gamestop, so make sure to like and

09:42 subscribe if you want to see us make a video on  that, and in the meantime go and watch our video

09:47 to find out if the world bank is really an evil  empire. Thanks for learning, How Money Works.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Why You Wouldn't Survive 1 Day in CECOT... World's Largest Mega Prison in El Salvador
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: Why You Wouldn't Survive 1 Day in CECOT... World's Largest Mega Prison in El Salvador
  • Video ID: mNlKWWgmpus
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 It’s 2023, you’re a hardened member of Mara  Salvatrucha - better known as the infamous

00:06 MS-13 - and the government of El Salvador has  just sentenced you to a fate worse than death.

00:12 You’re forced like cattle into the back  of a heavily armored vehicle; tight-packed

00:16 flesh covered in gang tattoos holds you in place.  There’s barely space in this scorching vehicle for

00:21 you and the others to breathe. The guards stripped  you and gave you an uncomfortable cavity search,

00:27 leaving you violated and humiliated in  nothing but a pair of white shorts. An

00:31 unsympathetic police barber shaved you bald,  row by row of hair, just like all the others.

00:37 If you raise your head in transit,

00:39 a guard barks at you in Spanish to  get your head down, you worthless dog!

00:43 He wields his nightstick. You get the  impression that there’s nothing he’d

00:46 like more than cracking open the back of your  skull, flecking the naked skin of your fellow

00:51 prisoners with your blood. Just to send a  single message: Where you’re going, you’re

00:56 not considered human anymore. You’re an animal,  and when animals misbehave, they get put down.

01:01 You bow your head again. A wise choice - There’ll  be plenty of beatings later, so why start early?

01:07 But before you disappear back into the  sea of anonymous prisoners, you see it:

01:11 A glowing fortress, wreathed in barbed wire  and illuminated by piercing floodlights. It

01:16 makes Alcatraz look like Disneyland. It makes  Rikers look like a resort in Cancun. Hell,

01:21 after a few years here, Guantanamo  Bay would look like a health retreat.

01:25 This is the Centro de Confinamiento del  Terrorismo, or the Terrorism Confinement

01:30 Center. We’ll call it CECOT. You won’t find  another prison like this anywhere in the world.

01:35 But you’re not being sent here alone. There  are trails of buses in front of and behind you,

01:41 like some almost endless centipede of human  misery. You’re just one tiny percentage

01:45 point in a statistic - A tidal wave of 2000  prisoners, all being transferred at once,

01:51 as part of El Salvador’s sweeping efforts to  bring the country’s gang activity to its knees.

01:56 At its worst in 2011, El Salvador was  considered the murder capital of the

02:00 world. Peaking at 71 murders per hundred thousand.  In 2015, that number had risen to over 100 deaths

02:06 per hundred thousand. One day even saw 62  people murdered in 24 hours. Gang violence

02:12 had completely overtaken the Central American  country. Year after year, brutal gang warfare

02:17 saw the army roaming the streets just to keep  the country from falling into total collapse.

02:22 The government needed to take drastic measures.

02:24 You’re about to enter one  of those drastic measures.

02:27 Opened in 2022, very few people have  had the chance to see inside CECOT,

02:31 aside from the flood of prisoners being sent  there - including you. The media are not

02:35 allowed in. Lawyers are not allowed in. Human  rights groups are not allowed in. It’s closed

02:41 down almost entirely to the outside world. All  that civilians know about the facility has been

02:46 gleaned from satellite imagery, footage that the  El Salvador government has filmed and released.

02:51 The buses grind to a halt in a large grid outside  the prison. Some deep animal part of you feels

02:57 like you’re outside a slaughterhouse, and your  skin begins prickling with panic. You were a

03:02 bad dude on the outside - a robber, a killer, an  unquestioning enforcer of one of El Salvador’s

03:08 most feared gangs. Here, you’re a frightened  little child again, wishing for your mommy.

03:14 But you don’t get your mommy. You get manhandled  out of the bus by a huge man in riot gear,

03:19 clapping you in long cuffs that bind your  hands behind your back and connect to your

03:23 legs. The same thing is happening to hundreds,  then thousands, of other men around you. You

03:28 feel a nightstick press against the back of  your neck and instinctively bend over before

03:33 they can even start applying pressure.  Good boy. That’ll serve you well here.

03:37 The guards bark orders and corral you inside  like sheep. Of course, you obey. You and all

03:42 the others are practically naked, and even if  you managed to overpower one of the riot squad

03:47 guards specifically trained to beat you into  a fine puree, an expert sniper in one of the

03:52 nearby guard towers would put a round through  your head before you even had time to fart.

03:57 Right now, there are estimated to be  around 16,000 men in CECOT. That would

04:01 max out most prisons around the world.  The second largest prison in the world,

04:05 Silivri Penitentiaries Campus in  Turkey, manages to host a population

04:09 of around 22,000 inmates. CECOT is built  to double that, with a capacity of 40,000.

04:16 Even getting to the prison is a challenge.  President Nayib Bukele wanted to build it

04:20 far away from civilization. There are  no towns or cities nearby. No public

04:25 buildings or schools. The prison itself has  its own water supply and electric generators,

04:30 meaning it has even less need to connect  with anyone or anything external. That’s

04:35 why you spent so many hours roasting with your  fellow convicts in the back of that prison bus.

04:40 As you’re dragged into the main hall and  forced to boy down in lines for inspection,

04:45 you find yourself wondering how  one prison complex could hold so

04:48 many people. And the answer to that  is simple: It’s unimaginably huge.

04:54 There are eight prison blocks covering around 57  acres total but the plot of land for the prison

04:59 is an enormous 410 acres total. There are 19  guard towers perched high above the complex,

05:05 surveying everything. There are four layers  of walls surrounding the prison blocks,

05:10 each one is nearly ten feet tall and two feet  thick, with coils of barbed wire draped over

05:15 the top. And of course, you can’t forget  about the 15,000-volt electric fence too.

05:21 Surveillance cameras are in operation  24/7 and cover practically every square

05:25 inch of the facility. Nothing happens  off-camera. Should a riot break out,

05:29 they have a fully stocked armory with racks  and racks of firearms as well as heavy riot

05:34 gear for their guards. Even the US army  would have a hard time storming CECOT.

05:39 And you’re just a common thug  for hire. You’ve got no hope,

05:42 buddy. So, what have you got to  look forward to now you’re here?

05:45 When you first arrive, prisoner or not, you’re  subject to an intense screening process. Even

05:50 if you’re not an inmate, the guards at  CECOT have large X-ray machines that scan

05:54 you from head to toe to look for contraband.  You’ll also be asked to disclose any tattoos,

05:59 and if you don’t, they have the right to strip  you to check for themselves. The gangs in El

06:03 Salvador have a culture of tattooing their  members to cement their allegiance for life.

06:07 If you’ve got gang ties, you’re not getting  in unless it’s in handcuffs and white shorts.

06:12 Once you’ve been scanned,  searched again, beaten down,

06:15 and noted in the prison inventory, it’s time  for your first night at CECOT to begin. Part

06:19 of you just feels relieved that you’ll  finally be able to sleep after what’s

06:23 felt like the longest day of your life - But  we’ve got some bad news for you there, too.

06:27 The guards organize you into groups by cell  block and chase you, your hands on your head,

06:32 your back bowed over. If you lag behind,  you might take a nightstick to the spine

06:36 or the ankle, or feel the electric  burn of a stun gun on your bare skin.

06:41 They run you like the bulls of Pamplona  until you reach your cell, at which point,

06:45 a swift kick to the ass sends you tumbling in,  the reinforced metal door slamming behind you

06:50 once all of the others assigned to  this cell have been trapped there,

06:53 too. This is when you start to notice a number  of horrifying things about your new home.

06:59 For starters, the lights are always on. They  don’t switch them off at night, they don’t even

07:03 dim them, they are on 24/7 at full blast. Bright  harsh artificial light floods every communal cell.

07:10 There are 80 beds to a cell. We say beds, they  have no mattresses or bedding on them. Instead,

07:15 they’re harsh bunk bed frames, stacked four  high, with nothing to lie on but flat metal.

07:21 In the corners of the cells, right by the bars,  are two toilets. Next to them are two wash basins,

07:26 but the flow of water in these  is controlled by a guard outside

07:29 the cell. So that’s 80 prisoners in a cell  sharing just two toilets. Except it isn’t.

07:35 It seems that El Salvador is actually  cramming more than 80 in each cell.

07:39 We hope you don’t mind having plenty of roommates.

07:41 When a BBC reporter asked the director of the  prison exactly what the capacity of CECOT was,

07:46 the man smiled and said “Where you  can fit 10 people, you can fit 20.”

07:50 Can you imagine a worse night’s  sleep? Being in a brightly lit cell,

07:54 with over 100 other people, all the most  hardened gangsters in Central America,

07:59 lying on a metal sheet, with two shared toilets  stinking out the cell. Human rights groups have

08:05 estimated that prisoners in CECOT have just  0.6 square meters of personal space each.

08:11 That number falls far below the 4 square  meters mandated in the European Union.

08:16 There are solitary confinement cells too,  and to many, they might be preferable,

08:21 but they’ve got their trade-offs  too. Instead of a metal bed frame,

08:24 you have a slab of concrete to lie on. You get  one toilet. One wash basin. And while the communal

08:29 cells are always bathed in artificial light, you  have the opposite problem. No light at all, either

08:35 artificial or natural, meaning you just have to  sit in darkness all day stewing in your thoughts.

08:41 And at CECOT, one thing is for sure:  You’re not having pleasant thoughts.

08:45 Before we tell you about the horrors that  await you when you wake up in the morning,

08:49 we’ve got an important question to  answer: Why does El Salvador need

08:53 such a massive prison? Who are the men  arriving here and when will they leave?

08:58 We mentioned earlier a particular day in  El Salvador when 62 people were killed.

09:03 This was the 26th of March 2022. It was the  bloodiest day in the country’s history and

09:08 the final straw for the Salvadoran people.  President Bukele announced a radical new

09:12 approach to combating gang warfare.  Have been nominated largely for his

09:16 tough stance on gangs back in 2019, it was time  for him to put his money where his mouth was.

09:22 His plan was a sweeping raft of changes  that removed almost all of the barriers

09:26 preventing the police from arresting gang  members. Known as the régimen de excepción,

09:31 it was a national state of emergency.

09:33 The changes affected almost every stage  of the legal system. Criminals no longer

09:37 had access to legal counsel and  they could be held five times

09:41 longer without charge. Options like  bail and house arrest were removed,

09:46 and police could now monitor civilian  communications without the need for a warrant.

09:50 Sentences were also massively increased.  Previously, a convicted gang lord would

09:55 get 6-9 years in prison. That shot up to 40-45.

09:59 Lower gang members saw their potential sentences  rise from 3-5 years up to 20-30. Even if you

10:05 were caught sharing gang-related information  you could end up behind bars for 15 years.

10:11 One of the ways that gangs all around the  world have avoided long prison sentences

10:15 has been by using children and teenagers for  the risky leg work. A young teenager can be

10:20 easily manipulated. What’s more, they  will get a lenient sentence and be out

10:24 sooner so they’re an expendable workforce  for the gang leaders to use as shields.

10:28 Not anymore. El Salvador lowered the age of  criminal responsibility from 16 to 12. That’s

10:35 right, actual 12-year-olds could get locked  up for decades for their roles in gangs.

10:40 Soldiers and heavily armed police swarmed the  streets, looking for any trace of evidence that

10:45 somebody was gang-affiliated. They would  raid houses indiscriminately and set up

10:50 security checkpoints on almost every major  road. Anyone passing through the checkpoint

10:54 would not only need to provide a photo ID  and proof of address but also demonstrate a

10:59 valid reason for travel. Their cars would be  searched from top to bottom. If the people

11:03 manning the checkpoints even suspected  the person could have ties to gangs,

11:07 they would ask the person to strip them and  then search their body for any gang tattoos.

11:12 This policy was massively supported up  and down the country. 78% of Salvadorans

11:18 ‘strongly support’ the crackdown. A staggering  91% of them are in favor. That’s just 9% of the

11:25 country that is neutral or anti-crackdown. The  measures were only supposed to last for 30 days,

11:30 but here we are well over two years later  and they’re still in place. That’s because

11:35 consistently every month parties across the  government of El Salvador vote to extend them.

11:40 So far, over 79,000 people have been arrested  for gang affiliation. In a country of just

11:46 6.5 million people, that’s over 1% of  their population being detained in just

11:51 two years. It’s a monumental shift and one  that has brought its own set of challenges.

11:56 The Salvadoran prison system was not  designed to house this many criminals,

12:00 nowhere close. Prisons all around the country  quickly filled to capacity. When the question

12:05 of funding came up Nayib Bukele drew a hard line  that only won him more favor. He would not take

12:11 funding away from schools, hospitals, or good  public services to feed these prisoners. Instead,

12:17 their meals went down from three to two per  day, consisting of just beans and tortillas.

12:22 But a longer-term solution was needed,  one that Bukele was already prepared for.

12:26 CECOT. A brand new 40,000-capacity prison  miles away from civilization. A proverbial

12:32 hole in the ground where they could throw  the country’s gangs and let them fester.

12:37 You know, the same hole in the ground  where you’re currently festering.

12:40 Let’s head back there and see how  your evening is going, shall we?

12:43 You don’t know what time you wake up. The  harsh lights overhead didn’t let you sleep

12:47 in the first place. The constant talking,  shouting, and fighting through the night

12:51 kept you from drifting off for more than  a few minutes at a time. At one point,

12:55 one of the tougher guys shoved you out of  the bed he wanted and you fell 8 feet onto

13:00 the concrete floor. It’s down here you  decided to spend the rest of the night,

13:04 rather than risk getting shivved for  something only marginally more comfortable.

13:08 You’re desperate to go to the bathroom, but  there’s not much you can do. One toilet in

13:12 your cell has been blocked for two  weeks now, the other got blocked

13:16 over the weekend. They’ll probably call in a  plumber… Sometime over the next year or two.

13:20 A guy shoves you in the back and you crack  your head against a bunk frame. It’s an

13:24 early lunch today. Plastic trays loaded  with cost-saving beans and tortillas,

13:29 with sickly boiled eggs on the side,  are passed through the bars one by one.

13:33 You join near the back of the line and  have to eat your cold food on the floor.

13:37 They never give out cutlery, the forks  and knives could be used as weapons,

13:41 so you have no choice but to eat with your hands  like some depressed chimp at the local zoo. A lot

13:43 of the guys in the cells have pretty poor hand  hygiene, especially with the toilet situation,

13:48 so stomach viruses are common - Which has, in  turn, made the toilet situation even worse.

13:53 You’ve avoided getting sick so far  but it’s only a matter of time.

13:57 Before you’ve even had a  chance to eat your nasty egg,

14:00 everyone is up and moving again. It’s  time for your 30 minutes. Lucky you.

14:05 Every day, you get to spend half an hour  outside. It’s easily the best part of the day,

14:09 as long as the handcuffs aren’t  done up too tight. As expected,

14:12 the guard takes a dislike to you and  pinches the shackles extra tight today;

14:17 you feel it chafe the skin of your  wrists with every movement you take.

14:20 You and your 100 cell mates shuffle meekly out  into the sweltering sun for your ‘exercise’. Some

14:26 guys try to do push-ups, some half run around  as best they can with their ankles chained,

14:31 and most just sit against the  fence breathing in the fresh air.

14:35 It’s over before you know it.

14:37 Bundled back inside by guards, the  excitement of your day is over before

14:41 it’s even 11 AM. Not that you know that.  Time’s long gone. Every day blends into

14:46 the next and the next. And most of them  are spent how you are spending your time

14:50 now. Sitting around on either a hard  bunk or hard concrete, doing nothing.

14:55 Every five days, you get your head shaved. The  four days in between usually have nothing to do,

15:00 the boredom slowly turning your brain as  soft and cold as those revolting eggs.

15:05 The fights are the only interesting part  of the day. The guards usually just let

15:08 the prisoners settle their own differences,  not worth wading into a cell with 100 angry

15:12 prisoners just to stop one criminal from getting  his face smashed in. Worst comes to worst,

15:17 they’ll flood the cell with tear gas  and send the riot squad in to drag

15:21 out the corpse. Everything else was  considered a waste of prison resources.

15:24 You think about your family. You never got to  say goodbye to any of them, it all happened

15:29 so quickly. One minute you were sitting on  your couch, the next the military police

15:32 were kicking down your door and hauling you  away. Does your mother know where her son is?

15:37 Does your daughter understand that her dad  loves her? Will she think you just abandoned

15:41 her? Will your younger brother see sense  and choose a different life? Or is he in

15:45 the next cell block over from you right  now going through the exact same thing?

15:49 While CECOT is immensely popular in El Salvador  and has indisputably helped the country get on

15:55 top of gang violence, you cannot ignore the  glaring human rights violations. So far,

16:00 not one person who has been sent to CECOT has been  released. Inmates arriving here face the very real

16:05 possibility that they will live out the rest of  their days stuck here without ever even getting

16:10 a hypothetical release date to hope for. Human  rights campaigners have accused it of being

16:14 the death penalty on a mass scale, minus the  injections, nooses, or lethal electric shocks.

16:20 With so many thousands of prisoners being  apprehended without access to proper legal

16:25 counsel, there inevitably will be a significant  proportion of innocent men behind bars. That

16:30 happens even in the best justice systems in the  world, but in one where the convicts’ rights have

16:35 been eroded to the point of almost non-existence,  it’s likely happening alarmingly often.

16:40 The lack of access to the prison is also  a massive red flag. Journalists, lawyers,

16:45 and NGOs are all either denied access or  taken around in very focused controlled

16:50 circumstances where the guards do their  best to show off the prison to the world.

16:54 The prisoners themselves have no  access to the outside world. They

16:57 are not allowed to make phone calls  or send letters like in other prisons

17:01 across the globe. They live totally  cut off from the rest of humanity.

17:05 There is a reason for this. In  countries overrun with gang warfare,

17:09 prisons can end up being pretty ineffective.  Gang leaders locked away can often still call

17:13 the shots from behind bars thanks to burner  phones that get smuggled in by visitors,

17:18 new inmates, or corrupt guards. The black market  in prison can become a hotbed of crime as drugs,

17:24 weapons, and other contraband are exchanged  freely amongst inmates. To a large extent,

17:29 gangs can continue to operate in  and through the prison system.

17:33 Not in CECOT. As extreme as the  measures are, they have snuffed

17:36 out communication among gang leaders. Lock  them away and they are dead to the world,

17:41 leaving a power vacuum in their wake. Inside  the prisons without a thriving black market,

17:46 they can’t disrupt and control things in the  way they once did. They’ve lost their power.

17:51 Some of that comes down to the way guards  are treated too. Bukele himself admits that

17:55 El Salvador had made mistakes in how they  treated their guards previously. Prisons

18:00 run by gangs saw many inmates living in  more luxury than the guards themselves,

18:04 as they’d enjoy a free flow of  drugs, prostitutes, and alcohol,

18:08 while the guards were working long shifts  in terrible conditions. Bribery was rampant.

18:13 But now, Bukele has made sure to treat  the guards much better. CECOT has great

18:18 recreational facilities for its staff.  They have gyms, lounges, and much better

18:22 working conditions. There are 1,000 guards, 600  soldiers, and 250 police officers working on

18:29 site. That works out at 40 inmates per guard,  a high ratio, but when you consider how many of

18:34 those inmates are packed into just one cell, you  can see how much more power the guards now have.

18:40 They monitor everything, they control  everything. The inmates have no power anymore.

18:46 Now check out “50 Things Nobody Tells You  About Being in Prison.” Or watch this instead!

00:00 Over the last year, the car market has kind of  been going through something. Toyota, Volkswagen,

00:06 GM, Ford, Nissan, Volvo, and almost every other  bigname car manufacturer has seen widespread

00:11 disruptions alongside massive profit drops.  And they were the lucky ones. Honda recently

00:17 posted its first annual loss in just under 70  years of operations. And not to be outdone,

00:22 Stalantis recorded the largest loss from an  automaker outside of a major global recession.

00:27 Embodying his company values, the Stalantis CEO  broke down a turnaround planned that involved

00:32 going allin on V8, which was announced exactly  two days before the start of the war in Iran. Now,

00:39 I know you guys don't want to hear me say tariff  disruption, consumer debt, and the K-shaped

00:44 economy for another 15 minutes this week. And  the well uh good news is that there is a little

00:49 bit more going on here. Even at the top end of  the market, Porsche saw its profits drop by 99%,

00:55 encouraging them to sell off the ultra premium  Bugatti brand Land Rover and the artist formerly

01:00 known as Jaguar also saw profit fall by 99%.  And even the king of the K, Ferrari themselves,

01:06 have seen their shares decline by around 30% since  the last time we covered the car market on this

01:11 channel just 6 months ago. Of course, this stock  trend was not helped by the Ferrari Magic Mouse,

01:17 but that's actually worth addressing later on.  For now, I know you might all be getting some

01:21 sort of schadenfreude, seeing these companies  start to struggle after taking advantage of

01:25 accommodating economic conditions to screw  consumers for the past 5 years. But like always,

01:30 it's important to understand what is actually  happening behind the scenes in these companies

01:34 to see how it is going to impact you. An auto  company with facilities here in Indiana tonight

01:40 is reporting losses of $2.7 billion. Profits  at German car maker Porsche plunged by nearly

01:47 96% in the first nine months of this year.  US auto giant Ford says it's taking a $19.5

01:54 billion right down as it kills off several all  electric models. BYD says it sold 2.3 million

02:00 battery powered cars globally in 2025. Car  payments are becoming harder to afford for

02:06 many families as rising costs for essential  items continue to strain household budgets.

02:11 There is a reason why I spend so much time on this  channel talking about cars, despite personally

02:16 driving a 15-year-old CRV, and that's because for  the past 100 years, the car market, alongside the

02:21 construction industry, has been the canary in the  coal mine for the wider economy. A healthy car

02:26 market normally employs a lot of people in good  paying union jobs. It helps a country maintain

02:31 its industrial base. And on the opposite side of  the same coin, if people are buying lots of cars,

02:36 it's a clear indication that they can at the very  least qualify for a loan to make seven years of

02:40 irresponsible monthly repayments. Car makers can  help to both build a healthy economy and indicate

02:46 its health at the same time. But they can also do  the opposite. So to put everything into context,

02:52 car sales in 2025 were actually at their highest  level since the pandemic here in America.

02:57 Worldwide, the number of new cars sold fully  recovered and actually exceeded pre-pandemic level

03:02 sales, which should be cause for celebration,  right? What's more is that because the average

03:08 new car has become so much more expensive,  even after adjusting for inflation, the amount

03:12 of actual revenue car companies are making has  never been higher, even though unit volumes are

03:17 still down from their all-time peak. But then  the question is why are all of these companies

03:22 doing so badly at the same time that the market  itself is theoretically doing better than ever?

03:28 Growing sales naturally shouldn't go handinhand  with collapsing profit, right? Or perhaps an even

03:33 better question is if this is what is happening  to these companies during a good sales year,

03:39 what's going to happen to them when sales  actually slow down again like what is kind

03:43 of already happening right now? Well, there are  really four big problems beyond the immediately

03:47 obvious that are hurting car makers today. And the  first is what I like to call the great flip-flop.

03:53 A name that I really hope catches on. If you go  back through almost every one of those headlines

03:57 talking about massive profit haircuts, you'll  find the car makers themselves all citing the

04:02 same thing, electric vehicles. Now, there are two  very big reasons why they are trying so hard to

04:07 point this out, and we will get to that soon. But  beyond some accounting trickery, this is still an

04:12 industry-wide problem. Honda's first loss since  1957 came with the company pointing straight at

04:18 the billions it had poured into getting ready  to build electric cars it now isn't going to

04:22 sell. Stalantis turned a $5.5 billion profit  into a $26 billion loss. And around 25 billion

04:28 of that was write downs as it quietly backed out  of its EV plans. Ford booked nearly $20 billion

04:34 in adjustments and admitted its electric division  alone lost almost 5 billion in a single year. Even

04:40 the ones that stayed in the black still took a  hit. GM turned a $2.7 billion profit for the year,

04:46 but quietly scrapped its plans to go all electric  by 2035 and wrote down around $ 8.7 billion of EV

04:52 investment. For the last decade, a lot of these  major car manufacturers thought they were playing

04:56 a game of catch-up to the EV leaders in the space,  pushed by significant investor pressure from

05:01 shareholders that wanted Tesla level valuation.  But a lot of them are now realizing that the

05:06 demand they were all chasing is a lot softer  than they were expecting. The early adopters

05:10 that wanted an EV have already purchased one.  And as the market is flooded with more options,

05:15 it isn't necessarily driving people to make  the switch. It's just dividing the original

05:20 pool of customers between more brands. According  to research from Cox Automotive, even existing EV

05:25 owners are considering a switch back to internal  combustion engine or hybrid vehicles. Across the

05:30 entire industry, outside of the purely electric  automakers, most companies have been quietly

05:35 rolling back their bold projections that  they would be a purely EV automaker within

05:39 a decade. In America, in particular, this has been  accelerated by a cut down in EV credits and, well,

05:45 up until recently, some pretty cheap gas that  made it a lot easier to keep the Canyon Narrow

05:49 on the road. So, the industry as a whole has seen  where this is going and they are all announcing

05:54 major resets on their EV strategy. Now, to be  completely fair and put this back into context,

05:59 part of that rethinking process is rethinking all  of the book value they assigned to the tooling and

06:06 research that went into developing EV platforms  and building the plants to produce them. A plant

06:10 that was supposed to stamp out a million electric  F-150s a year is just worth a lot more than one

06:16 that is only producing 10,000 in reality. A lot  of the companies that have announced those 99%

06:21 profit drops are really just taking this year to  readjust their balance sheet and record a loss

06:25 because they know everybody else in the industry  is doing the same thing so they won't look quite

06:30 as bad. They are kind of like the zebra crossing  the river. They know they need to do it and

06:35 they know there are angry shareholders in the  water. But if they all do it at the same time,

06:39 it's much less likely that they will  be singled out. Now, on the other hand,

06:43 I know this makes it all sound like nothing but  an accounting illusion. But behind all of this,

06:47 there is still a serious problem. These write  downs still represent real money that companies

06:52 piled into a technology and capital infrastructure  that they thought would be the future and generate

06:56 them substantial returns, but turned out just  to be underutilized and rapidly depreciating,

07:01 which is probably an important lesson to keep in  mind for no other reason in particular. Anyway,

07:07 on top of this, the ongoing cost of running  research, development, and production lines for

07:12 both EVs and internal combustion engine vehicles  is also not insignificant. Companies like to share

07:18 parts and processes where they can, which is a  lot more difficult when they have different models

07:22 operating off an entirely separate drivetrain.  Now, maybe this would all still be worth it

07:27 if they were growing sales by catering to new  markets, but this is also happening while unit

07:32 sales are still below where they were before the  pandemic. So, even though they might be selling

07:36 more expensive cars, they aren't exactly opening  up new markets. It sounds bad, but so far this is

07:42 only the flip. The flop is still playing out. In  response to these market trends, some companies

07:48 boldly and loudly pivoted back to expanding  their portfolios of big gasg guzzling cars,

07:54 just in time for gas prices to become a major pain  point all over again. Now, you might logically

07:59 think that anybody illogical enough to spend  six figures on a new V8 Jeep Wagon Ear wouldn't

08:05 be the first to feel the pinch of gas prices, but  well, I made a promise to keep irrational consumer

08:10 behavior until the end of this video. For the car  companies themselves, ongoing R&D is just part of

08:16 being a car manufacturer. It is by its nature  a highly capital-intensive business and most

08:21 manufacturers and their shareholders are prepared  for this by itself even if a lot of it has been

08:26 wasted chasing market trends. But there are also  other headwinds hitting them at the same time

08:30 making it a lot scarier to deploy this capital.  So it's time to learn how many works to find out

08:35 why the car market is eating itself all during an  otherwise good sales year. This video is sponsored

08:41 by Monarch. Monarch is a private ad-free personal  finance platform that brings all your accounts

08:46 into one clean dashboard. It automatically tracks  your spending and net worth and helps you stay

08:51 financially aligned without juggling spreadsheets.  Instead of just showing where your money went,

08:56 Monarch makes it easy to see the full financial  picture, make smart adjustments, and make progress

09:00 towards your goals with confidence. Plus, with  bank level encryption and readonly access,

09:05 it is secure, and thousands of users have given  it a 4.9 star rating. I started using Monarch for

09:11 my monthly budget check-ins, and it has been  a gamecher. All my accounts, cards, loans,

09:16 and investments sync from over 13,000 institutions  into one beautiful view on web or mobile, saving

09:22 me time hopping between apps. I love the flexible  budgeting that separates fixed and flexible

09:27 spending with customizable rules and categories.  And Monarch quietly comes through your numbers and

09:31 surfaces patterns for you. things like spending  changes or unusual transactions explained in plain

09:36 English, so you always stay aware without constant  alerts. There is also a built-in assistant you can

09:41 ask anything about your finances, like how much  you spent on travel last summer, or whether you

09:45 can afford a vacation without touching your  savings. It answers from your actual data,

09:50 not generic advice. Seeing my net worth trend,  and goal timelines for saving or paying down

09:55 debt makes progress feel real and motivating  without the stress. Try Monarch yourself. Start

10:00 your free trial, then scan the QR code on screen  or use code HMW50 for 50% off your first year.

10:11 So, the great flip-flop has left most major car  manufacturers bleeding cash on a technology bet

10:17 that hasn't paid off, at least not yet. But the  second big change is what is happening to badge

10:22 engineering. One of the most underappreciated  threats to these companies right now is the slow

10:28 erosion of what has historically been their  most valuable asset. High-end luxury cars and

10:33 especially performance cars are more expensive  to manufacture than regular mass market cars,

10:38 but not by as much as you might expect. So,  the significant markups they can charge come

10:43 overwhelmingly from their badge and the brand  value people give to it. The margins on cars

10:47 from Porsche, Ferrari, JLR, and up until recently  Tesla were huge. Porsche's's operating margin was

10:54 sitting around 19% in 2024. Ferrari has enjoyed  unit margins of over 50% on most of their models,

11:00 meaning that for every car they sell, they are  making a unit profit of almost a quarter of a

11:04 million dollars. Of course, a lot of this is used  to fund their racing teams, their R&D, and their

11:09 other branding. But even after that, they have  run off a profit margin several times greater

11:14 than most ordinary car makers. Now, more than  almost any other product, people have historically

11:19 been willing to spend money on cars as a status  symbol, even when the marginal utility was well

11:23 into the territory of diminishing returns. But  crucially, there was always still something there

11:29 to justify it. A Porsche GT3 may be twice the  price of a regular Porsche 911, which is twice

11:35 the price of a BMW M3, which is twice the price  of a BMW 320i. And for 99% of on-road driving,

11:42 they are all going to get around just as quickly  while also displaying some level of European

11:46 luxury. But the top of the market is willing to  pay 8 times as much, probably in addition to some

11:53 significant dealer markups because in theory, the  GT3 has better performance capabilities than all

11:58 of these other cars. So they could save 2 seconds  a lap on the track days they will never go to. The

12:03 same is true for people who wanted to be on the  cutting edge of luxury or even new technologies.

12:09 The problem is now capabilities are getting  democratized. Most modern cars are incredibly

12:14 fast by historic standards and performance EVs in  particular all basically have the same spec sheet.

12:20 1,000 plus horsepower, 0 to 60 in 2.5 seconds,  and a 100 kWh battery despite having huge price

12:26 differences. The Ferrari Luche is kind of just a  conveniently timed encapsulation of this. In the

12:32 past, Ferrari clearly had a performance edge over  most mass market cars. But the Luch is by most

12:38 metrics going to be slower than similar offerings  from Porsche, Tesla, and even the phone maker

12:43 Xiaomi. The Lucid Air Sapphire will beat the Luché  on almost every metric that matters. More power,

12:49 faster, longer range for $391,000 less. And they  are both equally likely to leave you locked out on

12:56 the side of the road. Now, I know it's hard to  reverse engineer irrational consumer behavior,

13:01 and people don't buy cars off a spec sheet,  especially in markets like high-end performance

13:05 cars, which are clearly emotional, not rational  purchases. But this still really matters because

13:11 in the past, people could at least justify buying  a very expensive performance car because this was

13:16 the only way to access those capabilities. This  is just like someone buying a $5,000 handbag and

13:22 talking about craftsmanship. It's clearly  primarily motivated by the flex, but there

13:27 is at least something there to justify it. The  only other way people will be able to justify a

13:32 luch over a Model S Plaid is because they will  like the badge, which still works obviously,

13:38 but it won't work forever. And eventually, people  will just be flexing how irrational they really

13:43 are. Even outside of EVs, the democratization  of performance is making it really hard for

13:48 high-end manufacturers to sell their capabilities  alone. Modern Corvettes are faster than almost any

13:54 European supercar at a fraction of the price.  A C8 ZR1X will be a new Lamborghini by almost

14:00 any performance metric for half the price. So,  the argument for spending significantly more is

14:05 getting even harder to justify. Now, I know there  are still a lot of rich people buying a lot of

14:10 expensive cars, but in these markets, the simple  idea that someone could pull up having paid half

14:15 the price for a comparable car is a surefire  way to deflate the egos these cars were there

14:20 to support in the first place. Even in the more  sensible segments of the market, the same kind

14:24 of thing is happening all the way down to the base  model of cars as well. For most people, their cars

14:30 are basically just appliances that are getting  harder to differentiate. Most manufacturers now

14:35 have efficient engines, Apple CarPlay, and a  decent safety rating with interiors that would

14:39 be considered luxurious just 10 years ago. The  channel Modern MBA did a great deep dive video on

14:45 this corner of the market recently. And one of his  big points is that even the biggest manufacturers

14:50 are really just assembling thirdparty components  from companies like Bosch, Harmon, and

14:53 Phillips. Meaning that it is becoming harder to  differentiate between cars to people who treat the

14:58 purchases like any other appliance. what has the  best features for the given price and financing

15:03 deal. Hot take alert and feel free to come back to  this video in 10 years time to call me an idiot,

15:08 but there really isn't anything stopping the car  market from going the way of the computer market

15:13 where it becomes a lot harder to flex a particular  brand when they are all using roughly the same

15:17 components. Most people don't really care if you  have an Acer or an HP laptop. They care about the

15:23 specs and the components. And as cars become more  appliance-like, there is really nothing separating

15:27 them from the same fate. Which leads us neatly  onto the China problem. We briefly touched on it,

15:34 but Chinese EVs and hybrids are here and their  cost to performance ratio is very hard to compete

15:39 with. Now, in America, this hasn't mattered yet  because trade barriers keep us isolated to the

15:44 point that we really do live in our own little  car bubble. A lot of the most popular cars in

15:50 North America simply don't exist outside of North  America. Seeing an F-150 in Europe, for example,

15:56 is extremely rare. This is either because our  cars are too large for roads in other major

16:00 markets of Europe and Asia, too inefficient for  local laws, or because there are just better,

16:05 cheaper local alternatives. Now, that's typically  been fine for us at least, because the USA is such

16:11 a large market that even foreign automakers  set up operations here to get inside the

16:15 bubble. But there are a lot of manufacturers,  particularly those from Europe and Japan,

16:19 that depend far more heavily on exporting cars  beyond their home country. And for a long time,

16:24 the single largest and fastest growing market was  China itself. European automakers in particular

16:30 enjoyed several years of selling high-end cars to  status-driven consumers in the rapidly developing

16:35 Chinese economy. And for most of that time, they  really didn't have any competition because locally

16:40 produced Chinese cars were almost embarrassingly  cheap, poorly engineered, lacking in features,

16:45 and most importantly, they couldn't compete  with the status of the European luxury brands.

16:50 But that has clearly changed. Even despite being  largely protected from Chinese competition on

16:55 their home turf, European automakers have run  into a serious problem trying to sell their cars

17:00 into China because local alternatives  are now far more competitive. Xiaomi,

17:05 a company that didn't even have a car division 5  years ago, delivered over 400,000 vehicles in its

17:10 first full year of making cars. And the base model  outsold the Tesla Model 3 in China in 2025. And on

17:16 the point of badge engineering again, a Porsche  Tekcon is still more of a status symbol than a

17:21 Xiaomi SU7 despite looking almost identical. But  in some cases, that's actually working against

17:28 the European automakers. Just like Americans like  to buy American cars, a level of nationalism is

17:33 pushing some Chinese consumers to buy Chinese  cars. Even before considering their exports,

17:38 the rise of Chinese automakers have hurt the  incumbent players that are losing one of their

17:42 most valuable markets. But well, it would also  be irresponsible not to include their exports

17:47 because they are coming. According to data  from the Rodeium Group, China exported over 1

17:52 million vehicles to the EU in 2025, accounting for  around 6 to 7% of the market. And in early 2026,

17:59 those exports accelerated by 62% yearonear. BYD  alone delivered 2.6 million vehicles last year,

18:06 commanding roughly 20% of the global EV market.  Australia is actually a really interesting case

18:12 study here because they are a nice little guinea  pig for the larger American market given some

18:16 important similarities. Big roads, consumers  with strong purchasing power and a surface

18:21 level cultural similarity to America. But because  they no longer have a local car industry, Chinese

18:27 manufacturers are treated the same as every other  manufacturer and they are dominating because of

18:32 their cost competitiveness. Now, of course, there  is the argument that China has subsidized these

18:37 auto manufacturers to make them as competitive  as they are today through co-investment and

18:42 vertically integrated industrial planning. This is  absolutely true, but it's also only fair to point

18:48 out that American and European automakers are also  the beneficiaries of generous government policy.

18:53 And for what it's worth, China has also let a lot  of their EV manufacturers fail. China has actually

18:59 let more EV companies fail than America has had  automakers in its entire history. We are now just

19:05 seeing the ones that have actually survived. Now,  all of these problems would be a serious threat to

19:10 a healthy car market. But the fourth big problem  is that over the next few years in particular,

19:14 a wall of debt is likely to mean they are fighting  for a smaller slice of a smaller pie. Now, we all

19:20 know people are spending irresponsible money  every month so they can drive a car they can't

19:24 reasonably afford. But there is one big piece  of this that often gets ignored. We are about to

19:30 hit peak refinance. The average transaction price  for a new vehicle in America has gone from around

19:36 $38,000 in 2019 to just under $49,000 today.  And a lot of the car loans from the cheap money

19:42 era are now expiring. Loans that were written  when interest rates were near zero and monthly

19:46 repayments were a lot more manageable. This means  if people want to upgrade into a similar vehicle,

19:52 they are going to be paying a higher interest rate  on a higher base price, making deals significantly

19:57 harder to do. According to data from Lending Tree,  the average monthly payment on a new vehicle hit

20:03 $773 in the first quarter of 2026, and one  in five buyers now commits to a payment of

20:09 $1,000 or more each month. Of course, people will  pay irresponsible amounts, but there are still

20:15 fundamental limits to what loans can be given with  any hope of repayment. Another underappreciated

20:20 factor is that these financing realities are just  making newer, more expensive vehicles harder to

20:25 sell. Again, people will sign up for some pretty  irresponsible lending if they see they are getting

20:30 themselves into a better car. But, as we saw  earlier, car features that most people care

20:35 about have pretty much plateaued while prices and  interest rates have increased. Higher repayments

20:40 for a downgrade, even if it is just the trim  level, is a lot harder to get people excited about

20:44 at a dealership negotiating table. The industry's  uh solution to this has basically been to just

20:51 make the loans longer. Effective loan terms after  refinancing now average over 90 months, or 7 1/2

20:57 years of repayment on a depreciating asset. In  January 2026, the 60-day delinquency rate on

21:03 subprime auto loans hit 6.9%. the highest level  recorded in more than three decades of tracking.

21:09 And roughly 31% of trade-ins towards new vehicles  now carry negative equity with the average

21:14 underwater amount sitting at around $7,200. EVs in  particular are now depreciating faster than their

21:20 internal combustion engine equivalent, averaging  around 58 to 59% depreciation over 5 years

21:26 compared to roughly 45 to 46% for IC. And beyond  that, cars are statistically lasting longer,

21:33 too. So, it's harder to make a new deal happen  while also easier to just keep driving the same

21:38 vehicle for longer, which for what it's worth is  exactly what people should be doing as long as

21:42 it's still safe. People can't afford to trade up  and the cars they're sitting in are in many cases

21:48 just as well equipped as anything they would be  able to trade into with the same repayment. The

21:53 final thing is that higher interest rates are also  hurting manufacturers themselves just as much as

21:58 their customers. Most large auto manufacturers  carry a lot of debt to finance their financing

22:04 divisions, but also to fund their ongoing, highly  capital-intensive operation. Ford, for example,

22:10 has closed $163 billion worth of debt on their  books, with 22 billion of that being for their

22:15 core business functions. Just the interest on that  debt now accounts for as much as half of their

22:20 free cash flow. Now, individually, these are all  problems that car manufacturers are worried about,

22:26 but together it is a bit of a perfect storm.  Companies are burning capital they are running

22:31 out of for products their customers are  struggling to afford in a market that is

22:35 getting more competitive and harder to stand  out in. It sounds bad, but it gets worse. This

22:41 is just what has been happening recently. So,  if you want the full breakdown, go and watch

22:46 this video next. And don't forget to like and  subscribe to keep on learning how money works.
