docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 What if NASA's next mission to the  Moon isn't exploration… it's control?

00:04 For decades, we were told the Moon belonged  to everyone. Since Neil Armstrong planted the

00:09 Stars and Stripes, the Moon has remained one  of humanity's few truly neutral frontiers.

00:13 A place where any nation capable of reaching  it could conduct research and exploration.

00:18 But is that era about to end? Could the future of the Moon look

00:22 less like one giant leap for mankind… and  more like a massive American stronghold?

00:27 Is NASA really preparing to build a  massive autonomous lunar fortress,

00:31 powered by cutting-edge drone technology, to  secure one of the Moon's most valuable locations?

00:36 Because if that's true, the new race to the  moon won't be about getting there first.

00:41 It'll be about deciding who gets to stay. Right now, Shackleton Crater is one of the

00:45 most important locations on the ,oon. Located at  the lunar south pole, it's one of the moon's most

00:50 unusual geographical features. The crater's  rim rises high enough that some of its peaks,

00:55 known as the Peaks of Eternal Light, receive  sunlight for nearly 90% of the lunar day.

01:00 But inside the crater, conditions  couldn't be more different.

01:03 Constantly shrouded in darkness, it creates a  cold trap that flash-freezes everything inside

01:08 it. The crater has been examined by unmanned  spacecraft, and its findings indicated that

01:12 water ice is likely present. It’s one of the  most inhospitable spots on our only satellite.

01:18 And one of the most valuable.

01:20 NASA recently revealed a 3-stage timeline that  will take the United States back to the moon

01:25 for the first time since 1972. The agency is  pouring more than $20 billion into the effort,

01:30 with the goal of putting astronauts back on  the lunar surface within the next few years.

01:34 But this isn't just about planting another flag.

01:37 It’s about dominance.

01:39 America wants to establish a foothold on the  moon. And that’s where phase three comes in.

01:44 Known as "Sustained Human Presence," the program  would create a lunar base capable of hosting

01:48 not just astronauts, but eventually long-term  residents. For the first time, humanity would

01:53 have a permanent station on another world. It  will be built in the Shackleton crater and result

01:58 in a massive perimeter around the crater that  covers over 31,000 square miles (80,209 sq km).

02:03 Astronauts won’t just be exploring the moon.

02:06 They’ll be claiming it.

02:08 The plan is for the base to be protected by  some of the most advanced drone technology ever

02:12 developed. Drones will map and track the lunar  surface as well as moving around independently.

02:17 But these aren’t only the cameras, they’re  the security. These drones will arrive on the

02:22 surface of the moon long before any humans  set foot there. They’ll eventually be used

02:26 to create an autonomous surveillance network as  the Shackleton Crater falls under U.S. control.

02:31 But NASA isn’t kickstarting the race to the moon.

02:33 It's been going for a long time already.

02:36 While the public only learned about these  ambitious plans in May 2026, NASA had already

02:40 been laying the groundwork for years. Phase 1  will take place between 2026 and 2029, and is

02:46 planned to involve 25 launches - 21 of which  will land on the moon. Most previous missions

02:52 to the moon using unmanned spacecraft have been  done to send a single surveillance spacecraft.

02:57 This time it’s different.

02:59 The goal is to deliver up to four tons of  infrastructure to begin the process of building

03:03 the moon base in stages and transform  one of the Moon's harshest environments

03:07 into somewhere hospitable. At the heart of  NASA's plan is the Mark 1 Endurance Lander,

03:13 built by Jeff Bezos' space company, Blue Origin. For years, Bezos watched from the sidelines as

03:18 Elon Musk's SpaceX dominated the modern space  race. Now, he's been handed one of the most

03:23 important missions in its history. And he'll have to deliver.

03:27 The first phase, known as Moon Base I, will see  the Endurance lander begin its initial missions

03:32 to the Moon. These early flights are designed to  test its capabilities by targeting the Shackleton

03:37 Connecting Ridge and ensuring its landing and  propulsion technologies can operate safely.

03:42 Once these missions are complete, the lander will  begin unloading its first payloads of technology.

03:47 This includes high-resolution cameras and  a laser-reflecting device designed to help

03:52 future spacecraft pinpoint and navigate  lunar locations with far greater precision.

03:57 Because many more will be coming.

03:59 Griffin Mission One, a lunar lander developed  by robotics company Astrobotic Technology will

04:04 play a key role in Moon Base II. While Blue  Origin will handle the human landing systems,

04:10 Griffin Mission One will focus on building the  heavy surface infrastructure. One of its key

04:14 developments is the FLEX Lunar Innovation  Platform. It’s a multi-purpose lunar rover

04:19 designed to operate across the surface  as the base begins to take shape.

04:23 This rover will carry the payloads delivered  from Earth, taking them exactly where they’re

04:28 needed as construction of the lunar base begins. For Moon Base III, Blue Origin and Astrobotic

04:33 will be joined by additional partners as the  mission moves into its most advanced stage yet.

04:38 This phase will see the deployment of the Nova-C  Trinity Lander built by Intuitive Machines.This

04:44 mission will be bringing in specialized  analytical technology that will explore to

04:48 study magnetic anomalies on the Moon and  investigate the mysterious lunar swirls

04:53 that continue to puzzle scientists today. For the first time, this stage of the program

04:57 also expands beyond the United States,  bringing in international cooperation from

05:01 partners including South Korea’s space  program and the European Space Agency.

05:06 But cooperation is just the  first step toward control.

05:09 As NASA begins to deliver the infrastructure  to pave the way for human habitation,

05:13 it’s also preparing for the biggest perimeter  in human history. While the first stages of the

05:17 Moon Base are advancing, Nasa’s Jet Propulsion  Laboratory is getting ready for a 2028 mission

05:23 that will determine whether the entire  mission is a success… or a failure.

05:27 The Moonfall Drones are autonomous “hopping”  devices inspired by the success of NASA’s

05:32 Ingenuity Mars Helicopter. They’ll be  carried aboard the Elytra spacecraft,

05:36 which will transport a quartet of 550-pound  (250 kg) drones toward the lunar surface.

05:42 But instead of landing with them, the main  spacecraft will release them in transit.

05:46 This will allow the drones to deploy  independently once they reach the Moon.

05:50 And from that moment on, there’s no  control ship… and no second chance.

05:55 They’re on their own. Once they reach the lunar surface,

05:57 they will use up to 10 high-definition  cameras to create a map of hard-to-reach

06:02 terrain within the crater. The drones will  reportedly feature technology that allows

06:06 information to be independently gathered. This  is important because it will allow NASA to create

06:12 a real-time survey grid over the lunar South  Pole, long before a crew sets foot on the moon.

06:17 Because what comes next is humans stepping into

06:19 one of the most unforgiving  places in our neighborhood.

06:22 There have been plans for moon bases for decades  now, although most of them fell more into the

06:27 realm of science fiction rather than reality. The  talk about how to power such a huge undertaking

06:32 often leaned towards solar power. It would be  sustainable, easy to maintain, and reliable.

06:37 There’s just one problem.

06:39 It wouldn’t work.

06:40 The lunar cycle only provides  solar power for 50% of the month,

06:44 which plunges the moon into  darkness for a 14-day night.

06:47 It’s not possible to create a level of storage  that would carry you through half the month.

06:51 Battery backups would be incredibly expensive,  hard to transport, and subject to failure.

06:56 And that would mean death. The Shackleton Crater is one of the coldest places

07:00 on the Moon, where the long lunar night can drop  temperatures to around -400°F (-240°C) for over

07:06 336 hours. That’s similar to conditions on Pluto,  the frozen dwarf planet at the edge of our solar

07:13 system. The goal is to create a climate-controlled  moon base that can sustain human life long-term.

07:18 Human excursions outside would be limited  and performed in climate-controlled suits.

07:23 But to do that, a new form  of power will be needed.

07:26 The crown jewel of NASA’s Moon base plan is  its Fission Surface Power project. Developed

07:31 in partnership with the Department of Energy, it  would use a self-sustaining nuclear power system

07:36 capable of keeping the base running  regardless of lunar night, solar storms,

07:40 or supply delays. The long-term goal  is to be used as part of a Mars colony,

07:44 but it will make its debut on the moon.  Fission has a lot of advantages. It’s

07:48 small and lightweight, and can be  duplicated for future outposts.

07:53 If it works, the power problems will be solved.

07:55 This fission power system - still in  active development and scheduled for later

07:59 deployment - is expected to generate up to 40  kilowatts of energy for the base. That’s roughly

08:04 equivalent to the electricity needed to power  around 30 households on Earth for an entire year.

08:09 But those households aren’t operating on the Moon. They don’t have the same stakes attached to them.

08:14 On the moon, a power failure will be measured  in hours before everyone on the base freezes

08:19 to death. There is no room for error here, and  the technology is experimental. There will be

08:24 an inherent level of risk for anyone who joins  this moon base project. But according to NASA,

08:28 it’s a risk worth taking. Because there’s a secret  in the darkest recesses of the Shackleton Crater.

08:34 One that might be worth dying for.

08:36 During the early days of the space  race, it was exactly that… a race.

08:40 The world was in the throes of the Cold War,  with 2 superpowers jockeying for advantage.

08:45 No one was sure what would happen if  the Soviets got to the moon first.

08:48 Would they declare it sovereign territory  and threaten military assaults if anyone

08:52 else tried to land there? In the end, the  US’ victory allowed for a future where

08:55 the final frontier would be neutral  territory that anyone could explore.

09:00 Now, people are trying to keep it that way. The Artemis Accords were introduced in 2020

09:04 as a set of non-binding agreements shaping the  future of space exploration under NASA’s Artemis

09:10 program. Today, 67 countries have signed on,  including the United States, much of Europe,

09:15 and rising space powers like India, Japan,  South Korea, Saudi Arabia, and the UAE.

09:20 But two major players are noticeably absent. Russia, and China, both long-standing space

09:25 rivals of the United States. And China,  in particular, has made no secret of

09:29 its ambition to build a lunar base of its own. So is the US about to violate its own principles?

09:35 One of the foundations of the Artemis Accords  is that all activities in space should be for

09:39 peaceful purposes. Nations should commit to  transparency and a mutually beneficial sharing

09:44 of scientific information. This would seem to  prevent national appropriation of the moon.

09:49 But the US has a loophole for that. Section 11 of the Artemis Accords

09:52 requires signatories to avoid any activity that  could cause harmful interference with another

09:58 nation’s operations in space. On paper, that makes  large scale development on the Moon difficult.

10:04 But further down, there’s a key caveat. The wording says “...the nature and existence

10:09 of safety zones is expected to change over time  reflecting the status of the relevant operation”.

10:15 That gives the governments some leeway in  creating so-called safety zones on the moon.

10:19 It just so happens that the US’ idea of what  constitutes a safety zone is very large.

10:24 Critics of the current program point to the  1967 Outer Space Treaty, which was signed before

10:29 the US had won the space race. It essentially  limited the moon and all other celestial bodies

10:35 to peaceful uses. This was signed by the USSR, at  a time when the United States had the high ground,

10:40 and has been abided by ever since. China was added  to the treaty in 1983. Of course, the fact that

10:46 only the US has ever landed people on the moon  has largely rendered it moot. But that might be

10:51 changing. Critics of the US’ current plan say it  stands the risk of creating a space arms race.

10:57 But it might be on the verge of already happening.

10:59 Because there’s something on the moon that  might be the key to the entire solar system.

11:04 People are watching the current US mission  with interest, because on the surface,

11:08 it has chosen one of the most difficult  spots on the moon to stake its set up base.

11:12 Anything exposed to the depths of  the crater will be flash-frozen.

11:15 That’s exactly why it has to be here.

11:18 Space might look peaceful at first glance, but  it’s constantly in motion. The cosmos is always

11:23 carrying particles from other celestial bodies,  with water ice being one of the most common.

11:28 It can drift in small amounts, or it can be  carried frozen solid on comets. What form it takes

11:33 will depend on where it lands. Any that lands in  the Shackleton Crater will remain frozen solid,

11:39 maybe for eons. It’s estimated that there  might be over 100 million metric tons of

11:43 water ice locked down there in the crater. That’s  more than 40,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools.

11:48 In the space race, that might be an ace card.

11:51 One of the biggest challenges of creating a  moon base will be keeping everyone who lives

11:55 there alive. Food will likely be a combination  of pre-packaged astronaut meals, delivered to the

12:00 base, and produce grown on the moon after  gardens are started in the early stages.

12:04 But water will be harder to come by. The  human body can go longer without food than

12:08 it can without water. Just a few days without  the latter can mean death. If the US can find

12:14 a reliable source of water on the moon, it  can make life on its moon base sustainable.

12:18 The US might have just unlocked the  key to long-time life on the moon.

12:22 But that’s just a jumping-off point.  NASA and many of its partners have

12:26 their sights set on Mars next,  and for that, you’ll need energy.

12:30 The Shackleton Crater is surrounded by the Peaks  of Eternal Light, the high ground of the crater’s

12:35 rim. They’re exposed to the sun for 90% of the  lunar year. By setting up solar panels there,

12:40 the base would be equipped with a strong  backup of energy that could be useful for

12:44 keeping the base running… or powering  any vessel that lands on the satellite.

12:48 But NASA isn’t the only space agency with its  eye on this incredibly valuable real estate.

12:53 The United States’ moonshot has a very  ambitious end goal. The goal is to first

12:57 deliver the infrastructure through unmanned  missions, then begin landing astronauts in 2028.

13:03 After that, a second phase follows:  27 launches, 24 lunar landings,

13:08 and more than 132,000 pounds (59,874 kg) of  additional payload delivered to the surface.

13:13 From 2029 to 2032, the focus shifts again:  building the infrastructure needed for sustained

13:19 human life on the Moon. During this time, early  colonists would work alongside autonomous systems

13:24 to expand and maintain the base, along  with its growing research networks.

13:28 It’s a wildly ambitious plan. One  many experts say is overly rushed.

13:33 But the United States is trying to beat the clock.

13:35 That’s because they have a rival. The  International Lunar Research Station,

13:39 or ILRS, is a joint China-Russia-led project  aimed at creating a lunar base of its own.

13:45 It will be operated by the 2 great powers with  a tense relationship with the United States,

13:50 alongside Pakistan, Egypt, Venezuela, South  Africa, and Serbia. They've been planning it for a

13:55 long time. China has been doing unmanned missions  on the moon since 2007. Russia’s Roscosmos agency

14:01 has been launching its own probes on the  moon, albeit with a more erratic record.

14:05 But now they want to beat the US to the moon.

14:09 The ILRS timeline looks a lot like the American  one at first, with the process starting in 2026.

14:14 That’s when joint operations will start, as cargo  deliveries begin to the surface of the moon.

14:19 Once that is pulled off, the next phase  will begin establishing facilities

14:23 both in-orbit and on the surface,  as the base starts taking form.

14:27 This will take place from 2031 to 2035, putting  it behind the US’ schedule. But no one is sure if

14:33 the US timeline can be pulled off. This base  is expected to be utilized from 2036 onward.

14:38 It’s the location that worries the U.S.

14:41 China and Russia have been fairly cagey  about the location planned for the base or

14:45 how large it will be. But the location is  planned for the lunar south pole as well.

14:49 It’s not clear if the target  is the Shackleton Crater,

14:51 but the location’s water-rich environment  makes it a highly inviting target.

14:55 That means the US isn’t just in a  moonshot to duplicate its past success.

14:59 It’s in a race to maintain  its domination of space.

15:02 Not since Sputnik has the United  States been behind in the Space Race,

15:06 and it’s never had to answer one big question.

15:08 What happens if someone else gets  there first and claims their territory?

15:12 With resources on the moon looking inviting  and Mars looming as the next great frontier,

15:17 a space war may become inevitable. That’s why the  United States is looking at the moon in a way no

15:22 one can ignore. A nuclear-powered fortress right  on top of the most resource-rich spot on the moon,

15:28 patrolled by the most advanced drones in the  world, would certainly send that message.

15:33 Now it just has to deliver.

15:35 When NASA had to beat the Soviets to the moon, it  relied on the best scientists who were willing to

15:39 work for the government. But now, it has access to  a whole new pool of talent from the tech sector,

15:44 motivated to deliver on this  impossible-seeming timeline.

15:47 They know that if they pull this off, the rewards  are massive both personally and professionally.

15:52 But they also know that if they fail, there’s  much more at stake than their stock holdings.

15:56 If the US loses the new space race,  there might be no catching up this time.

16:00 Because this one isn’t just for bragging rights.

16:03 It’s for the keys to the cosmos.

05:26 buy into if he wants to purchase more of

05:28 a company in the future. Obviously, you

05:30 are not Warren Buffett. But if everybody

05:32 became financially responsible, you

05:34 would share the same problem. If more

05:36 people were buying the same shares that

05:38 you wanted to buy to fund a long-term

05:39 goal like retirement, then you will end

05:41 up paying more for the same portfolio.

05:43 The only time that you actually want a

05:44 stock's price to be high is when you

05:46 want to sell it. Currently, if everybody

05:48 became savers and investors, the people

05:50 that would stand to gain the most are

05:51 wealthy people who already have large

05:53 holdings of assets to sell to people

05:55 entering the market for the first time.

05:57 The same thing would happen for other

05:58 financially responsible purchases like a

06:00 house. If people gave up vacations,

06:02 fancy dinners, and expensive cars to

06:04 save diligently for a house, they would

06:05 become even more expensive, making it

06:07 harder for you to buy one, thus making

06:09 it harder for you to be financially

06:11 responsible. Additionally, investments

06:13 like stocks and real estate only have

06:15 value because they make something to

06:16 sell to people. So, if everybody decides

06:18 that their 2-year-old iPhone is good

06:20 enough and they don't need to upgrade,

06:21 that would hurt the earnings of Apple as

06:23 a company and you as a shareholder. So,

06:25 you might be thinking that maybe it's a

06:27 good thing that so many people make so

06:29 many dumb financial decisions. It's

06:30 easier to get ahead if everybody else is

06:32 tripping over themselves. But then,

06:34 there are three reasons why despite the

06:36 extra competition, you should still want

06:38 people to be more financially

06:39 responsible. The first reason is that

06:41 people being better with their money

06:43 would be better for everyone. People are

06:45 afraid of a future where they will own

06:47 nothing and be happy about it. The

06:49 growth of subscription services, where

06:50 people pay monthly for entertainment,

06:52 applications, cars, food, housing, and

06:54 everything in between, has grown in

06:56 popularity in part because people no

06:58 longer have the means or discipline to

06:59 save up to make a one-time upfront

07:01 purchase. Companies have capitalized on

07:03 this to build a recurring revenue model

07:05 where people pay a monthly fee for

07:06 everything that works out to be a much

07:08 worse deal on a time value adjusted

07:10 basis. According to the subscription

07:12 economy index report, the market for

07:14 subscription services has grown by 435%

07:18 over the last decade. It is expected to

07:20 grow even more by reaching a market size

07:22 of 1.5 trillion by 2025. According to

07:25 the market research and consulting firm

07:27 Forester, the number one reason that

07:29 subscription services have become so

07:31 popular with consumers is exactly what

07:32 you would expect. People don't have

07:34 enough money to pay for things upfront

07:36 anymore. Now, subscription services are

07:38 not bad by themselves. Sometimes it's a

07:41 great way to try a product without

07:42 committing to a single upfront purchase.

07:44 And it has other advantages like forcing

07:46 companies to push through updates on

07:47 their services so they don't lose their

07:49 recurring revenue. What is bad is when

07:51 there is no other option that is not a

07:53 subscription. There are now some things

07:55 that are hard to buy without paying a

07:57 monthly subscription. This very video

07:59 was made using the Adobe suite, which is

08:02 no longer available for upfront purchase

08:03 and can only be used on a subscription.

08:06 Even if you want to buy something like a

08:07 car, dealerships are going to make more

08:09 money by putting you on a lease than

08:11 they would by selling you a car in all

08:13 cash. So, they have structured their

08:14 businesses to push those deals.

08:16 like this is only possible because there

08:18 are enough people that buy these

08:19 services that businesses have been able

08:21 to transition to them and in many cases

08:23 completely discontinue their upfront

08:24 sales offerings. The second reason you

08:26 should want everybody to be as

08:28 financially responsible as possible is

08:30 for exactly the opposite reason. An even

08:32 scarier future where you own everything

08:34 and are miserable. Poor financial

08:37 planning and overconumption go hand in

08:39 hand. According to data from the EPA,

08:41 the average American uses more than

08:43 their body weight in consumable products

08:45 every day. Reckless spending has

08:47 financed big cars, big houses, big

08:49 meals, and big convenience. That all

08:51 comes at a financial cost, but is also

08:53 an environmental cost. Even if you don't

08:56 personally care about the environmental

08:57 impact, this benefit is still important

08:59 to you. If people buy less of everything

09:02 and are more conscious of where they

09:03 spend their money, then there will be

09:05 more stuff left over for you. Less

09:07 consumption will also reduce how much we

09:09 collectively pay in environmental taxes,

09:11 which will make it even easier to be

09:13 financially responsible. And that's the

09:14 third reason why we can afford for

09:16 everybody to be financially responsible

09:18 and would be better off if they were.

09:20 Some companies need people to spend

09:21 their money recklessly to stay in

09:23 business. Fast fashion, consumer

09:25 lenders, automakers, debt collectors,

09:27 hotels, airlines, and restaurants all do

09:29 well from people yoloing their paycheck

09:31 away or signing up for irresponsible

09:33 amounts of debt. But other companies

09:35 like groceries, healthcare, and repairs

09:37 won't be as affected. Some companies

09:39 would actually do better as people have

09:41 more money to make investment purchases

09:43 into things that are expensive upfront,

09:44 but pay themselves off over time, like

09:46 new homes, solar panels, and

09:48 highquality, long-lasting clothes. If

09:50 you save money, you will eventually

09:51 spend it on something. And long-term

09:53 purchases are generally better for

09:54 everyone than easy consumables. More

09:57 responsible spending done by everybody

09:58 with the intention of being financially

10:00 secure will also mean services like

10:02 social security will have more to give

10:04 to people in need. The bonus fourth

10:06 reason is that if people are spending

10:07 less of their money on useless junk,

10:09 then we won't need to work as hard to

10:10 make that useless junk. Today, the

10:13 average American is not working as many

10:15 hours as they used to 100 years ago. But

10:17 we still haven't got our work life

10:19 balance perfected. To find out who might

10:21 have though, go and watch my new video

10:23 over on how history works to find out if

10:25 you work harder and have less free time

10:26 than a medieval peasant. If you want

10:28 more soul crushing content like this, I

10:30 write some of my even less

10:31 monetizationfriendly content on my

10:33 totally free email newsletter,

10:34 Compounded Daily. You can sign up to

10:36 that in the link below this video to

10:38 keep on learning how money works.

docs.title: YouTube Transcript: Dumb YouTube Videos That Got People Fired #2

docs.text:
• Title: Dumb YouTube Videos That Got People Fired #2
  • Video ID: pB6nlxuytLU
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 You’ve actually done it. You’ve landed the best  job in the world. The richest man on Earth is

00:04 cutting you a fat paycheck just to test-drive a  product that most people can only fantasize about

00:09 owning. Life couldn’t possibly get better, right? Well, not so fast. As you hurtle down the road in

00:16 one of your company’s cars, fate slams  into you. In a split second, your dream

00:20 gig goes up in flames… almost literally. This guy’s probably the least dumbest

00:25 person on this list so be prepared to  hear about some next-level stupidity

00:30 on today’s episode of The Infographics Show - Even  More Dumb YouTube Videos That Got People Fired.

00:37 16. Don’t poop where you eat As you’ve probably guessed,

00:40 Elon Musk is the richest man on the planet,  boasting a jaw-dropping fortune of $323.2 billion

00:48 at the time we started making this video. Let’s  be real, you don’t climb to the top of the wealth

00:52 mountain by hiring bad employees. Or do you? Back in 2022, a former Tesla employee named John

00:59 Bernal thought he’d showcase his driving skills-  or lack of- on YouTube. The video shows him behind

01:05 the wheel of a Tesla Model 3, veering off the  road and smashing into bollards. To top it off,

01:10 John provided a play-by-play commentary of his  chaotic off-road escapades, narrating every

01:16 collision like it was a sporting event. To make matters worse, the Tesla was in

01:20 full self-driving, or FSD, mode when it had  its unfortunate meeting with the stationary

01:25 object. It’s safe to say Musk and his  managers would not be impressed if this

01:29 guy showed the whole world his crash. Bernal was a Tesla Autopilot tester,

01:34 which made his YouTube video of the crash a  kind of company sabotage. He was basically

01:39 showing a weakness in Tesla’s software. He could have kept it quiet or just told

01:43 his bosses, but he posted it to his YouTube  channel, AI Addict. It was his first crash

01:48 video in FSD and it quickly garnered 200,000  views. A week later, he was out of a job. He

01:55 told the media he’d been told he’d, “broke  Tesla policy.” Tesla went a step further

02:00 and rescinded this guy’s access to the FSD Beta  in his own car. In short, they were pretty mad.

02:06 But let’s be honest here, what was he expecting? Still, in terms of our list today, this guy

02:10 is dumb-person-lite. He has nothing  on the woman we’ll talk about next.

02:15 15. Karen and the Cocker Spaniel On a sunny May morning in 2020,

02:20 Amy Cooper- later known as Central Park  Karen- was out for a leisurely stroll with

02:24 her dog. Her furry friend was off the leash,  as Amy blissfully ignored the park’s rules.

02:30 Enter the birdwatcher- a calm and considerate rule  enforcer- who gently reminded her of the policy.

02:36 And that’s when things took a turn for the worse.  Amy spiraled into full-blown hysteria after the

02:41 birdwatcher did the unthinkable. He offered her  dog a treat to lure it away from a flower bed.

02:47 Clearly, an act of extreme provocation, right? This should have been the biggest nothingburger

02:52 of the century, but Amy lost it, screaming,  “Don't you touch my dog!” The birdwatcher calmly

02:58 put down his binoculars and began recording  on his phone. Meanwhile, Amy dialed 9-1-1,

03:02 her voice breathless with urgency as she claimed,  'There is an African American man- I’m in Central

03:08 Park-he is recording me and threatening me  and my dog… please send the cops immediately!'

03:13 The sheer terror in her voice would have you  believe she was moments away from being torn apart

03:17 by Jason Voorhees himself. The reality was she'd  simply crossed paths with a birdwatcher- arguably

03:23 the most harmless variety of human on the planet." The cops didn’t do anything. But this story had

03:28 a life of its own once it hit YouTube. Karen,  sorry… Amy was fired from her investment firm

03:33 job on grounds of racism, which she took  to the courts for wrongful termination.

03:37 She was also charged with filing a false police  report, but the birdwatcher man said he didn’t

03:42 want to bring “her more misery.” Meanwhile, she  claimed this guy had a history of “confronting

03:46 dog owners in Central Park who walked their dogs  without a leash.” Hardly a crime of the century.

03:52 All the stress resulted in her having a  breakdown and leaving the US for her home

03:56 in Canada. She even received death threats so  she wasn’t the only one who needed to chill out.

04:01 There are so many first-world problems with  this story we don’t know where to start. We’d

04:06 say “People need to get out more” but it was  getting out more that started all of this.

04:11 Ok, now for something slightly ridiculous. 14. The Florida farter

04:16 Doug, better known online as Paul Flart, was just  an ordinary guy from New Jersey who unexpectedly

04:22 shot to internet fame. After moving to Florida  at 31 to help his mom after his father’s passing,

04:27 Doug took a job as a hospital security guard.  It was here, in the quiet hours of his shifts,

04:33 that his now-legendary ‘visual art’ first  made its way onto Instagram before going viral

04:38 on YouTube, racking up millions of views. Doug was something of an old-school comedy

04:43 connoisseur- a slapstick aficionado with a  very... unique specialty. On his shifts as

04:48 a security guard, he entertained the internet  by posting videos of himself farting on the

04:53 job. Anything to pass the time, right?  He did loud ones, long ones, short ones,

04:59 and those that sounded like they could be leaky. He explained to the media how he discovered his

05:04 talent for farting: “One day I ripped a rather  nice one and got a really good sound from it,

05:09 so the next time it happened I recorded  it and sent it to my group chat.”

05:13 Alas, his career as a  security guard was cut short.

05:17 In 2018, he had his video camera turned on  when his manager explained there were a bunch

05:21 of angry people at the hospital not happy with  Doug’s cutting the cheese routine. The manager

05:26 told him to hand in his badge like Doug was a  rogue cop in an 80s Hollywood movie. He wasn’t

05:32 fired for farting, which we guess under US  law is protected by freedom of expression,

05:38 but using his phone when the hospital  had a no-phone-use policy for workers.

05:43 If you think that’s ridiculous,  it’s going to get worse.

05:46 13. Vulgar students In 2013, the internet was introduced

05:50 to the viral meme known as the Harlem Shake,  a dance routine that was copied by others and

05:55 posted to YouTube thousands of times. Within days  of the original being posted, there were about

06:00 40,000 Harlem Shake spinoff videos on YouTube  which had garnered around 175 million views.

06:07 This would eventually increase to 700 million. Now, people in their right mind would see this

06:12 as a bit of harmless fun, or at worst,  slightly silly, but it seems - as we’ve

06:17 already discovered- some people in this world  are a little too uptight. After a group of US

06:22 high school kids did the shake and posted it  online, the school suspended 30 of them citing

06:27 the school’s code of conduct that related to the  “vulgarity” of the hip-thrust part of the dance.

06:33 One of the most iconic Harlem Shake stories  hails from across the pond in England. At

06:38 St Hilda’s College, Oxford, a student and  her band of brainiacs took the viral craze

06:43 to new heights by performing the dance  in the college’s centuries-old library.

06:48 One Oxford professor even dubbed  it 'the best example of the genre,

06:52 at least in the UK.' But the student’s employer  wasn’t so impressed- she was promptly sacked

06:58 from her part-time library job. Harsh feedback  for what many might call a viral work of art.

07:04 Talking about violence, let’s now see how the  UFC boss Dana White got a person fired after he

07:09 made a video that went viral. 12. The ultimate snitcher

07:13 The UFC’s CEO Dana White in 2024 filmed a  FedEx guy throwing packages into the back

07:19 of a truck with the power and precision  of a professional basketball player.

07:23 This guy could seriously throw. White posted  the video online and the man was sacked after

07:28 it was seen millions of times on Instagram,  YouTube, and other platforms. FedEx said in

07:34 response, “We are committed to treating our  customers’ packages with the utmost care,

07:38 and this driver is no longer providing service  for our company as a result of this behavior.”

07:43 To be fair to the guy, he should  probably concentrate on playing sports,

07:46 because he really did have good technique. Ok, this next one should be a lesson to you all:

07:52 Be nice to strangers. It doesn’t take any  effort, and not being nice might cost you… a lot.

07:59 11. The rancid passenger As everyone knows, some people have two faces,

08:04 one that they show to the public and people they  work with, and another that is mean and nasty.

08:10 An Uber driver in 2020 found that out when Hans  Berglund got into his car in Arizona. The driver,

08:16 a young African-American student, politely  asked Hans to sit in the back. While Berglund

08:21 insisted on the front seat, the driver stood  firm. Following a serious incident in 2018,

08:26 he implemented a backseat-only policy  for safety- something even Uber had on

08:30 record. A sign in his car explained the  rule, which stemmed from a past assault

08:35 But Berglund decided he didn’t play by the  rules. The student calmly warned him that

08:40 what happened in his car didn’t necessarily stay  in his car- he had a camera recording everything.

08:45 After being told the ride was canceled, the Hans  exploded into an expletive-laden diatribe filled

08:51 with racial slurs. The driver gave his video to  the media and before you could say “fired” the

08:57 foul-mouthed passenger was cleaning out his desk. But this wasn’t just any desk, it was a corner

09:02 office of the company he’d founded and of  which he was CEO and President. Yep, he was

09:08 fired from the company he’d spent years building. Berglund was apparently CEO of several companies

09:13 and now every time he met his prospective  clients and partners, they knew what kind

09:17 of man they were dealing with. He said he  was sorry and that his apology was “honest

09:22 and heartfelt” but don’t they all… And as we’ll now see, women can be

09:26 just as hurtful. 10. The savages

09:29 In 2024, a video surfaced online showing a woman  reading aloud from what appeared to be a diary.

09:35 Another woman, filming and giggling, stood  nearby, while a third woman sat on the floor

09:40 listening intently. A man in the room seemed  uninterested, focused on his phone instead.

09:45 Ok, so far, no problem, but this story takes  a darker turn when we discover the diary the

09:50 woman was reading from, which seemed hilarious  to them, was a cancer diary. Its writer had

09:56 written about her possible impending death. The three women worked at a dental clinic in

10:01 Kansas, and the diary they mocked belonged to  one of their patients. According to the media,

10:05 it contained “heartbreaking” entries  about the woman fighting for her life.

10:09 But one of the women, presumably the one filming,  posted the video online with the heading, “Found

10:14 a patient’s journal and now it’s story time.” It’s hard to see what was so funny about someone

10:19 who’d written she was running out of treatment  options. There was public outrage after,

10:24 as the media said, “the footage spread  across social media like wildfire.”

10:28 All three women were sacked and the dental  practice released the familiar “this

10:32 doesn’t reflect our values” apology. Now for a woman who was definitely

10:37 in the wrong job. 9. Airport Rage

10:41 We’ve all had that one teacher or boss so strict  or angry that we’ve jokingly called them a

10:46 dictator. Passengers at Hollywood Burbank Airport  in July 2024 may have felt the same way as they

10:52 watched in shock. A woman, whose demeanor seemed  ripped from a page of history’s harshest regimes,

10:58 screamed at them and barked orders  to 'shut up,' leaving them stunned.

11:02 Her job was a Spirit Airlines  customer service representative,

11:06 but we’d say she’s wasting her talents. Throwing her arms in the air and screaming

11:10 at the top of her voice, she told the 300 or  so passengers who’d had their flight delayed,

11:15 some who’d been waiting for eight  hours, to shut up and take the pain.

11:19 She later told the press, “I think it was just  everything. It was just the pressure, nobody was

11:24 listening.” It wasn’t just her who got the boot.  Her much quieter supervisor also lost her job.

11:30 If you’re going to scream at  people like a deranged maniac,

11:33 maybe don’t do it in a crowd where hundreds  of phones are ready to capture your meltdown.

11:37 What’s kind of funny is after she was fired,  she was hired by another company for crowd

11:42 management. We guess she’ll do quite well there. Enjoying these epic fails? Tell us your favorite

11:47 so far in the comments- we  know you’ve got thoughts!

11:50 8. Hot sauce war Fast-food work might

11:53 not seem like a stressful job, but at the end  of a long shift, all you want to do is unwind.

11:58 This is exactly what happened to employees  at a KFC/Taco Bell outlet in Vermont in 2019.

12:04 After a long day on the job, these young workers  did what any exhausted crew would do- they started

12:09 a food fight. And while it would’ve been  great to see KFC vs. Taco Bell as rival

12:14 teams, it seemed like a chaotic free-for-all.  Taco sauce flew through the air, and soon,

12:19 one employee was in a food-strewn restroom,  looking ready to hurl, while another frantically

12:24 tried to scrub hot sauce out of her hair. As any veteran food fighter knows, getting

12:28 sauce out of one’s hair is no easy feat. So this  employee gave her hair a soak in the large kitchen

12:34 basin… the one packed full of dishes. The video travelled into social media

12:38 hyperspace and before the day was finished  people were writing comments such as,

12:43 “Guess I don’t want Taco Bell anymore.” Restaurant chains don’t take kindly to their

12:47 staff diminishing their bottom line. KFC issued  a swift apology and informed the public that

12:52 everyone involved was “terminated”. Meanwhile  the Vermont Department of Health was probably

12:57 overdoing it when they issued a statement saying  the incident didn’t pose a public health risk.

13:01 The staff should have known better.  But the next group of workers? They

13:05 really should have known better. 7. What the F were they thinking?

13:09 Imagine scrolling through YouTube and stumbling  across a video of your trusted TV news anchors-

13:14 people who always seemed to love your community-  openly trashing it. As if that wasn’t bad enough,

13:20 they go on to rant about how terrible their  bosses are at the station they work for.

13:24 This happened in 2010. Four staff at Little Rock’s  KARK-TV produced two “profanity-laden” videos and

13:31 posted them to YouTube. The stars included two  news anchors, a sports anchor, and a photographer.

13:37 They talked about how much they hated Arkansas,  hated the people, hated the job, hated their

13:41 bosses, and wanted nothing more than to leave. The video might have been a spoof, but the public

13:47 didn’t know that. While the anchors realized  their mistake and quickly took the videos down,

13:52 it was too late- the damage was done,  and the public was already sharpening

13:56 their pitchforks. The station wasted no time,  announcing the anchors’ immediate termination

14:01 and issuing an apology for the 'unauthorized,  offensive, and distasteful videos' that they said

14:06 'degraded' and 'discredited' the community. Now for the maddest dad you’ve ever seen.

14:12 6. Furious father Let’s imagine you have a top job as a financial

14:17 advisor at one of the US’s biggest investment  management firms. You’ve got cash in the bank

14:23 and you’re putting your kids through college,  and then you lose it all over a… smoothie?

14:28 This happened in 2022 to a dad whose son had  bought a drink at a Connecticut smoothie shop. The

14:34 dad, who worked at Merrill Lynch, was outraged  when his son had an allergic reaction to a

14:39 smoothie that contained nuts. It’s understandable  that the father was upset, but things quickly

14:44 escalated. He began screaming at the workers- at  all of them- and at one point, hurled a smoothie

14:49 toward one of the employees. The cup glanced  off her shoulder but left everyone stunned.

14:54 Was he done? No… he was only getting started. "In a fit of rage, he tried to break into the

15:00 back where the terrified workers were hiding,  shaking with fear. His screams grew louder as

15:06 he threatened to kill every last one of them.  That’s right… he was threatening murder.

15:11 But there’s one crucial piece of information  missing here. The father hadn’t actually told the

15:15 staff his son had a peanut allergy. He’d only told  them he didn’t want peanut butter in the drink,

15:20 which isn’t quite the same thing. His son  collapsed and was rushed to the hospital in

15:25 anaphylactic shock- a life-threatening condition.  The situation was serious, but the workers hadn’t

15:30 known to warn the father that an ingredient  in the drink contained a trace of nut essence.

15:36 As the dad continued his rant, the girls in  the shop called the cops and he was arrested.

15:40 Millions of people saw his tirade on national  news and on social media. His investment firm

15:46 said they do not “tolerate behavior of this kind”  and that was the end of his time at Merrill Lynch.

15:50 Let’s now get back to some rudeness. 5. Mock the passenger

15:55 We’re sure part of the job when you’re  a flight attendant is having a good old

15:59 gossip about the passengers. But if you want to  keep your job, you probably shouldn’t mock them

16:03 when someone’s pointing a video camera at you. It seems two British Airways flight attendants

16:08 didn’t get this memo. They were caught on  video performing what the media described as

16:12 'racist gestures' aimed at mocking their Chinese  passengers. One of the attendants used her fingers

16:18 to pull the skin around her eyes to mimic a  stereotypical 'Chinese look' while doing a

16:23 crude and offensive impression of how she thought  a Chinese person sounded. According to reports,

16:29 their actions specifically 'targeted a  Chinese family…who struggled with English.'

16:33 The video ended up on TikTok, Instagram  and YouTube and was viewed by millions

16:37 of people. Not only that, their Asian colleague  saw the video, and as you can expect, she wasn’t

16:42 impressed and demanded that action be taken. And that’s what happened. Both women were accused

16:47 of violating the airline's policies against  racism and subsequently booted out of their jobs.

16:52 That seems fair, but this next  firing doesn’t sound fair at all.

16:56 4. The candid coffee maker In 2019, a former 21-year-old

17:01 barista at a Starbucks in Detroit said she  was sent packing from her job for just being

17:06 honest. The girl, a vlogger with about 73,000  subscribers on YouTube, made content telling

17:12 viewers how to make coffee at home and make  it taste just like the stuff at Starbucks.

17:16 This could have been great marketing for  Starbucks, but the girl didn’t sugarcoat

17:20 her opinions- especially when it came to drinks  she didn’t like. She told her fans she wasn’t

17:25 exactly a fan of the 'Pike Place Roast.' Ok,  maybe she phrased it a bit more... bluntly.

17:31 Surely, she deserved to have an opinion,  but her manager didn’t see it that way.

17:35 The vlogger said he saw the video and “it  all went downhill” from there, leading to

17:39 her receiving her marching orders. She admitted  her video could be construed as “defamation” but

17:44 criticized Starbucks for not caring about  her “well-being” right before Christmas.

17:48 But then, the plot thickened. Starbucks said it had nothing to

17:52 do with her side hustle as a coffee reviewer,  but what they said was a case of “theft.” She

17:57 denied it, saying the company was lying  and it was definitely over her channel.

18:02 Who knows what the truth is in this crime  of the century, but it all worked out well

18:06 for the woman whose video was seen 329,000  times, giving her a much bigger following.

18:12 The moral of the story is if you’re  going to get fired over a video,

18:15 make sure there’s something to be gained. As for this next guy, it was a lose-lose

18:20 situation for him. 3. Rotten Apple

18:23 It goes without saying that working on new  products for a tech company- especially

18:28 in a competitive industry- comes with strict  secrecy agreements. But if you’ve signed one,

18:32 you might want to think twice before  letting your YouTube creator daughter

18:36 get her hands on unreleased products your  company is desperate to keep under wraps.

18:40 This is what happened in 2017 when an engineer  at Apple working on the new iPhone X took his

18:46 daughter on a tour of the company. She  videoed the tour for her YouTube channel,

18:50 which was fine according to Apple, but at some  point in the video she picked up the iPhone X

18:55 and started playing with it. The issue for  Apple was the phone wasn’t even out yet!

18:59 Sitting in the cafeteria, she showed off all  the cool things you could do with it. Soon,

19:04 all the tech websites were having a field day.  A writer at 9to5Mac called it “probably our best

19:09 look yet at the device in action.” She took the video down, but Apple

19:13 wasn’t impressed, firing her dad on the  spot. The daughter, who seemed genuinely

19:17 naïve about Apple’s zealous secrecy, was  upset, saying in another video, “If you

19:21 break a rule, they just have no tolerance.” It seems a little cruel, but everyone knows

19:25 what happens at Apple stays at Apple. 2. The scariest police chief in America

19:31 You’d think a police chief would know  how to avoid upsetting his bosses,

19:35 but not Mark Kessler. He was let go from his job  at a small Pennsylvania police department in 2013

19:41 after becoming something of a YouTube celebrity. Kessler liked guns. Actually, he loved guns,

19:47 all kinds of guns, and he hated anyone who was  trying to reform the USA’s laws on gun ownership.

19:52 That’s all well and good, but he made what the  media called “expletive-laden” videos where he’d

19:58 pop off a few shots while going into a diatribe  against anyone who disagreed with him on gun laws.

20:03 Never one to hold back, he took aim at a target  he’d nicknamed 'Nancy Pelosi,' which, in his

20:08 creative touch, was depicted as an evil clown. To  top it off, after branding John Kerry a piece of…

20:14 poop, he unloaded about 20 rounds into another  target. Subtlety clearly wasn’t his strong suit.

20:20 Now, everyone has the freedom in the US to  say what they want about gun rights. But his

20:25 department and the borough council where  he worked took a dim view of this guy’s

20:29 YouTube channel. Still, they couldn’t really  fire him on the grounds he liked shooting up

20:33 politician targets and arguing about gun  rights. Instead, they got him for misusing

20:38 borough property - the gun- neglecting his duties,  and failing to turn over weapons to the borough.

20:44 He later said “It was because of my videos”  and we think we might have to agree with

20:49 him. At least he became famous, with some media  calling him “America’s scariest police chief.”

20:55 But as we all know, internet fame doesn’t  always lead to happy endings. Five years later,

20:59 Kessler found himself in the headlines again.  This time, he was under indictment for terroristic

21:04 threats and harassment, with additional  accusations of lying on a firearm application.

21:09 The moral of this story is: Be careful who  you choose as your shooting practice target.

21:14 Ok, the last one, and one with a difference. 1. YouTube viewer snitches

21:20 If you haven’t seen YouTuber Arlette Amuli’s  dating show, “Pop the Balloon or Find Love”?,

21:26 then you haven’t missed much. It’s kinda  cheesy and fake as all dating shows tend to be.

21:31 But that doesn’t mean a person should be  fired because they played a starring role in

21:34 the making of a particularly viral episode. That’s what happened to a young man named

21:38 Aaron. He walked down a line of women holding  balloons and had a chat with each of them,

21:43 and if they popped their balloon,  it meant they weren’t interested.

21:46 But Aaron seems to have upset some viewers  because he said he didn’t like cheating women

21:50 and he’d prefer they had good hygiene practices.  But things got awkward when he told one contestant

21:55 he wouldn’t approach her if he saw her in public. To be clear, he didn’t say he’d run away screaming

22:01 or vomit in the street, but his honesty didn’t  stop there. He crossed another line when he told a

22:06 different contestant he wasn’t a fan of her hairy  arms. Cue the sound of more popping balloons.

22:11 While Aaron didn’t think he was being offensive-  he saw himself as a straight-shooter- the women

22:16 took his remarks as arrogance. And  judging by the YouTube audience’s

22:19 reaction, they weren’t too impressed either. He later posted to Instagram, “All this clout

22:24 chasing got me fired from work.” 5.3 million  people watched that video, and it seems about

22:29 500 of them, according to him, found out where  he worked as a plumber and lodged a complaint.

22:34 Still, it seemed a little unfair that he lost  his job. He at least got some love online,

22:39 with one person saying, “Social  media takes things entirely too far.”

22:43 Yep, that sounds about right. Got a favorite firing fail from these stories? Or

22:48 know an even dumber one? Drop it in the comments. Now you need to watch, “Dumbest Ways to

22:52 Die - Florida Edition.” Or, have a look  at “Dumb Ways to Die - Celebrity Edition.”

133:04 And they're moving at a constant rate.

133:06 So you can kind of guess when the train

133:07 is going to get to the station.

133:10 There are strategies to-- you can move

133:13 your lines around a little bit.

133:15 But once your lines are in place, for the most part,

133:17 they're static.

133:18 You can't really change them all that much.

133:20 So there's some limitations going on

133:21 between how much you can move a line or not.

133:24 At the end, if you last a week, it's

133:26 going to give you one of three options

133:28 to do a power-up, basically.

133:29 Either you can build a new line, add a new train,

133:33 increase the capacity of a train.

133:34 So you're making a permanent choice there.

133:36 And that's going to affect the later game.

133:38 So you're making all sorts of these decisions

133:40 at both a macro and micro level.

133:42 And there's a really good write-up about the game

133:44 right there, if you just want to read that.

133:47 FTL-- I lost a ton of productivity

133:51 a few months ago because of this game.

133:53 It is a game about fighting in spaceships

133:56 without actually controlling all the fighting so much.

133:59 You're actually upgrading your ship, increasing your capacity,

134:04 buying crew members-- and hoping your crew members survive

134:07 is a lot of it.

134:09 You could-- and I do this-- manually

134:13 control all your weapons.

134:14 And actually to succeed, you really do have to.

134:17 Because the interesting thing with this game is it's

134:19 a perma-death game.

134:20 As soon as you die, it's dead.

134:22 You have to start over.

134:23 You have to restart the game.

134:24 Luckily the game only takes about three hours to play.

134:28 But you're lucky if you get through those three hours.

134:30 And when you finally get to the last boss,

134:32 and you're there-- the thing about this game is in order

134:36 to get to that boss, there's all sorts of different challenges

134:39 you're facing.

134:40 And you're making these decisions about,

134:42 do I buy this weapon or that weapon

134:44 to help me with the thing I know that I'm going

134:45 to face in the next sector?

134:46 Because I'm losing health.

134:48 I'm really dying here.

134:50 But is this weapon really going to help me

134:52 when I get to the boss?

134:54 You're constantly going back and forth.

134:56 So I'll often find, after three or four, that I'm at the boss

134:59 and I'm completely ill-equipped to fight this thing.

135:02 And I just die.

135:03 But I do play out to the end, because it's fun.

135:05 Last game I have-- this one's free online.

135:08 It's called Gridland.

135:09 If anybody's played the game, A Dark Room, a text-based supply

135:14 chain game, this is the Match 3 version

135:16 of that game, a little bit.

135:19 There's two stages in the game-- day and night.

135:21 It's Match 3, so you just collect three gems.

135:24 And you get whatever the gems represent-- resources

135:27 like clay, wood, and stone, food, paper, gems.

135:34 You can upgrade your little factories to make better gems.

135:38 Every time you upgrade one of these,

135:39 though-- so if you upgrade your wood,

135:41 you'll get a better sword.

135:42 If you upgrade your clay, which you

135:44 need to make the better wood, you're

135:47 going to get in the nighttime a stronger monster.

135:49 So in this case, this is immediately daytime

135:52 and then shifted over to night.

135:54 The exact same layout is there.

135:55 It's just the logs have become shields.

136:00 The little blue things that are supposed to be iron

136:03 become swords.

136:04 And all the other things become enemies.

136:08 So a lot of the strategy for this game

136:11 is, what's going to help me now?

136:14 What's going to help me in the future?

136:16 What's going to hurt me in the future?

136:17 And what's going to hurt me immediately

136:19 as I switch over to night?

136:21 Once I get into the night mode, I'll

136:24 have known exactly what I'm going to be facing.

136:25 Because I set that stage up.

136:27 So unlike Bejeweled where you're just constantly just clicking

136:30 things, or Candy Crush where you're just

136:32 constantly just clicking things, there's

136:33 actually no time limit on this.

136:34 And it took me-- it's embarrassing

136:35 how long it took me-- a day or two to realize that I

136:38 didn't have to play that way.

136:39 I could just wait, pause, and play.

136:42 There wasn't going to be a time limit pushing

136:44 me to continue moving forward.

136:48 And that's an interesting presentation thing.

136:50 When you're presenting your games,

136:51 especially if you're using a previous genre,

136:53 there's going to be genre conventions that the players

136:55 are going to understand.

136:56 That is going to shape their user experience.

136:59 And we'll be talking about that about project three.

137:03 So that's it.

137:05 If you want to play these games or watch these games

137:07 on YouTube, please do.

137:09 And if you want to know more about choice and conflict,

137:11 there's a nine-minute video at Extra Credits.

137:13 We use Extra Credits a lot, because they're short.

137:15 They're fun videos on game design.

137:18 I highly recommend it for this class

137:20 to give you a leg up on some of the design challenges

137:22 that we're facing here.
