docs.title: YouTube Transcript: $2.45 BILLION Debt. Ubisoft is DOOMED.
Video Information
docs.text:
• Title: $2.45 BILLION Debt. Ubisoft is DOOMED.
  • Video ID: q9GpzCudQb4
  • Published: Unknown
  • Views: Unknown
  • Language: en

docs.title: Transcript
docs.text:
00:00 Ubisoft fans aren't happy. The French gaming giant has

00:03 stumbled from one disappointment to the next.  Skull and Bones flopped. Star Wars Outlaws failed

00:08 to become the hit Ubisoft desperately needed.  Even Assassin's Creed isn't the untouchable

00:13 powerhouse it once seemed. So what happened?

00:15 Everyone has an answer...  and they might all be wrong.

00:18 Some fans blame woke writing. Industry  veterans blame overworked developers and

00:23 bloated management. But those explanations  don't fully explain what's happening.

00:27 Because the reality may be much darker. Is Ubisoft still trying to make great

00:32 games? Or has it become something else entirely,  shaped by outside interests, data harvesting,

00:37 and forces most players never see? The answer could reveal a future where

00:41 gaming faces its own Lehman Brothers moment. And where players stop being customers…

00:46 and become the product instead.

00:48 For those holding Ubisoft stock in 2018, things  were looking good. The French video game had a

00:54 huge stable of hit franchises including Far  Cry, Prince of Persia, and of course, the

00:58 Assassin’s Creed series. With over 20 installments  released and multiple spinoffs in TV and movies,

01:03 it was one of the most well-known brands in  video games. It was also one of the biggest

01:07 factors that sent Ubisoft’s stock rising  to a record high of over €102 a share.

01:13 But like any roller coaster, there’s a climb…

01:16 Then a meteoric fall.

01:17 By 2024, Ubisoft stock had cratered to around  €13, wiping out 87% of shareholder value on

01:24 a stock that many saw as a safe bet. This is  the equivalent of having a $100 bill in your

01:29 pocket, and when you pull it out, it’s  transformed into a single movie ticket.

01:34 It would be easy to assume this is a  general collapse of the tech industry.

01:38 It’s not. While Ubisoft was crashing,

01:40 almost everyone else was surging. Nintendo  has been consistently climbing since 2018, and

01:45 acclaimed game publisher Konami - seen as a rival  to Ubisoft - saw its stock soar from 2023 onwards.

01:52 It’s not the industry. It’s not the games.

01:54 It’s what’s going on behind the scenes.

01:56 Ubisoft is a giant in the video game  world. Alongside original titles,

02:01 they rely heavily on existing intellectual  property like Star Wars and Avatar,

02:05 with games involving a high level of action. The  company, led by chairman and CEO Yves Guillemot,

02:11 is also independent and can cut its  own deals with the console companies.

02:15 But that independence hasn’t  been easy to maintain.

02:17 The company consistently expanded and had resisted  pressure to sell. Until 2015. That’s when a

02:23 company tried to take that choice away from it.  Vivendi, a powerful French mass media corporation,

02:29 set its sights on the gaming company as part  of an expansion push. It had acquired a 10.4%

02:34 share in the company, and Guillemot feared  it was all part of a hostile takeover plan.

02:38 As Vivendi continued to acquire  shares through other companies,

02:41 Guillemot successfully rallied board members to  freeze out Vivendi’s representatives. In 2018,

02:47 the two struck a deal that ended  any risk of a hostile takeover.

02:51 That might have sown the  seeds of its own destruction.

02:54 Vivendi was the pressing threat, but the  cure might have been worse than the disease.

02:58 Battered by scandals, disappointing  games, and a costly fight for survival,

03:02 Ubisoft turned to Chinese tech giant  Tencent for billions in investment. Over

03:07 the last few years, that has made Tencent  the second-largest shareholder in Ubisoft.

03:12 Some would say, it’s the power behind the scenes.

03:15 Now, Ubisoft could find itself in  a hostage situation. But why would

03:19 the founders hand over the keys to the castle?

03:21 The war with Vivendi was over. But Ubisoft  couldn't stand alone. Its largest shareholder

03:26 was Guillemot Brothers Ltd., a company  controlled by the family that founded

03:30 Ubisoft. This is mostly done for tax purposes,  and it gives the founders more flexibility when

03:35 it comes to leveraging wealth, assets, and debt.  Tencent, which has been heavily investing in

03:40 video game assets for years, is the world’s  largest video game company based on revenue

03:44 And it had its sights on Ubisoft.

03:47 In 2022, Tencent invested €300 million  Euros into Guillemot Brothers Ltd.,

03:52 which gave the company just under half of the  investing power, 49.9%. Ubisoft has always

03:58 guarded its creative independence. But this deal  instantly made Tencent one of the most influential

04:04 players in the company's future. Meanwhile,  Ubisoft gained a powerful financial backer,

04:08 while Tencent expanded its reach into  one of gaming's biggest publishers.

04:12 It seemed like a win-win.

04:14 It also might have signed Ubisoft’s death warrant.

04:17 €300 million sounds like a lot, but it’s really  only the price of one Marvel blockbuster these

04:23 days. Large tech companies can throw that  money around like spare change. For Ubisoft,

04:28 though, it was an act of desperation. They were  scrambling to save board seats for the founders.

04:32 Now they found a partner who was known for  wanting to maintain a hands off approach.

04:38 Tencent’s business model generally centers around  being a silent partner and reaping the benefits.

04:43 There were several conditions included in the deal  that made this more than an investment. It made it

04:48 into a marriage. For Tencent, the deal included  an 8 year lockup period that kept Tencent from

04:53 selling its shares. This was to protect Ubisoft  from a backdoor deal that would see its investors

04:58 turn over control of the company. Ubisoft also  built in protections if the company is ever sold,

05:04 adding exit clauses in case a new owner takes  over. As Ubisoft actively managed its options,

05:10 this arrangement seemed beneficial for both  sides, stabilizing the company for the future.

05:14 Behind the scenes, Ubisoft was struggling.

05:16 And it had very few options.

05:18 A company carrying debt is no surprise. But often,  accumulating debt is the prelude to a big sale

05:24 or collapse. A bigger company that can absorb  the debt purchases it and gets all its assets,

05:30 in exchange for taking the up-front financial  hit. But with Ubisoft determined not to sell,

05:35 they had to figure out how to get  out from under their current debts.

05:38 Which, as of 2026, ran $2.45 billion.

05:42 Ubisoft was now in a catch-22. It had to  pay off its debt, but the method it would

05:47 normally use to do so - a quick sale - was  closed off to it for multiple reasons. That

05:52 left only one remaining suitor, Tencent itself,  which was eager to purchase more shares. But if

05:57 Ubisoft wanted to remain independent, it would  have to figure out a new way to do business.

06:02 What happened next is what many gamers say  is the death spiral of the company, as the

06:06 gaming house known for acclaimed, historically  accurate epics started turning out pure slop.

06:12 Although, was it doing it on purpose?

06:14 Ubisoft continued to crank out games at its  usual pace, and several of them had a lot of

06:19 hype behind them. One of the top picks  was Skull and Bones, which seemed like

06:23 a can’t miss pitch. It brought the historical  accuracy of Assassin’s Creed to a new genre.

06:28 Players would engage in piracy and naval warfare  on the high seas. The tactical action game

06:34 featured a realistic sailing mechanic that was  unlike anything ever seen in video gaming before.

06:39 It was innovative.

06:40 But was it fun?

06:42 The game had to be redesigned multiple times to  refine its combat and exploration mechanics. The

06:47 shipped game failed to include very little  of the original sailing mechanics. Instead,

06:52 it focused on treasure hunting,  ship combat and faction wars.

06:55 This made it feel less like a new game and  more like a reskinned Ubisoft classic that

06:59 cost $200 million to produce. It debuted  to poor reviews and middling sales after

07:05 an extended development that saw it slip from  being announced in 2017 to being released in 2024.

07:11 That was just the start.

07:12 It was a huge coup for Ubisoft when Star Wars:  Outlaws was announced in 2021. From there,

07:17 it was a fairly smooth development  process. The game was fully revealed

07:21 in 2023 and dropped on shelves in 2024.  The game featured original characters and

07:27 was a heist mission set in an open world.  While it got marginally favorable reviews,

07:32 it was generally seen as derivative and  many users noticed frequent glitches.

07:36 The middling sales likely put an end to future  collaborations between Ubisoft and LucasFilm.

07:42 Everyone had an opinion on what was to blame.

07:45 Many players expressed their frustration with  Ubisoft’s recent output for subjective reasons,

07:49 often accusing it of being “woke”. The Assassin’s  Creed franchise had diversified heavily since its

07:54 early days focused on Renaissance Europe,  featuring lead characters of all races and

07:59 genders. Star Wars: Outlaws featured a female  lead, while Skull & Bones let users customize

08:04 their own pirate lead and featured a diverse  supporting cast. Some fans felt that was

08:08 pandering to an audience who were unlikely to  play video games and ignored the original fans.

08:13 The reality was very different.

08:15 There’s a term in development, Minimum Viable  Product, which essentially means “Good enough”.

08:20 Companies will release an incomplete product  with just enough to get fans interested. They

08:25 will then let the fans tell them what’s wrong.  These betas are then either patched and released

08:29 in updated models with new features. Or, the  feedback is incorporated into the sequel,

08:34 which the studio can then sell  to the fans at full price.

08:37 One way or another, the studios win.

08:39 The fans, who get an imperfect  product, usually lose.

08:42 This might be becoming Ubisoft’s  modus operandi now: pushing out

08:46 unfinished code just to keep the  financial life support running.

08:49 But where is the money coming from?

08:51 It doesn’t seem to make sense at first  glance. After all, who would want to

08:55 put out games that don’t provide a satisfactory  experience? That might get some money up front,

09:00 but it would likely alienate most casual gamers,  making it harder to sell them future games.

09:05 Short-term benefit and long-term loss is very  rarely a good bet when it comes to marketing.

09:10 This strategy seems likely to push  Ubisoft further into debt as time

09:14 goes on and make it harder for the company  to maintain control of its own property.

09:18 Except… new gamers might  not be the target anymore.

09:21 One of the most important numbers in gaming is  player recurring investment. It’s the metric

09:26 that measures how much money players are willing  to spend on a game AFTER their initial purchase.

09:31 In the 1990s and early 2000s, you purchased a  complete game and that was it. But once game

09:36 systems connected to the internet, it became  possible to create a whole in-game economy

09:40 of microtransactions. The game wasn’t so much a  single product as your passport to a network of

09:46 features. The days of straightforward games  with a clear beginning, middle, and end are

09:50 gone. Welcome to the world of “Games as a service”  where updates are constant and the fun never ends.

09:56 And neither do the payments.

09:57 If the studio can get a gamer  addicted to this format,

10:00 they have a customer for life. That can  make up for losing dozens of other buyers.

10:05 Ubisoft has become one of the biggest subscribers  to this model, to the frustration of many fans.

10:10 But as long as it keeps  paying, they’ll keep doing it.

10:13 Ubisoft has had massive success with this model,  with its recurring player investment typically

10:18 averaging 43% of total annual revenue. When you  remove the big game launches that have an outsized

10:24 impact on the bottom line, it can top over  50% per quarter. That’s a lot of money for

10:29 doing little more than selling new digital  costumes and launching new PVP battle seasons.

10:34 And when you need to put in less effort  than before, you need less talent.

10:38 Over the last few years, Ubisoft has seen an  exodus of mid-level programming talent. The team

10:43 being replaced by engagement-minded algorithms  that focus on creating the next hot collectible.

10:48 It’s a good business, but  is it sustainable long-term?

10:51 Not for a company in as deep debt as Ubisoft. They  need something bigger, and they may have found it…

10:57 At your expense.

10:58 The announcement of a new Assassin’s  Creed game is the kind of thing that

11:02 could get people excited about Ubisoft again.  The franchise is still Ubisoft’s crown jewel,

11:07 and the last installment was in 2023. So  when Assassin’s Creed: Jade leaked in 2022,

11:13 it picked up some buzz. It would be set  during the Qin Dynasty in the 3rd century BC,

11:18 and would feature a customizable lead character  for the first time. But behind the scenes,

11:23 there were rumors of trouble,  and soon they proved to be true.

11:27 This wasn’t really Assassin’s Creed at all.

11:29 For one thing, the game was going to be  released exclusively on Android and iOS.

11:33 That usually comes with more limited gameplay  and a greater focus on level-based gameplay as

11:38 opposed to a single narrative. It’s  also where microtransactions live,

11:42 as everyone who’s ever played a match-3 game  knows. But beyond that, the move of one of the

11:47 world’s greatest video game franchises to mobile  raised worries of another plague of mobile gaming.

11:53 Welcome to the algorithm…  where you’re the product.

11:56 Assassin’s Creed: Jade isn’t an Ubisoft  production, it’s being outsourced to Tencent,

12:00 with the mobile RPG being handled by Level  Infinite, their mobile-gaming arm. Designed

12:05 as a free-to-play game, little is known about  its actual gameplay beyond some enticing-looking

12:10 trailers that hint at intense battles. But  veterans of mobile combat gaming know what

12:14 to expect: a never-ending supply of levels,  with new gear and features always available

12:20 to purchase. Many fans are dreading their favorite  game series being turned into a Hero Wars clone.

12:25 If it ever comes out, that is.

12:27 While the game hasn’t been officially cancelled,  it has been hit with massive delays since 2022

12:32 and word of its development has slowed to a crawl.  It’s possible that the Ubisoft budget crunch led

12:37 to it being cancelled. It's also possible  Tencent is helping fine-tune the formula,

12:41 using its expertise in player behavior  and engagement to make it harder to put

12:45 down. And if it works, this may be what  Assassin's Creed looks like going forward.

12:50 And maybe, of all of video gaming.

12:52 Ubisoft has effectively handed its most valuable

12:55 franchise to a company that  could one day be a rival.

12:58 But Tencent may be after something  even more valuable than your money.

13:02 One of the most significant acquisitions Ubisoft  has made in recent years didn’t make the headlines

13:07 at all. In 2018, the gaming company made an  offer for Dutch server-hosting company i3D,

13:13 which hosts over 10,000 servers globally, heavily  in the gaming sector. That means they have a

13:18 player base of over 840 million active users,  with the number varying dramatically by server.

13:24 The company also provides major infrastructure for  both Ubisoft and competitors. By acquiring them,

13:29 Ubisoft guaranteed that it could ensure server  stability for its multiplayer-heavy future.

13:35 But that same structure might be  enticing for a very different reason.

13:39 I3D grew massively under Ubisoft’s leadership.  What it has done is essentially create a digital

13:44 panopticon, a massive network of almost  a billion gamers playing, interacting,

13:49 and making microtransactions online on a  regular basis. If you wanted to build a

13:54 profile of the gaming industry, this is about as  close as you could get. Most modern games have

13:59 an online component, and their players cover  nearly every demographic and genre imaginable.

14:05 For Tencent, it could be the  most valuable intel imaginable.

14:08 Tencent is one of the most successful gaming  companies in the world because of its investments,

14:13 but it has also been making more aggressive  steps into being a provider. Its mobile gaming

14:18 subsidiary has had great success in China,  but it’s had limited impact in the United

14:23 States. Assassin’s Creed: Jade was the first  step in changing that, using a popular brand

14:28 to introduce the user to Chinese gaming  and media infrastructure. The next step?

14:32 Giving them access to the  entire gaming panopticon.

14:35 If Tencent gains control of Ubisoft’s media  infrastructure, they’ll have an express pass to

14:41 some of the biggest gaming companies in the world  and their most secure data. This is essentially a

14:46 backdoor into the secrets of the most popular  games in the world. Tencent will be able to

14:50 discover the gaming patterns of American players.  When they make their next big move into the

14:55 American market, this will be an invaluable tool  that could change the gaming industry forever.

15:00 And not in a good way.

15:02 Why would a Western gaming company  leverage its future and allow itself

15:05 to be turned into little more than a  vessel for foreign data harvesting?

15:09 Ubisoft is still a rarity in the gaming world,  a major game company that is controlled by the

15:13 family that founded it. It hasn’t been  absorbed into a larger gaming company

15:17 that turned them into little more than a  boutique imprint. When the chance for a

15:21 hostile takeover arrived, the Guillemot’s  were willing to pay anything to avoid it.

15:25 That’s what cost them.

15:26 The founding family had one priority: avoid being  pushed out of their own company. When Vivendi was

15:32 ready to make a move, the company thought the  deal with Tencent was worth making. However,

15:36 this may have been a short-term gain in exchange  for long-term pain. Because Ubisoft, a company

15:41 already in heavy debt, had leveraged its future in  exchange for maintaining its hold on the company.

15:46 Now, those chickens may be coming home to roost.

15:48 Ubisoft has never been like other gaming  companies… and that might spell its end.

15:53 Ubisoft has found itself locked in  with Tencent. Neither company can

15:57 easily disentangle itself from the other.  That’s fine for Tencent, which has money

16:01 to burn and has been investing heavily in  companies like Ubisoft. But for Ubisoft,

16:05 it’s given up some of its independence and now  has less leverage. It’s still heavily in debt

16:10 and staring down bankruptcy unless its gaming  fortunes turn around. If it was forced to sell,

16:15 it would find itself with only one feasible  seller, Tencent, who is lying in wait.

16:20 The trap is set, and Ubisoft’s outlook is grim.

16:23 Chapter 8 - Controlled Demolition What does Ubisoft’s future look like?

16:25 It’s likely that Ubisoft’s debt problems will  only get worse, with their release schedule

16:29 slowing down. Since Star Wars Outlaws released  in 2024, the majority of their releases have

16:34 been internally developed games. Major titles  like Just Dance are produced entirely in house,

16:40 alongside releases like Monopoly and mobile  games. Releases in the Assassin’s Creed and

16:44 Tom Clancy series haven’t provided  the impact that the series used to,

16:48 and it’s likely that due to their financial  problems, they’ll have to sell more shares.

16:52 As Tencent gains more shares and Ubisoft’s stock  price continues to sink, the best financial option

16:57 will be to take the company private. That would  make it easier for Tencent to continue to exert

17:02 control, eventually gaining a majority share or  buying the company outright. All the franchises,

17:07 including Assassin’s Creed, would be  Tencent property, and the 300 million

17:12 user base with it. They’d also have full  access to the servers owned by i3D as well.

17:17 They would immediately become one of the  biggest players in the entire gaming market.

17:21 And they’re ready to take full advantage.

17:23 China’s gaming market has been waiting for this.  Tencent has been making moves in the sector

17:28 for years, but they’ve only been able to get  shares in existing powerful companies. However,

17:33 Ubisoft’s determination to remain independent  has done the exact opposite. The company

17:37 has made itself the most enticing target  possible. Tencent is likely to take control,

17:42 transform it from a console gaming  powerhouse into a mobile-only label,

17:46 and complete the dramatic shift  of gaming power from east to west.

17:50 And if it works, they’ll likely be  looking ahead to see who’s next.

17:53 Ubisoft isn’t the only gaming  company in deep trouble. One

17:56 of the biggest names in the sector is  facing its own problems. Check out “The

18:00 $50,000,000 Employee. Why Electronic Arts  is DEAD” or watch this video instead.

docs.text:
00:00 Three days. That's how long your grocery store

00:02 lasts if diesel trucks stop moving today. You probably think the government has a

00:07 backup plan. It doesn't.

00:09 Officials already drained 172 million barrels  from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve in early

00:15 2026. It's now at its lowest level since 1983, and  they're refilling it at a fraction of the speed

00:21 they emptied it. America's emergency oil cushion  is thinner than it's been in over 4 decades.

00:27 And while you're just one disruption  away from empty shelves, the biggest oil

00:31 companies in the world are cashing out. Imagine stepping inside a grocery store

00:35 in the middle of one of the biggest and busiest  cities on the planet, only to find empty shelves.

00:40 No bread, no milk, no fruit. Now imagine that same scenario

00:44 playing out all over the globe. In New York, London, Tokyo,

00:48 stores that are usually a hive of activity  and filled with groceries are stripped bare.

00:53 It sounds like a scene from a Hollywood disaster  movie, a post-apocalyptic world with no hope.

00:58 Except… that reality might  be closer than you realize.

01:01 Because this is exactly what would happen if the  critical but incredibly fragile logistics system

01:06 powering major urban centers suddenly collapses.  It’s known as the “Just In Time” system,

01:11 and once you understand it, your entire view  of how big cities function may change forever.

01:16 Most people think there are giant warehouses  packed with endless supplies, ready to refill

01:22 empty grocery shelves at a moment's notice. The reality is completely different.

01:26 Modern cities work like funnels. Food and everyday  essentials flow in, get bought almost immediately,

01:32 and disappear just as fast. It's an efficient  system, but not a resilient one. Most major

01:37 cities only have about 3 to 5 days of physical  food inventory before the shelves run dry.

01:42 The rest has to arrive on board heavy-duty  trucks, traveling hundreds of miles

01:46 across the country on a daily basis. In other words, there isn't some secret

01:51 warehouse waiting to save the day. Your grocery  store survives because trucks keep showing up,

01:56 day after day, without fail. The moment those  trucks are delayed, disrupted, or stop altogether,

02:01 the illusion of abundance disappears. And it breaks down quickly.

02:05 If the “Just In Time” system fails, major  metropolitan centers could literally run

02:09 out of food in 72 hours. That’s less time  than it takes to get over a common cold.

02:14 The moment the wheels stop  turning, the countdown begins/

02:18 On day 1, deliveries that were supposed  to arrive fail to show. By day 2,

02:23 localized panic starts to spread. Shoppers rush to  their local stores and snatch up whatever supplies

02:28 they can get. By day 3, everything’s gone. We’ve been trained to believe that something like

02:33 this could never happen. We trust the system. We shouldn’t.

02:37 Every item you buy, every piece of food you eat  , is all dependent on a logistics network that’s

02:43 entirely dependent on a constant supply of fuel. Without fuel, the food stops moving.

02:48 That’s when people look  for a back up. A fail-safe,

02:51 an emergency system that has been put in place  by the government to kick in and save the day.

02:56 And there is. Unfortunately, it’s already been raided.

03:00 The US government wasn’t blind to  the risks of the logistics system.

03:03 It realized that if ever there was some sort of  global oil crisis or fuel shortage, transportation

03:08 networks could break down and millions of  Americans would be at risk of starvation.

03:13 So, it set up a safety net: the US  Strategic Petroleum Reserve, or SPR.

03:18 It acts as a buffer against a fuel  supply crisis, ensuring that there is

03:21 enough emergency petroleum to keep vehicles  moving and transport networks operational.

03:26 Other countries have similar strategic  reserves, but the US’ has always been

03:30 one of the biggest. At full capacity, it can  hold 714 million barrels, stored deep inside

03:37 gigantic underground salt caverns along  the Gulf Coast of Texas and Louisiana.

03:41 Now, those caverns are nowhere near  full. They're not even half full.

03:46 As of late June 2026, the US SPR  held barely 330 million barrels,

03:51 the lowest level in more than 40 years.  You'd have to go all the way back to 1983

03:56 to find the reserve this depleted. For  decades, the government steadily built

04:00 this emergency buffer, stockpiling  hundreds of millions of barrels.

04:03 Then, almost overnight, a  huge chunk of it was gone.

04:06 In early March, the government authorized the  release of 172 million barrels. This was a direct

04:12 response to the war in Iran, which had led to  skyrocketing oil prices after the Iranian military

04:17 effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz. 20% of  the world’s oil supply came to a dramatic halt.

04:23 This was the sort of situation  that the SPR was made for.

04:26 The massive emergency release managed to  provide some level of short-term relief to

04:30 global energy markets. But the biggest issue  isn’t how quickly the reserve was depleted,

04:35 but how slow it is to fill back up. The physics  and economics involved with replenishing such

04:40 a vast reserve are more complicated than  opening the valves to empty it. Bureaucrats

04:45 are already trying to buy back crude oil and  pump it back into the Gulf Coast salt caverns.

04:50 But they’re not doing it fast enough. The current refill rate is approximately 10 times

04:55 slower than the million barrel a day drawdown rate  witnessed in 2022. It’s like having one person

05:01 draining a lake using a fire hose while someone  else tries to refill it with a tiny bucket.

05:06 The numbers don’t work. If this pace continues,

05:08 it could take years to bring the SPR back  up anywhere close to its maximum capacity.

05:13 This doesn’t mean that the US has run out of  oil or lost its crisis buffer entirely, but that

05:19 buffer is significantly thinner and weaker than it  was just a few years ago. That means the margin of

05:24 error is far smaller than it has been in decades,  because the safety net is riddled with holes.

05:30 We don’t have to guess or  estimate what happens next.

05:32 We’ve already seen this exact  scenario play out before.

05:36 In 2022, Sri Lanka experienced a  sharp and violent collapse that

05:40 brought the entire nation to its knees. When the country’s usable foreign exchange

05:44 reserves dropped to near-zero levels,  it effectively found itself unable to

05:48 service its $58.7 billion external debt. As a result, it defaulted on its debt

05:54 payments for the first time in its history. To make matters worse, the Sri Lankan

05:58 government was no longer able to afford  essential imports, including food, fuel,

06:02 medicine, and fertilizer. This led to nationwide  shortages of vital resources. Literally overnight,

06:08 shipments of petroleum and other  products and materials stopped.

06:12 The nation’s distribution network  collapsed almost instantly.

06:15 Without fuel, it was no longer possible to  move goods from place to place. Food rotted

06:20 in fields since there were no trucks  around to transport it to markets and

06:24 grocery stores. The absence of fertilizer also  meant that agricultural yields began to drop.

06:29 People were forced to spend hours or even days  waiting in miles-long queues to buy what little

06:35 petrol remained. They were also dealing with daily  rolling blackouts that lasted up to 13 hours at a

06:41 time, because there wasn’t enough fuel for the  country’s power plants. Schools closed down.

06:46 Hospitals postponed treatments and surgeries.  The cost of simple, staple items skyrocketed.

06:51 By September of 2022, year on year food  inflation had reached an eye-watering 94.9%.

06:58 The cost of a basic meal effectively  doubled in a single year.

07:01 The people of Sri Lanka had to deal with  the cost of sustenance and survival rising

07:06 faster than a hyper-inflating currency. And  it’s not as though their wages were rising,

07:11 too. People were earning the same amount  or even less than before, but somehow had

07:15 to stretch their budgets twice as far. Over 6 million Sri Lankans fell into food

07:20 insecurity, unsure when or where their next  meal would come. More than 60% of households

07:25 resorted to coping strategies - like skipping  meals or eating smaller portions - to get by.

07:30 This is why a fuel crisis  quickly becomes a food crisis.

07:34 Sri Lanka provided the perfect example of what  happens to your wallet when the fuel stops

07:38 flowing; when a country runs out of fuel, it also  runs out of food. Whatever food that’s left over

07:43 becomes a luxury asset, with a far higher price. You might think that Sri Lanka

07:48 was a one-off. An anomaly. An isolated occurrence of economic

07:52 mismanagement in a developing nation. Something  like this couldn’t happen in the Western world.

07:57 You’d be wrong. The same systemic

07:59 vulnerabilities that caused the Sri Lanka crisis  also exist in the US, the UK, and other nations,

08:05 regardless of their status or economic standing. The idea that richer countries can reduce their

08:10 risk by transitioning towards a stronger  and smarter system is fundamentally flawed.

08:15 We're constantly told that new technology  is about to solve our biggest problems.

08:19 That the next breakthrough will make our lives  easier, safer, and less vulnerable to crises.

08:24 Like electric vehicles. They’re supposed to be  the solution to our dependence on oil. Every

08:28 year there are more EVs in driveways,  more electric SUVs on the highway,

08:33 and more headlines predicting the end of the  gas-powered car. The age of oil is ending.

08:38 This is a myth. And the data proves it.

08:41 Yes, global sales of electric vehicles are rising  and even breaking records in many countries. Yes,

08:46 governments are setting out plans to phase  out vehicles with internal combustion engines

08:51 and offer incentives so people buy EVs. But as of June 2026, electric vehicles

08:56 make up just 5% of the global passenger fleet  and almost 0% of the heavy-duty maritime and

09:02 aviation sectors. In other words, while  there are more EVs on the roads today,

09:07 the majority are used by families for  their morning commutes and shopping trips.

09:11 Very few of them are being used in the sectors  that sustain modern society. The trucks,

09:16 the planes, and the ships that move goods  from point A to point B are almost exclusively

09:21 dependent on petroleum-based fuels. It’s going  to stay that way for the foreseeable future.

09:26 Around 80% of all global trade is transported  by a vast maritime fleet that is, in effect,

09:32 the lifeblood of 21st century civilization. And  99% of that fleet needs oil to move a single mile.

09:39 Cargo ships need petroleum-based fuels,  like Heavy Fuel Oil (HFO) and Marine

09:44 Gas Oil (MGO), in enormous quantities. The idea of suddenly switching them over

09:49 to electric energy is a fantasy. There’s no  battery technology in existence today that’s

09:54 big enough or strong enough to allow these  giants to make their transoceanic voyages.

10:00 The same limitations apply in the air. Freight  planes that move high-value or time-sensitive

10:05 supplies, like pharmaceuticals, churn through  huge amounts of petroleum-based fuels. There’s

10:10 no electric fleet just waiting to replace them. When you understand this, the true danger of

10:14 a major global fuel crisis  becomes even clearer to see:

10:18 a total oil depletion is, in effect, a “Delete”  button for the global economy as we know it.

10:24 If the oil stops flowing, everything stops moving. The rising popularity of EVs has no influence on

10:30 that. That means the logistics systems we depend  on have to compete for a shrinking pool of oil. As

10:36 that competition intensifies, the cost of energy  is set to reach an unprecedented breaking point.

10:41 Energy analysts and financial experts,  like Goldman Sachs often talk about the

10:45 “Demand Destruction” threshold. There comes a point at which the

10:48 cost of a commodity is simply too high for  consumers to absorb. So they dramatically

10:53 and permanently adjust their behavior to  reduce their consumption of that commodity.

10:58 At that point, economic activity  invariably begins to decline.

11:01 Purchases are put-off, travel is  reduced, and investment slows down.

11:06 Research and consultancy firm Wood Mackenzie  believes that the Demand Destruction threshold

11:10 for oil is between $125 and $150 per barrel. Once we enter that range, everything changes.

11:17 That’s because the actual energy cost required  to physically move a product across an ocean,

11:22 along a rail line, or down a highway exceeds  the profit margin of the product itself.

11:27 Imagine a product making its way through the  global supply chain. It has to be manufactured,

11:32 packaged, stored and shipped across the  world. It’s then trucked to a warehouse,

11:36 delivered to a store, and sold to you. Every step costs money.

11:40 As long as fuel stays reasonably cheap, the  numbers work and everyone makes a profit.

11:44 But when fuel prices spike, transportation  becomes more expensive. If it costs more to move

11:49 a container of goods than the goods themselves are  worth, shipping them simply stops making sense.

11:55 Sure, companies can raise prices, but only  to a point. Eventually customers stop buying,

12:00 sales dry up, and products stop moving. That's when the economic engine begins to

12:04 stall. Not because the world ran out of products,  but because it became too expensive to move them.

12:10 This phenomenon doesn’t stop there. It ripples outwards across society,

12:14 impacting the middle and working classes the most. As long as oil sustains a price within or

12:19 above the $125 to $150 range,  global GDP growth contracts.

12:24 All of a sudden, basic goods that were  once cheap and accessible feel like luxury

12:28 purchases. Families are forced to do mental  arithmetic in the grocery store to work out

12:33 what they can and can’t afford. Job stability takes a hit, too.

12:37 As energy costs soar and consume larger parts of  corporate revenues, even large and established

12:42 brands are forced to scale down their operations  and lay off workers. Within what feels like the

12:47 blink of an eye, the average consumer is  stuck between the rock of rising costs

12:51 and the hard place of income insecurity. All of the comforts and conveniences of

12:56 their modern lifestyle are torn away. The solid  foundations of the system they grew to rely on

13:01 are replaced by increasingly shaky ground. And when we think about this scenario,

13:06 one obvious question emerges: why  doesn’t the US just use its own oil?

13:11 Honestly, there’s no way that would work. The US is often hailed as a colossus of the energy

13:17 sector, with domestic production rates and export  levels reaching record highs in recent years.

13:22 It’s easy to assume that the oil fields of  Texas and New Mexico should provide more

13:26 than enough fuel to insulate the domestic  market, even in cases of global shortages.

13:31 Except that’s not true. If you only read the headlines,

13:35 you'd think America has energy independence.  Record oil production. A booming fracking

13:39 industry. No more relying on the rest of  the world to keep the economy running.

13:44 The reality is far more complicated. Despite producing record amounts of oil,

13:48 the United States still imports huge volumes  of heavy crude every single day. It sounds

13:53 like a contradiction, until you look at how  America's oil infrastructure actually works.

13:58 Not all crude oil is the same.  Think of it as a spectrum.

14:01 At one end is heavy crude, thick, sticky, and  packed with impurities. Turning it into fuels

14:07 like gasoline and diesel requires large, complex  refineries. At the other end is light crude,

14:13 which is much thinner and easier to process.  These aren't just different grades of the

14:17 same product. They behave differently,  require different refining processes,

14:21 and can't always be used interchangeably. This is where the problem comes in.

14:25 The multi-billion dollar refinery infrastructure  in the US was engineered and optimized to deal

14:30 with heavy sour crude. It made sense at the  time, as the global energy market was highly

14:35 reliant on imports of this type of oil from  places like the Middle East and Latin America.

14:40 These days, however, America’s fracking  revolution produces enormous quantities

14:44 of light sweet crude from shale formations.  But the infrastructure wasn’t built for that.

14:49 Trying to refine light sweet crude in  facilities designed for heavy sour is

14:54 like pouring unleaded gasoline into a diesel  engine and expecting it to work just as well.

14:58 It won’t. The fuel

15:00 and the facilities are entirely mismatched. Because of this, the US is stuck. It has to

15:05 keep exporting millions of barrels of its domestic  light sweet oil everyday to markets around the

15:10 world. Meanwhile, it also has to import millions  more barrels of heavy sour from its international

15:16 partners just to keep its own pumps up and  running in the first place. In other words,

15:19 the fracking boom didn’t provide any sort of  energy independence; it just made the existing

15:24 dependency even more complicated. The oil companies at the top of

15:28 the food chain know this. They can see the limitations

15:31 of the infrastructure. They can  see the problems this causes.

15:35 So what are they actually doing about it? People picture these big oil brands as

15:39 desperate to preserve the age of petroleum,  at any cost. They refuse to accept that the

15:44 world is moving towards cleaner and  more sustainable sources of energy.

15:48 There is some truth in that. The oil firms are money-hungry.

15:51 They are desperately attempting to squeeze out  every last drop of profit they can get. But it’s

15:56 not because they want to stop the transition or  think that they can keep selling oil indefinitely.

16:01 They know their days are numbered. That’s why they’re planning their exit strategies.

16:05 Just follow the money. Major firms like Shell  and BP are funding carbon capture projects,

16:11 building alternative energy infrastructure,  and positioning themselves for what comes next.

16:15 Money that once went into searching for  new oil fields and expanding drilling

16:19 capacity is being redirected into laying  the groundwork for the next energy system.

16:24 They’re not doing all of this out  of the goodness of their heart.

16:27 It’s not some altruistic attempt to  atone for the errors of the past and

16:31 play a part in saving the planet. It’s a way  for these same companies that have dominated

16:35 the energy sector for decades to maintain  their monopoly as long as they possibly can.

16:40 They realize that the current  petroleum-dependent system is flawed,

16:43 unsustainable, and screaming towards a brick  wall. They know that the “Demand Destruction”

16:48 threshold will eventually be crossed,  and there’ll be no going back from there.

16:53 At that point, oil will become either physically  or economically un-extractable, or both.

16:58 Consequently, oil giants should become obsolete. But if they buy enough of that next-generation

17:04 infrastructure early, they can effectively lock  in a system where we still depend on the same

17:08 major corporations… just in a different form. That’s the emerging geopolitical reality.

17:14 Oil companies helped build a world  where modern societies run on thin

17:18 margins. Where we rely on small buffers  and just days of food and fuel in reserve.

17:23 Now, as those safety nets continue to erode  and inventories sit at multi-decade lows,

17:29 the same industry players are repositioning  themselves for what comes next.

17:32 Not by leaving the system… but by owning it. But while everyone is focused on the fuel crisis,

17:38 there's another indicator that we might be at  an economic tipping point. We explain it all in

17:43 “It's Not Oil You Should Be Watching.  It's Japan”. Or click on this video.

00:00 Your phone already knows more about  you than most people ever will.

00:03 If you think it's just cookies, location tracking,  chat logs, shopping habits, and every website

00:09 you've ever visited feeding endless corporate and  government databases... that's just the beginning.

00:14 Because right now, governments and some of  the biggest companies on Earth are building

00:17 something far more dangerous: backdoors into the  devices you spend hours using every single day.

00:23 Including the one you're  probably watching this on.

00:26 Mark never thought it could happen to  him. He was already dealing with one

00:30 of a parent’s worst nightmares: His infant  son was getting sick. In February of 2021,

00:35 the San Francisco stay at home dad noticed his boy  was experiencing painful swelling in his groin.

00:40 So, he did what every responsible father would do,  getting in contact with a medical professional.

00:45 He’d never expect that doing the right  thing could put his whole life in jeopardy.

00:50 The COVID-19 pandemic was in full swing at  the time, when even leaving the house could be

00:55 dangerous, especially to the very old and the very  young. They’d need to send evidence of the illness

01:00 to the advice nurse to schedule an appointment for  a video consultation. Mark grabbed his Android and

01:05 took some pictures of the affected area so that  he and his wife could send them to the nurse.

01:10 It was the right decision,  because using the images,

01:13 the nurse was able to easily diagnose the  infection and prescribed an antibiotic.

01:17 But Mark was about to deal  with a far worse infection.

01:21 In taking and sharing those photos, he’d  attracted the attention of a supposedly

01:25 world-class AI system that big tech uses to catch  some of the most monstrous people in the world:

01:30 Creators and distributors of online child abuse  material. And in the eyes of this system, a man

01:36 who was just trying to help his son was actually  another one of these truly despicable criminals.

01:42 That decision was about to  throw his life into chaos.

01:44 Programs that large companies like Google and  Apple use to stop monsters are peering into your

01:50 private digital photo library. Mark found this  out the hard way. Loyalty didn’t matter: Mark was,

01:55 in many ways, one of Google’s best customers. Not  only was he a lifelong Android devotee since the

02:01 phones became available, he backed up all of  his data and photos on Google Cloud. He synced

02:06 his Google Calendar with his wife, and had a phone  plan with Google Fi. So when Google turned on him,

02:12 it really was like the ground opening up  beneath his feet and swallowing him whole.

02:16 Two days after taking the photos, he  received a notification from Google

02:19 saying that his account was closed  due to harmful content. It was, quote,

02:24 “a severe violation of Google’s  policies and might be illegal.”

02:28 And here’s the first cruel twist.

02:30 Mark immediately realized what was happening,  because he’d once worked as a software engineer

02:34 for a company producing automated content  moderation tools. In his case, he believed,

02:39 it would be as simple as identifying and  appealing to the human being inside the system

02:44 who could exercise real judgment. The  problem here was that there was no human.

02:49 The system itself was his only judge.

02:51 Google had also flagged a different video, and the  case triggered a humiliating police investigation.

02:57 Thankfully, after the stress of the  probe, it was easy to prove to the cops

03:00 that this had been a misunderstanding.  He had the words of his wife, the nurse,

03:05 and the paper trails of the treatment on his side.

03:08 It would not reinstate the account or any of  his tools, and what did this mean in real terms?

03:13 He lost years of photos, emails, contacts, records  of his son’s early life, his email address, and

03:19 important business documentation. And thanks to  Google Fi, he even lost his phone number and plan,

03:25 despite having done anything wrong. Mark  would say of this whole nightmare scenario,

03:29 “I knew that these companies were watching and  that privacy is not what we would hope it to be,

03:33 but I haven’t done anything wrong.”

03:35 It’s a freak case, a nightmare scenario,  the kind of thing you’ll think about every

03:39 time you take or save a perfectly innocent  photo. But this wasn’t just an isolated case.

03:44 Literally the exact same thing happened  to a man identified as Cassio in Texas,

03:48 right down to the private parts infection and  the photos texted to a concerned pediatrician.

03:53 Cassio was in the process of buying  a house, and having all of his Google

03:56 accounts nuked almost ruined him and his  family’s chances of sealing the deal.

04:01 These are real families, real  lives, real consequences,

04:05 all in the hands of something that doesn’t even  have hands: Unthinking, unfeeling AI content

04:10 algorithms hard-coded into the systems that  we’ve all come to be so dependent on. In 2021,

04:14 Google flagged over 600,000 cases, and used  this as evidence to annihilate 270,000 users.

04:21 Are we to believe that all of these people  are criminals? Or are we seeing a mass cull

04:26 from overzealous systems, designed to look like  hammers and treat everything they see as a nail?

04:31 And the cull is just getting started. In  the UK, the tools to carry it out aren’t

04:35 just being hard-coded into phones, they’re  being hard-coded into laws themselves…

04:40 The UK has always been the spearhead of digital  surveillance efforts in the English-speaking

04:44 world. For proof of this, look no further  than the Investigatory Powers Act 2016,

04:50 or as it was commonly nicknamed, “The Snooper’s  Charter.” It gave the British police and

04:54 intelligence services sweeping powers to violate  the communication privacy of their citizens.

04:59 In the classic style, trading privacy and  liberty for the promises of safety and security.

05:04 In terms of more specific provisions, they  empower these authorities to intercept certain

05:09 communications, collect mass communication  data, and to bulk-intercept communications.

05:14 Americans will probably be getting deja vu for  the actions of the NSA after the passing of the

05:20 Patriot Act right about now. It also led to the  creation of the Investigatory Powers Commission,

05:25 requiring service providers to retain details  of every site that a user had been on for at

05:30 least a year. It gave law enforcement warrantless  access to this data, and reaffirmed the ability

05:35 of these authorities to remove any encryption  that private companies have placed on user data.

05:40 Under these new laws, at least 48 different  agencies can have warrantless access to the data.

05:46 These range from different police  forces and national security interests

05:49 to even the Food Standards Agency and the  Northern Ireland Ambulance Service Health

05:54 and Social Care Trust. To say all of this  was just “controversial” among free internet

05:59 activists and government watchdog groups  in the UK would be vastly understating it.

06:04 Anne Jellema, head of the World Wide Web  Foundation, said, “Does the UK really want

06:09 the dubious honor of introducing powers deemed  too intrusive by all other major democracies,

06:14 joining the likes of China and Russia in  collecting everyone's browsing habits?”

06:18 Article 19, an individual rights  and freedoms group from the UK,

06:22 went even further. They said that the law  “offers a template for authoritarian regimes

06:27 and seriously undermining the rights of its  citizens to privacy and freedom of expression.”

06:31 And they were right, because the Chinese  Government would later use this British

06:35 legislation to defend their own  draconian internet control laws.

06:39 It’s not exactly great international company.

06:42 It got so much worse on April 23rd, 2024.

06:45 The British Government argued that the  bounty of data and metadata out there

06:49 had grown by an order of magnitude since  2016. That meant the general public as

06:54 well as the corporate sector were already  able to access and take advantage of this

06:58 data. Giving the government even more  power to snoop into all of this data

07:02 was simply a way of leveling the playing field  against the so-called “Bad Actors” out there.

07:07 If you’re someone who believes that  encryption that private companies will

07:09 protect your information, then this legislative  framework should and frankly, will, scare you.

07:15 The biggest additions for the new 2024  amendment are two frightening details:

07:19 One: The law would force technology  companies, even ones based overseas,

07:23 to keep the British Government updated  on any improvements to encryption,

07:27 privacy, and security hardware and software.

07:29 And Two: When receiving this information, they’d  have limitless power to order these companies to

07:35 halt or alter these new developments so they  could always have a backdoor into everyone’s

07:40 online data and communications. It’s a  kind of terrifying digital skeleton key,

07:45 a one-way mirror that lets the UK Government stare  into anyone’s devices without them ever knowing.

07:51 It might be happening right now.

07:53 An open letter from 30 cybersecurity  experts, cryptographers, and academics said

07:57 that this whole thing could be an absolute  disaster for overall security. They wrote,

08:01 “these proposals would have disastrous  consequences for the security of users…

08:05 by introducing bureaucratic hurdles that slow the  development and deployment of security updates.”

08:10 Nobody with any knowledge in the field  could tell them that they’re wrong here,

08:14 but that doesn’t matter. Legislators  are more oriented towards scrambling for

08:18 power and control than taking things  slow and listening to the experts.

08:21 If you think this starts and ends in the UK,  then I’m afraid you’re living in a fairytale.

08:26 You might think these are just tools  to track down criminals and terrorists,

08:30 you’re safe and secure. After all,  you haven’t done anything wrong.

08:33 But that’s just what they want you to think.

08:36 Now that the tracks have been put down to slow  and sometimes even destroy the encryption,

08:40 the next question is how they can  look at everyone’s actual messages.

08:44 And if you’ve been paying attention, you’ll  know that they already have the answer…

08:48 The UK Government isn’t the all-powerful,  world-dominating force that it was in the

08:52 Imperial Era. There’s no putting the power of  End to End Encryption, and the security and

08:57 privacy it provides, back in the box. And you’re  right. So instead, they took a different route.

09:01 Hiding the poison pill  inside end to end encryption.

09:04 If you’ve never had it explained  to you in human terms before,

09:08 end to end encryption means that when you  send a message, the message is scrambled,

09:12 or “encrypted”. No one but its intended  recipient would be able to see it. The

09:16 decryption key would only be in the recipient’s  hand, and the message would only be decoded when

09:21 in this person’s possession. It’s a great  system that will keep your secrets safe.

09:26 Unless there’s a backdoor…

09:28 Like Client-Side Scanning.

09:30 It goes by many names, including “local  processing” and “endpoint filtering.”

09:34 But they all fundamentally mean the same thing.  It creates a filter between the two ends of the

09:39 encryption process. That filter is connected  to a database that has a series of hashes.

09:44 When a message or a file passes through, while  the encrypted message isn’t said to be “read”,

09:49 it is checked against the hash databases  of the Client-Side Scanning software.

09:53 If this filter deems the encrypted communication  to contain objectionable or forbidden material,

09:58 one of several things might happen.

10:00 If you’re lucky, on the most benign end, the  filter will just stop the message from sending. If

10:05 you’re unlucky, your message might be sent, but a  copy of it will also be sent to the relevant third

10:10 party, whether that’s a corporate moderation team  or the government imposing restrictions on it.

10:15 No matter how narrow the focus of this  filter, this is still a breach of security

10:19 that could be crowbarred open as wide  as a powerful enough entity likes.

10:24 If the end to end encryption you’ve been  promised contains Client-Side Scanning,

10:28 then the encryption is little  more than a comforting lie.

10:31 This little government black box  is hiding inside far more of your

10:34 favorite communication programs than  you’d ever feel comfortable knowing.

10:38 There’s no meaningful limit to what can  be put in this collection of hashes.

10:42 Some have suggested that you could easily put  the whole dictionary into one of these databases,

10:47 which would effectively make any  message susceptible to easy decryption.

10:51 Think of it like Dracula: He can’t enter  your house until he’s been invited,

10:55 but once he’s been invited in once,  he can come and go as he pleases.

10:59 Then you’re in real trouble.

11:01 In the days before the internet, would  you still send mail if you knew that USPS

11:05 was opening every single letter, every package,  to find out and record what’s waiting inside?

11:11 Which brings us back to the privacy-destroying  legislative experiments of the UK, such as the

11:15 Online Safety Act of 2023. This is the law that  keeps minors in the UK off of social media,

11:21 and has likely led to an incredible boost in  the sales of VPNs across the nation. But it

11:27 actually contains an even more sinister caveat  that the intrusive age checks: A mandate for

11:31 technology providers to include the exact kind of  Client-Side Scanning mechanisms we just described.

11:38 At this point, it probably goes without  saying that this is a terrible idea.

11:42 Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK  National Cyber Security Centre, said of this:

11:46 “Client-side-scanning, despite  the claims of its proponents,

11:49 does seem to involve some kind of level of access,  some kind of ability to sort and scan… there’s

11:55 no way of confining that to good use by lawful  credible authorities and liberal democracies.”

12:00 It’s not surprising that ComputerWeekly.Com has  declared, “Privacy will be under unprecedented

12:05 attack in 2026.” The UK seems to just be  the warning shot before the full onslaught.

12:11 The worst part is that all  these nightmarish new policies

12:14 are almost impossible to argue  against for one big reason:

12:18 You’re not against child safety online, are you?

12:22 It’s the vague notion of child safety that’s  been employed to prop up campaigns as baloney

12:27 at the original 1980s Satanic Panic against rock  music, to more modern attempts to paint games

12:33 from Pokemon to GTA as horrors that’ll  turn kids into cold-blooded murderers.

12:38 And the reason it keeps being used  is that it almost always works.

12:41 Purely because of the fact it looks really,

12:44 really bad if you argue against proposals that  aim to prevent child abuse and even terrorism.

12:49 But is this technology actually really stopping  criminals and terrorists? Or is it just making

12:54 things easier for governments across the world  to oppress people whose speech they don’t like?

12:59 Starting in 2023, the National Center for Missing  and Exploited Children saw a sharp rise in reports

13:05 thanks to the increasing role of  automated technological systems

13:08 in reporting sinister behavior  online. 36.2 million reports.

13:14 Sadly, while some of that actually is material  being made by truly awful people, it’s worth

13:19 remembering that people like Mark and Cassio from  earlier would be included in a tally like this.

13:24 This is a problem that cuts both ways.

13:27 Not only is it horrible for the  people who get falsely accused,

13:30 but all these false positives make it harder  for authorities to investigate actual culprits,

13:35 and save any victims involved. Anyone whose  primary motivation was actually protecting

13:39 children would be able to notice this glaring  flaw in the system and work to create more

13:44 specific tools. Well, unless “protect the  children” is really just a smokescreen.

13:49 And you inevitably have to ask: If they’re not  actually building this system to protect children,

13:55 then what’s the true purpose of these  massive, hidden surveillance machines?

13:58 What the UK is doing is just the start.

14:01 Obviously, restrictive systems like this have  existed in Russia and China for about as long

14:05 as the internet existed. But the UK were  the real trailblazers for destroying digital

14:10 privacy in the alleged liberal democracies of  the Western world. Now the EU and the United

14:16 States seem eager to follow that trail to a  potentially even more extreme destination.

14:21 The EU has been slowly but surely moving to take  up a policy called CSAR, but it’s more infamously

14:28 known by its nickname: Chat Control. Now why  might they call it something like that, huh?

14:33 Of course, this policy would feature the same age  verification traps that have been inconveniencing

14:38 people across the UK and Australia. But they’d  also take it just that little bit further:

14:43 Proposing that technological communication  programs “voluntarily” scan all the messages

14:48 of their users for forbidden content. When  the government of a major economic zone

14:53 strongly suggests that you “voluntarily”  do something, it’s a little like the Mafia

14:58 strongly encouraging you to “voluntarily”  give them protection money every week.

15:03 It’s kind of an offer you can’t refuse.

15:05 Critics have said that the systems the EU wants  to put in place are notoriously error prone.

15:11 While the legislation says that it will only  give the police access to data that the system

15:15 flags as potentially dangerous, you’ll realize by  now that tuna nets catch plenty more than tuna.

15:21 If you use an innocent word that’s been plugged  into the system as a terrorist code hash,

15:26 police and intelligence agencies will have  full legal access to all of your chats.

15:30 Even if you’re not doing anything illegal,  do you really want them seeing all that?

15:35 Let’s say you go to the beach and you and your  friends take a few photos in your swimwear.

15:40 You’re not the kind of person who posts stuff  like that to social media, it’d make you feel a

15:43 little self-conscious, but you still don’t want  to lose the memory. These photos sit there in

15:48 your photo album, but if you’re in the UK, the  EU, or - as you’re about to find out - the US,

15:53 something scary happens the next time  your device backs up to the cloud.

15:57 AI systems designed to scan photos  for bodies and bare skin suddenly

16:00 pick your photos out of the cloud. There  might never be any real consequences,

16:05 you might not even know it happened,  but they still got flagged. Somewhere,

16:09 a content moderation team or a cybercrime  division are looking at your swimsuit photos.

16:14 Pretty creepy, right?

16:15 But it could get worse. Imagine you  take an intimate selfie for a partner,

16:19 and it trips this same system.  There’s no cleaner way to put this:

16:23 A content moderation team or a group of anonymous  government agents could be looking at your nudes.

16:29 It’s totally legal… and there’s  nothing you can do about it.

16:33 The American flavor of this is the EARN IT  Act, which stands for Eliminating Abusive and

16:38 Rampant Neglect of Interactive Technologies Act  of 2023. In essence, it’s a reskin of all these

16:44 other laws and regulations we’ve seen popping up  over the Western world. They want to establish a

16:49 formal regulatory board that threatens to strip  tech companies of their immunity if they don’t

16:54 follow the board’s practices. This means they  can use the threat of legal coercion to force

16:59 companies to break the encryption in your devices  and look at your private photos and messages.

17:04 It’s preposterous, but when has anything  being absurd ever stopped it from happening?

17:09 And we all know where this leads…

17:11 We all look back fondly on the days of  the first Smartphones. Fruit Ninja, iBeer,

17:16 and the convenience of having a working  computer in your pocket. But that thing

17:20 you can’t do without is soon going to be a  double agent for the corporations and the Feds.

17:24 It’ll become a gateway onto an internet  panopticon that’ll never stop looking.

17:28 Want even more reasons to  feel justifiably paranoid?

17:31 Check out “Somebody Is Watching You  Right Now”, or watch this instead!

08:33 Laborintensive farmwork like handh harvesting is  almost always conducted by contractors since they

00:00 The animal kingdom is full of terrifying and deadly parasites.

00:12 that would love nothing more than to feed on you.
