00:19 #13.

00:20 Tapeworms

00:21 One of the most common parasites, tapeworms usually make their way inside the human body

00:24 as hitchikers alongside your lunch or dinner.

00:27 These tiny, ribbon-like worms lurk inside the flesh of animals, commonly fish, beef,

00:32 or pork.

00:33 When you unwittingly consume them, these creatures don’t get digested - they set up camp in

00:37 the digestive tract and can live there for a long time.

00:41 Their long bodies have hooks or suckers that embed themselves in the intestine, and they

00:46 then get all the energy they need to live by absorbing part of your food.

00:49 But they don’t stay invisible for long.

00:52 People who are infected with tapeworms soon report symptoms including nausea, vomiting,

00:56 digestive issues, unexplained weight loss, and signs of malnutrition including dizziness.

01:00 While most people eventually expel their tapeworm through their digestive tract - which can

01:05 be a disgusting sight in the bathroom - they can survive for up to twenty-five years.

01:09 And when ingested as eggs or larvae, the tapeworm can reproduce in the body.

01:14 Larvae can turn into cysts that migrate through the body - even in the brain, where they can

01:18 potentially cause serious illness or even death.

01:21 This parasite is often invisible - but the next makes itself very well known.

01:26 #12.

01:27 Bedbugs

01:28 These little insects are the scourge of anyone who has stayed in a hotel.

01:31 Tiny bloodsucking insects that are notoriously hard to find and eliminate, they spread in

01:36 high-density areas and can hide in mattress seams or wall cracks.

01:39 When they attach to a person, their bites cause a host of skin issues that become impossible

01:44 to ignore.

01:45 Skin rashes, blisters, and constant itchiness become a part of regular life until the bedbugs

01:50 are eliminated, and more severe cases can result in fatigue and fever.

01:54 While the insects aren’t known to spread serious diseases - unlike other pesky bloodsucking

01:58 insects - one of their biggest threats is causing allergic reactions.

02:02 And while many exterminators will promise to get rid of a bedbug infestation, these

02:06 little buggers can live up to seventy days without feeding and reproduce fast - making

02:10 them likely to be unwelcome guests for a long time.

02:13 These next parasites make their presence known in a very unpleasant way.

02:17 #11.

02:18 Pinworms

02:19 Roundworms are a common species of parasitic worm that lays eggs in the body, but many

02:23 of them don’t pose a serious danger to humans.

02:25 That’s not to say you don’t want to avoid them - especially the pinworm, a small worm

02:30 that spreads via its eggs.

02:32 It can be picked up via contact with the hands and then getting swallowed - and then it goes

02:36 where the sun doesn’t shine.

02:37 The pinworm likes to lay its eggs around the anus, and this causes a host of uncomfortable

02:41 symptoms for the unlucky humans.

02:43 Pinworm hosts report itching around the anus, painful bowel movements, and difficulty sleeping

02:48 due to the constant annoyance.

02:50 Fortunately, it can be treated with a number of medications - but the worms spread so quickly

02:54 that doctors recommend everyone who lives with the infected take the medicines.

02:58 This parasite is so common that it’s estimated that twenty percent of children in the United

03:02 States will get infected.

03:04 Some roundworms, though, can cause much more serious infections.

03:09 #10.

03:10 Filarial Worms

03:11 Everyone knows mosquitos are annoying, but some can carry something far more dangerous.

03:15 These pesky bloodsuckers are hosts to tiny roundworms that can cause a whole host of

03:20 diseases.

03:21 Mosquitos are a common transmitter of plague, and the World Health Organization estimates

03:25 more than 120 million people may have an infection of filarial worms.

03:29 While many of them don’t cause any symptoms at all, they have the nasty effect of clogging

03:33 lymphatic vessels in some cases.

03:35 Another variety affects the eyes.

03:37 These worms can usually be treated with antiparasitic medications, but if left untreated they can

03:41 cause serious ailments.

03:43 They’re one of the world’s leading causes of blindness, and in severe cases can cause

03:47 elephantiasis syndrome - a disorder that causes extreme swelling due to the inability of the

03:52 lymph glands to drain, mostly affecting the legs.

03:55 The next parasitic worm has more aggressive tastes.

03:59 #9.

04:00 Hookworm

04:01 The Hookworm is a species of roundworm that is common in many countries around the world

04:04 - especially those without access to clean water.

04:07 Its larvae infects people both orally and through the skin, at which points it sets

04:11 up camp inside the human digestive tract for a feast.

04:14 Pretty similar to other parasitic worms - except the hookworm doesn’t want your food.

04:18 It wants your blood.

04:19 These worms latch onto the intestinal tract and start acting like a vampire, causing major

04:24 health issues for the unfortunate host.

04:26 If left untreated, it can cause abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, and most seriously

04:31 anemia that can result in weakness and other serious health conditions.

04:35 This worm kills up to 60,000 people a year.

04:38 The good news is, it’s vulnerable to many anti-parasitic medications, but it’s hard

04:42 to detect before it reaches maturity.

04:44 But it’s not the most deadly parasitic worm.

04:47 #8.

04:48 Whipworm

04:49 The whipworm is a soil-based parasite that infects over half a billion people worldwide,

04:54 and is mostly spread by contaminated soil and often eaten through fruits and vegetables.

04:59 The eggs hatch and take up residence in the large intestine.

05:02 While many cases are asymptomatic, those who have heavy infections can find themselves

05:06 seriously sick.

05:07 Not only do these worms wreak havoc on the digestive tract, but it can trigger more serious

05:11 illnesses like appendicitis that require emergency surgery.

05:15 Its most dangerous effect, though, may be on children.

05:18 Kids who are infected can suffer delayed growth and cognitive impairment, as well as suffering

05:23 from nutritional ailments.

05:24 Experts estimate this worm kills upwards of sixty thousand people a year, but like other

05:29 parasitic worms, it can be killed off with antiparasitic medication.

05:32 But the biggest challenge of battling these worms is preventing infections and treating

05:36 people before they progress to serious cases.

05:39 One worm makes its presence known with a name that says “terror”.

05:42 #7.

05:43 Dracunculus Medinensis, or the Guinea Worm

05:46 Translated as “little dragon of the Mediterranean”, the proper name of the Guinea Worm gives away

05:51 that this worm is a killer.

05:53 The female worms are among the largest worms that can infect humans, growing to up to thirty-one

05:58 inches in length - longer than many snakes as they slither around in the human gut.

06:02 It’s not surprising that they can cause excruciating pain.

06:05 They infect people through contaminated drinking water and are most common in rural areas of

06:10 Africa and tropical regions like southwest Asia and India.

06:14 Once embedded in the human body, the effects can be deadly.

06:17 These worms cause a secondary disease as the female worm tries to emerge from the body

06:21 through the skin.

06:22 The chemicals she releases can cause infections, nausea, blisters, and itching.

06:27 But if she fails to emerge and gets stuck in the body, the worm can cause arthritis,

06:31 paralysis, or severe swelling from the infection and resulting immune response.

06:35 To treat this, doctors look for a blister where the worm is going to emerge and then

06:39 use warm water to lure the worm out.

06:41 They then slowly pull it out and wrap it around a stick.

06:44 It can take several days to remove a full-sized guinea worm, followed by treatment with antibiotics

06:49 and bandages.

06:50 These next parasites don’t wait for you to consume them.

06:54 #6.

06:55 Blood Fluke

06:56 Everyone is scared of leeches, those predatory worms that latch onto your skin in water and

07:00 start sucking your blood.

07:01 But the Blood Fluke takes that nasty MO to the next level.

07:05 After spending part of their life in a snail host, they lurk in water and enter the skin

07:08 of humans and proceed to feed on their blood.

07:11 They can live for decades, and can remain asymptomatic for years.

07:14 But when things go bad, they go VERY Bad.

07:17 When they cause a series of infections called schistosomiasis, they can affect almost every

07:22 part of the body.

07:23 Their most serious symptom is swelling, which can cause long-term damage to glands and can

07:27 even cause liver failure if left untreated.

07:30 While the parasite can be treated with the same antiparasitic medications useful against

07:34 other worms, these parasites are particularly common in Africa and are estimated to cause

07:38 up to two hundred thousand deaths a year - making the blood fluke one of the deadliest parasites

07:44 worldwide.

07:45 The next parasite is much more visible - and much more painful.

07:48 #5.

07:49 Jiggers.

07:50 Any dog or cat owner probably knows how annoying fleas are - constantly jumping everywhere

07:55 and biting.

07:56 But that’s nothing compared to the sand flea, also known as the jigger.

07:59 These fleas are common in Central and South America and have arrived in sub-Saharan Africa,

08:04 and they have an parasitic tactic that can make every step miserable.

08:07 The smallest known flea, they lurk in sand and attach to people as they burrow head-first

08:12 into the skin, usually on the foot.

08:14 This causes swelling and lesions as the female swells up with eggs.

08:18 This is just the beginning of the problem.

08:20 It’s common for victims of jiggers to have dozens or even hundreds of them embedded in

08:24 their feet.

08:25 As the fleas die off, this can cause infections that result in pain, scabbing, dead skin,

08:30 and permanent deformation of the toes.

08:32 As pulling the fleas out can cause their bodies to tear and leave parts behind, jigger infestations

08:36 are treated by a doctor to carefully remove any trace of the attached flea and disinfect

08:41 the area - which can be a lengthy process.

08:44 The next parasite also makes itself way too welcome in the human body.

08:48 #4.

08:49 The Human Bot Fly

08:50 Flies usually do little more than buzz around you, making that annoying sound.

08:54 But dermatobia hominis, or the human botfly, has a particularly invasive method of reproduction.

09:00 Its eggs are carried by other insects like mosquitoes which bite humans, transferring

09:04 the eggs into the open wound.

09:06 They hatch there, and the larva wedges itself in the human skin, growing there and creating

09:11 a visible grub sticking out of the skin.

09:14 Disgusting - but not dangerous...usually.

09:16 The biggest danger the human botfly poses is infection, because when you see a grub

09:21 sticking out of your skin, what’s the first thing you do?

09:23 You try to pull it out.

09:25 That’s a mistake, because while the body breaks off and the grub dies, the head and

09:29 jaws attaching it to the body stay in place.

09:32 That becomes a vector for potentially deadly infections.

09:34 The best way to safely remove a botfly larvae without medication or professional help?

09:39 To suffocate it with a coating of petroleum jelly.

09:42 After a day, it can be removed with tweezers.

09:44 It makes sense that Australia would have deadly parasites - and the next one adds a killer

09:48 kick to a common pest.

09:51 #3.

09:52 Australian Paralysis Tick

09:53 Ticks are common parasites, jumping from animal to human and sucking blood.

09:57 While they’re usually easy to remove with tweezers because they stay on the outside

10:01 of the body, their main threat is as a vector for deadly diseases - including the potentially

10:06 lethal Lyme Disease.

10:07 But one tick down under poses a bigger threat - one that can kill quickly.

10:11 Not only can it cause allergic reactions, but it secretes a toxin that can cause neuromuscular

10:16 function to fail.

10:17 Within eight to twelve hours of injection, paralysis can set in and even cause respiratory

10:22 failure if it is allowed to progress.

10:24 While these reactions aren’t common, with only about twenty fatalities reported in Australia,

10:29 this tick is one of Australia’s most feared animals.

10:32 And in the land of the bird-eating spiders, that’s saying something.

10:36 The penultimate parasite is invisible - and deadly.

10:39 #2.

10:40 Brain-Eating Amoeba

10:41 Not a true amoeba but a tiny shapeshifting organism, this microscopic bacteria-eater

10:47 lives in bodies of warm freshwater.

10:49 That means that it can be lurking anywhere people want to take a dip - rivers, lakes,

10:53 wells, or even swimming pools that aren’t treated with enough chlorine.

10:57 While it doesn’t function like other parasites and feed on humans long-term, this organism

11:02 has one major impact on humans - it causes a rare, but almost invariably fatal brain

11:07 infection that can kill a healthy person in days.

11:09 And it has shown up in the happiest place on Earth.

11:12 One of the earliest cases that brought this parasite to the public's attention was when

11:16 a young boy died of the infection after swimming at Disney’s River Country waterpark.

11:20 The parasite enters through the nasal cavity, usually when swimming but also occasionally

11:24 through rinsing out the sinuses.

11:26 It travels to the brain, where it changes up its usual diet of bacteria and starts eating

11:31 the brain’s astrocytes and neurons.

11:34 Symptoms appear after an average of five days - and by then, it’s already too late.

11:38 While this parasite can’t be spread between humans, it soon results in headache, nausea,

11:43 a stiff neck, decreasing brain function, seizures, and eventually death.

11:47 But no parasite causes as much death as our

11:51 #1.

11:53 Malaria Plasmoidium

11:54 When you think about the deadly disease malaria, you probably think about mosquitos.

11:58 These biting pests do spread disease - but the actual cause of malaria is a single-celled

12:03 parasite called Plasmodium.

12:05 These protozoans enter the body through the mosquito’s saliva, and they infect red blood

12:09 cells.

12:10 The cells swell and burst, infecting the bloodstream - thus spreading to mosquitoes when they bite

12:14 a host containing the virus.

12:16 This makes it one of the fastest-spreading parasitic infections in the world, affecting

12:20 up to 600 million people a year.

12:22 And things can get bad for the unfortunate victims.

12:25 Malaria starts with simple symptoms including fever and chills, but some cases evolve into

12:30 something deadly.

12:31 Vomiting and severe sweating turn to anemia, seizures, and possible damage to the body’s

12:36 vital organs and bloodstream.

12:37 This can cause the victims to slip into a coma, suffer serious neurological issues,

12:41 and potentially die.

12:43 Several hundred thousand people die of malaria each year, most in the global south, and while

12:48 no vaccine is available, treatments are available to lessen the severity of symptoms.

12:52 The challenge is to outrace this fast-spreading parasite, which spreads as quickly as the

12:56 mosquito flies.

12:58 For more on a tiny organism that caused mass chaos, watch “Why Spanish Flu Killed Over

13:03 50 Million People - Deadliest Plague in Modern History”, or check out “13 Most Dangerous

13:08 Animals in History” for some larger predators.

docs.text:
00:00 In January 1975, editors and senior reporters  from The New York Times gathered inside the White

00:05 House for what was supposed to be a routine  Q&A. But things got interesting - fast. The

00:11 topic turned to the CIA and a mysterious  collection of reports known as The Family   Jewels. Would the public ever see them? President Gerald Ford didn’t mince words.

00:20 He looked the reporters straight in the eye  and said if those files ever got out - even   redacted - they would “blacken the eye of  every President since Truman.” They could

00:28 destroy America’s image abroad. That was all the bait reporters   needed. What exactly had the CIA been up to? “...Assassination… and that’s off the record!”

00:37 The room fell silent. But it was too late.  Off the record or not, the secret was out.   The CIA had allegedly been involved in killing  foreign leaders - and it was only the beginning.

00:47 Hold on to your tin-foil hats, we’re taking  a deep dive into the murky world of the CIA   in today’s episode of The Infographics Show. The mid-70s weren’t a good time for the CIA.

00:57 It was on the verge of imploding, thanks to  a number of scandals and a 693-page internal

01:02 report known as The Family Jewels. Within those  pages were admissions of illegal wiretapping,

01:08 surveillance of American activists and  journalists, assassination plots against   world leaders, and mind-blowing Nazi-esque human  experimentation. The document offered a glimpse

01:18 into the murky depths of CIA operations,  with the worst of it conveniently left out.

01:23 Meanwhile, Washington was still reeling  from the political earthquake of Watergate.   President Richard Nixon had dragged the CIA  straight into the scandal, weaponizing the

01:32 agency to sabotage and smear his opponents.  That abuse of power led to the now-infamous   break-in at the Democratic National Committee’s  headquarters inside the Watergate complex.

01:41 Nixon wasn’t the first president to bend the  rules - but he was the one who got caught.   And sometimes, that’s all that matters. On June 23, 1972, Nixon got on the phone

01:51 with CIA Director Richard Helms - a man who knew  where all the bodies were buried - metaphorically   and literally. The contents of that conversation  were later made public by Supreme Court order in

02:01 what became known as The Smoking Gun tape. With the Watergate scandal just beginning to   unfold, Nixon and Helms engaged in what Politico  later described as “gangsterly dialogue.”

02:12 Nixon seemingly threatened to blow the lid off  the JFK assassination if Helms didn’t help him   get out of the very tight squeeze he was in. Nixon talked about the CIA’s “Dirty Tricks.”

02:22 He was referring to the US’s support of death  squads and dictators, to regime change. He also

02:27 referred to “hanky panky” - generally thought to  have meant secret assassinations. This is what

02:32 the CIA called “Health Alteration,” “Executive  Action,” and “Termination with Extreme Prejudice.”

02:38 Looking for leverage, Nixon confronted CIA  Director Richard Helms with a loaded question:

02:43 “Who shot John?” - a thinly veiled reference  to JFK’s assassination. Then he drove the

02:49 point home. “Is Eisenhower to blame? Is Johnson to  blame? Is Kennedy to blame?... Is Nixon to blame?”

02:55 The CIA had a lot of skeletons in its closet… and  Nixon knew it. He was issuing a warning: If I go

03:01 down, you go down. He then told Helms, “I have  done more than my share of lying to protect you,

03:06 and I believe it’s totally right to do it.” What did Nixon know, what was he threatening   to leak? It doesn’t prove the CIA had  anything to do with JFK’s assassination,

03:15 but it’s certainly interesting. It’s  also evidence the CIA was indeed dirty.

03:20 So, when Ford replaced Nixon,  the CIA and by extension the US   government had a lot of image cleaning to do. Presidential aide and political behemoth,

03:28 Henry Kissinger, told the new President  that the CIA’s “clearly illegal” actions   would “raise profound moral questions.” The most  shocking actions, he said, if they all came out,

03:38 “the CIA would be destroyed.” Ford called a secret meeting with   his Chief of Staff, Donald Rumsfeld,  and his deputy chief, Dick Cheney,

03:45 to devise a plan of action. That’s what led to  the White House luncheon and subsequent moral   outrage across America and the rest of the world. The congressional investigations that followed,

03:55 led by Senator Frank Church, would reveal the  CIA had conducted over 900 “major projects” and

04:01 “several thousand” smaller projects - with 75% of  them never being reviewed “outside the agency.”

04:07 As former President Kennedy had warned, the  CIA was “out of control.” Church described   them as a “rogue elephant” whose actions were  often minimized or ignored by a pliant media.

04:18 But was the CIA being made a scapegoat for the  President and other powerful elements of what   journalists today sometimes call the “deep state?” Congressman Otis Pike of the House Select

04:27 Committee thought so. He explained, “The  CIA does not go galloping off conducting   operations by itself…without approval from  higher up the line.” He added, “The CIA never

04:37 did anything the White House didn’t want.” Running the world’s most powerful country,   and attaining global supremacy was never  going to be a wholly democratic process.

04:46 But as a so-called beacon of liberty,  the U.S. had to keep up appearances.  Still, President Harry Truman, who signed off  the National Security Act of 1947 that created

04:56 the CIA, didn’t intend to create a monster  - it was never intended to be a “Cloak and

05:01 Dagger Outfit.” The agency, Truman believed,  should keep the President informed on global   affairs, not running covert wars in the dark. But as Pulitzer Prize-winning author Tim Weiner

05:11 put it in Legacy of Ashes, Truman’s vision was  “subverted from the start.” And that subversion

05:16 began with the CIA’s roots - planted firmly in the  wartime Office of Strategic Services, or the OSS.

05:23 When the OSS shut down after World War II,  its most powerful minds didn’t just fade into

05:28 retirement. They resurfaced as the CIA’s founding  elite. Among them were Frank Wisner, a brilliant

05:34 yet ruthless strategist, and Allen Dulles Dulles would one day become the CIA’s most   controversial boss. He was the man who’d once  protected a wealthy Nazi businessman and major

05:45 war criminal, SS General Karl Wolff - the  go-between for Hitler and Himmler. Wolff,

05:50 who would later be accused of sending 300,000  Jews to Nazi extermination camps, was just one

05:56 of the high-ranking Nazis secretly shielded  from the noose at the Nuremberg Trials. Why?

06:01 Because it served US interests. But this wasn’t  exactly something you could tell the public.  So, fascists in Europe were secretly supported by  the US to sabotage the Communists. This resulted

06:12 in one of the CIA’s most secretive operations,  Operation Bloodstone. Wisner enlisted European

06:17 anti-communist refugees and, in some cases, former  Nazis, for what he said would be “psychological

06:23 warfare, subversion, sabotage, and…assassination.”  Some were offered the carrot of: Do your job,

06:29 and you can come live in the USA. Many were already living in those   communist nations. But that didn’t stop Wisner’s  team from launching covert missions. For years,

06:38 they parachuted into countries like Albania,  Poland, and Ukraine aiming to cause trouble   and form a resistance. It sounded daring on  paper - but in reality, it was a disaster. Most

06:48 operatives gathered little useful intelligence.  Many were captured. Some disappeared entirely.   Others turned out to be double agents. This was  all thanks to Soviet moles embedded in British

06:57 intelligence. The toll of these sabotage  missions was likely one of the reasons for   Wisner’s mental breakdown and death in 1965. Under the similarly covert Operation Gladio,

07:08 CIA- and NATO-backed anti-communist paramilitary  forces would later be accused of terrorism,

07:13 bombings, false flag attacks, and political  assassinations across Europe. These stay-behind

07:19 armies, often made up of far-right extremists  and ex-fascists, were implicated in torture   and massacres that continued long after the war. All these operations needed millions in covert

07:30 funding, money that was secretly laundered  from the Marshall Plan. All added up,   it was about $685 million - around  5% of the total Marshall Plan funds.

07:40 So, the CIA hired some very nasty men, including  high-ranking Nazi intelligence specialists.

07:45 One of them was Alois Brunner, an Austrian  SS Captain who was a major component of the

07:51 Holocaust. He sent tens of thousands of  European Jews to the extermination camps,   including women and children. He was a torturer  who caused people untold pain and would become

08:00 one of the most sought after Nazi war criminals,  and yet, he was given a pass by US intelligence.

08:06 He admitted long after the war that he was given  papers by US officials. He said he worked as a

08:11 driver for the US Army and later fled to Egypt  where he rented a room from a Jewish couple who,

08:17 according to the New York Times, he  said were… “quite nice people, really.”  The reason he was protected was because  he was working for the highly secretive

08:25 Gehlen Organization, which was headed by top  Nazi intelligence officer Reinhard Gehlen.

08:30 Known as “Hitler’s super spy”, Gehlen had been in  charge of Nazi intelligence on the Eastern Front,

08:36 making him a prize asset for the CIA. On September  20th 1945, Gehlen was smuggled out of Germany on

08:42 a plane headed for Washington D.C. To save his skin, Gehlen agreed to   work for Uncle Sam, but this came with  requests. He wanted his men from the war,

08:52 other high-ranking Nazis: thugs, torturers, and  executioners whose intelligence work for the US

08:57 was later said to be mediocre at best. Then there was Otto von Bolschwing,

09:02 the man who was responsible for expropriating  Jewish property during the war. Yet in the

09:07 1960s and 70s he was enjoying a corporate  career in the USA surrounded by neighbors   in the affluent suburbs. They had no idea the  guy who served them up barbequed frankfurters

09:17 had once hanged people from meat hooks. He was behind 1941’s Legionnaires' rebellion and

09:23 Bucharest pogrom, when Jews were taken from the  streets in Romania and tortured; their homes set

09:28 on fire, their synagogues burned to the ground.  Some were forced to write letters saying goodbye   to their loved ones… and then shot in the head. In the most disturbing story involving von

09:38 Bolschwing, on January 23, a large group of  Jews were taken to a slaughterhouse where they   were tortured and shot: men, women and children.  When their bodies were found, someone had stuck

09:47 a sign to some of them that read, “kosher.” After being granted US citizenship in 1959,

09:53 von Bolschwing became wealthy from working with  large corporations, later landing a job with the

09:58 United States Agency for International Development  (USAID). The CIA helped to whitewash his past,

10:05 but his past eventually caught up with him.  The Office of Special Investigation would   have deported him, but he was so ill he died  in a hospital in California in 1982, aged 72.

10:16 The CIA could do whatever it wanted. The senior  operations officer Tom Braden later admitted as

10:22 much, saying, “It could hire armies, it could  buy banks. There was simply no limit to the   money it could spend and no limit to the people  it could hire and no limit to the activities…”

10:32 Part of that endless stream of money went  toward what Frank Wisner proudly called   his Mighty Wurlitzer - a super secretive  program designed to propagandize Americans

10:41 and turn Eastern Europeans against communism. Wisner was behind the Radio Free Europe/Radio

10:46 Liberty, a CIA funded radio station that provided  pro-West, anti-Soviet content to communist

10:52 satellite states. He was also behind the hydrogen  balloons which floated high above the Iron Curtain

10:57 and dropped propaganda leaflets on the people  below. They dropped over 590,000 balloons that

11:03 carried 301 million leaflets, posters, books,  over the Iron Curtain to Czechoslovakia,

11:09 Hungary and Poland. This was done under the  cover of plausible deniability. None of it

11:14 could ever be traced back to the US government.  It was, after all, major political interference.

11:19 But not all propaganda came in the form  of leaflets and loudspeakers. Sometimes,   it was much more subtle. The Congress for  Cultural Freedom was a seemingly innocent,

11:28 intellectual movement that drew in peace-loving  minds like Tennessee Williams, John Dewey,   Arthur Schlesinger Jr., and Bertrand Russell.  But what none of them realized was that they’d

11:38 unknowingly become part of a global anti-communist  propaganda machine secretly run by the CIA.

11:43 The CIA led operations in which certain books  would be smuggled into the Soviet Union,   a project that lasted throughout the Cold War.  It’s thought about 10 million books got through,

11:52 one of the reasons why so many Russians  read the works of George Orwell,   the British journalist and novelist who wrote  the famous book about totalitarianism, 1984.

12:01 Orwell was also a critic of imperialism and  was often skeptical of left-right politics,

12:07 but it seems the CIA wasn’t interested in nuance.  They liked the fact he was scathing when it came   to Soviet Communism. So, they made sure one  of his most critical communism-based works,

12:17 Animal Farm, was smuggled into Russia en masse. Spreading the anti-communist message in Eastern

12:22 Europe was one thing - but selling it at home  in the U.S. took a different strategy. Sure,   much of America already viewed communism as a  threat, but a growing anti-imperialist movement

12:32 was starting to push back. Books like War is a  Racket (1935), written by the highly decorated

12:38 Marine General Smedley Butler, were fueling  the fire. And with lines like,“I spent 33 years

12:43 and four months in active military service  and during that period… I was a racketeer,   a gangster for capitalism” his words hit hard. This kind of rhetoric didn’t sit well with

12:53 the CIA - especially when it secretly  orchestrated coups in Iran and Guatemala,   toppling democracies in favor of U.S.-friendly  regimes. To cover their tracks and polish the

13:02 image of those new puppet governments, the agency  needed more than just boots on the ground. This   is where Wisner’s Operation Mockingbird came in. It certainly didn’t hurt that Henry Luce - the

13:12 owner of Time and Life magazine - was close  friends with C.D. Jackson, president of the   CIA front known as the Free Europe Committee.  According to Rolling Stone journalist Carl

13:22 Bernstein, one of the first to expose Operation  Mockingbird, Jackson wasn’t just an ally - he

13:27 was Luce’s “personal emissary to the CIA.” Journalists in the US, and some worldwide,

13:32 wrote stories at the behest of the CIA or  at least had their stories approved by the   agency. Without psychological warfare, the  rest of the work would have been impossible.

13:41 The CIA had a habit of silencing critics,  especially those who dared to expose America’s   darker dealings abroad. And in 1963, it  faced a major headache. A book was about

13:52 to hit the shelves - The Invisible Government  by journalists David Wise and Thomas B. Ross.

13:57 The authors pulled no punches. They exposed  the CIA’s role in engineering coups in Iran   and Guatemala - replacing democratically  elected leaders with dictators. The authors

14:07 claimed the so-called ‘freedom-loving’  institutions of the U.S. government were   just a smokescreen for a covert empire  fueled by dirty wars and secret deals.

14:16 They also pointed fingers at the CIA  for masterminding the catastrophic   Bay of Pigs invasion in Cuba and for  supporting violent operations in Vietnam,

14:25 Laos, and Indonesia - conflicts that  collectively killed millions of civilians.  The CIA Director at the time, John McCone, called  the writers in for a meeting and talked to Random

14:35 House, saying that there were parts of the  book that MUST be deleted. Publishers Random

14:40 House refused, so the CIA went to plan 2. It  said it would buy every single copy itself,

14:46 to which Random House said it  would just print a second edition.  Today, The Invisible Government is considered  the first serious deep-dive into the CIA’s

14:53 covert operations - shattering the carefully  crafted image of America as always the good guy.

14:59 For many, it was the first time they saw  past the patriotic propaganda and glimpsed   the secretive agency operating behind the scenes. Little did the writers of that book know the CIA

15:09 promoted art exhibits, symphonies, ballet,  theater, jazz and opera, if the work was

15:14 seen as being pro-US. Its gloved hands were  everywhere, including in Hollywood movies - one

15:20 of the major sources of pro-US propaganda. Declassified letters show that C.D. Jackson

15:25 was in regular contact with Carleton Alsop, a  CIA officer who worked undercover at Paramount

15:30 Studios. He was following in the footsteps  of his father, Joseph Alsop, a journalist   and columnist for The Washington Post, who  was also a covert CIA asset and operative.

15:40 In the letters, Carleton was told by Jackson to  write certain narratives into movies. In the film,   The Caddy, Jackson suggested “planting spectators  in the crowd watching a golf game.” He said these

15:50 spectators needed to be black. That’s because  the left of American politics, as well as many   African Americans, were saying blacks weren’t  being treated on equal terms in the US. The

15:59 CIA wanted to make it look like they were. Even  today, critics believe the CIA sometimes plants

16:05 seeds in movies to help the public think a certain  way, and it’s not always about foreign policy.

16:10 We now know thanks to the US’s Freedom of  Information Act, the CIA over the years influenced   a number of scripts to ensure the US and the CIA  were portrayed positively. According to research

16:20 by the Age of Information, the Pentagon and the  CIA together have quote, “worked behind the scenes

16:25 on over 800 major movies and more than 1,000 TV  titles.” This has included making script changes

16:32 in the James Bond franchise, the Transformers  franchise, as well as the Marvel and DC universes.

16:37 Surprisingly, the CIA and Pentagon also had  input in the America’s Got Talent TV show, Oprah,

16:43 and various documentaries by the BBC, PBS, and  the History Channel. Not so surprisingly, it had

16:49 a hand in the writing of Homeland, The Americans,  Zero Dark Thirty, Argo, and Black Hawk Down.

16:54 In the 90s, it even had a go at creating  its own show, “The Classified Files of   the CIA.” However, the pilot was called  “a masterclass in humorless propaganda.

17:03 The movie propaganda thing started with  President Dwight D. Eisenhower. In 1953,   he said in a secret letter, “The hand of  government must be carefully concealed,”

17:12 explaining that there would be “arrangements with  all sorts of privately operated enterprises in the   field of entertainment, dramatics, music, and so  on.” This was par for the course in dictatorships,

17:23 in China or the Soviet Union, but it wasn’t  really supposed to be part of a democracy.

17:28 Big Hollywood blockbusters tended not to show  the grim reality of US foreign policy back then.   Even small criticisms have been expunged  from films by either the CIA or Pentagon,

17:38 such as when a CIA torture manual had  to be taken out of Meet The Parents.  The CIA’s Allen Dulles was a huge James Bond  fan, and he knew that by telling stories that

17:47 made intelligence work look cool would influence  the world’s public. Indeed, Dulles had a special

17:52 relationship with Bond’s creator Ian Fleming. In declassified letters, it was revealed that the   CIA developed 007-style gadgets, similar to  those used in the many failed attempts to

18:02 take out Cuban leader, Fidel Castro. In these  secret communications, Dulles put pressure on

18:07 Fleming to portray the CIA in a positive light. But maybe one of the most startling instances

18:13 of censorship was in the movie The Hulk. This  was when the codename of a military operation

18:18 was changed from ‘Ranch Hand’ to ‘Angry Man’.  The reason being the former was the name for a

18:24 real covert operation. It was a U.S. military  campaign during the Vietnam War that dumped

18:29 millions of gallons of toxic chemicals - like  Agent Orange - across Vietnam and Laos. The

18:35 aftermath was catastrophic. Farmland was  destroyed, ecosystems were poisoned, and,

18:40 according to the Vietnamese government,  an estimated 400,000 civilians killed..

18:45 The CIA pushed the story that the  death and destruction from Agent   Orange was Soviet propaganda… It wasn’t. As for Laos, the CIA ran a Secret War there,

18:54 dropping more than 2 million tons (1.8 billion  kg) of ordnance on Laos during 580,000 bombing   missions - making it the most heavily bombed  country per capita in world history. The

19:05 Agency trained Hmong people to fight, and with Air  America, its secret airline, turned a blind eye to

19:11 or gained black money from heroin trafficking. The CIA secretly sponsored or subsidized over

19:16 1,000 books that were published and circulated  in the U.S. Under the direction of E. Howard Hunt

19:22 - one of the men behind the Watergate break-in -  the Agency also recruited writers from mainstream

19:27 outlets to pen glowing or damning reviews  depending on what narrative they wanted to push.

19:32 Hunt allegedly ordered a New York Times  writer to slam Edgar Snow’s book on China   for being too soft on the Communist regime. Incidentally, on his deathbed, Hunt made a series

19:42 of shocking recorded confessions to his sons -  implicating himself and others in a conspiracy to

19:47 assassinate JFK. He even drew a diagram explaining  how it all went down. Some called it a cash grab,

19:53 others claimed it was the truth finally coming  to light. The LA Times called it “inconclusive.”

19:59 But it definitely left people talking. Still, it was a funky time for conspiracy   theorists, and as you’ll soon  see, they had a lot of ammunition.

20:06 The CIA was never a big fan of alternative JFK  assassination theories. Which is why on April 1,

20:12 1967, director Richard Helms secretly  launched a campaign to smear critics of   the Warren Commission report using friendly  US journalists and editors. James Angleton,

20:21 the CIA’s counterintelligence czar, established  a secret group to spy on New Orleans District   Attorney Jim Garrison, the man who was  questioning the Warren Commission’s findings.

20:30 Declassified documents show that Angleton  called this his “Garrison Group.”   CIA memorandum 1035-960, which went out to all CIA  station chiefs, said to use “propaganda assets”

20:42 in the media to discredit Garrison and other  troublesome characters trying to say anything   other than Lee Harvery Oswald acted alone. Some  media subsequently called Garrison an egomaniac,

20:52 a KGB asset, or on the payroll of the  mafia. It’s not certain if this was   CIA influenced, but it’s certainly plausible. The CIA even had a man inside Garrison’s team.

21:03 His name was Gordon Novel, who is reported  to have been Garrison's chief of security,   while at the same time working for the  White House to destabilize Garrison's

21:11 operation. This kind of thing hardly inspired  confidence in the Warren Commission report,   one of the reasons the House Select  Committee on Assassinations later said

21:20 there was “probably” a “conspiracy” to  kill JFK - but it didn’t finger the CIA.  Then there was the US attorney Mark Lane, whose  JFK assassination book Rush to Judgment became a

21:31 best-seller and kicked off decades of skepticism.  He said most media wasn’t interested in his story

21:36 and publishers snubbed his work. He had no  idea why. Through Freedom of Information   requests he discovered both the CIA and FBI  had put pressure on publishers to ignore him.

21:46 He eventually went to a British publisher.  The book exploded and Lane was a marked man.

21:51 FBI agents went to his lectures and forwarded  their reports to the Warren Commission.  Some journalists refused to work with the CIA,  such as Wayne Phillips of the New York Times,

22:00 who said he was offered $5,000 a year to write  friendly narratives.The deal didn’t go through

22:06 because of complications. That was less than Keyes  Beech of the Chicago Daily News who was offered

22:11 $12,000 a year - about $120,000 in today’s money. Propaganda was incredibly important, but it wasn’t

22:18 enough. The CIA needed to be more hands on at  home in the USA, which fell under the domestic

22:23 spying program Operation Chaos. The agency  reportedly illegally spied on 7,200 Americans,

22:30 with about 300,000 civilians and 1,000 groups  in its index. This included journalists,

22:36 civil rights groups, women’s liberation groups,  socialists, communists, and anti-war groups.

22:41 The agency had a large file on Martin Luther King,  who’d become a major critic not just of racism,

22:47 but poverty and imperialism. He was really only  deemed a serious threat once he’d branched out

22:52 from civil rights, which was when even  left-wing media started criticising him.  In a declassified memo, a CIA officer  talks about King being assassinated,

23:01 stating that this would be problematic because  it might make him a “martyr.” He was right.   Years later, the House Select Committee  on Assassinations said there was likely a

23:10 conspiracy in King’s actual assassination, but  it didn’t believe it included the FBI or CIA.

23:16 What the CIA might have liked to  have done is modify King’s behavior,   and it just so happens the agency tried to  do that to Americans without their consent.

23:26 This brings us to mind control. In  European safehouses and across Asia,   powerful drugs were tested on people in an attempt  to brainwash them. But the CIA wanted to bring the

23:35 program home and test on what one memo called the  “weaker” or “less intelligent” members of society.

23:42 The infamous memos, the ones that survived  after the CIA took the unprecedented step to   destroy every single document concerned with  MKUltra, contain lines about making a person

23:52 commit an assassination or sabotage against  their “natural will.” But could you make

23:57 someone do something terrible and then make  it so they couldn’t remember anything? Or,   could you plant false memories? Documents show  this was a major pillar of the MKUltra agenda.

24:08 One of the men hired to make this possible was  Louis Jolyon “Jolly” West. West became well-known

24:13 as one of the psychiatrists sent to visit Jack  Ruby in prison after he’d shot Lee Harvey Oswald.

24:19 West was the first person to declare Ruby  delusional and psychotic, rendering anything   Ruby said the words of a madman. This was strange,  according to the journalist Tom O’Neil. Strange,

24:29 because O’Neil found documents showing  Ruby was fine prior to West’s visit.  West said Ruby had an “an acute psychotic break”  and “was now positively insane” which he said was

24:40 “unshakeable” and “fixed.” Psychiatrists have  since said it’s unusual for a sane 52-year-old

24:45 man with no history of serious mental illness  to completely lose his mind overnight…Well,

24:50 unless powerful drugs weren’t involved… In a sworn affidavit, West said that Ruby   believed all Jews in the US would be slaughtered  and Ruby’s name was top of the list. West then

24:59 claimed that Ruby hid under a table thinking  they were after him at the jail. According   to O’Neil’s book, Ruby claimed he could  hear the screams of his brother outside,

25:08 who was being tortured in the street. Ruby  believed this “pogrom” was ordered by Washington.

25:13 This came after half a dozen other psychiatrists  had found Ruby to be sane. So, the judge wasn’t

25:18 sold on West’s diagnosis. According to O’Neil,  the judge was also suspicious that West had   been sending applications to treat Ruby for a  long time. The judge ordered a second opinion,

25:28 having himself spoken to Ruby numerous times  and seen no signs of insanity. Ruby’s jailer,

25:34 Sheriff Bill Drecker, said the same. So, Dr. William Beavers went to visit Ruby.   He was surprised by what he saw. Ruby did seem to  be hallucinating and he was definitely paranoid.

53:33 which would not have looked good to the public. Time magazine later talked about how the disgraced   Challe landed by airplane in Paris looking  like a broken man. Despite JFK’s offer,

53:42 the French people were still crying out in  protest over how the CIA had tried to relieve   them of their leader. Admiral Pierre Lacoste  said outright that the CIA supported the OAS.

53:52 As Kennedy was already thinking about splintering  the CIA into pieces, the French press called the

53:58 agency a “state-within-a-state,” which was more  fuel to fire up Kennedy’s wrath. He had the power,

54:03 not the CIA and whoever the  CIA was taking orders from.  De Gaulle started firing his security  officers, the ones close to Dulles,

54:11 just as JFK was about to fire Dulles. Then  in 1962, as de Gaulle was still clearing out

54:16 suspected CIA friends in his government, he was  almost killed. With Algeria newly independent,

54:22 President Charles de Gaulle was driving down the  Avenue de la Liberation OAS in his government   issued car. OAS assassin Bastien-Thiry gave the  signal for the other assassins to open fire on

54:32 de Gaulle’s car. Five men in cars belonging to  the organization’s Commando Delta death squad,

54:38 lit up the street with submachine guns. 187 bullets were fired in the ambush - but

54:43 only 14 struck de Gaulle’s moving car. One  lodged in the headrest of the passenger seat,   inches from where de Gaulle had ducked his head.  One of the assassins swung out of a car door,

54:52 his submachine gun blazing. But somehow, de  Gaulle wasn’t hit. Two motorcycle officers   in his motorcade weren’t so lucky - they were  killed instantly. The car skidded, the chauffeur

55:02 spun it around and shot off down the road. T The assassins were later imprisoned and   Bastien-Thiry became the last Frenchmen  to be executed by firing squad.

55:11 De Gaulle later laughed about it, joking, “They  are such bad shots.” But the fun was over in 1970

55:17 when in his armchair while watching the news on  TV, a heart attack finally took him out aged 79.

55:23 So, did the CIA have anything to do with the  attempt on de Gaulle’s life? We don’t know,   but the evidence shows the agency and its shadowy  overlords in Washington would likely have quietly

55:32 celebrated had those assassins pulled it off. In 2015, the Guardian in the UK reported that the   CIA was indeed asked to help kill de Gaulle, but  under President Johnson after Kennedy’s demise.

55:42 The evidence was in files about to be released,  and Congress had been told. The CIA had twice

55:48 been approached after the failed coup  and asked by dissidents to help them.   The story said an “old soldier” was to wear  a poisoned ring on one of his fingers and

55:57 shake de Gaulle’s hand in what was to be “a  clasp...of lethal friendship.” The Chicago   Tribune said the documents didn’t make it clear  if the CIA went any further than “entertaining”

56:06 this option, or if Johnson was informed. On November 28, 1961, Dulles was given his

56:12 ceremonial send off at the brand-new CIA HQ  in Langley, Virginia. Despite his contempt,

56:17 Kennedy was outwardly kind, bestowing Dulles with  the National Security Medal. J Edgar Hoover was

56:23 in the audience, likely wondering where he stood  with Kennedy’s administration. Nothing was certain

56:28 for the old guard while JFK was at the helm. Dulles' invite list, the people he’d supported,

56:34 watched on with pride. This included the CEOs of  Chase Manhattan, General Electric, General Motors,

56:40 Coca Cola, DuPont, Ford, US Steel, Standard  Oil, IBM, CBS, and Time Life. He’d made US

56:47 multinationals a fortune with his neoliberal  maneuvering over the years. The doctrine was   that money always trickles down on the populace.  Maybe it did, but at great cost to many millions

56:57 of people a long way from the USA. When it was over, Kennedy flew away   in a helicopter. Dulles, watching from  a distance, waved, his face forlorn,

57:06 a beaten man… but he’d be back. He still had power, but he conducted

57:11 it from the shadows. Two years later, after  Kennedy took a bullet to the head in Texas,   Dulles was on the Warren Commission. A move which  is now regarded as a clear conflict of interest.

57:20 The Dulles era at the CIA had come to an  end - but the conspiracies, allegations,   and dark secrets didn’t fade. Instead, they  erupted into a supernova of suspicion that

57:30 would shadow the Agency for decades to come. Is the truth finally out, or are we only   scratching the surface? Drop your  wildest CIA theory in the comments.  Now you should watch, “CIA LEAKED DOCUMENTS That  SHOCKED the World.” Or check this video instead.

  • Video ID: sRavs-1HMoI

docs.text:
00:00 On January 5th, 2012, the following cryptic  message was posted in the paranormal section

00:05 of an infamous Internet message board. Hello. We  are looking for highly intelligent individuals.

00:11 To find them, we have devised a test. There  is a message hidden in the image. Find it,

00:17 and it will lead you on the road to finding  us. We look forward to meeting the few

00:22 who will make it all the way through. Good luck.  3301. And so would begin the most complex and

00:30 maddeningly difficult challenge that the Internet  had ever seen. While at first some wrote it off

00:35 as a clever marketing stunt, over the span of  the next ten years it would become increasingly

00:40 clear that it could be no such thing. But what,  then, could it be? Who, or what, was 3301?

00:47 Many speculated that the whole thing was a  recruiting tool for an intelligence agency

00:50 like the NSA, CIA, or MI6. Others believed that  perhaps it was a secret society or cult, but why

00:58 then the need for complex skills in steganography,  cryptography, mathematics and so on? And what was

01:04 the purpose? Where did it lead to, and how far  would it take those who followed the trail?

01:08 And to what end? Many would become obsessed with  finding out. Where individuals would fail,

01:14 groups would form, bringing their collective power  and expertise to bear on solving the puzzles.

01:19 But that always runs the risk of one individual  in the group going rogue with a discovery.

01:23 Based on recently leaked information that  appears to bear the correct PGP signature,

01:28 it would appear that at least one person succeeded  in solving the riddle of 3301. But who or what,

01:34 precisely, did they find? All that and more  today, right here in Dave's Garage. [Intro]

01:46 I'm Dave Plummer, a retired software engineer from  Microsoft going back to the MS-DOS and Windows 95

01:52 days, and today we're investigating the one of the  greatest technological mysteries that the world

01:56 had ever seen: Cicada 3301. It all began with that  simple JPEG image posted to the web. It claimed to

02:04 contain a secret message, but how, and where? The  file posted that day appeared to be a simple JPG

02:09 image, but hidden away within it was plain text,  easily extracted from the file with Unix "strings"

02:15 command. When run upon the image, it revealed  a messages string that contained a reference to

02:20 TIBERIVS CLAVDIVS CAESAR followed by text  that had clearly been scrambled by encryption.

02:25 But what kind of encryption? The reference to  Caesar implied that this was likely a simple

02:30 "Caesar Cipher", wherein each letter is offset by  some number within the alphabet, or in this case,

02:34 ASCII code. If offset by 3, then A becomes D,  B becomes E, and so on. A few iterations of the

02:42 cipher solver reveals that, sure enough, in the  3301 image each letter is offset by 4, and once

02:49 corrected, the result is a URL to an image hosting  site. Each step was getting slightly harder,

02:55 and this trend would continue until the challenges  became maddeningly obscure and difficult - and yet

03:01 some would persevere, even through the Mayan  alphabet, disappearing ink, ancient poetry

03:05 and cryptic ruins. Loading the linked image into  the web browser, we get an image of a duck. More

03:11 specifically, a decoy duck, and one that openly  admits to being a decoy at that: The text on the

03:17 message reads "Looks like you can't guess how to  get the message out". This text is actually our

03:22 one and only clue: combining guess and out to  yield the name of the outguess tool, a program

03:27 that is able to hide and retrieve information that  has been intentionally hidden within an image.

03:32 By changing a mathematically predictable set of  pixels by tiny subtle amounts, the tool is able

03:37 to encode data within an image that can't be  seen by the naked eye. As a contrived example,

03:43 let's say we decided to hide text in an image by  offsetting the blue value in every 131st pixel

03:48 up or down by one bit depending on whether  we were trying to store a one or a zero.

03:53 Because we're changing the least significant bit  of the color least sensitive to the human eye,

03:58 it's going to be entirely imperceptible in most  non-trivial images. And that's basically how

04:01 steganography hides data inside of an image in a  manner that's hard to detect. The outguess tool

04:03 applies a number of techniques to extract that  hidden data for you automatically. And indeed,

04:08 using the outguess tool we can extract a  character string from the duck decoy's image:

04:12 "Here is a book code. To find  the book, and more information,

04:16 go to https://www.reddit.com/r/a2e7j6ic78h0j/"   Apparently, the next stage of the clue was hidden

04:22 within the subreddit. The header contained a  numeric code of some kind and a picture of a

04:26 welcome mat. By applying outguess again, we would  receive perhaps the single most important piece of

04:31 information that 3301 would encode: it's public  PGP key. A PGP key is a private-public keypair.

04:40 Only the person with the private key can  generate messages that will have a signature

04:43 that matches the public key. Thus, you can  send the public key out freely and then anyone

04:48 at any point can use it to verify that a signed  message you later send out MUST have been signed,

04:53 with mathematical certainty, by whomever possessed  the original private key. Put more simply,

04:59 it's a foolproof manner of verifying that a  message really did come from a particular sender.

05:04 And it meant that from this point forward, no one  could pretend to be 3301. Only the person truly

05:10 in possession of the official 3301 private  key could send officially signed messages,

05:15 so it became impossible for anyone else to  impersonate 3301. A second image on the subreddit

05:21 also contained a steganographic payload that could  be extracted with outguess. The message read: "The

05:26 key has always been right in front of your eyes.   This isn't the quest for the Holy Grail. Stop

05:31 making it more difficult than it is. Good luck.   3301" The subreddit also contained encrypted

05:39 text messages, which were found to be a Vigenere  cipher, where 0 is A, 1 is B, 2 is C, and so on.

05:46 Decoding the text in the subreddit revealed  an ancient English tale by Thomas Bullfinch

05:50 on King Arthur and his quest for the Holy  Grail. The original subreddit message header,

05:55 when translated from Mayan, is the key to use with  the cipher. It all decoded to a phone number,

06:00 214-390-9608. When called, that  number played the following message.

06:37 Besides pointing out that the group's numeric  name was, in fact, prime in its own right,

06:41 this message sent investigators on a quick hunt  to find two more prime numbers hidden somewhere

06:46 in the image. A few quickly noted that the  height and width of the image, 509 and 503,

06:52 were also prime numbers. Combined and multiplied  with 3301, they would yield the number 845145127.

07:00 With a .com appended, it led them to a website  that contained an image of a Cicada and a

07:05 countdown timer. With outguess applied to the  cicada image, the follow message was revealed:

07:10 "You have done well to come this far.   Patience is a virtue. Check back at 17:00

07:16 UTC. 3301" Everyone following the puzzle was now  confronted with the same fate: waiting for the

07:19 countdown timer to expire. It was apparently a way  to start the race anew, with everyone at the same

07:19 point. What happened next would solidify 3301's  reputation as an international group and largely

07:20 eliminate the possibility that this was all a  ruse created by a single hacker. Was the image

07:21 of the cicada important? An interesting fact about  cicadas is that while there are over 1500 species,

07:27 they generally gestate underground for periods of  7, 13, or 17 years. The most popular theory has

07:34 been that this is to eliminate competition amongst  cicadas by reducing the frequency of how often

07:38 their various gestation periods would overlap with  each other. Others have advanced the theory that

07:44 a prime gestation period would overlap less often  with predators that emerged on a 2-year, 3-year,

07:48 or 4-year cycle, for example. Regardless of what  evolutionary pressure led to the prime gestation

07:53 periods, it is likely that this characteristic -  the prime numbers associated with the gestation

07:58 period - is why 3301 has used cicada imagery.  Primes are incredibly important to cryptography.

08:21 When the countdown timer reached zero, the  image changed. It now contained 14 pairs of

08:26 GPS coordinated scattered around the globe:  California, Australia, Hawaii, South Korea,

08:32 Poland, and many more. In each of those  physical locations could be found a poster,

08:37 in plain view, that contained an image of a  cicada and a QR code. The sudden appearance and

08:53 world-wide distribution of the posters meant that  at a minimum, cicada was a broadly distributed

08:58 group. Those who believed that 3301 might simply  be a few hackers in the basement now were faced

09:04 with the reality that at a minimum, 3301 had the  resources to make a physical appearance in 14

09:09 international locations within a reasonably short  time period. But how short? Assuming the posters

09:15 might last a week or two, they would have to  be all placed within that time limit. A careful

09:20 analysis of the GPS locations reveals that most  of the locations are within 90 minutes drive an

09:25 international airport, but this is true for most  urban centers. It also meant that the puzzle was

09:30 now going "off the grid", or at least offline.  To continue meant the solvers would have to

09:35 venture out into the real world. There were two  variants of the poster. The QR code on the poster

09:40 led to an image from which could be extracted  a riddle and taken as a whole they contained

09:43 new book ciphers and a curious admonition: "You've  shared too much to this point. We want the best,

09:50 not the followers. Thus, the first few there  will receive the prize. Good luck. 3301"

09:57 There was only one problem: the book ciphers  were plain enough except that the messages never

10:02 indicated to WHICH books the ciphers should  be run. The hunt was now on to find the very

10:06 books which would contain the encoded message. It  would take centuries to do so by hand in even a

10:11 modest library, but thanks to the power of the  internet and modern search, both were found in

10:16 reasonably short order. The first was found  to be Encyclopaedia Britannica, 11th Edition,

10:21 Volume 6, Slice Number 3. The second book was  even more obscure: though written by popular

10:27 author William Gibson, the book Agrippa was  only released in a book printed in disappearing

10:32 ink and on self-erasing 3.5 inch floppy disc  back in 1992...and no, I'm not kidding. The book

10:36 was literally printed on photosensitive paper,  whose pages, when exposed to light even a single,

10:42 would the fade to nothingness. The floppy would  entirely encrypt itself after a single use.

10:47 The result of these puzzles was a link to a page  on the web. But it was Tor link, meaning it was a

10:53 link to the Dark Web. The Dark Web, for lack of a  more thorough explanation, is largely encrypted,

10:59 secret, and unindexed. You generally don't surf  it, you go directly to it for a particular page.

11:04 The reasons for a page's existence on the dark  web range from a severe need for privacy to pretty

11:09 much every illegal activity imaginable. You can't  get there accidentally with a regular web browser,

11:14 in fact. You need special software such as the  Tor browser. The Tor link led to a message that

11:19 read: "Congratulations! Please create a new email  address with a public, free, web-based service.

11:26 Once you've never used before, and enter it below.  We recommend you do this while still using Tor,

11:32 for anonymity. 3301" It further explained  where to send the email, but shortly after,

11:37 the message was replaced the following:   "We want the best, not the followers."

11:45 Those who did so promptly received an email that  lead to a page that contained an image of artwork.

11:50 That artwork contained a message with a link that  purported to offer latecomers a second chance.

11:55 It also contained text that encoded another Tor  link, which, via a series of prime numbers and

11:59 other puzzles, ultimately led to an audio file,  known as a MIDI file. The musical contents of

12:05 the audio file seem unimportant, but the MIDI file  contents could be laboriously decoded to produce

12:10 the next message: "Very good. You have proven  to be most dedicated to come this far to attain

12:16 enlightenment. Create a gpg key for your email  address and upload it to the mit key servers

12:22 then encrypt the following word list." It also  provided a gmail address to send the encrypted

12:28 results to. Those who did so promptly were  provided with an interesting amonition by email.

12:33 "Each person who has come this far has received  a unique message encrypted with a unique key. You

12:40 are not to collaborate. Sharing your message or  key will result in not receiving the next step."

12:46 Those whom were selected were also provided  with a Tor link, this time to login page.

12:51 For the vast majority, as far as we know,  this is where the trail went cold.

12:55 Once month later, the following  message appeared on the subreddit.

12:59 "We have now found the individuals we sought.  Thus our month-long journey ends. For Now.

13:05 Thank-you for your dedication and effort. If  you were unable to complete the test, or did not

13:10 receive an email, do not despair. There will be  more opportunities like this one. Thank you all.

13:17 3301." A select few, however, received the  following explanation. In at least one case

13:23 it was leaked to the web, which is how we know  of its existence. "We are not a hacker group.

13:29 We do not engage in illegal activity, nor do our  members. If you are engaged in illegal activity,

13:35 we ask that you cease any and all illegal  activities or decline membership at this time.

13:40 We will not ask questions if you decline.  However, if you lie to us, we will find out."

13:47 "You are undoubtedly wondering what it is that  we do. We are much like a think tank, in that

13:53 our primary focus is on researching and developing  techniques to aid the ideas we advocate: liberty,

14:00 privacy, security." Next, it produced  three questions to be answered by email:

14:07 "Do you believe that every human being has  a right to privacy and anonymity?" "Do you

14:12 believe that information should be free?" "Do  you believe that censorship harms humanity?"

14:19 Nothing more was heard from 3301. That  is until precisely one year later, when,

14:25 on the anniversary of their original  image, the next puzzle appeared.

14:40 Make sure you're subscribed to my channel for  part 2, where we learn about the encypted Liber

14:50 Primus and the man who ultimately cracked  the 3301 puzzle and was offered a chance

14:51 to join. All next time, right  here in Dave's Garage.

15:12 [https://votiro.com/blog/image-steganography-example-how-i-created-an-attack/]

docs.text:
00:00 Chernobyl is a city in the Ukraine located about 56 miles (90 kilometers) northeast of

00:04 the capital, Kiev.

00:05 Prior to the disaster and a subsequent evacuation, it was home to around 14,000 people.

00:11 At that time, it was still part of the Soviet Union.

00:14 The city was the location of the first ever nuclear power station to be built in Ukraine,

00:18 but on the 26th of April, 1986, disaster struck when Reactor No. 4 exploded.

00:25 The town is still home to around 690 people, although it’s now somewhat of a ghost town,

00:30 with animals occupying many abandoned buildings.

00:33 Most of the residents live about 19 miles (30km) from the disaster site in the Chernobyl

00:37 Exclusion Zone, and surprisingly, international tourists flock to the area.

00:42 But what exactly happened in Chernobyl?

00:44 That’s what we’ll find out today, in this episode of the Infographics Show, What Caused

00:49 the Catastrophic Nuclear Accident in Chernobyl?

00:52 As CNN reported in 2016, if you visit Chernobyl now as a tourist, you’ll be taken on a strict

00:57 guided tour of what was once a busy, if not small, city.

01:02 Photographs show a place that has been frozen and overgrown, a kind of spooky remnant of

01:06 a town where people once lived and worked, and where kids played on the now unused ferris

01:11 wheel.

01:12 The explosion at the nuclear plant is rated as the worst nuclear disaster in the history

01:16 of the world.

01:18 Radioactive dust was sent far and wide, transported by winds as far as Sweden.

01:22 The number of deaths directly related to the initial explosion is thought to be about 31,

01:27 although the WHO reports that a further 50 deaths happened later as a result of massive

01:32 exposure of radiation on the day.

01:35 These deaths were mostly workers and rescue workers.

01:37 Two people died as a result of injuries suffered because of the blast of the explosion.

01:42 The WHO further states that around 4,000 deaths in total can be attributed to radiation exposure

01:47 because of the event.

01:49 On the day of the disaster, thousands of people were exposed to high levels of radiation,

01:54 with the WHO saying these people are at high risk of having cancer in their lifetime.

01:59 Even the millions of people that lived miles away from the site in other parts of the then

02:03 Soviet Union, were exposed to low levels of radionuclides ( or atoms that contain excess

02:08 nuclear energy) and they too are more at risk, regarding cancer.

02:13 On top of that, many of those displaced suffered financially and psychologically, especially

02:18 because some were never given sufficient information regarding the danger they had been exposed

02:22 to.

02:23 According to recent reports, areas at least 19 miles (30 km) away from the accident site,

02:28 are mostly radiation free, although some lakes and forestland are no-go areas or are at least

02:33 restricted to the public.

02:35 “In most areas the problems are economic and psychological, not health or environmental,”

02:40 said Dr. Mikhail Balonov, a radiation expert and the scientific secretary of the Chernobyl

02:46 Forum.

02:47 So yes, this is now a tourist spot for those who want to see what a ghost town looks like.

02:51 We looked at blogs written by travelers who have visited the exclusion zone.

02:55 One of them wrote that when she was invited, she thought it was a joke, thinking like many

02:59 people that visiting such a place was too dangerous.

03:02 She wrote that in the absence of people, the area has once again become home to wandering

03:06 bears, wild horse, deer, foxes, wolves…and dogs, lots of stray dogs.

03:13 While you are told not to touch things, or eat or drink while on the tour, the radiation

03:17 levels are checked by your guide throughout the visit.

03:20 “I felt like I was walking through a horror themed park,” she said of an abandoned kindergarten,

03:25 saying dolls were still hanging around.

03:27 Anyway, you get the picture, let’s now talk about what happened on that fateful day.

03:31 Ok, so according to the World Nuclear Association, this is how it went down.

03:35 We will try and explain it as clearly as we can, because it’s not all that simple if

03:39 you don’t work as a nuclear power engineer.

03:41 The workers at Chernobyl reactor 4 were performing a test to see if the turbines could provide

03:46 enough energy to keep the coolant pumps running if there was a loss of power, and if they

03:51 could keep them running until the emergency diesel generator kicked in.

03:55 They’d done this test before, but the tests had been unsuccessful.

03:58 They turned down the reactor to 25 percent of its capacity, but a problem arose when

04:03 the power plummeted to one percent.

04:05 They then tried to increase the power, but what ensued was a massive power surge.

04:10 The reactor’s emergency shutdown failed.

04:13 One engineer had wanted to abort the test but was told by a senior to carry on.

04:17 The reactor then became even more unstable.

04:20 This caused considerable pressure, and according to one step-by-step report one engineer witnessed,

04:25 “the 1.5 ton (350 kg) blocks atop the fuel channels of the Upper Biological Shield began

04:30 jumping up and down and you could feel the shock waves through the building structure.”

04:35 What did he do then?

04:36 Of course, he ran for it, down a series of steps to report what he had seen to others.

04:41 The pumps failed, there was no water flow, and the reactor started to make loud noises.

04:45 As another website tells us about the sudden increase in power, “A peculiarity of the

04:49 design of the control rods caused a dramatic power surge as they were inserted into the

04:54 reactor.”

04:55 Hot fuel combined with cool water, created a mass of steam that couldn’t escape and

04:59 caused lots of pressure.

05:00 This lifted a 1,000-ton lid and here we have the start of the radiation leak.

05:05 Air got into the reactor and caused a graphite fire.

05:08 A second explosion happened when hydrogen was formed by hot water steam contacting zirconium.

05:14 This was a much bigger explosion than the first, and it threw debris everywhere.

05:18 Power went out, except for battery-powered lighting.

05:21 The air was filled with dust.

05:23 One man died, and his body was encased in all the debris.

05:27 Burning fuel started fires everywhere and radiation was cast into the atmosphere.

05:31 All the internal phone lines went down, and workers fled from the scene.

05:35 Firefighters arrived, apparently unaware of the danger they were in due to the radiation

05:39 leak.

05:40 One even joked about it, saying, “There must be an incredible amount of radiation

05:44 here.

05:45 We’ll be lucky if we’re all still alive in the morning.”

05:46 He was kidding, but he wasn’t far off.

05:49 As one woman explained, the next day she found out there had been a fire, but the kids still

05:53 played, they went to school, people still milled around in the street, even though she

05:58 said, “All the roads were covered in water and some white liquid.

06:02 Everything was white, foamy.”

06:04 She added that she wasn’t told about the danger of radiation, stating, “About radiation,

06:08 that radioactivity was escaping, there was not a word.”

06:12 The reactor was filled with water, but then flooding was a problem.

06:15 After that, for days, thousands of tons of clay, sand, boron, and dolomite, were dropped

06:21 by helicopter into the burning reactor to quell the fire, but also to try and prevent

06:25 the spread of radiation.

06:27 For 10 days, a large amount of radioactive substances pervaded the air, most of it falling

06:32 as dust into nearby areas, but smaller particles spread far and wide carried by the wind.

06:37 We all know what happened next.

06:39 We should add that there are numerous scientific theories as to exactly what happened that

06:43 day, and this is just a basic summary of the most widely held belief.

06:47 Hopefully, something like this never happens again.

06:50 So, would you ever consider visiting Chernobyl?

06:53 Tell us why or why not in the comments.

06:55 Also, be sure to check out our other video called Russia vs the European Union - Who

06:59 Would Win?!

07:00 Thanks for watching, and, as always, don’t forget to like, share, and subscribe.

07:04 See you next time!
