00:00 The middle class has been sterilized. Most people think the collapsing birth rate

00:04 is just about money. Couples need two incomes just  to survive, and adding children feels impossible.

00:09 They're wrong. The biggest forces

00:11 driving birth rates down aren't war, climate  change, or even the economy. They're bureaucracy,

00:16 safety regulations, and planning decisions.  The real crisis hasn't even started yet…

00:22 And almost nobody is talking about it. When the boys came marching home from war,

00:26 they got busy… in more ways than one. After  World War II, there was a massive boost to the US

00:31 infrastructure and economy. The high of surviving  the war made a lot of people feel like the time

00:36 was right to have kids. And many kept having them.  The birth rate continued to stay relatively steady

00:41 during the 1950s. But the Baby Boom couldn’t  last. It started to decline in the 60s,

00:47 dipping from an all-time high of 25.3  per 1,000 people to 14.76 in 1978.

00:54 And it just kept dropping.

00:56 As of 2026, the birthrate  currently stands at 11.96,

01:00 the lowest in over 70 years, but still  far from the worst in the developed world.

01:05 France is currently at 10.76, while Japan is  at 6.96, well below the replacement level.

01:11 People just aren’t having kids.

01:13 While the United States population isn’t  dropping yet, many people are looking at

01:17 the trends and wondering just how bad the  fallout will be. After all, the US is on the

01:21 verge of the biggest retirement wave in history  as the Boomers all age out of the job market.

01:26 So who’s going to replace them?

01:28 Across the United States, we’re already seeing the  fallout of declining birth rates in the form of

01:33 empty buildings. Chicago is ground zero for what  people are calling the “Ghost School” phenomenon.

01:39 Regions don’t have enough kids to fill all  the seats and buildings they’ve dedicated to

01:42 the next generation. A March 2026  study by the Manhattan Institute,

01:47 found that at Frederick Douglass Academy High  School - built to seat over 1,000 students - only

01:52 27 students were currently enrolled. This  wasn’t an isolated case. Across Chicago,

01:58 255 schools were identified as underutilized,  with 145 being more than half empty.

02:05 Now, municipalities are facing  some difficult decisions.

02:08 Maintaining staff for half-empty schools is  expensive and pointless, and many schools sit

02:12 on valuable real estate. So districts are  choosing to close schools, repurposing or

02:17 selling the land and redistributing the students.  This is most noticeable in elementary schools.

02:23 Young students being shipped off to new schools,  disrupting their education and friendships. But if

02:28 there aren’t enough students, the district isn’t  going to keep operating it out of good intentions.

02:33 But this might be just the  prelude to a much bigger problem.

02:36 The problem isn’t just people choosing not to have  children - it’s that those who do aren’t having

02:41 nearly as many as they used to. Large families  used to be commonplace, to the point where it was

02:46 a regular staple of TV shows and movies. It wasn’t  just entertaining, it was aspirational for many.

02:52 Today, it might as well be science fiction.

02:55 The idea of an America hostile to large families  started gaining traction when a mom-blogger and

03:01 activist, Bethany Mandel, described the  strange catch-22 she found herself in.

03:06 She tried to sign her family up for a community  center membership. Mandel and her husband have 6

03:11 kids and the family membership only had space for  up to 4 kids. It wasn’t that the institution was

03:16 actively trying to exclude large families, they  just didn’t expect to have to accommodate them.

03:21 It’s the same story in cities across  America.Many parents think about how

03:25 the system often feels to punish  them for having larger families.

03:29 And ironically, it’s all in the  name of keeping the kids safe.

03:33 For all the talk about how this is a terrible  time to have kids, the truth is it’s never been

03:37 safer to be a child in many ways. Mortality from  childhood diseases including cancer is decreasing,

03:43 kidnappings - which peaked in the 80s - are way  down - and deaths from accidents have decreased

03:48 as well. This is partially because of  increased safety measures all around.

03:52 But those improvements have also made  raising a large family much harder.

03:56 Having a kid doesn't just mean another mouth  to feed. It means buying specialized equipment,

04:01 baby-proofing your home, and  often upgrading your car.

04:04 Every new baby means another crib, another  car seat and eventually, another bedroom.

04:09 Raising a child up to the age of 18  hovers around $300,000 in the US today.

04:14 Over 10% of that goes to the first year,  when the child is at their most vulnerable.

04:19 For many large families, it was common for the  new kid to be born just over a year after the

04:23 previous one. "Three under three" sounds like  a nightmare to many parents today. Every new

04:28 baby means another layer of safety. And in some  cases, it isn't just about buying the equipment.

04:33 It's about having a home that's actually big  enough to accommodate a fast-growing family.

04:37 But big cities are making that impossible.

04:40 The inflation in the housing market means  that single-family homes in the suburbs

04:44 can easily reach $500K for a starter home.  It’s more like a pipe dream than an attainable

04:50 goal to many. That leaves millions deciding  that it’s just easier to rent permanently,

04:54 even if it means that a majority of  their paychecks go to the landlord.

04:58 But even on that front, it’s not easy to  find the perfect place to grow a family.

05:02 Because family-sized apartments  are disappearing altogether.

05:05 Any apartment building above 3 stories is  required to have 2 separate staircases.

05:10 In the event of a fire or another disaster,  no one is cut off from an exit. Sadly,

05:15 this was a building code born in tragedy.  A century old rule that effectively removes

05:21 the center of any building and forces long  narrow hallways. What’s left is a thin ring

05:26 of space along the windows. That works  fine for studios and small one-bedrooms.

05:31 Anything bigger becomes a problem.

05:33 The most sought-after apartment in New York  City at the moment is the 3 bedroom setup.

05:37 It’s almost an essential if a  family wants to have multiple kids.

05:41 But big apartments aren’t big business.  Thanks to the fire code, and profit margins,

05:45 it’s much more appealing to divide the  building into as many units as they can.

05:50 The result is a housing market  that wasn't built for families.

05:53 In New York City’s large new buildings, 1 bedroom  units outnumber 3 bedrooms by roughly 10 to 1.

05:59 So to no one’s surprise that rates for larger  apartments have skyrocketed by 7% in the fourth

06:04 quarter of 2025 alone. Brokers describe  the hunt for an affordable three-bedroom

06:09 as close to hopeless. The few that reach  the market disappear into bidding wars.

06:14 It’s not the only problem facing parents.

06:16 If there’s one area where having  multiple children has become onerous,

06:20 it’s the vehicle. Most 4 door  vehicles are equipped for car seats.

06:25 For most families, that will be  fine, even if they have 2 kids.

06:28 Once it gets larger than that, things get tricky.

06:31 Three children families weren't even  considered large during the Boomers' time,

06:35 but now the infrastructure  simply isn’t there for them.

06:38 Only a handful of the top 50 vehicles on  the market - including the Toyota Sienna,

06:42 the Honda Pilot, and the Volkswagen Atlas - are  equipped to hook up 3 car seats in the back seat.

06:47 Three car seats seems unlikely unless  the family has kids in quick succession.

06:51 It’s all down to safety.

06:52 But some say it’s gone too far.

06:55 Many people associate car seats with babies and  toddlers, but you’d be surprised by how many

07:00 states regulate things. In New Jersey, typically  seen as one of the most safety-minded states,

07:05 strict regulations are in place that keep many  kids in boosters far longer than expected.

07:09 Up until the age of 2, children must be in  rear-facing car seats with a 5 point harness.

07:15 But even up to the age of 8, kids are required  to be in forward facing seats or boosters.

07:20 The lack of room for three car seats  in the back seat doesn’t sound like

07:24 a big issue when you think that it’s  just babies and toddlers using them.

07:28 Having three kids in five years is pretty rare  today. But it’s a much bigger concern when you

07:33 need to have space well into childhood.  Suddenly, the prospect of buying a whole

07:37 new car to accommodate a growing family seems  imposing. Or they put off having another child.

07:43 It’s the Minivan Tax.

07:45 And it’s having a real impact.

07:47 Studies show that since 1977, the surge in laws  raising the ages for car seat use have actively

07:53 depressed births in these states. When a woman has  2 children of car-seat age in one of these states

07:58 with stricter regulations, they’re 0.73 percentage  points less likely to have a third child. That

08:04 means a reduction of around 8,000 births per year.  Overall, there have been approximately 145,000

08:10 fewer births since 1980. And this process has only  sped up. 90% of the decline has been since 2000.

08:18 It’s getting harder to have a large family.

08:20 That’s why many people are opting out.

08:22 But even if we fixed every zoning law  and every car-seat regulation tomorrow,

08:27 there'd still be another problem. People  have to meet each other in the first place.

08:31 In the past, people had no choice but to  get out there and meet people in person.

08:35 Dating was done by introducing yourself  to someone at school or a public event,

08:39 arranging a public date, and  seeing how you connected. But now,

08:43 people are able to form connections and end  them without ever seeing someone in person.

08:48 It’s all thanks to that magic  little rectangle in our pockets.

08:51 Smartphones mean that everyone has access to  dating apps at all times. For many people,

08:56 forming connections or rejecting them  is as simple as swiping left or right.

09:00 And that’s meaning a lot less fun… for everyone.

09:03 There’s been a significant decrease  in sex overall. American adults are

09:07 now having sex around 9 fewer times per  year, down to only 54 as compared to 63.

09:13 But these numbers are heavily driven by  married couples. For young people who

09:17 have never had the chance to date offline, it  can be hard to find the right person to form

09:21 connections with and get that cycle started.  Life becomes a series of missed connections.

09:27 And even for those who do find the right partner,

09:29 life becomes a game of Netflix  and Chill… minus the chill.

09:34 Life is full of distractions now, and  the smartphone is a double-edged sword.

09:38 Every minute of every day, we’re  besieged by information, notifications,

09:42 and flashy offers for entertainment. While  previously a couple might have come home,

09:46 enjoyed each other’s company, now they’re in  their own world even when they’re together.

09:51 They might be a couple, but they each  have their own tailored algorithm.

09:54 That’s often more powerful than sexual attraction.

09:57 It’s becoming a crisis… and  governments are taking notice.

10:00 South Korea has one of the world’s lowest  birthrates, coming in at 6.69, well below

10:06 replacement level. This is due to many of the  same reasons as the United States, including a

10:10 tech-heavy culture. But it also relates to the  incredibly competitive academic and workplace

10:15 atmosphere in the country. People often spend the  vast majority of their time grinding for success,

10:20 leaving them little time to court a  partner. Many of the factors that play

10:23 a role in the United States, like high  housing prices, are even more extreme.

10:28 It’s led many analysts to consider the fast slide  in the birthrate to be an existential threat.

10:33 The government is running out of options.

10:35 So they’re throwing money at the problem.

10:37 Back in 2022, South Korea had the world’s  lowest fertility rate, 0.78 children per woman.

10:44 That’s barely a third of the 2.1 needed  to guarantee replacement-level population.

10:49 With an aging population and a looming pension  crisis, the government wanted to invest heavily

10:54 in encouraging young people to consider  family a critical part of their future.

10:58 Over $200 billion had been invested in  programs aimed at boosting the birth rate.

11:02 But would any of them get  to the root of the problem?

11:05 Some of the new initiatives included more than  doubling the monthly allowance for new parents,

11:10 from 300,000 won to 700,000,  around $500 each month. By 2024,

11:16 that had increased to 1 million won or  $770 dollars. Companies were encouraged

11:21 to hold “baby fairs” advertising their  products to new and potential parents.

11:25 It was South Korea’s fertility Hail Mary.

11:28 It didn’t work.

11:30 The birthrate kept sliding. And if  you ask the people on the ground,

11:33 the government is throwing money at nothing,  because they keep on sabotaging themselves.

11:37 South Korea is still relatively hostile  towards unconventional families,

11:41 with most benefits only being available to  traditional male-female couples who have children.

11:46 That makes this a process  with many failure points.

11:49 For some people, having a baby still seems  like a joyous, spontaneous event. But they’re

11:54 quickly awakened to the other side. It’s a  massive life-changing decision that comes with

11:59 incredibly heavy financial costs and strategic  decisions that you don’t get to opt out of.

12:05 For many couples, there’s a series of  events that need to take place first.

12:09 First you get out there and you date, then  you find the right partner. Then you both

12:13 get settled in your careers to the point where you  can afford to have a kid. Only then do you start…

12:19 Assuming time doesn’t catch up first.

12:21 The boomers and Gen xers can’t understand  why the new generations don’t follow suit,

12:26 but the fact is, the world they grew up in no  longer exists. One of the reasons big families

12:31 were possible back then was because there was  a traditional family structure. Dad worked a

12:36 hard but steady full-time job, often the same  one for 40 years. Mom stayed home and looked

12:42 after the growing brood. But today, only 20% of  families have a stay-at-home parent, with those

12:47 being heavily concentrated in rural areas. In  cities, two-income households are almost essential

12:52 even without kids in the picture. A two-income  household ups the money, but drastically alters

12:58 the logistics, creating big gaps of time  where neither parent might be available.

13:03 The world has changed and it’s the  family unit that’s feeling the effect.

13:07 It’s easy to blame the economy for the  declining population. It’s an issue,

13:11 but it’s not the root cause. Rules and  regulations have essentially been the

13:15 deathknell for the larger family. One child  seems like a massive milestone in life,

13:19 2 seems like a huge undertaking. Three seems  like an insurmountable mountain to climb.

13:24 For most couples, they’re not going to  strap on their mountaineering equipment.

13:27 They’re just going to sit down at the  base and be happy with what they have.

13:31 The declining population rate is a serious crisis,

13:34 but how bad could things be without  any births? Watch “ What if No Babies

13:38 Were Born for a Year” to discover the  horrifying truth. Or click on this video.

00:00 Over just the last 6 months, the job market  has changed dramatically. Again, back in the

00:05 good old days of 2024, all workers had to worry  about was ghost jobs, quiet firing, job washing,

00:11 career cushioning, invisible overtime, application  black holes, resentism, digital downsizing,

00:16 compensation compression, burnout attrition, and  when all else fails, good old-fashioned rolling

00:21 layoffs. But today, the job market is dealing  with a whole new set of trends. And don't worry,

00:26 they come with a whole fresh list of dumb  corporate buzzwords. New economic data, if we are

00:32 allowed to believe that anymore, is revealing some  stark realities about the ways that people are

00:36 finding a job, keeping a job, and progressing in  a job. Unfortunately, as you have probably already

00:41 guessed, a lot of these changes are throwing young  workers, and in particular, young men, out of the

00:46 frying pan and into the fire. For the first time  ever, unemployment amongst young male college

00:51 graduates is the same as non-graduates. The share  of unemployed people entering the job market for

00:56 the first time is the highest it has been since  1988 and job mobility has effectively frozen. Now,

01:01 I know what you might be thinking. All things  considered, the unemployment rate still looks

01:06 pretty good, right? Well, that might actually be  part of the problem. And if all of this wasn't

01:11 bad enough already, there is now a good chance  that art history majors are earning more than

01:16 you are. So, ever since you found out about  AI, you've learned that your computer science

01:20 degree is actually a complete joke. New college  graduates are facing one of the most challenging

01:25 markets for entry-level jobs in a decade. It's  just like getting the first job. That's so hard.

01:30 I've tried to apply for jobs for like a year  now and just like most places like don't get

01:34 back to me or they just like say no. I make fun  of my college degree all the time cuz I'm not

01:39 self-conscious. Realize it wasn't worth it. Even  though society deems it as a great accomplishment.

01:43 I'm about to call my school up and say that this  degree that I spent four years trying to get four

01:50 years was a waste of money. There is a funny but  not totally inaccurate anecdote amongst business

01:56 analysts that if you want to find an industry  that's about to have really bad job security

02:00 then just look where all the Ivy League grads  are going. For a while that was oil and gas

02:04 companies before the 1980s oil crisis. Then it was  outsourcing operations before the Asian financial

02:09 crisis. Then early technology before the do crash.  finance before the global financial crisis and now

02:15 over the most recent decade it's been big tech  paying huge salaries to talented graduates early

02:19 in their careers. Now obviously there is a lot of  hindsight here. Nothing can boom forever and of

02:25 course a lot of young graduates from top schools  are going to try to find a job that pays them as

02:29 well as possible if for no other reason than to  start paying back that tuition. The problem is

02:35 that everybody else sees these growing industries  where people can make good money earlier in their

02:39 career and they try to get qualifications to  move into those roles too. But no industry can

02:44 boom forever. And by the time most people catch  up, they find themselves overqualified for a role

02:48 that doesn't exist anymore. For the last 10 years,  the story has been that everybody getting laid off

02:53 from their factory job should just learn to code.  But before that, it was everybody should go and

02:58 get an MBA. According to the Graduate Management  Admissions Council, 2022, right after the.com

03:04 crash was the all-time peak of people enrolling  in post-graduate business school in the hopes

03:09 that it would boost their stalling careers.  According to the numbers today, it looks like

03:13 that well-intentioned but ultimately flawed advice  may be going to college at all as the unemployment

03:18 rate is now the same between graduates and  non-graduates. After this data went live,

03:22 there were several articles concluding that this  signifies the end of the higher education payoff,

03:27 which is probably a bit of an oversimplification  for the sake of hyperbole. This is absolutely a

03:33 concerning trend, but there are two important  details you need to understand about it before

03:37 you go canceling that college admission. The first  is that if both of these groups have the same rate

03:42 of unemployment, that doesn't necessarily mean  that the earnings advantage of college is gone.

03:47 Looking for a job as a qualified engineer is  normally going to be better than looking for

03:51 a job as an unskilled laborer. So even though the  same share of these two groups may be out of work,

03:55 the earnings of the college graduates is still  higher. Also something I feel I need to repeat

04:01 as often as I can, the unemployment rate is a  really narrow statistic that people pay far too

04:06 much attention to as a singular data point. To  count as unemployed, you need to be out of the

04:11 job and actively looking for more work. Today,  according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics,

04:16 about 72% of people with a bachelor's degree  or higher qualification are actively working

04:20 or looking for a job. That number is falling every  year, which we will address soon. But it's still

04:26 significantly higher than the 56% of high school  graduates who are actively engaged in the labor

04:31 force, and it's even worse for people who didn't  graduate high school. But they are getting more

04:35 involved. And again, we will get to why soon. For  now, what you need to remember is that even though

04:40 this particular statistic looks bad, and don't get  me wrong, it is bad, you are still more likely to

04:45 have a job and have a higher paying job with a  college degree. But that's still not the whole

04:51 calculation. Degrees are not free. And a lot of  people are realizing that lifetime earnings are

04:55 great and all, but sometimes a little bit of money  early in life with no debt is better than more

05:00 money later in life with big repayments the moment  you are handed a piece of paper. The trend is that

05:04 every year the math is looking a little bit worse.  And that is something that should be carefully

05:09 considered for any investment with a 40 or 50year  payoff period. But that's just the statistical

05:15 details that you need to understand about this  graduate unemployment problem. The second and

05:19 much more important point is that this only  applies to men. The unemployment gap for graduate

05:25 women is lower than it has been historically,  but is still pretty wide. And it's actually

05:30 been growing at the same time the gap for men has  been disappearing. And the question is why? Well,

05:36 this strange difference actually reveals a lot  about other recent trends in the job market. So,

05:41 it's time to learn how money works to find out  how it's all changing. Again, this week's video is

05:46 sponsored by Cape. Cape is a privacy first mobile  carrier that gives you premium nationwide service

05:52 without tracking your data, selling it, or storing  it longer than necessary. Traditional carriers

05:57 build profiles on you, who you call, where you  are, and what you do. Cape does none of that.

06:03 They don't even ask for your name or address  to get started. And what really sets them

06:07 apart is their cryptographic SIM protection. Your  number is secured with a 24word recovery phrase,

06:12 similar to how you'd protect sensitive digital  assets. Honestly, what got me was how they handle

06:17 SIM swaps. Instead of relying on some call center  agent, Cape gives you full control over your

06:22 number. If you don't have the key, no one does. No  resets, no override. It's a level of security that

06:28 finally feels built for how things work today.  And if you're into privacy tools, there's more.

06:33 Encrypted voicemail, real-time threat blocking at  the signal level, and a partnership with Proton

06:37 that lets you bundle on services like ProtonVPN  Plus for just a dollar. Cape is also trusted

06:42 by security leaders at OpenAI, Crowdstrike, and  more. If you're ready to take your mobile security

06:47 seriously, check out cape.co/sim swap. And you  can use my code how works 333 to get 33% off your

06:54 first 6 months of Cape. To switch to Cape, visit  cape.co/gipcape. Another subtle but extremely

07:01 important change that has been recorded in the  job market is the changing payoff for job hopping.

07:06 We've mentioned multiple times that workers who  are overly loyal to their company statistically

07:10 earn significantly less over their working careers  when compared to those who hop jobs for promotions

07:15 or pay bumps. But that has changed and over the  last year the benefit has all but disappeared.

07:21 Now a little bit of that is because wage growth  is just slowing down overall. But a larger trend

07:26 is that the job market is encouraging staying put  and doing absolutely nothing. Nobody is hiring.

07:32 Nobody is leaving their job. Nobody is pushing  for a promotion. And nobody is doing anything

07:36 that could open them up to the next round  of layoffs. According to industry reports,

07:41 some people are even avoiding new jobs that could  be considered career advancements so they can

07:45 stay with a company in a role where they are past  probation and feel less at risk of being let go.

07:50 This is also benefiting people in less boom and  bust careers like those who went and got an arts

07:56 degree. Generally, these people go into their  fields because they are genuinely passionate about

08:00 it over people who are chasing a lucrative career.  They generally take less career risks and hold

08:05 on to roles that they become extremely proficient  at, which makes them harder to replace than random

08:09 business and commerce graduate number A3113. This  is not the best strategy in good times if all you

08:16 care about was making money. But it gave them a  head start on what everybody is doing right now,

08:20 which is holding on to their job for dear life.  This trend of people holding on to the rules has

08:24 its own buzzword because of course it has its own  buzzword, and it's called job hugging. Overall,

08:30 it's not a great sign when combined with the  less than stellar new jobs data, but it is

08:35 the logical response by all parties dealing with  increased uncertainty, which is where we get back

08:40 to this growing gap between young men and women  in the workplace. There is a lot to unpack there,

08:45 but there are three key differences driving this  trend. The first is the push to equalize gender

08:50 balance in certain roles, but not all roles.  The push has been toward getting women into

08:54 male-dominated fields that require a college  degree, like STEM and business management,

08:59 but not as much the unskilled fields that are also  dominated by men, like the trades and labor roles.

09:04 Women in STEM has been a big focus of government  programs, corporate initiatives, and school

09:08 enrollments for decades at this point, and it's  been highly successful at opening up the field

09:13 to more talent. This means that men are competing  with a wider base of competition than they would

09:17 have in the past. And the simple fact is that  there are only so many of these jobs to go around.

09:22 But at the same time, the men in roles that don't  require a college degree haven't had the same

09:26 increase in competition. This isn't a new trend.  Before the pandemic shook up a lot of this data,

09:31 male college grads had an unemployment rate of  around 5% while their non-graduate peers had an

09:36 unemployment rate of 6%. Female college graduates  at the same time had an unemployment rate of

09:41 around 3%. But their non-graduate peers also  had 6% unemployment, so the gap was much wider.

09:48 Now, it's important to point out that there  have been similar programs to try to get men

09:52 into historically women dominated graduate fields  too, especially nursing, age care, and elementary

09:57 school teaching. But overall, they have been  less successful. Now, there are a few reasons

10:02 for this. If we were being completely honest with  one another, there is still a stigma around this.

10:07 A woman landing a role as an engineer or office  executive is seen as empowerment where a guy

10:12 becoming a nurse is still the butt of the joke  and an elementary school teacher is the target

10:16 of suspicion and raised eyebrows. It absolutely  should not be like this and it is getting better

10:22 but it's silly to pretend it doesn't exist. The  second reason is that historically these roles

10:27 have not paid as well and men have generally  been attracted to more lucrative careers

10:31 either because they need to support a family or  simply because that's what they valued. The job

10:36 market has changed faster than those cultural  expectations, which is why men seek out more

10:40 typically prestigious jobs. This current gap is a  reflection of that reality. Safe, stable jobs like

10:46 nursing are doing really well in a bad time thanks  to an aging population while we are on the tail

10:51 end of trendy jobs that would have made a lot of  money in a better environment. This also explains

10:55 why unemployment amongst non-college educated  men has been pretty stable because construction,

11:01 the trades, and other semi-skilled jobs have been  pretty stable between increased home construction

11:05 and infrastructure. You can also see the beating  they took after construction slowdowns from the

11:09 global financial crisis, which were not nearly  as bad for their college educated peers. Now,

11:14 these differences hurt women in the workforce,  too. When women do go into these trendy fields

11:19 like technology, they actually tend to do  worse when it comes to downsizing. A study

11:23 on the recent round of tech layoffs sweeping the  industry found that women accounted for 44% of

11:28 job losses while only representing 28% of the  workforce. Now, the companies obviously didn't

11:33 release comprehensive data on why they chose  to lay off who. But generally, there are three

11:38 explanations for this. The first is that these  companies may have hired evenly, but they still

11:42 segregated genders within different departments,  hiring more women for jobs in HR, marketing,

11:47 corporate culture, and internal development. These  are coincidentally the first departments to get

11:52 cut in downsizing. The second explanation is that  in some ways cultural expectations work for men.

11:58 They are seen as a bread winner supporting  a family where the #girl boss is more likely

12:02 to land on their feet. This is another example  of something that employers should clearly not

12:06 be doing. But women are consistently judged more  harshly in high performing roles compared to men.

12:12 Unfortunately, this often happens particularly  from other women who disproportionately work in

12:17 departments like HR, which can have a lot of sway  over layoff decisions. The third crude explanation

12:22 is that hiring practices that targeted a diversity  objective over just hiring the best person for the

12:27 job favored people who would underperform compared  to their peers. So, when performance-based layoffs

12:32 were conducted, these people were more likely  to be below the cutoff. It's no secret that a

12:37 lot of the cultural forward companies have built  a hard 180 on a lot of these initiatives in the

12:41 last year. Now, I am sure you can probably tell,  but I am trying to be really careful about sidest

12:46 stepping the whole culture war rabbit hole here.  But it's still important to acknowledge these

12:51 realities when looking at these issues because  even though it shouldn't, it will have a big

12:55 impact on everybody's career. One of the best  things to do with this information is to use it

12:59 to your advantage. Despite the stigma, one of the  safest groups from trouble in the job market are

13:04 men in previously female-dominated fields. Fields  like healthcare already have a low unemployment

13:10 rate, and men often find it particularly easy  to get these roles because of the practical

13:14 realities that they can more easily do a lot of  the physical work these roles involve. This was

13:19 dubbed the glass elevator effect all the way back  in 1992 in a University of Texas article. It found

13:25 that men often found it much easier to progress  in these roles. And even though initial salaries

13:29 were lower compared to male-dominated fields,  after accounting for the higher chance of career

13:33 progression, the lifetime earning shifted back  into their favor. Now, obviously, don't pick a job

13:38 because of some video on the internet. Healthcare  and teaching are no joke, but also don't let some

13:42 business school douchebag talk you out of it  because chances are you will end up earning more

13:47 than them. Genuine professions like this are also  more reliant on performance compared to office

13:52 politics. Go and watch this video next to find  out how we forgot what professionalism even means

13:56 in the modern workplace. And don't forget to like  and subscribe to keep on learning how money works.

docs.text:
00:00 Chaos has erupted in Iraq as a gang of bloodthirsty ISIS commandos attack the US Embassy.

00:05 Wielding assault rifles, improvised explosives, and lethal machetes, they lead a cunning assault

00:11 that takes the guards by surprise and puts the diplomats and embassy staff inside at

00:15 risk of a terrible fate.

00:17 But just when things start looking hopeless, salvation arrives: An elite thirty-man platoon

00:22 swoops in, routing the attackers and putting them down with some well-placed shots from

00:27 their assault rifles, while another among their numbers lays down a hail of suppressing

00:31 fire with his M240 bravo.

00:34 The day is saved by this crack team of US military operatives, but all this raises one

00:39 question: Was that the Marines or the Army?

00:41 You might have heard the terms ‘Army’ and ‘Marines’ used interchangeably in

00:44 movies or on TV, but the Marines and Army are two entirely different entities.

00:49 Heck, they’re not even in the same military branch!

00:52 Whether you call them Jarheads, Devil Dogs, or Leathernecks, there’s a lot more to the

00:56 USMC than you probably know.

00:58 So let’s give our boys in scarlet and gold a Semper Fi, an OORAH, and plenty of yummy

01:04 crayons, as we find out exactly what makes the United States Marines different from the

01:07 regular army.

01:09 There are way more differences than you think!

01:11 With over a million members serving in active duty, the US has one of the largest militaries

01:16 on the planet, divided into six distinct branches.

01:19 There’s the Army, the Navy, the Air Force, the Coast Guard, the Space Force (yes, really),

01:24 and, of course, the United States Marine Corps, or USMC.

01:28 Most of the time, it’s pretty easy to deduce the general function of each military branch

01:33 from its name alone; the Air Force, for example, specializes in aerial warfare.

01:37 Then there’s the Navy, which wouldn’t be out of place patrolling the seas in large,

01:41 heavily armed ships.

01:42 The Marines don’t feel quite so obvious - From name alone, you might correctly assume

01:47 they conduct missions at sea.

01:49 But hold on, isn’t that what the Navy’s for?

01:52 Yes, but that’s because the Navy and the US Marines often work hand in hand, with the

01:57 Marine’s primary job being conducting amphibious operations- something no other branch of the

02:01 US military can do.

02:03 The missions the US Marines are sent on typically involve landing on a hostile piece of beachfront

02:08 property, and kicking the current proprietors out- permanently.

02:12 But you’ll also find Marines hundreds of miles inland- doing the same job you’d expect

02:16 the Army to do.

02:17 Sounds confusing right?

02:19 Don’t worry, when you break it down it makes much more sense.

02:22 The Army’s purpose is acting in defense of the United States, typically by completing

02:26 missions that take place primarily on land against hostile forces that have acted against

02:31 the national security interests of the US.

02:33 So, the Marines are, in essence, the Army for the Navy.

02:38 Or, if you prefer to think of it like this, you can imagine them as a smaller and more

02:42 pinpointed hybrid of both these branches - with the training and equipment to conduct missions

02:47 on land and at sea.

02:49 While Marines need to be prepared for any type of mission, wet or dry, the Army is only

02:53 tasked with duties that take place on solid ground, although it’s not uncommon for the

02:58 different specialized branches of the US military to work together collaboratively.

03:02 Joint operations like these are vital for securing objectives that call for the skills

03:06 of multiple different branches of the military.

03:09 In the case of the Marines, being a force that can operate from both land and sea, its

03:13 members can assist other military units in missions that require getting personnel from

03:18 sea to land where they may not have been previously trained to do so.

03:22 But the Marines’ other specialty is their role as a quick reaction force, United States

03:27 Marines are often referred to as ‘the tip of the spear.’

03:30 They consist of combat-ready specialized units that are trained to respond to urgent situations

03:35 and conflict operations wherever and whenever necessary.

03:39 Marine Expeditionary Units must remain prepared for combat at all times and are among the

03:44 first to respond to dangerous situations.

03:46 However, Marines aren’t meant to conduct heavy combat operations on their own- they

03:51 don’t even have tanks anymore.

03:53 This is where the Army comes in, with the Marines acting as a fast, agile, and flexible

03:57 quick-reaction force, and the Army bringing the big guns right behind them.

04:01 Although the two forces undergo different types of training, there is often room for

04:05 overlap between the Army and the Marines, and their capabilities can even complement

04:09 each other.

04:10 That being said, even though all Marines are trained to engage in amphibious warfare, very

04:15 few in the US Army are.

04:17 Most Army units are assigned a specific terrain or type of warfare to specialize in.

04:22 These can include airborne or mountainous infantry or even the famed US Army Rangers.

04:27 This is by far one of the hardest specialties to achieve, but doing so will result in a

04:31 soldier serving in the United States Ranger Regiment - an elite special operations unit

04:37 famous for conducting missions deep within enemy territory, amongst severe adverse conditions.

04:42 Meanwhile, all Marines are considered amphibious troops- but lack the type of training that

04:47 a US Army mountain division might have, for instance.

04:49 When it comes to who out of the Army or Marines is better equipped, it’s definitely the

04:54 former.

04:55 The US Army has consistently been the first of the two to receive rollouts of newer weapons.

04:59 Take the M4A1 carbine, for example.

05:02 This assault rifle is a shorter version of the M16, capable of both semi-automatic and

05:06 automatic fire.

05:08 While it’s now used by both forces, the Army was the one equipped with it first, long

05:12 before the Marines eventually adopted the weapon.

05:14 This also applies to newer weapon add-ons and attachments such as optical sights, lasers,

05:20 and hand grips.

05:21 We’ve seen this recently with the M4, as the Picatinny rails on the weapon’s receiver

05:25 and handguards make it compatible with various attachments.

05:28 This includes the M203 under-barrel grenade launcher, which is widely used by the US Marines.

05:34 Meanwhile, the Army is adopting the M320 as its primary grenade launcher, which can be

05:39 fired as a stand-alone firearm or mounted to other weapons like an M4.

05:44 The point is, the Marines do get their hands on all the fancy new firearms and attachments

05:48 eventually, it just tends to be much later than the Army.

05:51 A further difference between the Marines and the US Army is their flags and iconography.

05:56 The US has several separate flags that are each designed for specific branches of the

06:00 military.

06:01 The flag of the US Army was originally designed with the seal of the US War Office, as well

06:05 as the words ‘United States Army,’ their star emblem insignia, and the year 1775 emblazoned

06:12 over a white background.

06:13 1775 is the year in which the US Army was officially established, making it the oldest

06:18 branch of the United States’ vast military.

06:21 The official motto of the US Army is ‘This We’ll Defend’ and has been ever since

06:26 they played a pivotal role in gaining independence for the US during the Revolutionary War.

06:31 The branch has an impressive service record, being involved in nearly every major armed

06:35 conflict that the US has been a part of, either domestically or overseas.

06:40 This includes both World Wars, as well as the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.

06:44 Meanwhile, the flag representing the Marine Corps has changed numerous times over the

06:48 years, largely due to it being a part of the US Navy for so long before becoming its own

06:53 distinct entity.

06:54 In fact, the modern-day incarnation of the Marines’ flag did not see use until as recently

06:59 as the twentieth century.

07:01 Their official insignia is the Eagle, Globe, and Anchor, which are all present on the current

07:06 iteration of the Marine Corps flag.

07:08 First adopted in 1955, this flag features a globe intersected by an anchor, with an

07:13 eagle standing on top of the globe with its wings spread and a ribbon in its beak.

07:17 The flag also bears the Latin phrase ‘Semper Fidelis,’ the official motto of the United

07:22 States Marines, which has become something of a legendary phrase amongst its members.

07:27 Translating to ‘Always Faithful,’ and frequently shortened to “Semper Fi,” it

07:32 can often be heard being yelled, cheered, or used as a greeting among current and former

07:36 Marines, intended to remind them of their close commitment to their comrades and nation

07:41 both.

07:42 But enough sweating the small stuff.

07:43 Let’s talk about size, duties, and operational structure.

07:47 The US Army is split into three distinct units: the Army, the Army Reserve, and the National

07:52 Guard.

07:53 As well as engaging in warfare on battlefields outside of the US, the Army also has a responsibility

07:58 to protect America domestically, meaning in times of national crisis or even invasion,

08:03 you’d be more likely to see the US Army on United States soil, while the Marines handle

08:08 things in foreign territory.

08:10 Compared to the Army, there are also a comparatively small number of Marine Corps personnel in

08:14 service.

08:15 As of 2020, there were over 180,000 Marines actively serving, with a further 32,000 in

08:21 reserves, compared to the over 450,000 active duty soldiers in the US Army, 325,000 in reserves,

08:28 and almost 177,000 active personnel in the National Guard.

08:32 These reserve forces operate in extremely similar manners across the Army and the Marine

08:36 Corps; in the case of the Army Reserves, they provide additional troops and support to the

08:41 regular Army, with many reservists serving in their spare time.

08:45 For the Marines, their reserves are expected to be ready to leave civilian life and join

08:49 their fellow Marines in combat assignments or assist in national emergencies should the

08:53 need arise.

08:55 Given that they are a smaller force that operates with fewer service members than the Army,

08:58 it’s no surprise that the Marine’s main recruiting slogan is ‘the Few and the Proud,’

09:03 emphasizing that they only accept the highest caliber of troops.

09:07 Engaging in operations on both land and sea, Marines can be found stationed at military

09:11 bases on land and aboard warships.

09:14 Marines are often tasked with protecting US naval bases, as well as the Navy’s warships

09:19 and other areas of national interest that are located near coastlines.

09:23 Members of the US Marine Corps also have a particular responsibility that the Army does

09:27 not have: They’re charged with protecting United States embassies on foreign soil.

09:32 Being the only part of the US military with this duty, the Marine Corps has its own specific

09:36 sub-group that deals with providing the heightened levels of security required for guarding American

09:42 embassies: the Marine Corps Embassy Security Group.

09:45 Another key factor that differentiates the Marine Corps and the US Army is their training

09:50 programs.

09:51 Basic training for new recruits in the US Army is roughly ten weeks long and is normally

09:55 followed up by Advanced Individualized Training, where soldiers are given additional training

10:00 to prepare them for their future specialties we mentioned earlier, whether that be a specialty

10:05 in certain environments and terrains, or specific tactics.

10:08 According to some – although certain members of the US military will disagree on this - Marine

10:13 boot camp is generally considered to be more mentally and physically challenging compared

10:17 to the Army’s basic training program or that of other US military services.

10:22 Lasting around twelve to thirteen weeks, approximately 40,000 Marine hopefuls undergo this training

10:27 every year.

10:28 Beforehand, they have to be screened, have their overall health assessed, and must pass

10:32 a fitness test in order to begin their training.

10:35 Any recruits that fail this physical examination will go on to receive individual, personalized

10:40 attention and additional training until they can pass and enter the Marine Corps.

10:45 While these processes are similar in timeframe, each training course differs based on the

10:49 routes each prospective candidate decides to specialize in.

10:52 In either case, both the Marines and the Army expect all those who enlist to complete their

10:57 basic recruitment training before they are permitted to advance into specialization training.

11:02 Where successful Army recruits go on to Advanced Individualized Training schools after their

11:06 basic training, Marine hopefuls are enrolled in Military Occupational Specialty schools.

11:11 Both the Marines and Army also receive higher education training.

11:15 Annapolis, Maryland, is the home of the US Naval Academy.

11:18 This is a university dedicated to training both male and female officers, referred to

11:23 as midshipmen, over the span of four years.

11:25 Full tuition costs are sometimes even covered if a candidate enters active duty with the

11:30 Marines directly after they graduate.

11:32 Both the Navy and Marines receive graduates from the Naval Academy, given that the Marines

11:37 operate under the Navy.

11:39 Meanwhile, over in Quantico, Virginia, you’ll find the United States Marine Corps Officer

11:44 Candidates School.

11:45 This one is slightly different, instead of offering a four-year degree course, it provides

11:49 potential candidates with either two six-week courses or the same thing condensed into one

11:54 ten-week version.

11:55 These are usually attended by those enrolled in commissioning programs aimed at college

11:59 students and graduates who have previously completed degrees prior to enlisting with

12:04 the Marines.

12:05 Any midshipmen who complete the program are entitled to receive a commission as a second

12:09 lieutenant; this will often see them placed in command of a platoon consisting of 16 to

12:14 44 soldiers, including two or more rifle squads.

12:17 Meanwhile, the Army has the United States Military Academy located in West Point, New

12:22 York.

12:23 Much like the US Naval Academy, it provides Army recruits with a separate four-year course,

12:28 one designed to prepare these students for active service following their graduation.

12:31 Also, much like the aforementioned Naval Academy, West Point will grant free tuition to anyone

12:37 who enters active military duty upon the completion of their degree.

12:40 The Army’s equivalent of the Marine’s officer training program is their own Officer

12:45 Candidate School in Fort Benning, Georgia.

12:47 This school also offers courses specifically for college graduates, and after they have

12:52 completed a vigorous twelve week course, these graduates will also be awarded the rank of

12:55 Second Lieutenant, only within the United States Army instead.

12:59 So, while their training might be different, and the courses for enlistees will also differ,

13:04 the ways in which the Marines and Army recruit and teach their prospective soldiers follow

13:08 a similar pattern.

13:10 After all, if it ain't broke, don't fix it.

13:12 Speaking of similarities between the two, the US Army and Marine Corps also share many

13:16 organizational elements when it comes to basic unit structure.

13:20 A platoon normally consists of three to four small squads of between 25 and 50 troops and

13:25 is usually commanded by a lieutenant.

13:27 The Army and Marines both organize their soldiers into large companies, which are typically

13:32 made up of three to four platoons.

13:34 These are then further split up into squads, and then fire teams.

13:38 Although these can vary depending on mission requirements, a typical fire team will consist

13:42 of only four members, sometimes even fewer.

13:45 Among these are an automatic rifleman, a grenadier, another rifleman, and a designated fire team

13:51 leader.

13:52 The role of the leader is to ensure that the other members of the fire team are operating

13:55 as a cohesive unit, with the rifleman acting as the primary asset for both the US Marines

14:00 and the Army.

14:01 A typical Marine Corps rifle platoon contains three rifle squads.

14:05 Each squad is led by a sergeant who has three fire teams under their command.

14:09 Then, every one of these smaller fire teams is led by a corporal, who oversees the automatic

14:14 rifleman, assistant automatic rifleman, and rifleman.

14:17 In some cases, a fire team leader will be equipped with an M16 assault rifle that has

14:21 an M203 grenade launcher attachment, allowing him to act as a quasi-grenadier.

14:25 A platoon of the US Army, however, will normally contain squads with fewer troops despite their

14:32 greater overall number of active duty personnel.

14:35 Sergeants or staff sergeants are normally the ones assigned to lead rifle squads, as

14:38 well as fire teams consisting of about four soldiers.

14:42 Army fire teams have a team leader present, and their composition can vary but typically

14:46 includes an automatic rifleman, a grenadier, and another rifleman.

14:50 One of the riflemen in each Army squad is also sometimes designated as the marksman,

14:56 specially trained to engage targets with precision fire.

14:59 In each of the Army’s platoons, given that their fire teams are much smaller, there are

15:02 usually enough troops to form an additional fire team: the infantry weapons squad.

15:07 This squad contains fire teams that are proficient in the use of the M240B machine gun and the

15:13 Javelin missile system.

15:14 The organization of these two military branches’ troops is not perfectly identical, however,

15:19 as an Army platoon will typically have a radiotelephone operator and a medic on duty.

15:24 By contrast, Marine platoons have a radio transmitter operator and a corpsman, although

15:29 these troops essentially fulfill the same functions.

15:32 The Marine Corps and US Army’s platoons also operate under the orders of commanders

15:36 who are in charge of entire companies and battalions.

15:40 These commanding officers also have heavy weapon elements at their disposal, such as

15:44 a Mortar Section.

15:45 Naturally, neither the soldiers of the US Army nor the Marines are made to occupy the

15:49 same rank or position for the entire duration of their active service.

15:53 The specialization options that are offered to both can extend well into their military

15:58 careers, should troops seek to progress and further develop their skills.

16:02 For example, one of the more challenging options that US Army soldiers can pursue is airborne

16:07 qualification, which requires a soldier to undergo a three-week course in parachuting.

16:12 This also applies to soldiers who wish to join the aforementioned Rangers, although

16:16 success isn’t guaranteed here.

16:17 This elite unit of the Army, and mainstay of plenty of action movies and Call of Duty

16:23 games, is so prestigious that they require members to graduate from a specific Ranger

16:27 School or be selected by the Ranger Assessment and Selection Program.

16:31 Or, should a soldier also be trained as a sniper, by being selected for and graduating

16:36 from a specialized sniper school.

16:38 There are also additional specialization options for US Marines who are looking to advance

16:43 in their military career.

16:45 Marines can compete to become scout snipers, who, as you can imagine, provide accurate

16:49 long-range fire support for infantrymen on the ground.

16:52 Then, there’s the Reconnaissance Marines and Force Recon Marines.

16:56 These sub-divisions are designed to track down enemy forces and then relay their locations,

17:01 troop numbers, and activities back to commanding officers.

17:04 Although the two branches have their differences, in ideal military operations, they can work

17:08 in unison to ensure that the US Military achieves even its most challenging objectives.

17:13 And to avoid that wrath being directed towards you, make sure you don’t ask a former Marine

17:19 what unit he served in during his time in the Army!

17:22 Now check out “US Special Forces vs Wagner Group - Battle of Kasham.”

17:26 Or watch “What Actually Went Wrong In Afghanistan”
