00:00 [SQUEAKING] [RUSTLING] [CLICKING]

00:16 ANA BELL: All right, so welcome to the first lecture of 6.100L.

00:21 That's our new number. My name is Ana Bell. That's two separate names, first name Ana,

00:26 last name Bell-- super confusing. But I've been a lecturer here in the EECS Department for probably almost 10 years now.

00:33 And I've been doing the intro course for a while. I'm really happy to be teaching this full semester version

00:39 of 6.100A. So today what we're going to do is go over

00:45 a little bit of course administrative information, and then we'll dive right into some thoughts

00:50 about computers, high level how they work. And then we'll start going into some Python basics.

00:56 So we're going to get coding right away. So I highly encourage you, since you're in this class,

01:01 to download the lecture slides beforehand, to take notes, and run code when I do.

01:08 Some of the lectures are interactive. And we'll have breaks, so there'll be a place where you can take a break

01:14 to actually do some coding. And that's important-- I call them "you try it" breaks. That's important to make sure that you're actually

01:21 practicing what we are learning right at this time. The main idea for lectures is, yes, I will do some teaching,

01:28 but there will also be opportunities for questions and for you guys to try some programming

01:33 right on the spot. Even if you don't finish writing a program that we start talking about, I will finish it,

01:39 and we can all talk about it together. And I'll show you some pitfalls and things like that.

01:46 There will be lots of opportunities to practice in this class at various degrees of granularity.

01:52 And then there's also lots of opportunities that I have in the handouts to do extra practice

01:58 at home and through a bunch of different resources as well. The reason why I stress participation and practice is

02:05 because part of the reason you're here is you want to learn how to program. You don't know how to program yet.

02:12 And programming is actually a skill. it's like math or reading. It's something that you have to practice.

02:18 You can't just watch me type in a bunch of lines of code And then when it comes time to do the quiz,

02:23 you automatically know how to do it. You need to do it often, more and more so that it

02:29 becomes sort of second nature. So the three big things you'll get out of this class are

02:35 knowledge of concepts, obviously-- we're going to learn some computer science ideas-- programming skill, and problem solving--

02:43 problem solving skills. Lectures and exams basically help you with your knowledge of-- test your knowledge of concepts

02:50 and help you get knowledge of concepts. Finger exercises give you the programming skills.

02:56 And the problem sets help you with problem solving. Basically, if you're given an English version of-- a problem

03:04 in English, how do you go from that to thinking about what computer science concepts can I apply?

03:10 And then after that, how do I take those computer science concepts and actually do the programming?

03:17 So what are some topics we'll be covering? We will be, at the core of it, learning

03:23 computational thinking. So in the future, when you encounter a problem,

03:28 your first thought shouldn't be, How do I mathematically solve this? or, How do I brute force

03:34 or manually solve this problem? How can I apply computation to help me solve this problem?

03:39 And throughout these lectures, you're going to see some examples of us applying computation

03:44 to a problem you might have already seen and maybe solved mathematically, which is pretty cool.

03:51 Obviously, to get that, we're going to learn the Python programming language. Once we get the basics, we're going

03:56 to see how we can start to structure our code to look a little bit better so we don't just

04:01 have a bunch of code dumped in a file. We're going to start to organize our code and see how we can make it neat, readable, and modular.

04:11 And then towards the-- not in this lecture but in a couple of lectures

04:16 and as a theme throughout this class, we're going to look at some algorithms. They're not super complicated, but they're

04:23 kind of the base algorithms for a bunch of algorithms you might see in the future if you decide to take more CS classes.

04:30 Lastly, towards the end of the class, we're going to see algorithmic complexity, which basically means we're going to start asking or trying to answer

04:37 the question, how do we know the programs we write are efficient? We can write programs, but how do we know that they're fast,

04:44 and how do we know that they don't take up all the memory in the computer? So things like that, comparing different algorithms

04:51 that do the same thing against each other. So if there's no questions--

04:58 again, as I said, a bunch of this information is already in the handout plus more-- we can begin.

05:05 OK, so let's start by talking about knowledge.

05:11 Declarative knowledge is a statement of fact, and a lot of us probably in math and in the past

05:17 have worked with declarative knowledge. But this is not how computer science, this is not how this class works.

05:23 In computer science what we do is we work with imperative knowledge, which is basically a recipe,

05:28 how to do something. And when we're programming, all we're doing is writing a recipe for the computer to do something.

05:35 That's it. So here's a numerical example. The first statement is a declarative statement.

05:44 The square root of a number x is y such that y times y is equal to x. There are many possible values for x and y

05:50 that this statement can be true, right? But if we gave that statement to a computer,

05:55 it wouldn't know what to do with it. What we need to do is tell the computer how to find the square root of a number

06:03 and then tell us what the square root of that number is. And so the computer then needs a recipe.

06:09 So the recipe, a really simple one for finding the square root of a number, is steps one, two, three.

06:15 So what we do is-- let's say we want to find the square root of 16.

06:20 We obviously know it's four, but the computer doesn't. And so we give it an initial guess. Let's say the guess is three.

06:27 How do we go from there? So the steps we follow-- step one, if 3 times 3, 9, is close enough to 16,

06:35 we can stop. It's not really close enough for me. So let's keep going.

06:41 Step two-- otherwise, we're going to make a new guess by averaging g,

06:46 which is our original guess, 3, and x over g, which is 16 over 3.

06:52 16 was the square root we wanted to find. So our next guess is 4.17.

06:58 OK, using the new guess, repeat the process until we are close enough. So we go back to step one.

07:03 That's the first part of the process. We find guess squared. 4.17 squared is 17.36.

07:10 So now we say, is that close enough? Not really. It's not. It's 17.

07:15 It's not really even close to 16. So let's do it again. We make a new guess by averaging 4.17 and 16 divided by 4.17.

07:26 That gives us our new guess, 4.0035. OK, next step, using the new guess, we repeat the process.

07:34 So 4.0035 squared is 16.277-- .0277.

07:40 Is that close enough to x? Yeah, I could be happy with this. I could stop there because we're within sort of plus/minus 1.

07:47 So I'm OK with that. But if we want it to be within plus or minus 1 times 10 to the negative 6 or 7 or something like that,

07:55 then we would continue the process. So really what we had there is an algorithm.

08:01 It's a sequence of steps-- step one, step two, step three. There's some sort of flow of control.

08:07 We had a place where we said if the guess is close enough, then we can stop.

08:13 Otherwise, we do something else. We had another flow of control where we said repeat this thing.

08:19 So we're kind of not going linearly, but we're changing the flow. And then lastly is a way to stop.

08:25 We don't want the algorithm to go on forever. We would like to stop at some point. And this stopping point, I was kind of vague about it.

08:32 But it could be when we were within plus or minus 1 of the actual answer.

08:39 And so recipes are basically algorithms, right?

08:44 My grandmother was basically teaching algorithms when she would teach me to bake a cake.

08:52 She didn't call it that, but she was really. And so even recipes have that same structure.

08:58 There's a sequence of steps. There's a flow of control. Like, if you don't have egg, use egg substitute. Or repeat sticking a toothpick to see

09:06 if it comes out clean every minute or something like that. And then there's a way to stop.

09:12 When the toothpick comes out clean, you take it out of the oven, and you eat it. And so computers are machines that execute these algorithms.

09:19 They're actually dumb. Computers are not very smart. They don't make decisions on their own.

09:26 They just follow these sequences of steps that we told them to do. Computers are good at storing lots and lots of data.

09:35 We can't really do that, but computers can store gigabytes of storage, terabytes even.

09:40 And computers can do operations really, really quickly, which is something we can't do. They're good at those two things,

09:46 but they're not very smart. They can't make decisions unless they're told to make the decisions.

09:54 So really, the computer only does what you tell it to do.

09:59 And that's one of the big ideas that I want you to come away from this lecture with.

10:05 Computer only does what you tell it to do. The sequences of steps that you tell it to do, that's the only thing it follows.

10:12 So a little brief history just to make you appreciate programming, Python programming language before we actually get

10:19 started with it is-- so before the 1940s, we had these things

10:24 called fixed program computers. A pocket calculator as an example of that. Every button was an operation.

10:33 In the little screen, you could use parentheses to put a bunch of different operations together, but there was no way to store all these operations together

10:41 to later put in different inputs for that same sequence of operations.

10:46 You had to input it every single-- input those sequences of operations every single time.

10:52 After the 1940s, stored programs computers came into play. And they were able to store instructions to do things

11:03 as data. And there was a special program called an interpreter that

11:09 executed these instructions. It knew how to follow simple sequences of steps. When the program told it to go to a different location,

11:17 it did. So it was basically executing these instructions.

11:23 And the instructions that it did were arithmetic and logical, so addition, subtraction, things like that;

11:30 simple tests like checking for equality between two values; and moving data, so taking this value

11:36 and putting it at a different memory location. So I just wanted to give you a really brief overview,

11:41 and this is not super accurate, but it gives you a sense of how exactly things happen

11:47 low level in the computer. So the computer basically has memory,

11:52 where things are stored. It has an arithmetic logic unit that does operations.

11:57 It knows how to add things, subtract things, multiply things, compare things. And then it has the control unit, where

12:03 this program counter is set. And this is where you put a program in. So let's see if this works.

12:10 This is a program. And up here is our memory. So we have a bunch of memory locations, 3456, 3457.

12:18 And at each of these memory locations, we have some values stored, prefilled.

12:24 So when we first run this program, what ends up happening is that the interpreter sees the first instruction,

12:31 Add, the values at 3456 and 3457 together. So it goes to these memory locations here,

12:38 grabs the 3 and the 4, and sends them to the Arithmetic Logic Unit. The ALU knows how to do the addition.

12:44 So it adds 3 plus 4, 7, and sends the result back here. Now, we never told it to store that result anywhere.

12:52 But the next instruction says Store the value you just got back from the ALU at this memory location, 3458.

12:59 So the next step basically takes that 7 and stores it at memory location 3458.

13:08 Super tedious-- all we did was add 3 plus 4. We do that again.

13:14 We add the values at 7889 and 7890. So it goes in the memory.

13:19 It grabs the 5 and the 2, sends it to the ALU. The ALU calculates it as 7, brings it back,

13:26 and then we store that in location 7891.

13:32 And then after that, all we've done is two additions. And then the next instruction says Compare the values

13:38 at memory locations 3458 and 7891. So we're going to compare the 7 with the 7.

13:45 The ALU again does this comparison and says, all right, well, 7 and 7 are equivalent.

13:51 So this is true or whatever it wants to give back to the interpreter.

13:56 And then the last instruction here we have is Print the result of that comparison. So we print True because they were equal.

14:04 Again, super high level, but it kind of gives you an appreciation for programming languages

14:10 these days. This is very tedious to write if we had to write programs in this manner.

14:16 Alan Turing a long time ago showed that you can compute anything with actually an even more basic set of primitives,

14:22 not addition, subtraction. But instead, with a tape, you would actually have six primitives-- move the tape left, move the tape right,

14:29 read the value at the tape, put a value on the tape, erase the value from the tape, and no operation.

14:38 And so since he showed this what the result of it actually was

14:43 is down here. Anything computable in one language is computable in any other programming language.

14:50 So if we had some program written in Java, that basically boils down to something super

14:57 long but something that is made up of these six primitives.

15:02 That means that if we boil down this program to these six primitives, we can build back up the same program

15:08 in a completely different language. And that's really powerful. That's a really cool statement.

15:14 Now, we're not going to be working with those primitives. We're going to be using the Python primitives, which

15:21 are more convenient, and they allow us to do a lot more things in much less time. I'm going to do a little comparison

15:28 as we talk about the primitives of Python with English. So in English, some of the primitives might be words

15:36 or even we can do letters or characters. But we can say it's words.

15:41 With characters, we can build up words. With words, we can build up sentences. With sentences, we can build up stories. With stories, we can build up books and things like that.

15:50 In programming languages, the primitives are numbers, sequences of characters, operators

15:58 like addition, multiplication, division,

16:04 checking for equality, checking that something is greater than, things like that. So once we have these primitives in a language,

16:12 we can start to build up the syntax of the language. So in English, having something like noun and noun and noun

16:20 doesn't make any sense. Cat dog boy doesn't make much sense. It's not syntactically valid.

16:26 But noun verb noun is syntactically valid.

16:31 Similarly, in programming languages, we can have two objects kind of side by side.

16:37 So here, this is a sequence of characters h and i. And this is the number 5 right beside that sequence

16:43 of characters. But that doesn't make any sense, right? What does it mean to have this sequence of characters

16:49 and that number right beside it? It has no meaning in Python. Instead, what we have to do is we

16:54 have to add an operator in between these two objects. So here we add a little star operator in between the sequence of characters "hi"

17:01 and the number 5. And in Python, the meaning to this is I want to repeat the sequence of characters "hi,"

17:08 h-i, five times. So this would basically give me hi, hi, hi, hi, hi.

17:13 So once we have sentences in English and expressions that are syntactically valid,

17:21 we can now talk about the static semantics of the language. So in English, saying something like "I are hungry"

17:27 is syntactically correct, but it's not static-- it's not-- sorry, it doesn't have good static semantics.

17:37 There's no meaning-- there is no meaning to that because the "are" is for you or plural.

17:44 Similarly, in programming languages, and this will differ depending on what programming language you use--

17:51 here, in the previous slide, we saw that you can use the star operator between the sequence

17:56 of characters and the number. And that meant repeat that sequence many times.

18:01 But if we use a plus operator in between the sequence of characters and a number, that doesn't

18:07 have any meaning in Python. So it has a static semantic error, even though it's syntactically valid, right?

18:14 We have operator-- sorry, object operator object.

18:21 So, so far, we've been able to find really nice parallels with English, the English language and the programming

18:28 languages. But this is kind of where things break down, when we talk about the semantics of a language.

18:33 So in English, you can have many different meanings. The chicken is ready to eat means let's eat this chicken.

18:41 Or the chicken is ready to eat means the chicken wants to eat something. Programming languages, there is no multiple meanings

18:49 to a program that you write. Because the computer, the machine, the language follows the set of instructions to a T,

18:58 there is no ambiguity about what it needs to do. It just follows the instructions and does

19:03 what it needs to do to the end, till it reaches the-- it terminates the program.

19:10 And so programs only have one meaning, but the problem is it might not be the meaning that you intended it to have.

19:17 And that's when things start to go wrong. We can have syntactic errors in our program, spelling errors

19:24 and indentation errors, things like that. And those are easy to catch. Static semantic errors are 90% probably easy to catch.

19:31 But the problem comes in with the semantics. The meaning that you intended this program to have

19:39 might not be what it's actually doing. And that's where most of my errors happen.

19:44 And that's where I get super frustrated when I program. And that's probably where you guys will get super frustrated too because you write a program that you think

19:51 is doing one thing, but instead, either it crashes right away, or it runs forever and doesn't really stop, or it terminates,

19:59 but it gives you an incorrect answer. It's not what you were expecting. And we'll talk about this in a few lectures.

20:08 So when we write programs, we're basically writing sequences of definitions and commands.

20:14 And we're going to write these either in a file editor or in a shell. The first, today at least, we're writing in the shell directly.

20:22 And half of tomorrow, we'll write in the shell because we're not really writing any--

20:30 we're not really writing many lines of code. We're just going to be-- I'm just going to be showing you some really quick things

20:39 that we can do with the Python programming language. So hopefully you all have installed the programming

20:45 environment. This is the Code Editor. So tomorrow, we'll start working in here.

20:51 But for today, we're really just going to work in the shell. And even in the future, you can still

20:57 type commands in the shell. I find the shell very useful if there's just something really quick that I want to check, that I

21:04 don't want to write a program for and then run. It's just like a simple command that I want to check to make sure it's doing

21:09 what I think it's doing before I insert it in my code editor. So here we have this.

21:19 So mine is-- I guess I'm using the white theme just because I find it easier for you guys to see.

21:25 This is the file editor. And this is just a bunch of expressions or-- yeah, a bunch of code that we're going to type in today.

21:32 And we're going to type it in the shell today, so the thing on the right-hand side.

21:40 OK, so what exactly do we do when we write a program?

21:45 At the base of it, we are going to create objects inside our programs, and we're going to manipulate them.

21:53 That's it. That's what programming is mostly about at its core.

22:00 Now, when we create objects, it's important-- this is kind of something we're going to come back to again

22:06 and again in a more high-level setting. But right now what I want you to understand is that when we create an object, an object has a type.

22:16 And the type that an object has tells Python the things you're allowed to do with that object.

22:23 So here are two examples. The number 30, it's a number.

22:29 The type we'll talk about it in a bit. The type is an integer. It's a whole number. But basically, what are the things

22:35 we can do with this integer, with this number? We can add it to another number. We can subtract it to another number.

22:40 We can take it to another power. We can take some other number to this power of 30.

22:47 A bunch of mathematical operations, as you would expect. So that's pretty straightforward.

22:53 What about this one here, this quotation capital A, lowercase a--

22:59 lowercase n, lowercase a quotation? So this is something we'll talk about next lecture. It's called a string.

23:05 And it's a sequence of characters. The quotations tell Python it's a sequence of characters.

23:10 And the characters part of it are capital A, lowercase n, and lowercase a. The kinds of things I can do with this string

23:19 are not the same kinds of things I'm allowed to do with the number, right? If I tried to take Ana and divide it

23:25 by the sequence of characters Bob, Python would complain very much because you

23:31 can't divide a string by another string, a sequence of characters. It doesn't make sense to divide it by another sequence of characters.

23:37 Similarly, I can't take Ana to some power. I can't multiply--

23:42 I can't multiply by itself, things like that. But the kinds of things that I am allowed to do on a sequence of characters

23:48 is different than the kinds of things I'm allowed to do on a number. So the things I can do with a sequence of characters

23:53 is I can say, well, what's the character at the first position? What's the middle character?

23:59 How long is the sequence of characters? How many characters do I have? And so now you can see that the type of the object

24:07 is actually really important. Python uses it to know the kinds of operations you're allowed to do with it.

24:13 And so there's actually scalar objects, and these are Python's primitives, numbers

24:19 and truth values. And there are nonscalar objects. We're not talking about these yet. We'll talk about these in a few lectures.

24:26 But these have some sort of structure. So for example, a list of numbers has a structure because there's a number at the beginning

24:33 of the list, there's a number at the end of the list, things like that. But a number itself doesn't have a structure.

24:39 It's just the number. So what are the types of the scalar objects?

24:44 What are the types of the primitives in Python? Integers, so number 5, 0, negative 100, 1 million.

24:52 Float is another type. It represents all the real numbers, so 3.27.

24:58 2.0 is a float because it has a decimal number even though to us that just means 2.

25:04 But to Python, if you put in 2.0, it says that's a type float. Negative 3.14159, things like that.

25:12 Bool is a Boolean. It represents truth values. And there's only two possible values that a Boolean type has,

25:20 True and False. And it has to be capital T True and capital F False.

25:26 And the last one is this NoneType type. It's literally called NoneType.

25:33 And it has only one special value, None. We're not going to talk about it for a bit, but we will sometime in the future.

25:41 So to figure out the type of an object when you create that object, you use the type command.

25:47 So we can say something like type parentheses. And this is a command. And inside the parentheses, you say, what do you

25:54 want to find the type of? So if we do type of 7, it tells me it's an int.

25:59 And if you want to do the same command again, I hit the up arrow, and it automatically puts in what I wrote previously.

26:04 And then if I want to do type of 0.0, it's a float because there's a decimal point.

26:13 So this is basically what I said. So we type this in the shell. And the shell tells us what the output is.

26:23 So just to reiterate, int, float, bool, and NoneType are types of objects.

26:31 And there can be many different objects you can create of that type. So if you think about it, ints and floats,

26:38 we basically have an infinite number of objects we can create of those types

26:44 because we can have 0, 1, 2, 3, 100, 200, 300, 1 million, and all the negatives.

26:49 There's almost an infinite number of values or objects that we can create of type int and float.

26:56 But bool, there's only two, the truth values True or False. And the NoneType, there's only one, this None.

27:04 So that's the type, and these are the possible values, possible objects we can create.

27:11 You try it. So you can just yell out the answers. There's nothing to type unless you want to check yourself so

27:17 what is the type of 1234? AUDIENCE: Int. ANA BELL: Int. Type of 8.99?

27:24 Float. Type of 9.0? Float. Type of True?

27:29 Bool. And type of False? Bool. Perfect. If you ever wonder what the type of something is,

27:35 you type it in here. You guys are doing well. Type is bool. Type of lowercase t true is an error,

27:43 just wanted to point that out just to reiterate the fact that capitalization matters in Python.

27:49 This is our first error, by the way, guys. Very exciting. The error is a NameError, and this is

27:55 the message associated with it. You also know that it's something special in Python

28:04 when you have color-coded stuff. So you see capital T True, capital F False are

28:10 this dark blue here, whereas anything that's not special in Python is just black.

28:17 So type is a special command. This is a float, so you see they're color coded.

28:23 OK. So once we create objects, one thing we can do with these objects is to cast them

28:30 to a different type. Now, this is a little bit maybe confusing

28:36 because we're not actually changing the object once we've created it. So once we create the integer 3, it's there in memory.

28:46 If we cast that integer to a float version of it, we're creating a new object in memory.

28:52 We're not changing the 3. The 3 already exists. We're just getting the float version of it

28:57 and storing it as a new object in memory. So when we do float 3, this is a command

29:03 that gets for me the float version of the integer 3. So that will give me 3.0.

29:10 So for example, this is what I had, float 3.

29:16 The output is 3.0. If I do int of 5.2, it truncates it,

29:26 and it gives me the integer portion of this float. If I do int of 5.9, it still truncates it

29:33 and gives me the integer version of this float. It doesn't round. I'm just asking for the integer version of this float.

29:42 Some operations like round is an operation we can do has an implicit cast in it.

29:48 So if I round 5.9, it's actually going to round it to 6.0 and then cast it to an integer.

29:55 So notice it doesn't give me as an output 6.0. It then rounds it to just six.

00:00 A horde of feral creatures  tears through the street.

00:03 They might look human, but they no longer have  the brain capacity to do anything but consume.

00:07 God help you if you find yourself in their path.

00:10 No, it’s not the latest  toilet paper hoarding frenzy,

00:12 it’s the zombie apocalypse - and  it might not be entirely fiction.

00:16 Could the zombie apocalypse actually  happen? Possibly - in more ways than one.

00:21 These are the potential undead outbreaks  scientists are keeping their eyes on.

00:25 Surprisingly, some people believe zombies  actually walk among us - and have for hundreds

00:29 of years. The origin of the concept dates back to  Haitian folklore, where the dead are resurrected

00:34 by dark magic. A necromancer uses potions and  rituals to revive a corpse, but what comes back

00:40 isn’t entirely human. It may have full physical  function, but something in its soul stays behind.

00:45 This usually creates a zombie who is lacking  the ability to make complex decisions,

00:49 but can complete simple tasks when instructed  - making it the perfect slave for a sinister

00:54 witch doctor looking for some free labor. These  zombies can often be kept in this unfortunate

00:58 stasis for the length of their natural life,  but the spell can be broken if they are not

01:02 given the proper substances to keep them  in their stupor. And when they’re awoken,

01:06 they often don’t remember anything of their time  as a zombie - even if they’ve been missing years.

01:11 But is this only folklore?

01:13 It was believed to be an odd tale from traditional  Voodoo religion, but during the US occupation

01:18 of Haiti, they were surprised to discover that  people were actually reporting to know residents

01:22 who were turned into zombies! People would show  up after being missing for years, and would

01:27 claim they had been enslaved by witch doctors  with only fitful memories of the missing time.

01:31 Scientists looked into these claims and found a  possible explanation for this - right down to the

01:35 supposed return from the dead. These people might  have been given a powerful neurotoxin that would

01:40 have paralyzed them completely and slowed their  body functions to the point of appearing dead,

01:44 followed by the application of the toxin  Datura stramonium. Derived from Jimsonweed,

01:49 this can cause long-term disorientation  that would leave someone in a fugue state

01:53 and highly suggestible - leaving  them in a zombie-like state.

01:57 Could this create a zombie plague?

01:59 In a word…no. While this is one of the only cases  known of actual zombie-like behavior in humans,

02:05 it might be the least terrifying prospect. For  one thing, there are no detailed case studies

02:09 of this behavior long-term, just stories  of it happening in the past. Many of the

02:13 case studies have been doubted by scientists  who think it couldn’t be sustained long-term.

02:18 If these chemicals were applied effectively, it  would only take one missed dose for the person to

02:22 start regaining their full mental faculties - and  a slight overdose of the toxic jimsonweed extract

02:27 could kill. These cases aren’t the  precursor to a zombie apocalypse,

02:31 they’re a case of kidnapping and enslavement.  More importantly, they’re not contagious in

02:35 any way. If someone under the effects of  Datura stramonium bit an unaffected person,

02:39 all that might happen is a nasty infection  from the bacteria in a person’s mouth.

02:43 But outside of the human world,  more threatening cases await.

02:46 Fungi. They take many forms, like mushrooms that  grow on trees - and make for a tasty topping on

02:52 pizza! But in the fungal kingdom, a surprising  number of them are parasitic - and some display

02:56 a disturbing ability to affect other organisms.  That’s the case for Ophiocordyceps unilateralis,

03:02 an insect-pathogenic fungus that spreads  itself in a disturbing fashion. And it has

03:06 a particular target - the ants crawling  along the canopies of tropical forests.

03:11 They crawl through the trees, except when  the tree gaps become impossible to cross

03:15 and they head down to the forest floor.  That’s where this sinister fungus is waiting,

03:19 spreading its spores. They attach to the  exoskeleton of the ant and start growing there,

03:24 using enzymes to weaken the exoskeleton and  allow them to take root in the ant’s body.

03:28 And once they work their way in, that’s  when the transformation truly begins.

03:32 Because the fungus doesn’t just affect  the ant’s body - it affects their brain.

03:36 The fungus’ yeast spreads through the ant’s body  and starts generating compounds that affect the

03:41 ant’s behavior, starting with causing it to have  seizure-like convulsions that knock it from its

03:45 usual perch down to the forest floor. And there  it stays, because it now has one function - to

03:50 spread the fungus growing off its body. When the  ant is about to reach the end of its life cycle,

03:55 it will attach itself to a leaf with its mandibles  and die there, spreading the fungal spores from

04:00 the massive growth on its head. This creates a  morbid garden of dead ants to infect the entire

04:04 population of ants in the area. And as the  ant dies, the fungus continues to grow until

04:09 the area is covered in a large growth of fungus.  In between four to ten days, the ant transforms

04:13 from a creature with its own mind to one solely  devoted to propagating another species’ survival.

04:19 This has led scientists to give these  creatures a disturbing nickname - zombie ants.

04:23 But could they jump species to bigger targets?

04:26 While the idea of a fungal infection targeting our  brains is terrifying, the odds of them breaking

04:30 that species barrier are limited. For one thing,  the fungus is designed to target small animals

04:36 with an exoskeleton, and if they jumped species  it would likely be to a larger insect or spider.

04:41 Humans don’t have an exoskeleton, they have bones  - which are much harder to break through. While

04:45 humans do have some weak, unprotected points like  our eyes, there’s another element that protects

04:50 us from a fungal zombie infection like this - we  can notice and react to weird things happening

04:55 to our body much easier than ants can. If we see  a weird fungal infection coming out of our body,

05:00 we’ll either pull it off or go see a doctor.  So the odds are that even if a fungus did

05:04 start affecting humans, it would never be able to  transform any of us into mind-controlled zombies.

05:08 Assuming no one decided they liked their  new mushroom hat and just let it grow.

05:12 But some species more terrifying than  fungi are using the same tactics.

05:16 Pretty much everyone hates wasps, from those  nasty yellow jackets that haunt every summer

05:21 picnic to the terrifying “Murder Hornets”  of Japan. But smaller creatures have far

05:25 more reason to fear them, because many wasps  have a truly disturbing method of reproducing.

05:29 They lay their eggs inside a still-living  creature, usually a large insect or a spider,

05:34 and the eggs hatch inside and eat the creature  from the inside out. Usually, the wasp uses

05:38 its venom to paralyze the creature before  laying the eggs and just uses it as a cocoon,

05:43 but one wasp named Zatypota percontatoria  may have taken this tactic to the next

05:48 level. It has the same sting and ovipositor that  its larger and more dangerous counterparts does,

05:53 but it doesn’t render the host completely  paralyzed while the larvae are gestating.

05:58 Instead, it might do something worse.

06:00 It mostly targets small spiders, usually younger  ones. But as the larvae grow inside the spider’s

06:04 body, something unusual happens. The spider may  be aware of the creatures growing within it,

06:09 but it finds itself unable to affect or remove  them. As the growth of the larva advances,

06:13 the spider will even build a cocoon to immobilize  itself while the larva emerges and consumes

06:18 its host. The initial thought was that the  wasp was directly affecting the brain of the

06:22 spider - which would be a terrifying prospect -  but now scientists believe it’s more likely the

06:27 larva exudes hormones that guide the behavior of  the spider in a certain direction. Until the end,

06:32 the spider doesn’t behave in ways that  are completely atypical for the species,

06:36 but instead seems to be mutually  protecting itself and the wasp.

06:39 Of course, there’s only going to be one survivor  at the end - exactly the way the wasp wants it.

06:45 But is this deadly wasp a threat to humans?

06:47 Zatypota percontatoria is a much smaller wasp  than the ones that attack humans, but there are

06:51 wasps that pose serious threats to large animals.  The Asian Giant Hornet even has the nickname “Yak

06:56 Killer” because a swarm of them can kill a massive  animal with their stings - and they do kill dozens

07:01 of humans a year. But these attacks are usually  defensive, seeking to drive humans away from them.

07:06 No wasp has ever tried to parasitize a human  for the same reason no fungi has ever made a

07:11 go of that big game. If a wasp injected a human  with its eggs, the human would likely go to the

07:15 doctor and get them removed. And even if hormones  were affecting their behavior to make them want

07:20 to protect their carry-on, the odds are another  person would notice and get them some help. That’s

07:24 why the species that do lay their eggs in humans  - like the bot fly - mostly do surface-level

07:29 infections and hope that the person just doesn’t  notice. So no wasp zombies coming any time soon.

07:34 But is a far deadlier threat  lurking under our noses?

07:37 Plants. They make our yard beautiful, and  they make for a lot of work pulling weeds.

07:42 But these leafy organisms are the backbone of the  global ecosystem - and that makes them uniquely

07:46 vulnerable to parasites. A bacteria known as  phytoplasma has been affecting plants since it

07:51 was discovered in the 1600s, but at first they  were assumed to be plant viruses. They create

07:56 fast-spreading blight, abnormal plant  growth, and odd growths that seem to

07:59 have one purpose - spreading the bacteria  further. The bacteria starts in plants,

08:04 spreads through insects, and moves back to plants  once they’re pollinated by exposed insects.

08:08 Some of the signs include yellow leaves and  growths that attract insects, but otherwise the

08:13 plants just seem to continue existing just fine  regardless of the bacteria parasitizing them.

08:17 But the truth goes deeper.

08:19 These bacteria literally rewire  the morphology of a plant,

08:23 switching it from growing flowers that  would help it to spread healthy plants

08:26 to growing the odd leafy growths that spread the  bacteria. While plants lack any brain function,

08:30 this bacteria manages to get deep down into the  base components of the plan and permanently change

08:35 its core function. This is considered dangerous  to the health of the plant, but it doesn’t have

08:39 all negative consequences for those who cultivate  plants - the bushy appearance of infected plants

08:44 can actually be desirable for those breeding  certain plants because they can then produce

08:49 more flowers. But in the wild, these bacteria  spread fast and furious - turning every plant they

08:54 infect into a puppet of their spread and every  insect that touches them into a disease vector.

08:59 But could this affect humans  and create a zombie apocalypse?

09:02 This is probably the most dangerous case yet,  because unlike parasitic wasps and fungi,

09:07 humans are just as vulnerable to bacteria  as anything else. Countless diseases start

09:12 from bacteria and devastate populations. But if  this bacteria started using humans as a vector,

09:17 it’s not likely to turn us into zombies the way  it does to plants. That’s because we lack the

09:21 tools it needs to spread - and any change  where it makes people start growing plant

09:25 growths is the stuff of science fiction.  What it could do is hitch a ride on us and

09:29 use us to spread the way it does to insects  - but it doesn’t use the insects in any way

09:33 besides being an insect-shaped bus. So if this  bacteria infected us, the odds are we wouldn’t

09:38 even know it - and the only ones who need  to be worried about phytoplasmas are plants.

09:43 But at least none of these have  made the jump to mammals…right?

09:46 Parasites are everywhere - as any pet owner  knows when they have to give their beloved

09:50 Fido or Fluffy their dewormer medicine. Your cat  may have just turned into a furry buzzsaw as soon

09:55 as you uncapped the pills, but at least they’re  not infected with a zombie parasite, right? Well,

10:00 probably - but a parasite making the rounds is  actually displaying the terrifying ability to

10:04 puppet the largest animals yet. Toxoplasma  gondii isn’t some new parasite that’s just

10:10 making its way into the population, it’s a widely  spread parasite common in developing countries,

10:15 and it’s estimated that as many as fifty  percent of the global population may have

10:18 been exposed. But the good news is,  it’s not too serious - in most cases.

10:23 It can cause flu-like symptoms, but most  humans who get infected might not even know it.

10:27 What’s scary about it is that it can infect  almost any warm-blooded animal - including pets.

10:32 But it’s the interaction with two common  animals that gives it a disturbing x-factor.

10:36 While Toxoplasma gondii can infect almost any  mammal, its sexual reproduction needs much more

10:41 specific conditions - it can only reproduce in  the digestive tract of a domestic cat. It doesn’t

10:47 affect the cat much, but how it gets there is  what’s terrifying. When it infects mice, it has

10:52 an unusual effect that is unlike anything else it  does - it affects the mouse brains, reducing their

10:57 sense of anxiety and self-preservation. Infected  mice are less likely to hide when confronted by

11:02 danger, and more likely to explore risky areas.  This puts them at greater risk of getting eaten

11:08 by - you guessed it, cats, who now have the  infected mouse meat in their digestive tract.

11:13 The heavier the parasitic load in the mice,  the more they’re affected. This microscopic

11:18 parasite does everything short of making the mice  deposit themselves directly in the cat’s mouth.

11:22 Could it do the same to humans?

11:24 Unlike the previous four zombie apocalypse  candidates, Toxoplasma gondii has one scary

11:28 advantage - it’s already able to infect humans and  it’s already shown the ability to affect mammal

11:33 brain chemistry. We share a lot of common DNA with  mice, and it’s not hard to make humans do risky

11:38 things - as every episode of a popular TV stunt  show indicates. Parasites can mutate quite easily,

11:44 especially with fast reproduction, but the odds of  this particular parasite mutating are slim to none

11:49 for one reason - targeting humans doesn’t make  sense for its life cycle. With the parasite only

11:54 being able to reproduce inside cats, it only makes  sense to evolve to target something that cats eat.

12:00 Birds and other small rodents might be at risk,  but Fluffy probably can’t eat you - even if

12:05 they seem like they’d like to every time  you’re three minutes late with dinner.

12:09 But one potential zombie plague  creator is already among us.

12:12 It’s one of the most terrifying diseases in the  world - Mad Cow Disease. Unlike most diseases,

12:17 its not a virus or bacteria - it’s a prion disease  that affects the other prions in the brain,

12:22 causing them all to mutate in the same way.  Its effects are terrible - memory problems,

12:26 behavior changes, clumsiness, visions,  and eventually blindness, dementia,

12:31 coma, and death. The disease is mysterious,  degenerative, untreatable, and invariably fatal.

12:37 While a small number of cases are  inherited or caused by genetic factors,

12:40 it became infamous in the 1990s when  it spread due to contaminated beef.

12:45 One bite of a bad hamburger could kick-start  someone’s slow decline - and before the end,

12:49 things could get terrible, not just for  the victim, but for the people around them.

12:53 And many people say it reminds  them of something terrifying.

12:56 Most zombie films have a standard type of  zombie - slow, shambling, and decomposing.

13:01 They usually want brains…braaaaaaaains. But  a movie series starting with 28 Days Later

13:07 introduced us to a different kind of zombie. They  were fast, smart - and still technically alive.

13:13 They were infected with a “Rage virus” that made  them viciously attack anyone they encountered,

13:17 and the virus could spread rapidly through  contact, including biting. While there were no

13:22 actual undead zombies in the movie, the world that  resulted looked a lot like a zombie apocalypse.

13:27 And the origin was a released Chimpanzee carrying  a pathogen that jumped to humans. While it was all

13:33 fiction, it was more scientific than most zombie  outbreak plots - and many people pointed out

13:37 that this origin sounded a lot like how Mad  Cow disease made its way into the population.

13:42 Could it turn into something deadlier?

13:44 Mad Cow Disease, also known as Variant  Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, is already pretty

13:49 deadly - invariably killing anyone it infects over  a period of years. It’s also highly contagious,

13:54 being spread not just through contact with  tainted beef but through blood transfusions

13:58 and potentially even donated sperm. It can also  be contracted through eating squirrel brains,

14:03 so sorry to anyone who appreciates that  delicacy. What it doesn’t have right now

14:07 is the active desire to spread - the slow decline  of victims usually incapacitates them and makes

14:12 it unlikely they’ll actively spread it after  being diagnosed. But a mutation could make it

14:17 faster-acting and make victims display more  aggressive behavior. It’s no surprise that

14:21 governments around the world are determined to  keep a lid on this horrible disease - with the

14:25 disease staying dormant for years, it’s hard  to tell if anyone is a carrier, and countries

14:29 like Finland even ban British residents  during the 90s from donating blood for life.

14:34 But buried deep in the Arctic might  be the start of a horror movie…

14:38 The year was 2000, when scientists were exploring  ancient ice in the Siberian permafrost. This area

14:43 has not defrosted for tens of thousands of years,  and provides a rare time capsule into a world long

14:48 gone. But when a sample taken from a riverbank was  exposed to some test amoebas, scientists noticed

14:53 something disturbing - the amoebas were rapidly  dying off. A series of tests revealed that the

14:58 permafrost contained a virus - but not just any  virus. It was the largest virus humans had ever

15:03 discovered, a creature named Pithovirus  that measured a whopping 1500 nanometers.

15:09 Looking vaguely like a honeycomb when examined,  it was unlike any virus in the modern day - and it

15:14 was active and killing its target like no time had  passed since it was frozen. Unlike most viruses,

15:19 it could easily be seen under a microscope, and  it contained as many as five hundred unique genes.

15:24 Each of those ripe for a possible mutation.

15:27 Already deadly viruses, like  the ones that cause HIV,

15:30 only contain about twelve genes. While  this virus doesn’t infect humans,

15:34 that’s only for lack of opportunity - it  may have evolved in a time before humans,

15:38 and developed to target small single-celled  organisms. Naturally, humans responded to this in

15:42 the sensible way - throwing the samples back into  the permafrost and backing slowly away from the

15:47 resurrected virus that had been waiting thirty  thousand years, right? Not so much. The French

15:52 scientists who discovered Pithovirus have been  examining it since and testing its interactions

15:56 with its targets to figure out how it’s most  likely to affect people in the modern day.

16:01 The good news is, it’s purely  a relic of the past, right?

16:04 Not so much - a modern species of the same genus  was found in 2016, and studies indicate it has

16:10 very similar DNA to its ancient counterpart. The  good news is, this indicates this giant virus is

16:14 not likely to evolve to target humans in any way -  it has a very specific spot in the food chain, and

16:20 humans couldn’t be further away from amoebas. But  what worries scientists about the Pithovirus isn’t

16:25 this specific virus - it’s that viruses from tens  of thousands of years ago are still hanging around

16:30 in the permafrost. Could something down there be  more likely to affect humans? Entirely possible,

16:35 although there’s no current evidence of any  virus that would create a zombie apocalypse.

16:39 Scientists are advocating caution when  possibly disturbing these frozen organisms.

16:43 Good thing the ice is staying right where it  is - hey, why is it feeling so hot lately?

16:48 But scientists might not just uncover the source  of a zombie plague - they might create it.

16:53 The human body is incredible at regenerating  itself. If you cut yourself, there’ll be a fresh

16:58 layer of skin over it in a week. A broken bone  will knit itself together after a few months in a

17:02 cast. But there are some areas that cause a little  more problems - namely anything in the nervous

17:07 system. While the process of neurogenesis - the  generation of new neurons - does happen naturally,

17:12 the body is incapable of healing certain  injuries. A person who breaks their neck

17:16 might be in a wheelchair for life, while  someone who hits their head in the wrong way

17:19 might never wake up from a coma. This has been  one of the last frontiers in medicine - curing

17:24 brain and spinal cord injuries through  triggering the body to regenerate. The

17:28 key to this might be stem cells - cells that  can adapt to become any other type of cell.

17:32 When applied in the right way, they might  be able to regenerate dead nerve cells.

17:36 But can they rewire the brain itself?

17:39 So far, this is very much in the realm  of science fiction - but scientists have

17:42 been trying to figure out how to beat death for  decades. Cryogenics research has been ongoing,

17:47 with thousands of people volunteering to have  their bodies frozen in hope of being awoken at

17:51 a later date when science has developed the  means to resuscitate them. The problem is,

17:55 no one knows what kind of damage the freezing  process has done to either the body or the

17:59 brain tissue - which is why any resurrection  attempt would require some additional help.

18:04 That’s where stem cells come in, as some…less  than ethical scientists have proposed using

18:09 this treatment to reverse brain death  or experiment with the already deceased.

18:13 After all, these cells can regenerate dead  cells in other parts of the body - what

18:17 about the most complicated machine  the human body has ever reproduced?

18:20 What would happen? That’s the scary part.

18:23 The human brain is still a mystery in many ways,  and one tiny thing going wrong can result in an

18:27 entirely different person. Regenerating new  tissue in the brain might essentially do a

18:31 factory reset on the person, creating someone  highly suggestible. The result could make for

18:36 a high-tech modern version of the people who are  under the effect of a toxin in the rumored Haitian

18:41 zombie plague. Could this be a great way for an  unethical mad scientist to create compliant labor?

18:46 Possibly. Could it create a zombie  plague? There’s no evidence of that,

18:49 because there is no pathogen the  “Zombie” would want to spread

18:53 and it’s unlikely someone in this situation  would have the higher brain function to attack

18:56 anyone. This scenario is the most far-off in  the future, as research into neurogenesis is

19:01 focusing more on reversing short-term damage at  the moment - but be careful what you wish for.

19:06 Because the most deadly scenario for a zombie  apocalypse could be developing as we speak.

19:10 Technology is getting smaller all the  time. Remember when a cell phone was a big,

19:14 bulky thing that barely fit in your pocket? Now a  smartphone is basically a thin sheet that shatters

19:19 if you drop it. The same is happening to robots  - at a much smaller scale. Nanorobotics is a

19:24 fast-developing field that creates tiny  machines that are roughly a nanometer.

19:28 So what could one of these do? Not much - but a  whole lot of them could make a big difference.

19:32 These devices are mostly in the research and  development phase right now, but the basic

19:36 theory is that they could all be programmed  with the same function from a central point,

19:40 then released in the thousands or millions to  tackle a task. Each one would attack a certain

19:45 point, but together the cloud of them would have  a huge effect. This could be used to repair damage

19:50 in areas where it’s not easy for humans to  go, like outer space or deep in the ocean.

19:54 Or even the human body.

19:56 These microscopic robots could be used to perform  minimally invasive surgery if programmed right,

20:01 or even perform long-range repair while staying  in the body. But some experiments scientists

20:05 are doing are much more worrisome. Designs are in  the works for nanobots to not just repair things,

20:10 but to build more of their own system -  essentially becoming self-replicating.

20:15 But scientists weren’t satisfied with designing  the self-replicating smart robots too tiny for

20:19 anyone to see - they’re trying to see how  they can be fused with living organisms.

20:23 Scientists at the University of Nebraska  experimented on integrating a silicone

20:27 chip into a virus, and discovered that the  virus died - but the mechanical component

20:32 still kept it running as a humidity  gauge for a month after its death.

20:36 That’s right - the University of Nebraska  successfully created a zombie virus.

20:41 What could go wrong?

20:42 Is this going to create a zombie outbreak now?

20:44 No - the nanobot wasn’t programmed to  reproduce and its function was limited.

20:48 But that won’t always be the case. One of the  areas scientists are most interested in is using

20:52 nanobots to potentially repair brain tissue  - neurogenesis with a cybernetic twist. To do

20:58 this job, the nanobots would need to be able to  self-replicate. So in a few years, there could

21:02 be people with self-replicating intelligent robots  in their brains, rewiring their brain chemistry.

21:07 A central computer would be regulating their  function- unless something went horribly wrong.

21:11 Because if the nanobots went off their  designated function and wanted to spread,

21:15 who knows what they would be capable of. So  while the origin of zombies may have started

21:19 in Haitian folklore, it may be headed somewhere  much different - the technology of the future.

21:24 Are you prepared for the worst? Check  out “Could You Survive A Zombie Attack?”,

21:28 or watch “Why Did Scientists Create Zombie  Dogs” for more disturbing tales of the undead.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: Large-scale genome-wide association meta-analysis combining ADHD symptoms and diagnosis data from 70,953 children across 28 cohorts identified 39 independent loci (17 new) and 22 potential effector genes. Key finding: clinical ADHD represents the extreme end of a continuous genetic liability indexed by ADHD symptoms, with strong genetic correlations (rg > 0.8) with aggressive behavior and antisocial behavior.

docs.title: Sample Characteristics
docs.text:
• Total Participants: 70,953 unique individuals
  • ADHD Measures: 290,134 observations from multiple raters and instruments
  • Diagnosis Cohort: 38,691 cases and 186,843 controls
  • Age Range: 1.5-18 years (with retrospective adult assessments)
  • Cohorts: 28 population-based cohorts from ACTION and EAGLE consortia
  • Raters: Mothers, fathers, teachers, self-reports
  • Instruments: 20 different ADHD assessment instruments

docs.title: Methodological Approach
docs.text:
• Meta-analysis: N-weighted multivariate GWAMA
  • Gene Mapping: FUMA, FINEMAP, CAVIARBF, PAINTOR
  • Effector Gene Identification: FLAMES analysis
  • Pathway Analysis: MAGMA gene-set analysis, FUMA GENE2FUNC
  • Genetic Correlations: LDSC in genomicSEM

docs.title: ADHD Symptoms Alone
docs.text:
• No genome-wide significant variants found
  • SNP heritability: h²SNP = 0.04 (s.e. = 0.01)
  • Genetic correlation with diagnosis: rg = 1.00 (s.e. = 0.06)
  • Interpretation: Strong support for continuum model

docs.title: Combined Analysis (ADHD Symptoms + Diagnosis)
docs.text:
• 39 independent loci identified
  • 17 loci were newly discovered (previously not genome-wide significant)
  • 2,039 genome-wide significant variants (P < 5 × 10⁻⁸)
  • SNP heritability: h²SNP = 0.11 (s.e. = 0.01)
  • Interpretation: Combining symptom and diagnosis data increases power to detect genetic variants

docs.title: New Effector Genes (Previously Unknown in ADHD)
docs.text: Gene FLAMES Score Biological Function EMCN 0.08+ Cell adhesion, endothelial cell function STK32C 0.08+ Serine/threonine kinase PCDH17 0.08+ Protocadherin, cell adhesion TCF12 0.08+ Transcription factor, basic helix-loop-helix PEAK1 0.08+ Pseudopodium-enriched atypical kinase IGF1R 0.08+ Insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor CTNNA2 0.08+ Catenin alpha 2, cell adhesion ABCA12 0.08+ ATP-binding cassette transporter

docs.title: Previously Known ADHD Risk Genes
docs.text: Gene Function Association Type DRD5 Dopamine receptor Neurotransmission SLC9A9 Sodium/hydrogen exchanger Ion transport CDH13 Cadherin 13 Cell adhesion GCKR Glucokinase regulator Metabolism PPM1K Protein phosphatase Signal transduction KANK1 Ankyrin repeat domain Cytoskeletal organization LPP Lipoma preferred partner Cell migration MACROD2 Macrodomain 2 Chromatin regulation NCKAP5L NCK-associated protein 5-like Cytoskeletal organization POU3F2 POU class 3 homeobox 2 Transcription regulation

docs.title: Enriched Biological Processes
docs.text:
• Frontal cortex expression: Significant enrichment in genes differentially expressed in frontal cortex
  • Synaptic pathways:
  • Postsynaptic density membrane (q = 1.46 × 10⁻³)
  • Postsynaptic density (q = 1.57 × 10⁻³)
  • Synapse organization (q = 1.62 × 10⁻³)
  • Postsynaptic modulation of chemical synaptic transmission (q = 3.28 × 10⁻⁵)
  • Transcription factor targets: 52 enriched gene sets
  • MicroRNA targets: 13 enriched gene sets
  • Cell-type signatures: 8 different cell types enriched

docs.title: Functional Categories
docs.text:
• Neural development: Key theme across effector genes
  • Cell adhesion: Multiple genes involved (EMCN, PCDH17, CTNNA2)
  • Signal transduction: Kinases and regulatory proteins
  • Metabolism: IGF1R and metabolic regulators

docs.title: Strong Positive Correlations (rg > 0.8)
docs.text: Trait Genetic Correlation Interpretation Childhood Aggressive Behavior rg = 1.13 Very strong genetic overlap (likely both biological and statistical pleiotropy) Antisocial Behavior rg = 0.97 Strong genetic overlap Major Depressive Disorder rg = 0.57 Moderate overlap Autism Spectrum Disorder rg = 0.39 Moderate overlap

docs.title: Moderate Positive Correlations (0.4 < rg < 0.8)
docs.text: Trait Genetic Correlation Smoking habits rg = 0.46-0.60 Number of children rg = 0.38

docs.title: Negative Correlations (Cognitive/Health Traits)
docs.text: Trait Genetic Correlation Interpretation Educational Attainment rg = -0.55 Higher ADHD risk associated with lower educational achievement Childhood IQ rg = -0.43 Higher ADHD risk associated with lower cognitive ability Overall Health Rating rg = -0.59 Higher ADHD risk associated with poorer health Birth Weight rg = -0.10 Small negative correlation

docs.title: Substance Use Patterns
docs.text: Trait Genetic Correlation Pattern Alcohol intake frequency rg = -0.28 Negative correlation (may reflect socioeconomic confounding) Drinks per week rg = 0.14 Positive correlation (may reflect different construct) Cannabis use rg = 0.20 Positive correlation

docs.title: Physical Health Correlations
docs.text: Trait Genetic Correlation Childhood obesity rg = 0.21 Adult BMI rg = 0.30

docs.title: 5. Polygenic Score Performance
docs.text:
Tested in three independent cohorts (ALSPAC, MoBa, NTR):

Polygenic Score Variance Explained Performance Rank ADHDOVERALL (Combined) 0.3-3.1% Best ADHDDIAG (Diagnosis only) 0.2-2.5% Moderate ADHDSYMP (Symptoms only) 0.1-1.2% Lowest

Key Finding: Combining ADHD symptoms with diagnosis data significantly improves polygenic risk score prediction accuracy.

docs.title: Study Design Advantages
docs.text:
1. Large Sample Size: 70,953 unique individuals provides substantial power
  2. Multiple Raters: Reduces measurement bias and increases validity
  3. Longitudinal Data: Multiple assessments across ages improve reliability
  4. Instrument Diversity: 20 different assessment instruments capture ADHD comprehensively
  5. Rigorous QC: Comprehensive quality control including LDSC intercept analysis

docs.title: Advanced Statistical Methods
docs.text:
1. FLAMES Analysis: Novel method for identifying causal effector genes
  2. Multivariate Meta-analysis: Accounts for sample overlap and phenotypic covariance
  3. Fine Mapping: Multiple methods (FUMA, FINEMAP, CAVIARBF, PAINTOR) for credible variant sets
  4. Genetic Correlations: LDSC-based estimates with genomicSEM

docs.title: Comprehensive Analysis
docs.text:
1. Gene-set Analysis: MAGMA and FUMA GENE2FUNC for pathway enrichment
  2. Tissue-specific Expression: Brain tissue expression analysis
  3. Functional Annotation: Integration with multiple functional datasets

docs.title: Population Limitations
docs.text:
1. European Ancestry: Primarily European ancestry limits generalizability to other populations
  2. Age Focus: Childhood-focused; adult ADHD less represented
  3. Sex Distribution: Sex included as covariate but detailed sex-specific analysis limited

docs.title: Methodological Considerations
docs.text:
1. Heterogeneity: Different assessment instruments may introduce measurement variance
  2. Phenotype Definition: Clinical diagnosis definition may vary across cohorts
  3. Statistical Power: Some analyses may be underpowered for rare variants

docs.title: Interpretation Challenges
docs.text:
1. Correlation vs. Causation: Genetic correlations don't imply causal relationships
  2. Pleiotropy: Complex patterns of genetic overlap with other traits
  3. Population Stratification: Despite QC, some residual population structure may exist

docs.title: Clinical Implications
docs.text:
1. Continuum Model: Supports viewing ADHD as a quantitative trait rather than categorical disorder
  2. Early Identification: ADHD symptom measures can help identify genetic risk before full clinical diagnosis
  3. Personalized Medicine: Polygenic risk scores may inform early intervention strategies
  4. Comorbidity Understanding: Strong genetic correlations with externalizing behaviors inform treatment approaches

docs.title: Research Implications
docs.text:
1. Novel Targets: 8 new ADHD risk genes provide new avenues for research
  2. Biological Pathways: Synaptic and cell adhesion pathways highlight potential mechanisms
  3. Developmental Perspective: Findings support neurodevelopmental hypotheses
  4. Cross-Trait Genetics: Pleiotropic effects inform understanding of psychiatric comorbidity

docs.title: Future Research Directions
docs.text:
1. Diverse Populations: Include non-European ancestry samples
  2. Functional Validation: Experimental studies of novel effector genes
  3. Longitudinal Studies: Track genetic effects across development
  4. Gene-Environment Interactions: Investigate environmental modifiers of genetic risk
  5. Treatment Response: Study genetic predictors of treatment response

docs.title: vs. Demontis et al. (2019)
docs.text:
• 2019 Study: 12 loci identified, 20,183 cases and 35,191 controls
  • 2025 Study: 39 loc identified, 17 new, much larger sample
  • Improvement: More than 3x increase in loci detected

docs.title: vs. Demontis et al. (2023)
docs.text:
• 2023 Study: 27 loci identified, broader case definition
  • 2025 Study: 39 loci, 17 new, combined symptom + diagnosis approach
  • Key Difference: Symptom data addition increased power to detect new variants

docs.title: Clinical Practice
docs.text:
1. Risk Assessment: Polygenic scores may help identify high-risk children
  2. Early Intervention: Early identification of genetic risk enables preventive strategies
  3. Treatment Planning: Understanding genetic correlations may inform treatment approaches

docs.title: Research Applications
docs.text:
1. Gene Discovery: Novel genes provide targets for functional studies
  2. Pathway Analysis: Synaptic pathways inform drug development
  3. Biomarker Development: Genetic correlations suggest potential biomarkers

docs.title: Public Health
docs.text:
1. Resource Allocation: Understanding genetic burden informs public health priorities
  2. Prevention Strategies: Early identification enables targeted prevention
  3. Education: Genetic understanding reduces stigma and improves support

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
This landmark study significantly advances our understanding of ADHD genetics by:

  1. Novel Discovery: Identifying 17 new risk loci and 8 novel effector genes
  2. Continuum Validation: Strong evidence for ADHD as a quantitative trait
  3. Pathway Insights: Enrichment in synaptic and cell adhesion pathways
  4. Comorbidity Mapping: Comprehensive genetic correlations with other traits
  5. Methodological Innovation: Advanced statistical approaches for gene discovery

The findings provide a solid foundation for future research into ADHD biology and may eventually contribute to improved diagnosis, treatment, and prevention strategies for this common neurodevelopmental disorder.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: A specialized DNA extraction protocol that utilizes agarose plugs to encapsulate biological samples, enabling gentle handling and preservation of high-molecular-weight DNA for applications requiring intact genomic DNA.

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
1. Agarose encapsulation of biological samples
  2. Preservation of high-molecular-weight DNA integrity
  3. Gentle extraction process minimizing DNA shearing
  4. Optimized for sensitive applications requiring large DNA fragments
  5. Step-by-step procedural guidelines for consistent results

docs.title: Notable Quotes
docs.text:
"Agarose plugs provide mechanical protection during extraction"

"Method preserves DNA integrity for downstream applications requiring large fragments"

docs.title: Method Overview
docs.text: The agarose plug DNA extraction method involves embedding biological samples within agarose matrix before extraction, providing structural support and minimizing mechanical stress on DNA molecules.

docs.title: Key Steps
docs.text:
1. Sample Preparation: Biological samples mixed with molten agarose
  2. Solidification: Agarose solidifies around embedded sample
  3. Cell Lysis: Gentle lysis within the agarose matrix
  4. DNA Purification: Standard purification methods applied
  5. Plug Removal: Agarose matrix dissolved or removed

docs.title: Applications
docs.text: This method is particularly valuable for: - Pulsed-field gel electrophoresis requiring large DNA fragments - Genomic DNA extraction from sensitive tissues - Archival sample processing where DNA integrity is critical - Long-read sequencing applications requiring high-molecular-weight DNA

docs.title: AI's Impact on Science - Nature 2026
docs.text: Source: Hao, Q., Xu, F., Li, Y., & Evans, J. (2026). "Artificial intelligence tools expand scientists' impact but contract science's focus." Nature, 649, 1237-1244. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-025-09922-y.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: AI tools provide dramatic individual career advantages (3× more papers, 4.8× more citations, faster leadership transitions) but collectively narrow scientific focus (-4.63% topic breadth, -22% follow-on engagement). AI appears to automate established fields rather than explore new ones, creating a tension between personal advancement and collective progress.

docs.title: Study Design
docs.text:
• Scale: 41.3M papers (1980-2025), 6 disciplines (biology, chemistry, geology, materials science, medicine, physics)
  • AI Detection: Fine-tuned BERT model (F1=0.875), validated by 12 experts (κ=0.964)
  • AI Papers: 310,957 (0.75% of total)
  • Eras: ML (1980-2014) → DL (2015-2022) → GenAI (2023-)

docs.title: Individual Career Impact
docs.text:
• Productivity: AI users publish 3.02× more papers annually
  • Visibility: AI users receive 4.84× more citations
  • Career Velocity: AI users become project leaders 1.37 years earlier
  • Establishment Rate: AI-using juniors: 45% (13.64% higher than non-AI)
  • Team Size: AI teams have 31.14% fewer junior scientists, 10.77% fewer established scientists

docs.title: Collective Scientific Impact
docs.text:
• Knowledge Narrowing: Topic breadth shrinks by 4.63%
  • Subfields Affected: >70% of 200+ subfields show contraction
  • Citation Inequality: Top 20% of AI papers capture 80% of citations; top 50% capture 95%
  • Follow-on Engagement: Papers citing the same AI work interact 22% less with each other

docs.title: Core Paradox
docs.text:
"AI automates established fields rather than exploring new ones"

Individual gains vs. collective contraction. AI optimizes known problems, reinforcing hot topics, reducing exploration of frontier domains.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text: Individual Impact Value Annual papers 3.02× baseline Annual citations 4.84× baseline Leadership timing -1.37 years Establishment rate +13.64% Collective Impact Value Topic breadth -4.63% Follow-on engagement -22% Top 20% citation share 80% Top 50% citation share 95%

docs.title: Entities/Concepts Mentioned
docs.text:
• Authors: Qianyue Hao, Fengli Xu, Yong Li, James Evans
  • Institutions: Tsinghua University, University of Chicago, Santa Fe Institute
  • Methods: BERT, two-stage fine-tuning, birth-death model, knowledge extent, follow-on engagement
  • AI Techniques: Support vector machines, PCA, CNN, GAN, large language models
  • Datasets: OpenAlex, Web of Science

docs.title: Takeaways
docs.text:
1. For individual scientists: AI tools accelerate careers dramatically
  2. For collective science: AI concentrates research around data-rich areas
  3. For research policy: Incentivize exploration beyond optimization
  4. For scientific progress: Balance individual benefits with collective breadth
  5. For AI development: Design tools that encourage exploration, not just efficiency
